China slams US claims of ‘industrial-scale’ AI theft
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
19:21:50 UTC
04:21:50 KST

China slams US claims of ‘industrial-scale’ AI theft
The response comes after three US agencies accused Chinese AI companies of exploiting American AI models.
China has issued a forceful reply against claims by the United States that top Chinese artificial intelligence companies have engaged in “industrial scale” theft of their US counterparts’ AI models.
The response on Wednesday comes after three US federal agencies – the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), National Security Agency (NSA) and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) – accused Chinese AI companies of exploiting American AI models to benefit their own systems.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3OpenAI unveils latest AI model amid rising scrutiny and safety concerns
- list 2 of 3As the China-US AI race reaches Cairo, Egypt faces a strategic decision
- list 3 of 3AI researcher quits Anthropic saying AI race ‘could kill us all’
The joint advisory on Tuesday said Chinese companies like DeepSeek, Alibaba and Moonshot AI had distilled “billions of tokens” from US models since “at least late 2024”, likely with the Chinese government’s “awareness”.
Tokens are the smallest units of text that AI models read, or generate.
On Wednesday, China’s Commerce Ministry dismissed the allegations and accused the US of seeking a “monopoly of the AI industry”.
“If the U.S. suppresses Chinese AI companies under the pretext of targeting distillation, China will take resolute countermeasures,” the ministry said in a statement to the Associated Press.
Distillation is a method in which lesser AI models are trained on more advanced ones. The ministry said the practice is commonplace in the AI industry, including by US AI companies. But American firms say the volume in which it’s being done by Chinese AI models amounts to stealing.
“The sheer scale of these campaigns and their sophistication indicate that distillation is not a supplement to these companies’ AI model development, but the critical core of it,” the US advisory claimed.
The AP reported that China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs called on the US to “refrain from making unfounded accusations or smears” against China.
“China’s AI development is the result of high-level technological self-reliance and strength,” ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told reporters at a news conference. “We maintain that all parties should strengthen cooperation to promote AI development that is open, inclusive, universally beneficial and oriented toward the common good.”
Xi visit
The US advisory comes just weeks before Chinese President Xi Jinping is set to visit the US, where President Donald Trump will host a summit on a range of topics, including AI.
In a rare move, Xi could be accompanied on his US visit by a large number Chinese executives, according to the Reuters news agency. It is not clear which executives would join the delegation, but past meetings between the two countries may indicate AI leaders could be in the mix.
Xi brought Alibaba founder Jack Ma during his 2015 visit to the US. When Trump visited Xi during a trip to Beijing in May, the US president was joined by more than a dozen American executives, including Tesla CEO Elon Musk.
Under Trump, the US government has taken a hardline against efforts to advance Chinese AI models. China is aggressively investing heavily in artificial intelligence and robotics, pouring nearly $300bn into what the government sees as the country’s next economic engine.
While speaking in Dallas on Tuesday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told an audience that China can “never get ahead” of the US in AI.
“The Chinese distill our models and they can never get ahead of us,” Bessent said.
The Chinese companies named in the US advisory did not immediately respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment.

04:21:18 KST

It’s a brand new era for Apple. The company is turning over leadership for the first time in 15 years, with former CEO Tim Cook handing off the reins last week to the new CEO, former Apple VP of hardware John Ternus.
At the first Apple product soiree hosted by Ternus, the company made an even bigger change: it announced its first ever folding device, the iPhone Duo.
The company also announced its new line of iPhone 18 Pro phones, some updates to its Apple Watch line, new AirPods, and new software capabilities powered by Siri AI.
As expected, there were no base-model iPhone 18 announcements; those are likely coming early next year. There was also no mention of Vision Pro, iPads, or Macs. Apple touted new desktop Macs in August.
Here’s everything Apple showed off today.
Apple iPhone Duo
Apple’s first ever folding device is the Duo, a “passport sized” foldable iPhone. It starts at $1,999 for a model with 256 GB of storage.
It’s a product category that Apple has been working toward for a decade. Now, it hopes to do that very Apple thing where it may not be the first company to the new tech party, but it definitely aims to be the snazziest.
The Duo is a landscape style foldable, meaning it has a vertical magnetic hinge that lets you open the device like a book. Closed, it has a 5.3-inch screen on the outside. Open it up, and the landscape display is 7.7 inches. The Duo is also heavy, weighing in at 254 grams, which might be a little too hefty for some users.
The Duo is made with a titanium frame and what Apple calls a “custom polymer” screen for increased durability. It runs on Apple’s proprietary A20 Pro chip (the same chip in the new Pro-model iPhones 18) and the company’s custom C2 modem. The horizontal format also means it's capable of running iPad-like apps, albeit ones that can adjust on the fly when folding the screen or setting the phone up at an angle. The Duo will also be able to work with the Apple Pencil Pro stylus.
On the back of the Duo are two 48-megapixel cameras, one standard, one for ultrawide shots. There are two 12-megapixel selfie cameras, one on the main screen and one on the inside when the screen is opened. The cameras can also capture 4K video.
Untypical of Apple, the Duo does not have Face ID. Instead, it uses a TouchID sensor in the power button. This is likely due to Apple’s desire to minimize the device’s bulk and allow for more components inside the device.
Like, for example, the massive battery. Apple says the iPhone Duo gets 31 hours of battery life, and up to 44 hours just using the smaller front screen. Storage options start at 256 GB for the base model, with options up to 2 terabytes of space. That top configuration puts the Duo at $3,199.
Expensive, yes, and very in line with Apple's upward adjustment to its prices due to the memory shortage. But Apple is also keen on enticing users to rent the most premium devices with Apple Upgrade, the leasing program the company introduced in July.
For more details about the Duo, check out WIRED’s deeper look at the company's very first foldable.
iPhone 18 Pro
As predictions suspected, Apple is not releasing its base model iPhone this year. Instead, the company focused on highlighting its new iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max.
These look almost identical to the iPhone 17 Pro models, albeit slightly smaller. The iPhone 18 Pro is 6.3 inches and the iPhone 18 Pro Max is 6.9 inches. They come in black, silver, glacier, and burgundy color options.
They come with Apple’s new A20 Pro chips, which have been repackaged into a silicone casing that can connect directly to the new redesigned vapor chamber, a design flourish that aids in keeping the components from overheating and helps the phone last longer. Wireless charging is even faster, able to juice the phone up to 50 percent battery life in 15 minutes.
The iPhone 18 Pro battery is capable of up to 36 hours of video playback per charge. The 18 Pro Max gets around 45 hours of video playback.
The 18 Pro phones are also getting juiced up with a new and improved Siri AI. There is an all new Siri AI app on the iPhone. Siri AI is rolling out as a beta in English now, and will be available in French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish in October.
Adjustable Aperture
The iPhone 18 models also get a number of big improvements to their cameras. The biggest: a variable aperture on the iPhone 18 Pro's 48-megapixel main camera. Users can dial in their preferred aperture, which adjusts mechanically in the lens. This opens up new possibilities for shooting in different light environments, as well as adjusting the depth of field for adding real—not digital—bokeh effects to photos.
Apple is also touting improved photography and video capture controls, called Pro Controls, that let you change settings like white balance, aperture, and shutter speed. So if you’re a camera nerd, you have new software and hardware tools to play with.
Apple is also introducing Apple Reference Image, a watermarking tech that maintains an image the way it was originally shot. Apple refers to it as something close to “a digital photo negative” that you can reference if you need to prove a photo’s provenance.
The iPhone 18 Pro is $1,199, and the iPhone 18 Pro Max is $1,299. You can preorder the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max this Saturday, September 12. Apple says they’ll officially start selling September 18.
Apple Watch
Apple announced some revamps to its Apple Watch. There is a reengineered Apple Watch 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4.
Both watches get new sensor arrays. Apple’s new Health Sensing System includes LEDs that measure high-frequency heart rate data as often as every five seconds. This gives wearers a constant stream of health data all day long.
The Apple Health app gets some revisions that better track sleep and show personalized guidance about your daily readiness. This is something Google’s Pixel watches have had for a while, though Apple’s reports will benefit from its new sensor array.
Also on the watch are some features that make use of Apple’s ambient listening tech to record and log the things around you. That means the watch can transcribe the things people say and show the text right on your smartwatch’s screen. In a demonstration video today, Apple showed a server at a restaurant reciting menu specials, and the person sitting at the table was able to scroll back through a transcript of the last 15 seconds on their Apple Watch’s screen to read what the server said.
These features are opt-in—at least for the person wearing the watch—and the features that record audio will emit a chime when somebody uses them. You can learn more about how the Apple Watch listens in Lily Hay Newman’s report for WIRED.
The listening feature can also send alerts to your wrist when it detects important sounds like sirens, doorbells, and babies crying. Apple says the audio is not stored, the raw audio is inaccessible even by Apple, and that the transcriptions do not identify the people talking.
There are new ceramic cases and color options for the Series 12 Watch, including gray, black, light gold, and bronze. The Apple Watch Series 12 is $399. The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is $799.
For more about the Apple Watch updates, read Boutayna Chokrane’s WIRED story about all the details.
AirPods 5
Apple’s new, cheaper AirPods 5 come with some of the features that the AirPods 4 had. The AirPods 5 come with noise canceling and adaptive sound controls. You can also use Siri AI directly on the AirPods and communicate via chat. They also have live language translation, though it’s not clear how well that will function out in the real world—of course, it works great in Apple’s demo videos.
The base model costs $129. There’s also a version with touch volume controls on the stems, a little more battery, and a wireless case-charging puck that also can charge your Apple Watch. Those nicer options cost $149.
Some rumors had predicted that Apple would show off a new pair of AirPods with cameras in the earbuds. Those are possibly still coming eventually, but Apple didn't say anything about them this time. We’re expecting at least one more Apple event before the end of the year, and they may show up then.

Canadian Muslim groups welcome Ottawa's decision to ban illegal Israeli settlement trade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
19:19:06 UTC
04:19:06 KST

Merve Gül Aydoğan Ağlarcı
09 September 2026•Update: 09 September 2026
Canadian Muslim organizations and a leading human rights advocate on Wednesday welcomed Ottawa's decision to join 11 countries in the long "overdue" but "monumental" move to ban trade with illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
Ahmad Al Qadi, Government Affairs and Public Policy Officer at the National Council of Canadian Muslims (NCCM), said at a news conference in Ottawa that the organization was "here to welcome the government's announcement on a categorical ban on products emerging from illegal Israeli settlements."
"Although this step should have been taken long ago, September 8th, 2026, will mark a monumental day in Canada's history," he said.
Al Qadi said future generations of Canadians "will use this date as a precedent for Canada's commitment to upholding values of human rights, sovereignty, and territorial integrity, values that the Prime Minister (Mark Carney) spelled out clearly during his Davos address."
He added that the ban "demonstrates that, indeed, as the Prime Minister stated, Canada is not powerless," and it has "the capacity to build a new world order that respects these values."
Al Qadi thanked Carney and Foreign Minister Anita Anand on behalf of the NCCM for advancing the ban, stressing that "Canadian businesses operating internationally have a duty to respect human rights and ensure that activities do not contribute to adverse impacts."
Imam Sikander Hashmi, executive director of the Canadian Council of Imams, said Canada's trade policy "should not help sustain the dispossession and abuse of another people," calling the ban "overdue."
He said Islamic teachings do not bar business dealings based on ethnicity or religion, noting that Prophet Muhammad “conducted business with Jewish people and others."
"Honest and respectful trade can benefit everyone. It can build relationships and bring communities together," said Hashmi, adding that "trade that sustains injustice demands a different response," and "refusing to support dispossession is a matter of basic fairness and human dignity."
Amira Elghawaby, a human rights advocate and Canada's former special representative on combatting Islamophobia, said the decision was "grounded in clear principles of international law, including the Fourth Geneva Convention and numerous other United Nations resolutions and international court findings."
She said the move by Canada and its allies sends "an unmistakable signal" that they "refuse to be complicit in the violation of international law," describing it as "the mainstream of international law finally being enforced through policy."
Citing public opinion, Elghawaby said that "far more Canadians oppose illegal settlements than support them, and far more Canadians support banning settlement products than oppose that step."
"Canada's responsibilities do not end at our borders," she said, adding that upholding international law "consistently and without exception is how a country like ours earns the right to speak about human rights at all." 
12 countries announce measures on illegal Israeli settlements
The foreign ministers of the 12 countries announced in a statement Tuesday that they would impose or consider trade restrictions on goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
The countries said Israel's actions in the West Bank were undermining prospects for a two-state solution and stressed the need to preserve the possibility of establishing a Palestinian state.
Israel subsequently announced that it would close the UK's consulate in occupied East Jerusalem, which serves Palestinians, in response to the measures.

Poland Presents Heavy CBWP Infantry Fighting Vehicle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
19:18:55 UTC
04:18:55 KST

Poland has presented the domestically produced CBWP heavy infantry fighting vehicle (IFV).
A Militarnyi correspondent reported this from the MSPO exhibition in Poland.
The CBWP is being developed by companies from the Polish Armaments Group, including Huta Stalowa Wola, in response to the Polish Armed Forces’ need for a vehicle that is heavier and better protected than the Borsuk IFV.
In the configuration shown at the exhibition, the CBWP is equipped with the remotely controlled ZSSW-30 turret used on the Borsuk IFV and Rosomak armored personnel carrier, a 30 mm Mk 44/S Bushmaster II cannon, a machine gun and a Spike-LR anti-tank guided missile launcher.
Other CBWP weapon configurations are also possible, including a 40 mm or 105 mm cannon.
The IFV weighs approximately 40 tons, compared with 28 tons for the Borsuk. The demonstrator is equipped with an 800 kW MTU engine, producing more than 1,000 hp, as well as a U.S.-made transmission.
The CBWP will have two troop compartment configurations, with seating for 6-8 troops.
In this configuration, the vehicle meets the requirements of the SAFE program and uses at least 65% EU technologies.
According to Defence24, the Polish Armaments Group announced plans to produce two prototypes in 2027 and be ready to begin serial production of the IFV in 2029.
Huta Stalowa Wola first revealed the specifications of the new IFV, then known as the Ratel, at last year’s MSPO exhibition in September.

Rutte warns delays in Ukraine aid cost lives
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
20:18:52 BST
04:18:52 KST

NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte has urged allies to accelerate military support for Ukraine, warning that delays in delivering weapons and funding are costing lives.
Speaking at the latest Ukraine Defence Contact Group meeting, Rutte said Ukraine’s war against Russia was directly affecting the wider security environment across NATO and called on countries to increase their contributions.
Rutte said: “Ukraine’s fight shapes the entire Euro-Atlantic security environment. It directly impacts, as we all know, our own security, and as we work on modernising the alliance and building a stronger Europe and a stronger NATO, we must continue to support Ukraine’s security and help them defend from Russia’s brutal attacks.”
He added: “That means supporting Ukraine with the utmost urgency. And here, let me say that delays simply cost human lives.”
Rutte said the level of civilian deaths had reached its highest point since May 2022 and told members of the group that more military assistance was required. He said: “Nations must dig deeper. We do not have a choice, I believe.”
The NATO Secretary General identified air defence, drones and extended-range ammunition as priority requirements for Ukrainian forces. Rutte also said allies were seeing changes in the weapons employed by Russia, including greater use of North Korean missiles and jet-powered attack drones.
He stressed the continuing role of the PURL mechanism, under which NATO allies and partners finance the purchase of American weapons for Ukraine. According to Rutte, around $10 billion had been allocated over the previous year through PURL and US foreign military sales for Ukraine, including $3.5 billion originating from the Ukraine support loan.
He described those figures as evidence of European countries taking on a greater share of the effort to sustain Ukraine. Rutte said continued deliveries were particularly important for maintaining Ukrainian air defences and enabling forces to hold positions on the front line.

Ukraine seeks 300 Patriot missiles from allies
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
20:18:38 BST
04:18:38 KST

Ukraine has asked allied countries to provide 300 Patriot interceptor missiles from their existing stocks as Kyiv attempts to strengthen its air defences before another winter of Russian missile and drone attacks.
Ukrainian Defence Minister Evgeniy Khmara set out the requirement during his first appearance at the Ukraine Defence Contact Group, alongside requests for 500 air-to-air interceptors capable of engaging cruise missiles and $2 billion in funding for drones.
Khmara said a recent Russian attack had involved cruise missiles, ballistic missiles and jet-powered Shahed-type drones. Ukrainian air defences had intercepted 31 of 32 cruise missiles, he said, but ballistic missiles were proving more difficult to counter because of shortages of Patriot ammunition.
He said: “Our air defence managed, among other things, to intercept 31 of the 32 cruise missiles, but the situation with ballistics is much more difficult, and that difficulty is precisely down to the lack of Patriot missiles.”
Ukraine is already contracting around 1,000 Patriot missiles with support from partner countries and through European Union financing, according to Khmara, but most of those weapons are not expected to arrive immediately.
He therefore appealed to countries to transfer missiles currently held in their own inventories, saying: “we ask that you supply us the missiles from your stockpiles today, in exchange for future improved missiles from our contracts.”
Khmara also warned that Ukraine faces a substantial defence funding gap. He said €70 billion in security assistance had been promised this year, with around €62 billion currently expected from bilateral assistance and European funding.
That leaves €8 billion of the earlier commitment outstanding, while Khmara put the wider Ukrainian defence funding shortfall at €23 billion, equivalent to around $27 billion. He asked partners to take the necessary funding decisions by November so that equipment could reach the battlefield during the winter.
Drones also featured prominently in the Ukrainian presentation. Khmara said: “Up to 90 percent of our success in the battlefield is down to drones.”
He said Ukrainian companies were developing lower-cost methods of intercepting jet-powered Shahed-type drones, with some interceptor systems already being tested in combat. Khmara also said Ukrainian assessments indicated that Russia was planning to mobilise around 300,000 additional personnel on top of existing recruitment and could seek a similar mobilisation effort in 2027.
He argued that Moscow was attempting to turn the conflict into a competition over manpower and resources, while Ukraine intended to rely increasingly on technology, drones and rapid battlefield adaptation.

====================================================================================================

Staggering price tag for states worst hit by rising seas revealed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
19:18:14 UTC
04:18:14 KST

Sea level rise threatens more than a quarter of a million properties as bill surges to $855b
Climate change means Australia's love of the coast is facing a multi-billion-dollar reckoning, research suggests, as rising seas threaten to turn its prized coastal lifestyle into a question of who will foot the bill: property owners or governments.
In the first nationwide assessment of economic losses from sea level rise, researchers from the University of Melbourne, the Australian National University and Global Environmental and Economic Modelling have found that all coastal states and the Northern Territory face hefty damage bills this century.
Australia could face damage costs of more than $850 billion, with more than $274 billion going to property losses and $580 billion spent on land-use damage.
Co-author Tom Kompas said the findings were "alarming", and the economic toll would mount as fossil fuel emissions continued to drive global temperatures higher.
"We keep warming the planet … so you get more sea level rise, you get higher tides, higher king tides, higher maximum tides," the professor of environmental economics and biosecurity at the University of Melbourne said.
"You get more intense, and maybe even more frequent storms and storm surges, and that causes localised flooding."
Sea level rise hits hard across the board
As temperatures rise, melting ice and the thermal expansion of warmer seawater raise sea levels, threatening coastal communities worldwide.
The Australian research found more than 267,000 coastal properties and 2 million hectares of land across the country will face flood damage by 2100 based on global carbon emissions peaking around 2040 and global warming being limited to about 2.7C.
The United Nations has warned that warming will reach at least 1.8C above pre-industrial levels and projects it could reach up to 2.6C by the end of the century under current policies.
The findings also put a price tag of more than a trillion dollars on impacts associated with global warming exceeding 4C. However, that level of warming was predicated on growing fossil fuel use, and scientists have deemed it unlikely to eventuate due to the uptake of clean energy.
Queensland has been identified as having 93,000 properties at risk of damage due to sea level rise, resulting in an expected damage bill of $214 billion for the state.
The Gold Coast is Australia's most exposed urban area, with projected economic losses of $84.4 billion.
Western Australia faces the largest total losses, while in New South Wales, communities in the state's north and Central Coast region face higher property losses than in Greater Sydney.
With Victoria the only jurisdiction where property damage costs exceed those associated with land use, Professor Kompas said the research underscored the significant costs of inundating farmland and recreational areas.
"Much of it is badly, badly damaged with sea level rise and storm surge … damaged reserves, parks, beaches," he said.
"So it's not just individual properties, commercial and residential properties; it's a wide range of assets that are being impacted."
Consequences with every centimetre
The economic assessment forms the basis of a Climate Council report, which highlights how coastal floods previously considered severe will become a regular occurrence in the future.
It found that every 10cm of sea level rise will triple the frequency of "once-in-a-century" flood events.
Global sea levels have already risen by over 22cm since 1900, with projections there could be an additional 14cm by 2050.
Narrowneck Beach and other northern Gold Coast shores suffered severe sand loss, exposed rock walls, and high tides crashing against infrastructure three months after Tropical Cyclone Alfred. (ABC News: Nicholas McElroy)
Report author and Climate Councillor Andrew Watkins said the impacts were already being felt.
"We have seen quite a rapid increase in what we call extreme water levels along the coast, and that gives coastal inundation, coastal flooding and coastal erosion as well," the Adjunct Professor at Monash University's School of Earth, Atmosphere and Environment said.
Sea level rise can damage coastal land and infrastructure in multiple ways, including permanent inundation. Scientists often use the "1 to 100 rule" to describe this — meaning seawater will go about a metre inland for each centimetre of sea level rise.
So 10cm of sea level rise can actually move water 10 metres further inland, inundating any land or building in its path.
The Land and Environment Court has granted consent for a 90-metre seawall at The Entrance North, a coastal village in NSW's Central Coast. (Supplied: Horton Coastal Engineering)
Rising seas can also contribute to isolated coastal flooding events when combined with storms.
"When you have that sea level rise, and then you get a storm surge where the storm is pushing the water up against the coast, it makes the water go even higher," Dr Watkins said.
"Then you get waves on top of that, and if it happens at high tide, that's when you get the full combination of impacts."
Storm surges and wind-driven waves linked to Ex-Tropical Cyclone Alfred led to severe erosion along the coastline between south-east Queensland and north-east NSW last year, with the Insurance Council of Australia announcing more than 125,000 claims totalling $1.36 billion.
Higher sea levels will push storm surges further inland. (X: Lisa Garnham)
Associate Professor of Climate Adaptation at Griffith University Johanna Nalau said recovery from that event was still ongoing.
"There has been a lot of work on beach nourishment and then more acute damage, so we talk about power, power networks, transport, water and sewage; those were resolved within weeks to months," she said.
"But the coastal erosion part is still an ongoing effort, and there has been some reporting in the news as well that some of the housing damage that people experience hasn't been resolved yet."
Bracing for the future
Experts are calling for improved efforts to help coastal regions adapt as climate change not only contributes to rising sea levels but is also expected to increase the frequency and intensity of storms.
Storms last year caused significant erosion damage at Fox Beach, Robe, SA. (Supplied: District Council of Robe)
Warnings of a mounting economic toll have also raised questions around who will foot the damage bills going forward, particularly given insurance generally does not cover "actions of the sea".
"Most coastal properties would have some level of insurance, although the insurance sector is also very, very aware of risks that come with climate change," Dr Nalau said.
"So insurance premiums are increasing quite heavily in some coastal areas."
Dr Watkins said it was becoming "prohibitively expensive" for some councils to pay for adaptation and recovery.
In the 1970s, old car bodies were used to prevent sand dune erosion in front of a sand mining site at Belongil in Byron Bay. (Supplied: NSW Public Works)
"A lot of councils are effectively having to dip into their own coffers to support resilience building, but also to recover from damage that's done when we have these storm events and sea level events along our coastlines," he said.
"We do need to look at this as a national problem and develop plans with the communities and with the local, state, and federal level about the best ways to go forward."

UK deepens NATO-first defence industry cooperation
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
20:18:03 BST
04:18:03 KST

The UK is expanding defence industrial cooperation with NATO allies and international partners, including the United States, as part of a wider effort to strengthen production capacity, supply chains and military readiness, the Ministry of Defence has said.
Defence Minister Luke Pollard set out the position in response to a written parliamentary question from Labour MP Callum Anderson, who asked what discussions the Government had held with allies on increasing defence industrial cooperation.
Pollard said work had accelerated since publication of the Defence Industrial Strategy in September 2025, with greater emphasis on exports, strategic partnerships, information sharing and what the department describes as a NATO-first approach to industrial cooperation.
He said: “Since publication of the Defence Industrial Strategy on 8 September 2025, the Department has strengthened collaboration with industry, NATO Allies and international partners, including the United States, to support UK defence exports, deepen strategic partnerships, improve information sharing and promote a NATO-first approach to industrial co-operation.”
The MOD also pointed to the role of National Armaments International in helping British defence companies compete for overseas contracts.
Pollard said: “National Armaments International is supporting UK companies to compete overseas, with record successes in 2025 including the UK’s biggest ever warship deal to Norway and the largest fighter jet exports agreement in a generation, promoting global security while boosting growth at home.”
The department is linking that international activity with efforts to expand industrial capacity inside the UK. This includes giving companies clearer indications of future demand, investing in priority capabilities and strengthening supply chains in sectors considered important to military readiness.
A further element is expected to come through the planned Defence Readiness Bill, which Pollard said is due later in the current Parliament. At alliance level, the UK is continuing work on NATO initiatives intended to increase defence production and make supply chains more resilient across member states.
The UK also backed a new NATO strategy for cooperation with industry at the recent Ankara summit.
Pollard said: “The UK also joined Allies in endorsing the new Strategy for Industry NATO Cooperation at the recent Ankara summit and maintains a strong partnership with the UK delegation to the NATO Industrial Advisory Group (NIAG), enabling senior industrialists to offer expertise and strategic insight on a wide range of security policy, defence planning, and capability issues.”
The NATO Industrial Advisory Group provides a route for defence companies and industrial specialists to feed expertise into alliance planning and capability discussions. Britain hosted the NIAG plenary in June 2026, an event the MOD said demonstrated a shared government and industry commitment to NATO capability development and further cooperation between allied defence sectors.

Pollard says he does not want kit that fails in Ukraine
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
20:17:19 BST
04:17:19 KST

Equipment that would not survive the war in Ukraine has no place in the British armed forces, the Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry has told an audience of financiers and defence firms at Mansion House, in a speech setting out how the government intends to bring private capital into defence.
Luke Pollard was speaking on Tuesday at an event hosted by the Lady Mayor, ahead of remarks by the Ukrainian Ambassador, and used the address to announce a Defence Finance Investment Strategy to follow the autumn budget along with a defence investment summit in December.
Warning that Britain must “discard the warm comfort blanket that we are used to, of polishing old things and pretending that that will protect us”, he put the test in a single sentence: “If our technology and kit will not work in Ukraine, I do not want it in our armed forces.”
That, he argued, opens the door to “new technology, new thinking, new weapons”, and to designing for “the conflicts of today and the battles of tomorrow”.
“The way that the United Kingdom would now fight is fundamentally different today than it was at the point when Putin launched his full-scale invasion of Ukraine only those four and a half years ago,” he told the room, adding that learning from Ukraine means changing how Britain itself operates.
Finding, funding and firing up
Much of the speech turned on speed, and on where the useful ideas are now coming from. Many of the most critical advances in defence, in the minister’s account, are emerging from technology startups and scale-ups, agile businesses “seizing the opportunities on offer and driving change at speed”. The challenge he set the room was framed as a question. “How can we get better at finding, funding and firing up the most creative minds and enterprise to get the best technology into the hands of our armed forces and those of our allies as fast as possible?”
He was unsparing about the position two years ago, describing a defence programme that was “to be honest and to be frank, unfit to counter the dangers that we now face”. Industry, he suggested, needs no reminding. “Those who work in our supply chains know how painfully slow, wasteful and costly the procurement the MOD previously undertook was,” he said, singling out small businesses and scale-ups with good products who “struggled sometimes to find the right buyer within the MOD”.
Small firms
Against that, Pollard set out the machinery now in place: a new National Armaments Director in Rupert Pearce, recruited from a FTSE 100 company and bringing what the minister called a new corporate approach and energy to procurement; the Defence Office for Small Business Growth, established to cut red tape and remove obstacles to entry; and an SME Action Plan published so the department can be held to account for the change.
The headline commitment is a 50 per cent increase in departmental spending with medium and small firms by summer 2028, which the minister described as “moving an extra two and a half billion pounds into the pockets of SMEs by changing the way we procure”.
Regional defence and security clusters have proved successful enough that more regions are developing them, he said, creating local routes that bring together major suppliers, devolved and local government, and giving investors a forum in which to meet them.
Bringing in the City
Running through the address was an argument that public money alone will not build the capacity required in the time available, however welcome rising budgets are. “As a defence minister, of course, I would like more defence spending,” he said.
“But it’s not just from the taxpayer that there’s opportunities for investing in defence. It’s how you crowd in private capital, how you use the institutions, the networks, the structures of the City of London and the UK’s place at the heart of global financial trade, to bring more private capital into defence, creating more good jobs and more deterrence.”
Waiting was not, in his view, an option: “In a more dangerous world, we need to build more capacity now, rather than just wait for the increase in defence money that we know is coming over the next 10 years.”
Whether the two sides can understand one another is a separate problem, and one he acknowledged. “There’s a risk that we sometimes speak past each other,” he said, arguing that a shared language and shared data would improve the department’s ability to deliver. The Defence Investment Unit announced in the Defence Investment Plan is meant to close that gap, giving investors a clearer interface with the department while bringing financial expertise in to turn priorities into market-facing propositions.
Companies already through the door
To show the approach producing results rather than remaining theoretical, the minister turned to firms that have already taken the route.
Thirteen British startups won contracts of up to £4 million in May under the Defence Unicorn Fund programme. Among them was Kraken Technologies, which builds maritime uncrewed surface vessels and has since raised $175 million in a Series B round on the back of a $1 billion valuation. Green Jets, one of three firms selected to develop a low-cost drone interceptor, has also secured significant funding. Both drew money from the National Security Strategic Investment Fund and the NATO Innovation Fund, with the British Business Bank financing Kraken as well.
JET Connectivity, a small business building 5G and 6G communications tools, was the only British firm admitted to the NATO DIANA mission track programme this year from more than three and a half thousand participants, which Mr Pollard called “fantastic recognition of British innovation at its best” while adding that it is “just the tip of the iceberg”.
There was a moment of self-deprecation over how the language has shifted under the current Prime Minister, with the Minister saying, “I used to be incentivised by the MOD press office to say defence is an engine for growth in all my interviews,” he told the audience. “With Andy Burnham in Downing Street I now say re-industrialisation, but the fundamental truth is there. Investment in defence creates good jobs. It provides opportunities in particular for our young people and we should be unafraid and unapologetic of saying that truth loudly.”
His closing argument was that none of this rests with his department alone, describing defence as “a whole of society endeavour, a whole of government endeavour” which the Ministry of Defence must lead but cannot deliver by itself.
He finished on deterrence, and on what follows if it does not hold, saying “That’s why increasing our deterrence matters with new technologies. But if deterrence fails, we must be ready to fight, and we must be ready to win.”

Company behind pulled sunscreens sued for 'misleading' conduct
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
19:16:48 UTC
04:16:48 KST

Wild Child Laboratories sued for 'deceptive' conduct over recalled sunscreens
In short:
Wild Child Laboratories, the manufacturer of 20 sunscreens recalled for not meeting their SPF claims, is being sued in the Federal Court.
The sunscreen industry was rocked last year by a spate of product recalls that followed an ABC investigation and testing by consumer group Choice.
Wild Child Laboratories went into liquidation in August after selling its assets to new company Heliora, which denies it was set up to avoid its predecessor's debts.
The manufacturer of the base formula used by 20 sunscreens pulled from sale for failing to meet their SPF claims is being sued for "misleading" and "deceptive" conduct.
High-profile brand Ultra Violette is seeking millions of dollars from Wild Child Laboratories, following the recall of one of its signature SPF50+ sunscreens last year in the wake of testing by consumer group Choice showing an SPF of just four.
But the status of the litigation is uncertain after Wild Child went into voluntary liquidation in August.
In the month before the liquidation, Wild Child sold its assets to a new company that shared the same CEO and director, which continued the company's sunscreen manufacturing business under the name Heliora.
Ultra Violette told the ABC it understood Wild Child's liquidators were reviewing the transaction and the circumstances surrounding it.
In a statement, Heliora said it "firmly rejects any suggestion that it was established as a means of avoiding Wild Child's liabilities".
"The liquidators have not raised concerns with us about the transaction," the statement said.
"The conduct and scope of any review of Wild Child's affairs is a matter for the liquidators, and they are the appropriate party to answer questions about it."
Liquidator PKF has not responded to questions.
Wild Child Laboratories' liquidation leaves creditors, including multiple sunscreen brands and the Australian Taxation Office, claiming debts totalling about $20 million.
In addition to Ultra Violette's Lean Screen SPF50+ product, 19 other sunscreens which shared the same base formula were recalled due to low SPF test results, all of which were made by Wild Child Laboratories.
Wild Child is also being sued by Advanced Skin Technology, owner of the high-end Aspect Skincare brand, which recalled two products.
Wild Child's creditors also include prominent Australian brand Naked Sundays, which is listed as being owed $8.2 million on the liquidator's report.
In documents filed to the Federal Court before it went into liquidation, Wild Child indicated it would defend the claims and said the sunscreen brands were responsible for ensuring the products met their regulatory obligations.
Heliora was registered about a month before the liquidation.
It was set up by Wild Child director and major shareholder Paul Waldren and is headed by former Wild Child chief executive officer, Tom Curnow.
In Heliora's statement, Mr Curnow said the purchase was negotiated with the involvement of a secured lender to Wild Child and a restructuring advisory firm.
Heliora is backed by investors who originally had stakes in Wild Child Laboratories, including Mr Waldren.
"No Wild Child shareholder received any payment or distribution from the transaction," Mr Curnow said in the statement.
"Heliora also assumed agreed liabilities … including obligations to many Wild Child suppliers and creditors.
"All Wild Child employees were offered employment with Heliora, and their employee entitlements carried forward."
Heliora has taken on Wild Child Laboratories' clients and manufacturing business and is continuing under its TGA manufacturing licence.
"Heliora has submitted the required dossier to the TGA to support the transfer of the [Good Manufacturing Practice] licence and is working through that process with the regulator," the statement said.
Millions of dollars in claims
Documents filed as part of the liquidation show 11 sunscreen companies are claiming a total of more than $19 million.
The debts also include more than $400,000 to the Australian Taxation Office.
In its statement of claim lodged in the Federal Court, Ultra Violette alleges that Wild Child Laboratories made six separate representations that the sunscreen in question had an SPF of 50 or 50+.
Ultra Violette said it commissioned its own SPF tests on the product, which all returned low results.
"Between July and September 2025 Ultra Violette received seven test results from four laboratories which returned average SPF ratings of 2.9, 3.0, 3.6, 4.1, 10.5, 21.5 and 25.18," the statement of claim says.
The claim also refers to additional testing commissioned by Wild Child Laboratories which showed a result of SPF 21.7.
The company has accused Wild Child of misleading and deceptive conduct and breach of contract.
The liquidator's creditor report listed Ultra Violette as being owed $7 million.
In its statement to the ABC, Ultra Violette said the liquidation has had an "immediate impact on our Federal Court proceeding".
"We cannot ordinarily continue proceedings against a company in liquidation without leave of the court," it said.
In response to questions about Ultra Violette's claim, Mr Curnow said "the liquidators are the appropriate party to respond to … those matters".
He added: "Wild Child's insurer has confirmed in writing that the liquidation has not altered or withdrawn indemnity previously confirmed in respect of relevant claims, and that the relevant insurance continues to respond to those claims following the liquidation, subject to its terms and conditions."
Separate suit
Advanced Skin Technology, which recalled two of its Aspect Skincare sunscreens last year, has also alleged misleading and deceptive conduct on the part of Wild Child Laboratories.
Its statement of claim filed in the Federal Court said the manufacturer failed to take reasonable care in the development, manufacture and supply of the sunscreens and in ensuring they were SPF50+.
The company is suing for losses for refunds, credits, write-offs, lost sales and profits and staff management time spent on the recall, as well as reputational damage.
It has not put a dollar figure on the damages it is seeking, but the creditors' report from the liquidator lists almost $2.5 million in debts owed to the brand.
Wild Child indicated it would defend the court action from Advanced Skin Technology in a defence lodged with the court in April this year.
Advanced Skin Technology said: "As the matter is ongoing, it would not be appropriate for us to comment on the details at this time."
In its defence filed in the Ultra Violette proceedings in July, Wild Child Laboratories argued the brand was responsible for making sure the SPF of the product met its label claim.
"Ultra Violette undertook responsibility for meeting all the legal obligations required of a sponsor of therapeutic goods in Australia in relation to the Lean Screen SPF50+ sunscreen," it said.
The defence also stated while Wild Child was not liable, the companies it engaged to perform SPF testing on the failed sunscreen were "concurrent wrongdoers".
One of those companies was Princeton Consumer Research (PCR), used by a significant number of Australian sunscreens, which was found to provide unreliable SPF testing data.
The Wild Child defence stated that PCR "engaged in conduct which was misleading and deceptive or likely to mislead and deceive."
The sunscreen formula used by the 20 products that were recalled last year has been discontinued by Wild Child Laboratories.
The TGA said at the time, "preliminary testing indicates that this base formulation is unlikely to have an SPF of greater than 21" and some products may have an SPF as low as four.
A TGA Good Manufacturing Practice audit of Wild Child facilities last year "did not identify any manufacturing issues that could have contributed to the low SPF results".

Apple Doesn’t Want You to Worry About the New Apple Watch's Listening Features
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
19:14:26 UTC
04:14:26 KST

The new Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 come not just with better fitness tracking and upgraded noise reduction, but also a whole new way to listen.
Apple announced on Wednesday that the two smartwatches come with four opt-in “audio intelligence” tools that are powered by audio gathered by the watches’ microphones. They include sound and music recognition, a conversation recap feature, and “Live Rewind” so a user can see a transcription of anything that was said in their environment in the previous 15 seconds.
Seemingly wary that the features could make it feel like the walls have ears, Apple is emphasizing that all of them are built to prioritize privacy and security using the extensive infrastructure the company has developed to protect its other Apple Intelligence and Siri services. As more and more of these types of features debut, though, the audio intelligence announcements are a reminder that AI-powered tools are becoming increasingly universal in all areas of computing and life.
“These features do not create or store audio recordings, and raw audio used for processing is completely inaccessible to the operating systems, apps, the user, or Apple,” the company wrote in a report shared with WIRED.
The new Apple Watch features are designed to process as much data locally on devices as possible, so potentially sensitive data doesn’t go to the cloud. Sound Recognition, for example, alerts users about sounds in their environment—including doorbells, sirens, alarms, or, say, a baby crying—without sending any data off the watch. The tools that do send information out to the cloud preprocess the data so it isn’t raw audio files, then use Apple’s Private Cloud Compute infrastructure.
Apple emphasizes that its on-device capabilities for Apple watches have expanded thanks to the company’s new S11 chips. The chips include a special memory-protected space that Apple calls the Secure Exclave. Designed specifically for sensor data, the exclave is an isolated buffer that is inaccessible to the rest of the operating system where Apple Watch can hold and process audio data in a protected space.
A new Shazam feature “listens” for music and will generate a signature of a song that is stored in the Secure Exclave. If the user navigates to Shazam to find out what the music is, the tool will send that signature—not an audio file—to Shazam’s servers for identification. (Shazam is an Apple-owned service.) If the user doesn’t prompt to identify the music, or as soon as they do, the special signature is “immediately” deleted from the watch.
The recap feature, known as Siri Recap, can be set to be on all the time and generate recaps of any substantive conversation, or it can be given a schedule to listen in at certain times during the day. A dedicated AI model determines when speech is occurring without recording or transcribing any data. If it detects a conversation, audio goes into a protected buffer within the Secure Exclave on the Apple Watch, the watch encrypts it, and then transmits it using Apple’s special secure Bluetooth pairing to the Secure Exclave on a user’s iPhone. Then the audio is immediately deleted from the Apple Watch.
The iPhone uses local speech recognition and language models on-device to transcribe the audio and then generate a minimal version of the transcript that removes nonessential elements like extra words and repeated phrases. Then the raw audio is immediately deleted from the iPhone as well. The last step on the iPhone is a safety model that “screens the text to omit potentially harmful terms,” according to Apple. From there, the distillation of the conversation is encrypted, and the iPhone sends it out to Private Cloud Compute.
“Contextual information is also sent to improve summary quality,” Apple says. “For example, Now Playing data helps the model understand that speech may have originated from music or a podcast. Calendar data can help generate accurate titles of summaries. High-level location labels such as home, work, and school, along with locality information such as city, state, and country, add context to the summarization. Point-of-interest categories like ‘grocery store’ or ‘park’ may also be included. Precise location and specific points of interest are not included.”
Finally, the condensed transcript is run through Apple’s foundation models in Private Cloud Compute to create a title and summary, which is then encrypted and sent back to the iPhone and Apple Watch. Apple says that Siri Recap is built to remove sensitive information like financial data, ID numbers, or other personal identifiers from its summaries.
The Live Rewind features that lets users ask for a text version of the last 15 seconds of what was said in their environment uses the Secure Exclave buffer to continuously hold audio on a rolling basis, where old sound is replaced by new audio and doesn’t amass. To get a transcript through Live Rewind, users must double-press the Apple Watch’s Digital Crown each time. Once activated, the watch sends the last 15 seconds of buffered audio from its Secure Exclave to the Secure Exclave of the paired iPhone. If the iPhone is not available, the transfer will fail, and the audio will automatically be deleted. (Siri Recap has similar fail-safes if the transfer from the watch to the iPhone fails.) If the transfer goes through, the iPhone does on-device speech-recognition processing to make a transcript and then deletes the audio and sends the text back to the Apple Watch. Users read the transcript and then can discard it or save it in the Siri app.
It's hard to ignore that, in spite of all of these data protections, anyone wearing a new Apple Watch could be siccing “audio intelligence” on, say, your intimate vent session, private family update, or accidental slip-up about a secret. To try to mitigate blatant privacy violations, Apple says that the watch produces an audible chime when a watch owner initiates a Live Rewind transcript to alert other people in the area—even if it is on silent mode or paired with headphones. And the features are built to omit or filter out potentially identifying information about speakers. But the sheer scope and breadth of the tools is extremely noteworthy.
Apple has invested significantly over many years in its secure AI processing infrastructure—far beyond what almost any other company has done. The new audio features highlight, though, that over time the AI attack surface, or sheer quantity of services and systems that could include flaws or mistakes and be attacked, is growing faster than the implications can be fully understood.

-  Pearl White ceramic;

-  Light Gold aluminum;

====================================================================================================

The UK was right to sanction Israeli settlements. Now it must do more to protect Palestinians under occupation.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
19:08:21 UTC
04:08:21 KST

The UK has crossed a political Rubicon on Israel’s occupation of the West Bank. Yesterday, the Government recognised that Israel’s continued control over Palestinian territory is unlawful, bringing it into line with the International Court of Justice’s 2024 Advisory Opinion.
For decades, British governments have condemned Israel’s settlements as illegal while allowing the settlement project to expand with impunity. Palestinian communities have been displaced and Israeli control over the West Bank has become ever more entrenched. Yesterday’s announcement matters because it puts a concrete consequence behind that position: it will ban trade in goods and some services with illegal Israeli settlements.
The ban is welcome. But it should be the beginning, not the end, of this shift in policy. The UK now needs to address the wider policies and relationships it has pursued over the years that have allowed Israel’s unlawful occupation of the West Bank to become so deeply entrenched.
But this is not simply about where the dates and avocados on our supermarket shelves come from. It is about Palestinian land being violently seized, communities being fragmented, and Palestinians being denied the basic conditions to live safely, move freely and access healthcare. For Palestinians who have lived with this reality for decades, the question is whether and when this will begin to change the reality on the ground.
In July, a three-month-old Palestinian boy, Ahmad Maarouf Zaid, died after Israeli forces prevented his family from crossing a checkpoint for more than an hour as they tried to get him to hospital in critical condition. Weeks later, a Palestinian woman who was six months pregnant and suffering severe bleeding was held at a military checkpoint for more than 30 minutes while the ambulance carrying her was searched. Doctors saved her life, but her baby tragically died.
For Palestinians, these restrictions are part of everyday life. In the West Bank, there are now 925 movement obstacles, including checkpoints and road closures. A journey that should take minutes can take hours, or become impossible altogether. On average, Palestinians in the West Bank spend around 90 hours a month dealing with checkpoints, road closures and other restrictions on movement.
Between January and July this year, the World Health Organization recorded 98 attacks on healthcare in the West Bank, including 92 incidents involving the obstruction of healthcare. Eighty-three ambulances and other health transport were affected, as well as 11 health facilities. In July alone, there were 37 attacks on healthcare.
Yesterday’s announcement also had implications beyond the issue of settlement trade alone. The Government has now accepted what the International Court of Justice found in 2024: that Israel’s continued presence in the occupied Palestinian territory is unlawful. That should have consequences for how the UK responds to the system of control that has entrenched Israeli rule over Palestinian land and restricted Palestinians’ access to healthcare.
The Government also struck a new tone on Gaza, acknowledging that “there must be accountability” for what has happened there and hinting at further possible sanctions. Nearly a year into the so-called “ceasefire”, more than 1,300 Palestinians have been killed, while Israel’s “Yellow Line” has advanced to cover around 70% of Gaza, displacing our colleagues and communities we serve in the process. At the same time, vital aid and medical supplies remain critically obstructed while Gaza’s health system lies in ruins. Gaza cannot wait – the UK must follow its words with rapid action to puncture Israel’s impunity.
For Palestinians who have lived under this system for decades, the question is whether the UK’s ‘reset’ will make a difference to their lives. Can Palestinians move freely, reach healthcare and live safely in their own communities? For those living with the consequences of the occupation every day, recognition of their plight will only mean something if it is followed by an end to Israel’s violent occupation, its genocide in Gaza, and the escalating state-backed settler violence against communities across the West Bank.
Yesterday’s decision should mark a complete circuit break in the way the UK has dealt with Israel’s occupation for far too long. Israel’s control over Palestinian land has deepened while condemnation has too often stopped at words. The UK should now make sure this decision is followed by decisive and comprehensive action.
The UK has crossed a political Rubicon. It should not turn back.

UK Lawmakers Are Freaking Out Over AI’s Summer of Chaos
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
19:07:42 UTC
04:07:42 KST

A leading British politician has urged the United Nations to intervene in “the unsafe development of super intelligence” after an Anthropic team leader posted: “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!”
Whether “marketing hype” or signposting of a genuine extinction threat, “governments must step in,” Labour MP Darren Jones wrote in an open letter also addressed to the UK prime minister and international Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development.
Jones is the latest lawmaker scrambling to find ways to protect the British public from AI threats to safety. Just one day earlier, Labour MP Alex Sobel had introduced a parliamentary bill proposing to ban the “development, deployment, and operation of artificial superintelligence”—systems which can fully replace and outmatch humans at any task. The legislation would also give the government powers to monitor and control the development of the technology at different points in the supply chain, including at chip level.
“We are not alone in this effort,” said Sobel while introducing the bill, pointing to the US government’s temporary export ban on Anthropic’s Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models in June. "If the Trump Administration, who are perceived as historically against AI regulation, can contemplate drawing a line on models that are too powerful and dangerous, it would be strange for us not to ask what our response should be," he argued.
MPs from across political parties put their names on the bill, including Labour MP Jess Asato, who is suing Elon Musk’s xAI after its Grok chatbot was allegedly used to generate fake sexualized images of her. Lawmakers have become increasingly worried about the threat of AI to national security after a string of incidents of AI agents going rogue in recent months. They want to introduce guardrails against worst-case scenarios, such as these systems seizing control of critical infrastructure and running sophisticated influence operations.
The Hugging Face hack by OpenAI’s models that escaped containment in July “is why it’s even more important that we move quickly to regulate and legislate on superintelligent AI,” Sobel tells WIRED, “because AI is developing at pace, and I’m afraid to say those developing it don’t know exactly what’s in it.”
In an unusual move, the parliamentary bill was drafted by the nonprofit ControlAI, which is backed by Skype founding engineer and former DeepMind investor director Jaan Tallinn. It was founded by Andrea Miotti, who had previously been working at AI safety startup Conjecture but tells WIRED he wanted to make the public and policymakers aware of the “open secret” that “developing superintelligence could cause human extinction.”
Conjecture founder Connor Leahy now leads ControlAI’s US arm, which consulted on Bernie Sanders and Greg Casar’s bill to ban superintelligence development, in addition to having briefed nearly 200 congressional offices and more than 20 members of the Senate and House of Representatives on the extinction risk of superintelligence.
Sobel will present his bill in full in November. While he accepts it’s rare for the UK government to accept private legislation like this, Sobel hopes it may lead the government to work with other countries on an international ban.
Sobel has previously tried in vain to introduce a “kill switch” into the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill, which would allow the government to pull the plug on any data center hosting an AI agent that presented a threat. The mechanism, which was also proposed by ControlAI, is similar to a law pushed for by both Republican and Democratic lawmakers in the US. AI minister Kanishka Narayan, then working under former prime minister Keir Starmer, shot it down, pointing out that the bill already allows the government powers to intervene if compromised network and information systems cause a national security risk. That could include requiring an entity to cease using and isolate an AI model, he noted.
But that may not be enough, Sobel says, hoping to meet with the government to hammer out details of which companies would be included within the scope of the proposed rules. “I think this might be the crucial year,” he says. “If we leave it too long, things may move past our ability to regulate it.”
Peers across parties in the UK parliament’s upper house, including former AI minister Viscount Camrose, tried unsuccessfully to reintroduce the measure last week. They have been frustrated as the binding regulation on frontier AI firms promised by the Labour government when they won power in 2024 has failed to materialize.
While peer Tim Clement-Jones admitted they shouldn’t be trying to “shoehorn” AI regulation into a cybersecurity bill. In the absence of any other AI legislation, “we have no choice,” he said in a speech to parliament. “We must have more control and oversight over that sort of behavior, because you can see its consequences,” said Alexandra Freeman in the debate, referring to the Hugging Face incident. “This legislation is our only opportunity now.”
Nearly nine out of 10 Britons support independent regulation of the technology, a poll by the Ada Lovelace Institute showed in December. Meanwhile, nearly three times as many (38 percent) believe that the risks of AI outweigh the benefits as vice versa (13 percent), according to official statistics. But “the government has been completely deaf to this, and they have paid no attention to those who are advocating for this,” Clement-Jones says, arguing that the public's lack of trust in the technology will curb adoption.
The UK government evaluates the capabilities and safety of advanced artificial intelligence models through the research body the AI Security Institute. Cooperation is voluntary for AI companies, as the organization has no legal powers to access unreleased models for testing or ban their public release. For example, the agency reportedly did not get access to Anthropic’s latest model, Claude Mythos 5.1, for testing.
“I think it's a rather naive position to imagine that we can do things on a voluntary basis,” says Clement-Jones. “Do you really think that the big AI companies have got everybody's welfare at heart?”

UK details £16bn military support for Ukraine
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
20:06:51 BST
04:06:51 KST

The Ministry of Defence has set out how £16 billion of UK military support for Ukraine has been allocated across five financial years, while declining to provide a departmental breakdown of the Government’s wider non-military assistance.
The figures were disclosed in a written parliamentary answer to Conservative MP Ben Obese-Jecty, who asked for a breakdown of the UK’s stated £25 billion total support for Ukraine, including £16 billion in military assistance and £5.6 billion in non-military support.
Armed Forces Minister Louise Sandher-Jones said: “The UK has committed to providing at least £3 billion in military support a year to Ukraine until Financial Year (FY) 2030-31 and for as long as needed.”
She added: “To date, the MOD has committed £16 billion in military support, including the £2.26 billion ERA loan contribution.”
According to the figures provided by the department, military support amounted to £2.5 billion in 2022-23, £2.3 billion in 2023-24 and £3 billion in 2024-25. For 2025-26, the MOD lists £3.2 billion of Ukraine funding alongside £1.5 billion through the Extraordinary Revenue Acceleration loan, producing a total of £4.7 billion for that financial year.
For 2026-27, the department lists a further £3 billion in Ukraine funding and £750 million through the ERA mechanism, giving a total of £3.75 billion. The MOD table puts direct Ukraine funding across the five years at £13.8 billion and the ERA contribution at £2.26 billion, producing a stated overall military-support total of £16 billion when rounded.
The Extraordinary Revenue Acceleration mechanism forms part of the wider G7 arrangement intended to provide Ukraine with financing backed by revenues generated from immobilised Russian sovereign assets.
Sandher-Jones said the department regularly accounts for the support it provides directly, stating: “The MOD routinely publishes the support it has directly provided to Ukraine in its Annual Report and Accounts.”
Obese-Jecty’s question also sought a breakdown by department and year of the £5.6 billion in non-military support referred to in the Government’s July statement on UK assistance to Ukraine. The MOD did not provide those figures. Sandher-Jones said: “We do not comment on spending by other Government departments.”

Winners and losers of Labor's $560m community grants
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
19:03:30 UTC
04:03:30 KST

Which seats won and which missed out on Labor's $560m community grants?
There were 45 electorates that missed out on any funding from Labor's $560 million grants program set up to pay the party's election commitments.
The Centre for Public Integrity examined the 220 projects invited under the scheme and found it heavily favoured Labor at the election.
Among them was a $6 million grant to the Marrickville Golf Club in Anthony Albanese's seat of Grayndler, where the ABC revealed yesterday the prime minister held an undisclosed honorary membership.
Mr Albanese told the House of Representatives he had been advised he received that membership in 2012, but that he had no member card and had not set foot in the clubhouse for years.
Three quarters of the money committed under the Major and Local Community Infrastructure (MLCI) program went to seats notionally held by Labor heading into the 2025 federal election.
Centre for Public Integrity chair, former justice Anthony Whealy, said it appeared to be a case of "serious pork-barrelling".
On Thursday, the Greens will move to refer the MLCI program to a Senate inquiry for closer scrutiny.
The committee will be asked to examine the program's design, the process by which projects were identified for funding, the role of the prime minister and other ministers in determining who was invited to apply, as well as any potential or perceived conflicts of interest where it relates to grant recipients.
"This, on its face, is a significant misuse of public funds and warrants scrutiny," Greens senator Steph Hodgins-May said.
"[And] the fact that $6 million has gone towards the Marrickville Golf Club in the prime minister's electorate I think raises significant questions for the prime minister to answer.
"He's given some wishy-washy answers that, frankly, I think are sidestepping the core issue here, [which] is why was that money expended there?"
Winners and losers
Among the seats that received funding were a few big winners.
Victorian Labor MP Sam Rae's seat of Hawke received $27.5 million for two projects, most of that for a new swimming centre.
In NSW, Labor MP Kristy McBain's seat of Eden-Monaro received funding for eight projects worth a combined $26.47 million, the largest being for a new pool in Bega.
Those seats received more than any other under the program.
The single largest project promised funding was a $45 million redevelopment of the Nunawading Indoor Sports Centre.
For its analysis, the Centre for Public Integrity considered the grant shared across the seats of Chisholm, held by Labor with a margin of 3.3 per cent, and Deakin, held by the Liberals with effectively no margin.
Braddon, Blair, Solomon, Tangney, Wills and Corangamite rounded out the top-ten highest funded seats under the MLCI program.
Meanwhile, 45 seats received no funding through the program.
The federal government said it had made more than $1.7 billion available through other competitive grant schemes.
But under the MLCI, One Nation leader Barnaby Joyce's seat of New England, Opposition Leader Angus Taylor's seat of Hume, and former Liberal leader Sussan Ley's seat of Farrer missed out on any funding.
There were also seven Labor seats that received nothing, including the safe seats of Rankin (Jim Chalmers), Sydney (Tanya Plibersek) and McMahon (Chris Bowen).
The Centre for Public Integrity found more than $220 million went to marginal seats at the federal election where Labor was competitive and another $270 million to fairly safe and safe Labor seats.
Across all seats where Labor was not competitive, just $66 million was promised.
On Tuesday, Senator David Pocock asked Finance Minister Katy Gallagher if election commitments were overwhelmingly committed to marginal seats and how that differed from pork barrelling.
Senator Gallagher defended their allocation, saying they had been allocated "across the board, in seats we don't hold, in seats we would never hold".
"If you think you can demonstrate that our commitments were targeted on marginal seats, you do that," Senator Gallagher said.
"Now, unfortunately for those that seek to smear on this program, we have followed every single rule to the letter."
The Centre for Public Integrity challenged the assertion, saying the government still had not explained why it chose a closed process for the $560 million fund, or how it decided which projects would get access.
"A value-for-money assessment after a project has been hand-picked doesn't tell us whether the hand-picking itself was fair," research strategy director Gabrielle Appleby said.

New laws aim to make black market tobacco easier to prosecute
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
19:02:10 UTC
04:02:10 KST

Labor moves to make illicit tobacco prosecutions easier with new laws
In short:
Labor is cracking down on the illicit tobacco trade with new offences targeting organised crime, distributors and retailers selling illegal cigarettes.
The changes would also make it easier to seize the profits and assets of criminals involved in the black market.
What's next?
The federal government will introduce the bill on Thursday, while the Coalition and One Nation continue to push for a cut to the tobacco excise.
Organised criminals importing black market tobacco and retailers selling illegal cigarettes will be easier to prosecute under a federal government crackdown on the illicit trade.
New offences would allow authorities to rely on factors including suspiciously cheap prices, non-compliant branded packaging or concealed products to show tobacco had entered Australia unlawfully.
Under existing laws, prosecutions are routinely frustrated because it must be proven an accused person knew the tobacco was illegally imported and subject to customs duty.
Assistant Minister for Customs Julian Hill will introduce legislation to modernise the Customs Act on Thursday as the government moves to strengthen its response to the illicit tobacco market largely controlled by organised crime.
"Anyone involved in the illegal tobacco and vapes trade — whether high up in the crime groups, mid-level operatives, distributors or those running and working in the shops — would be wise to get a new job and do so quickly," he told the ABC.
Mr Hill said the current offences were designed for "another era" where low-level criminals had tried to "defraud a bit of revenue".
"Today, the scale, complexity and sophistication of organised crime demands a new approach to go after the criminals — anyone involved in the illicit tobacco trade," he said.
Mr Hill said "serious criminals" would be the focus, but it would also be "easier" for law enforcement to take action against retail premises in possession of illegal tobacco.
"Commonwealth laws cover companies, meaning tobacconists, warehouse or distribution companies could also be targeted," he said.
Cheap cigarettes could be used to prove illicit import
The proposed new laws create separate offences covering the importation of tobacco and its possession or movement within Australia.
Prosecutors would be able to point to circumstances that would lead a reasonable person to suspect tobacco was illicit.
This could include cigarettes being sold for less than the value of the excise and GST that would apply to a legal product, or the absence of documentation showing where the tobacco came from.
Another indicator could be non-compliant products, such as cigarettes that do not meet Australia's plain-packaging rules or banned variants like menthol flavouring.
The bill would also strengthen proceeds of crime laws, including expanding investigators' powers to obtain documents and tightening rules designed to prevent criminals shielding their assets.
Mr Hill said this would make it easier to "strip" criminals of the profits made through illegal tobacco sales.
"Prosecutions will be pursued, but what really hurts these criminals is to take their cash, their cars, their houses, their boats and their toys," he said.
Tobacco excise fight divides parliament
Labor had flagged plans to strengthen laws around illegal tobacco prior to the recent proposals by the Coalition and One Nation to slash the excise on legal cigarettes.
The opposition last week promised to cut the rate by 80 per cent, reducing the tax on a packet of 20 cigarettes by $24.
It would also legalise and tax nicotine vapes and pouches for adults, spend an additional $200 million on enforcement and $60 million on a public education campaign.
One Nation earlier announced it would reduce the tobacco excise by 75 per cent, which the party argued was sufficient to quash the black market.
On Wednesday, the Coalition used Question Time to accuse Prime Minister Anthony Albanese of failing to give a straight answer about whether Labor would cut the excise.
Health Minister Mark Butler responded, saying the government had taken the view that enforcement was the best approach to tackle the black market.
"Of course we are open to other sensible ideas about how we can fight organised crime, while not prejudicing our most important public health campaign," he said.

Why are borrowing costs rising across the world?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
19:00:36 UTC
04:00:36 KST

Counting the Cost
Why are borrowing costs rising across the world?
Rising bond yields are lifting borrowing costs for governments, businesses and households across the global economy.
For more than a decade, governments got used to cheap borrowing. That era may now be ending.
Government bond markets are flashing warnings around the world.
Across major economies, yields – the interest rates governments pay to borrow – are climbing to levels not seen in years and, in some cases, decades.
Investors are pricing in more risk before they’ll lend to governments already carrying heavy debt loads.
Inflation remains stubborn, geopolitical tensions are adding pressure, and central banks may have to keep interest rates higher for longer.
Those higher borrowing costs are pushing up what banks charge companies and homeowners.
