The US now learns what Taiwan knew before
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:37:55 UTC
01:37:55 KST

Taiwan does not need a CIA deputy director to explain that Beijing treats commerce as a battlefield. It has been living that lesson for decades, watching its chip designers get poached, its retired officers get recruited for cash, and its companies get pressured to choose between the Chinese market and their own government’s security priorities. What changed this month is that Washington finally said the quiet part out loud.
CIA Deputy Director Michael Ellis told a Washington audience that China’s threat to the US is now “fundamentally different,” because the competition is economic, not military, and that a Chinese company cannot be treated as genuinely private when the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) can absorb or direct it at will.
This is not a new insight in Taipei. It is the working assumption behind every export control on advanced lithography equipment, every debate in the Legislative Yuan about Chinese investment in the semiconductor supply chain, and every prosecution of a retired general caught building a spy network for a bowl of noodles and a modest stipend. Taiwan has spent 30 years treating Chinese capital as a potential delivery mechanism for state power. Washington is only now updating its assumptions to match the country Taiwan has always had to live next to.
The same week Ellis spoke, federal agents in Detroit charged a Chinese national, Zeng Weiheng, with lying about why he had spent 20 minutes photographing cargo planes at O’Hare International Airport. Zeng was not a trained intelligence officer. He was a college student in Canada, allegedly paid by a contact he believed was tied to the CCP to photograph specific aircraft and tail numbers, a task cheap enough and deniable enough that losing him cost Beijing nothing.
Taiwan’s own counterintelligence record is full of Zengs: low-ranking, financially motivated, recruited through family ties or business contacts and disposable by design. The scale is different, the method is not. What the O’Hare case demonstrates on US soil, Taiwanese security services have been documenting for a generation, usually with far less international attention.
The useful thing about Washington’s shift is not that it discovered anything new. It is that it removed a piece of cover that Beijing-friendly voices in Taiwan have relied on for years: the argument that treating cross-strait economic integration as a security risk is paranoid, protectionist or an overreaction driven by Taipei’s politics.
If the CIA argues publicly that a Chinese semiconductor firm cannot be assumed independent of the CCP, then the same logic applies with more force, not less, to a Chinese-linked investment vehicle courting a Taiwanese supplier or to political factions here who insist that deeper economic ties with China are merely business. That argument was always thin; it just got a lot thinner.
None of this should be read as vindication for its own sake. The point of Washington catching up is not that Taipei gets to say it told you so, although it would be entitled to. The point is that shared threat assessment is the precondition for shared policy, on export controls, on investment screening, on the defense package still stalled in the legislature by parties more interested in denying the threat than countering it.
Taiwan has spent years explaining what it is like to share a border with an authoritarian state that does not recognize the line between its companies and its intelligence services. It is a strange kind of relief to watch Washington arrive, slightly out of breath, at the same conclusion.

MOL warns foodpanda over docking couriers’ pay for late deliveries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:37:55 UTC
01:37:55 KST

Delivery platform foodpanda could face fines up to NT$100,000 (US$3,178) per affected worker for illegally docking couriers’ pay for late deliveries based on unilaterally imposed time limits, the Ministry of Labor (MOL) said yesterday.
At multiple recent meetings with local labor officials, the ministry declared that such practices by foodpanda violate the Delivery Workers’ Rights Protection and Delivery Platform Management Act, according to a statement issued by the ministry.
Local labor bureaus can impose fines ranging from NT $20,000 to NT$100,000 per affected courier once they determine the validity of the complaints filed by workers, MOL Department of Labor Relations Director-General Wang Hou-wei (王厚偉) told CNA.
Photo: Chiu Chiao-jen, Taipei Times
Wang did not disclose how many complaints had been filed with local authorities, citing a lack of complete data, but said all reported cases involved foodpanda.
According to Wang, delivery couriers reported facing pay deductions for exceeding estimated delivery times by as little as one to five minutes, calling the policy “unfair” due to “numerous unforeseen and uncontrollable factors on the road.”
When delivery delays occur, platforms should look into the causes and handle them via proper mechanisms instead of making unilateral pay deductions, the ministry said.
“Unlawful practices will absolutely not be tolerated,” it added.
Under the law, which came into force on July 21, platforms must pay riders based on the exact time a delivery takes, using a rate of 1.25 times the minimum wage, and no order can pay less than NT$45.
Unions voicing support
Earlier yesterday, the National Delivery Industrial Union and two other unions issued a joint statement accusing foodpanda of “maliciously scapegoating delivery workers for order delays” as a pretext to unlawfully dock their pay.
Separately, the Preparatory Committee for the Taiwan Federation of Delivery Industrial Unions said couriers frequently encounter delays caused by factors beyond their control.
Such situations include understaffed retail stores, long peak-hour restaurant waits, GPS and system glitches, unreachable customers or faulty delivery addresses, as well as traffic congestion, road closures, and severe weather, it said.
The union coalition called on couriers to submit formal complaints to local labor departments if they experience illegal pay deductions.
foodpanda’s response
In response, Emma Kuo (郭昕宜), foodpanda’s director of public affairs and public relations, told reporters that the platform has never refused to disburse rider pay due to delivery delays.
Kuo said the company only asked delivery couriers to clarify unusually long trips, adding that full pay will be disbursed as long as a valid explanation is provided.
Kuo made the remarks yesterday afternoon at a press conference announcing a new commercial partner, according to reports by local media.

Seyit Şamil Kurt
09 September 2026•Update: 09 September 2026
The foreign ministers of Türkiye, Egypt, Indonesia, Jordan, Pakistan, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates on Wednesday welcomed the UK government's decision to ban imports of goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territory and restrict services linked to such settlements.
In a joint statement, the ministers expressed hope that the decision would help mobilize the international community to take similar action in line with international law and hold accountable settlement organizations and individuals engaged in illegal settlement activities.
They also welcomed a joint statement on the two-state solution issued by the foreign ministers of Canada, Denmark, Finland, France, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain, Sweden and the UK.
The 12 countries confirmed their intention to introduce national restrictions and/or support European restrictions on trade in goods with settlements that are illegal under international law, or to actively consider these and other measures in accordance with their respective national procedures.
The ministers of the eight countries urged the international community to build on these steps and adopt concrete measures to end activities that support or sustain illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territory.
They said the announced measures were in line with international law and relevant UN resolutions, including UN Security Council Resolution 2334 and the International Court of Justice's advisory opinion of July 19, 2024.
The statement cited the obligation of all states not to recognize as legal the situation arising from Israel's unlawful occupation of the Palestinian territory and not to provide aid or assistance in maintaining the situation created by the occupation.
The ministers reiterated their call for Israel to rescind all measures taken in connection with settlement activities, as well as other measures aimed at altering the geographic and demographic character of the occupied Palestinian territory.
They also stressed that Gaza is an integral part of the occupied Palestinian territory and called for the "full and immediate implementation" of US President Donald Trump's Comprehensive Plan to End the Gaza Conflict.
The ministers said the plan should be implemented to ensure security and stability, address the humanitarian situation, facilitate reconstruction and recovery, and lay the foundations for lasting peace.
They reaffirmed that "the only viable path" to achieving a just, lasting and comprehensive peace is the implementation of the two-state solution through the establishment of an independent, sovereign, contiguous and viable Palestinian state based on the June 4, 1967 lines, with East Jerusalem as its capital. 
12 countries announce measures on illegal Israeli settlements

The countries said Israel's actions in the West Bank were undermining prospects for a two-state solution and stressed the need to preserve the possibility of establishing a Palestinian state.
Israel subsequently announced that it would close the UK's consulate in occupied East Jerusalem, which serves Palestinians, in response to the measures.

Who controls the data controls the future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:37:52 UTC
01:37:52 KST

In March, Iranian drones targeted three Amazon Web Services (AWS) facilities in Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates (UAE), striking two directly and almost hitting the third. It was the first time a commercial data center had been a military target, yet almost nobody outside specialist circles noticed. They should have. The servers holding a country’s data, and the chips running the artificial intelligence (AI) models on which its economy increasingly leans, are no longer background infrastructure. They are as strategic as ports or power grids — and just as exposed.
For most of the past decade, data was something companies mined, and AI was something companies sold — regulated at the margins through privacy law, if they were regulated at all. This framing no longer works. AI now sits inside finance, defense, healthcare and public administration, and it runs on two things most governments do not actually control: the data that train it and the compute that processes it. Countries that ignore this would find their futures being decided in boardrooms where they have no seat.
Many governments have taken note. Global spending on “sovereign AI” would reportedly surpass US$100 billion this year. Over the past few months, Canada, France, Saudi Arabia and the UAE have rolled out national compute funds and GPU allocations. The EU has gone further, treating sovereign AI infrastructure almost as doctrine, which has meant backing Gaia-X to build out European data infrastructure and financing projects such as Mistral AI’s new data center outside Paris.
Illustration: Mountain People
On paper, this looks like sensible diversification away from a handful of US and Chinese firms. In practice, it risks creating something more brittle: a patchwork of national fortresses, each self-sufficient and none capable of talking to the others. Part of the problem is that “AI sovereignty” encompasses at least three things, and most governments are only working on one.
Data residency — keeping citizens’ data within national borders — is the oldest of the three, the easiest to legislate, and the one most policy actually addresses. Compute sovereignty — who owns the chips and data centers doing the processing — is more difficult: a country can wall off its data, but it loses control if those data are processed on infrastructure someone else owns. Governance sovereignty — the ability to set the rules AI systems have to follow, rather than importing whatever standard the country hosting the dominant developers happens to set — is the one almost nobody talks about.
A fragmented regulatory landscape does not help any of this. Roughly 90 countries have some kind of national AI strategy; at least 33 have passed binding legislation. The approaches often clash. The EU’s AI Act, whose main provisions became applicable last month, carries penalties of up to 35 million euros (US$40.6 million) or 7 percent of the offender’s global annual turnover. The US’ AI Action Plan takes the opposite approach, treating deregulation itself as a competitive edge. China’s Global AI Governance Action Plan offers cooperation on AI governance with developing economies, but on Chinese terms.
The Council of Europe’s Framework Convention on AI — the first binding international AI treaty — represents real progress, but its enforcement is modest next to the scale of what it is meant to govern. Coordination beyond that has barely started. The UN’s Independent International Scientific Panel on AI has warned of a “race to the bottom,” with jurisdictions competing to offer the most permissive rules rather than the safest ones. Companies running high-risk AI deployments are already shopping for the softest jurisdiction.
Genuine AI sovereignty requires four things, none of which is complicated in concept. Start by putting AI data infrastructure in the same legal category as power grids, with someone clearly on the hook for physical and digital security.
Next, countries building sovereign compute need shared interoperability standards, not just national champions — Gaia-X’s work on data portability is a useful template. A hospital in Lagos or a ministry in Warsaw ought to be able to verify that a system meets baseline safety requirements, regardless of whose infrastructure it is running on.
Oversight needs teeth: audit rights, mandatory incident reporting, and licensing for the handful of frontier models capable of touching critical infrastructure or financial stability. These models should be treated more like nuclear material than ordinary software.
The world needs a real mechanism to stop AI sovereignty from turning into just another axis of inequality. That US$100 billion investment in sovereign compute is happening almost entirely in rich countries. Pooled regional compute, financed and governed jointly by smaller countries, would deliver better results than each of them trying to go it alone.
None of this requires a grand global treaty. The components of a governance framework — including the EU AI Act, the Council of Europe convention, Gaia-X, and the UN’s scientific panel — already exist. The scaffolding connecting them is missing, and building that takes deliberate work. Every year it is delayed, the infrastructure gets bigger and harder to reconfigure. Nobody pouring billions of dollars into data centers and GPUs is waiting around for governance to catch up.
The strikes on those AWS facilities in the Gulf sent a message (whether or not anyone intended it): The infrastructure underpinning a growing share of consequential decisions — who gets a loan, which patients get flagged for treatment, which factories keep running — sits in buildings most governments do not control and cannot fully protect. Data sovereignty, compute sovereignty and governance sovereignty are not conference-room abstractions. They are the precondition for a future shaped by countries’ own citizens — not whoever happens to own the servers.

Kenyan start-up makes limbs to sign for deaf kids
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:37:50 UTC
01:37:50 KST

In a school for the deaf in Kenya, children signed their excitement as a team demonstrated how a robotic arm could revolutionize their studies.
About 300,000 children in the east African nation have a hearing impairment, according to the Kenya Society for Deaf Children, but just 20,000 were enrolled in schools as of 2024.
Kenyan start-up ZeroBionic, cofounded by 22-year-old Norah Kimathi, hopes to tackle some of the educational difficulties they face.
Photo: AFP
It has built a mechanical hand that can translate a teachers’ voice into sign language in real time, allowing deaf children to learn alongside their hearing counterparts.
For the pupils at the Kasarani Treeside Secondary School for the Deaf in Nairobi, there is another element of the technology that is even more promising.
The robotic arms are trialed by deaf teachers to record and store signs using a bodysuit, which ZeroBionic imported for the task.
In the process, they are building a database of technical terms — drawing on English, American and Kenyan signs — that is helping to expand the language and make it easier for deaf children to learn and communicate.
“The biggest challenge we faced actually was in Africa we don’t have a standardized African sign language dataset,” Kimathi said at the company’s tiny lab in Nairobi.
“No one else had built this on the continent... We had to start from scratch,” she said.
Many deaf children in Kenya learn a patchwork of makeshift signs, and the local dialect lacks many technical terms used to teach subjects like math and biology.
Sharon Mumbe, 19, one of the pupils at the deaf school, said it gives her “hope for the future.”
“I’ll be able to understand different concepts better,” she said.
Numerous prototype limbs litter the surfaces in Kimathi’s lab.
The team works with Africa One, a humanoid robot they built, to refine and expand the signs their mechanical arms are able to produce.
Everything has been designed and built in-house, using recycled materials to reduce costs and environmental impact, produced using 3D printers that thump away constantly in the background. Each hand costs about US$350 and can last for up to two years. They are already in 78 schools across Kenya.
They boast a 92 percent speech-to-sign accuracy rate and Kimathi said the results have made all the long hours in the lab worthwhile.
“We know we’re going to put a smile on someone else’s face,” she said.

Thai authorities yesterday said they are investigating a Bangkok clinic where a Nigerian-born British businessman and influencer underwent a penis enlargement procedure that led to his death.
A coroner in London last month ruled that the March 6 death of Igho Ubiribo, 43, in the Thai capital was caused by the hyaluronic acid injection he received hours earlier.
The case has reignited debate about medical tourism, with Thailand a leading destination for visitors from abroad seeking healthcare, including aesthetic procedures.
Photo: AFP
Ubiribo, reportedly known as “Tiny” and “Ego,” had 185,000 followers on Instagram, regularly posting pictures with his wife, Daniella Simba Allen, enjoying a luxury lifestyle.
The Thai Ministry of Public Health ordered an investigation into his death and officials on Monday visited the central Bangkok clinic where Ubiribo was treated.
Authorities are looking into whether it holds a valid license and followed health and safety protocols, a health ministry official said.
He was having a massage after receiving the filler when he complained of chest pains and collapsed, according to a report last month from the British coroner, which formally determines cause of death.
He was taken by ambulance to hospital, suspected of having a pulmonary embolism, but lost consciousness before he could have a computed tomography scan.
Medics tried to resuscitate him for more than 100 minutes, but he was declared dead around 1am.
“Post-mortem examination and toxicology determined the cause of death to be due to the hyaluronic acid injection,” the report said.
Senior Bangkok police official Utit Soodjai told AFP his officers were also investigating.
“When it comes to medical procedures, we advocate for the highest level of caution,” Thai Minister of Public Health Pattana Promphat told reporters.
The probe was intended “to ensure fairness for everyone and to reassure both local and international patients that they are receiving safe, high-standard and valuable care in Thailand,” he added in a statement.
The clinic’s managers said Ubiribo had been a regular patient since 2024 and had undergone five penile enlargement injections, according to the health ministry.
The first four procedures took place in 2024 and last year, while on his fifth visit on March 5 he received 40 milliliters of filler.
The doctor had recommended splitting the procedure into two sessions, but Ubiribo requested that the entire amount be injected in one session, clinic management told investigators.
Hyaluronic acid fillers are widely used in aesthetic medicine, considered minimally invasive and relatively low risk.

Global notebook computer shipments are expected to fall 8 percent year-on-year to 167.9 million units this year, dragged by weak demand, high component prices and supply constraints, the Market Intelligence and Consulting Institute (MIC) said on Tuesday.
Next year, shipments are expected to decline by a further 4.7 percent to 160 million units as higher retail prices weigh on consumption, MIC deputy director-general Edward Lin (林柏齊) told a news conference in Taipei.
The downtrend is expected to extend into 2028, with replacement demand unlikely to recover before supplies of key components rebound and costs decline, Lin said.
Photo: AFP
Surging demand for artificial intelligence (AI) servers has led to a broader tight supply of standard DRAM and high-bandwidth memory chips, high-end multilayer ceramic capacitors, advanced microscopic bridge substrates and build-up films, high-end copper-clad laminates and T-glass, which is likely to persist until 2028, he said.
However, NAND flash memory shortages could ease by the end of next year, he added.
MIC expects wider adoption of AI PCs in 2028, with penetration rate projected to reach 76.1 percent, from 54.1 percent projected for this year and 66.3 percent next year, Lin said.
The next AI PC opening is in devices that run meaningful agentic workloads locally, he said.
Unlike basic AI assistants, the systems can handle workflows and execute tasks, requiring greater computing power and memory, he added.
A trend among PC makers to cut memory specifications to offset rising costs in the past year is likely a short-term response rather than a lasting strategy, Lin said.
The measure can help maintain prices, but could weaken the user experience for AI, he said.
As AI shifts from an optional feature to an expected capability, products with overly compromised specifications could lose competitiveness, he added.

Book review: The Cold War’s hidden hands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:37:45 UTC
01:37:45 KST

Alfred McCoy has been a thorn in the side of the CIA at the very least since 1972, when he published The Politics of Heroin in Southeast Asia, a book the agency tried — and failed — to kill.
Now, with his latest, The Cold War on Five Continents, McCoy continues to hammer the CIA for its crimes of the Cold War, including anti-democratic political assassinations, coups and other covert foreign interventions. At the same time, he also presents a startlingly novel analysis of the Cold War itself — this is most of the book, and it’s great — and a less good prediction for the advent of a new Cold War.
Taiwan is mentioned only a few times in the book, but McCoy’s grand narrative of the late 20th century has big implications for the country. It allows us to consider the nation’s post-World War II history against broader trends, and shows this history to be less unique than is often assumed.
McCoy’s theory of the Cold War goes something like this. The 40 or so years following World War II combined two defining historical moments, the Cold War and the era of decolonization. These overlapped almost perfectly.
As scores of new nations stepped out from under the yolk of colonialism to be born in Asia, the Americas, Africa and Eastern Europe, two major powers — the Western liberal bloc led by the USA and the Communist bloc led by the USSR — vyed to bring them into their respective folds. It was a geopolitical competition for influence, and the superpowers played it by carving up the globe.
But with the horrors of World War II fresh in the world memory, there was little appetite for “hot war.” There were a few exceptions of course — Korea and Vietnam for the US, Afghanistan for the USSR.
But on the whole, the superpowers preferred covert operations — espionage, insurgencies and secret wars. (Think: Laos, Angola, Congo, Nicaragua). These types of interventions were much cheaper, didn’t kill off hometown boys and there was no moral backlash as long as the news stayed in the back pages.
The chaotic milieu of new nations — which especially from the late 1940s to the 1960s mixed nationalists, democrats, communists and warlords — was perfect for the deployment of covert operatives, or spies.
McCoy calls these “men on the spot,” an archetype he models on 19th century solo agents like T.E. Lawrence, or “Lawrence of Arabia,” and James Brooke, the “White Raja of Sarawak.” One could also imagine Joseph Conrad’s Colonel Kurtz or Lord Jim.
Such men were parachuted into local, factional conflicts and, based on their personal wiles, often managed to win the day for one empire or another.
Characterizing these men on the spot as “ambitious, cunning and often amoral,” McCoy identifies around three dozen such Cold War operatives, from French military officer Roger Trinquier, who pioneered methods of counter-insurgency in Indochina in the late 1940s, to US marine Oliver North, who ended his career at the center of the Iran-Contra scandal in the 1980s.
Such covert actors often fueled what were essentially civil wars — though in the new Cold War terminology, they were labeled anti-communist or anti-imperialist insurgencies--with arms, cash and secret directives from Washington or Moscow.
The pity here is that each of McCoy’s spy stories offers a potential thriller, but he is so ploddingly deadpan in the telling. Mainly, we are left with a history lesson.
As the superpowers squared off throughout the third world, McCoy argues that the US found it much easier to achieve its political goals by backing “absolute monarchies, dictatorships and juntas,” as long as they were reliably pro-Western.
The pattern was perhaps predicted by US president Franklin D Roosevelte, who, after having backed Nicaraguan dictator Anastasio Somoza Garcia in 1939, is supposed to have said, “He may be a son of a bitch, but at least he’s our son of a bitch.”
For Washington, autocrats were often easier to deal with. Democracies, by comparison, were messier and far less predictable.
So the US, in large part through the CIA, funded dictators who ruled with iron fists, jailed and killed their political opponents and in many cases operated death squads. Cumulative death tolls ran up into the millions.
Many of these Cold War autocracies however came to an end in the late 1980s and early 1990s. As the Berlin Wall came down and the Soviet Union split apart, a series of “people power” revolutions sprung up across the globe, spurring their downfall. The US Congress also became far less tolerant of anti-democratic rulers and the CIA’s dirty tricks.
In this new climate, repressive regimes from the Philippines to Eastern Europe suddenly fell apart. With varying degrees of success, they were replaced by democracies.
These overarching trends were geographically dispersed and remarkable in their variety. The way McCoy weaves them together is extraordinary.
Taiwan’s Cold War history is not specifically described, but it fits McCoy’s pattern almost perfectly. (McCoy probably found Taiwan less interesting, as the country didn’t contain rival superpower proxies fighting it out.)
Following Taiwan’s decolonization from Japan at the end of World War II, the US backed an authoritarian ruler Chiang Kai-shek (蔣介石). Then Washington stuck with his regime through 38 years of martial law, largely turning a blind eye to the human rights abuses of the White Terror.
Taiwan’s martial law came to an end in 1987 — right at the tail end of the Cold War and marking the twilight of what some would call the Chinese Nationalist Party’s (KMT) colonization of the country. Domestic democracy movements were key in pushing this change.
Viewed in McCoy’s framework, it becomes easy to place Chiang alongside other US-supported dictators like Mobotu in the Congo (then called Zaire), Chilean president Augusto Pinochet, Philippines president Ferdinand Marcos and Indonesia’s General Suharto.
It also reminds us that Taiwan’s democratic era arrived in the same wave with the Philippines’ People Power Revolution (1988), the fall of the Berlin Wall (1989), and the end of apartheid in South Africa (1994).
Where McCoy directly addresses Taiwan is in looking towards a “New Cold War.” Here, he sets it alongside Ukraine and Gaza, but it is hard to see how these conflict zones fit his classic pattern. Though Taiwan and Ukraine can be considered as part of great power competitions, Gaza is a harder fit. If anything, what these places have in common is that they are resisting the annexation of aggressors who are not only intent on taking their territory, but on obliterating their cultural identity as well.
No matter where one sits on the political spectrum and who one blames for the ongoing struggles between the executive and legislative branches or the latest food scandal, there has been noticeable frustration with the way democratic institutions are functioning. Attempts to circumvent political opposition and institutional checks can begin a slide toward authoritarianism, even when presented as short-term solutions to gridlock. While that might solve problems in the short term, it inevitably evolves into a system that serves the rulers and the powerfully connected at the expense of the rights of regular folks. One interesting lens to examine the

They were not simply trying to sell programs. They were trying to change an idea of Taiwan. International perceptions of Taiwanese television, PTS executives recalled in interviews conducted for my joint research with Chairman Hu Yuan-hui (胡元輝), were still strongly associated with the idol dramas that had enjoyed enormous regional popularity

Caring for migrant care workers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:37:44 UTC
01:37:44 KST

Taiwan has nearly 1 million people in need of long-term care, yet the proportion of people with severe disabilities receiving long-term care benefits has been declining year by year. The gap is not being filled by the government, but by more than 200,000 live-in migrant care workers who are not covered by the Labor Standards Act (勞動基準法).
Wages are rising in the home countries of most of Taiwan’s care workers, such as Indonesia, the Philippines and Vietnam. Meanwhile, Japan, South Korea and Hong Kong are competing to attract those workers. The question is not whether families can afford carers, but whether any will still be willing to move to Taiwan three years from now.
The Ministry of Labor’s Diversified Companion Care Service Pilot Program is a step in the right direction. Under the program — which was launched last year — nonprofit organizations hire care workers who are covered by the Labor Standards Act. After 90 hours of training, they provide in-home services in shifts of at least two hours, demonstrating that migrant workers do not have to be tied to a single household to work with dignity.
However, with just 13 participating organizations and 41 foreign care workers, the program is nowhere near large enough to meet the demands of even a single district of Taipei.
There are three keys to solving the problem:
First, care services should be a part of long-term care benefits. Under the diversified companion-care system, services running at NT$300 to NT$400 per hour are difficult for struggling families to afford.
If the services provided by migrant domestic care workers for people with severe disabilities were incorporated into the long-term care benefits system — with partial subsidies based on the individual’s level of disability and the household’s financial circumstances — that could ease the burden on families, and improve migrant workers’ pay and access to days off.
The long-term care budget for this year has already exceeded NT$100 billion, yet people with severe disabilities have among the lowest takeup rates. Redirecting funding toward those who need it most should be at the heart of long-term care policy.
Second, talent pools and career pathways must be built up. The system treats migrant workers as disposable labor: When their work permits end, one group is replaced by another and the process starts over. Japan, by contrast, allows skilled care workers pathways to extend their work visas and transition to other forms of residency. Taiwan should allow trained foreign care workers who have accumulated experience to move into institutional care, advance to supervisory positions and ultimately qualify for long-term residency.
Third, cultivate differentiated pathways rather than a one-size-fits-all approach.
People with mild or moderate care needs could receive services through institutional staffing agencies, using multiple caregivers working in shifts and flexible hours. For people with severe or profound disabilities, one-on-one care could be retained, but wages should be supported through long-term care benefits, with mandatory respite care shift rotations implemented.
Neither employers nor the government wants to shoulder the additional costs, but the cost of care does not disappear simply because no one is willing to bear it; it is merely shifted onto people with disabilities, the careers of family members and the years of migrant workers’ lives.
Taiwan is using the silence of more than 200,000 foreign care workers to subsidize a society that refuses to confront the true cost of care.
As Long-Term Care 2.0 enters its 10th year, migrant domestic care workers have been waiting outside the system for two decades. The overdue bill for care is one the government must start facing up to.
Huang Jin-shun is a former Presidential Office national policy adviser and an honorary president of the Federation of Taiwan Pharmacists’ Associations.

The Panamanian National Assembly on Tuesday established a friendship group with the Legislative Yuan, a move welcomed by Minister of Foreign Affairs Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍) as an opportunity to facilitate bilateral exchanges and advance mutual interests.
The multiparty interparliamentary exchange group was established at an inaugural ceremony at the assembly in Panama City.
Forty-five of the assembly’s 71 lawmakers have joined the group, including National Assembly President Shirley Castanedas and vice presidents Manuel Cohen and Manuel Cheng, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement released yesterday.
Photo: Huang Ching-hsuan, Taipei Times
In a congratulatory video message played during the inaugural ceremony, Lin said that Taiwan and Panama share universal values, including democracy, freedom and respect for human rights.
“Through the Taiwan-friendly parliamentary group, we look forward to further deepening parliamentary diplomacy and expanding bilateral cooperation and exchanges, thereby promoting the well-being of both peoples and fostering mutual benefit and shared prosperity,” the ministry quoted Lin as saying in the video.
The ministry said that the group was formed after more than 20 Panamanian lawmakers visited Taiwan over the past six months.
Taiwan and Panama ended formal diplomatic ties in June 2017.
In a separate video message played during the ceremony, US Representative Mario Diaz-Balart, cochair of the US Congressional Taiwan Caucus, congratulated the Panamanian National Assembly on establishing the parliamentary exchange platform, the ministry said.
Panamanian lawmaker Jose Antonio Perez-Barboni said the establishment of a Taiwan-Panama parliamentary exchange group was “a step in the right direction” and marked the beginning of closer economic and trade ties between the two sides.
He said he looked forward to advancing bilateral diplomatic relations.
Another lawmaker, Joan Manuel Guevara, said the formation of the parliamentary exchange group demonstrated that Taiwan and Panama could continue to develop “parliamentary diplomacy” despite the absence of formal diplomatic relations.
Such cooperation is particularly important as both sides seek to defend their sovereignty and withstand external pressure, Guevara said.
Perez-Barboni and Guevara are members of the Inter-Parliamentary Alliance on China (IPAC).
Panamanian lawmakers have stepped up parliamentary exchanges with Taiwan over the past two years, with multiple delegations visiting Taiwan.
IPAC members led delegations to Taiwan in November last year and February, while Orlando Carrasquilla, chairman of the Panamanian National Assembly’s Committee on Agricultural and Fisheries Affairs, led a delegation to Taiwan in July.
When Perez-Barboni led a delegation to Taiwan in February, he was chairman of the National Assembly’s Committee on Infrastructure and Canal Affairs.
The itineraries of the delegations, their membership and the lawmakers’ public remarks indicate that Panama has been interested in Taiwan’s technological and economic development, suggesting that parliamentary exchanges between the two sides are increasingly focused on practical cooperation in technology and trade.

Photo: Liu Yung-yun, Taipei Times
According to local news reports, Chen met with Chang at around 10 a.m. on Sunday. The two shared a meal for under an hour, during which time Chang is suspected of giving her unspecified objects, the reports said.

An arrest warrant was issued for Chang, but as of yesterday he had not been located.
Kao Chin Su-mei corruption case
Kao Chin, Chang and 22 others were indicted June 8 on corruption and fraud-related charges related to the embezzlement of public funds and the importation of unapproved COVID-19 test kits from China.
Kao Chin, who has denied wrongdoing, was accused of fraudulently obtaining more than NT$7.87 million in public funds through fraudulent claims for legislative assistant salaries, bonuses, overtime pay and childcare subsidies.
This included registering several individuals, including her siblings, as legislative assistants, despite them not actually performing any duties, prosecutors alleged.
Chang, meanwhile, was accused of conspiring with Kao Chin to fraudulently obtain funds earmarked for assistant salaries, as well as using an Indigenous cultural association to fraudulently obtain over NT$9.33 million from government agencies and state-owned enterprises.
Prosecutors said that during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2022, Kao Chin also authorized Chang to enlist others to illegally import 74,400 unapproved rapid test kits from China, circumventing medical device regulations.
Kao Chin, however, has claimed that the rapid test kits were intended to help Indigenous communities amid a shortage of the devices in Taiwan.
In the indictment, prosecutors recommended a sentence of at least 16 years for Chang and 12.5 years for Kao Chin.
Chang, who was held incommunicado for nearly four months before his indictment, was released on NT$10 million bail in June.
At the time, Chang’s lawyers sought his release on health grounds, noting that he was over 70 years old and battling lung cancer.
During the first day of his trial on Sept. 1, Chang denied the corruption charges but admitted to other offenses, such as document forgery. He argued that he was not merely a legislative aide in name only, but had actually performed his duties and lacked criminal intent.

Exports hit record on 41% rise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:37:43 UTC
01:37:43 KST

Exports hit a record last month as artificial intelligence (AI) demand continued to spread across semiconductors, servers and other high-tech products, the Ministry of Finance said yesterday.
Exports rose 41 percent from a year earlier to US$82.4 billion, the highest monthly level on record, the ministry said.
The gain marked the 34th consecutive month of year-on-year growth and exceeded the ministry’s expectations of growth of 31 to 35 percent on better-than-expected AI demand.
Photo: CNA
“We underestimated the strength of AI, which is spreading rapidly into more technology sectors,” Department of Statistics Director-General Beatrice Tsai (蔡美娜) said.
The momentum is likely to continue into the final months of the year, with the ministry expecting exports to grow by more than 40 percent this month as the peak season for high-tech products begins.
Monthly exports in the fourth quarter could average as high as US$83 billion, Tsai said, a level Taiwan has never reached.
The increasingly broad adoption of AI is helping to support global economic activity and cushion the effects of short-term disruptions such as tariff uncertainty, Tsai said.
Information, communications and audiovisual products, as well as electronic components remained the main engines of growth, with the categories together accounting for 78.7 percent of total exports last month, the ministry said.
The concentration highlights Taiwan’s pivotal role in the global AI supply chain, while also underscoring the economy’s increasing dependence on technology-related demand.
“AI has created a wave that keeps strengthening demand,” Tsai said, adding that Taiwanese companies occupy key positions in global semiconductor and server supply chains.
The upcoming launch of new mobile devices also provided an additional boost as international brands began building inventories, Tsai said.
However, supply constraints across parts of the electronics industry have yet to be fully resolved, supporting prices and increasing the value of shipments, she said.
The release of Apple Inc’s latest iPhone lineup, including an expected foldable model, is likely to provide support for Taiwan’s electronics suppliers as buyers and manufacturers prepare for the new devices, the ministry said.
Mineral products were another major contributor to Taiwan’s exports growth, with outbound shipments jumping about 70 percent last month as higher oil prices increased the value of petroleum-related goods, it said.
Last month, imports rose even faster, climbing 44.3 percent to US$60.1 billion, it said.
The increase reflected the increasingly international division of labor in AI supply chains, as Taiwanese manufacturers sourced more components and materials from overseas, including memory chips from South Korea, the ministry said.
Capital goods imports jumped 41.6 percent to US$13.06 billion, pointing to continued investment by local technology companies as they expand production capacity to meet customer demand, it said.
The export performance pushed the trade surplus to a record US$22.3 billion that month, up 32.9 percent from a year earlier, the ministry said.
For the first eight months of this year, exports jumped 44.2 percent to US$574.34 billion from the same period last year, while imports rose 40.4 percent to US$437.4 billion over the period, it said.
The ministry expects export momentum to remain strong through the end of the year, Tsai said.

Brace for new AI threats ahead of elections, AIT head says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:37:43 UTC
01:37:43 KST

Taiwan must guard against artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled information manipulation ahead of local elections on Nov. 28, American Institute in Taiwan (AIT) Director Raymond Greene said yesterday.
Although Taiwan has earned acclaim for its efforts to counter disinformation, it must still brace for a new wave of sophisticated, AI-powered cognitive warfare, Greene said during his keynote speech at the Taipei Security Dialogue hosted by the Institute for National Defense and Security Research.
Taiwan also urgently needs to defend financial institutions and critical infrastructure against AI-powered cyberattacks, he said.
Photo: Tien Yu-hua, Taipei Times
The US’ top diplomat in Taiwan also touched on issues such as defense spending, military reforms and energy resilience.
Taiwan has made great progress in energy resilience by increasing the importation and storage of liquefied natural gas, which the international community has taken note of, Greene said.
The nation has also made less visible, but equally impressive, improvements in its electricity allocation policy, power-grid decentralization, use of coal-fired plants and renewables, and exploration of alternative energy sources, including small modular reactors and geothermal energy, he said.
Washington welcomes President William Lai’s (賴清德) commitment to increase defense spending to 5 percent of GDP by 2030, as US allies face rising security threats around the globe, he said.
US President Donald Trump has been calling on European countries to take on greater responsibilities for their self-defense, he said, adding that Ukraine has shown that sustained military spending can improve a nation’s military capabilities.
Compared with many other US partners, Taiwan is far better placed financially to boost its defense, Greene said.
Military preparedness should not just aim to win a war, but to prevent a conflict from breaking out altogether, he said.
Deterring Chinese aggression is paramount for Taiwan and the world, he said.
“Beyond the human toll, any conflict across the Taiwan Strait would have a bigger impact on the global economy than the Second World War,” Greene said.
The Trump administration has made preserving peace in the Indo-Pacific region one of its top priorities, he said.
That includes “vigorous” diplomacy, especially at the highest levels, he said.
“The upcoming US-China summit is an opportunity to further advance a relationship of strategic stability, on the basis of fairness and reciprocity, that can avoid misunderstandings and miscalculations,” Greene added.
At the same time, the US is reinforcing its presence and partnerships in the Indo-Pacific region to maintain a “favorable regional balance of power,” while supporting Taiwan’s work to enhance its ability to defend itself, he said.
Claims that Taiwan’s efforts to bolster national defense are provocative and accusations that the US aims to change the “status quo” in the region are false, he said.
Taiwan has been rapidly implementing lessons learned from Ukraine’s use of asymmetric warfare and emerging technology to fend off Russia’s invasion, Greene said.
Taiwan has many strategic advantages Ukraine and many other countries do not have, including advanced manufacturing capabilities, sea barriers and formidable natural geography, he said.
Taiwan’s armed forces are rapidly adapting to mission-command concepts, as demonstrated in the latest Han Kuang exercises, he added.
Such flexibility has been vital in Ukraine’s defense against Russia’s military, which has been hobbled by its rigid and hierarchical command structure, Greene said.
Taiwan and the US must constantly improve their defensive capabilities to safeguard peace, he said.

Taipei to launch more food-safety inspections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:37:37 UTC
01:37:37 KST

The Taipei City Government is to conduct more unannounced inspections to ensure food safety at schools, Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) said yesterday, following an alleged food poisoning incident at a high school on Monday, in which 87 students became ill.
The school was ordered to suspend lunch services on Tuesday.
Taipei on Monday last week launched a free school lunch program for all elementary and junior-high school students.
Photo: Chang Chia-ming, Taipei Times
On Tuesday, Democratic Progressive Party Taipei City Councilor Lin Liang-chun (林亮君) said she received complaints from parents saying that the lunch provided at a school on Monday contained suspected spoiled meat and some students complained about the smell.
Lin said she has asked the Taipei Department of Health to clarify the situation.
Taipei Department of Health Food and Drug Division Director Lin Kuan-chen (林冠蓁) on Tuesday said the department received a report from the school at about noon on that day saying that 87 students experienced diarrhea and displayed suspected food poisoning symptoms from 10pm on Monday.
The department sent inspectors to the school to investigate and collect samples for examination, and it also ordered the lunch service to be suspended, Lin Kuan-chen said.
On-site inspection found five hygiene deficiencies, and the department ordered the school to implement improvements before tomorrow, or face fines of up to NT$200 million (US$6.35 million), she said.
The health department said it also collected 11 food, environment and hand swab samples from the kitchen for testing.
All the affected children have returned to school, and the city government would set up a special project to follow up on the case and the children’s health, Chiang said yesterday.
The ingredients are being traced to the source and environmental sanitization has been conducted, he said, adding that the city government would increase unannounced campus food safety inspections.
The health department yesterday evening said that education department officials also went to the school to investigate the case, and the preliminary inspection showed that the meat in Monday’s lunch met Certified Agricultural Standards requirements for traceability.
People should pay close attention to the hygienic conditions of food-handling and eating venues, avoid raw or undercooked food, and eat meals promptly to prevent food poisoning, the health department said.
Those who experience suspected food poisoning symptoms should seek medical attention immediately and report the incident, it said.

Imported mpox cases rise from last year: CDC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:37:35 UTC
01:37:35 KST

The Centers for Disease Control (CDC) yesterday reported two new cases of mpox, including a locally acquired case infected with the newer Mpox Clade Ib strain.
It added that mpox cases this year had reached 30, double the number for the same period last year.
The two new confirmed cases include a local case and an imported case, the centers said.
Photo: Lin Chih-yi, Taipei Times
Both cases reported having unsafe sex before the onset of symptoms and were unvaccinated against mpox, it said.
The local case is a man in his 40s who began having symptoms last month, including mouth sores, a fever and rash. The imported case is a man in his 30s, who traveled to Cambodia last month and engaged in unsafe sexual activity, and later experienced fever, chills and rash, it said.
CDC Deputy Director-General Lin Ming-cheng (林明誠) said that as of Monday, 30 cases of mpox have been reported this year — 20 locally acquired and 10 imported — all men aged between 20 and 60.
While the number of local cases has been declining, the percentage of imported cases has increased, he said, adding that the 10 imported cases reported this year were double the figure for the same period last year.
The risk of contracting mpox overseas cannot be overlooked, he said.
Of the 10 imported cases this year, six were from Thailand, and one each from Vietnam, India, Hong Kong and Cambodia, the CDC said.
Epidemiological data from other countries show that both Clade II and the newer Clade Ib virus strains of mpox might cause symptoms including fever, swollen lymph nodes and rash or blisters, but systemic rashes are more widely distributed over the body in Clade Ib, Lin said.
Clade Ib can spread more readily through household contacts compared with Clade II, and immunocompromised people, young children, pregnant women, or those with chronic illnesses are more likely to experience severe illness, he said.
The overall symptoms and fatality rates of Clade Ib and Clade II are similar, and the severity of mpox infection depends heavily on the status of a person’s immune system, the CDC said.
Mpox vaccines can provide effective protection against Clade Ib infection, and the antiviral drug Tecovirimat can help treat a severe Clade Ib infection, it added.
Getting the first dose of the standard two-dose mpox vaccine regimen only provides about 40 to 80 percent protection, while completing the full two-dose series can increase effectiveness up to 90 percent, Lin said.
Since the mpox vaccine was introduced in Taiwan, 111,908 people have received the first dose, while 80,033 people completed two doses, he said, adding that the CDC strongly urges the roughly 29 percent who did not get their second dose to get fully vaccinated as soon as possible.

Mao’s shadow hangs over China 50 years on
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:37:34 UTC
01:37:34 KST

China yesterday marked half a century since the death of Mao Zedong (毛澤東), founder of the People’s Republic, who brought roughly one-quarter of the world’s population under communist rule and whose specter still haunts China’s future.
Mao’s death on Sept. 9, 1976, at age 82, mourned by many and welcomed by some who suffered under his nearly three-decade rule, also hastened the end of the Cultural Revolution, a frenzied mass movement he launched in 1966.
The party later condemned the Cultural Revolution as a grave error for which Mao bore primary responsibility, but still reveres him, saying his achievements outweigh his mistakes.
Photo: EPA
Mao’s 6m-high portrait overlooks Beijing’s Tiananmen Square, the symbolic center of Chinese political power. His preserved body lies in the Chairman Mao Memorial Hall, where visitors from across the country queue to pay respects.
Many still idolize Mao as the nation’s savior. The mausoleum extended hours for the anniversary, expecting a surge in visitors.
During the Cultural Revolution, a distrustful and aging Mao mobilized students and supporters against perceived “class enemies,” including leaders accused of “taking the capitalist road,” unleashing upheaval that fractured the bureaucracy, paralyzed the economy and triggered violence and persecution.
The decade of turmoil also left a complex imprint on generations of leaders who followed Mao, including Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平).
Xi’s father, former Chinese vice premier Xi Zhongxun (習仲勛), was purged and brutally persecuted in the lead-up to and during the Cultural Revolution, while the family home was ransacked.
The teenage Xi Jinping was labeled a “reactionary student,” subjected to interrogation and coercive political study and even threatened with execution.
“Because I had a stubborn streak and refused to be bullied, I offended the rebel faction,” Xi Jinping said in a 2000 interview with a state-run magazine. “Everything bad was blamed on me... I wasn’t even 15.”
In 1969, like many others of his generation, Xi Jinping was sent to the countryside and spent seven years in a poverty-stricken village in northwestern China.
“The Cultural Revolution was a profoundly disillusioning experience for Xi,” said Joseph Torigian, an expert in Chinese politics at American University.
However, “he still saw something redemptive in the campaign,” which toughened him and showed the dangers of state collapse and that the party needed a clear road map to socialism, Torigian added.
Xi Jinping has not publicly blamed Mao for either his family’s suffering or other tragedies he witnessed.
Since becoming China’s top leader in 2012, he has instead argued that the post-Mao reform era should not be used to repudiate the Maoist years, while increasingly echoing Mao-era practices.
Unlike his immediate predecessors who — prompted by Deng Xiaoping’s (鄧小平) reforms in the aftermath of Mao — sought to cautiously loosen the leader’s grip, Xi Jinping has unapologetically consolidated power, cultivated personal authority and stressed ideological conformity and strict party discipline.
He is on course to become the longest-serving paramount leader of the People’s Republic of China, after Mao, having broken with reform-era term limit norms meant to curb excessively concentrated power and reduce the risk of another personality cult.
Xi Jinping has also had his own name formally attached to the state ideology enshrined in both the party and state constitutions, a feat no other since Mao has managed while in office.
“The iconography of Maoism, the charisma, and very specific language and symbols — these remain immensely powerful,” said Kerry Brown, director of King’s College London’s Lau China Institute.
“Xi has reinstated some of this with strong nationalism and populism,” he added.
One reason Xi Jinping shies away from more direct criticism of Mao is that he “wants to take the party back to its glory days when everyone was shaped by zeal and enthusiasm,” Torigian said.
The question is whether Xi Jinping’s approach will prove lasting, “or whether, like Mao before him, Xi is unintentionally creating pressure for change that will push China in a new direction after he’s gone,” he added.

CIA director may take leading role in US talks on Russia-Ukraine war – FT
CIA Director John Ratcliffe may take a leading role in Washington's diplomatic efforts to end Russia's war against Ukraine.
Source: Financial Times citing informed sources, as reported by European Pravda
Details: The White House is reportedly considering reducing the involvement of US special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, son-in-law of US President Donald Trump, who have so far played a key role in contacts with Moscow and Kyiv.
Officials close to Ratcliffe told European counterparts that he will play a larger role in "shuttle diplomacy" between Russia and Ukraine.
Ratcliffe is expected to continue maintaining contacts with the intelligence services of both countries. However, the sources said Trump has not yet made a final decision.
The sources said Witkoff, for his part, is likely to retain his position as US special envoy for peace missions, which includes negotiations in the Middle East. They said he may continue to take part in the Ukraine process in parallel with Ratcliffe.
Two of the sources said Ratcliffe and Witkoff are engaged in a struggle over who will be responsible for what.
Background:
- On 25 August, it was reported that the CIA director visited Moscow. Speaking about Ratcliffe's trip, US President Donald Trump has said "something may come out of it".
- On 6 September, after talks in Kyiv involving the Ukrainian side, Trump's special envoys and national security advisers from the E3 countries, an agreement was reached to repeat the meeting in the same format in the near future.

Watch: Norway bids farewell to King Harald
Tributes have been paid to King Harald V after his funeral in Norway's capital Oslo, with the Prince of Wales and other European royals among attendees.
Flags were raised from half-mast to mark the conclusion of a private ceremony at Akershus Fortress, where the king was laid to rest in the crypt of the Palace Chapel after a public service at Oslo Cathedral.
Tens of thousands of people lined the streets to pay their respects after 13 days of national mourning.
The new king Haakon VIII - Harald's son - and his family stood on the balcony of the Royal Palace and waved to thousands of people gathered outside.
The late monarch died in August after 35 years on the throne.

Poland and Indonesia hold political consultations

Poland and Indonesia hold political consultations
07.09.2026
On 7 September, MFA Secretary of State Władysław Teofil Bartoszewski met with Grata Endah Werdaningtyas, Director General of American and European Affairs at Indonesia's Ministry for Foreign Affairs. The talks focused on fostering bilateral relations, security in Europe, and the situation in the Indo-Pacific region.
The interlocutors emphasised the importance of regular political dialogue for the furthering strengthening of Polish–Indonesian relations. They discussed opportunities to intensify economic cooperation, particularly in the agri-food, energy, new technologies, and green technology sectors. They also noted the need to continue supporting cooperation between businesses from Poland and Indonesia.
Deputy Foreign Minister Władysław Teofil Bartoszewski highlighted the significance of Poland’s accession to the Treaty of Amity and Cooperation in Southeast Asia (TAC) in July 2026. The accession reflects Poland’s growing engagement in the Indo-Pacific region and creates additional opportunities for developing cooperation with the member states of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN). Poland regards Indonesia as an important partner in the region and is interested in a further deepening of relations, both bilaterally and within the framework of EU–ASEAN cooperation. The Indonesian side pointed to the success of Poland’s economic transformation and emphasised its interest in Poland’s experience, which serves as an important reference point for cooperation between the two countries, including within the G20 framework.
An exchange of views on international affairs and security was an important element of the talks. Among other topics, Deputy Minister Władysław Teofil Bartoszewski and Director General Grata Endah Werdaningtyas discussed the situation in Europe and the Indo-Pacific, Russia’s aggression against Ukraine, and the key challenges to the international order. They stressed the importance of respect for international law, the principles of the Charter of the United Nations, and effective multilateralism.
The talks confirmed the broad potential for strengthening relations between Poland and Indonesia, both bilaterally and in the context of cooperation with ASEAN.
***
ASEAN (Association of Southeast Asian Nations) was established in Bangkok in 1967. It is a political and economic organisation based in Jakarta.

Meta launches personal AI agent Muse that can shop, book travel, negotiate for users
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:35:32 UTC
01:35:32 KST

Halis Sünnetci
09 September 2026•Update: 09 September 2026
Meta launched a new personal artificial intelligence agent on Tuesday called Muse, designed to carry out tasks on users' behalf rather than simply respond to questions.
The US technology company said Muse can make purchases, book travel, send emails, fill out forms and negotiate on behalf of users.
Once given a task or broader goal, Muse can develop a personalized plan and continue working independently, including after users close the app.
The agent can return when circumstances change or when it needs approval, with Meta saying it seeks permission before sensitive actions such as sending an email or making a purchase.
Muse can complete online purchases using Stripe's Link payment service, which can generate a single-use virtual card for an approved purchase while keeping users' underlying payment details hidden from the agent.
Muse can also remember information users previously shared and use it to make suggestions without being prompted.
The agent operates through what Meta calls a Secure VM, a dedicated virtual computer in the cloud with its own browser that allows it to interact with websites and connected services.
A separate AI agent called Sentinel governs Muse's access to the internet and connected services, determining whether an action can proceed, should be blocked or requires the user's approval.
Users can choose which services Muse can access and what it is allowed to do within them, while Meta said the agent cannot see users' passwords or payment methods, and provides an audit trail of its actions.
The company said conversations and data stored in Muse's virtual machine are not shared with its advertising systems, while users can opt out of having their interactions used to train Meta's AI models.
The launch comes as AI companies face questions about the security and privacy risks of giving autonomous agents access to users' personal accounts and data.
Muse is initially available to those aged 18 and older in the US through a dedicated app or WhatsApp, with support for Meta's AI glasses planned.
The service is free for most uses, while subscription plans for heavier use are priced at $20 and $100 per month.

“Sistema Italia” Mission to Cabo Delgado in Northern Mozambique
Italy

The second “Sistema Italia” mission to the province of Cabo Delgado in northern Mozambique has been underway since Monday, led by Italian Ambassador Gabriele Annis along with the head of the Maputo office of the Italian Agency for Development Cooperation (AICS), and the president of the Mozambique-Italy Chamber of Commerce, Simone Santi. The goal is to strengthen Italy’s presence in the province by promoting collaboration with local institutions, communities, and the private sector.
                                    
                                       
				   On the first day, the delegation—accompanied by Minister of Youth and Sports Caifadine Paulo Manasse—met with Pemba Mayor Satar Abdulgani, Governor Valige Tauabo, and Provincial Secretary of State Plácido Nerino Pereira, before visiting the Ifpelac vocational training institute and participating in a business forum organized by the Chamber of Commerce.    
   “Italy has a presence in the province with about 30 companies and is one of the countries investing the most in the region,” Annis noted.
                                    
                                       
				   On the second day, the Cambio program was launched, funded by Italian cooperation with two million euros to strengthen the climate resilience of the cities of Pemba and Beira and the island of Ibo, implemented by a consortium led by the NGO AVSI in collaboration with the Polytechnic University of Milan and Lúrio University. “Cabo Delgado is a region of particular importance to Italy, where the presence of major Italian companies, such as Eni, goes hand in hand with the growing commitment of Italian development cooperation,” the ambassador stated.

European Parliament to debate Ceuta crisis amid fierce political backlash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:33:44 UTC
01:33:44 KST

The EPP and other right-wing groups are pushing for a resolution that would criticise Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez and call for a tougher migration policy, while the Socialists and Democrats are expected to defend Spain and call for greater European solidarity.
The European Parliament will debate the situation in Ceuta next Tuesday in Strasbourg, in what is expected to be a heated political confrontation, following a decision by the Parliament’s political group leaders in Brussels on Wednesday.
The centre-right European People’s Party (EPP) and the European Conservatives and Reformists (ECR) also pushed to add a resolution to be voted on by lawmakers after the debate, in a move widely seen as an attempt to attack the Spanish government led by Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez.
The debate is expected to be contentious, with the EPP poised to confront Sánchez directly.
“The Prime Minister said [the Ceuta crisis] has been an attack on Spain's territorial integrity. But he has not acted consequently”, EPP senior MEP Javier Zarzalejos said at a press conference on Tuesday.
Besides the EPP, otherright-wing conservative and far-right parties are also ready to attack Sánchez, linking the massive influx into Ceuta to the Spanish plan for the mass regularisation of undocumented migrants.
The Socialists and Democrats (S&D) group will be on the defensive, calling for European solidarity with Spain and criticising other governments for failing to present a united front following the sudden arrival of thousands of migrants in Ceuta.
“The narrative adopted by some prime ministers was simply shocking. They attacked Spain instead of showing support,” a senior S&D MEP told Euronews on condition of anonymity.
The final title of the debate reflects a compromise between differing political positions. The Parliament’s agenda lists it as: “The recent hybrid attacks and instrumentalisation of migrants in Ceuta and the need for a coordinated response to protect the EU’s external borders.”
The resolution, expected to be put to a vote next Tuesday, is likely to trigger a dispute over amendments shaping its final wording, with right-wing groups expected to press for a tougher stance on migration and criticism of Spain’s handling of the crisis.
The Spanish exclave is “on the brink of collapse”, according to its president, after the massive arrival of some 80,000 irregular migrants on 30 July. Several thousand of them, including unaccompanied minors, are still in the city, sparking a humanitarian crisis and making the overall situation “untenable”, Ceuta’s president said.
Meanwhile, Madrid has been plunged into further chaos after a leaked police report suggested that Moroccan forces played a role in pushing migrants into Ceuta, a claim Sánchez has so far not confirmed.
The crisis also had consequences at the European level, with twenty-two EU countries calling for an emergency meeting in August and Italy reintroducing border checks at its air and maritime borders with Spain.
On Wednesday, the European Commission decided to provide Spain with €114.7 million in emergency assistance to help manage the situation, following a request submitted by Madrid on 24 August.
