plywood and reflective steel build retro-futurist print shop in tbilisi’s former factory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
14:15:09 UTC
23:15:09 KST

JPG Print Shop Reframes Fabrika’s Industrial Interior in Tbilisi
Designed by Sandro Kvirikadze, JPG Print Shop transforms an existing Soviet industrial space at Tbilisi’s Fabrika into a contemporary environment for graphic design and urban culture. Plywood structures, stainless steel, and retro-futurist forms introduce a new architectural layer within the existing space, creating a dialogue between industrial memory and contemporary creative culture. The result is a space where design becomes part of the everyday urban experience. The print shop brings together graphic design, fashion, and the culture of on-site customization. Alongside collaborative T-shirts created by notable graphic designers, the space allows visitors to print their own ideas directly onto garments. The interior was therefore conceived as more than a commercial setting, becoming a continuation of the printing process as well as the surrounding urban culture and contemporary design scene.
The space deliberately preserves traces of the existing environment at the entrance. The original architectural condition is neither concealed nor completely replaced; instead, it becomes the first layer from which the new interior develops. The existing space gradually transitions into a system of rigid geometric plywood structures that defines the architectural language of the interior. The warm, tactile character of plywood is contrasted with the cold, technological surfaces of stainless steel, creating an interior that combines industrial rigor with the qualities of a carefully constructed object. Structural elements are not used solely for technical purposes but are transformed into shelving, hanging systems, and architectural details that organize the space.
Reflection and Retro-Futuristic interiors define the print shop
The hanging system follows the principles of Light Weight Architecture, in which the synthesis of different structural elements becomes part of the design itself. Functional objects are therefore integrated into the architectural structure rather than treated as separate decorative elements. One of the central elements of the space is a mirror almost three meters in height, composed of three movable panels. Sandro Kvirikadze Design Studio utilizes the reflective element to alter the perception of the interior. When closed, the three panels correspond precisely with the wooden structure positioned opposite them, creating a visual continuity between the two elements. When opened, the mirror changes the spatial composition, introducing movement and transformation into the interior.
The design is rooted in the principles of retro-futurism. Rather than directly quoting historical forms, it reinterprets them through contemporary materials and new functions. The strict geometry of the wooden structures and the forms of the panels refer to traditional architectural and furniture principles, while their execution in stainless steel and contemporary construction systems gives them a contemporary character. The interior of JPG Print Shop does not attempt to erase the industrial past of the Soviet-era building. Instead, it adds a new architectural layer to it. The existing architecture of Fabrika becomes a fragment of the city’s memory, while the structures introduced into the space represent contemporary youth culture and design. The old and the new coexist within the same interior, allowing the city’s industrial past to continue through the language of contemporary design.

Strategic folly of Iran war: a global economic catastrophe
TEHRAN- The recent war waged by the United States and Israel against Iran has been a catastrophic miscalculation, inflicting severe and likely irreversible damage on the global economy. While Americans grapple with soaring gas prices and inflation, the deeper, more systemic impacts of this conflict expose the reckless shortsightedness of U.S. policy in West Asia.
The most significant change has been the permanent alteration of control over the Strait of Hormuz. Before the war, this vital waterway was an international passage. Now, Iran has demonstrated its effective control by regulating traffic and directly challenging U.S. naval dominance. This shift has introduced a permanent risk premium into global energy markets and cemented a precedent for nations to exert sovereign control over strategic waterways. This is not a hypothetical "tail risk" but a proven, permanent geopolitical reality that threatens the foundation of global energy security.
Furthermore, the war has established China as the undeniable "most powerful force in the oil market”. Through its strategic stockpiles and rapid energy transition, China has demonstrated a unique ability to modulate its demand, effectively cushioning itself from an oil shock that the U.S. itself precipitated. The resulting surge in electric vehicle adoption and coal usage in China suggests that global oil demand may have permanently peaked, a direct consequence of the instability fostered by the U.S. war.
The United States has not only destabilized a critical region but has also accelerated the global energy transition on its adversaries' terms, weakened its own economic standing, and created a geopolitical environment from which it struggles to extract itself. This conflict stands as a stark example of how misguided foreign policy can boomerang, damaging the initiating nation's own economy and global standing far more than it harms its intended target.

23:12:47 KST

Germany will transfer additional Patriot and AIM-9 missiles from Bundeswehr stocks to Ukraine while financing tens of thousands of long-range artillery rounds, Defence Minister Boris Pistorius has announced.
Speaking at the opening of the latest Ukraine Defence Contact Group meeting, Pistorius said Berlin would urgently provide PAC-2 Patriot interceptor missiles and called on other countries to examine whether they could release weapons from their own inventories ahead of the winter.
Pistorius acknowledged the tension between maintaining national reserves and supplying Ukraine, but told participants: “I am aware that it is not easy to strike a balance between one’s own security requirements and urgently needed support to Ukraine. But please, if in doubt, decide in favor for Ukraine.”
Germany will also increase deliveries of AIM-9 air-to-air missiles from Bundeswehr stocks, with Pistorius saying the weapons were already being supplied to Ukraine. The additional missiles form part of a wider effort to strengthen Ukrainian air defences before temperatures fall, with the German minister warning that Russian attacks against power stations, ports and other infrastructure could increase during the winter.
Germany is also continuing deliveries of IRIS-T air defence systems and missiles. Pistorius said Ukraine was preparing to order several thousand additional IRIS-T guided missiles using funding from the EU-Ukraine Defence Loan.
According to Pistorius, the size of that procurement will allow industry to expand production by establishing another missile production line. He said the order represented an example of how support for Ukraine could also increase European defence manufacturing capacity, allowing production to serve both Ukrainian requirements and wider European rearmament.
Pistorius also referred to the City Dome project, through which Germany is supporting the establishment of additional defences for Ukrainian cities against missile and drone attacks. Beyond air defence, Germany will finance several tens of thousands of long-range artillery rounds for Ukraine. The ammunition will be procured through the British Artillery and Air Defence Consortium before being transferred to Ukrainian forces.
Pistorius thanked UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting and his team for helping arrange the procurement, describing it as an example of cooperation between countries participating in the Ukraine Defence Contact Group.
Germany will also continue deliveries of drones and long-range ammunition as part of its support for Ukrainian forces operating on the front. The commitments were announced as members of the contact group focused heavily on preparing Ukraine for another winter of Russian air attacks, with air defence missiles identified by Kyiv as its most immediate requirement.

Would you let AI design your next tattoo? Tattoo artists say AI is changing the way they work
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
14:12:45 UTC
23:12:45 KST

Customers are increasingly using generative AI to visualise tattoo ideas, while artists use it for photo restoration and design references.
Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing how people decide what to permanently put on their bodies.
Many tattoo artists also rely on reference material as they work, particularly when making extremely detailed and realistic designs.
"This is also edited with AI. But this is my tattoo. It's not going to look like my reference exactly. Because I want that to look more realistic on the skin than on the photo itself,” said Brigi Fuzes, a Hungarian tattoo artist who has used AI to create reference images and believes AI can be an important tool for artists.
“That's something you do from your head. You can't do that with photos all the time."
Fuzes says around 70% of her customers now arrive with AI-generated images.
AI-generated images do not necessarily account for how light, shadow and fine details need to be adapted for tattooing, according to Fuzes, who has a background in fine art.
Extremely fine details that look convincing in a generated image may also fail to translate well into ink or remain clear as a tattoo ages.
"They think that's something possible on the skin. Like way too detailed. It might not stay in,” Fuzes said.
“Don't get me wrong, I do love details and my work is known for details, but at the same time, you want to make it right so it's going to last forever."
'AI as another design tool'
Edinburgh-based tattoo artist David Corden sees AI as the latest addition to tools artists were already using.
He previously used software such as Photoshop to build detailed reference images. AI can now help him improve old or blurry photographs, including pictures of deceased relatives that customers want tattooed.
However, he is frustrated by the growing assumption that highly detailed digital artwork must be AI-generated.
"You see videos come up on Instagram and somebody's zooming in on an iPad that an artist is working from going, 'Oh, AI image.' No it's not," he said.
"Some artists are better than you can possibly imagine."
Some tattoo artists still keep AI out of their creative process.
Tiago Miranda of Disturbia Ink creates his dark horror designs from his own imagination.
Unlike many tattoo artists, he does not use a reference photo to produce his work, and it all comes from the moment and the hundreds of pencil sketches he makes in his books.
Tattoo artist Ellie Diamond is also wary of AI, although she increasingly sees customers arrive with images they have generated themselves.
"If somebody brings us an idea and they're like, 'I've mocked this up,' I'm like, 'Okay, well, we can take that, but I'm going to draw you something much better than a computer can,'" she said.
"Most of the time the best tattoos come out of somebody just saying, 'Here's my idea, I love your work, you do your thing with this idea.'"
Can AI replace the tattoo artist?
The debate comes as tattooing has become increasingly mainstream in Europe.
A 2026 study found that 29% of adults in Sweden aged 20 to 68 have at least one tattoo, while a 2025 study involving more than 111,000 adults in France found that 11.5% were tattooed.
Veteran tattoo artist Dan Gold does not expect AI to take over his job. His bigger concern is how generative AI systems obtain the material used to train them.
"There ought to be some kind of AI tax or something like that," he said, "because they are using all of this data for free."
Diamond is also unconvinced that machines can replace the human appeal of tattooing.
"There's obviously something very innate and human about it," she said. "So I'm not worried that the machines are going to take over."

14:12:00 UTC
23:12:00 KST

Lithuania’s Energy Ministry on Wednesday proposed significantly increasing the country's reserve of generators following a storm last month that left almost 270,000 consumers without electricity.
"Storms are becoming stronger and more frequent, so we need to have a larger reserve. Our proposal is to increase the number of generators not by hundreds, but by thousands, and distribute them in a decentralised way through municipalities and elderships, so they can be deployed when people need them most," Energy Ministry Chancellor Eglė Radišauskienė told the Seimas Committee on Energy and Sustainable Development on Wednesday.
"We don't have a generator reserve [in Lithuania]," said the committee's chairman, Algirdas Butkevičius, an MP from the Democratic Union "For Lithuania".
Energy Minister's adviser Artūras Ketlerius told BNS that the reserve would be decentralised and that a manager would be appointed if the government approved the proposal.
Renaldas Radvila, head of ESO, said the company had bought 500 generators following the 2024 storm, 200 of which were delivered to municipalities. However, the August storm showed that the reserve was not sufficient.
"Obviously, when putting the whole plan together, if such a storm were to happen again, the number should not be hundreds but much larger. It may not even be ESO's responsibility, but rather something closer to customers, municipalities and elderships," Radvila said at the committee meeting.
Radišauskienė also said that the action plan submitted to the government proposed greater investment in putting electricity lines underground.
"We have proposed greater investment in cabling – an additional 1,200 kilometres, as proposed by the minister [Lukas Savickas – BNS]. We will see what decisions are made," she said.
According to Radvila, 1,000 kilometres of underground cables are expected to be laid by the end of this year, and 2,000 kilometres by 2028.
Radišauskienė also said the ministry was proposing to look for additional funding for residents to install autonomous electricity systems – solar power plants with battery storage.
According to the chancellor, households with such systems were able to avoid power disruptions, but only around 15,000 consumers have installed them.
Following the storm on August 22, electricity supplies were disrupted for more than 268,000 consumers. Since Monday, ESO customers who have been without electricity for more than 72 hours have been receiving compensation.
The Finance Ministry estimates that the financial impact on ESO will be around €18m.
However, the figure will be revised as damage assessments and network restoration work are still underway.

Egypt, Greece and Cyprus back plans to bring Cypriot gas to Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
14:11:29 UTC
23:11:29 KST

Cyprus’ Cronos gas is expected to reach European markets via Egypt from 2028, with Greece offering an onward route into southeastern and central Europe. The three countries renewed their backing for the plan at their El Alamein summit.
Egypt, Greece and Cyprus have renewed their backing for plans to send Cypriot gas to Europe through Egyptian export facilities, with Greece offering a possible onward route into southeastern and central Europe.
The plans come as disruption to Gulf liquefied natural gas (LNG) supplies due to the ongoing Iran war and the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz continues to put pressure on European buyers to find alternatives.
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis and Cypriot President Nikos Christodoulides met in El Alamein on Egypt’s Mediterranean coast on Tuesday.
In a joint declaration, they called for work connecting Cyprus’ offshore gas fields to Egyptian infrastructure to be completed as soon as possible.
Cronos, Cyprus’ first gas development, is expected to start producing gas in 2028, according to Eni.
New contract for Cypriot gas project
On the same day as the summit, engineering company McDermott announced that Eni’s Cyprus subsidiary had awarded it a contract worth between $500m (€429.6m) and $750m (€644.4m) for work on Cronos.
McDermott said it would provide engineering and installation support and help manage the offshore development.
The contract follows Eni and TotalEnergies’ approval of the project on 28 July. The Italian and French companies each hold a 50% stake.
Cronos is to be developed through four offshore wells, with gas carried by an undersea pipeline to Egypt. It will use existing processing facilities linked to Egypt’s Zohr field before being sent to Damietta, where it will be liquefied and exported by ship.
The Italian energy group said in July that using existing Egyptian facilities would reduce costs and speed up development. It also said the project would help restore regular LNG exports from Egypt.
At its planned production level, Cronos is expected to supply the equivalent of around 2.8 million tonnes of LNG a year. The field contains more than 3 trillion cubic feet of additional gas, according to Eni. The two companies will each market half of the output.
“This new gas route in the Mediterranean will contribute to Europe’s energy security by diversifying its LNG supply sources,” TotalEnergies chief executive Patrick Pouyanné said when the project was approved.
Where Greece fits in
Mitsotakis outlined a route through Greece’s Revithoussa and Alexandroupolis terminals, where LNG would be turned back into gas and sent to southeastern and central Europe through the Vertical Corridor.
He said the gas “could, in theory” enter Europe through Greek facilities.
Greece would therefore be one possible gateway rather than a compulsory stop. Eni said it would sell the gas primarily in Europe and other international markets, rather than send it exclusively to Greece.
The Vertical Corridor is not a single pipeline. It links existing gas networks running north from Greece through countries including Bulgaria and Romania towards Moldova and Ukraine, allowing LNG arriving at Greek terminals to reach markets further into Europe.
The proposed route would keep shipments from Egypt to Greece within the Mediterranean, avoiding Hormuz and the Red Sea. It would carry newly produced Cypriot gas rather than reroute existing Gulf cargoes.
In its July outlook, the International Energy Agency estimated total LNG supply losses of 140 billion cubic metres between 2026 and 2030, with the biggest impact on supply growth expected in 2026 and 2027.
Europe is also preparing to end its remaining Russian gas imports. EU rules provide for a full ban on Russian LNG from the beginning of 2027 and pipeline gas from autumn the same year, with Europe looking for alternative suppliers.
Wider energy ties and regional tensions
The cooperation extends beyond gas. El-Sisi and Mitsotakis discussed plans to connect their countries’ electricity systems during bilateral talks on Tuesday, according to the Egyptian presidency.
The proposed GREGY undersea power cable would carry renewable electricity from Egypt to Greece, with a planned capacity of 3,000 megawatts.
Developer Elica Interconnector said the electricity could supply Greek industry and be exported to other European markets.
All three leaders renewed their backing for the project in the summit declaration.
The trilateral partnership dates back to a first summit in Cairo in November 2014. The latest declaration also addressed maritime boundaries, saying agreements should comply with international law, including the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea.
Greece and Egypt signed an agreement covering part of their maritime boundary in 2020. Turkey rejected it at the time, arguing that the area covered overlapped with Ankara’s claimed continental shelf.
Mitsotakis said on Tuesday that the partnership between Egypt, Greece and Cyprus was “not directed against any country”.

Russian hackers may have used fake CAPTCHA to hack Ukrainian government computers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
14:11:13 UTC
23:11:13 KST

Researchers say the attack was likely part of a wider operation to steal cryptocurrency and login credentials by tricking users through a fake Google verification check to trick victims.
A suspicious cyberattack using fake CAPTCHA checks to target a Ukrainian government organisation has been linked to Moscow, according to a new report.
US tech giant Cisco said its cybersecurity researchers noticed unusual activity in the organisation's computer systems in April, asserting “with moderate confidence” that a Russian threat actor carried out the attack.
Cisco's researchers found malware known as Amatera running on the system, capable of stealing sensitive information.
It was also used to install software that could give an attacker access to the computer, including the ability to inspect files, transfer data and run commands, according to the company.
Cisco found that the software was configured to connect to a server with an IP address based in Russia.
The report could not verify whether any information was actually stolen from the Ukrainian organisation, whether hackers actively used that access or how the computer was initially infected.
Cisco researchers however assessed that it was part of a broader operation designed to steal cryptocurrency and credentials.
“It was not clear what started the execution chain,” the report said.
CAPTCHA checks as traps
In the Ukrainian system, Cisco researchers had seen a malicious file disguised with the name “verification.google” but could not trace what had caused it to run.
To understand how the Ukrainian infection might have been started, they searched for similar attacks and found another infection involving the same Amatera malware.
This time, they traced it back to compromised websites showing fake versions of Google’s CAPTCHA verification check, used to distinguish human visitors from automated bots.
But instead of simply asking users to tick a box or identify images, the fake check told them to open a window on their computer and paste in text that would run malware.
In that infection, Amatera was also used to install a program designed to steal cryptocurrency.
The program could monitor cryptocurrency wallet addresses victims copied and replace them with addresses controlled by the attackers, potentially redirecting payments.
Cisco says similarities between the infections suggest the attack against Ukraine may have started in the same way.
However, researchers could not confirm that the two infections began the same way or that the same group carried them out.

Public transport strike halts nearly all train services across Netherlands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
14:09:56 UTC
23:09:56 KST

İlayda Çakırtekin
09 September 2026•Update: 09 September 2026
A public transport strike on Wednesday brought nearly all train services across the Netherlands to a halt, while also disrupting other forms of transportation, according to Dutch broadcaster NOS.
Trade union FNV said a few thousand public transport employees were taking part in the strike, although the exact number was not immediately known.
The strike brought virtually all train services across the country to a standstill for 24 hours, while also disrupting urban and regional public transport.
The disruption resulted in a sizable number of people working from home, NOS reported.
Meanwhile, a primary school in Amsterdam arranged a tour boat for students and teachers after ferry services were disrupted.
Passenger organization Rover criticized the unions' approach to the campaign, saying that while they aim to stand up for vulnerable people, taking away their mobility further isolates them.
The organization called for other forms of campaigning.
The public transport strike was announced by the FNV trade union as part of broader action against planned cuts to social security.
The unions are calling for the cuts to be completely scrapped. Although the government has since announced that it would reverse part of the planned measures, the unions do not consider the move sufficient.

Serbian leader calls snap elections after dissolving country’s parliament
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
14:06:40 UTC
23:06:40 KST

Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić has dissolved his country’s parliament and announced snap elections for the end of October as he seeks to assert control over the febrile political situation in the country.
“I am convinced that the citizens of Serbia will choose the right path into the future,” Vučić said Wednesday, adding that “preserving our democratic system” and avoiding divisions were his priorities. The snap elections will take place on Oct. 25, according to reports in Serbian media.
Vučić acknowledged “turbulence” in Serbian society but blamed “significant interference by foreign powers” for inspiring student-led anti-corruption protests that have fueled the country’s political turmoil over the past two years.
On Monday, Prime Minister Đuro Macut asked Vučić to dissolve parliament and call fresh elections. “If we want to mitigate tensions in society there is no better way than to ask people,” Macut said.
Vučić, who has been in power as president or prime minister for 12 years, has faced calls to step down since the 2023 parliamentary elections, amid allegations of electoral fraud. His second and final term as president is set to end in 2027 and his powers will not expire with the dissolution of parliament.
In June, Vučić said he would resign as president “within weeks,” but his ambitions to remain in power continue. His Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) has nominated him for prime minister if the party secures a majority in the upcoming snap election.
Serbia has been a candidate for EU membership since 2012, but its bid has stalled over concerns about democratic backsliding in Belgrade and its refusal to sanction Russia for the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

EU to give cities more power to curb Airbnb and short-term rentals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
14:06:19 UTC
23:06:19 KST

"Short-term rental activity" grew 93 percent across four major letting platforms between 2018 and 2024, according to the EU.
European cities will have greater powers to restrict short-term rentals such as Airbnb under EU plans unveiled on Wednesday aimed at tackling rising housing costs in popular tourist destinations.
The European Commission set out conditions under which local authorities will be able to limit short-term lets as part of its affordable housing package, designed to address what Commission Vice-President Teresa Ribera described as a “terrible crisis”.
“When the market fails to deliver something as fundamental as an affordable home, public authorities have a responsibility to act”, Ribera said.
Short-term rentals are popular among tourists, but residents in cities such as Lisbon, Barcelona and Prague have blamed platforms like Airbnb for reducing the supply of homes available for long-term rent and driving up prices, sometimes forcing locals to move elsewhere.
EU data from 2024 shows that nearly 10% of people living in EU cities spend more than 40% of their disposable income on housing.
However, the Commission's upcoming restrictions would be allowed only in areas with clear evidence of serious housing pressure.
For Airbnb-style rentals, the EU is particularly concerned about commercial operators running several properties as holiday lets, rather than people occasionally renting out their own home.
Under the proposal, cities would be able to target professional multi-property operators, but a person's ability to rent out their main residence would be protected.
However, the Commission acknowledges that short-term rental restrictions and limits on second homes can't solve Europe's structural housing shortage. Other challenges include high construction costs, expensive land, planning restrictions and lengthy permit processes.
"Europe's housing crisis needs structural solutions, and the implementation of this act should focus on increasing the supply of homes," said an Airbnb spokesperson.

Finland backs Foreign Ministers' statement on two-state solution
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
17:05:54 EEST
23:05:54 KST

Finnish Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen (NCP) said on Wednesday she would stand behind a joint statement condemning Israeli settlements, even if she were the only one doing so.
The statement also aims to restrict imports of products from Israeli settlements. According to Valtonen, the aim is to prevent Israel from continuing to build settlements in the West Bank and thereby help safeguard the prospects for a two-state solution.
"If it's a question of respecting international law, I'm prepared to stand alone on this," Valtonen said at Parliament on Wednesday.
Finland's participation in the joint statement with several other European countries has drawn criticism from the Finns Party and the Christian Democrats.
Speaking at a press conference in Parliament, Valtonen said she is not alone in the government on the issue.
Earlier on Wednesday, Jani Mäkelä, chair of the Finns Party parliamentary group, said on X that Valtonen had acted on her own and that the government did not share a common position on the matter.
On Tuesday, Finland said it would begin restricting imports from Israeli settlements alongside the Nordic countries, Canada, the UK and France. Valtonen said the volume of such imports is small, though products including cosmetics are imported from the settlements, according to Finnwatch.

Russia developing protective system to safeguard warehouses from drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
14:04:36 UTC
23:04:36 KST

MOSCOW, September 9. /TASS/. Russia is developing a four-level system to protect warehouse facilities against drone threats and attacks, Roman Belyayev, head of the Severstal Engineering JSC’s commercial construction project, said in an interview with TASS.
"Four-level protection systems are being developed in Russia to protect warehouses from the threat of and attacks by drones. The system consists of three types of netting, ropes, cables, and special protective mats. This provides the highest level of protection with good fire resistance and anti-corrosion treatment. In addition, the company (Severstal) manufactures quick-release anti-UAV defense systems that can later be removed, returned, and certified," he said.
According to Belyayev, warehouses are in desperate need of a system like this. "We have 90 designers booked two months in advance; we don’t have enough people to keep up with all the design work. Demand is very high," he added.
Demand for protection systems is coming from both commercial warehouses – such as Wildberries and Ozon – and state-owned companies. "If we look at the market as a whole, right now, as a rule, everyone wants at least minimal, standard protection," the expert noted. Chinese companies are also delivering protective nets to Russia.

Ukraine Presents Domestically Developed Pegas IFV
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
14:04:12 UTC
23:04:12 KST

Ukraine has unveiled Pegas, its domestically developed tracked infantry fighting vehicle (IFV) that could eventually become the country’s first locally designed vehicle of its kind to enter serial production.
Ukrainian Defense Industry, the country’s state-owned defense conglomerate, showcased the Pegas at the MSPO 2026 defense exhibition in Poland.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The vehicle is being developed by the Kharkiv Morozov Machine Building Design Bureau, the same firm behind Ukraine’s T-84 main battle tanks (MBTs), Ukraine’s modernized version of the Soviet T-80 MBT.
Ukraine currently operates a broad range of Soviet- and Western-made tracked IFVs. Pegas is intended to be a domestic addition to that fleet, though the project remains under development and no production schedule has been announced.
NATO-standard armors
According to the specifications presented at the exhibition, the vehicle’s frontal armor is designed to meet Level 6 of NATO’s STANAG 4569 protection standard, while the remaining sections of the hull are rated at Level 4.
The stated protection levels are intended to allow the front of the vehicle to withstand 30mm ammunition and its other sides to resist 14.5mm armor-piercing rounds.
According to the presentation, additional armor can be installed to protect the vehicle against weapons such as the RPG-7 anti-tank rocket launcher. Pegas is also expected to carry electronic warfare (EW) equipment to counter drones.
Russian Strikes Could Add Up to 0.6 Points to Ukraine’s Inflation, NBU Says
Mixture of onboard armaments
The proposed armament includes a 30mm automatic cannon, a coaxial 7.62mm machine gun, two anti-tank guided missiles and a 30mm automatic grenade launcher.
The weapons are mounted in a remote combat module. The module shown on the model resembles Ukraine’s BM-7 Parus, but the vehicle is expected to enter production with a different module called Topaz, if the project reaches that stage.
Performance and capabilities
Pegas is 8 meters (26 feet) long, 3.2 meters (10.5 feet) wide and 3.3 meters (10.8 feet) tall. Its stated combat weight is 35 metric tons.
The vehicle is designed to reach a maximum speed of 70 kilometers per hour (43 mph) and has a stated operational range of 500 kilometers (310 miles).
Developers said it could operate at altitudes of up to 3,000 meters (9,840 feet) above sea level and emphasized its intended cross-country mobility.
Based on the stated dimensions and weight, Pegas is larger and heavier than Poland’s Borsuk infantry fighting vehicle and is roughly comparable in weight to an unloaded German KF41 Lynx.
The presentation did not provide information on how many troops Pegas can transport, its engine or the current stage of prototype testing.
Pegas has not yet entered serial production. If development is completed and manufacturing begins, it would become Ukraine’s first domestically developed tracked infantry fighting vehicle to reach mass production.
Ukraine previously pursued several projects in this category, including designs based on tank chassis and other existing armored platforms. Those efforts remained limited to models or prototypes.

The head of the Sverdlovsk regional chapter of the liberal Yabloko party has left Russia amid a growing number of arrests of other party members, local media reported Wednesday, just weeks before parliamentary elections are scheduled to be held.
Regional party chairman Maxim Petlin has not been seen in the capital city Yekaterinburg for “several months,” anonymous sources told the news outlet 66.ru. It was not immediately clear when he left Russia or where he is currently located.
Petlin later told the newspaper Kommersant that his lawyer advised him not to comment on reports of his departure “for the safety of my family and myself.”
In June, the politician withdrew his candidacy in this month’s State Duma elections due to reported pressure from law enforcement authorities, including short-term detentions and police searches at his home.
Yabloko is Russia’s oldest liberal party and is the only registered party campaigning on a pro-peace platform. Several of its candidates have been disqualified from running in next week’s elections over various violations.
On Monday, Sverdlovsk region police arrested at least six Yabloko members running for federal or regional office in connection with public displays of “extremist” symbols. The charges disqualify them from the upcoming elections.
Yabloko’s Sverdlovsk regional chapter said Wednesday that Petlin was in communication with one of its arrested members.
Candidates of the party campaigning in single-member districts are still allowed to run for office after Russia’s Supreme Court last month ruled to cancel the registration of Yabloko’s federal slate of candidates for the State Duma.

Hungary takes one more step to normalise relations with Brussels over rule of law
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
14:04:00 UTC
23:04:00 KST

Hungary has formally notified Brussels it has met its rule-of-law conditions, a step that could unlock €4.2bn in EU funds and restore access for researchers and students who were left out of European programs.
The Hungarian government has formally notified the European Commission of the reforms it has passed to address the EU's rule of law concerns, in a move that could unlock €4.2 billion in cohesion funding and restore access to EU programmes.
"The European Commission has received Hungary's written notification under the Rule of Law Conditionality Regulation. The notification sets out measures to remedy the situation that led to the adoption of protective measures," the European Commissioner for Budget, Anti-Fraud and Public Administration, Piotr Serafin, wrote on X on Wednesday.
The notification follows an agreement struck in May between Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar and Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, which included funding blocked over corruption and rule-of-law concerns.
At the end of 2022, the Council of the EU formally suspended €6.3 billion in cohesion funding to Hungary under the conditionality mechanism, citing shortcomings in the country's anti-corruption framework, conflicts of interest and systemic irregularities in public procurement.
That initial sum has since been reduced due to losses, meaning Budapest could now recover €4.2bn as part of a broader normalisation in relations with Brussels that began after Magyar ousted Viktor Orbán from power in April.
Resolving the issue goes beyond unlocking this amount: the conditionality mechanism also blocked funding to Hungarian public interest trusts and related entities, a legal structure the government uses to take control of public institutions such as universities.
As a result, Hungary-based students and researchers were locked out of EU programmes such as the Erasmus+ exchange scheme and Horizon Europe research grants.
In recent weeks, the Commission and the Hungarian government have worked closely together, meaning Brussels does not expect any surprises when assessing whether the reforms passed sufficiently address its concerns, Euronews understands.
Hungary remains eligible for €10bn under the Recovery and Resilience Facility, the EU's post-pandemic stimulus instrument, with a payment request expected later this month.
Just over €2bn in cohesion funding remains blocked due to concerns about the asylum system, child protection law and academic freedom.
The Commission now has one month to complete its assessment, after which it will refer the matter to the Council with a draft decision — only member states can terminate the conditionality mechanism.
"We will now carefully examine the notification," Serafin added.

Russia’s new ballistic missile could reach western Ukraine—and it may be tested there within months
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
14:03:40 UTC
23:03:40 KST

Russia plans to test-fire a new type of ballistic missile before the end of 2026, one built to fly farther than the Iskander missiles it now launches at Ukraine, according to Ukraine's military intelligence. Its deputy chief outlined the plan at a Ukraine-NATO meeting on 8 September, ZN reported.
A longer-range missile would erode the relative safety of western Ukraine, where the routes carrying Western aid run beyond the front, and stretch air defenses already struggling against ballistic strikes.
A longer reach into western Ukraine
Russia plans final tests of a new ballistic missile with a range of up to 800 kilometers, or about 500 miles, by year's end, Vadym Skibitskyi, deputy head of the Defense Intelligence of Ukraine (HUR), told the Ukraine-NATO Interparliamentary Council, citing the agency's own assessments. Russian forces may try to hit targets in western Ukraine during those tests, he said.
The deputy chief noted that Moscow is raising both the output and the range of its ballistic missiles to intensify strikes and push Ukraine into a social and economic crisis. He urged partners to tighten sanctions until Russia loses access to the foreign components in its long-range weapons.
Russia's modernized 9M723-2, also called the Iskander-1000, reaches up to 550 km, HUR says, and the older 9M723-1 covers 390 km. An 800-km weapon would carry strikes well past the front.
The missile Russia already fields
Russia already fields a longer-range Iskander variant. This summer, its forces first fired the modernized 9M723-2—part of the Bora-M system—in a combined missile strike on Kyiv. A bigger engine and a larger launcher gave that missile its extended reach, HUR said. Ballistic missiles are the hardest of Russia's strikes for Ukraine to stop, and Moscow has poured them out in recent months, running its plants above quota and firing them in larger salvos.
Losing more soldiers than it signs up
Russia is waging a war of attrition despite heavy losses and has not given up on destroying Ukrainian statehood, Skibitskyi said. Skibitskyi put Russia's August losses at 43,000 soldiers against 39,000 recruited. Russia has struggled to fill its ranks for months. Russia's General Staff sees intensified mobilization as the only way to reach its main goals—fully occupying the Ukrainian Donbas and seizing the strategic initiative—he explained.
The Kremlin plans to mobilize about 600,000 people across 2026 and 2027, half of them by the end of this year, he said. Russia will also try to close the Black Sea to Ukraine and to drag Belarus into the war and into hybrid operations against NATO, he added, though HUR sees no signs of Russian strike groupings forming there yet.
Each new kilometer of range puts more of Ukraine within reach from deep inside Russia, without moving a launcher closer to the border.

EU universities struggle to cut ties with Israeli defense-linked partners: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
14:03:33 UTC
23:03:33 KST

Melike Pala
09 September 2026•Update: 09 September 2026
European universities are struggling to withdraw from research projects involving Israeli institutions and companies linked to the defense sector, despite public commitments to suspend the cooperation amid the genocidal war in the Gaza Strip, according to an investigation by Investigate Europe and Reporters United that was released Wednesday.
The investigation found that 34 universities in Spain, the Netherlands, Italy and Belgium are involved in 38 new Horizon Europe projects with Israeli entities linked to defense or technologies with potential military applications.
The projects have received €15 million ($17 million) in EU funding.
Across Horizon Europe, 386 European higher education institutions are involved in 205 projects with Israeli entities that have defense or defense-technology links, said the report.
Some universities have cited legal, financial and reputational risks as reasons for maintaining partnerships.
The University of Ghent, for example, estimated that unilateral withdrawal from Horizon Europe projects could cost tens of millions of euros.
The University of Granada is meanwhile fighting a legal battle about its decision to suspend cooperation with Israeli entities, while continuing to participate in another Horizon Europe project involving Mellanox, now owned by US technology company Nvidia, and European defense companies.
In the Netherlands, universities, including Groningen and Eindhoven, have also faced scrutiny for cooperation with Israel's Technion Institute of Technology, which has close ties to Israel's defense sector.
The European Commission said requests to terminate Israeli participation in Horizon projects are assessed on a case-by-case basis, stressing that all beneficiaries must comply with ethical principles and relevant national, EU and international law.

12 Questions You’ll Be Glad You Asked Your Grandparents
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
14:02:39 UTC
23:02:39 KST

Elizabeth Keating’s students learn about World War II in history books. But when one of them asked her grandmother what it was like to live through the wartime mobilization and bombing in the U.K., the past suddenly felt real. Talking to her grandmother, the student told Keating, felt like “talking to a celebrity.”
“It gives us a link with history that’s very personal,” says Keating, a professor emerita of anthropology at the University of Texas at Austin and author of The Essential Questions: Interview Your Family to Uncover Stories and Bridge Generations.
Your grandparents might not think of themselves as eyewitnesses to history—or realize that anyone is interested in the ordinary details of their lives. Asking an unexpected question can make the past come alive while helping you discover who they were, and who they still are.
These questions can help you get beyond the familiar family stories—and start conversations you’ll be glad you had.
“What’s something you believed when you were my age that you don’t believe anymore?”
Your grandparent has probably changed their mind about more than a few things over the years. Maybe they swore they would never get married or that they’d stay in their hometown forever. Ask what they felt certain about at your age—and what eventually made them reconsider.
The answer can make a younger person think, “Oh my God, you were my age,” says Mike O’Krent, founder of LifeStories Alive, a company that preserves family histories on video. It might also be reassuring to discover that your grandparent once shared some of your fears or wrestled with questions you’re confronting right now. Hearing what happened next can open up a larger conversation about how they became the person they are today.
“Tell me about the dinner table in the house where you grew up.”
“What was your childhood like?” is an enormous question—the conversational equivalent of handing someone a blank book and asking them to fill it. It’s better to zoom in on one specific setting. “The dinner table is a window into an entire family, sometimes an entire childhood,” says Lauren Befus, founder of Memory Lane Jane, a family-biography company that preserves people’s life stories in heirloom books.
Ask who sat where, who cooked, and whether everyone ate together. Was dinner loud and chaotic or silent and formal? Did people linger or bolt the moment they finished? Was there always enough food? Could friends drop in?
One person told Keating that “there was no talking at the dinner table.” In Keating’s own family, her mother occasionally made the children prepare little reports from the encyclopedia to present during dinner. “We hated it,” she recalls. Whether your grandparent remembers laughter, pinching under the table, or strictly enforced silence, you’ll learn much more than what was on the menu.
“What was considered a waste of money in your house?”
Every family has at least one expenditure it considers financially unhinged. Perhaps your grandparent’s parents refused to pay someone to repair anything they could conceivably fix themselves. Maybe restaurant meals, store-bought clothes, or long-distance phone calls were treated as scandalous extravagances.
The question can reveal what money represented in your grandparent’s childhood home: security, freedom, status, or a source of constant stress. You might also recognize a few financial commandments that have traveled down the family line. Oh, that’s why your mom refuses to pay for shipping or regards full-price cereal as a personal affront!
“Tell me about a time you got into trouble—and how you got out of it.”
Your grandparent wasn’t always the person reminding everyone to be careful. Once upon a time, they might have sneaked somewhere forbidden, played hooky from Sunday school to take a nap in the cornfields behind the church, concocted an impressive lie, or attempted to conceal a mishap from their parents.
Keating particularly likes asking about trouble because it comes with a built-in plot: What happened? How did you respond? Did anyone find out? The story doesn’t need to involve a wild act of rebellion. She’s found that “you can get into trouble with small things, too, that evolve into bigger things.” Either way, you’ll get to meet the mischievous younger person behind the grandparent you know and love.
“What object have you kept from childhood—and what’s its story?”
That battered book, recipe card, or piece of jewelry might look unremarkable. Then you hear the story about why it’s still a prized possession.
Keating recalls talking to a woman who had grown up poor and dreamed of owning a particular doll. When she received it for her birthday, she treasured it so deeply that she eventually passed it down through her family. “We attach relationships to objects,” Keating says. Eventually, “an object isn’t just a thing anymore.” It evokes a person, place, yearning, or moment someone wants to keep close.
If your grandparent still has the item, ask to see it. Their act of holding it again—or simply studying its scratches, faded colors, or fraying edges—might shake loose a story they didn’t even realize they remembered.
“Who believed in you before you believed in yourself?”
The answer could introduce you to a teacher, mentor, neighbor, boss, or friend you’ve never heard about—yet whose encouragement altered the course of your family’s history.
For O’Krent, it was his third-grade teacher, Mrs. Glaze. One day, despite making him stay inside during recess because he couldn’t keep his mouth shut, she looked him in the eye and said: “You’re going to be somebody important someday.”
He never forgot it. An influential person isn’t always who you would expect, O’Krent says, and the best part of the story may emerge when you ask why your grandparent connected with them. What did they see in your grandparent—and how did their belief change what your grandparent saw in themselves?
“What decision did you make that everyone else thought was wrong?”
Maybe your grandparent pursued a career their family didn’t approve of, moved somewhere unexpected, ended—or began—a relationship, or took a risk everyone else considered foolish. Ask why people objected. Then borrow O’Krent’s favorite follow-up: “Do you agree with that?”
Your grandparent might still insist everyone else was wrong. Or perhaps the decision led directly to something they’d love to forget. “Everybody makes mistakes,” O’Krent says. What matters is “the lesson you learn from it.” Either way, you’ll discover how your grandparent responded when their judgment collided with other people’s expectations—and whether they’d make the same choice again.
“What are you proud of that would never appear on a résumé?”
Résumés are good for recording promotions and degrees. But they don’t capture the time someone took care of an aging parent, raised children through a miserable year, started over after a failure, repaired a relationship, or became the friend who always showed up.
The accomplishments you associate with your grandparent might not be the ones that matter most to them. This question “gives people permission to define accomplishment for themselves,” Befus says. You may discover that the chapter of their life they value most is one you barely knew about.
“What are you still figuring out?”
There is, apparently, no birthday at which a person wakes up with life completely sorted out. Grandparents still have evolving identities, relationships, hopes, and uncertainties, says Claudia Johnson, a licensed marriage and family therapist in Seattle.
Asking what your grandparent is still figuring out communicates: “I don’t only want to know who you were. I’m interested in who you are now,” Johnson says. Maybe they’re learning how to enjoy retirement, trying to understand a changing friendship, or deciding what they want the next few years to look like.
Answer the question yourself, too. That reciprocity transforms the interaction from an interview into a real conversation—and reminds both of you that nobody ages out of uncertainty.
“If you were naming a baby today, what name would you choose?”
Not every meaningful question requires rummaging through the past. That’s especially important when you’re talking to someone with dementia, says Cristina Rodriguez, founder of Mind&Melody, a nonprofit that connects musicians with people living with dementia and other neurological conditions.
Rodriguez’s grandmother was diagnosed with dementia a few years ago. As her memory changes, Rodriguez has realized that “connection can’t always depend on asking her to recall the past.”
During one FaceTime call, when Rodriguez was thinking about having children, she asked her grandmother what she would name a baby girl today. Estefania, she replied, because it sounded strong and powerful. Rodriguez had known her grandmother her entire life—and knew she had raised six children—but had never thought to ask her anything like that.
The exchange showed Rodriguez “how much possibility there is in questions that aren’t about remembering at all.” Ask what song should belong to the two of you, or what your perfect day together would look like. These types of questions let you be curious about who your grandparent is right now, including what they imagine and what makes them laugh.
“If you could ask me anything right now, what would you want to know?”
After putting your grandparent in the hot seat, turn the interview over to them. What have they always wondered about you?
“The grandparent’s not expecting that one,” O’Krent says. That’s exactly why he likes it: The question gives your grandparent some control over where the conversation goes and makes the exchange feel mutual.
Once the conversation is flowing, don’t cling too tightly to your prepared questions. O’Krent teaches people an unusual listening trick: “The next thing you say has to include at least one word from the last sentence they say.” Because you don’t know when that last sentence is coming, you have no choice but to pay close attention. It might feel awkward at first, he acknowledges, but it helps the other person feel heard. Plus, the best question is almost always the follow-up you didn’t plan.
“What do you wish you’d asked your own parents or grandparents?”
This question might expose the blank spaces in your grandparent’s own family history. Maybe they know their mother moved across the country alone but never learned what compelled her to go. Perhaps they inherited a house without ever asking why their grandparents chose it—or what brought their parents together in the first place.
The answers often involve what Keating calls “huge identity questions”: Where did I come from? Who am I? Why did my family’s life unfold the way it did? Most people know the milestones, she says, but what they really want is “the story behind everything.”
Listen closely. Your grandparent might be telling you not only what they regret leaving unanswered, but which parts of their own story they hope you won’t.

What is the nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
14:02:29 UTC
23:02:29 KST

What is the nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty?
Sept 9 - Western powers have submitted a proposed resolution to the U.N. nuclear watchdog's 35-nation Board of Governors that would report Iran to the U.N. Security Council for the first time in 20 years for breaching its obligations under the nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty.
Diplomats at the International Atomic Energy Agency say the text proposed by the United States, Britain, France and Germany is almost certain to pass, with a vote expected later on Wednesday or on Thursday.
Below are some key facts about the treaty.
PURPOSE OF THE NPT
The objective of the treaty, which took effect in 1970, is to halt the spread of nuclear weapons-making capability, guarantee the right of all members to develop nuclear energy for peaceful ends and for the original five nuclear-weapons powers to take steps towards phasing out their arsenals.
The treaty defines nuclear-armed states as those that “manufactured and exploded a nuclear weapon or other nuclear device prior to January 1, 1967. They are the United States, Britain, France, China and Russia, which assumed rights and obligations from the former Soviet Union. Those five nations are the permanent members of the U.N. Security Council.
SIGNATORIES
A total of 191 countries are party to the NPT. Nuclear-weapons states agree not to transfer those weapons or to help non-nuclear states obtain them.
NON-SIGNATORIES
Two non-signatories, India and Pakistan, developed nuclear weapons. Another, Israel, is widely assumed to have a nuclear arsenal but has not confirmed or denied it publicly.
North Korea signed the treaty in 1985 but announced its withdrawal in 2003. After a rapprochement, North Korea expelled IAEA inspectors again in 2009, and they have not returned since. It has tested several nuclear weapons.
ESCAPE CLAUSE
The treaty is divided into 11 articles, including one that enables a state to withdraw “"if it decides that extraordinary events ... have jeopardized the supreme interests of its country". A state must give three months' notice to other treaty members and the U.N. Security Council.
IRAN
Iran has been a non-nuclear-weapon signatory to the NPT since 1970. It has a uranium enrichment programme that it says is for peaceful purposes, but Western powers and Israel suspect it intends to develop the means to make atomic bombs.
The International Atomic Energy Agency's 35-nation Board of Governors passed a resolution on June 12 of last year declaring Iran in breach of its non-proliferation obligations for the first time in almost 20 years.
Actually reporting Iran to the Security Council for that breach is a separate step requiring a second resolution.
The June 2025 resolution cited Tehran's "many failures to uphold its obligations since 2019 to provide the Agency with full and timely cooperation regarding undeclared nuclear material and activities at multiple undeclared locations in Iran".
ISSUES OF CONCERN
Israel and the United States bombed Iranian nuclear facilities in June of last year, badly damaging or destroying Iranian uranium-enrichment plants. Iran has not let the IAEA return to those sites or accounted for its stocks of enriched uranium, some of which is close to weapons grade, since then.
In its latest report on Iran to member states last week, seen by Reuters, the IAEA said "it is critical for the Agency to conduct verification activities in Iran without further delay in accordance with the NPT Safeguards Agreement".
Last year's resolution declaring Iran in breach of its safeguards obligations under the NPT, which was passed the day before Israel launched its attacks, was to do with a separate issue, however.
The issue of concern there was Iran's failure to provide credible explanations of how uranium traces detected atundeclared sites came to be there despite the agencyhaving investigated for years. They largely concerned activities carried out more than 20 years ago.
Iran says it has always adhered to its safeguards obligations. It has criticised IAEA findings as politically motivated and lacking technical or legal foundation.
Iran has often responded to previous IAEA board resolutions against it by escalating its nuclear activities or scaling back cooperation with the IAEA, though there is limited scope for that now since no inspections were carried out in the past three months and many of its nuclear facilities are badly damaged.
NUCLEAR SANCTIONS
Sanctions were imposed on Iran in 2006 after it failed to comply with a U.N. Security Council resolution demanding a halt to its uranium enrichment programme.
Iran agreed to restrain its nuclear programme, while still enriching to a low level, in return for relief from economic sanctions under a deal reached with six major powers in 2015, but President Donald Trump pulled the United States out of the agreement in 2018, reimposing U.S. sanctions.
Iran subsequently retaliated by ramping up its nuclear programme, abandoning the restrictions imposed by the deal. REUTERS

Burç Eruygur
09 September 2026•Update: 09 September 2026
Azerbaijani Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov said Wednesday that his country and neighboring Armenia agreed to conduct the delimitation process between their borders from north to south.
Citing his remarks to journalists on the sidelines of the 4th Climate Week (CW4) under the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change in Baku, Azerbaijani news outlets, including the APA and Trend news agencies, reported that Bayramov said the composition of Baku and Yerevan’s delimitation commissions remains unchanged.
Bayramov said Deputy Prime Minister Shahin Mustafayev continues to lead Azerbaijan’s commission, and that the commission and its Armenian equivalent hold regular meetings and discussions.
“There is an agreement and mutual understanding that the work should be carried out and progressed from the north to the south, starting from the more difficult northern border, the intersection of Azerbaijan, Armenia, and Georgia,” he said. "As for more specific details, all issues will be discussed in due course and are expected to be resolved. More specific issues, including issues related to these or other settlements, will be discussed as part of the delimitation commission's work.”
Bayramov also said he is in regular contact with his Armenian counterpart, Ararat Mirzoyan, and that a meeting between them in the near future is “not excluded.”
Azerbaijan and Armenia continue discussions to determine their mutual border, with talks having been held between their border commissions on 13 occasions since their inaugural meeting in May 2022.
Following the eighth meeting of the commissions in April 2024, the two countries agreed to carry out their border delimitation process based on the 1991 Alma-Ata Declaration, which established the founding declarations and principles of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS).

US scrambles to match China’s air-breathing hypersonic missiles with Darpa programme
US defence agency launches next-generation weapons project a year after PLA unveiled pioneering hypersonic missiles in military parade
The US Defence Advanced Research Projects Agency (Darpa) will bring contractors together later this month to lay out what it wants from the Next Generation Hypersonic Cruise Missile, with air-breathing propulsion at the heart of the project, according to the agency’s website.
Unlike rocket-powered missiles, air-breathing weapons draw oxygen from the atmosphere instead of carrying all they need on board, freeing up weight for fuel or payload.
Darpa has made clear it is looking for more than an upgrade to existing technology. In an industry request issued last month, the agency called for radically new propulsion, fuels, boosters and systems to cope with the extreme heat of hypersonic flight.
The new missile could come in varied sizes, from weapons carried by tactical aircraft to much larger systems launched from bombers or the ground.

The brain’s fuel system rapidly recovers after you stop heavy drinking
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
14:00:04 UTC
23:00:04 KST

New research suggests that when people with alcohol use disorder stop drinking, their brains show a sudden, sharp drop in the ability to burn a secondary fuel source called acetate, before recovering just a few weeks later. The study, published in Neuropsychopharmacology, provides evidence that the brain’s metabolic adaptation to heavy alcohol consumption is highly reversible.
Alcohol use disorder is a medical condition characterized by an inability to stop or control alcohol use despite adverse social, occupational, or health consequences. Chronic drinking alters the balance of chemical messengers in the brain, contributing to the intense physical and emotional symptoms that occur when a person tries to quit. However, alcohol also changes how the brain fuels itself.
The human brain usually runs on glucose, a simple sugar. But when a person drinks, the liver breaks down the alcohol into a chemical called acetate, which floods the bloodstream. A 2012 study showed that drinking alcohol leads the brain to rely less on glucose and instead take up this circulating acetate for energy. Specialized brain cells called astrocytes eagerly absorb the acetate, using it to power their operations and support nearby neurons.
“There are examples of the brain changing fuel sources, changing to one and changing away from another,” Graeme F. Mason, a professor of radiology and biomedical imaging and psychiatry at the Yale Biomedical Imaging Institute at the Yale School of Medicine, told PsyPost. “One example is in starvation, when the brain reduces its reliance on sugar and increases its capacity to consume ketone bodies. Another is that in diabetes with hypoglycemia unawareness, the brain increases its capacity to consume things other than sugar.”
“Newer data also look like people with chronically high blood sugar are down-regulating their ability to transport glucose into the brain, which may be protecting the brain against having high sugar inside,” Mason continued. “Well, long ago, T.K. Li, the former director of the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism, was talking with me about metabolism and highlighted that when people drink alcohol, it raises blood concentration of acetate.”
Because heavy drinkers are constantly exposed to this alternative fuel, their bodies adjust to the surplus. Previous research published in 2013 indicated that the brains of heavy drinkers develop an increased capacity to burn acetate compared to the brains of light drinkers. The brain essentially gets used to running on the breakdown products of alcohol.
“If somebody binges on the weekends, they have intermittently high blood acetate levels,” Mason explained. “And if somebody reaches a state at which they have difficulty not drinking, where they may want treatment, then their blood acetate levels are elevated almost constantly, even when they’re asleep. We have been wondering if there’s something in there that we might be able to use to help people stop drinking.”
Given these adaptations, scientists are exploring how this energy shift relates to the severe symptoms people experience during detoxification. When alcohol is removed, the sudden loss of acetate might shock the brain’s energy systems. Providing alternative brain fuels during detoxification might ease this transition. For instance, a 2021 clinical trial found that giving patients in alcohol detox a high-fat, low-carbohydrate diet reduced withdrawal severity. This aligns with a study covered by PsyPost in 2026 noting that ketone supplements lowered alcohol cravings by providing the brain with a substitute energy source.
Building on this line of research, a team led by Chathura Kumaragamage of the University of Calgary and Mason investigated what happens to acetate metabolism in the brains of people with alcohol use disorder as they undergo detoxification and maintain sobriety. They wanted to see if the brain’s heightened ability to burn acetate would persist or normalize after drinking stopped.
“We found about 15 years ago that people who drink at risky levels are much more able to use the acetate in their blood, but that was a smallish study,” Mason said. “We really needed to test this finding to see if it was real, to see if we could reproduce it, or if it was just a fluke. The National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA) gave us funds to test it in a new, larger group of people, and to extend the test to people who were seeking treatment.”
The researchers recruited four groups of participants. The sample included 13 light drinkers who consumed fewer than three standard drinks a week, and 15 heavy drinkers who drank at risky levels over the past six months. They also recruited six individuals in long-term recovery who had been abstinent for at least six months. Finally, they included a group of treatment-seeking individuals with alcohol use disorder who were undergoing medically supervised inpatient detoxification.
Of the treatment-seeking group, nine provided usable data at roughly one week of abstinence, and ten provided data at roughly one month of abstinence. Seven of these participants successfully completed scans at both time points, allowing the researchers to track their progress directly.
During the testing session, participants received an intravenous infusion of a specialized form of acetate containing a stable carbon isotope. This harmless carbon-13 isotope acts as a tracking tag. By taking frequent blood samples, the researchers could monitor how much acetate was in the bloodstream and how quickly the body was clearing it.
To see what was happening inside the head, the team used magnetic resonance spectroscopy, a non-invasive imaging technique that measures chemical signatures in the body. They focused the scanner on the occipital cortex at the back of the brain. They measured how quickly the tagged acetate was taken up by astrocytes and converted into neurotransmitters like glutamate and glutamine.
The researchers also calculated a metric called energy per cycle. This ratio compares the brain’s basic cellular energy consumption to the rate of chemical signaling between neurons. It provides a snapshot of whether the brain’s energy supply is keeping up with its communication demands.
Going into the study, the research team expected the newly abstinent group to show a massive capacity for acetate consumption, given their history of heavy alcohol use. Instead, the results went in the opposite direction. After one week of abstinence, the detoxification group showed a 64 percent lower rate of brain acetate oxidation compared to the heavy drinkers, and a 41 percent lower rate compared to those in long-term recovery.
“This latter group consumed way more alcohol than the risky drinkers, and so we assumed that the people seeking treatment would also use way more acetate,” Mason said. “To our surprise, we found that the people looking for treatment had a far lower capacity to consume acetate.”
“We think that this may happen because, just like with chronically elevated glucose leading to less capacity to transport glucose into the brain, the chronically elevated acetate may lead the brain to lower its transport capacity and protect itself,” Mason explained. “Acetate can do things like interact with the genome to change how DNA gets expressed, so there’s one reason that the brain might not want so much acetate around all the time.”
The blood tests confirmed this metabolic slowdown was happening across the whole body. The newly abstinent group had higher levels of acetate remaining in their blood during the infusion, indicating that their systems were clearing acetate unusually slowly.
The heavy drinking group, meanwhile, showed a 58 percent higher rate of brain acetate oxidation than the light drinking group. This confirmed the team’s 2013 findings, demonstrating that active heavy drinking increases the brain’s reliance on acetate.
“Maybe it is the intermittent acetate exposure of risky drinking can increase acetate consumption capacity, while chronic heavy acetate of dependence reduces the capacity to protect the brain,” Mason noted. “It is likely that the people who drink to the point of dependence have nearly constant elevations of acetate, and the brain resets so that it lets in a little bit, so that the brain, sitting behind its protective barrier, sees some acetate, but not as much as if it had not protected itself.”
The metabolic slump seen during early abstinence was strictly temporary. When the researchers tested the detoxification group again after one month of abstinence, their brain acetate consumption had increased by 43 percent. At this one-month mark, their acetate metabolism was nearly indistinguishable from that of the light drinkers, suggesting the brain rapidly readapts to functioning without alcohol.
“The good news is that after a month, this aspect of alcohol dependence has gone back close to normal,” Mason said. “There are other changes in the brain that can also normalize, given more time, like the volume loss (the brain shrinks with that heavy drinking and can return at least partway to normal).”
Despite the dramatic shifts in how quickly the brain burned acetate, the energy per cycle measurement was similar across all groups. This indicates that the fundamental balance between energy consumption and neurotransmitter cycling remained stable. Even as the type of fuel being burned shifted, the basic energetic health of the neuronal networks appeared intact.
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. Sample sizes were small, particularly for the long-term recovery and one-week abstinence groups. This limited the researchers’ statistical power, making it difficult to assess how other variables, such as sex differences or tobacco use, might influence brain metabolism.
The categories of light and heavy drinking were based on self-reported histories, which can sometimes be imprecise compared to objective medical markers. Additionally, the acetate was administered directly into a vein during the scan. This differs from real-world drinking, where acetate is produced gradually by the liver.
Mason also warned against drawing incorrect conclusions about drinking alcohol for a quick energy boost. “I have encountered two misinterpretations: just because acetate can be consumed for energy does not mean that alcohol is helpful when you are tired,” he said. “The process of getting from alcohol to acetate creates oxygen free radicals, hydrogen peroxide, and acetaldehyde, which is a powerful carcinogen and toxin. So, don’t drink alcohol in search of energy.”
Similarly, he cautioned against using household vinegar as a home remedy for withdrawal. “The second misinterpretation is that people should drink vinegar to help them stay sober,” Mason added. “To get the amount of acetate your body provides from a couple of margaritas, you would need to drink about a quart of grocery store vinegar. That will damage the enamel on your teeth and is a huge acid load that is hard on the throat and stomach.”
The authors suggest that the depressed acetate metabolism during early withdrawal might be a protective mechanism that limits the brain’s exposure to high acetate levels, or it could simply reflect temporary cellular sluggishness as the brain adjusts to the sudden absence of alcohol. Exploring how other alternative energy sources might smooth this transition could lead to new dietary or medical therapies for alcohol withdrawal.
“One practical outcome is another piece of evidence that alcohol dependence as a physical condition, one that can benefit from medical interventions,” Mason said. “I know that it’s difficult to stop, but the benefits are great, and there are FDA-approved medications proven to help people stop or reduce their drinking. The NIAAA web site has something called the Treatment Navigator to help people find resources.”
The study, “Reversible alterations of brain acetate metabolism associated with alcohol consumption,” was authored by Chathura Kumaragamage, Lihong Jiang, Gustavo A. Angarita, Robin A. de Graaf, Elizabeth Guidone, Anastasia Coppoli, Kevin L. Behar, Barbara I. Gulanski, Brian Pittman, Stuart A. Weinzimer, Douglas L. Rothman, John H. Krystal, and Graeme F. Mason.

Seven of my colleagues were killed in Gaza. There and in Ukraine, aid workers are no longer safe | José Andrés
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
14:00:01 UTC
23:00:01 KST

In times of war, the hard and vital work of supplying food, water and medicine has been protected by international agreements for almost 80 years. Yet those protections have been systematically and repeatedly ignored in the two most bloody wars of recent years: Ukraine and Gaza.
Russia has attacked healthcare targets in Ukraine more than 3,200 times since the full-scale invasion in February 2022, according to the World Health Organization: about twice a day on average. That includes many “double-tap” attacks on the same target in quick succession, which are especially lethal for first responders.
In April, the UN security council heard that in the past three years, at least 1,010 humanitarian workers had died in 21 countries. More than half of those were in Gaza and the West Bank. That is three times more than the 377 killed in the previous three years.
“This is not an accidental escalation,” said Tom Fletcher, the UN’s undersecretary-general for humanitarian affairs. “It is the collapse of protection.” This collapse of protection has led directly to the airstrikes on aid workers in Gaza, including seven of my own World Central Kitchen (WCK) team, who were killed by the IDF in April 2024 despite full cooperation and coordination with the military.
At the time, the IDF concluded that the attacks had been “a grave mistake” and a breach of its own standard operating procedures. It stated: “We consider the vital humanitarian activity of international aid organizations to be of utmost importance, and we will continue to work to coordinate and assist their activities, while ensuring their safety and safeguarding their lives.” The reserve colonel who ordered the strikes, Nochi Mendel, was dismissed for his actions.
However, these fine words were undercut by the IDF itself, when its military prosecutor decided last month not to open a criminal investigation into the airstrikes on our convoy. Now we understand, because of a Guardian investigation, that the targeting of the WCK convoy was the result of a military tactic of guilt by association. It means that lethal force can be triggered by suspicions, shadows, or simply prejudice. This undefined, unjustified and unlawful tactic is a mortal threat to all humanitarians. What are the protections under these conditions?
It is worth remembering why the fourth Geneva convention was created in 1949 and embraced by the world, with the express intention of protecting civilians in war and meeting basic humanitarian needs. In the immediate aftermath of the second world war, the scale of civilian suffering shocked the world’s conscience. Indeed, one of the key architects of the convention was Georges Cahen-Salvador, a French Jewish civil servant, whose family was imprisoned at the Drancy internment camp. They were being deported to Auschwitz in 1943 when they managed to escape to Switzerland. He was one of several survivors who drafted the fourth convention.
The convention’s assertions of shared values in war are not lost today, but they are struggling to survive.
David Ben-Gurion, Israel’s founding father, famously said: “The fate of Israel depends on two things: its strength and its righteousness.” It’s something that Israel’s military leaders like to quote, but their record falls far short. Humanitarian values are the foundation of righteousness; they are what separate responsible nation states from terrorist groups or rogue states who don’t care about civilian suffering. The protection of aid workers allows the world to ensure that civilians are cared for.
We might be numb to the sight of Russia disregarding our values. But we surely cannot tolerate the only democracy in the Middle East behaving the same way.
- 
  José Andrés is the founder of the food aid charity World Central Kitchen, and a Michelin-starred chef
