These 9 midterm races will decide control of 100-seat US Senate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
14:00:00 UTC
23:00:00 KST

Democrats need to pick up four seats from Republicans to win control of the 100-seat Senate in the midterm elections on November 3.
While voters will pick candidates in 35 states, independent analysts only see nine of those races as competitive.
Most of these contests take place in states that President Donald Trump won in 2024, but his approval rating stands at 33 percent, the lowest of his political career, according to Reuters/Ipsos polling.
Alaska
Incumbent Republican Senator Dan Sullivan faces two liabilities in his reelection campaign: a credible challenge from a Democrat and another person on the ballot with the same name.
Democrat Mary Peltola previously held the state's sole House seat for a single term and has campaigned as a centrist. She garnered 82,000 votes to Sullivan's 69,000 in the state's nonpartisan primary in August, in what could be an ominous sign for the incumbent.
Sullivan also will have to contend with another Republican, retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan, who got enough votes to advance to the November election despite Republican attempts to knock him off the ballot.
Peltola could also benefit from the state's ranked-choice voting system, which takes voters' second choices into account.
Polling has been sparse in this race, but analysts see it as a toss-up.
Georgia
Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff is running for reelection against Republican Representative Mike Collins, a conservative backed by Trump.
Georgia has emerged as a top battleground state. Trump narrowly won the state in 2024, while Ossoff, 39, narrowly won his seat in a 2021 runoff. Analysts see him as a possible 2028 presidential candidate.
In recent weeks, Collins has been under scrutiny for racist posts by a former aide, which his campaign has disavowed.
Most polls have shown Ossoff leading Collins, and nonpartisan analysts say he currently holds the advantage in this race.
Iowa
After a decade of Republican dominance, Iowa is home to competitive races this year, as the farm state struggles with high fuel prices.
Representative Ashley Hinson aims to keep the seat in Republican hands following the retirement of incumbent Senator Joni Ernst.
She faces state representative Josh Turek, a former Paralympic basketball player who has emphasised his bipartisan work in the state legislature.
Polls show a close race, and analysts say it should be one of the most competitive contests this fall.
Maine
Democrats scrambled in July to find a replacement for Graham Platner, the progressive oyster farmer and political newcomer who dropped out after facing accusations of sexual assault, which he denied. The party quickly coalesced around Troy Jackson, a former lumberjack and state legislator who shares Platner's progressive politics.
Jackson, 58, takes on incumbent Republican Senator Susan Collins, a moderate who occasionally breaks with her party.
First elected in 1996, Collins has won reelection easily even as the northeastern state has consistently backed Democratic presidential candidates.
Recent polls have shown Jackson holding a three- to four-percentage-point lead.
Michigan
Democrats are playing defence in Michigan, where they hope to retain the seat held by retiring Senator Gary Peters. A loss in this closely contested state would complicate their efforts to win control of the chamber.
Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive, faces lingering skepticism as he tries to consolidate support after narrowly defeating centrist Representative Haley Stevens in a bitter primary.
He faces Republican Mike Rogers, a former House member who lost a Senate race in 2024.
Polls show a close race, and nonpartisan analysts rate it a toss-up, saying El-Sayed's left-wing candidacy could give Rogers a greater opportunity to win independent voters.
New Hampshire
Republican John Sununu is running to return to the Senate, where he previously served from 2003 to 2009, while Democrats have nominated Representative Chris Pappas for this open seat.
Nonpartisan analysts say Pappas holds the edge.
North Carolina
Democrats have a good chance to pick up a seat in North Carolina, where incumbent Republican Senator Thom Tillis is retiring.
Opinion polls show former Democratic Governor Roy Cooper holding a steady lead over Republican operative Michael Whatley, a Trump ally who most recently chaired the Republican National Committee.
Cooper is well known to North Carolina voters, having won four races as state attorney general and two more as governor in 2016 and 2020, even as Trump carried the state in those years.
Whatley also has decades of experience in politics but has not previously run for office.
Ohio
Former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown is hoping voters in Ohio remember his long record of economic advocacy as he tries to win back his old job.
First elected in 2006, Brown was defeated by Republican Bernie Moreno in 2024, a year when Trump won the once-competitive state by 11 percentage points.
He is now trying to unseat incumbent Republican Senator Jon Husted, who was appointed to the seat in 2025 after then-Senator JD Vance resigned to serve as Trump's vice president. Husted previously served as lieutenant governor and secretary of state.
Ohio has trended steadily Republican over the past decade, but recent polls show Brown leading Husted by three to four percentage points and analysts view the race as a toss-up.
The winner of this race will serve the remainder of Vance's term, through January 2029.
Texas
This Republican-dominated state has emerged as a surprise battleground this year. Polls show a close race between Democrat James Talarico, a state representative and former seminary student, and Republican Ken Paxton, the state's attorney general.
Despite allegations of marital infidelity that nearly forced him from office in 2023, Paxton unseated incumbent Senator John Cornyn with Trump's backing in a divisive primary. Since then, he has struggled to raise money — forcing his party to spend money shoring up what would normally be considered a safe seat.
Talarico has sought to win over independents and disaffected Republicans. Analysts see this race as a toss-up.

Trump blamed for decline in Swiss travel to US
US President Donald Trump is contributing to a decline in travel to the United States among Swiss travellers.
After falling last year, bookings for the US dropped even further in the first half of 2026.
More
Explainer: How the new US tariffs are already impacting the Swiss economy
Between January and June, 120,000 Swiss travellers visited the US. That was 16.5% fewer than during the same period last year, according to Andrea Beffa, managing director of the Swiss Travel Association. Speaking to the AWP news agency on the sidelines of a press conference on Wednesday, she said the decline had accelerated.
More
US tariffs force Switzerland to rethink trade ties
The sharp downturn is continuing. Last year, the number of Swiss visitors to the US fell by 10.6% to just over 361,000.
Lowest level in two decades
The outlook is equally bleak. “If this trend continues for the rest of the year, around 300,000 arrivals from Switzerland can be expected in 2026,” Beffa said. That would be roughly in line with the number recorded in 2007.
+ How Trump is manoeuvring Switzerland closer to the EU
Over the past two years, since Trump began his second term in office, the US has lost around a quarter of its Swiss visitors. By comparison, 404,434 arrivals from Switzerland were recorded in 2024.
Scepticism grows
At the same time, scepticism towards the US has also increased, according to surveys conducted by insurer Allianz Partners.
“65% of Swiss respondents do not currently plan to travel to the US,” Pia Bodner, Head of Marketing and Products at Allianz Travel, said at a media briefing. “Last year, the figure was 53%.”
In addition, 7% of Swiss respondents said they intended to cancel a planned trip to the US, up from 2% a year earlier.
The increase in scepticism was surprising because “people have more or less become accustomed to the political situation in the US as it is”, the Allianz executive said.
There was only a slight countertrend: 9% of under-30s said they planned to travel to the US more often. The Allianz manager suggested this could be linked to lower air fares.

Ukroboronprom Reveals Designation of Palianytsia Missile-Drone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
13:59:26 UTC
22:59:26 KST

Ukroboronprom has revealed the designation of the Ukrainian-made Palianytsia missile-drone, which Ukraine’s Defense Forces use to strike targets in Russia.
The weapon was displayed under the designation UAV-290 at MSPO 2026, an international defense exhibition in Kielce, Poland.
Previously, the missile-drone was displayed at various exhibitions and events, sometimes as Palianytsia and other times as UAV-290.
It has now been officially confirmed for the first time that the two names refer to the same weapon, developed and manufactured by the state-owned Luch Design Bureau.
UAV-290 Palianytsia is designed to autonomously strike various stationary ground targets at the enemy’s tactical depth.
The missile-drone is equipped with a turbojet engine that provides a cruising speed of up to 800 km/h.
Palianytsia is launched from a trailer or semitrailer using a solid-fuel booster.
After launch, it switches to autonomous flight using an integrated INS+GPS navigation system.
The UAV-290 carries a 100 kg warhead and weighs 350 kg. Its stated range is 650 km.
The missile-drone is 3.5 meters long, with a 1.7-meter wingspan.
The manufacturer states that navigation and terminal guidance are performed using a combination of an autonomous inertial navigation system, immune to electronic warfare, and satellite navigation to correct deviations.
In August 2026, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky reported that Ukraine’s Defense Forces had used, among other weapons, the UAV-290 to strike a Russian Navy base and port in Novorossiysk.

Supreme Court to examine marital rape exception under IPC, BNS
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
13:59:08 UTC
22:59:08 KST

NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Wednesday agreed to examine whether the law excluding non-consensual sexual intercourse by a husband against his wife from the definition of rape can withstand constitutional scrutiny. The court is hearing challenges to the marital rape exception under both the Indian Penal Code (IPC) and the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS).The issue came before a Bench hearing a batch of petitions challenging Exception 2 to Section 375 of the IPC. The pleas also question the corresponding exception under Section 63 of the BNS and seek its reading down to allow non-consensual sexual acts within marriage to be treated as rape.The Bench indicated that the matter involved a fundamental question about the limits of judicial interpretation, particularly whether courts can permit prosecution for conduct that Parliament has expressly excluded from the offence.The court also raised the question of whether an individual could be prosecuted for marital rape while the constitutional challenge to the statutory exception is yet to be decided.
“We would definitely protect the victims but is it within the domain to prosecute a person where there is direct exclusion of a person under 375,” the court observed.The proceedings also covered an appeal arising from a March 2022 Karnataka high court ruling, which refused to quash rape charges against a husband accused of sexually assaulting his wife.Senior advocate Indira Jaising, appearing in the appeal, submitted that the Karnataka high court had held that prosecution could proceed where a wife was treated as a “sexual slave”. She also pointed to the subsequent raising of the age of consent from 16 to 18 years.Senior advocate Karuna Nundy argued that the constitutional challenge would require the court to consider whether the exception could be read down or interpreted in a manner consistent with constitutional guarantees.The Bench said the question before it was ultimately one of constitutional validity rather than social morality.“What is social morality? When people speak through their representatives - what we do is test it with the Constitution. It’s for the people to decide. Court says it can only speak its constitutional language,” the court observed.The Bench also made clear that it would not prejudge individual criminal proceedings while considering the larger constitutional challenge.
“We don’t want to pronounce on that. We will take up constitutionality. We will examine the question,” the Court said.Counsel also raised questions about the BNS provisions relating to gang rape and the exception available to a husband.Solicitor general Tushar Mehta, appearing for the Union government, said its counter-affidavit had already been filed. The court directed that it be circulated among all counsel within two days.The constitutional challenge will now be heard in detail on a date to be fixed.

PARIS — The National Rally, the party of French far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen, fired a volunteer security official on Wednesday after body camera footage emerged showing the individual, a municipal police officer, making racist remarks.
The clip, published by local daily Midi Libre, showed a group of local police officers in the southern city of Carcassonne — which the National Rally took control of during the French local elections in March — using racial and homophobic slurs and uttering a series of hateful comments about minorities, migrants and women. The individual was not named and appears blurred in photos and video.
In a statement, the city said the clip was from 2025 — before Mayor Christophe Barthès took office— and that Barthès unequivocally condemned the remarks.
Advertisement
“Proceedings will be initiated, and the sanctions will match the seriousness of the facts,” the statement said.
The Carcassonne local police did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment.
The National Rally said in a statement that the volunteer was “immediately removed” from his role and “expelled” from the party after its leadership learned of the video. The prosecutor’s office in Carcassonne told the AFP news agency it had opened an investigation on the basis of the footage.
But the party’s opponents said the incident was evidence of the National Rally’s inability to fully extract itself from its racist, xenophobic and antisemitic roots. Le Pen’s father founded the party, then known as the National Front, alongside a ragtag group of political misfits andNazi collaborators. The elder Le Pen was repeatedly convicted for hate speech, including downplaying the Holocaust.

Yet her party has frequently been forced to address offensive remarks made by lower-ranking officials and members, especially during election cycles.
“This is what France would look like if it were led by the National Rally,” Gabriel Attal, the candidate for French President Emmanuel Macron’s Renaissance party wrote on X.
Olivier Faure, the leader of the center-left Socialist Party who is vying for his party’s backing in the presidential race in a primary contest, said on X that voters should not give the National Rally “the keys to France.”

An American startup will begin producing low-cost cruise missiles in Germany next year
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:58:04 EEST
22:58:04 KST

An American startup will begin producing low-cost cruise missiles in Germany next year
Kyiv • UNN
The American company Covenant plans to produce low-cost Anthem missiles in Germany starting in 2027. The company aims to manufacture 5,000 units each year.
The American defense startup Covenant plans to begin mass production of low-cost cruise missiles in Germany in early 2027 to meet demand from European countries seeking to procure long-range weapons to counter the growing threat from Russia, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
Details
Covenant said that, at present, the company has signed one contract to supply its Anthem missile in Europe and is negotiating with other potential customers, but declined to specify which countries are involved. The first deliveries of this ground-launched missile are expected in early 2027.
"Our goal is to reach 5,000 units by 2028 or, at a minimum, achieve a production rate of 5,000 missiles per year during 2028," Covenant co-founder and CEO Michael Kaufman told Reuters in an interview, referring to the company's production facility.
Germany and the United Kingdom are developing a long-range missile with a range of more than 2,000 kilometers (which would allow it to reach Moscow), seeking to reduce their dependence on the United States in the defense sphere. Currently, the only long-range precision weapon Berlin possesses is the Taurus cruise missile; Germany's stockpile of these missiles amounts to approximately 600 units.
The publication notes that, amid declining trust among European countries in Washington and growing demands for the use of weapons that do not contain American components, Covenant said it procures most of the components for Anthem missiles assembled in Europe directly on the European continent.
"The supply chain (for the facility in Saxony) does not depend on the United States... Less than 5% of the components come from outside Europe, and our goal is to reduce this figure to zero," Kaufman said.
The media outlet adds that the Anthem missile could become a new option for countries seeking to expand their long-range weapons arsenals, which currently consist of a limited number of expensive missiles—a quantity considered insufficient to confront the enormous arsenals of a country such as Russia. According to Covenant, the Anthem missile not only addresses the need for mass deliveries but is also a more affordable option compared with weapons such as the Tomahawk manufactured by Raytheon (RTX.N): the cost of a single Tomahawk missile runs into the hundreds of thousands of dollars (between $400,000 and $600,000).
The American defense giant Raytheon plans to increase Tomahawk production to 1,000 units per year; currently, annual output ranges from 60 to 90 missiles.
Covenant also said that the company is working on a sea-launched version of the Anthem missile; it will be equipped with a warhead weighing more than 200 kg and designed to strike targets both on land and at sea.
Covenant did not disclose Anthem's range, but said that the missile is ideally suited for use in the European theater of operations.
"To win a war or deter an adversary, it is necessary to have a sufficient arsenal and depth of resources to conduct combat operations... for many days, weeks, or even months," Abby Denburg, president and chief development officer of Covenant, told Reuters.
According to Kaufman's estimates, Germany and other European countries would need tens of thousands of long-range missiles to confront a distant adversary with a large territory.

Met police launch inquiry into alleged overseas donations to Reform UK
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
13:56:03 UTC
22:56:03 KST

The financial scandal around Reform UK has deepened as police expanded their investigation into allegations of illegal foreign donations and the elections watchdog said it was considering regulatory steps.
Police confirmed on Wednesday they would broaden their inquiries into Reform after Channel 4 News broadcast an undercover sting by a group called Verbatim, in which a reporter posed as a foreign donor seeking to fund Reform.
The Electoral Commission also said on Wednesday that it was “considering all relevant information and regulatory steps” in parallel with the police inquiry.
Two of Nigel Farage’s close advisers, Dan Jukes and James Orr, resigned last week after footage was broadcast showing them discussing ways to get around electoral law with a reporter posing as the son of a foreign businessman.
The fake US-based donor also paid for more than £30,000 of polling intended to benefit Reform that was not publicly declared. In the footage, Jukes also appeared to suggest the impermissible US donor could contribute through his UK-based son as a way to get round election law banning foreign donations.
The police investigation will form part of an existing inquiry into Reform’s political funding before July 2024, including allegations that it took impermissible donations.
It means the party is facing intense scrutiny on multiple fronts, with a separate parliamentary standards investigation into Farage’s gift of £5m received from an overseas donor, first revealed by the Guardian, and calls for a wider investigation into his undeclared funding from his unpaid aide, the fraudster George Cottrell.
It also raises the prospect that Farage and other senior figures linked to the party could end up being interviewed by detectives, although the force stressed that no arrests had been made so far, and no one had been interviewed under caution, in relation to the latest allegations.
The initial police investigation into Reform, launched in February last year, relates to allegations about £500,000 donations to Reform UK before the 2024 election from Fiona Cottrell, the mother of George Cottrell. Both have been interviewed under caution.
The financial scandals overshadowed Reform’s autumn conference last week, with the party beginning to slip in some polls into second place behind Labour and opinion surveys suggesting voters are have noticed stories about the party’s funding.
A Metropolitan police spokesperson said: “Following a broadcast by Channel 4 News on Thursday 3 September, the Met received a number of reports relating to donations and polling involving a political party.
 “Detectives have assessed the information provided and determined that there are potential offences requiring investigation.
“The potential offences are similar in nature to matters already under investigation by the Met’s special enquiry team relating to donations made to the same political party. As a result, these matters will form part of that ongoing investigation. 
 “Detectives are now seeking to obtain relevant footage relating to the broadcast and are liaising with the Electoral Commission and Crown Prosecution Service as inquiries progress.”
A Reform UK spokesperson said the party “denies any wrongdoing and will fully cooperate with the investigation”. It added: “We won’t be commenting further while a live investigation is under way.” Jukes and Orr have both also denied wrongdoing.
In the undercover investigation, the journalists posed as a potential Reform supporter and his wealthy American father, an impermissible donor, who paid for £30,000 of polling commissioned by Reform and which benefited the party when it was published in national newspapers.
If found to have been a donation in kind and made from abroad, it would have been impermissible as it was a foreign source and was not registered with the Electoral Commission.
Farage was subsequently caught on camera in a meeting with the fake US donor in Clacton where he appears to be celebrating the success of the poll, saying it was “amazing” and provided “bang for buck”. He said: “It worked. Boom.”
In footage of another meeting, Jukes appeared to suggest to the fake UK-based supporter that his US-based father could make a substantial donation by channelling it through the son.
When the possible structure was explained to Farage, footage of a meeting between him and the fake donors shows him saying: “Thank you both.” Farage has since said he was not listening.
At another point, Orr appeared to suggest that the fake UK-based donor and his US father might secure a meeting with Farage if he could promise a five- or six-figure sum. The meeting later took place in Clacton with Jukes over oysters and champagne.
In a different clip, Orr can be heard saying of the poll funding arrangement that Farage “doesn’t know, won’t know” and it was the kind of thing he would “rather not know”. At one point the footage shows him saying it was “totally legit” and with “nothing untowards about it at all”.
The Guardian reported last week that the police were highly likely to launch a full investigation into the allegations.
Reform initially dismissed the investigation by Verbatim as a hoax and Farage responded by reading out a legal statement in which he described it as “a little local difficulty” and an “an exercise in entrapment”.
Farage claimed Orr and Jukes had merely been “contractors” who engaged in “loose pub talk, including a couple of boasts that simply were not true” – despite Jukes having been the Reform UK leader’s very close adviser for more than decade.
A spokesperson for Verbatim, which was founded by the Centre for Climate Reporting, said the group would cooperate with the police investigation.
The initial police investigation into Reform was launched in February last year after a referral from the Electoral Commission. Lawyers acting for George Cottrell, who lives in Montenegro, have previously said he had no comment to make. In a prior letter to the Guardian, the lawyers stated that “his mother’s donations have been entirely her own decision, and are a matter for her”.
Both George and Fiona Cottrell were previously interviewed under criminal caution by Scotland Yard detectives. They attended voluntarily.
Fiona Cottrell, who lives in Worcestershire and once dated King Charles, has not responded to questions from the media about any issues involving her support for the Reform party.
Lisa Smart, the Liberal Democrat Cabinet Office spokesperson, said: “Thanks to Channel 4’s investigation we all saw with our own eyes Farage’s true colours … we welcome the Met police’s criminal inquiry into their finances, and if proven, Nigel Farage and his cronies should face the full force of the law.”

Iran threatens maritime sanctions on vessels entering newly declared zone without authorization
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
13:55:47 UTC
22:55:47 KST

Şahin Demir
09 September 2026•Update: 09 September 2026
Iran said Wednesday that enemy and commercial vessels entering a newly designated maritime zone without Tehran’s authorization would face sanctions, according to Iranian media reports.
IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohibi said any enemy vessel or commercial ship entering the area without coordination with Iranian authorities would be placed on a sanctions list, the semi-official Fars News Agency reported.
He said the measure would mean Iran would halt the provision of maritime, insurance and support services to those vessels, and that they would remain barred from receiving the services even if they later transit the Strait of Hormuz.
The remarks follow an announcement by Iran’s Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei that Tehran would declare a new restricted zone outside the strait.
Rezaei said the zone would begin from what Tehran describes as the US Navy’s “blockade line” and extend into parts of the Arabian Gulf.
Any vessel entering the new zone without Iranian permission with the intention of passing through the Strait of Hormuz would be added to Iran’s sanctions list, he said.
In separate remarks by Iran’s Student News Network, Mohibi said that although the fighting with the world’s “greatest apparent powers” had ended at certain stages, “the nature of the war continues.”
He claimed that the war had, for the first time, inflicted “strategic damage” directly on the US and affected its security and economic calculations.
Mohibi said if the enemy wanted the situation to end, it must completely halt the war and refrain from renewed threats.
He also listed several other demands, including the withdrawal of the Israeli army from Lebanon, an end to the blockade of Yemen, the release of $24 billion in frozen Iranian assets, and an end to interference in Iran’s nuclear and missile capabilities.
“We have reached a point where if the enemy hits two or three of our targets, we respond firmly against 20 targets,” said Mohibi.
The remarks come amid continuing US-Iran hostilities and heightened maritime tensions in and around the Strait of Hormuz.
Earlier Wednesday, the IRGC said its naval forces targeted two US vessels and eight oil tankers in response to American attacks on five Iranian oil tankers.
The Strait of Hormuz has emerged as a key flashpoint in the conflict, with Tehran maintaining restrictions on maritime traffic and demanding that vessels coordinate their passage with Iranian authorities.

Switzerland-EU electricity agreement: the key issues it must tackle

Kremlin War Drone Flies 30 Minutes Over Romania Unimpeded by NATO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
13:55:01 UTC
22:55:01 KST

A jet-propelled Russian war drone penetrated at least 50 kilometers (31 miles) into NATO-defended airspace over Romania and flew there for about a half an hour before being lost by alliance radars and returning unmolested to Moldova, Romanian and Moldovan news and official sources reported on Wednesday.
The Russian military aircraft’s extended violation of Atlantic Alliance airspace took place on Tuesday afternoon as NATO was running a massive air surveillance and defense exercise nearby with fighters, air tankers and AWACS air surveillance planes from at least six NATO member states participating.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Notwithstanding the beefed-up NATO air presence in the region and two Romanian F-16 fighter jets launched specifically to intercept the encroaching Russian robot plane, the drone was not interfered by NATO air and ground forces and ended its combat sortie by blowing up in a Moldovan farm field.
The seemingly unimpeded excursion by the Russian Air Force strike drone into and out of Romanian airspace came in the wake of a July 30 penetration by a Russian cruise missile over Poland. In that incident a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile that had been tracked by Ukrainian air defenses for more than two hours flew across central and western Ukraine and approximately 100 kilometers (62 miles) into Poland, before impacting the ground and without interception by NATO forces.
                                                                                                                                                                         
Russian Strikes Could Add Up to 0.6 Points to Ukraine’s Inflation, NBU Says
NATO/Polish air defenses failed to launch fighters before the weapon had already crashed deep inside Poland, radar data and radio transmission data subsequently published by Ukraine’s Air Force showed. On Aug. 16 a Russian drone flying into Romanian airspace from Moldova was detected by NATO air defenses and intercepted by a pair of Spanish F-18s and shot down.
According to Moldovan and Romanian media, on Tuesday, Moldovan and NATO air defense radars detected a Russian Shahed drone entering Moldovan airspace from Ukraine several minutes before NATO’s air frontier was violated. Moldovan air defense subsequently identified it as a jet-powered Shahed drone, an Iran-designed flying wing usually carrying a 50-100-kilogram (110-220-pound) explosive warhead.
Russia earlier that day launched a major missile/drone strike with a reported 166 Shahed-type drones, 32 cruise missiles, and one-to-two dozen ballistic and hypersonic missiles, targeting primarily the capital Kyiv and the seaport Odesa. Ukrainian air defenses claimed shoot-downs of 149 drones and 22 cruise missiles. Ukraine since early 2025 has suffered a critical shortage of interceptor missiles, the only weapon able to knock down a ballistic or a hypersonic missile.
The single Russian drone entering Romanian airspace according to a Romanian Defense Ministry statement breached the Moldovan air frontier at between 4:20-4:33 p.m. local time, about eight hours after the massive air battle over Ukraine had ended. One of Europe’s poorest countries, Moldova has no air force and only obsolete ground-based air defense systems to protect its airspace.
NATO radars based in Romania and possibly aboard surveillance aircraft detected the drone in Moldovan airspace west of the Moldovan capital of Chișinău at 4:33 p.m., and registered the Russian aircraft’s violation of Romanian airspace at 4:37 p.m., with a heading in the direction of the northeastern Romanian city of Iași. The calculated speed of the aircraft – between 600-750 kph (380-460 mph) was well above maximum speed for older propeller-driven Shahed drones, and consistent with reported speeds of more modern jet-propelled Shahed drones.
Romania scrambled a pair of Spanish Air Force F-18s stationed at Mihail Kogălniceanu serving as part of a standing NATO air-policing operation, and Romanian authorities locked down Iași airport and issued air raid warnings in four Romanian districts.
According to the Romanian Defense Ministry statement, the Spanish fighters were unable to intercept the Russian Shahed and radar contact was lost with it around 5:02 p.m., while the transgressing aircraft was near the administrative border of Romania’s Iași and Botoșani districts.
At 5:08 p.m., Romanian radar detected the same aircraft in Moldovan airspace, by its heading seemingly having exited Romanian airspace from the Iași district. NATO radars lost track of the drone at about 5:14 p.m. while the aircraft was near the Moldovan city Bălți.
At about 5:26 p.m., Moldovan authorities received a report, quickly re-reported via Moldovan news platforms, that a drone-line aircraft had crashed in a field near Mihăileni Vechi, in Rîșcani district, igniting a small fire. Romanian authorities confirmed the drone had crashed in Moldova about 25 kilometers (16 miles) east of the Romanian border.
The Russian war drone probably spent about a half an hour flying above NATO territory and through NATO’s air defense network and penetrated at least 50 kilometers (31 miles) into Romanian airspace before returning unmolested to Moldova, Romanian, Moldovan and Ukrainian news and open-source intelligence (OSINT) reports of the incident agreed. Prior to Tuesday the most recent reported failed intercepts of Russian drones by NATO, likewise over Romania, took place on July 24, 25 and 26.
According to open-source flight tracking platforms and regional OSINT monitors, the latest Tuesday failed interception by NATO of encroaching Russian attack drones took place at the same time the alliance was running a major air operation over and near the western Black Sea to help airmen from at least five NATO states practice sustained air surveillance and defense.
Among the NATO warplanes confirmed participating in the exercise was a French Air Force E-3F AWACS “flying radar” (registration 36-CB, callsign FAF902), a pair of A330 MRTT flying tankers (one identified as Dutch Air Force), the Italian itamilradar.com reported.
Along with those support aircraft, two French Dassault Rafale fighter jets, two Belgian F-16 fighter jets, two Polish F-16 fighter jets, a Turkish Bayraktar Akinci heavy drone and a French Air Force Breuguet Br. 1150 Atlantique II maritime patrol plane participated in the day-long NATO exercise mostly over waters east of the Danube Delta, the Ukraine-based Crimean Wind reported, citing local sources on Tuesday.
The Russian drone flying almost to Iași committed a confirmed violation of Romanian airspace about 200 kilometers (124 miles) to the north, about a 10-15 minutes’ flying time from the French, Belgian and Polish fighter jets participating in the training, and at close range to the advanced detection systems aboard the French AWACS that had been practicing air defense and air combat control operations, Kyiv Post review of published flight tracks found.
NATO conducts intermittent patrols over the western and central Black Sea usually using one to three aircraft for reconnaissance and one or two fighter jets for security and defense. If confirmed, Tuesday’s concentration of 11 combat, air watch and air tanker planes over the western Black Sea would be the most substantial combined air operation in that sector conducted by NATO in memory.
Romania’s armed forces parallel with the NATO operation on Tuesday conducted an exercise called SAREX 2026, during which national inter-agency maritime search-and-rescue units practiced response to distress calls. The training involving helicopters, C-130 search planes and seagoing cutters took place in Romanian territorial waters east of Cape Aurora.

In an earlier update on Tuesday, officials said they were responding to the “collapse of a driveway” and a resulting gas leak, which had been reported at about 5.45am local time. The Los Angeles county sheriff’s department and Los Angeles county fire department closed the private road and identified the gas leak.
Actor Nicolas Cage is reportedly the owner of the home where the sinkhole formed. Cage purchased the home in 2024, the New York Times noted. A representative for Cage did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
“Conditions are continuing to be evaluated, and the full extent of the impacts is not yet known,” Malibu city officials said on Tuesday evening, warning that the sinkhole “poses imminent danger to the homes and residents along Sea Level Drive”.
By Tuesday evening, 31 properties were under an evacuation order. Officials said that seven homes had been red-tagged because of “hazardous conditions resulting from the sinkhole” while another 24 residences were red-tagged “due to the loss of safe vehicular access”. Sheriff’s deputies notified residents in person and a digital alert had been issued.
Gas service to the affected area was shut off by Tuesday evening and city officials warned that water service “may also be discontinued as conditions warrant”.
They also cautioned that “conditions are likely to worsen with forecasted high tides and rains”. Additionally, Post-tropical Cyclone Marie could continue to bring “increased rainfall and high surf” to the area.
The National Weather Service said on Tuesday that “swells generated by Marie will continue to affect portions of the coast of the Baja California Peninsula and southern California for the next couple of days”.
A coastal flood advisory had been in effect until 11pm local time on Tuesday, Malibu officials said. A temporary shelter was also established by the American Red Cross at Malibu high school.
City officials said that emergency personnel access “is severely constrained and may be impassable, due to the large portion of the road that has collapsed”. They said that as of Tuesday evening, the “intact portion of the roadway is too narrow to accommodate emergency response vehicles, including fire engines and other large apparatus, creating a substantial risk to public safety and emergency response capabilities”.

Scientists find a bone-building switch that could fight osteoporosis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
13:52:53 UTC
22:52:53 KST

Scientists find a bone-building switch that could fight osteoporosis
- Date:
- September 9, 2026
- Source:
- Universität Leipzig
- Summary:
- An experimental compound called AP503 significantly strengthened bones in mice by activating GPR133, a receptor that boosts bone formation while slowing bone loss. Because the same treatment has also been linked to stronger muscles, researchers see intriguing potential for combating age-related decline and osteoporosis.
- Share:
Osteoporosis, a condition that weakens bones and increases the risk of fractures, affects millions of people and remains a major challenge for doctors seeking safe treatments that can be used over long periods. In Germany alone, about six million people are affected, most of them women.
Because existing therapies can have limitations and side effects, researchers are looking for new biological targets that could lead to more effective ways of preserving or rebuilding bone. Scientists at Leipzig University have now identified one such target in GPR133, a receptor that appears to play an important role in keeping bones strong.
A Little-Known Receptor With a Major Role in Bone Health
GPR133 belongs to a group known as adhesion G protein-coupled receptors. These receptors sit on the surface of cells and help them respond to signals from their surroundings. Although this family of receptors is still not fully understood, the new findings suggest GPR133 is closely involved in the processes that build and maintain healthy bone.
"If this receptor is impaired by genetic changes, mice show signs of loss of bone density at an early age - similar to osteoporosis in humans. Using the substance AP503, which was only recently identified via a computer-assisted screen as a stimulator of GPR133, we were able to significantly increase bone strength in both healthy and osteoporotic mice," explains Professor Ines Liebscher, lead investigator of the study from the Rudolf Schönheimer Institute of Biochemistry at the Faculty of Medicine.
The results point to GPR133 as a potentially valuable target for future osteoporosis treatments. The researchers found that stimulating the receptor with AP503 increased bone strength not only in healthy mice, but also in mice with osteoporosis-like bone loss.
How GPR133 Helps Build Stronger Bones
Inside bone tissue, GPR133 responds to physical forces and interactions between nearby bone cells. When the receptor is activated, it sets off signaling that changes the balance between the cells that build bone and those that break it down.
Bone-forming cells (osteoblasts) are responsible for producing new bone tissue. Bone-resorbing cells (osteoclasts), by contrast, remove old bone as part of the skeleton's normal cycle of renewal. Healthy bones depend on maintaining the right balance between these two processes.
Activation of GPR133 encourages the activity of osteoblasts while reducing the activity of osteoclasts. This shifts the balance toward stronger and more durable bone.
AP503 appears to imitate the natural process that activates GPR133. That raises the possibility that the compound could eventually be used to increase bone strength or help restore bone that has already been weakened. One potential application would be osteoporosis associated with menopause, when declining hormone levels can accelerate bone loss in women.
Potential Benefits for Both Bone and Muscle
The findings could have broader implications because AP503 may affect more than the skeleton.
In an earlier study, researchers at Leipzig University had already found that activation with AP503 also strengthens skeletal muscle.
"The newly demonstrated parallel strengthening of bone once again highlights the great potential this receptor holds for medical applications in an aging population," says Dr. Juliane Lehmann, lead author of the study and a researcher at the Rudolf Schönheimer Institute of Biochemistry.
A treatment capable of improving both bone and muscle strength could be especially relevant for older adults, who often experience declines in both tissues at the same time. Maintaining stronger muscles can also support mobility and stability, while stronger bones can reduce vulnerability to fractures.
The Leipzig team is now pursuing several follow-up projects aimed at understanding GPR133 more fully. Researchers are also investigating whether AP503 could have applications in other diseases and are continuing to examine the receptor's wider functions throughout the body.
Leipzig's Longstanding Research Into GPR Receptors
For more than a decade, Leipzig University has made adhesion G protein-coupled receptors a major research priority through Collaborative Research Center 1423, Structural Dynamics of GPCR Activation and Signaling.
The program focuses on understanding how these receptors change shape, become activated, and transmit signals inside cells. Leipzig University is internationally recognized as a leading center for research in this area.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Universität Leipzig. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Juliane Lehmann, Hui Lin, Zihao Zhang, Maren Wiermann, Albert M. Ricken, Franziska Brinkmann, Jana Brendler, Christian Ullmann, Luisa Bayer, Sandra Berndt, Anja Penk, Nadine Winkler, Franz Wolfgang Hirsch, Thomas Fuhs, Josef Käs, Peng Xiao, Torsten Schöneberg, Martina Rauner, Jin-Peng Sun, Ines Liebscher. The mechanosensitive adhesion G protein-coupled receptor 133 (GPR133/ADGRD1) enhances bone formation. Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy, 2025; 10 (1) DOI: 10.1038/s41392-025-02291-y

Hiking in the Holyland: A new year brings a change in the air
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
13:52:42 UTC
22:52:42 KST

There’s a change happening out there. I know this because I’m a sunrise person. For the past few months, dawn has been hard to come by. In summertime, the heat arrives early in the day and with intensity – it can feel oppressive by six in the morning.
Last week that changed. The weather doesn’t always cooperate here in Israel, but the seasonal clock is reliable, and darkness has begun to gain ground again. It’s getting lighter later every morning. With our recent bout of rainy weather, I’ve had two signs of fall at once: darkened skies and a cool breeze as I set out on my morning runs.
When I see clouds outside at dawn, I lace my shoes with lightning speed. I head up toward the hills past the synagogue, where the shofar pours through an open window like an alarm clock announcing the shifting season.
Although both Rosh Hashanah and Passover are referred to in our tradition as a new year, the fall holiday season couldn’t look more physically different from our springtime festivities. In Tishrei, the land of Israel isn’t green, or boisterous, or painted in hues of fragrant flowers. It’s uniformly golden and dusty. The aroma of sweet figs hangs low in the air.
Rather than calling our attention to the world of possibility outdoors, this season invites introspection and contemplation, a preparation for the quiet, determined growth of the long year ahead.
The world treats Autumn as an ending, Judaism sees it as an opening
It’s strange, when you think about it, that this should feel like a beginning at all. The school year starts now, but that’s an invention of the last century or two.
Agriculturally, this is an ending: the last fruit coming off the trees, the grain already gathered and stored.
The rest of the world treats autumn as the year winding down.
We treat it as the year opening up. I’ve been wondering whether there’s something real underneath that, or whether we’ve simply learned to lean into what we’re told to feel.
The Torah is of two minds about it
Standing in Egypt on the eve of the Exodus, God tells Moses and Aaron: “This month shall be for you the beginning of months; it shall be the first month of the year for you” (Exodus 12:2). That is Nisan, in the spring. The year begins with freedom.
And yet, a few chapters later, describing the pilgrimage festivals, the same book places the autumn holiday at “the Feast of Ingathering, at the going out of the year” (Exodus 23:16), and later at “the turning of the year” (Exodus 34:22). A year going out. A year turning over. In autumn.
Stranger still is what the Torah does not say. The day we call Rosh Hashanah is never called that. It appears only as the first day of “the seventh month,” a sacred occasion “commemorated with loud blasts” (Leviticus 23:24). The seventh month, which is somehow also the beginning of the year.
The usual resolution is that two calendars run at once. One counts the life of a nation and begins with the Exodus. The other counts the life of the earth and mankind, and begins with Rosh Hashanah. But growing up outside of Israel, I never fully grasped what it meant for the calendar of creation to begin in autumn.
What crystallized it for me was living here long enough to watch this calendar at work.
There’s no clean break in an Israeli autumn. No frost, no changing leaves, none of the sweater weather and pumpkin lattes so prevalent in the United States.
While camping in northern Israel a couple of weeks ago, I lay awake under a star-filled sky trying to figure out what season it was exactly. Sleeping in our tents on the dusty ground, we enjoyed a cool breeze at night.
That day, we had seen grapes heavy on the vine on a nearby nature trail. Olives were everywhere, still green and hard in their clusters. It was clearly going to be a good year for olives.
Here, summer just sort of bleeds into fall. The changes are almost imperceptible – ripe fruit, more migratory birds. The earth itself has settled into seeming dormancy, dusty and cracked from five rainless months.
But a plot of earth at its most barren is just a field ready for planting, for human effort, and the hope of divine blessing. So the feeling isn’t invented after all. Here, the agricultural year really does begin now, in the dust, before a single drop has fallen. Rosh Hashanah coincides with the season that asks us to plan diligently and to put our faith in God at the same time.
Rambam said the call of the shofar is there to awaken us from our slumber. During this new year, we can tune in to the rhythm offered so naturally by our surroundings here in Israel. Just like those empty fields, we are ready and waiting for the slow growth we aspire to in the long year ahead.
The writer is the author of From Southerner to Settler: Unexpected Lessons from the Land of Israel and the founder of Hiking the Holyland.

Swarming the battlefield: Elbit-FUSE reveals mass drone and robot armies as IDF plans new AI branch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
13:52:32 UTC
22:52:32 KST

The Jerusalem Post and a limited number of other media outlets on Wednesday visited the Elbit-FUSE facility for building mass-scale robot and drone armies.
The visit was timed to coincide with Elbit-FUSE’s unveiling of a range of new and updated products, enabling small numbers of human soldiers to direct dozens or even hundreds of robots and drones to perform defensive and offensive functions in large-scale swarms.
Imagine hundreds of drones combining with dozens of tank-style autonomous vehicles and smaller tactical bat-shaped, dog-shaped, and otherwise specialized robots to defend a border or take over an enemy urban neighborhood.
The drones provide air cover, the autonomous tank-style vehicles provide tactical firepower, and the smaller robots enter structures where the enemy forces are hiding to defeat them up close or neutralize their booby traps without a single soldier setting foot in the neighborhood.
This is the vision Elbit-FUSE presented on Wednesday. The company did not enter this arena in a vacuum. Ukraine announced in July that it had reached a production rate of 10 million small tactical drones per year and was looking to double that volume.
Drones, autonomous weaponry increasingly defining global warfare
China, the United States, and others are all starting to mass-produce drones and robots in astronomically larger quantities than in the past.
In line with these developments, IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir on Tuesday night announced that by Hanukkah (December), the IDF would have opened an entirely new branch to focus on robots, drones, and AI battle forces.
“Military forces are entering a new operational era in which combat effectiveness will increasingly depend not only on autonomous platforms themselves, but also on the ability to integrate and coordinate large numbers of autonomous systems within existing maneuver forces in real time,” Eyal Dahan, CEO of FUSE, said. FUSE is a recently developed Elbit unit focusing on these issues, having combined at least four other related entities into one.
“FUSE was established to deliver that capability today – combining autonomous platforms, operational AI, and scalable One2Many command capabilities into integrated operational solutions that can be rapidly deployed and integrated into modern combat formations,” Dahan explained.
Speaking at a private briefing on Wednesday, he explained that even mass swarms of robots and drones would not completely replace human soldiers.
Other Elbit officials clarified to the Post that, on defense, fewer human soldiers could be needed in general to manage the autonomous vehicle swarms.
In contrast, on attack, the officials explained that a larger number of soldiers could be required, depending on the mission.
As an ethical matter, Elbit officials said that humans would and must remain in the loop to sign off on targeting decisions and reduce collateral harm to civilians.
In that sense, the AI systems installed in Elbit’s myriad types of drones and robots, including extremely advanced sensors for distinguishing combatants from civilians, are still not the final line for approving an attack.
If an attack was in an area where few civilians and sensitive items were known to be in play, fewer human soldiers might need to be involved.
But if an attack was against a highly sensitive location or one where many civilians could be at risk if the strike was not precise, then more soldiers would be involved to analyze the situation, as currently occurs.
At the facility, the Post saw five different versions of the Firefox drone, with each version having different uses, abilities in day vs nighttime, and varying price ranges depending on whether a client-buyer seeks cheaper, less fancy machines or smarter, high-end ones.
Some drones might cost as little as $2,000, while others might be in the hundreds of thousands of dollars.
Large variety of machines in production
The Post also saw FPV drones; drones disguised as items in nature, something which has been previously reported on; machines with shorter and longer range capabilities; and machines with laser-guided capabilities
In another section of the facility, the Post witnessed multiple stages of drone and robot assembly.
Some Elbit-FUSE technicians were assembling single parts, such as cameras or wings; others were meeting to discuss ongoing technical issues; and others were assembling all of the many parts of a drone or a robot.
Many dozens of robots and drones were already assembled on shelves, and many others were secured in special wrapping material for delivery.
There were special rooms for simulating intense wind environments, as well as others for handling special laser-related issues.
These laser-related issues are important but not as complex as those in a different Elbit facility that the Post visited in June, which is at the heart of Elbit’s most complex laser production.
FUSE has 160 employees, with 110 at the main facility which the Post visited, of whom around 65% are engineers, with many others being programmers or having other special skills, all at just one subsidiary of Elbit’s much larger operations.
Dahan emphasized that having many engineers available was critical to constantly updating each product, noting that one drone had been updated four times in the last three years to stay on the cutting edge of developing technologies.
A major focus of the FUSE product launch was its One2Many operational capabilities, which are powered by a unified AI operating system enabling centralized coordination of autonomous swarms and distributed aerial and ground formations at scale.
FUSE said that at the core of the portfolio is Dominion-X, “an AI-powered unified operating system enabling One2Many operations in GNSS-denied environments, supported by advanced automatic target recognition (ATR) and homing capabilities.”
It added that “Dominion-X enables centralized real-time coordination and management of autonomous aerial and ground systems, including real-time mission data exchange between platforms and distributed operations across battlefield environments through a shared mission network.”
Designed for contested and GPS-denied environments, FUSE’s solutions “support resilient mission execution, distributed autonomous operations, and manned-unmanned teaming (MUM-T) alongside maneuvering forces and crewed platforms within existing military formations and command structures.”
FUSE said that it “delivers mature military-grade autonomous systems designed for scalable and resilient multi-domain operations, supported by Elbit Systems’ operational experience and high-volume manufacturing infrastructure.”
According to Dahan, FUSE’s solutions have accumulated more than 1,000,000 operational flight hours and over 100,000 autonomous ground operation hours, with thousands of platforms delivered worldwide.
Generally, FUSE’s products are focused on medium-to-longer range missions as opposed to competitors such as SpearUAV, an Israeli defense tech company based in Tel Aviv, which announced on Monday that it had close to 1,000 Viper 300 loitering munitions (LM) ready to deliver to customers around the world.
While Elbit-FUSE is focused first on Israel as a client, the US and many European countries remain strong customers.
Although there are large American and other foreign competitors in this field, Elbit-FUSE has shown that its products not only perform at a higher level product-to-product but also excel over many others in being able to connect the operations of swarms of products in the air and on the land simultaneously.
Dahan said that FUSE is also working on expanding into drone and robot swarm operations at sea.
It was previously reported that the Israeli navy has been operating autonomous sea vehicles in recent years, though it is unclear when operating swarms at sea will be ready to be rolled out.
Elbit Systems has already been among the Israeli companies developing such technologies, including its already publicized 12-meter Seagull autonomous surface vessel designed to patrol offshore infrastructure for up to four days. The Seagull “incorporates mine countermeasures (MCM), anti-submarine warfare (ASW), maritime security (MS), electronic warfare (EW), and other advanced systems and technologies.”

Israel can protect Sweida’s Druze without supporting Syria’s separation - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
13:52:29 UTC
22:52:29 KST

Sweida has become one of the most sensitive issues in the new Syria, not only because of violations suffered by Druze and Bedouin civilians, but also because of questions over the province’s future and its relationship with the Syrian state.
This raises an important question for Israel: if protecting Sweida’s Druze population is a genuine objective, is supporting separation or keeping the province outside state institutions really the best way to achieve it?
Or would a more realistic option be to encourage a political settlement inspired by the path taken by the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF), whereby the Druze receive political guarantees, rights, and meaningful participation in state institutions without turning Sweida into a separate entity?
In my view, the second option is more realistic and safer.
Sweida is not the SDF, but its experience offers a lesson
The SDF fought Damascus for years, including in Aleppo and Sheikh Maqsoud, while tensions and clashes also occurred in Raqqa, Deir ez-Zor, and elsewhere. Yet the conflict did not lead to an independent Kurdish state.
Instead, the SDF moved toward negotiations with Damascus over a formula guaranteeing Kurdish rights and participation within a united Syrian state, followed by arrangements for integration into state institutions.
The lesson is not that Sweida should copy the SDF. It is that conflict with the state does not make separation the only option.
The students’ crisis reveals the core of the problem
The case of Sweida’s students illustrates the crisis clearly.
After the disruption of examinations, the Syrian state took exceptional measures to ensure that students could sit their exams. It prepared examination centers, staff, and materials and made special arrangements for them.
But according to media reports, the so-called “National Guard”, affiliated with Sheikh Hikmat al-Hijri, prevented students from leaving Sweida to reach examination centers prepared by the Syrian state.
The question is simple: if the state prepared the examinations and provided the centers, who is preventing the students from reaching them?
Students should not become parties to a political conflict. When an armed force can prevent citizens from accessing state services, the issue becomes one of authority: who is responsible for providing basic services and protecting citizens’ rights?
Al-Hijri does not speak for all Druze
Sheikh Hikmat al-Hijri has become one of the most prominent political voices in Sweida, but it would be wrong to treat him as the exclusive representative of Syrian Druze.
This matters to Israel because building long-term policy around one individual can lead to strategic miscalculations.
Reports concerning the detention, mistreatment, or killing of opponents and critics of al-Hijri also make independent investigations essential.
Al-Hijri’s past also matters
Israel should assess al-Hijri’s political record, rather than looking only at his current opposition to Damascus.
He has a history of political positions and relationships during the era of Bashar al-Assad, including positions that raised questions about his relationship or interaction with forces associated with various Iranian militias during different stages of the Syrian conflict.
If Israel is looking for a partner capable of producing stability in southern Syria, it should ask whether that person can build institutions capable of protecting the entire community, including those who disagree with him.
Violations do not make separation inevitable
The violations suffered by Druze and Bedouin civilians are unjustifiable and condemnable. Anyone who committed crimes against civilians should be held accountable, regardless of affiliation.
But justice does not require dividing Syria.
A state capable of investigating, prosecuting, and holding perpetrators accountable may provide stronger protection than local armed authorities operating outside a clear national judicial system.
Sweida therefore does not have to choose between submission to Damascus and separation from Syria. There is a third option: a genuine partnership within a united Syrian state.
Why should Israel think twice?
It is natural for Israel to view Sweida through a security lens and to care about protecting the Druze.
But this does not mean that supporting a separatist project is the best policy.
Israel can encourage a settlement between Sweida and Damascus that guarantees Druze rights rather than a permanent rupture.
If the Syrian state is responsible for security, services and the judiciary, while the people of Sweida participate in its institutions, clear arrangements can be established and monitored.
Keeping the province as a separate armed sphere of influence, by contrast, means continued uncertainty.
What if a Druze entity becomes a problem for Israel?
Even if establishing an independent Druze entity/state in southern Syria were possible, Israel should consider its long-term consequences.
Creating a political entity based on Druze identity would establish a new precedent in the region.
This raises a hypothetical question: what if the emergence of an independent Druze entity creates new identity dynamics among some of Israel’s Druze citizens?
This does not mean that Israel’s Druze citizens would seek separation or join such an entity. There is no basis for asserting that.
But an independent Druze entity across the border could, over time, open new debates about identity, belonging and relations between Druze communities across borders.
A state without recognition is not a guarantee of stability
There is also a practical question: who would recognize, finance, and protect an independent entity in Sweida?
A small entity without broad international recognition, surrounded by a complex regional environment and dependent on external support, could become a permanent zone of influence rather than a stable state.
Israel could ultimately face a new responsibility rather than more secure borders.
Damascus should put forward a political initiative
The Syrian government should build on the steps it has already taken (for example, students’ examinations) and make the people of Sweida see tangible benefits in remaining within the state.
What is needed now is a broader political initiative that includes holding accountable everyone who committed violations against civilians, ensuring a fair and transparent judiciary.
Sweida’s population needs to be included in state institutions and integrated into the state’s armed groups through clear and gradual arrangements, while ensuring the continuation of government services, particularly education and healthcare.
No settlement can succeed if an armed force remains capable of preventing state institutions from reaching citizens.
The SDF model offers Israel a third option
Israel does not have to choose between abandoning the Druze and supporting their separation from Syria.
It can encourage a third formula: Druze who are secure within Syria enjoy political representation and clear rights, while the Syrian state remains responsible for sovereignty and institutions.
Sweida can be part of the solution
The Druze do not need a new state to obtain their rights. Syria does not need to eliminate Sweida’s distinctiveness to preserve its unity. And Israel does not need an independent Druze entity to ensure the security of the south.
There is political space between these options: a united Syrian state, genuine Druze participation, justice for victims, and weapons organized under state institutions.
Protecting the Druze does not require dividing Syria, and preserving Syria’s unity must not mean ignoring Druze rights. If Israel genuinely wants to protect the Druze and contribute to the stability of its southern frontier, it should encourage this path rather than bet on continued division.
Stability in Sweida will not come from creating new borders, but from building a new relationship between Sweida and the Damascus government.
The writer is the Editor-in-Chief of Syria Focus.

Trump’s Iran war has left him without a clear path to victory - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
13:52:16 UTC
22:52:16 KST

US President Donald Trump keeps telling us he started the war with Iran so that the Islamic Republic “cannot have a nuclear weapon.” His energy secretary just gave the world reason to doubt his boss. Trump is unlikely to get what he called “the kind of deal that I feel is necessary.”
Energy Secretary Chris Wright told ABC News Sunday, “There may not be a nuclear agreement,” and the US will focus instead on “degrading their capacity to develop nuclear weapons.”
Sensing his humiliation, a dismissive Trump took to social media to say he “could not care less” if Iran makes a deal. He bounces back and forth between threatening to walk away and destroying the entire Iranian civilization.
Dealmaker Trump dramatically tore up the 2015 Iran nuclear pact (JCPOA) negotiated by the Obama administration, and said he could do better. He never really tried. There were limited but unproductive talks in his second term, with enough bombastic rhetoric going back and forth to destroy anyone’s hope.
Many believe the major flaw in the JCPOA from Trump’s standpoint was less its substance than the name most associated with it: Barack Obama. There is scant expectation that Trump could even get that deal today.
On March 25, 2025, Tulsi Gabbard, the director of national intelligence, told the Senate Intelligence Committee that America’s intelligence leaders “assess that Iran is not building a nuclear weapon, and Supreme Leader [Ayatollah Ali] Khamenei has not authorized the nuclear weapons program that he suspended in 2003.”
In Senate testimony a year later, she refused to say whether Iran posed any “imminent nuclear threat.” That’s not what Trump wanted to hear. “I don’t care what she said,” Trump told reporters. In his view, Iran was “very close” to having a nuclear bomb, PBS reported.
In private, Gabbard had advised against going to war and many of her arguments turned out to be spot on, according to leaked reports. Speaking truth to power apparently cost the intelligence chief her job; after weeks of rumors that Trump was planning to push her out, Gabbard resigned in May, citing her husband’s health.
Trump declared in June 2025 that US B-2s (stealth bombers) had “obliterated” Iran’s nuclear program. Apparently he oversold his achievement. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu convinced him that the job was unfinished, and they went back on February 28 this year.
Iran has taken a hell of a beating in a war Trump refuses to call a war but can’t find an exit. Iran’s navy, air force, and even much of its air defense system have been decimated, but the regime persists, as does much of its drone and proxy terror network.
The old leadership was killed on the first day, only to be replaced by even more hard-line rulers. The popular uprising Trump called for never materialized.
Iran causes global economic shock
Iran retaliated with its oil weapon, closing the Strait of Hormuz and shocking the global economy. Trump and his party are reeling.
The president has been promising that the resulting huge jump in gas and grocery prices will soon disappear, but no serious economist agrees. That terrifies Republican candidates in this fall’s midterm elections as they are being hammered by Democrats talking about “affordability.” Trump dismissed the talk of the high cost of living as just a “hoax” and a “con job” just before he flies off in Qatar Force One for a tournament at his Irish golf course.
Secretary Wright, who is also presiding over Trump’s takeover of major Venezuelan oil fields, told ABC News Sunday, “We are degrading [Iran’s] capacity to develop nuclear weapons and ultimately to deliver them, if they develop them.”
That’s a big and dangerous “if.” For decades prior to this war, Iranian leaders publicly swore off going for the bomb. US and Israeli intelligence largely agree, as Gabbard told the president and the Senate, Iran was enriching uranium to near-weapon levels but that it had not yet made the breakthrough decision. Now, the new leadership is said to be reconsidering that policy, pointing to North Korea, Pakistan, India and Israel, which went nuclear as deterrence insurance against hostile neighbors.
If you're picking winners and losers, Iran is a big loser just because of the military, economic and human damage that has been inflicted on it. But Trump cannot declare victory – despite doing so dozens of times – until Hormuz is open to the free and unfettered flow of shipping by all and there is an enforceable nuclear deal.
Trump may not be able to get either. His energy secretary said a deal “may await a next administration in Iran.” Thanks to the US and Israel, Iran got a new administration six months ago, and you know how that went.
Trump started an unnecessary war of choice without a clear operational plan or an endgame, without the support of Congress, the American people, or America’s allies.
Bombs are not the only things falling. The president’s approval rating has dropped to historic lows. Nearly two-thirds of Americans oppose his war and disapprove of the president’s handling of it. Four in five tell pollsters they blame the high and increasing cost of living on this war.
The president will try to stem the defection of disapproving Republicans when he speaks at this week’s mid-term convention in Dallas, but many Republican candidates won’t be there. They know their constituents are unhappy with how this war is hurting their pocketbooks, and candidates worry that on Election Day those folks may be staying home or pulling the wrong lever. The last thing they need is to be seen on television cheering Trump’s unpopular war.
The writer is a Washington-based journalist, consultant, lobbyist, and former legislative director at the American Israel Public Affairs Committee.

EU plan aims to help cities crack down on Airbnb, holiday rentals
The European Commission’s Affordable Housing Act lays out conditions under which local authorities can limit short lets
European cities will gain more leeway to curb short-term rentals such as Airbnb under new EU plans that aim to bring down housing costs in tourism hotspots.
The European Commission laid out conditions on Wednesday under which local authorities can limit short lets, under a proposal seeking to address Europe’s “housing crisis”.
“Short-term rentals are a part of the problem in many cities,” Dan Jorgensen, the 27-nation bloc’s housing commissioner, told a press conference in Brussels.
Though hugely popular with visitors, short-term lodgings are blamed by residents in many popular travel destinations for depriving locals of flats for long-term rental and pushing up prices – something holiday-let providers dispute.
Cities from New York to Tokyo and Barcelona have imposed or considered restrictions on tourist flats in recent years. But curbs have often been met with court challenges, resulting in legal uncertainty.
The commission’s Affordable Housing Act – which still has to be negotiated with lawmakers and EU countries – aims to provide cities with legal cover, clarifying when authorities can take action without falling foul of the bloc’s single market rules.

France’s record heatwave pushes champagne alcohol levels to historic high

France’s record heatwave pushes champagne alcohol levels to historic high
France’s record-breaking summer heat has forced champagne producers to contend with unusually high sugar levels in grapes, forcing authorities to allow alcohol content of up to 15 percent in the region’s sparkling wine for the first time. Champagne is usually capped at 13 percent.
Drinking this year's champagne might give you a heftier headache as France's record heatwaves are forcing some producers to up the alcohol levels, industry officials said Wednesday.
French authorities have allowed champagne houses to make their bubbly with alcohol content of up to 15 percent, a historic first for a wine usually limited to 13 percent.
Read moreFrench wine yields drop to new historic low after searing summer heat
Growers had to harvest exceptionally early this year as extreme heat sped sugar buildup – and hence natural alcohol production – in the grapes, according to the Comite Champagne industry association.
Nonetheless, "the crop already has all the hallmarks of producing great, perhaps even exceptional, wines", the group said in a statement.
Authorities have also allowed a temporary easing of strict rules for making several types of cheese after heatwaves scorched grazing pastures.
France is the world's second-largest wine producer after Italy, and this summer's heat and drought have deepened fears for many growers about how they will cope with climate change.
The 2026 harvest was the earliest ever recorded in the Champagne region, with the first grapes cut as early as August 6 and the harvest becoming widespread on August 17, two weeks earlier than in 2025, when it was already considered to be early, according to the association.
Read moreClimate crisis pushes French winemakers to bet on warmer future in Brittany and Normandy
Due to climate change, "this unusual harvest will probably become the norm in 10 to 15 years", said Maxime Toubart, the co-chairman of the Comite Champagne.
It "should prompt reflection on the champagne of tomorrow", he said.
Fellow co-chair David Chatillon said the relaxed alcohol content would concern just a small number of growers.
"The average after the harvest is below 12 percent," Chatillon said. "Not all winegrowers in Champagne will be above that level."
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

European Heritage Days 2026: protecting Europe’s heritage at risk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
13:48:48 UTC
22:48:48 KST

European Heritage Days 2026: protecting Europe’s heritage at risk
The 2026 European Heritage Days highlight how communities and EU-supported initiatives are protecting and adapting cultural heritage in response to climate change, societal shifts and other forms of threats, including conflict.
The EU strives to preserve cultural heritage under all circumstances, as reflected in the EU preparedness union strategy. Across Europe, communities are finding diverse ways to respond to these pressures with the support of the European Union.
Revive, resist, reimagine
Throughout September and October, the European Heritage Days 2026 invites people across Europe, under the theme “heritage at risk: revive, resist, reimagine” to discover how communities are protecting, restoring and reimagining their heritage for the future.
Protecting heritage from a changing climate
As climate change increases pressure on cultural sites and landscapes through extreme weather, flooding, fires and other natural hazards, protecting heritage also means finding ways to adapt. These challenges highlight how closely Europe’s natural and cultural heritage are connected.
Natura 2000, the EU’s network of protected areas, reflects this connection. In France’s Camargue, for example, protected wetlands and exceptional biodiversity – including one of Europe’s top breeding sites for greater flamingos – coexist with centuries-old traditions such as rice cultivation and salt production, both recognised through EU geographical indications.
EU-funded research is helping these landscapes adapt. The RescueME project, funded under Horizon Europe, works with communities in five European coastal areas – including Crete, Cinque Terre and Zadar – to develop solutions that strengthen the resilience of their cultural landscape in the face of climate change.
Giving old places a new purpose
Heritage can also become vulnerable when societal and economic changes leave historic buildings without their original function. Vacancy and neglect can gradually put their heritage value at risk. Adaptive reuse can help reverse this process, preserving the character of historic buildings while giving them new functions and keeping them part of community life.
In Rathfarnham, Ireland, the historic Castle Stables and Courtyards are being transformed into spaces for cultural, community and hospitality activities. Co-funded by the European Regional Development Fund (ERDF), the THRIVE project shows how giving heritage a new purpose can contribute to its long-term preservation while creating new value for the local community.
Safeguarding heritage in times of conflict
Armed conflict and other types of threats can cause irreversible damage to heritage. Safeguarding it during and after armed conflicts requires both immediate protection and long-term commitment to restoration and recovery.
Europe’s recent history offers powerful examples. In Dubrovnik, Croatia, the Society of Friends of Dubrovnik Antiquities has worked for decades to safeguard the historic city, including during and after the conflicts of the 1990s. Its contribution was recognised with a 2024 European Heritage Award / Europa Nostra Award, supported by Creative Europe.
The Team Europe for Cultural Heritage in Ukraine supports 89 initiatives from EU countries and the European Commission to safeguard Ukraine’s cultural heritage from the impacts of Russia’s war of aggression – from emergency protection and recording damage to cultural sites and digitally preserving endangered heritage, to training heritage professionals and supporting restoration.
