Who should be in charge of the war?
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:11:00 EEST
22:11:00 KST

Who should be in charge of the war?
This article is based upon my experiences in MOD UK and Army and Joint staff during the first Gulf War, Bosnia and with NATO in Kosovo.
I turned for support to my US defence academic friend and author Dr Thomas Durell Young a former member of staff at the US war college, and a former Policy Director in MOD Bulgaria Retired Colonel Vladimir Milenski. We all worked variously together with MOD Ukraine in 2014 and 2015 and between us on reform in over 15 other countries worldwide.
I apologize in advance to my female military friends for using he throughout this article, but it reflects simplicity of writing before translation not denigration of your amazing contribution to the national war effort.
Introduction: War Does Not Suspend Democratic Defence Governance, it severely tests it
In a democratic state at war, the defence system must be able to fight effectively while remaining politically controlled, legally accountable, strategically coherent and operationally agile.
War increases pressure on institutions, but the defence system must not become insular or a power on its own. War does not remove the need for clear authority, lawful responsibility and public accountability. On the contrary, the greater the stakes, the more important it is to know who governs defence, who advises government, who generates forces, who plans strategy and campaigns, who commands operations, and who answers for results. Today this is not totally clear in Ukraine.
The institutional question is therefore not primarily one of terminology. Different democratic states use different titles for organisations and posts.
What matters is whether these offices form a coherent system in which authority, responsibility, military advice, operational command, force generation, political control and accountability are clearly separated where necessary and integrated where useful – and most importantly society can see who is in charge and responsible for each task.
There is no doubt that to achieve a well–oiled, well–managed system the key requirement is outstanding teamwork. The fastest and best process is always two friends working together with a common purpose. Lack of trust, institutional arrogance, poor teamwork, bureaucracy or unclear tasks lead to delay – and delay kills.
In this regard the Minister and senior commanders, MOD, General Staff (GS) and Joint Staff (JS) must function as a single organism, working closely together not in opposition.
I have been lucky to work in a combined MOD/General Staff in UK with teams of officers and civil servants serving together. Meetings contained staff from all relevant HQs from MOD to units and many key decisions could be made and implemented immediately without need for bureaucracy. The civilian component came with different, less narrow thinking and skills, and added to achieving results hugely. Sharing work openly is vastly better than strict ownership.
In Ukraine, the main headquarters are the MOD and the General Staff (GS) (Most countries would call this HQ, Defence Staff as it is more than just army). We suggest a third strand is needed as Joint Staff, which should manage the fighting. UK and many NATO countries have an operational Joint Staff HQ and US have the regional combatant commands (COCOMS) reflecting their world view. Together, these three HQs would form a leadership triangle with clear and separate tasks. I have worked variously at all three levels. Depending on the issue in need of resolution, one headquarters leads the staff work, while the others support it.
The next day the task and leadership requirement may be totally different. States that inherit command structures from the Soviet military tradition and then introduce institutions associated with modern democratic and NATO ways of defence management are always challenged in who does what, how and when.
The problem is not that one idea, or vocabulary is "Eastern" and another "Western." The problem is that mixed systems often create parallel chains of authority, overlapping staff, unclear responsibility and commanders who are held accountable for outcomes without being given the authority or resources to achieve them. The current Ukrainian Joint Staff is a case in hand. It was given a role on the battlefield for which it was not intended. And in truth, it was never Joint either.
For a democratic state at war in 2026, the central principle should be simple: responsibility must follow authority. No institution or part of an institution should be able to use power without accountability, and no commander should be given responsibility without sufficient authority and resources to complete the task.
The Ministry of Defence: Civilian Authority, Policy, Resources and Accountability
The Ministry of Defence is the civilian political–administrative authority responsible for governing and enabling defence. In a democratic state, MOD is an arm of government and not an operational headquarters. It should not function as a parallel military command. Its legitimacy comes from constitutional authority, ministerial responsibility, parliamentary oversight and the rule of law.
In wartime, the responsibilities of the Minister remain the same, but he must do them faster and with more focus. He not only has to lead the whole defence system but also be a hands–on manager for MOD encouraging the staff to be proactive, supportive, innovative, and fast working. His ministry must also be operational 24/7, ready and able to react to emergencies. And the strong political role of this post is why a civilian, preferably an experienced politician, should always be appointed.
Military ministers may think and understand well the fighting task but are unused to the political and civil signals. They rarely understand the requirements for political briefing, networking and consensus building to get the best overall defence result.
The ministry task is complex. It must translate national political objectives into defence policy and strategic guidance; managing resources, the budget, procurement, mobilisation policy, personnel policy, international assistance, defence industry and sustainment. It must coordinate with government, parliament, other ministries, allies and civil emergency structures; and at the same time ensure legality, transparency, democratic oversight and anti–corruption controls.
The minister must also personally keep the defence committee constantly briefed about problems with any of the above tasks and especially the possible requirements for new or changed laws. Some Ministers in Ukraine have seen working with Parliament as the enemy instead of a vital and fundamental part of the defence system. The failure to pass many vitally needed laws in 12 years of war highlights this mistake exactly.
The ministry must also hold the military leadership accountable for readiness, plans, performance and use of resources. This does not mean political micromanagement of operations. It means that civilian authority as part of government sets objectives, provides means, defines limits, demands professional advice, evaluates performance and accounts to the democratic state. Its role is not to be military but to brief government and parliament, set strategic direction, provide the maximum resources available, oversee performance and carry political–administrative responsibility.
There is no doubt that to achieve a well–oiled, well–managed system the key requirement is outstanding teamwork across the whole system. I learned this well in MOD, but I also learned that we military are poor at arguing and getting our point across. Too often we use emotions and military arrogance to make our point where our civilian colleagues want hard logical arguments and facts. I learnt the hard way with papers and briefs returned covered in red ink and questions like "Why?" and "where is the proof?" spread all over them.
In this regard the Minister and senior commanders, MOD, General Staff (GS) and Joint Staff (JS) must function as a single organism, working closely together not in opposition. To do this, however, they all need common and high–quality briefings from the staff. They usually only know what the staff presents to them; they are not deity. Honesty is everything. Where there is a combined MOD/GS with teams of officers and civil servants working in tandem such as in UK or the Pentagon, most decisions can be made and implemented immediately.
In Ukraine with a separate MOD and General Staff the leadership must constantly look for new processes and better ways to design coordinated and collective team work to get the fastest and most coordinated results. The NATO or Continental Staff system for the military is arguably the best method for this, but it must be used in all its concepts and methods not just a renaming of the old methods. Ukrainian staff still have not grasped the essence of this tool. But this needs another article.
The Chief of Defence / Commander–in–Chief: Strategic Military Leadership and Professional Advice
The Chief of Defence, or Commander–in–Chief (CinC) of the Armed Forces is the senior professional military authority of the state. The title may vary, but the function must be totally clear. This officer is the principal military adviser to the President, government, Minister of Defence and national security bodies, and is responsible for the strategic military leadership of the armed forces as an institution. All three authors agree they have seen more Commanders–in–Chief fail than succeed.
The main reason is failing to grasp that they are not there to run defence like a CEO, and they are not just king of the castle as too many want to be. They must be the expert conduit between society and government, and the military system, ensuring that information and activity flows both ways smoothly and correctly.
The role requires translating political objectives into military strategic options; advising honestly on risk, feasibility, costs and consequences; directing the development of campaign–level plans through the staff system; ensuring jointness and equality across every aspect of the defence system; maintaining morale, readiness, discipline, professional standards and strategic coherence. The list and scope is enormous in its breadth and importance. This is why the Commander–in–Chief should not be the fighting commander. When he takes this role to himself the other key defence tasks that need his time suffer from neglect of proper command attention – and then like the TCC and mobilisation, the whole system degrades.
A further key role for any Commander–in–Chief is to select and provide advice to the President on which officers of all services, not just army, are suitable for high ranks, especially for operational command. Equally, the Commander must advise the President about senior officers who must be moved for failing to achieve results because of lack of ability, staleness or physical tiredness.
Accountability for the Commander–in–Chief flows upward to the civilian leadership through lawful oversight mechanisms like briefing President, Minister and Parliament regularly.
The Commander–in–Chief is responsible for the professional quality of this personal military advice, which means that those below him must also brief him honestly with trust that even when giving bad news they will not be judged or punished for this as has happened too often in the past. He is also responsible for the strategic employment of the armed forces, the integrity of the command system and the readiness and morale of the force.
The Commander–in Chief should be strong enough to lead the military institution through good and bad, but he must always remain subordinate to democratic authority.
The Chief of Staff: Staff Authority, Not Independent Command
The role of Chief of Staff is often the most sensitive in a mixed system. Chief of Staff is subordinate to the Commander–in–Chief and in Ukraine should be the daily manager of the defence system on his behalf by managing the General Staff. He is responsible for staff processes and quality at all levels, planning quality, coordination, staff discipline and ensuring military options developed inside the Joint Staff are fully supported by the system. This officer may be powerful in practice because good staff work shapes strategic decisions, but the authority should be exercised under the Commander–in–Chief and not as an independent command function.
If the Chief of General Staff issues orders, those orders should be staff orders issued under the authority of the Commander–in–Chief not personal command directives. The guiding formula is straightforward: the Chief of General Staff should be powerful as a staff coordinator and the lead manager of the armed forces, but not independent as a commander.
The General Staff: Strategic Staff, The Engine Room of Change and Creating a Stronger Future.
The General Staff, or Defence Staff as named in many contemporary systems, should be understood as the strategic staff that serves the Commander–in–Chief. Its purpose is to convert political direction and strategic military guidance into business plans, force development, mobilisation arrangements, readiness systems, doctrine, training policy, logistic priorities and strategic assessments. With these activities General Staff has a simple three–fold role.
First is supporting the Joint Force Commander with the resources he needs to conduct the fight.
Second is to create new and innovative military resources for the future, and third is to ensure that the whole defence system in the rear is focused upon supporting war as efficiently as possible. This means creating tight processes and effective organisations everywhere with no waste or delays.
Thus, the General Staff is the military brain of the institution and must remain focused upon the future. It should not become a rival command chain and should not be involved in the daily direction of the war or pull tasks to itself that are proper tasks of the subordinate services and agencies like the army or air force.
This distinction is especially important in countries shaped by the Soviet military inheritance. In Soviet–derived systems, the General Staff often accumulated planning, force management, mobilisation, operational direction, intelligence and direct command functions. That model reflected a different political–military logic: centralised control, vertical authority, limited civilian policy capacity, staff–driven command and secrecy over accountability.
In a contemporary democratic system, such concentration of functions creates serious risks: duplication of authority, unclear responsibility, staff interference in command, excessive centralization, extremely slow decision cycles, weakened joint command and poor accountability for operational outcomes. The more intense the war becomes, the more damaging these frictions and disfunctions become to the fighting force.
The General Staff should therefore not directly command operational formations and be involved in warfighting. When they are the staff risk being busy with the wrong tasks, slowing decision–making, weakening operational commanders and destroying the clear link between authority and responsibility. They also lose the focus of their own key tasks and create delays that slow the others they deal with.
The Joint Force Commander: Commander of all Current Joint Warfighting Operations
The Joint Force Commander should be the operational commander responsible for the conduct of assigned campaigns and operations. His task is to win the war. This role is essential because modern war is Joint by nature. Every single capability including civil–military cooperation cannot be managed as separate single service efforts. They must all be integrated under an operational commander with real authority over assigned forces.
The Joint Force Commander's responsibilities should include commanding assigned forces in the operational area; planning and executing campaigns and major operations; identifying needed resources for the upcoming operations, integrating service and functional components; allocating operational priorities; synchronizing effects; reporting progress, risk, losses, needs and opportunities; and adapting operations within the strategic guidance received. He must also highlight operational gaps and weaknesses.
The key is that the title must be matched by authority. If every significant tactical or operational decision is controlled by the General Staff or the political center, the appointment becomes hollow and accountability disappears. A Joint Force Commander who is responsible for operational outcomes must have the authority to command assigned forces, set operational priorities and make timely decisions within strategic guidance.
The Joint Force Commander should be accountable to the Commander–in–Chief for his military performance, and through that chain to civilian authority. This accountability should be based on mission, resources, constraints and delegated authority. It should not be reduced to blame after failure or praise after success; it should be continuous discipline of reporting, assessment, adaptation and lawful command.
Joint Staff: The Operational Warfighting Machinery of Joint Integration
The Joint Staff should manage and coordinate the war fighting organization. It should focus on fighting the war through Joint operational and intelligence integration, translating and directing strategy to subordinate formations and then supporting their operations. It is the staff mechanism through which the armed forces integrate all possible capabilities into a coherent and coordinated war fighting system focused on a single warfighting strategy. When a state has both a General Staff and a Joint Staff, the distinction between them must be precise and with no overlap of cause for misunderstanding.
A well–designed Joint Staff enables the Joint Force Commander to plan, coordinate, assess and adjust joint operations on behalf of the country. His staff support operational–level planning both for close, medium and deep operations with a key aim to both focus battlefield effect and to direct resources where the strategic and operational needs demand. The staff prepare orders and directives for joint operations, work closely with MOD and the General Staff on resource requirements, maintain the recognized operational picture, coordinate with allied headquarters and link national military strategy with campaign execution.
There is always a danger that a Joint Staff can become either redundant if the General Staff take too much operational power, or too weak to integrate the services effectively if the legal authorities are not strong enough. Either outcome is deeply harmful for the war effort. Equally if the Joint Staff try to duplicate the General Staff, they add bureaucracy without authority. When the staff lack influence and real authority, joint operations remain dominated by service and agency interests or by improvised ad–hoc coordination. The result is operations that lack focus, coherence and coordination. Operations and ammunition are wasted on activities that do not have the desired cumulative effect of defeating the enemy. The Joint Staff must therefore have a defined role and clear access to the Commander–in–Chief. It is also vital that the Joint Commander and Chief of Staff have common purposes, are like minded with shared experiences, and even better, are good friends.
The Central Democratic Principle: Responsibility Must Follow Authority
The principle that responsibility must follow authority is the normative heart of democratic wartime defence governance. It protects the state from two equally dangerous failures: institutions that exercise power without accountability, and commanders who are blamed for outcomes they were not empowered or resourced to influence.
In such a system, accountability should be distributed as follows:
- Political leadership is accountable for political objectives, war aims, mobilisation of society, alliances, national resilience, and acceptable risk.
- The MOD is accountable for defence policy, resources, institutions, procurement, personnel, sustainment, and oversight.
- The Commander–in–Chief is accountable for professional military advice, strategic military leadership, readiness, and use of the armed forces.
- The General Staff is accountable for the quality of development plans and R&D, assessments, readiness systems, mobilisation, force development, and staff work.
- The Joint Staff is accountable for war fighting, joint integration and operational planning.
- The Joint Force Commander is accountable for the conduct of assigned operations.
- Armed forces (army/navy etc.) are responsible for delivering trained forces ready and equipped for combat
This distribution of accountability does not fragment command; it clarifies it. Political leaders remain responsible for political aims and national risk. Civilian defence authorities remain responsible for policy, resources and oversight. Senior military leaders remain responsible for professional advice, readiness and strategic coherence. Operational commanders remain responsible for the conduct of assigned operations. The system works when each level has enough authority to discharge its responsibility and enough oversight to prevent abuse.
Each principal defence office should therefore have a statutory duty list that answers five questions: what decision or product the office must deliver; by when it must be delivered; to whom it must be submitted; what authority is granted to deliver it; and what evidence will be used to assess compliance. Legal accountability should include periodic reporting to the Minister of Defence, government, President or parliament; written records of military advice and decisions; deadlines for operational assessments and readiness reports; audit trails for resources; and explicit consequences for failure to perform lawful duties.
Conclusion: Clarity Is a Strategic Capability and Battle Winner
For a democratic state at war in 2026, the decisive institutional test is not the number of headquarters, staff or command titles, but the clarity of authority, responsibility and accountability among them. A state may have a Ministry of Defence, a Chief of Defence or Commander–in–Chief, a General Staff, a Joint Staff, a Chief of General Staff and a Joint Force Commander. But unless their roles are clearly distinguished, the result may be duplication and weakness rather than strength.
Ukraine's challenge is especially demanding because it must fight a high–intensity war while transforming inherited command structures. The aim should not be cosmetic adoption of Western terminology, nor rejection of every inherited practice simply because of its origin. The aim should be a genuinely democratic and joint wartime defence system: civilian–led, professionally advised, operationally effective, legally accountable and clear enough that every major decision and action has an identifiable owner.
Institutional clarity is not an administrative luxury. It is a strategic capability. It shortens decision cycles, strengthens trust between civilian and military leaders, improves the use of resources, enables joint operations, reduces politicisation and makes accountability possible. In war, these are not secondary virtues. They are the key conditions for endurance, adaptation and victory.
Glen Grant

It is the first project that Mogotel Hotel Group is implementing in cooperation with Marriott International, one of the world’s leading hospitality companies. The launch of Four Points Flex by Sheraton in the Latvian market marks an important milestone in the company’s development, while adding another internationally recognised hotel brand to Latvia’s hospitality market.
Four Points Flex by Sheraton Riga Old Town is located in the heart of Riga’s Old Town at 49 Vaļņu Street, on the site of the former Wellton Riga Hotel & SPA. It is one of Marriott International’s newest brands, created for modern travellers who value quality service, thoughtful functionality and a convenient location.
Before the rebranding, the hotel underwent a phased renovation, including the refurbishment of guest rooms, updated design and improvements to the interiors of public areas. Most of the investment was directed towards upgrading the lobby, reception, breakfast area and bar. The hotel will offer 174 comfortable, contemporary rooms, the Tapas Tapas restaurant serving lunch and dinner, a breakfast area, as well as the Wellton SPA Oasis with a sauna, jacuzzi and Turkish bath. The hotel also offers a modern conference room for small meetings, presentations and business events, providing comprehensive facilities for both individual guests and corporate clients.
“Renovation is not cosmetic refurbishment; it is the only way to change the economics of an asset: increase its value and occupancy, reduce energy costs, significantly enhance the company’s appeal to employees and minimise staff turnover. We make renovation decisions taking into account the natural lifecycle of equipment, energy-efficiency rules and requirements, as well as the rebranding process. Equally important are the technologies we introduce into the day-to-day management of our hotels. We only use solutions that either free up employees’ time for interaction with guests or directly reduce operating costs. In practice, this means a digital guest journey – online check-in, mobile keys, cloud-based management systems and artificial intelligence in revenue management, which we have been using across every hotel in the group for several years. This is not technology for the future — it is our everyday reality,” says Ivan Dokitsans, Executive Director of Mogotel Hotel Group.
Four Points Flex by Sheraton Riga Old Town will be the first hotel under the brand in Latvia, strengthening the presence of Marriott International’s brands in the Baltic region. The next stage in Mogotel Hotel Group’s development will be the launch of the StudioRes by Marriott brand. This will enable international hotel brands to expand their presence in the Latvian market even further.
“One of the most notable trends today is the affiliation of independent hotels with global brands. In Europe, chain hotels account for around 40% of hotel rooms, compared with around 70% in the US. This gap represents the entire growth potential in a single figure, which is why the largest operators today are growing not through new construction, but through conversions. In Latvia, there is still insufficient awareness that sustainability is becoming not merely part of marketing communications, but a full-fledged criterion in hotel selection. Already 76% of corporate clients include sustainability requirements in their hotel tenders, and a hotel that cannot provide data on its energy consumption effectively loses the opportunity to participate. At the same time, price remains one of our challenges: our revenue per available room is lower than in the other two Baltic states. This cannot be solved through discounts — the answer must be product quality and brand strength. A global brand with hundreds of millions of loyalty programme members becomes a distribution channel that works for a small country’s market every day,” comments Vadim Mukhin, Chairman of the Board of AS Mogotel Hotel Group.

Gaming tycoon ordered to pay ex-wife $1.8B in South Korea’s biggest divorce settlement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

13:10:45 UTC
22:10:45 KST

Faisal Mahmud
09 September 2026•Update: 09 September 2026
A South Korean court on Wednesday ordered gaming tycoon Kwon Hyuk-bin to transfer shares and cash worth 2.55 trillion won ($1.8 billion) to his former wife, in what is believed to be the country’s largest-ever divorce settlement, according to the Korea Times.
The Seoul Family Court granted a divorce petition filed by Kwon’s wife, identified only by her surname Lee, and divided their marital assets 65% to Kwon and 35% to Lee.
Kwon, founder of gaming giant Smilegate, was ordered to transfer shares worth about 2.49 trillion won ($1.83 billion) and pay a further 65 billion won ($47.7 million) in cash.
The court included Kwon’s Smilegate holdings among the assets subject to division, noting that Lee held a stake in the company during its establishment and growth and had served as a registered director and CEO.
It also cited her long-term role in managing the household and raising their children.
The court said, however, that Kwon’s business judgment and management played a decisive role in Smilegate’s growth when it set the 35%-65% division.
It found both spouses equally responsible for the breakdown of their marriage and dismissed Lee’s damages claim.
Lee was granted parental rights over their minor child, while Kwon was ordered to pay 20 million won ($14,700) a month in child support.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said a “roadmap” for resuming direct talks between Russia and Ukraine could emerge within the next few weeks.
Rubio called the meetings between American mediators in Moscow and Kyiv “substantive,” saying “new ideas were bandied about, it’s a very difficult conflict.”
For now an extended period we haven’t seen much movement on either side in terms of their willingness to make accommodations, and both side have very bright red lines.

Putin publicly backs Nabiullina
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
13:09:21 UTC
22:09:21 KST

Putin publicly backs Nabiullina
Vladimir Putin this week showed that he has no intention of allowing Central Bank chair Elvira Nabiullina to stand alone against mounting criticism from big business over her interest rate policy. His support had been in doubt after a summer in which the president twice called on the bank to reduce rates. But in a speech at the Eastern Economic Forum, Putin unambiguously supported Nabiullina, saying that monetary policy was not too tight, warning that it would be dangerous to flood the economy with money, and that the bank was tackling inflation.
- Putin had several times in recent months made a de facto call for a cut in borrowing costs, in double digits for the past several years. At a government meeting in June, he said that the economy had grounds to expect a rate cut. In July, in a meeting with the leader of Yakutia, Putin said that a rate reduction would be “a natural process.” Since then, the Central Bank went for two cautious rate cuts, taking the key rate down to 14%.
- The verbal interventions came amid a bitter public spat between the Central Bank and Russian businesses. In April, Alexander Shokhin, the head of the Russian Union of Industrialists and Entrepreneurs (the so-called “Oligarchs’ Union”) called for cuts at one-percentage-point intervals and said that a key rate “somewhere close to 10%” was essential to revive investment. In July, Nabiullina responded to another rate-cut advocate, Sberbank boss German Gref, with the argument that cutting too fast would spark a “rapid surge in inflation” and stagnation, as she dismissed talk of economic “overcooling” as inappropriate.
- But when Putin spoke this week at the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok, he stuck up for Nabiullina and left business with little hope of a swift rate cut. In response to a statement about a recent survey by the oligarch’s union which found that only 9% of companies have resources for a fresh round of investment, while 31% said they were “very restricted”, Putin said: “Investment activity has indeed declined recently for a number of reasons, primarily due to the deliberate policies of the regulator — the Central Bank — and the government of the Russian Federation. The aim is to curb inflation. We could not allow a threatened hypersurge, and such a threat existed. Right now, our inflation rate is 6.3% per year. We’re achieving our goal.”
- Putin also said he understood the risks: “It’s important not to overcool the economy, we understand this very well.” But as he went on, it was clear he was taking a side in the dispute. “Getting ahead of ourselves, pumping up the money supply and assuming that this will not affect inflation, it seems to me, is dangerous,” he said, adding that the government and the bank had “on the whole, managed to navigate between Scylla and Charybdis so far.”
- The Central Bank’s two most recent rate cuts had surprised analysts, who had expected a hold due to rising inflation risks. The few available consensus forecasts predict that it will finally pause rate cuts at its next meeting on Sep. 11 due to the weakening ruble, rising fuel prices and high government spending.
Why the world should care
Long-serving Central Bank chief Nabiullina only has six months left of her current term, meaning Vladimir Putin will either have to name a replacement, or pass a law allowing her to serve a third term. Since May, when we first wrote about this succession issue, there has been no apparent progress or more details revealed publicly. In the summer, many felt that Putin was openly siding with the defense industry lobby and big business, but now he seems to have reversed his position.

Minister: Estonia will have to shelve some investments in tight fiscal situation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09

Minister: Estonia will have to shelve some investments in tight fiscal situation
Budget talks are continuing within the government. On the one hand, the government is seeking to keep the deficit below 4.5 percent, but ministers acknowledge there is little room for spending cuts.
According to Minister of Economic Affairs and Industry Erkki Keldo (Reform Party), the government is drawing up the budget on the assumption that defense spending must remain at no less than 5 percent of GDP, meaning other areas will have to cut costs.
"We have promised to reduce the shortfall, or deficit, to below 4.5 percent. We are trying to do that. It simply means spending has to be reined in. Operating costs, technical costs. We will also have to forgo investments that might be possible in better times — buildings and other construction projects. We cannot afford those when a large share is going toward defense investments," Keldo said.
Making cuts within the Ministry of Interior's area of responsibility is difficult, Interior Minister Igor Taro (Eesti 200) said. Instead, additional funding would be needed to develop capabilities such as counter-drone defenses. Taro did not say Tuesday how much additional funding would be needed.
"I cannot imagine telling society right now that we are simply not going to deal with civil protection at all. We need shelters. Everyone agrees on that. Everyone is asking where those shelters are — where they are in schools, where they are in residential buildings. Or could we say, for example, that we are no longer going to build the national border infrastructure?" Taro said.
Social Democratic Party Vice Chair Riina Sikkut said the minority government needs opposition support to pass the state budget, but the government has not discussed its budget plans with the opposition.
"If everyone had the same information about the forecast and the use of foreign funding, it would be much easier to find support in the Riigikogu because otherwise questions inevitably arise about where a particular figure came from, why a particular choice was made and what the alternatives were," Sikkut said.
The government wants to make the major decisions on the 2027 state budget by the end of next week.

Melike Pala
09 September 2026•Update: 09 September 2026
Nearly half of Belgians are skeptical about the use of technology at events, mainly due to concerns over privacy and data sharing, according to a survey by the Event Confederation, cited by Belga news agency on Wednesday.
The survey, conducted among 1,000 Belgians, found that only half of respondents believe digital applications make events more efficient and better organized, the umbrella organization for Belgium's events sector said.
Despite significant investments in digitalization by the events industry in recent years, many attendees remain reluctant to use technologies such as QR codes for ordering food and drinks or event-specific mobile applications for practical information.
Three-quarters of respondents said they prefer "simple events without too much technology," while one-quarter said technology improves the event experience more than personal contact.
Privacy is another major concern.   
More than half of those surveyed said they are worried about their privacy and want to be cautious about sharing personal data at events.  
Artificial intelligence is also viewed with skepticism.   
About 70% of respondents in Flanders and Wallonia regions said they are wary of AI technologies, compared with 55% among respondents in Brussels.

Brazil top court judge orders reinstatement of federal police chief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
13:07:27 UTC
22:07:27 KST

Brazil judge steps into Supreme Court power struggle, orders police chief reinstated
BRASILIA, Sept 9 - Supreme Court Justice Flavio Dino ordered Brazil's federal police chief be immediately reinstated on Wednesday, a day after his firing, stepping squarely into a power struggle that has exposed rare public divisions on Brazil's highest court.
Dino's ruling reverses Tuesday's decision by his colleague, Justice Andre Mendonca, who had ordered the removal of federal police chief Andrei Rodrigues and his intelligence chief over allegations they helped produce intelligence reports intended to monitor Mendonca and other authorities.
According to a court document seen on Wednesday, Dino said the firings were unsupported by evidence and had a direct impact on ongoing investigations, citing an "equally real and immediate" risk of harm.
Mendonca's firing of Rodrigues had been backed by the majority of a five-member court panel but challenged by the government of President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva. Dino was Lula's former justice minister — and Rodrigues' boss — before Lula tapped him for the court.
The firings were the latest chapter in an unfolding clash between Mendonca and another justice, Alexandre de Moraes, who accused Mendonca last week of abusing his authority when Mendonca made public material from an investigation into alleged fraud at the now liquidated Banco Master. The material exposed dozens of messages from the bank's disgraced president to Moraes, prompting calls for an unprecedented investigation into a sitting Supreme Court justice.
The clash between the justices has thrust the court into its biggest crisis since Brazil's return to democracy over four decades ago, just weeks before Brazilians elect a new president and most of Congress.
GROWING UNCERTAINTY
While Dino's decision takes immediate effect, it will be submitted to the full Supreme Court for final confirmation. But in a rare move, Chief Justice Edson Fachin canceled the court's planned session on Wednesday.
Brazil's institutions are being roiled by the widening investigations into Banco Master and alleged ties between the bank's president Daniel Vorcaro and top government officials.
The court crisis has injected new uncertainty into the country's tightly contested presidential race between leftist Lula and leading right-wing opponent Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, as Bolsonaro's supporters attempt to conflate Moraes and the corruption case with the leftist president, whose lead over the senator has all but been eliminated in polling.
In a post on X on Wednesday, Lula referred to the Banco Master case as the "greatest financial crime in Brazil's history" and said "the Brazilian people need explanations and immediate measures to confront the institutional crisis that has taken hold of the judiciary."
Campaigning in the city where his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, survived a stabbing attack eight years ago, Flavio Bolsonaro on Wednesday blamed Lula for the escalating crisis.
"Brazil is without a president, Brazil is without leadership. Everything that is happening is chaos left behind by Lula," he said.
Brazilian markets rallied on Tuesday as traders pointed to two polls showing Bolsonaro and Lula statistically tied in a potential runoff ahead of the election. REUTERS

British radar firm pushes for more sales across Eastern Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
13:07:03 UTC
22:07:03 KST

- British radar maker Blighter is showcasing its border and low-altitude surveillance radars at MSPO 2026 in Kielce, Poland, targeting more Central and Eastern European sales.
- Blighter's radars are designed to detect drones flying low enough to evade many conventional air defense and counter-drone systems.
British radar maker Blighter is pushing for more sales in Central and Eastern Europe, showcasing its border and low-altitude air surveillance radars this week at the MSPO defense exhibition in Kielce, Poland.
The company builds ground-based radars that use electronic scanning array antennas rather than the mechanically rotating dishes found on older radar systems, letting them track multiple targets while running on very little power. Blighter’s B422 long-range radar, for example, uses just 4 watts of transmit power and can detect and track people, vehicles and low-flying drones out to 32 km (20 miles), even in cluttered terrain and fog, according to the company.
“Central and Eastern European countries are investing significantly in strengthening their borders against an increasingly diverse range of threats,” said Mark Radford, co-founder and chief technology officer at Blighter. “Operators must be able to detect people, vehicles and, in coastal regions, small and covert vessels.”
“It’s been another strong year for sales of our border surveillance radars across Central and Eastern Europe, as customers recognise the advantages of adopting our COTS-based radar products along their borders,” Radford said. “At MSPO, we aim to establish new contacts, strengthen existing partnerships, and discuss the highly effective drone-detecting capability of ground radars.”
Blighter says its engineering addresses a specific gap in typical air defense coverage: drones that fly low enough to exploit ground clutter and radar signal bounce, letting them slip past conventional air defense radars and many counter-drone systems built to watch higher altitudes. The company’s radars use micro-Doppler signal processing, which reads the distinct vibration patterns of small propellers and rotors, to pick these low-flying threats out from ground noise.
The company won a contract in March to supply its B400 series radars and BlighterNexus software to an unnamed Eastern European army, deploying the systems to fixed border posts and onto army reconnaissance vehicles. That win followed what Blighter’s chief executive at the time called a record 2025 order book, alongside deals in the Middle East and Asia-Pacific.
Blighter says its radars are already used by the UK Ministry of Defence for forward operating base protection, by South Korea’s army along the Demilitarized Zone, and by the U.S. Air Force for drone detection. The company has deployed more than 800 units in over 40 countries.
During MSPO, Blighter representatives also met with senior UK government officials to discuss the company’s expanding presence in Central and Eastern Europe. The company has not disclosed the value of its recent regional contracts or named specific customers beyond the March deal with the unidentified Eastern European army.

Ozempic and Wegovy linked to nearly 40% fewer asthma attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
13:06:53 UTC
22:06:53 KST

Ozempic and Wegovy linked to nearly 40% fewer asthma attacks
Semaglutide, the active ingredient in Ozempic and Wegovy, may have an unexpected benefit beyond diabetes and weight loss.
- Date:
- September 9, 2026
- Source:
- European Respiratory Society
- Summary:
- Semaglutide, the drug found in Ozempic and Wegovy, was linked to nearly 40% fewer asthma attacks in a large real-world study. It was also associated with about 20% fewer COPD flare-ups. Researchers say GLP-1 drugs may offer respiratory benefits in addition to their effects on diabetes and obesity, but clinical trials are needed to confirm the findings.
- Share:
Semaglutide, a medication widely used for type 2 diabetes and weight loss, may also provide an unexpected benefit for people with asthma. New research presented at the European Respiratory Society (ERS) Congress in Barcelona, Spain, found that semaglutide use was associated with a reduction in asthma attacks of nearly 40%.
The study was led by Professor Chloe Bloom, Clinical Associate Professor in Respiratory Epidemiology at the National Heart & Lung Institute, Imperial College London, UK, and presented by Dr. Bohee Lee.
Exploring GLP 1 Drugs and Lung Health
Dr. Bloom said: "GLP-1 receptor agonists are widely used to treat type 2 diabetes and obesity. Previous research suggests that they may have anti-inflammatory effects and may improve lung-related outcomes. However, asthma and COPD outcomes have not been included as outcomes in GLP-1 drug trials.
"We wanted to use real-world health records to investigate whether people with asthma or COPD who started GLP-1 receptor agonists had fewer acute respiratory attacks."
To investigate that question, the researchers analyzed electronic medical records from the UK. They carried out four parallel studies, each involving between 20,000 and 22,000 people who had started treatment with either a GLP-1 medication or a different type of diabetes drug known as a sulfonylurea.
The results suggested that people with airway diseases such as asthma and COPD who received GLP-1 therapies experienced fewer asthma attacks and COPD flare-ups than comparable patients who were prescribed other diabetes medications.
Semaglutide Showed the Strongest Effect
Among the GLP-1 drugs examined, semaglutide appeared to stand out, particularly for people with asthma.
Bloom explains: "The effect was strongest with semaglutide, especially in people with asthma, where use of semaglutide appears to be associated with nearly a 40% reduction in asthma attacks. Semaglutide also led to a 20% reduction in COPD flare-ups."
The findings suggest that people who already qualify for GLP-1 receptor agonists because they have obesity or type 2 diabetes could potentially receive an additional benefit for their respiratory health.
However, Bloom emphasized that the results are not enough to recommend these medications specifically as treatments for asthma or COPD.
She explains: "The findings from this study are encouraging, but they should not change treatment decisions on their own. People with asthma or COPD should not start GLP-1 receptor agonists specifically for their lung condition outside current prescribing guidance. While the findings suggest that some people taking GLP-1 receptor agonists may experience fewer respiratory attacks, this needs confirmation in clinical trials."
Why Metabolic Health May Matter for the Lungs
Dr. Alexander Mathioudakis, Chair of the European Respiratory Society's Group on Airway Pharmacology and Treatment and Senior Lecturer in Respiratory Medicine at the University of Manchester, UK, was not involved in the research.
He said: "Obesity and metabolic dysfunction are common in airways disease and are often under-recognized as problems that can and should be addressed.
"This is one of the largest real-world studies to investigate GLP-1 receptor agonists and airways disease, and one of the first to examine whether effects differ between individual GLP-1 receptor agonists.
"It highlights the need to consider metabolic health as part of respiratory care. It also supports the case for including respiratory outcomes, such as asthma attacks and COPD exacerbations, in future trials of metabolic therapies.
"We need clinical trials that include respiratory outcomes, such as asthma attacks, COPD exacerbations, lung function, symptoms and quality of life, to determine whether metabolic treatments could become part of a broader, more personalized approach to managing airways disease."
Story Source:
Materials provided by European Respiratory Society. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

U.S. drone maker AEVEX picks up another kamikaze drone deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
13:03:50 UTC
22:03:50 KST

- AEVEX Corp. won $20.5 million in new U.S. government contracts to build and develop one-way attack drones, announced September 9.
- The company has now landed at least three separate one-way attack drone awards in 2026, following $18.5 million in May and $41 million in August.
AEVEX Corp. has won $20.5 million in new U.S. government contracts to build and develop one-way attack drones, the company announced September 9.
AEVEX did not name the government agency behind the awards or specify which of its drone models are covered. The work includes delivering the aircraft themselves along with engineering, development and integration support, and the resulting systems will be used both in combat-ready units and for training, according to the company.
“AEVEX customers continue to rely on our ability to design, build, and deliver autonomous capabilities with precision, reliability, and speed,” said Roger Wells, CEO of AEVEX. “Our one-way attack systems are informed by real-world operational demands and built to perform in contested and dynamic mission environments. We are proud to deliver affordable, scalable capabilities that strengthen warfighter effectiveness and meet the pace required by today’s operational tempo.”
One-way attack drones, also called loitering munitions, are unmanned aircraft that fly to a target and detonate on impact rather than returning to base, combining elements of a cruise missile with a small aircraft. AEVEX’s product line in this category traces back to the Phoenix Ghost program, which the U.S. Air Force accelerated in April 2022 to rush drones to Ukraine. The company has since expanded that family to include models such as the Disruptor, a Group 3 drone weighing under 1,320 kg (2,910 pounds) with a service ceiling of 18,000 feet, as well as the Dagger and Dominator systems.
This is the third publicly disclosed U.S. government award AEVEX has landed for one-way attack systems in 2026. The U.S. Air Force awarded the company $18.5 million in May for a Group 3 tactical drone, and the government awarded AEVEX $41 million in August for additional one-way attack systems, an order industry analysis firm Shephard Media’s Defence Insight estimated would cover more than 300 aircraft. Defence Insight has calculated that AEVEX has received $1.29 billion of the $6.58 billion the U.S. has spent on loitering munitions to date, or about 19.5% of that market.
AEVEX also builds the Atlas Precision Strike System, a smaller Group 2 drone the U.S. Army selected as the first platform fielded under its Launched Effects-Short Range program in October 2025. The company manufactures its drones across facilities in Alabama, California, Florida, Ohio and Virginia, and has said it relies on additive manufacturing, or 3D printing, to speed production.

How TIME and Statista Determined the World's Best Companies of 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
13:02:48 UTC
22:02:48 KST

The research project "World’s Best Companies 2026" is a comprehensive analysis conducted to identify the top performing companies around the world. The study is based on three primary dimensions: Employee Satisfaction, Revenue Growth and Sustainability Transparency (ESG).
Methodology
The first dimension, Employee Satisfaction, was investigated based on survey data from a large sample of over 200,000 employees from around the world. The evaluation encompassed direct recommendations of verified employees as well as indirect evaluations from industry peers.
The second dimension, Revenue Growth, was assessed using data from Statista’s revenue database, which contains company growth data for the last three years. The companies had to meet certain criteria to be considered for the evaluation, including generating a revenue of at least $100 million in 2024 or 2025 depending on when the most recent data was published during the research phase. Additionally, the companies had to demonstrate positive revenue growth in the last three years. Both relative and absolute growth were considered in the evaluation.
The third dimension, Sustainability Transparency, was evaluated based on ESG data among standardized KPIs from Statista’s ESG Database and targeted data research. To formulate a comprehensive ESG index, multiple Key Performance Indicators were collected. For the environmental evaluation, this included the 2024 carbon emissions intensity and reduction rate compared to 2022, as well as the Carbon Disclosure Project (CDP) score. The social dimension assessed the share of women on the board of directors and the existence of a human rights policy. The governance dimension evaluated whether a company had a Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) report adhering to the Global Reporting Initiative (GRI) guidelines and a compliance or anti-corruption guideline.
Once the data was collected and evaluated, it was consolidated and weighted within a scoring model. The scores of all three dimensions were added on an equal percentage basis to form the final ranking score of a maximum of 100 points. The 1,000 companies with the highest score were awarded as World’s Best Companies 2026 by TIME and Statista.

The World's Best Companies of 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
13:02:20 UTC
22:02:20 KST

The economy built around AI has continued to boom even as experts and leaders work to hammer out the technology's execution problem and debate the guardrails that should be put around it. Demand for AI chips remains strong, as Nvidia holds its top spot in TIME and Statista’s 2026 statistical ranking of the World’s Best Companies, highlighting top performing companies around the globe based on evaluations of employee satisfaction, revenue growth, and sustainability transparency. But new companies are also entering the scene as the AI boom reaches down the supply chain.
Companies like Wistron (no. 16), Lenovo (no. 51) and Zurich Insurance Group (no. 70) are new additions to the 2026 list. Major Nvidia supplier Wistron reports that the demand for its AI servers continues to exceed supply. The Taiwan-based manufacturing company recently opened a plant in Texas to ramp up production. Chinese computer company Lenovo, known for being a maker of devices like PCs, smartphones and tablets, saw annual profits rise to record sales driven by the newer AI server part of their business. And the wave of growing demand for physical infrastructure to support AI has created an opportunity for firms like Zurich Insurance Group to cash in on selling more data center construction-related insurance. Zurich plans to expand its dedicated insurance and risk management solution for large-scale data center projects soon into Europe and Latin America. S&P Global puts total insurable values for each data center at up to $30 billion per location.
Beyond AI, European defense technology companies are seeing cashflow as a result of European NATO allies committing in 2025 to spend a projected €800 billion on defense readiness by 2030. “The increased defense spending in Europe is actually one of the largest demand signals we have seen in generations,” says Hugues Lavandier, senior partner in McKinsey’s Aerospace & Defense Practice. A good portion of that spending is still going outside of Europe, but Lavandier “won't be surprised that we increasingly see more of that spend going to Europe for sovereignty reasons.” The war in Ukraine among other recent geopolitical tensions has shown Europe that the art of war fighting and the equipment needed is also changing. “The share of that money being spent on equipment is actually going up,” Lavandier says, especially on new technologies like drones and unmanned vehicles, and addressing technical challenges like navigation, electronic warfare, intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance.
Traditional companies in the space like French defense electronics maker Thales (no. 22; up from no. 224 in 2025) and Italian defense and aerospace company Leonardo (no. 25; up from a no. 126 in 2025) are seeing uptick in orders. At the same time, “non-traditional players are entering into the field, especially as suppliers,” Lavandier says. “In particular, a number of automotive players have entered into the fray…sometimes even selling plants, making capacity available.” Thales, for example, recently announced a sovereign drone partnership with French carmaker Renault (no. 42). A number of new startups are also taking this opportunity to translate the investment into innovations, sometimes as standalone products or in partnership with other companies, similar to Anduril’s ventures in the U.S. For example, German drone-maker Quantum Systems, which is currently supplying armed forces in Ukraine, announced significant investment from German telecomm giant Deutsche Telekom (no. 7), which owns the T-mobile brand, and also announced a new partnership with Rheinmetall (no. 287) to co-create an anti-drone shield.

Meet Nazym Kyzaibay, Kazakhstan’s first female world boxing champion and Olympic bronze medallist

Nazym Kyzaibay recounts her rise from a young boxer to Central Asia’s first female three-time world boxing champion and an Olympic bronze medallist.
Nazym Kyzaibay is one of Central Asia’s leading athletes and a pioneering figure in women’s boxing in Kazakhstan.
She is a three-time world champion and a bronze medallist at the Paris 2024 Olympics. In 2026, she continues to compete internationally and has already won a World Cup stage in China.
But her journey began at a time when women’s boxing in Kazakhstan was only starting to grow.
She began her sporting career in rhythmic gymnastics, but in 2008 Kyzaibay chose boxing instead. As one of the first female boxers of her generation to make the national team, she was part of a group of athletes who helped lay the foundation for women’s boxing in Kazakhstan.
“My first competition was the Kazakhstan Championships in Almaty. I had four fights there and won the national title for the first time,” said Nazym Kyzaibay.
After winning her first national title, Kyzaibay began competing internationally.
“My first World Championship was in the junior category. I was already part of the women’s national team, but I was still very young,” she added.
“In 2011, the championship was held in Turkey, where I won bronze. Then, in 2012, I competed in the senior category in China and won another bronze medal.”
Her first breakthrough came in 2014. At the World Championships in Jeju, South Korea, Kyzaibay won a gold medal, becoming the first Kazakh woman to win a world boxing title. Two years later, she won the title again at the World Championships in Astana.
In 2024, she made her Olympic debut in Paris. She reached the semi-finals, where she lost to China’s Wu Yu. Nazym Kyzaibay took bronze, marking a historic achievement for women’s boxing in Central Asia.
Her Olympic medal was not the end of her career.
In 2025, Kyzaibay returned to the top of world boxing. At the World Championships in Serbia, she won her third world title.
Looking beyond the ring
Nazym Kyzaibay is not planning to leave competitive boxing yet. Her main goal is still Olympic gold.
“Kazakhstan does not have an Olympic gold medal in women’s boxing or a gold medal at the Asian Games yet. Winning gold is the dream of all of us on the national team,” she said.
She is also thinking about what comes after her boxing career. She says she would like to become a coach.
“I have spent so many years in boxing and gained a lot of experience. I want to share it with other athletes, especially young boxers, and help create new champions

Icelandic Prime Minister Kristrun Frostadottir on Tuesday condemned a map shared by US President Donald Trump that depicted several countries, including Iceland, as part of the US.

Frostadottir said Iceland had not experienced problems in its direct relations with the US but agreed that Trump's post should not be dismissed as insignificant.

Elbit Systems unveils new brand for its autonomous combat drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
13:00:06 UTC
22:00:06 KST

- Elbit Systems unveiled FUSE, a new portfolio uniting its autonomous drone and ground vehicle systems under software called Dominion-X.
- The technologies have logged more than 1 million flight hours and are already in service with customers in Israel, the United States and Europe.
Elbit Systems has introduced FUSE, a new business line bringing together the Israeli defense contractor’s autonomous drone and ground vehicle systems under one portfolio, the company announced September 9 in Rosh HaAyin, Israel.
FUSE centers on software called Dominion-X, which lets a single operator control multiple autonomous aircraft and ground vehicles at once, a setup Elbit calls “One2Many.” The system is built to work in GPS-denied environments, using automatic target recognition to help unmanned systems identify and track targets without relying on satellite navigation that can be jammed. Elbit first unveiled Dominion-X in February 2025, and the software has since reached Technology Readiness Level 9, the U.S. government’s top maturity rating, meaning it has been proven in real operational use rather than only in testing.
The portfolio includes several previously announced products now grouped under FUSE. Among them are the Pirani-X loitering munition drones for ambush and strike missions, ground and air robots designed to fight alongside armored vehicles, and a family of backpack-portable reconnaissance drones called X-intra, THOR and Magni-X. Elbit also folded in systems built for urban combat against fortified positions and for automated border surveillance with minimal staffing.
“Military forces are entering a new operational era in which combat effectiveness will increasingly depend not only on autonomous platforms themselves, but on the ability to integrate and coordinate large numbers of autonomous systems within existing maneuver forces in real time,” said Eyal Dahan, CEO of FUSE. “FUSE was established to deliver that capability today, combining autonomous platforms, operational AI and scalable One2Many command capabilities into integrated operational solutions that can be rapidly deployed and integrated into modern combat formations.”
Elbit says the technologies behind FUSE have logged more than 1 million flight hours in the air and over 100,000 hours of ground operation, with thousands of drones and hundreds of unmanned ground vehicles already delivered to customers. The company says FUSE systems are currently in service with military customers in Israel, the United States and Europe, though it did not name specific units, countries, or contracts.
Elbit has built earlier versions of this concept before. The company’s Legion-X program, which combines autonomous drones with the ROOK unmanned ground vehicle, has been demonstrated for missions including reconnaissance, urban warfare and casualty evacuation. FUSE appears to extend that approach into a formal product line spanning both air and ground systems.

====================================================================================================

Farage is clearly struggling – I saw that for myself. But his legacy will be a poison that runs deep | Andy Beckett
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
13:00:03 UTC
22:00:03 KST

For much of the time since Nigel Farage resumed the Reform UK leadership two long years ago, his party has been an island of relative stability in the increasingly rough sea of British politics. While other parties plunged queasily in the polls, messily purged dissidents, argued publicly about their direction and changed leaders, Farage dominated Reform UK and gave impregnably self-assured interviews. The party’s popularity moved steadily upwards, comfortably above that of all the others.
It is a paradox that a new party with wildly expectant members, not many experienced politicians and few properly worked-out policies became the pole around which the country’s political debate revolved, and yet this seemed to do no harm to Reform’s chances of winning the next general election. As with rising rightwing populist parties across the world, Reform’s tendency to make it up as it went along appeared to be not a weakness but, for many voters, much of its appeal.
That seems less the case now. Amid multiple, worsening funding scandals, and with the party openly divided about how to respond to them, this year Reform has lost about a quarter of its support and its poll lead over Labour. There are internal mutterings about the attention-seeking and leadership ambitions of its home affairs spokesperson, the relentlessly abrasive Zia Yusuf, and its Treasury spokesperson, the slippery former Tory Robert Jenrick.
Meanwhile, Farage himself, who at 62 is two decades older than them, and has been active in politics for more than 40 years, may be finally losing his composure. Interviewed by the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg last weekend, after months of largely and uncharacteristically avoiding journalists, he switched between anger at his enemies, claims to victimhood and unconvincing insouciance: eyes bulging with fury one moment, head bobbing with forced laughter the next. Even by the feverish standards of modern British politics, it was a strange, almost manic performance.
What might happen to Reform and our wider politics if the party’s troubles continue and deepen? The answers may be less reassuring than Reform’s enemies like to think. While the diminishing likelihood of a Reform government is welcome, the party’s crisis could change Reform, and the forces massing further to the right of it – both in parliament and on the streets – in unpredictable and dangerous ways.
At the party’s conference last week, the mood felt brittle and volatile. Whereas speakers insisted that Reform was still a “government in waiting”, and banners, lanyards and speeches relentlessly hyped its potential “first 100 days”, the delegates I spoke to were worried about the party’s slide in the polls and general election chances, Andy Burnham’s assured start as prime minister, and the growing pressure Farage was under. After his speech was repeatedly interrupted by hecklers from the green group Climate Resistance, I overheard two delegates, mild-looking, middle-aged men in suits, discussing the protest. “It’s got to stop,” said one. The other said: “Smash ’em in the face!”
Another Reform reaction to the party’s difficulties has been to announce ever more extreme, dramatic policies, such as deporting foreign prisoners, possibly to the infamously brutal jails of El Salvador, and deploying the Royal Navy and Royal Marines to intercept and take all small boat migrants back to France, in “the biggest military operation in the English Channel since the second world war”. In his conference speech, Yusuf described “Operation Fortress” with lingering detail, while huge images of a military helicopter and warship were projected on to the set behind him, and a storm of applause came from the packed hall. Perhaps the potential for such authoritarian political theatre and performatively aggressive policy was always there in Reform, but both feel much more central to its activities now.
“All parliamentary recesses will be cancelled,” declared Farage in his speech. “Parliament will sit, if necessary, for 24 hours a day, six days a week, until we pass the necessary legislation.” Nothing would be allowed to obstruct “the will of the people” – even though, with modern election turnouts low and half a dozen parties now competing seriously across the country, a Reform victory might represent the will of only a fifth of voters, or less.
This year, with the party losing the electoral initiative, new movements have appeared on the anti-migrant right: the even more hardline Restore Britain, and Patriot Platform, the black-clad blockaders of Dover and Portsmouth. Though Farage has criticised both groups, the latter for wearing balaclavas at their protests, the boundaries between Reform and these rivals are not as firm as he would like more mainstream rightwing Britons – whose support Reform badly needs – to think. Restore and Reform’s rhetoric and policies can be hard to distinguish, while on Monday, Yusuf visited Portsmouth and spoke amicably with Patriot Platform’s organiser, Daniel Thomas, a convicted attempted kidnapper.
Thomas told Yusuf he was upset by Farage’s criticism, and that the protests were not meant to intimidate, but that he still considered Farage a “hero” for his campaigning against the small boats. “You have done really well,” said Thomas. “A lot of people support you.” “Thank you,” said Yusuf, who listened to him at length, nodding respectfully. Then Yusuf replied: “I will take that message – you’ve got my word … take that back to him [Farage].”
The encounter suggested that Reform’s problems may create new alliances and opportunities for the hard right, reshaping but not weakening anti-migrant politics. While the Conservative shadow home secretary, Chris Philp, condemned the Portsmouth violence, he added: “People are genuinely angry at the government’s failure to stop the boats.” Even Labour dares not challenge the legitimacy of what the policing minister, Sarah Jones, called on Monday “the frustration we see in our communities today” about the boats. Just as Reform’s rise made both Labour and the Tories more nationalist and socially conservative, there is a danger that its decline, temporary or otherwise, could continue that process, as they compete for its former supporters.
If you’re opposed to Reform’s policies, and especially if you might become one of their victims, then its setbacks this year may be a relief. But that relief will only be partial while its ideas and claims remain so thoroughly embedded across politics and the media, and in many people’s everyday conversations and thinking. One day, Farage will retire, but what he represents will be even harder to stop.
- 
  Andy Beckett is a Guardian columnist

New study reveals how depression twists our perception of fairness
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
13:00:03 UTC
22:00:03 KST

People experiencing symptoms of depression often view social situations differently than others. A recent study found that individuals with depressive symptoms are more likely to perceive unfair financial offers as fair, but only if they consider themselves to have a high social standing. The research was published in the journal PLOS One.
Depression involves more than just a persistently low mood or a loss of interest in daily activities. It frequently brings about cognitive distortions, which are biased ways of thinking that negatively alter how a person perceives themselves and the world around them. These mental filters can change how someone evaluates risk, assesses their personal value, and judges the intentions of others in everyday social exchanges.
Researchers often use a behavioral economics task called the Ultimatum Game to study how people process fairness. In a typical version of this game, one person is given a sum of money and proposes how to divide it with a second person. The second person then decides whether to accept or reject the offer.
If the responder accepts the deal, both players keep their respective shares of the money. If they reject the offer, the money is forfeited, and neither player receives anything.
From a purely logical standpoint, a responder should accept any offer greater than zero, since walking away with a small amount of money is better than walking away with nothing. However, human behavior rarely follows strict economic logic.
Typically, people will reject highly uneven splits, such as an offer where the proposer keeps 90 percent of the money and offers only 10 percent to the responder. Participants are often willing to sacrifice their own financial gain to punish the other player for violating social norms of fairness.
This behavior, known as altruistic punishment, relies heavily on a person’s emotional state and their cognitive ability to recognize a situation as inequitable. Studies show that facing an unfair offer triggers negative emotions and activates brain regions associated with conflict and disgust.
Psychology researcher Yin Hanmo of Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia and a team of colleagues wanted to understand exactly how depression influences these decisions. Previous studies on depression and the Ultimatum Game have yielded conflicting results. Some research indicates that depressed individuals reject more offers due to heightened negative emotions, while other studies show they reject fewer offers.
The researchers suspected that a person’s subjective socioeconomic status might explain the discrepancy. Subjective socioeconomic status refers to how an individual views their own rank in society, regardless of their actual income or education level.
To test this idea, Hanmo and the research team recruited 274 university students in China and Malaysia. The participants completed a standardized questionnaire designed to measure the frequency of depressive symptoms over the past week, such as feeling sad, experiencing restless sleep, or struggling to get going.
The students also completed a widely used assessment to gauge their subjective socioeconomic status. They looked at an image of a 10-rung ladder representing where people stand in society. The top rungs represented people with the most money, most education, and best jobs. Participants selected the rung that best matched their own perceived position.
Next, the participants played a modified, paper-based version of the Ultimatum Game. They received a list of 18 proposed monetary splits from anonymous partners. Some of the offers were equal, splitting the money evenly down the middle, while other offers were highly skewed in favor of the proposer.
For each proposed split, the participants had to choose whether to accept or reject the deal. They also rated the perceived fairness of each offer on a scale from one to seven, with one being very unfair and seven being very fair.
The researchers found that depressive symptoms alone did not directly dictate how often a participant rejected an uneven offer. Instead, the effects of depression depended heavily on a participant’s self-reported social standing.
Among individuals who ranked themselves high on the social ladder, having higher levels of depression was associated with viewing unequal offers as more fair. Because these individuals perceived the bad deals as relatively fair, they were subsequently less likely to reject them.
This pattern did not appear among participants who placed themselves lower on the social ladder. For these individuals, experiencing depressive symptoms did not alter their perception of unequal offers. Consequently, their likelihood of rejecting a bad deal remained unchanged regardless of their depression levels.
The researchers suggest that differing baseline expectations may drive this divergence. People who feel they have a high social status generally expect to be treated equitably and with respect. When they face a highly unequal financial offer, the gap between their expectations and reality creates psychological friction.
The authors propose that individuals with both high social standing and depressive symptoms might subconsciously cope with this friction by rationalizing the bad offer. By mentally reframing the unequal split as acceptable, they can avoid the emotional distress of acknowledging unfair treatment. This cognitive reappraisal acts as a defense mechanism, reducing immediate discomfort but ultimately leading to skewed financial decisions.
In contrast, people who view themselves as lower on the social ladder may frequently encounter systemic disadvantages and social inequality. Because they do not expect strict equity in the same way, an unequal offer does not trigger the same intense psychological conflict. As a result, depression does not force them to artificially adjust their perception of fairness to cope with the situation.
The current study focused on university students experiencing varying levels of depressive symptoms, rather than patients clinically diagnosed with a major depressive disorder. Studies involving clinical populations have occasionally found that severe depression leads to higher rejection rates in the Ultimatum Game. The regulatory mental strategies that cause people to rationalize bad offers might break down as depressive symptoms become more severe, leaving patients overly sensitive to unfairness.
Additionally, the researchers measured subjective social standing rather than objective financial metrics like household income or accumulated wealth. Because university students typically share similar educational environments and do not yet have established careers, their sense of social status might function differently than it would in older adults in the workforce.
Future studies will need to test whether objective income levels produce similar effects on financial decision-making. Researchers also hope to measure participants’ baseline expectations of fairness directly to confirm whether expectation violations drive these behavioral shifts.
The study, “Subjective socioeconomic status moderates depression’s impact on fairness perception in the ultimatum game: A moderated mediation model,” was authored by Yin Hanmo, Rozainee Khairudin, Shi Yixin, Zhang Xi, Chen Xinyu, Syakirien Yusoff, and Nasrudin Subhi.
