Taking care of people with dementia left up to loved ones in Estonia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
12:28:00 UTC
21:28:00 KST

Taking care of people with dementia left up to loved ones in Estonia
A recent study finds that a unified system for helping people with dementia should be established so their loved ones do not have to seek assistance from multiple agencies.
Nearly 27,000 people with dementia currently live in Estonia and in an aging society, the issue is becoming increasingly acute. A dementia diagnosis affects not only the person with the condition but also their loved ones. Hanna-Stiina Heinmets, who counsels family members on a daily basis, said the loved ones of people with memory disorders most need services that give them a break.
"Their daily job is providing care and they may also be working at the same time. They essentially have two full-time jobs and for the most part, they cannot afford to take days off. They simply need someone to come in and take over the caregiving for a few days," said Hanna-Stiina Heinmets, a consultant at the Dementia Competence Center.
In many municipalities, home care is understood to mean little more than bringing firewood inside and delivering food to a person's home. But if a person with dementia needs help taking medication, for example, Heinmets said the recommendation is often to send them to a nursing home, even though they could still continue living at home. At the same time, nursing homes are reluctant to accept people with severe dementia and some have effectively been thrown out of five or six different nursing homes. A recent study found that access to assistance often depends on where a person lives.
"The situation is generally better in larger population centers. They have day centers and more services. There are more options and more resources. The most difficult situation is in sparsely populated, outlying areas," Praxis analyst Jane Ester said.
Ester said the first step should be to create a comprehensive support system for both people with dementia and their loved ones. Each family affected by dementia should have a designated person responsible for their case who would proactively contact family members, regularly assess what assistance the family needs and help them find it, rather than leaving people to navigate between different agencies on their own.
According to the Ministry of Social Affairs, the planned health and social care reform should improve the situation to some extent. In two years, the ministry hopes to begin testing, with the support of EU funding, solutions that will help people with dementia continue living at home for longer.
"I think these people's lives can be made easier. If we think about what can provide support right now, today, there is the Dementia Competence Center and its information line. That is somewhere people can turn for help today," said Kadri Mets, head of disability rights policy at the Ministry of Social Affairs.

====================================================================================================

1 billion customers can be wrong
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
12:27:21 UTC
21:27:21 KST

For decades, Europe’s China strategy rested on a simple premise: more than a billion people, a rising middle class, and an insatiable appetite for European goods. Improve political ties, secure market access, and European industry would thrive.
That logic is not just outdated. It is dangerously delusional.
The China-Europe economic relationship has undergone a structural transformation. China is no longer Europe’s complementary consumer market.
It is Europe’s primary, state‑backed industrial competitor, explicitly aiming to reduce dependence on European imports at home while challenging European manufacturing abroad.
The old model assumed mutual benefit. Europe supplied high‑value technology, specialized machinery and premium cars.
China supplied low‑cost manufacturing and vast demand. For years, especially in export‑driven economies like Germany, the arrangement worked.
Numbers behind the story
That division of labor is vanishing. China did not merely grow richer, it became an industrial and technological powerhouse.
It now leads in batteries, solar panels and electric vehicles, and is rapidly closing the gap in robotics, artificial intelligence and industrial machinery. Beijing’s drive for technological self‑reliance functions, in practice, as import substitution in many high‑value sectors that underpin European prosperity.
The numbers tell the story. In 2025, the EU exported NT$7.3 trillion (199.5 billion euros, US$231 billion) in goods to China and imported NT$20.5 trillion, leaving a goods deficit of nearly NT$13.2 trillion.
More tellingly, the two sides are moving in opposite directions. EU exports to China fell 6.5%, while imports from China rose 6.4%.
Germany, long the biggest European beneficiary of China’s rise, offers a sharper warning. Its exports to China dropped 14.5% in early 2025, driven in part by a 26.1% plunge in automobile shipments.
This is not a temporary cyclical slump. It signals the erosion of the industrial complementarity on which Europe’s China strategy was built.
BYD or Mercedes
Why, then, are China’s 1.4 billion people not delivering the consumer bonanza Europe once imagined?
Part of the answer lies in the structure of the Chinese economy. Beijing’s state‑led industrial policies channel enormous resources into manufacturing capacity, while household consumption remains unusually low as a share of GDP. The result is a double squeeze on European industry.
Inside China, state incentives, technological advancement and increasingly capable domestic firms are replacing European products with Chinese alternatives. A consumer who once aspired to a Mercedes may now choose a BYD. The same shift is underway across machinery, electronics, renewable‑energy equipment and other sophisticated goods.
Outside China, the problem reverses. Manufacturing capacity that cannot be absorbed domestically seeks markets abroad.
Chinese companies therefore compete not only with European firms in China but increasingly with them in Europe and in third‑country markets across Asia, Africa, Latin America and the Middle East. Europe is being squeezed at both ends, losing ground in the Chinese market it once expected to dominate while facing ever‑formidable Chinese competitors in its own backyard.
That is why the familiar European prescription, improve relations with Beijing to gain greater market access, is no longer sufficient. Even if China eliminated every tariff and trade barrier tomorrow, European industry would still face the deeper challenge of competing against highly capable Chinese firms embedded in a state‑supported industrial ecosystem.
Strait peace
The political implications are profound. For years, the promise of the Chinese market encouraged Europe to tread carefully on Taiwan, invoking its “one China policy” to justify caution. But the economic relationship is no longer so one‑sided.
China needs European markets as much as Europe needs China. The fear of displeasing Beijing should therefore carry less weight.
Indeed, a war in the Taiwan Strait could do far more damage to Europe’s prosperity than better relations with China could ever offset. Peace across the strait is not separate from Europe’s economic interests. It is essential to them.
Taiwan sits at the nexus of global semiconductor production and vital maritime trade routes. Bloomberg Economics has estimated that a war over Taiwan could cost the global economy about US$10 trillion in its first year, roughly 10% of global GDP, with Europe suffering severe consequences of its own.
The precise figure is necessarily hypothetical, but the broader conclusion is hard to dispute. A major conflict in the Taiwan Strait would deliver an economic shock dwarfing almost any commercial advantage Europe might gain through improved access to the Chinese market.
For European policymakers, preserving stability across the Taiwan Strait is therefore not an act of distant idealism, nor should it be understood simply as ideological solidarity with a small democratic state. It is a matter of economic self‑preservation. Spending decades negotiating incremental access to Chinese markets means little if an Asian geopolitical crisis can erase those gains many times over.
None of this requires Europe to decouple from China or enter an ideological cold war. China remains a major trading partner, and Chinese competition can spur European innovation.
Nor should Europe abandon dialogue with Beijing. The question is not whether Europe should engage China, but what assumptions should guide that engagement.
Nostalgia no longer works
European leaders must replace nostalgic expectations with a strategy grounded in economic security. That means responding selectively to heavily subsidized overcapacity when it threatens strategically important European industries.
It means reducing dangerous dependencies in critical raw materials, green technologies, pharmaceuticals, semiconductors and other essential supply chains so that commercial dependence cannot easily become political leverage. It also means taking a more active diplomatic interest in Indo‑Pacific stability, particularly the preservation of peace across the Taiwan Strait and the security of the maritime routes on which European trade depends.
The political temptation to revive the old promise will remain strong. China still has 1.4 billion people. The number is enormous, easily understood and electorally seductive.
Better relations mean better access. Better access means more exports. More exports mean more jobs and prosperity. But population is not a market strategy.
The promise of 1.4 billion Chinese consumers was enticing when China needed what Europe made. Europe must now adapt to a world in which China increasingly makes those goods itself and, in many cases, wants to sell them to Europe.
European strategy can therefore no longer begin by asking what Europe can sell to China. It must begin with the harder question: What can Europe continue to make when China can make almost everything Europe can?
John Cheng is a retired businessman from Hong Kong who lives in Taiwan and is the author of “Taiwan Is Taiwan.”

EU proposes more restrictions for Airbnb, holiday rentals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
12:27:00 UTC
21:27:00 KST

EU proposes more restrictions for Airbnb, holiday rentals
September 9, 2026
Airbnb and other companies providing short-term home rentals could face tighter restrictions after the European Commission proposed new rules on Wednesday to help tackle housing shortages in tourist hotspots.
A surge in short-term holiday rentals has contributed to a shortage of affordable housing and a spike in housing prices in many of Europe's most popular tourist destinations, prompting residents to protest in recent years .
What do we know about the EU's affordable housing proposal?
The EU's executive branch unveiled the measures as part of an "affordable housing" package, which will allow local authorities to limit short-term rentals to address what European Commission vice-president Teresa Ribera described as a "terrible crisis."
"When the market fails to deliver something as fundamental as an affordable home, public authorities have a responsibility to act," the Spanish politician said.
The measures seek to harmonize rules across the bloc, after attempts to crack down on Airbnb-style rentals by authorities in cities such as Paris, Berlin and Barcelona, among others, were met with legal challenges by rental and tourism companies.
The European Commission's Affordable Housing Act — which still needs to be approved by EU legislators and EU member states — would provide cities with legal support by clarifying when local authorities can act against housing companies without breaking EU single market rules.
Under the proposal, city and local authorities would be allowed to limit short-term and holiday rentals as well as curb the purchase of property for short-term letting in areas considered to be "under housing stress," the European Commission said.
For an area to be defined as "under stress," certain parameters — including the ratio between local housing prices and incomes — would have to be met.
Before restrictions can be introduced, cities would have to show that holiday rentals have had a major negative impact on the affordability or availability of housing for at least three years.
The proposed legislation will not impact landlords renting out their primary residence for short-term periods.
The Commission also recommended that authorities free up land for more housing and modernize planning and construction of new homes to address housing shortages.
How have rental companies reacted?
CCIA Europe, a lobbying group that represents Airbnb, among others, said the EU's measures fail to address the need for independent assessment of the restrictions.
"Europe will not solve its housing crisis by giving cities an EU framework to restrict short-term rentals and then letting them police their own compliance," CCIA's head of policy Alexandre Roure said in a statement.
"Without independent scrutiny or effective redress, this proposal will remain a paper tiger, leaving disproportionate restrictions in place and undermining the legal certainty the Affordable Housing Act is meant to provide," Roure added.

As a public figure, Sisic had spoken openly about her health condition. In 2024, she shared a post on Instagram thanking her paediatric medical team who looked after her as a young person.
"Thanks to the medical staff and the dedicated doctors - who time and again saved my life through their tremendous efforts - I have overcome many difficult moments and been able to lead a fulfilling life," she wrote at the time.
Speaking to Austrian outlet Heute in 2024, the Miss Austria winner said her first operation was right after her birth.
She also spoke of how her health impacted her childhood.
"Sports weeks took place without me. My childhood was simply different, but it also made me strong," she said.
Herzkinder Österreich, a charity in Austria which supports children with heart conditions, also paid tribute to Sisic.
In a Facebook post, the organisation said it is "deeply saddened by the untimely death" of Sisic, adding "at just 22 years old, she left us far too soon".
The tribute says: "Lucia herself was a true child at heart. A young woman who knew what it meant to grow up with a congenital heart defect, to endure surgeries, and still to pursue her own path with courage and joy.
"We will remember her as a warm-hearted, joyful, and impressive young woman – and as an adult child who wanted to give courage to others affected."

13 people die in avalanche in southern Russia. Most were National Guard troops who had traveled there for training.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
12:25:19 UTC
21:25:19 KST

13 people die in avalanche in southern Russia. Most were National Guard troops who had traveled there for training.
At least 13 people have died in an avalanche that struck the Bezengi Gorge in Kabardino-Balkaria. The avalanche broke off Mount Mizhirgi on the evening of September 6 and buried a group of 33 climbers on the slope. Ten people made it down on their own, while six others were injured and hospitalized. By the morning of September 9, rescuers from Russia’s Emergency Situations Ministry had found the bodies of 13 dead climbers, with the search continuing for four more. Rescue efforts are being complicated by “dangerous, rugged terrain” and the risk of another snow collapse, the ministry stated.
According to sources cited by the Russian business daily Kommersant, the avalanche killed 12 National Guard troops and other security personnel who had traveled to Bezengi for mountain training. The Russian law enforcement-linked Telegram channel Shot and the Russian security services-linked Telegram channel Baza claimed that fighters from the elite “Vityaz” Special Forces Center of Rosgvardiya were among the dead. Rosgvardiya confirmed that some of the dead had served in its ranks but denied reports that “Vityaz” fighters were among them.
Albert Izotov, a 70-year-old climber from St. Petersburg, was also killed in the avalanche. He had traveled to the gorge as a civilian instructor training security personnel, the Alpine Climbing Federation of Russia stated. At the time the avalanche struck, Izotov’s group was carrying out a training exercise. “Nothing of this size had ever come down before. It all collapsed, jumped over the glacier, and fell on the group that was holding the exercise,” said Alexander Yakovenko, chairman of the federation’s sport climbing committee.
The Bezengi Gorge disaster is the deadliest mass fatality event in Russia’s mountains since 2002, when the film crew of Sergei Bodrov Jr. died. That year, a glacier collapsed onto the camp of the crew filming Svyaznoy “The Messenger” in the Karmadon Gorge in North Ossetia, killing at least 125 people, including the actor himself. Russia has recorded four mass fatality events in its mountains over the past 25 years, according to the Russian state news agency TASS.
Russia’s Investigative Committee has opened a criminal case on charges of negligence, and military investigators are handling the investigation. The federation emphasized that the training involved experienced climbers at a site it considered safe. “I really don’t understand where the negligence is here. Everything that needed to be done was done correctly, as part of conducting exercises like this,” said Yakovenko, a representative of the federation.

71% of Ukrainians Say They Are Happy Despite Russia’s War, Poll Shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
12:24:18 UTC
21:24:18 KST

More than seven in 10 Ukrainians consider themselves happy despite more than four years of Russia’s full-scale war, according to a survey released by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology (KIIS).
The poll found that 71% of respondents described themselves as happy. Of those, 31% said they were definitely happy, while 40% selected “rather yes than no.”
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Another 11% gave an ambivalent response, saying they felt both happy and unhappy. Sixteen percent described themselves as unhappy, while 7% said they were not happy.
The proportion of Ukrainians who consider themselves happy has changed little since December 2025 – rising from 69% to 71%. However, it has increased significantly from the 58% recorded in December 2024.
The latest figure also matches the level recorded in December 2021, two months before Russia launched its full-scale invasion, when 71% of respondents considered themselves happy.
KIIS President Volodymyr Paniotto said the results may initially appear paradoxical because Ukrainians have faced deaths, displacement, financial hardship, separation from relatives, and the loss of homes and their previous way of life.
He said the recovery in reported happiness did not result primarily from a decline in the proportion of unhappy respondents. That figure remained at about 16% in both December 2024 and the latest survey.
Instead, the share of people who answered “both yes and no” fell from approximately 25% to 11%. According to Paniotto, many respondents moved from an uncertain or conflicting perception of their lives toward a more positive assessment.
Russia Suspends Flights 1,800km From Ukraine as Drones Threaten Siberian Oil-Producing Heartland
The survey cannot establish a definitive reason for that change. The institute suggested that psychological adaptation to a prolonged war could be one possible explanation but stressed that the data did not directly test that hypothesis.
“Seventy-one percent being happy does not mean Ukrainians do not notice the war or that their lives have become easier,” Paniotto said.
He said the findings instead demonstrated people’s capacity to adapt to extremely difficult circumstances, reconsider their expectations and values, and maintain a positive assessment of their lives.
At the same time, Paniotto cautioned that the 16% who described themselves as unhappy represented millions of people struggling with bereavement, health problems, financial hardship, and other consequences of the war.
Age, health, and income affect happiness
Age remained a significant factor. Seventy-five percent of respondents under 40 described themselves as happy, compared with 60% among those aged 70 and older.
KIIS said the relationship between happiness and financial well-being was almost linear. The share of happy respondents ranged from 48% among those reporting very low incomes to 91% among the wealthiest group.
Health showed a similar pattern. About half of respondents who rated their health as poor or very poor considered themselves happy, compared with 91% among those who reported the best health.
The poll also found a strong connection between happiness and a sense of purpose. Forty-one percent of respondents who said they did not know the meaning of their lives considered themselves happy, compared with 79% among those who said they did.
KIIS surveyed 2,007 Ukrainian adults by telephone between May 7 and June 3. Respondents lived in areas controlled by the Ukrainian government, although the sample included internally displaced people who had left Russian-occupied territories.
Residents of occupied areas and Ukrainians who moved abroad after Russia’s full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, were not included.
Under normal conditions, the survey’s margin of error would not exceed 2.8 percentage points.

Estonians hope to choose a site for NPP construction by spring
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
12:24:02 UTC
21:24:02 KST

The best location for building a nuclear power plant is being considered in Estonia, and given that sufficient water for cooling can only be obtained from the sea, the selected sites are located on the coast, writes ERR News.
The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) guidelines set out a number of prerequisites that must be considered when choosing a site for the construction of a NPP. Agnes Lihtsa, Advisor for Land and Spatial Policy at the Estonian Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communications, pointed out that the ministry’s list of requirements includes 40 criteria. She said that these are not only nuclear safety requirements, but also geological criteria, hydrological criteria (availability of water for cooling), as well as the project’s impact on natural or environmental values, and socio-economic criteria.
Lihtsa pointed to examples that must be considered when choosing a site for a NPP. According to her, six potential locations for the NPP are currently being considered, all near Kunda and Lüganuse. Lihtsa said that the most important factor is the availability of water for cooling, and in Estonia’s case, the only place where it is possible to obtain enough water is the sea, as there are no rivers in the country that could provide a sufficient flow of water. However, there are also not many suitable places on the coast, and the best options have been found near Kunda and Lüganuse. Three potential construction sites have been looked at near both villages.
The geological situation is also important, as the bedrock must be very stable. Another important factor is the proximity of power lines to connect the NPP to substations. Two possible connection points have been found so far – a substation near Rakvere and a substation near Püssi. The proximity of ports should also be considered, so that nuclear fuel or construction materials can be delivered more easily.
The councillor said people don’t want a nuclear power plant in the immediate vicinity of their homes,
so officials are trying to find a location with as little population as possible. In August, the ministry held public consultations to get a broader reflection of local residents’ opinions, and received a lot of feedback. Lihtsa said that local residents are mainly concerned about how the proximity of the nuclear power plant will affect property values, groundwater and the environment. According to her, the feedback has varied widely – from the recognition that residents simply do not want a nuclear power plant in their vicinity to dozens of pages of detailed letters.
The proposals are still being reviewed, but it is already clear that the evaluation and selection of potential construction sites will require more explanation. Lihtsa said that it will probably be necessary to outline the methodology more clearly so that everyone understands how the comparison is made, how the locations are evaluated and how the selection is made.
The Ministry of Economy and Communications hopes to make sufficient progress by spring to select a construction site.

Rethinking Russia, Re-evaluating Risk: The Changing Face of Kyrgyz Migration
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
12:24:00 UTC
21:24:00 KST

Labor migration to Russia has traditionally played a central role in Kyrgyzstan’s economy. Between 2012 and 2021, average remittance inflows were the equivalent of 30 percent of Kyrgyzstan’s GDP. Following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the share of remittances in GDP has fluctuated, falling to approximately 17.6 percent in 2024. Despite this instability, remittance inflows have remained historically high in absolute terms. The volatility of recent years nevertheless points to a broader shift in the relationship between remittances and the Kyrgyz economy, suggesting that the country’s long-standing dependence on migration income is becoming more complex and potentially less predictable.
Russia’s war in Ukraine has contributed to changes in migration flows from Kyrgyzstan to Russia. According to estimates based on Kyrgyzstan’s 2022 National Population Census, approximately 854,000 Kyrgyz citizens were working in Russia. By 2026, the Kyrgyz Ministry of Labor reported that around 502,242 Kyrgyz citizens were engaged in labor migration in Russia. While differences in methodology and timing mean that these figures should not be treated as a precise measure of the decline, the overall trend is significant. Russia has not ceased to be the dominant destination for Kyrgyz labor migrants, but the changing scale of migration suggests that the long-standing Russia-centered migration system is undergoing a broader transformation.
Kyrgyzstan’s citizens have benefited from relatively open access to the Russian labor market through membership in the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) since 2015. Problems certainly existed: migrants frequently encountered arbitrary treatment by police, informal payments, document checks, and other forms of everyday insecurity. Yet the basic institutional framework remained relatively stable, and migration continued to be understood primarily as an economic and labor-market issue.
The system has experienced crises before. Since the mass development of labor migration to Russia in the early 2000s, migrants have experienced several major disruptions, including the 2008-2009 global financial crisis and the COVID-19 pandemic. Yet the current crisis is fundamentally different. Earlier shocks were primarily economic or epidemiological and, after a period of disruption, the established migration system largely recovered to its prior state. The war in Ukraine, by contrast, has produced a much longer-term transformation of the institutional and political environment in which migration takes place.
The most important change since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine has been the securitization of migration in Russia. This involves more than simply tightening migration controls; migrants are increasingly treated as objects of national security governance, with migration policy becoming more closely linked to counterterrorism, border control, and internal security.
In addition, Russia has increasingly sought to draw Central Asian migrants into its wartime manpower system, as the prolonged war in Ukraine created sustained demand for military personnel. Since 2022, Russian authorities have offered foreign nationals simplified access to citizenship in exchange for military service, while police raids and other forms of administrative pressure have increasingly been used to identify and recruit migrants and recently naturalized citizens of Central Asian origin.
This has created a striking duality in Russia’s approach to migration: migrants remain economically important because of persistent labor shortages, yet their precarious legal status also makes them a particularly accessible population for military recruitment. In this sense, migration governance has become intertwined not only with border and internal security, but also with the state’s efforts to sustain wartime manpower.
For migrants from Kyrgyzstan the significance of these changes extends beyond the immediate risk of detention or deportation. The rules governing everyday life in Russia have become more complex and restrictive, including requirements relating to registration, documentation, medical examinations, language testing, and other forms of administrative control. Migration is therefore becoming not simply more difficult, but less predictable.
This unpredictability is particularly important because the traditional Russia-Central Asian migration system depended on predictability. Families could plan around seasonal migration, circular movement, and the expectation that migrants would return to Russia after spending time at home. When the rules governing entry, employment, and residence become uncertain, the entire household migration strategy becomes harder to sustain.
A Gendered Transformation of Migration
This ongoing transformation is also likely to change the gender composition of migration. Historically, men dominated migration to Russia, particularly in construction, transport and other physically demanding sectors. The prospect of increasingly restrictive migration controls, detention, military recruitment, and uncertainty over legal status changes the calculation. Women have become a significant part of Kyrgyzstan’s migration system. Kyrgyzstan has historically had a relatively high proportion of female migrants compared with other Central Asian countries and war has accelerated this feminization of migration.
The gender implications of the current transformation require more attention. If young men increasingly avoid Russia while women become more visible in migration corridors, the social organization of migration, and potentially household roles and care responsibilities, will change as well. For women especially, these may include more precarity. Recent research from the International Organization for Migration (IOM) shows that female migrants from Kyrgyzstan continue to experience significant vulnerabilities throughout the migration cycle.
The asymmetric risks facing men in wartime Russia – specifically military mobilization and targeted security sweeps – are accelerating the structural feminization of Kyrgyz migration. This shift changes not only domestic division of labor and remittance flows within households, but also transfers the burden of economic survival onto female workers who navigate highly precarious service sectors.
The Family Implications
One of the most consequential developments is that the new restrictions increasingly affect not only workers but also their families. A particularly important example is education. Since 2024, foreign children seeking admission to Russian schools have been required to demonstrate sufficient knowledge of Russian through testing, alongside requirements concerning their legal status in the country. Children who do not meet the language requirement cannot be enrolled in school. In June 2025, the State Duma approved a bill requiring schools to report information about migrant children and their parents to the Ministry of Internal Affair. In August, a draft amendment to the Law on Education prohibiting free education for migrant children was submitted to the State Duma for discussion.
The significance of this change should not be underestimated. For many migrant families, migration to Russia was not simply an individual labor strategy. It was a family strategy in which children could live with their parents and attend Russian schools. The new rules therefore challenge one of the assumptions on which family migration had been built.
The Kyrgyz government has subsequently had to wrestle with how to provide education and social support to children whose parents work abroad.
In March 2025, the Kyrgyz government established the Tunguch online school as a pilot state institution for 2025–2028. The school provides education for students in grades 5-11 and was explicitly designed to expand access to education for children who cannot attend conventional schools because of geographical distance. By September 2025, the school had 43 classes – 28 in Kyrgyz and 15 in Russian – and children from more than 15 countries were studying through the online school, with Russia housing the largest group.
Tunguch represents an important change in the way the Kyrgyz state approaches migration. For more than two decades, the economic contribution of migrants was treated as a given, while many of the social costs of migrant children left behind, fragmented families, access to education, and reintegration were largely managed by households themselves.
By targeting the educational access and legal standing of migrant dependents, Russian policy has dismantled the “family migration” model. This systemic exclusion has forced the Kyrgyz state to pivot from passive economic beneficiary to active social mediator. Initiatives like the Tunguch online school mark the institutionalization of state-supported transnational living, signaling the state’s growing need to build infrastructure to mitigate its social externalities.
Preparedness for Migrant Reintegration
A potentially more consequential shift in Kyrgyzstan’s migration policy is emerging around the question of what happens when migrants return. On May 14, 2026, the Cabinet of Ministers approved the Program for the Reintegration of Returning Migrants for 2026–2030. This is the first national policy document specifically dedicated to migrant reintegration and signals an important change in how the state is beginning to understand migration: not only as a mechanism for absorbing domestic labor-market pressures and generating remittances, but also as a process that can reshape the country’s labor force, skills base, and economic development.
For much of the post-Soviet period, Kyrgyzstan’s migration policy was largely oriented toward managing outward mobility. Labor migration offered an important pressure valve in an economy with limited employment opportunities, while remittances became a major source of household income and foreign exchange. The policy challenge was therefore primarily how to facilitate migration, protect citizens abroad, and channel its economic benefits home. The new reintegration program suggests a different policy problem is now being centered: how to absorb and make use of the human, professional, and financial capital accumulated through migration when migrants return.
The program includes measures to support employment and self-employment, provide economic assistance, expand vocational retraining, and develop mechanisms for recognizing qualifications acquired abroad. Yet the adoption of the program should not be confused with evidence that Kyrgyzstan is prepared for a large-scale return. A policy framework is a first step; implementation capacity will determine whether reintegration becomes a viable alternative to renewed migration. The more fundamental question is whether the Kyrgyz economy can generate sufficient productive employment, wages, and opportunities for entrepreneurship to make staying economically meaningful for returnees. If these conditions are absent, reintegration programs may end up functioning primarily as short-term assistance schemes while migrants continue to view re-migration as the most viable livelihood strategy.
Diversification Beyond Russia, A Migration Crisis Unlike Any Before
The changing environment in Russia is also pushing Kyrgyzstan to diversify migration destinations. The United Kingdom has become one of the most visible alternatives. Kyrgyzstan began participating in the U.K.’s Seasonal Worker visa program in 2022. The quota available to Kyrgyz citizens increased from around 1,500 places in 2022 to 10,000 in 2025.
South Korea represents another increasingly important destination. Under the Employment Permit System, the quota for Kyrgyz workers increased by approximately 18 percent between 2023 and 2024, reaching more than 3,000 places. At the same time, South Korea has also been accessible through another route: Kyrgyz citizens who acquired Russian citizenship could take advantage of Russia’s visa-free arrangement with South Korea, which allow Russian passport holders to enter the country for short stays without a visa. This created an additional channel of mobility for some Central Asian migrants holding Russian passports, although visa-free entry should not be equated with legal authorization to work. Taken together, these developments illustrate how migration system is becoming more diversified, combining formal labor-migration programs with alternative mobility channels.
The current migration system crisis should therefore not be understood simply as another temporary decline in migration to Russia. The post-2022 crisis is different because it affects the foundations of the system. Russia is not simply becoming a more difficult labor market. It is becoming a more securitized environment in which migrants face greater uncertainty over entry, residence, employment, education for their children and personal security.
This is a profound shift. For more than two decades, Russia occupied a particular place in the social imagination of Kyrgyzstan as the most accessible foreign labor market, a familiar destination connected through networks and post-Soviet institutions, and a place where generations of Kyrgyz citizens had built their livelihoods. That perception is now changing. The significance of this transformation may ultimately extend far beyond migration statistics.

This shift changes not only domestic division of labor and remittance flows within households, but also transfers the burden of economic survival onto female workers who navigate highly precarious service sectors.
The Family Implications
One of the most consequential developments is that the new restrictions increasingly affect not only workers but also their families. A particularly important example is education. Since 2024, foreign children seeking admission to Russian schools have been required to demonstrate sufficient knowledge of Russian through testing, alongside requirements concerning their legal status in the country. Children who do not meet the language requirement cannot be enrolled in school. In June 2025, the State Duma approved a bill requiring schools to report information about migrant children and their parents to the Ministry of Internal Affair. In August, a draft amendment to the Law on Education prohibiting free education for migrant children was submitted to the State Duma for discussion.
The significance of this change should not be underestimated. For many migrant families, migration to Russia was not simply an individual labor strategy. It was a family strategy in which children could live with their parents and attend Russian schools. The new rules therefore challenge one of the assumptions on which family migration had been built.
The Kyrgyz government has subsequently had to wrestle with how to provide education and social support to children whose parents work abroad.
In March 2025, the Kyrgyz government established the Tunguch online school as a pilot state institution for 2025–2028. The school provides education for students in grades 5-11 and was explicitly designed to expand access to education for children who cannot attend conventional schools because of geographical distance. By September 2025, the school had 43 classes – 28 in Kyrgyz and 15 in Russian – and children from more than 15 countries were studying through the online school, with Russia housing the largest group.
Tunguch represents an important change in the way the Kyrgyz state approaches migration. For more than two decades, the economic contribution of migrants was treated as a given, while many of the social costs of migrant children left behind, fragmented families, access to education, and reintegration were largely managed by households themselves.
By targeting the educational access and legal standing of migrant dependents, Russian policy has dismantled the “family migration” model. This systemic exclusion has forced the Kyrgyz state to pivot from passive economic beneficiary to active social mediator. Initiatives like the Tunguch online school mark the institutionalization of state-supported transnational living, signaling the state’s growing need to build infrastructure to mitigate its social externalities.
Preparedness for Migrant Reintegration
A potentially more consequential shift in Kyrgyzstan’s migration policy is emerging around the question of what happens when migrants return. On May 14, 2026, the Cabinet of Ministers approved the Program for the Reintegration of Returning Migrants for 2026–2030. This is the first national policy document specifically dedicated to migrant reintegration and signals an important change in how the state is beginning to understand migration: not only as a mechanism for absorbing domestic labor-market pressures and generating remittances, but also as a process that can reshape the country’s labor force, skills base, and economic development.
For much of the post-Soviet period, Kyrgyzstan’s migration policy was largely oriented toward managing outward mobility. Labor migration offered an important pressure valve in an economy with limited employment opportunities, while remittances became a major source of household income and foreign exchange. The policy challenge was therefore primarily how to facilitate migration, protect citizens abroad, and channel its economic benefits home. The new reintegration program suggests a different policy problem is now being centered: how to absorb and make use of the human, professional, and financial capital accumulated through migration when migrants return.
The program includes measures to support employment and self-employment, provide economic assistance, expand vocational retraining, and develop mechanisms for recognizing qualifications acquired abroad. Yet the adoption of the program should not be confused with evidence that Kyrgyzstan is prepared for a large-scale return. A policy framework is a first step; implementation capacity will determine whether reintegration becomes a viable alternative to renewed migration. The more fundamental question is whether the Kyrgyz economy can generate sufficient productive employment, wages, and opportunities for entrepreneurship to make staying economically meaningful for returnees. If these conditions are absent, reintegration programs may end up functioning primarily as short-term assistance schemes while migrants continue to view re-migration as the most viable livelihood strategy.
Diversification Beyond Russia, A Migration Crisis Unlike Any Before
The changing environment in Russia is also pushing Kyrgyzstan to diversify migration destinations. The United Kingdom has become one of the most visible alternatives. Kyrgyzstan began participating in the U.K.’s Seasonal Worker visa program in 2022. The quota available to Kyrgyz citizens increased from around 1,500 places in 2022 to 10,000 in 2025.
South Korea represents another increasingly important destination. Under the Employment Permit System, the quota for Kyrgyz workers increased by approximately 18 percent between 2023 and 2024, reaching more than 3,000 places. At the same time, South Korea has also been accessible through another route: Kyrgyz citizens who acquired Russian citizenship could take advantage of Russia’s visa-free arrangement with South Korea, which allow Russian passport holders to enter the country for short stays without a visa. This created an additional channel of mobility for some Central Asian migrants holding Russian passports, although visa-free entry should not be equated with legal authorization to work. Taken together, these developments illustrate how migration system is becoming more diversified, combining formal labor-migration programs with alternative mobility channels.
The current migration system crisis should therefore not be understood simply as another temporary decline in migration to Russia. The post-2022 crisis is different because it affects the foundations of the system. Russia is not simply becoming a more difficult labor market. It is becoming a more securitized environment in which migrants face greater uncertainty over entry, residence, employment, education for their children and personal security.
This is a profound shift. For more than two decades, Russia occupied a particular place in the social imagination of Kyrgyzstan as the most accessible foreign labor market, a familiar destination connected through networks and post-Soviet institutions, and a place where generations of Kyrgyz citizens had built their livelihoods. That perception is now changing. The significance of this transformation may ultimately extend far beyond migration statistics.

Lee and Macron Pledge Deeper Security Ties After Paris Summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
12:22:00 UTC
21:22:00 KST

South Korean President Lee Jae-myung and French President Emmanuel Macron pledged on September 8 to deepen defense cooperation and coordinate on securing free passage through the Hormuz Strait. Their summit was the centerpiece event of Lee’s two-day state visit to France, which also produced new agreements on artificial intelligence, nuclear energy, and trade.
Lee laid a wreath at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier beneath the Arc de Triomphe and took part in an official welcome ceremony before a one-on-one lunch with Macron at the Élysée Palace. An expanded summit followed, and the two leaders then addressed reporters together.
“We agreed to achieve a genuine leap forward in defense and security cooperation in order to jointly respond to the uncertainties of the international order,” Lee said in the joint press conference after the summit, adding that the two governments would move quickly toward signing a reciprocal military logistics support agreement. South Korea and France also signed an amended protocol to their existing pact on protecting military secrets, expanding the list of French officials with access to classified material and tightening rules on its handling.
Hormuz Strait security featured prominently in the talks.
“South Korea and France agreed to continue close coordination so that freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz and the stability of global supply chains can be restored as soon as possible,” Lee said.
Meanwhile, Seoul officials cautioned that the discussion should not be read as a decision on troop deployment. South Korea has been weighing a range of contributions, including military options, but officials say no decision has been made. Any deployment, even of a small number of personnel, would require National Assembly approval under South Korean law.
On the economic side, Lee said the countries agreed to pursue $20 billion, or about 27 trillion won, in two-way trade by 2030. Roughly 20 Korean and French companies took part in a business roundtable on new investment opportunities, and trade promotion agencies KOTRA and Business France signed a cooperation document meant to expand support for companies entering each other’s markets.
The visit also produced a private investment agreement between Samsung Electronics and French AI startup Mistral, announced alongside government-level memorandums on artificial intelligence, semiconductors, and quantum technology. Samsung led a 3 billion euro funding round for Mistral, valuing the company at more than 21 billion euro. The investment gives Samsung a strategic stake as the two work on an in-house AI model for the Korean firm’s chipmaking operations.
Nuclear cooperation advanced too. Lee said the countries would sign further documents on nuclear research and fuel supply to push forward next-generation reactor development and diversify long-term supply chains, building on a nuclear fuel cycle cooperation agreement KHNP and French firm Orano signed during Macron’s April visit to Seoul. The two governments also agreed to open a high-level dialogue channel for private-sector nuclear cooperation.
Biotechnology cooperation also expanded. The Korea Research Institute of Bioscience and Biotechnology signed three memorandums of understanding with French research institutions and companies covering eco-friendly materials, climate-resilient crops, and quantum-computing-assisted drug discovery, agreements Lee said would help Korean biotech firms gain a foothold in the European market.
Lee added that the two sides modernized a bilateral aviation agreement dating to 1974, concluding talks that began in 2016. The updated pact adds fair-competition protections for consumers, expands code-sharing routes, strengthens mutual assistance during emergencies, and sets environmental standards for flight operations.
The countries also expanded people-to-people exchange programs. An agreement widening eligibility for their working holiday program, reached in April, takes effect October 1, and Korean teaching assistants will be dispatched to France starting in October under a language-exchange agreement also signed in April. The two sides also signed a memorandum expanding research ties between Korean scholars and Paris-Saclay University, whose mathematics and physics researchers have produced 12 Fields Medalists, along with a police cooperation agreement targeting transnational crime.
On Ukraine, Lee said France has played a central role in rallying European support for ending the war and restoring peace. He added that South Korea has backed Ukraine in various ways and would keep working with the international community on its recovery and reconstruction. Lee also thanked Macron for inviting South Korea to this year’s Group of Seven summit, saying the invitation allowed Seoul to add its voice to discussions on rebuilding international solidarity and restoring balanced, sustainable economic growth. He pledged that South Korea would keep contributing responsibly to challenges facing the international community through its cooperation with the G7.
Macron, in turn, reaffirmed French support for Lee’s approach to the Korean Peninsula. The two leaders agreed to keep cooperating on regional peace and stability, citing close links between security in Northeast Asia and in Europe. Macron also criticized North Korea’s military support for Russia’s war in Ukraine, saying Paris and Seoul share a commitment to upholding an international order based on law.
The peninsula was a recurring theme of Lee’s visit. Le Monde published a written interview with Lee on September 6 in which he said he wants to serve as a “pacemaker” in reviving dialogue between the United States and North Korea. Lee’s hope is that North Korea-U.S. diplomacy could lead to concrete and effective measures to halt Pyongyang’s nuclear buildup. The president acknowledged that “the wall of distrust built up over many years” cannot be torn down overnight. Still, he said he would keep working toward peaceful coexistence, a concept he laid out last month in his Liberation Day address.
The September 8 summit came five months after Macron’s state visit to Seoul in April, when the two governments upgraded their relationship to a global strategic partnership. This year also marks the 140th anniversary of diplomatic ties between South Korea and France.
Before arriving in Paris, Lee spent two days in southern France. He and Macron co-chaired the inaugural Lumière Summit on Monday at the Maeght Foundation in Saint-Paul-de-Vence, a gathering on the future of film and video that drew about 150 participants from more than 30 countries. The two governments launched a Lumière Partnership worth a total of 1 billion euro, aimed at promoting the growth and globalization of the film and video industry. Lee opened the summit with remarks on cultural cooperation. He later met with Korean film figures – including directors Lee Chang-dong and Jung Ju-ri and actors Sul Kyung-gu and Jeon Do-yeon – before chairing a roundtable with executives from CJ ENM, Naver, Netflix and other companies.
Lee is scheduled to meet French National Assembly President Yaël Braun-Pivet on September 9, hold a luncheon with the Korean community in France and meet with OECD Secretary-General Mathias Cormann before concluding his four-day state visit.

Russia plans final test of new ballistic missile with 800-kilometer range by end of 2026, Ukraine's military intelligence says
Russia plans to conduct final tests of a new, unspecified type of ballistic missile with a range of up to 800 kilometers (about 500 miles) by the end of 2026, Vadym Skibitskyi, deputy head of Ukraine's military intelligence agency (HUR), said on Sept. 8 at a meeting with NATO member states.
The statement comes as Russia continues to target Ukrainian cities with ballistic missiles, against which Ukraine has a critically limited supply of interceptors. Kyiv relies entirely on its international partners for these systems, while its own ballistic missile programs remain under development.
Russia may intend to strike targets in western Ukraine during these missile tests, Skibitskyi said.
Moscow is seeking to ramp up both missile production and the range of its weapons, according to Skibitskyi. Russia's ultimate goal, he added, is to intensify missile and drone strikes to push Ukraine into a socioeconomic crisis.
Skibitskyi also called on Ukraine's partner countries to tighten their sanctions to cut Russia off from using foreign components, particularly in its long-range weapons.
Russia has attacked Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities day and night, with little respite in recent weeks, using both ballistic missiles and large numbers of drones and causing civilian casualties.
The strikes prompted President Volodymyr Zelensky to announce a change in Ukraine's air alert system. Under the new plan, alerts will be divided into two levels: yellow for drone threats and red for incoming missiles and large-scale combined attacks.
Kyiv and the surrounding region have been among the main targets of Russia's intensified aerial campaign in recent days, facing near-constant attacks by jet-powered drones. Ukraine's air defenses remain critically stretched, leaving much of the country vulnerable not only to missiles and drones but also to glide bombs. The toll is mounting: July was the deadliest month for civilians since the start of the all-out war.
Separately, HUR announced on Sept. 9 that its cyber specialists had breached the networks of the Moscow Institute of Thermal Technology, a state-run research and design institute that develops Russia's missiles and military satellite communications.
HUR also said it identified 2,648 employees of the Moscow Institute of Thermal Technology, among them its chief executive, Sergei Ponomaryov, a retired lieutenant general.
The institute works on the Yars and Topol-M intercontinental ballistic missiles, the submarine-launched Bulava, the Iskander-M and the Oreshnik system, according to HUR.
Apart from missiles, the institute is also developing a system for rapidly launching military satellites into low Earth orbit, between about 160 and 2,000 kilometers (100 to 1,200 miles) above Earth's surface, HUR said.
Russia is accelerating the deployment of its Rassvet satellite communications system, a domestic alternative to Starlink, ahead of schedule, Skibitskyi said on Aug. 10.
Russia launched its first 16 Rassvet satellites into low Earth orbit in March 2026 and is continuing to expand the constellation, according to Skibitskyi. Earlier reports said Russia launched a second batch in July.

Europe's gas inventories top 67%, remaining at historic lows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
12:21:33 UTC
21:21:33 KST

MOSCOW, September 9. /TASS/. Gas stocks in European underground storage (UGS) facilities have exceeded 67%, which remains the lowest level for this time of year since records began in 2011, according to TASS calculations based on data from Gas Infrastructure Europe (GIE).
Average gas injection rates into EU storage facilities in early September are among the highest in recent years. At the same time, gas prices at European hubs are approaching late-2022 highs, reflecting the European Union's frantic drive to fill its storage ahead of winter, even at steep prices. However, Europe has already missed the summer months, which are the most favorable for injection.
As of September 7, European storage facilities were 67.12% full (16.41 percentage points below the five-year average for this date), compared to 79.5% a year earlier. This is the lowest level for this date since monitoring began in 2011. EU storage facilities hold approximately 73.5 billion cubic meters of gas -- 14 billion cubic meters less than last year's level and the lowest volume since 2013. Gazprom previously forecast that gas stocks in European storage might not even reach 75% by the start of the upcoming heating season.
TASS previously reported that Europe risks starting the heating season with record-low gas stocks. Average replenishment rates in EU storage facilities in July were among the lowest since records began in 2011, accelerating only slightly in August. Given these figures, Europe may fill its storage facilities to just 70-75% capacity by the traditional start of the autumn-winter period -- an all-time low for the beginning of the heating season.
Under European Commission regulations, EU member states must ensure their gas storage facilities are 90% full between October 1 and December 1 each year. A 10% flexibility margin is permitted if filling underground storage (UGS) facilities proves challenging. Consequently, net injection into European storage must total at least 68 billion cubic meters by the start of the 2026-2027 autumn-winter season to meet the target. Since the beginning of April, Europe has managed to inject only 63% of the volume required for the upcoming winter, amounting to 43 billion cubic meters.
Storage replenishment rates this year have been heavily capped by a lost "battle" with Asia for available liquefied natural gas (LNG) supplies during the Middle East conflict, higher fuel prices, and extreme heat in June and July. Such summer periods trigger a sharp surge in power demand for cooling systems and air conditioning. Gas remains a primary source of electricity generation, alongside nuclear, wind, and solar energy.

A special SIDLETSKIY show took place at UFW in partnership with PUMB’s &quot;Live to Meet Life&quot; platform

2026-09-09

21:21:04 KST

A special SIDLETSKIY show took place at UFW in partnership with PUMB’s "Live to Meet Life" platform
Kyiv • UNN
SIDLETSKIY presented an adaptive collection with interchangeable prosthetic covers. Five veterans and a civilian woman took part in the show.
PUMB Bank continues to work on integrating wounded male and female veterans into all spheres of our lives. The “Living Towards” platform, initiated by the bank, and the SIDLETSKIY brand held a presentation of the designer’s new collection, complemented by special accessories—stylish covers for prostheses. In addition to professional models, five veterans and a civilian woman who lost limbs as a result of the war took to the runway, reports UNN.
Since the beginning of the full-scale war in Ukraine, the number of people who have experienced severe injuries and amputations—both military personnel and civilians—has increased significantly. Tens of thousands of Ukrainians currently use limb prostheses. They are a familiar part of their lives and appearance. Can a prosthesis also be part of a person’s style, rather than merely a functional medical device that people try to conceal?
The SIDLETSKIY show, held with the support of “Living Towards,” Timelapse, U+System, and the Yanko Foundation on September 6 as part of Ukrainian Fashion Week, provided an affirmative answer to this question.
The brand presented the “Woven by Nature” collection, some of whose looks were created with consideration for the experience of people who use prostheses every day. For the first time, the adaptive clothing collection was complemented by special accessories: interchangeable prosthetic covers that allow people to integrate a prosthesis into their look, make it an accent of the outfit, or turn it into a stylish addition.
The covers for the collection were created by the veteran-owned business Timelapse, founded by former combat medic Hlib Bieshkariev, now an entrepreneur and winner of the second season of the “Living Towards” educational and grant program. Especially for the show, Timelapse created covers that echoed the collection’s visual language through their shape, texture, and natural motifs.
Five veterans who underwent prosthetic fitting and rehabilitation at U+System, as well as Olha Dolha, a civilian resident of Dobropillia who lost her leg as a result of a Russian airstrike, took part in the presentation of the unique collection.
Their appearance on the runway was not merely a way to present adaptive clothing, but also a convincing demonstration that adaptive fashion is—and can be—an organic part of fashion culture. There was not a single empty seat at the show, and guests watched the looks with interest, greeting the models wearing prostheses with loud applause. This is the best confirmation that integrating male and female veterans and building an inclusive society means moving towards one another.
Background
“LIVING TOWARDS” is a platform for integrating male and female veterans into employment relations, entrepreneurship, financial processes, and society as a whole, created at the initiative of PUMB Bank. In 2024, an educational and grant program supporting veteran entrepreneurship was launched במסגרת the platform. Over the program’s three seasons, 1,045 applications were submitted, 110 teams completed training and prepared business plans, and 57 received financial support from PUMB Bank. The total amount of grants provided is UAH 41.5 million.
U+System is a prosthetics and rehabilitation center working toward the comprehensive return of people who have suffered severe injuries to active lives. The center combines prosthetics, physical recovery, and subsequent programs for social, professional, and sports reintegration.
Timelapse is a Ukrainian veteran-owned business specializing in the production of adaptive products for people with amputations, injuries, and limited mobility. The brand was founded by veteran and former combat medic Hlib Bieshkariev to facilitate the rehabilitation of wounded military personnel and civilians and help them adapt to everyday life.
SIDLETSKIY is a Ukrainian conceptual clothing brand founded by designer Ihor Sidletskyi in 2020. Among other things, the brand creates adaptive clothing lines and invites Ukrainian veterans wounded in the war to participate in its shows.

I am only saying that the matter be heard and de-tagged," he said, as cited by PTI.Bhatia said the matter had not been listed despite a judicial order directing that it be taken up, adding that the situation did not augur well for the institution."He is not a VVIP that the matter will not be listed. He is enjoying the stay," he said.
"You follow the procedure and file an application seeking early hearing. All are treated equally. You file your separate application," the bench observed.The High Court had dismissed Rahul’s plea challenging the trial court’s summoning order in the case over his alleged derogatory remarks against the Indian Army during his 2022 Bharat Jodo Yatra.On August 4 last year, the Supreme Court had stayed further proceedings in the complaint case pending before a Lucknow court until the next date of hearing.On December 4, the apex court had admitted Rahul’s appeal and said it would hear the matter in detail. It had subsequently listed the case for hearing on April 22.The Supreme Court had earlier issued notices to the Uttar Pradesh government and complainant Udai Shankar Srivastava, seeking their responses to Rahul’s plea.
Before the trial court, the complainant had alleged that Rahul made several derogatory remarks against the Indian Army in connection with the clashes between Indian and Chinese troops during his December 2022 yatra.The trial court subsequently summoned Rahul as an accused to face trial on the alleged charge of defamation.Rahul’s counsel had denied the allegations and argued before the High Court that the trial court had failed to consider the complete facts and material before determining whether a defamation case was made out against him.

====================================================================================================

Documents show Vilnius knew about waste crisis before Energesman deal – LRT Investigation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
12:18:00 UTC
21:18:00 KST

Documents obtained by LRT show that authorities in the Lithuanian capital were already aware of the looming waste crisis in the spring, but decided to take a risk.
The city authorities expected the company to rebuild, at its own expense, the plant that burned down in April 2025, meaning the deal would cost the Vilnius region nothing extra. Thus, Vilnius decided in May to sign a settlement agreement with Energesman, a waste processing company.
But after the contract with the waste operator was terminated amid the subsequent crisis, the reconstruction work will have to be paid with public funds.
"Could we, as a municipality, have said immediately after the fire: thank you, you've made a mess, you didn't have insurance, you don't look like reliable partners, so go away? We could have done that. But the decision was made to let the company rebuild the plant at its own expense. We can see that this decision did not work," says Adomas Bužinskas, director of the Vilnius city administration.
Further reading
According to the LRT Investigation Team, the municipality knew that Energesman had other problems as well. For example, last summer it was found that flammable materials were being stored improperly and that the fire safety systems were technically defective. A year later, the waste operator had still not resolved all of these problems.
Environmental authorities had also raised concerns about the company.
In May, waste incineration also had to stop because of scheduled maintenance at the cogeneration plant, causing piles of waste at the site to grow.
"The lack of storage capacity caused this drama, because any planned shutdown of the plant, which the entire market knows about because it is scheduled, has these consequences: physically, there is simply nowhere to put the waste," says Mantas Burokas, director of the Vilnius Cogeneration Power Plant.
By the beginning of the summer, the waste management centre already knew there was not enough room for the waste, that it was being diverted elsewhere and that Energesman's financial situation was deteriorating.
"Our operations were so paralysed after the fire that all the activities that generated any kind of profit disappeared, and in reality only the least financially attractive ones remained," says Algirdas Blazgys, director of Energesman.
It has now emerged, however, that Energesman expected to receive €10m to fulfil the settlement agreement – in May, Energesman won a public procurement contract from the waste management centre.
The contract was worth €14m for the modernisation of the plant. Energesman believed the money would allow it to resolve some of its problems.
"In terms of cash flow, it would have addressed that immediate cash-flow shortfall. And then, one way or another, we would have entered a good period," says Algirdas Blazgys, director of Energesman.
But at the beginning of the summer, Vilnius city authorities suddenly became aware of the operator's other debts and realised that the situation was getting out of control. They decided not to pay a €4m advance for equipment.
"We were happy to agree to transfer the money directly to the manufacturer rather than to their account. So, as a party to the contract, we were paying late-payment penalties, but we could see that the money might not necessarily reach the ultimate beneficiary," says Bužinskas, director of the Vilnius city administration.
And that is when the waste crisis began.
In May and June, waste began piling up, bringing construction work to a halt. The new head of the waste management centre also began withholding payments for waste processing.
"When we see that the continuity of Energesman's operations, its solvency and its debts are having a negative impact on the entire regional system, we probably have to take action," says Marius Švaikauskas of the Vilnius Regional Waste Management Centre.
Eventually, the municipality drew a line under the matter.
The waste management centre terminated both contracts with Energesman – the settlement agreement and the modernisation contract. It is now becoming clear that the risk taken by the capital's authorities in ignoring the company's problems has not paid off.
The waste management centre will have to launch a new tender, while the buildings will have to be rebuilt at a cost of several million euros, paid for by taxpayers.

How has Israel hit back against sanctions by the UK, others?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
12:17:50 UTC
21:17:50 KST

How has Israel hit back against sanctions by the UK, others?
Israel announced four countermeasures ranging from the closure of the British consulate in occupied East Jerusalem to the banning of MPs from Israel.
Israel has announced four retaliatory measures against the UK in response to its decision to ban the import of all goods produced in illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, calling the move a “series of anti-Israel decisions by the Labour Government”.
On Tuesday, British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said in a speech to parliament that the rapid expansion of Israeli settlements across the occupied Palestinian territory was “unlawful” and accused Israel of carrying out “ethnic cleansing”. He also announced sanctions against companies providing services to illegal settlements as well as tougher new restrictions on arms exports to Israel.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Medicine shortages grow in Iran as US tightens sanctions, blockade
- list 2 of 3What ‘right’ and ‘left’ mean in Israel today
- list 3 of 3Israeli parties submit slates for October Knesset elections
Twelve countries, including the UK, France, Canada, Spain and others, also shared a joint statement supporting a two-state solution for the Israel-Palestine conflict and announced their plans to impose their own trade restrictions on Israeli settlements.
After Miliband’s speech, Israel announced four countermeasures against the UK, including the closure of the British consulate in East Jerusalem.
Israel’s Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said: “Accusations made today by the Foreign Secretary of the Labour Government in the British Parliament were outrageous lies.” He accused the UK of trying to interfere in Israeli elections, which are due in late October.
President Isaac Herzog said sanctions would prove to be a “grave miscalculation, a gross interference in the democratic elections of a sovereign nation, and a decision that will fall on the wrong side of history”.
Here’s what we know:
What four measures are being implemented against the UK?
These are:
- The closure of the British consulate in Jerusalem within 30 days.
- The removal of British representatives from the International Gaza Support Center located in Kiryat Gat, southern Israel.
- The termination of British activities to train Palestinian Authority forces in the occupied West Bank under the “British Support Team in Ramallah”.
- A ban on entry to Israel for 12 British MPs and other British nationals involved in “antisemitic and anti-Israel activity, as well as those who deny the very existence of the State of Israel”.
Saar said this response should be viewed as a message to every country, adding: “Whoever acts against Israel, Israel will act against them, and they will lose their influence and relevance in the region. Measures against Israel will not go unanswered.”
How important is the closure of the British consulate?
The British consulate in occupied East Jerusalem focuses on the needs of British nationals in the occupied West Bank and Gaza.
It was first opened in 1839 but closed in 1914 at the start of World War I. It was later re-established as a consulate-general in 1948 after the British Mandate in Palestine ended.
According to the British government website, the consulate provides assistance to British nationals in the Palestinian territory.
Meanwhile, the British embassy, where the British ambassador is based, is located in Tel Aviv.
With the UK recognising Palestinian statehood last year, the East Jerusalem consulate has functioned as its de facto embassy to Palestine.
This is a significant move because East Jerusalem, where the consulate is located, is considered Palestinian territory illegally occupied by Israel. By ordering its closure, Israel is reaffirming its position that the whole of Jerusalem is the undivided capital of Israel, analysts say.
“United Jerusalem is the capital of Israel and is under its full sovereignty,” Saar said. “Any foreign activity in the area must be conducted through accepted and agreed channels and without violating Israel’s sovereignty.”
What are the British Support Team and the International Gaza Support Centre?
For years, the UK has provided training to support PA security forces in managing tensions on the ground in the occupied West Bank.
According to a British government document from 2018, the team oversees the delivery of courses to security forces personnel in the occupied territory, ranging from conflict resolution to media skills.
At a basic level, terminating the support team in Ramallah would mean the PA forces lose British expertise.
On the removal of Britain from the United States-led International Gaza Support Center, which was set up to support a post-war Gaza, the biggest impact for the UK is that it no longer has direct influence in shaping the besieged enclave’s future.
Who has been banned from travelling to Israel?
Those banned from Israel are mostly left-wing parliamentarians, including:
- Jeremy Corbyn MP – former Labour Party leader
- Zarah Sultana MP
- Fahad Ansari, Director of Riverway to the Sea
- Naz Shah MP
- Diane Abbott MP
- Hannah Spencer MP
- Carla Denyer MP
- Sian Berry MP
- Ellie Chowns MP
- John McDonnell MP
- Richard Burgon MP
- Adrian Ramsay MP
Saar accused those denied entry to the country of being involved in “antisemitic and anti-Israel activity, as well as those who deny the very existence of the State of Israel”.
How has the UK responded?
On Wednesday morning, Miliband condemned Israel’s decision to close its consulate in Jerusalem, calling it “regrettable and damaging”.
“We anticipated this might happen because we saw other countries, the Dutch, for example, who had announced sanctions, who had seen these reprisals from Israel,” Miliband told the BBC.
“We have important intelligence and security relationships with Israel, and I’m confident they will continue,” he said, declining to elaborate.
“And I was very clear yesterday that we do believe in working with our Israeli partners when it comes to the threats they face from Iran,” he added.
What about other countries which signed the joint declaration?
So far, Israel has not applied any countermeasures against the other countries that have called on the Israeli government to stop the expansion of settlements.
Those countries include: France, Canada, Denmark, Spain, Finland, Ireland, Iceland, Norway, Poland, Portugal and Sweden.

Serbia's Vucic calls snap elections after nearly two years of protests

Serbia's Vucic calls snap elections after nearly two years of protests
Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic on Wednesday called snap parliamentary elections for October 25. They are expected to be a key test of his right-wing populist Serbian Progressive Party after nearly two years of student-led anti-corruption protests.
Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic on Wednesday dissolved parliament and called snap parliamentary elections for October 25, a key demand of the country's long-running protest movement.
Parliamentary elections were not due until December 2027, but Vucic called the early vote after nearly two years of anti-government demonstrations.
"I am calling parliamentary elections for October 25," Vucic said in a nationally televised address.
An anti-graft protest movement has gripped the country since the November 2024 collapse of a railway station canopy in Novi Sad, which killed 16 people.
The tragedy was widely blamed on entrenched corruption and fuelled demonstrators' anger, drawing some of the largest crowds since the fall of strongman Slobodan Milosevic in 2000.
Initial calls for a transparent investigation evolved into demands for snap elections, which Vucic had repeatedly promised, but without setting a date.
Read moreSerbia’s student-led protesters wanted accountability. Now they’re calling for elections
"We have seen major turbulence on the domestic political scene over the past year and a half," Vucic said.
"We need election results that will clearly reflect the will of the people," he added.
The protest movement, emerging from student-led university blockades, has demanded early elections since May 2025 and is preparing its own electoral list.
It poses the biggest challenge yet to nationalist Vucic, 56, who has dominated Serbian politics for more than a decade as prime minister or president.
Since the start of the protest movement, Vucic and his allies have accused the students of seeking to stage a "foreign-funded revolution".
He repeated the accusation while calling the election.
"We have seen not only signs of foreign interference, but significant involvement by foreign powers, as well as unrest, disorder and clashes, and above all a divided society," Vucic said.
Elected president in 2017 and re-elected in 2022 for a five-year term, Vucic recently said he would resign after formally calling the election to campaign, signalling his ambitions to return as prime minister.
Vucic faced widespread criticism from EU leaders in the past week over the public homage to war criminal Ratko Mladic, the former Bosnian Serb army commander, who was buried as a hero in Serbia on Monday despite his conviction for genocide by a UN court.
His right-wing populist Serbian Progressive Party decided at a weekend meeting to ask him to head its electoral list and stand as its candidate for prime minister.
