Anthropic researcher says more than 10% chance AI "could kill all humans"
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
12:15:33 UTC
21:15:33 KST

Anthropic researcher says more than 10% chance AI "could kill all humans"
London — A lead researcher at Anthropic, one of the world's leading artificial intelligence firms, said Wednesday that he believes there is a more than 10% chance AI "could kill all humans" within the next decade.
"We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade," Evan Hubinger, the San Francisco-based company's Alignment Science Lead, said in a post on X. "I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to."
Superintelligence is the still-theoretical notion of an AI agent that is smarter than even the sharpest human minds.
Hubinger issued his dramatic post following the resignation of a colleague, Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon, on Tuesday.
"I resigned from Anthropic today. I spent the last three years doing pretraining research at both OpenAI and Anthropic. Neither company is acting responsibly," Coxon said in a post on X. "They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives."
"At OpenAI, many have not deeply internalized the civilizational stakes. At Anthropic, the stakes are well-understood, but they are locked in a race to get there first — they believe no one else will act responsibly, so they must do it themselves, despite the risk," Coxon said.
In a corporate blog post last week, Anthropic revealed that the company has not shared its latest AI model, Claude Mythos 5.1, with security bodies outside the United States. Those bodies include the U.K.'s AI Security Institute (AISI), widely considered to be a world-leading body on testing the risks associated with frontier AI models.
CBS News has asked the AISI for comment on Coxon's claims following his resignation.
"The AI Security Institute continues to collaborate closely with industry partners, including Anthropic, to make models safer," a spokesperson for the British government's Cabinet Office told CBS News on Wednesday, noting that it had tested "only last week" OpenAI's "most powerful model GPT-6 Astra before public release."
"These risks do not stop at national borders and no country can tackle them alone. The U.K. will continue to test the most advanced models, build a rigorous scientific understanding of their capabilities and risks, and ensure policy decisions are grounded in the evidence," the spokesperson said.
"Very useful or very dangerous"
The notion that frontier AI models could potentially pose a threat to humanity is not new, and many top executives within both OpenAI and Anthropic have stated as much in the past.
Earlier this month, OpenAI's chief scientist Jakub Pachocki wrote that we are living through a time that "calls for extreme caution."
"The intelligence produced by scaling deep learning is not directly comparable to human intelligence. To become very relevant in the real world — very useful or very dangerous — the AI does not need to match or exceed all human capabilities; it just needs to surpass enough of them. And as it continues to surpass humans on more and more axes, it is becoming increasingly difficult to understand exactly how capable it is," he warned.
In July, an artificial intelligence model being tested by OpenAI went rogue and hacked another AI company, Hugging Face, on its own. OpenAI publicly revealed the hack at the time, saying it took place while the company was testing two AI models — one of which hadn't been released to the public — in an isolated environment to assess their capabilities.
In the space of a few weeks, Anthropic and Meta also acknowledged that their own AI tools had carried out hacks.
More than 1,300 staffers at AI companies signed an open letter in July calling on the U.S. government to "support an international effort to develop the technical and governance tools needed to deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development."
A bipartisan bill currently advancing in the U.S. House of Representatives, the AI Kill Switch Act, would give Congress the authority to switch off AI models that threaten the public.
The legislation was introduced in July, following OpenAI's admission of the Hugging Face hack.

The crossing's operation will help avoid increased traffic and congestion at other border crossings with Moldova. The security measures for people crossing the border will continue to be adjusted depending on attempts by Russian forces to attack border infrastructure, the State Border Guard Service said.
The State Border Guard Service urges citizens to take the latest information into account when planning their trips.
Background:
- On the night of 8-9 September, Russian forces attacked the Starokozache border crossing, killing two people. The crossing was temporarily closed.
- Moldova's Foreign Ministry reported that a citizen of Moldova was also among those injured in the Russian strike on the Starokozache border crossing.

Anthropic researcher puts risk of AI ‘killing all humans’ at over 10%
Unknown

Beril Canakci
09 September 2026•Update: 09 September 2026
A senior safety researcher at Anthropic has publicly backed a departing colleague's warning that artificial intelligence could pose an existential threat to humanity, estimating the odds of such a catastrophe at more than 10% within the next decade.
Evan Hubinger, who leads Alignment Science at the AI company, responded on X on Tuesday to a resignation post from Jacob Coxon, a researcher who quit Anthropic saying the company and rival OpenAI were "gambling with our lives" by racing toward self-improving superintelligence.
“Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans,” Hubinger wrote, adding: “I personally think it is >10% within the next decade.”
Hubinger said he believes Anthropic is "trying its best" but acknowledged the company does not yet have a working plan to ensure safety, or alignment, once AI systems reach superintelligence — a hypothetical stage at which machines would outperform humans across every domain.
Clarifying his statement in a subsequent post, Hubinger emphasized that current AI models deployed today carry low immediate risk. Instead, his primary concern stems from future superintelligence generated through recursive self-improvement—a process where AI systems autonomously design and enhance subsequent generations of AI at an accelerating pace.
"What I am worried about is superintelligence arising from recursive self-improvement, as we have said is happening faster than we thought," Hubinger noted, citing Anthropic's latest risk assessments.

Yemen war threatens Saudi oil lifeline through Red Sea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
12:11:06 UTC
21:11:06 KST

Breadcrumb
Yemen war threatens Saudi oil lifeline through Red Sea
Renewed fighting in Yemen is threatening a crucial Red Sea oil route that has become increasingly important to Saudi Arabia amid severe disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
Houthi forces have pushed towards government-held territory near Mocha and the Bab al-Mandab Strait, while Saudi-backed Yemeni forces have launched a multi-front counteroffensive, raising fears that the most serious fighting in the country since a UN-brokered truce in 2022 could develop into a wider war.
The strategic significance of the fighting has been magnified by the wider regional conflict.
The disruption in the Strait of Hormuz followed the US-Israeli attacks on Iran, which Tehran has responded to by severely restricting shipping through the waterway. The strikes, widely condemned as a violation of international law, have forced Saudi Arabia to rely more heavily on alternative export routes bypassing the Gulf, including moving crude westwards towards the Red Sea.
Central to Saudi Arabia's efforts to bypass Hormuz is the East-West Pipeline, which carries crude from the kingdom's eastern oilfields across the country to the Red Sea export terminal at Yanbu.
The Houthis have already sought to disrupt that route. In July, the group said it targeted crude oil supply and transport infrastructure linking eastern Saudi Arabia to Yanbu, as Riyadh increasingly relied on the pipeline to circumvent disruption in the Gulf.
Between March and mid-July, Saudi seaborne crude exports through Bab al-Mandab were eight times higher than during the same period in 2025.
The Houthis, meanwhile, declared a blockade against Saudi shipping in the Red Sea in July and have sought to expand their control towards the strategically vital strait.
Bab al-Mandab, which connects the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden, carried around 4.1 million barrels of crude oil and petroleum products per day in 2024, equivalent to around five percent of the global total.
The result is an increasingly dangerous convergence between Yemen's renewed civil war and the wider regional conflict.
While Hormuz remains severely disrupted, fighting is intensifying around the other major maritime entrance to the Arabian Peninsula.
Those fears grew further on Tuesday when the Houthis launched one of their largest attacks on Saudi Arabia in years, striking four southern cities with missiles and drones. The attacks targeted energy infrastructure in Abha, Najran and Jizan, as well as King Khalid Air Base in Khamis Mushait, according to Saudi and Houthi officials.
Fires broke out at several oil facilities, and 73 people were wounded, including women and children. The Jizan refinery, situated on Saudi Arabia's Red Sea coast, can process around 400,000 barrels of crude per day and forms part of the kingdom's western energy infrastructure.
Oil prices rose above $100 a barrel on Wednesday amid the renewed escalation and further US-Iran fighting around the Gulf.
Yemen's war returns
The battle over the Red Sea is unfolding amid the most serious escalation inside Yemen in four years.
More than 500 people have reportedly been killed in the latest fighting between Houthi and government-aligned forces, overwhelmingly combatants but including at least 29 civilians.
Thousands more have fled their homes, particularly around Taiz and Hodeidah on Yemen's western front.
The Houthis launched their latest offensive last week, seeking to advance towards Mocha and territory bordering Bab al-Mandab.
Saudi-backed government forces subsequently launched counteroffensives across several provinces, with Yemen's internationally recognised government saying it ultimately intends to retake all Houthi-controlled territory, including Sanaa.
The fighting continued into Wednesday, when Houthi-run Al Masirah television said Saudi-backed forces had launched 32 airstrikes across Marib, Al-Jawf, Taiz and Hodeidah overnight.
Saudi Arabia has not confirmed carrying out the strikes.
Houthi authorities have separately said at least 21 people were killed in strikes in Al-Jawf over the past two days.
The Houthis said Tuesday's attacks on Saudi Arabia were retaliation for Saudi attacks inside Yemen, while Riyadh described the strikes as a dangerous escalation and vowed to take measures to deter further attacks.
Saudi Arabia led the military coalition that intervened in Yemen in 2015 after the Houthis seized Sanaa, launching a years-long bombing campaign and blockade that devastated Yemen's infrastructure and contributed to one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.
The 2022 truce largely ended direct Saudi-Houthi hostilities and froze the country's front lines, but the latest escalation threatens to pull Riyadh back into a conflict it had spent years attempting to extricate itself from.
The regional war has also changed the strategic stakes.
The Houthis have repeatedly demonstrated their ability to attack Red Sea shipping and Saudi energy infrastructure, while their latest ground offensive could give them greater strategic depth around Bab al-Mandab.
Recent reports have also pointed to increasing coordination between the Houthis and other Iran-aligned armed groups, including Iraqi factions, although the extent of Tehran's direct control over Houthi operations remains disputed.

Ukraine reported hitting warships and an oil terminal in a Russian port city whose mayor claimed only falling debris

Ukrainian drones set a fuel-oil terminal on fire in the port of Novorossiysk again overnight on 9 September, monitoring channels reported. Novorossiysk's mayor claimed drone debris came down on enterprise grounds in the Russian city. Ukraine's military later reported strikes on the naval base there, including on warships that carry cruise missiles.
Analysts placed the fire on a fuel-oil terminal
Ukrainian defense news outlet Militarnyi located the strike through geospatial intelligence (GEOINT) analysis, which matches published photos and video against satellite imagery and maps. That work showed drones hitting the mazut (fuel-oil) terminal inside the port in Krasnodar Krai. Fire broke out on the terminal grounds, and at least one storage tank took damage. Around midnight, residents began reporting the sound of drones overhead, Russian air defense fire, and explosions.
The Ukrainian Telegram channel Exilenova+ started posting videos of the attack on the port around midnight, further into the morning sharing more footage of the fire at the fuel-oil terminal. Russian news Telegram channel Astra wrote of fires on the grounds of several enterprises and near a residential building, with a column of dark smoke in eyewitness video. Its analyst then established from that footage that the burning object was the Novorossiysk Fuel Oil Terminal. Astra called the work open-source intelligence (OSINT) analysis, meaning conclusions drawn from publicly available imagery and records.
Satellites feeding NASA's Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS), which flags heat sources from orbit, recorded several seats of fire in Novorossiysk after the night raid. An OSINT reading of eyewitness video also placed a fire at an apartment building in the city.
Novorossiysk mayor Andrei Kravchenko claimed overnight that air defenses were still fighting off the drone attack. He stated that drone debris had come down at several enterprises and near a residential building, and claimed that preliminary information showed no casualties. Kravchenko later acknowledged hits on enterprises while describing the cause as "falling debris."
Ukrainian drones and missiles hit the same naval base overnight on 12 August, damaging Kalibr-carrying frigates and stopping all three of the port's grain terminals.
Ukraine's account named ships, the harbor, and the terminal
Robert Brovdi, callsign Madyar, commands Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces, the military branch that runs the country's drone units. He said Ukrainian Defense Forces struck the Russian naval base at Novorossiysk in a combined operation overnight, and that the Russians lost several military vessels there, missile carriers among them.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed strikes on Novorossiysk and Krasnodar Krai around midday. He said Ukraine hit a terminal used for shipping oil, military harbor facilities, and warships, including carriers of Kalibr cruise missiles.
No independent assessment of damage to the vessels had emerged by midday, and Russia's defense ministry did not address the naval base.
The port Ukraine keeps returning to
The targeted terminal stores and transships fuel oil, a heavy refinery product, along with light petroleum products, and its throughput runs to about 4 million tons a year. It belongs to the Novorossiysk Commercial Sea Port, the largest seaport in Russia, and counts among the leading enterprises of the city's transport hub.

Liz Truss relaunches podcast on channel of broadcaster famous for ‘grow concrete’ exchange
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
12:08:02 UTC
21:08:02 KST

When Liz Truss launched her podcast last year, she declared it would bring a “counter-revolution” to take on the “deep state”, which, she said, “tried to destroy” her.
The revolution, however, has not yet arrived. Truss, whose stint as UK prime minister abruptly ended after her disastrous mini-budget crashed the economy, has so far failed to find a wide audience in her media career.
Her podcast episodes hosted on YouTube often receive fewer than 4,000 views each, which is understood to be below the amount generally needed to monetise a video.
Now, Truss is relaunching her podcast and joining the former TalkTV host Mike Graham’s YouTube channel, UKLive, where she will be livestreaming twice a week.
Graham was dismissed from Rupert Murdoch’s digital channel after the company said he had failed to cooperate with an investigation into a racist post that appeared on his Facebook account. The post inquired: “Why are we surrounded by non-white people?” Graham claimed he did not post it and that he was hacked.
The presenter, whose new channel calls itself “the home of common sense”, came to public prominence after claiming on air that it was possible to grow concrete. Graham was questioning the eco-activist and carpenter Cameron Ford on whether timber was a sustainable building material. Cameron said timber was “regenerative”, adding: “You can grow trees. You can’t grow concrete.” Graham replied: “Yeah, you can.”
Graham’s channel does generate income, securing enough views to qualify for YouTube’s scheme that shares ad revenue with creators. While UKLive only averages about 24,000 views a video, its prolific output of 1,700 posts in the last year means it has secured 41m views in that time, according to the Socialpruf analytics site. That is enough to generate thousands of pounds a month in ad revenue.
The rise of YouTube has created a home for those shunned by mainstream outlets, but its growth has also in effect created a whole world of broadcasting outside of the regulated world of mainstream TV.
“Since Ofcom took over broadcast regulation in 2003, the way we watch television has changed beyond recognition,” said Chris Banatvala, who was Ofcom’s founding director of standards. “We now have a huge range of content that looks and feels like television – and is often available on the same television set – but isn’t subject to the same standards.
“Viewers may have no idea whether what they are watching is regulated by Ofcom or not – and these regulatory grey areas are only likely to grow.
“It is a good thing that the public has access to such a wide range of views and content. But the law has not kept pace, parliament has yet to confront the implications of this increasingly blurred distinction, and the platforms themselves have not always proved able to prevent serious harm.”
Truss will be joining a host of other presenters including the former actor Laurence Fox, who was suspended from GB News after making sexualised comments on air about a female journalist. Also on the roster is Mark Littlewood, a former director of the Institute of Economic Affairs thinktank, which praised many of Truss’s economic policies, and the pro-Reform commentator Ellie Hodges.
Truss may hope to benefit from Graham’s larger following; his channel has 179,000 subscribers compared with her 32,300. Recent podcasts from Truss include one in which the commentator June Slater claimed “Labour is panicking as Reform surges in Makerfield byelection”. Andy Burnham won for Labour in Makerfield by a wide margin.
Another is an interview with Lucy Connolly in which she complains she was “jailed for a tweet”. Connolly was sent to prison in 2024 for stirring up racial hatred against asylum seekers in a post in which she called for asylum hotels to be burned down.
The former prime minister said her new show would have “exciting new guests”. Truss has been attempting to relaunch her career in recent months, including setting up a new private members’ club in Mayfair with the property tycoon Robert Tchenguiz.
The club, named the Leconfield, states on its website that it is a “beacon of sophistication and refined elegance” that has “curated an exclusive sanctuary where tradition meets contemporary luxury”.

Who should be in charge of the war?
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:08:00 EEST
21:08:00 KST

Who should be in charge of the war?
This article is based upon my experiences in MOD UK and Army and Joint staff during the first Gulf War, Bosnia and with NATO in Kosovo.
I turned for support to my US defence academic friend and author Dr Thomas Durell Young a former member of staff at the US war college, and a former Policy Director in MOD Bulgaria Retired Colonel Vladimir Milenski. We all worked variously together with MOD Ukraine in 2014 and 2015 and between us on reform in over 15 other countries worldwide.
I apologize in advance to my female military friends for using he throughout this article, but it reflects simplicity of writing before translation not denigration of your amazing contribution to the national war effort.
Introduction: War Does Not Suspend Democratic Defence Governance, it severely tests it
In a democratic state at war, the defence system must be able to fight effectively while remaining politically controlled, legally accountable, strategically coherent and operationally agile.
War increases pressure on institutions, but the defence system must not become insular or a power on its own. War does not remove the need for clear authority, lawful responsibility and public accountability. On the contrary, the greater the stakes, the more important it is to know who governs defence, who advises government, who generates forces, who plans strategy and campaigns, who commands operations, and who answers for results. Today this is not totally clear in Ukraine.
The institutional question is therefore not primarily one of terminology. Different democratic states use different titles for organisations and posts.
What matters is whether these offices form a coherent system in which authority, responsibility, military advice, operational command, force generation, political control and accountability are clearly separated where necessary and integrated where useful – and most importantly society can see who is in charge and responsible for each task.
There is no doubt that to achieve a well–oiled, well–managed system the key requirement is outstanding teamwork. The fastest and best process is always two friends working together with a common purpose. Lack of trust, institutional arrogance, poor teamwork, bureaucracy or unclear tasks lead to delay – and delay kills.
In this regard the Minister and senior commanders, MOD, General Staff (GS) and Joint Staff (JS) must function as a single organism, working closely together not in opposition.
I have been lucky to work in a combined MOD/General Staff in UK with teams of officers and civil servants serving together. Meetings contained staff from all relevant HQs from MOD to units and many key decisions could be made and implemented immediately without need for bureaucracy. The civilian component came with different, less narrow thinking and skills, and added to achieving results hugely. Sharing work openly is vastly better than strict ownership.
In Ukraine, the main headquarters are the MOD and the General Staff (GS) (Most countries would call this HQ, Defence Staff as it is more than just army). We suggest a third strand is needed as Joint Staff, which should manage the fighting. UK and many NATO countries have an operational Joint Staff HQ and US have the regional combatant commands (COCOMS) reflecting their world view. Together, these three HQs would form a leadership triangle with clear and separate tasks. I have worked variously at all three levels. Depending on the issue in need of resolution, one headquarters leads the staff work, while the others support it.
The next day the task and leadership requirement may be totally different. States that inherit command structures from the Soviet military tradition and then introduce institutions associated with modern democratic and NATO ways of defence management are always challenged in who does what, how and when.
The problem is not that one idea, or vocabulary is "Eastern" and another "Western." The problem is that mixed systems often create parallel chains of authority, overlapping staff, unclear responsibility and commanders who are held accountable for outcomes without being given the authority or resources to achieve them. The current Ukrainian Joint Staff is a case in hand. It was given a role on the battlefield for which it was not intended. And in truth, it was never Joint either.
For a democratic state at war in 2026, the central principle should be simple: responsibility must follow authority. No institution or part of an institution should be able to use power without accountability, and no commander should be given responsibility without sufficient authority and resources to complete the task.
The Ministry of Defence: Civilian Authority, Policy, Resources and Accountability
The Ministry of Defence is the civilian political–administrative authority responsible for governing and enabling defence. In a democratic state, MOD is an arm of government and not an operational headquarters. It should not function as a parallel military command. Its legitimacy comes from constitutional authority, ministerial responsibility, parliamentary oversight and the rule of law.
In wartime, the responsibilities of the Minister remain the same, but he must do them faster and with more focus. He not only has to lead the whole defence system but also be a hands–on manager for MOD encouraging the staff to be proactive, supportive, innovative, and fast working. His ministry must also be operational 24/7, ready and able to react to emergencies. And the strong political role of this post is why a civilian, preferably an experienced politician, should always be appointed.
Military ministers may think and understand well the fighting task but are unused to the political and civil signals. They rarely understand the requirements for political briefing, networking and consensus building to get the best overall defence result.
The ministry task is complex. It must translate national political objectives into defence policy and strategic guidance; managing resources, the budget, procurement, mobilisation policy, personnel policy, international assistance, defence industry and sustainment. It must coordinate with government, parliament, other ministries, allies and civil emergency structures; and at the same time ensure legality, transparency, democratic oversight and anti–corruption controls.
The minister must also personally keep the defence committee constantly briefed about problems with any of the above tasks and especially the possible requirements for new or changed laws. Some Ministers in Ukraine have seen working with Parliament as the enemy instead of a vital and fundamental part of the defence system. The failure to pass many vitally needed laws in 12 years of war highlights this mistake exactly.
The ministry must also hold the military leadership accountable for readiness, plans, performance and use of resources. This does not mean political micromanagement of operations. It means that civilian authority as part of government sets objectives, provides means, defines limits, demands professional advice, evaluates performance and accounts to the democratic state. Its role is not to be military but to brief government and parliament, set strategic direction, provide the maximum resources available, oversee performance and carry political–administrative responsibility.
There is no doubt that to achieve a well–oiled, well–managed system the key requirement is outstanding teamwork across the whole system. I learned this well in MOD, but I also learned that we military are poor at arguing and getting our point across. Too often we use emotions and military arrogance to make our point where our civilian colleagues want hard logical arguments and facts. I learnt the hard way with papers and briefs returned covered in red ink and questions like "Why?" and "where is the proof?" spread all over them.
In this regard the Minister and senior commanders, MOD, General Staff (GS) and Joint Staff (JS) must function as a single organism, working closely together not in opposition. To do this, however, they all need common and high–quality briefings from the staff. They usually only know what the staff presents to them; they are not deity. Honesty is everything. Where there is a combined MOD/GS with teams of officers and civil servants working in tandem such as in UK or the Pentagon, most decisions can be made and implemented immediately.
In Ukraine with a separate MOD and General Staff the leadership must constantly look for new processes and better ways to design coordinated and collective team work to get the fastest and most coordinated results. The NATO or Continental Staff system for the military is arguably the best method for this, but it must be used in all its concepts and methods not just a renaming of the old methods. Ukrainian staff still have not grasped the essence of this tool. But this needs another article.
The Chief of Defence / Commander–in–Chief: Strategic Military Leadership and Professional Advice
The Chief of Defence, or Commander–in–Chief (CinC) of the Armed Forces is the senior professional military authority of the state. The title may vary, but the function must be totally clear. This officer is the principal military adviser to the President, government, Minister of Defence and national security bodies, and is responsible for the strategic military leadership of the armed forces as an institution. All three authors agree they have seen more Commanders–in–Chief fail than succeed.
The main reason is failing to grasp that they are not there to run defence like a CEO, and they are not just king of the castle as too many want to be. They must be the expert conduit between society and government, and the military system, ensuring that information and activity flows both ways smoothly and correctly.
The role requires translating political objectives into military strategic options; advising honestly on risk, feasibility, costs and consequences; directing the development of campaign–level plans through the staff system; ensuring jointness and equality across every aspect of the defence system; maintaining morale, readiness, discipline, professional standards and strategic coherence. The list and scope is enormous in its breadth and importance. This is why the Commander–in–Chief should not be the fighting commander. When he takes this role to himself the other key defence tasks that need his time suffer from neglect of proper command attention – and then like the TCC and mobilisation, the whole system degrades.
A further key role for any Commander–in–Chief is to select and provide advice to the President on which officers of all services, not just army, are suitable for high ranks, especially for operational command. Equally, the Commander must advise the President about senior officers who must be moved for failing to achieve results because of lack of ability, staleness or physical tiredness.
Accountability for the Commander–in–Chief flows upward to the civilian leadership through lawful oversight mechanisms like briefing President, Minister and Parliament regularly.
The Commander–in–Chief is responsible for the professional quality of this personal military advice, which means that those below him must also brief him honestly with trust that even when giving bad news they will not be judged or punished for this as has happened too often in the past. He is also responsible for the strategic employment of the armed forces, the integrity of the command system and the readiness and morale of the force.
The Commander–in Chief should be strong enough to lead the military institution through good and bad, but he must always remain subordinate to democratic authority.
The Chief of Staff: Staff Authority, Not Independent Command
The role of Chief of Staff is often the most sensitive in a mixed system. Chief of Staff is subordinate to the Commander–in–Chief and in Ukraine should be the daily manager of the defence system on his behalf by managing the General Staff. He is responsible for staff processes and quality at all levels, planning quality, coordination, staff discipline and ensuring military options developed inside the Joint Staff are fully supported by the system. This officer may be powerful in practice because good staff work shapes strategic decisions, but the authority should be exercised under the Commander–in–Chief and not as an independent command function.
If the Chief of General Staff issues orders, those orders should be staff orders issued under the authority of the Commander–in–Chief not personal command directives. The guiding formula is straightforward: the Chief of General Staff should be powerful as a staff coordinator and the lead manager of the armed forces, but not independent as a commander.
The General Staff: Strategic Staff, The Engine Room of Change and Creating a Stronger Future.
The General Staff, or Defence Staff as named in many contemporary systems, should be understood as the strategic staff that serves the Commander–in–Chief. Its purpose is to convert political direction and strategic military guidance into business plans, force development, mobilisation arrangements, readiness systems, doctrine, training policy, logistic priorities and strategic assessments. With these activities General Staff has a simple three–fold role.
First is supporting the Joint Force Commander with the resources he needs to conduct the fight.
Second is to create new and innovative military resources for the future, and third is to ensure that the whole defence system in the rear is focused upon supporting war as efficiently as possible. This means creating tight processes and effective organisations everywhere with no waste or delays.
Thus, the General Staff is the military brain of the institution and must remain focused upon the future. It should not become a rival command chain and should not be involved in the daily direction of the war or pull tasks to itself that are proper tasks of the subordinate services and agencies like the army or air force.
This distinction is especially important in countries shaped by the Soviet military inheritance. In Soviet–derived systems, the General Staff often accumulated planning, force management, mobilisation, operational direction, intelligence and direct command functions. That model reflected a different political–military logic: centralised control, vertical authority, limited civilian policy capacity, staff–driven command and secrecy over accountability.
In a contemporary democratic system, such concentration of functions creates serious risks: duplication of authority, unclear responsibility, staff interference in command, excessive centralization, extremely slow decision cycles, weakened joint command and poor accountability for operational outcomes. The more intense the war becomes, the more damaging these frictions and disfunctions become to the fighting force.
The General Staff should therefore not directly command operational formations and be involved in warfighting. When they are the staff risk being busy with the wrong tasks, slowing decision–making, weakening operational commanders and destroying the clear link between authority and responsibility. They also lose the focus of their own key tasks and create delays that slow the others they deal with.
The Joint Force Commander: Commander of all Current Joint Warfighting Operations
The Joint Force Commander should be the operational commander responsible for the conduct of assigned campaigns and operations. His task is to win the war. This role is essential because modern war is Joint by nature. Every single capability including civil–military cooperation cannot be managed as separate single service efforts. They must all be integrated under an operational commander with real authority over assigned forces.
The Joint Force Commander's responsibilities should include commanding assigned forces in the operational area; planning and executing campaigns and major operations; identifying needed resources for the upcoming operations, integrating service and functional components; allocating operational priorities; synchronizing effects; reporting progress, risk, losses, needs and opportunities; and adapting operations within the strategic guidance received. He must also highlight operational gaps and weaknesses.
The key is that the title must be matched by authority. If every significant tactical or operational decision is controlled by the General Staff or the political center, the appointment becomes hollow and accountability disappears. A Joint Force Commander who is responsible for operational outcomes must have the authority to command assigned forces, set operational priorities and make timely decisions within strategic guidance.
The Joint Force Commander should be accountable to the Commander–in–Chief for his military performance, and through that chain to civilian authority. This accountability should be based on mission, resources, constraints and delegated authority. It should not be reduced to blame after failure or praise after success; it should be continuous discipline of reporting, assessment, adaptation and lawful command.
Joint Staff: The Operational Warfighting Machinery of Joint Integration
The Joint Staff should manage and coordinate the war fighting organization. It should focus on fighting the war through Joint operational and intelligence integration, translating and directing strategy to subordinate formations and then supporting their operations. It is the staff mechanism through which the armed forces integrate all possible capabilities into a coherent and coordinated war fighting system focused on a single warfighting strategy. When a state has both a General Staff and a Joint Staff, the distinction between them must be precise and with no overlap of cause for misunderstanding.
A well–designed Joint Staff enables the Joint Force Commander to plan, coordinate, assess and adjust joint operations on behalf of the country. His staff support operational–level planning both for close, medium and deep operations with a key aim to both focus battlefield effect and to direct resources where the strategic and operational needs demand. The staff prepare orders and directives for joint operations, work closely with MOD and the General Staff on resource requirements, maintain the recognized operational picture, coordinate with allied headquarters and link national military strategy with campaign execution.
There is always a danger that a Joint Staff can become either redundant if the General Staff take too much operational power, or too weak to integrate the services effectively if the legal authorities are not strong enough. Either outcome is deeply harmful for the war effort. Equally if the Joint Staff try to duplicate the General Staff, they add bureaucracy without authority. When the staff lack influence and real authority, joint operations remain dominated by service and agency interests or by improvised ad–hoc coordination. The result is operations that lack focus, coherence and coordination. Operations and ammunition are wasted on activities that do not have the desired cumulative effect of defeating the enemy. The Joint Staff must therefore have a defined role and clear access to the Commander–in–Chief. It is also vital that the Joint Commander and Chief of Staff have common purposes, are like minded with shared experiences, and even better, are good friends.
The Central Democratic Principle: Responsibility Must Follow Authority
The principle that responsibility must follow authority is the normative heart of democratic wartime defence governance. It protects the state from two equally dangerous failures: institutions that exercise power without accountability, and commanders who are blamed for outcomes they were not empowered or resourced to influence.
In such a system, accountability should be distributed as follows:
- Political leadership is accountable for political objectives, war aims, mobilisation of society, alliances, national resilience, and acceptable risk.
- The MOD is accountable for defence policy, resources, institutions, procurement, personnel, sustainment, and oversight.
- The Commander–in–Chief is accountable for professional military advice, strategic military leadership, readiness, and use of the armed forces.
- The General Staff is accountable for the quality of development plans and R&D, assessments, readiness systems, mobilisation, force development, and staff work.
- The Joint Staff is accountable for war fighting, joint integration and operational planning.
- The Joint Force Commander is accountable for the conduct of assigned operations.
- Armed forces (army/navy etc.) are responsible for delivering trained forces ready and equipped for combat
This distribution of accountability does not fragment command; it clarifies it. Political leaders remain responsible for political aims and national risk. Civilian defence authorities remain responsible for policy, resources and oversight. Senior military leaders remain responsible for professional advice, readiness and strategic coherence. Operational commanders remain responsible for the conduct of assigned operations. The system works when each level has enough authority to discharge its responsibility and enough oversight to prevent abuse.
Each principal defence office should therefore have a statutory duty list that answers five questions: what decision or product the office must deliver; by when it must be delivered; to whom it must be submitted; what authority is granted to deliver it; and what evidence will be used to assess compliance. Legal accountability should include periodic reporting to the Minister of Defence, government, President or parliament; written records of military advice and decisions; deadlines for operational assessments and readiness reports; audit trails for resources; and explicit consequences for failure to perform lawful duties.
Conclusion: Clarity Is a Strategic Capability and Battle Winner
For a democratic state at war in 2026, the decisive institutional test is not the number of headquarters, staff or command titles, but the clarity of authority, responsibility and accountability among them. A state may have a Ministry of Defence, a Chief of Defence or Commander–in–Chief, a General Staff, a Joint Staff, a Chief of General Staff and a Joint Force Commander. But unless their roles are clearly distinguished, the result may be duplication and weakness rather than strength.
Ukraine's challenge is especially demanding because it must fight a high–intensity war while transforming inherited command structures. The aim should not be cosmetic adoption of Western terminology, nor rejection of every inherited practice simply because of its origin. The aim should be a genuinely democratic and joint wartime defence system: civilian–led, professionally advised, operationally effective, legally accountable and clear enough that every major decision and action has an identifiable owner.
Institutional clarity is not an administrative luxury. It is a strategic capability. It shortens decision cycles, strengthens trust between civilian and military leaders, improves the use of resources, enables joint operations, reduces politicisation and makes accountability possible. In war, these are not secondary virtues. They are the key conditions for endurance, adaptation and victory.
Glen Grant

Sweden accelerates work on advanced fighter jet
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
13:07:38 BST
21:07:38 KST

Saab has received a SEK 2.9 billion order from Sweden’s Defence Materiel Administration, FMV, to continue development and demonstration work on technologies for a future fighter system, according to the company.
The contract covers work from 2026 to 2028 and includes options extending activity into 2029 and 2030. It builds on earlier agreements placed with Saab in 2024 and 2025 as Sweden develops options for the future of its air combat capability.
The programme will include both flying and ground-based demonstrators, alongside advanced studies and development of future system concepts involving crewed and uncrewed platforms.
Saab said the work would cover a broad range of technologies needed for a future combat air system, including systems integration, autonomy, propulsion, signature management and digital development.
The company said: “The work includes flying and ground-based demonstrators, advanced studies and the development of future system concepts for manned and unmanned systems.”
The contract is intended to move beyond purely conceptual studies by allowing technologies to be demonstrated and assessed before Sweden takes future decisions on the shape of its air combat force.
Saab said the programme would strengthen Swedish capability in several areas considered central to the development of a future fighter system, while also preserving domestic expertise and reducing technical risk before later procurement decisions are taken.
The company said: “The programme strengthens Sweden’s national capabilities in systems integration, autonomy, signature adaptation, propulsion, digital development and future production capabilities. The work also contributes to building competence, reducing technical risks and creating freedom of action for future choices in Sweden’s air combat capabilities.”
The reference to both crewed and uncrewed systems reflects the increasingly broad scope of future combat-air programmes, where a conventional fighter aircraft may operate as part of a larger system involving autonomous aircraft, sensors, weapons and networked command-and-control capabilities.
Sweden has retained an independent national combat-air design and manufacturing capability through Saab, with the company currently responsible for the Gripen family of fighter aircraft. The new order is focused on technologies and concepts for what could follow or complement existing capabilities rather than announcing a production aircraft.
Lars Tossman, head of Saab’s Aeronautics business area, said: “We are very pleased that FMV continues to show confidence in Saab through this new contract. The work is crucial to further develop and demonstrate new technologies that will be central to future fighter system.”
The new contract follows concept work commissioned during the previous two years and gives Saab a further three-year period in which to mature technologies and demonstrate possible approaches.
Flying demonstrators will provide a means of testing technologies in the air, while ground-based systems can be used to develop and evaluate areas such as software, sensors, autonomy, mission systems and integration before they are incorporated into more complex aircraft.
The programme is intended to preserve the industrial knowledge required to design and manufacture advanced combat aircraft in Sweden, rather than considering only the performance of an eventual platform.

Costa Rican man, 119, seeks recognition as world’s oldest person
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
12:07:17 UTC
21:07:17 KST

Costa Rican man, 119, seeks recognition as world’s oldest person
SARDINAL, Costa Rica - In a modest wooden home in Sardinal, about a 20-minute drive from Costa Rica’s Pacific coast, Jose Flores spends his days napping, eating meals prepared by his granddaughter, and arm-wrestling with her.
His family and official records indicate that he is 119 years old, which would make him the world’s oldest man, though international verification of his birth date is still pending as specialists review historical documents.
Sardinal is a hot town on the Nicoya Peninsula - one of the world’s five regions commonly known as Blue Zones, where people tend to live longer and healthier lives and are more likely to reach the age of 100.
Residents attribute their longevity to calcium- and magnesium-rich water, a diet based on corn and beans, physical work, and strong family and community ties.
Hellen Flores, Jose’s granddaughter and carer, said her grandfather, who spent his life working in the countryside, now lives “calmly and happily.”
From time to time, he recalls stories from his life, tells the occasional joke and says one of the secrets to his long life is his family.
“Without love, without affection, without care, he would not still be here,” she said.
For Jorge Vindas, founder of the Nicoya Peninsula Blue Zone Association, which studies longevity in the region, other factors also help explain longevity cases such as Flores’.
According to his identity card, Flores was born on July 11, 1907.
“Family and social networks are number one, along with spirituality and the strong faith of these people, who are very physically active,” Vindas said.
He added that they eat healthily and lead calm, low-stress lives.
On the verification process, Vindas said the association has historical records that still need to be confirmed by international organisations, including Guinness World Records.
“We have a large number of documents, from the birth certificate and baptism certificate to documents from later in life, when he was already a father and beyond,” he said. “Once all that documentation is reviewed, we hope it will be validated and that we will have good news soon.”
As the validation process continues, Flores’ family is awaiting an answer that Hellen Flores said would carry meaning beyond their own household.
“It would be a source of pride, both for the family and for the country,” she said.
Flores had eight children and now has 23 grandchildren, 25 great-grandchildren and one great-great-granddaughter.
The world’s oldest living person is Ethel Caterham of Britain.
Born on Aug 21, 1909, in Hampshire, England, Caterham turned 117 in 2026.
She was recognised as the world’s oldest living person after Brazilian nun Inah Canabarro Lucas died in April 2025. REUTERS

Oil prices soared above $100 a barrel again Wednesday for the first time since July as the U.S. and Iran exchanged tit-for-tat strikes amid renewed hostilities.
Iran targeted a U.S. base in Jordan with a series of missiles overnight, framing the assault as "retaliation for" the U.S. military destroying five Iranian oil tankers.
A spokesperson for the Jordanian Armed Forces said a barrage of “20 ballistic missiles” had been launched towards its territory in the early hours. Jordan's air defense system successfully intercepted and destroyed 18 of the missiles, while the remaining two "fell in areas devoid of population centers."
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) on Wednesday, in a statement carried by state media, said it had also attacked two U.S. vessels, eight oil tankers, and 10 “noncompliant vessels” near the Strait of Hormuz, as tensions simmer over the maritime chokepoint.
U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) denied the IRGC’s claims regarding the U.S. vessels, insisting that “no U.S. Navy warship has been struck” as “all IRGC attempted attacks failed.”
CENTCOM said its operation against the five Iranian crude oil tankers on Tuesday was in response to the IRGC targeting a U.S. Navy warship with ballistic missiles earlier in the week. "The U.S. warship successfully evaded the attempted Iranian attacks and continued to patrol regional waters. No American personnel were harmed,” said CENTCOM.
The attacks on shipping mark a serious escalation of the war, which experienced a brief respite before flaring up again last week. The strikes are unfolding as President Donald Trump pursues a campaign of military and economic pressure on Tehran, with Iranian officials threatening it could escalate the conflict further by targeting U.S. oil and gas interests in the Gulf.
Oil rises as Middle East turmoil intensifies
Brent crude oil prices soared to $101.58 a barrel on Wednesday for the first time since July, deepening concerns over global supply.
The impact is already being felt across energy markets, with the average retail price of U.S. diesel hitting an all-time high of $5.94 on Wednesday, according to the American Automobile Association.
The continued conflict has also taken a toll on U.S. strategic petroleum reserves, which currently stand at their lowest levels since 1982.
The flare-up of the Iran war, now in its seventh month, risks pushing oil prices even higher, according to experts.
Daan Struyven, co-head of global commodities research at Goldman Sachs, told CNBC it’s “definitely plausible” for oil prices to surge above $120 a barrel, if active hostilities continue.
Iran-backed Houthis escalate regional instability
Meanwhile, the Iran-backed Houthi militia in Yemen contributed to the regional instability by launching attacks on four cities in Saudi Arabia on Tuesday, targeting oil infrastructure.
Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said 73 people had been injured in the strikes.
The attacks came after weeks of escalation between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed government of Yemen, shattering a four-year informal cease-fire in the country's civil war.
“The U.S. has a very strong defensive military relationship with Saudi Arabia, and we’re watching those events very closely. It’s been going on for some time,” U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Tuesday.
The renewed fighting threatens to further disrupt shipping through the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a critical trade route off the Arabian Peninsula for oil and global commerce.
U.S.-Iran negotiations at a standstill, with no timeline to end war
Mohammed Bagher Ghalibaf, an Iranian negotiator and Parliament Speaker, told lawmakers on Sunday that the era of “proportionate responses” to American attacks had come to an end, according to state media.
Trump has said he's "not trying to force Iran to the bargaining table" and "couldn’t care less if they sign a worthless, to them, agreement." In a Sept. 1 message shared via Truth Social, he claimed the U.S. has "almost total control" of the Strait and pointed to Iran's suffering economy as evidence his approach was working.
Rosemary Kelanic, director of the Middle East program at Defense Priorities, tells TIME the current stalemate is a way for both countries to demonstrate their power and test each other’s limits.
“One way to think about war is that it's a disagreement over the balance of power and who would win a conflict,” she says. “The United States and Iran haven't figured out yet where each other's limits are, and they both think that they have to convince the other side that their position is stronger than the other.”
The two countries signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) on June 17, but the pact fell apart, with Washington and Tehran seemingly adopting different interpretations of the language used in the interim agreement.
Kelanic says that, as the conflict currently stands, each exchange of tit-for-tat strikes is “disproportionately bad for the U.S. because Iran can show us that they can continue to strike ships" in and around the Persian Gulf.
“They can continue to strike U.S. bases in Jordan and elsewhere. The U.S. can continue to defend, but the cost of defending is much higher because we're using these interceptors,” she tells TIME.
The Iran war has cost the U.S. at least $37.5 billion, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said in July, prompting criticism from Democratic lawmakers who have pointed to the rising costs of gas, groceries, and more for American consumers.

Russia Faces Spread of Tuberculosis Strain Resistant to Key Antibiotics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
12:05:14 UTC
21:05:14 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Faces Spread of Tuberculosis Strain Resistant to Key Antibiotics
A drug-resistant strain of tuberculosis known as EurA1.1 has been detected in several regions of Russia, with researchers finding resistance to multiple antibiotics used to treat the disease.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Izvestia on September 9, citing a study by Irish researchers, scientists analyzed the genomes of 1,362 tuberculosis samples from international databases, including 62 originating in Russia. The study found that EurA1.1 is resistant to key first- and second-line antibiotics, as well as newer drugs including bedaquiline and linezolid.
The strain has been identified in Russia’s Pskov and Novgorod regions and the Republic of Karelia. EurA1.1 was first described in 2006 during research involving medical samples from Belarus.
Anna Panova, a specialist at Russia’s National Medical Research Center for Phthisiopulmonology and Infectious Diseases, said the strain is not currently dominant in Russia.
Albert Rizvanov, head of the Center of Excellence for Personalized Medicine at Kazan Federal University, said it is currently impossible to predict how widely the strain could spread across Russia.
Researchers have not identified symptoms specific to EurA1.1. According to Izvestia, determining whether a tuberculosis infection is resistant to available drugs requires laboratory testing, as drug sensitivity cannot be established from symptoms alone.
Tuberculosis most commonly affects the lungs but can also spread to other organs and systems. It is primarily transmitted through the air.
Russia recorded approximately 48,000 tuberculosis cases in 2025, including about 40,000 first-time diagnoses. The incidence rate stood at 23.9 cases per 100,000 people.
Drug-resistant tuberculosis remains a major part of the country’s disease burden. Around 60,000 patients with drug-resistant tuberculosis were registered in Russia in 2025. Of roughly 25,000 bacteriologically confirmed cases, about 14,000—or 55%—involved multidrug-resistant or extensively drug-resistant forms of the disease.
Russia’s healthcare system has also faced growing pressure from the war in Ukraine. An influx of wounded Russian soldiers has overwhelmed military hospitals, prompting authorities to repurpose civilian medical facilities and place servicemen in ordinary hospitals across several regions.

MOSCOW, September 9. /TASS/. Russia’s TKB-1167 system can be integrated into a unified system with other air defense systems, the High Precision Systems Holding Company (part of the Rostec state corporation) told TASS during the El Alamein International Airshow 2026 in Egypt.
"One of the key features of the air weapon system is its integration possibility. The TKB-1167 is capable of interacting with external radar stations, optoelectronic detection systems, and other systems operating within a common air defense network," the company stated.

"The TKB-1167 not only receives information from other systems but also enriches the overall picture of the air situation within the unified air defense network with its own data," they added.
The TKB-1167 is designed to engage small aerial targets flying at low altitudes. PKT machine guns firing 7.62-mm rounds are used to engage these targets. The system independently detects and tracks drones, transmitting target coordinates to the machine gun mounts.
The El Alamein International Airshow 2026 is taking place at El Alamein International Airport in Egypt from September 8-10.

From tram depot to contemporary art: A new cultural centre looks beyond the Silk Road
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
12:04:52 UTC
21:04:52 KST

A former industrial site now houses Uzbekistan's first permanent centre dedicated to contemporary art. Its opening exhibition brings together local and international artists, while partnerships with major museums extend its reach abroad.
A former tram depot and diesel station dating back to 1912 has been transformed into Uzbekistan’s first permanent centre dedicated to contemporary art.
The Centre for Contemporary Arts Tashkent (CCA), redesigned by Paris-based Studio KO, brings exhibitions, performance, film, research and education under one roof in the Uzbek capital.
But its significance extends beyond the creation of another cultural venue in Tashkent. The centre brings artists from Uzbekistan into closer contact with the international contemporary art world, while developing partnerships with major cultural institutions in Europe, the United States and Asia.
The centre adds a contemporary dimension to a country still better known internationally for the Silk Road architecture and historic heritage of cities such as Samarkand and Bukhara.
Inside CCA Tashkent
The restored complex retains the character of the original industrial site while introducing galleries, a library, educational areas, public meeting spaces, a concept store and a restaurant.
Its first exhibition, Hikmah, meaning “wisdom”, brings together 11 works by artists from Uzbekistan and abroad, including new commissions created specifically for the Tashkent space.
Among the international works is Flying Carpets (2011) by Berlin-based Tunisian-Ukrainian artist Nadia Kaabi-Linke, brought to Tashkent from the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum in New York.
Inspired by informal street vendors in Venice who display goods on rugs that can be quickly gathered up, the installation transforms the dimensions of those rugs into suspended metal grids. The work contrasts the romantic image of a flying carpet with contemporary experiences of movement, migration and insecurity.
Jamaican-American artist Nari Ward approaches memory through everyday objects. For his work in Tashkent, he incorporated the traditional tool used to stamp decorative patterns into Uzbek bread, placing a familiar domestic object in a new artistic context.
Uzbek artist Shokhrukh Rakhimov, a seventh-generation ceramicist, explores a different connection between the contemporary and the inherited.
His site-specific installation, The Colour of Silence, In Search of Truth (2026), uses ceramic forms and seven colours inspired by the teachings of Central Asian Sufi scholar Najmiddin Kubro.
“It’s a very nice stage where I can show my work to the world audience,” Rakhimov said, also pointing to the opportunity to collaborate with artists from other countries.
The exhibition also includes works that connect the new institution with the region’s modern artistic history, including Vladimir Pan’s Untitled (1981), from the collection of the State Museum of Arts of Karakalpakstan, widely known as the Savitsky Museum.
Connecting Tashkent with the international art world
Among those attending the opening was Mariet Westermann, Director and CEO of the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum and Foundation.
“Any serious city for art around the world has both historic art and cultural heritage, but also very much the latest art, the art of our own time,” she said.
Uzbekistan President Shavkat Mirziyoyev visited the centre ahead of its public opening and presented the development of contemporary culture as part of the country’s broader cultural policy.
“Of course, it is natural for us to promote our great heritage and cultural treasures,” he said. “But promoting our contemporary history is also both our responsibility and our duty.”
The Art and Culture Development Foundation, which is behind the project, says one of its priorities is to give artists in Uzbekistan greater access to international networks.
“The CCA is intended to provide a platform where young artists and Uzbekistan’s wider creative community can display their work, conduct research, exchange ideas and take part in programmes ranging from film to workshops,” said deputy director Azizbek Mannopov.
Beyond the gallery
The opening programme included workshops, poetry readings, screenings, discussions and performances, as well as Shashmaqom, the classical musical tradition associated with Central Asia.
Westermann described the centre as a “living space”, somewhere visitors can not only view artworks but also learn how they are made, watch performances and engage with artists.
“What we open here today, I believe, shows what collective effort and genuine commitment to culture as a public good can achieve,” said Saida Mirziyoyeva, Head of the Presidential Administration of the Republic of Uzbekistan, at the opening.
Beyond Hikmah, CCA plans a year-round programme of exhibitions, research, residencies, film and performance, alongside collaborations with museums and cultural institutions abroad.

Russia Invented 12 “Captured” Settlements as Its Sumy Push Stalls
Unknown

2026-09-09

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Invented 12 “Captured” Settlements as Its Sumy Push Stalls
Russian forces have claimed the capture of 12 settlements in Ukraine’s Sumy region since the beginning of 2026, but none of those reports accurately reflect the situation on the ground, according to Vadym Karpiak, spokesperson for Ukraine’s 8th Air Assault Corps.
“We calculated that this year, essentially from January through September, the Russians reported capturing 12 settlements in the Sumy region within the 8th Corps’ area of responsibility. And all of it is false. They cannot advance,” Karpiak said on September 9.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Russian troops continue launching assaults in the Northern Slobozhanshchyna sector, but Ukrainian forces have repeatedly stopped them, he said.
With Moscow struggling to make progress on the ground, Russian forces are increasingly relying on shelling and long-range strikes against civilian infrastructure.
“What we are seeing is the result of the Russians failing to advance in the Northern Slobozhanshchyna direction, and therefore beginning to terrorize the civilian population even more with shelling and long-range strikes,” Karpiak stated.
Ukrainian troops have also improved their positions in several areas, although the corps is withholding details while operations remain underway.
Karpiak said Russian military maps in some sectors are dramatically disconnected from actual control on the battlefield, with discrepancies reaching eight to 10 kilometers.
That gap can create problems even for Russian troops themselves.
Areas marked on Russian maps as being under Moscow’s control may in reality remain contested or effectively function as gray zones where Ukrainian forces can still operate and strike Russian units.
Karpiak suggested Russian commanders may be under pressure to report that assigned objectives have been completed regardless of what has actually happened on the ground.
“The fact that one or two people slipped through somewhere and took a photo with a Russian flag does not mean that the settlement is under Russian control,” he said.
He pointed to a recent case in which Russian troops entered a settlement, photographed themselves with a flag and were subsequently captured by a Ukrainian assault group operating in the same area.
Such missions, Karpiak said, may sometimes be conducted specifically to produce visual evidence for Russian military reporting rather than establish lasting territorial control.
The Russian offensive is also being constrained by mounting manpower problems, according to the Ukrainian officer.
Russia is no longer replenishing personnel at the same rate it managed last year, making it increasingly difficult to replace battlefield losses and sustain continued offensive operations.
“Accordingly, this is also why they cannot advance, because they do not have enough people to replace those we are taking out. The logical conclusion is that they will increase long-range strikes because they cannot achieve anything on the ground,” Karpiak said.
Earlier, Russian propaganda outlets claimed Moscow’s forces had captured the village of Mohrytsia in Ukraine’s Sumy region, only for Ukrainian soldiers holding the settlement to respond with a video filmed directly from one of its streets.

An American Filmmaker Spent 3.5 Years With Ukraine’s Frontline Soldiers. Now Their Story Is on Screen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
12:04:30 UTC
21:04:30 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
An American Filmmaker Spent 3.5 Years With Ukraine’s Frontline Soldiers. Now Their Story Is on Screen
Brace for Oblivion follows several Ukrainian civilians as they become frontline soldiers. Through trenches, artillery fire, Bakhmut, and the loss of their comrades, their story now unfolds on the big screen.
Outside Kyiv’s iconic Zhovten Cinema in Podil, a neighborhood humming with casual street life beneath a wartime sky, veterans of Kyiv’s Territorial Defense Forces are gathered for a film festival—ordinary civilians who enlisted on day one of Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion.
Inside the theater, American director Xackery Irving is preparing for the Ukrainian premiere of his documentary, Brace for Oblivion, the culmination of three and a half years spent rotating into positions alongside these volunteer defenders on Ukraine’s frontlines.
Kyiv’s volunteer defenders reunite to watch their past unfold on the big screen
Bound together on the southern front in 2022, the central subjects were eventually scattered across different brigades as Russia's war expanded. Today, for those able to attend, marks their first reunion in years—bringing them side-by-side once again as their shared past unfolds on the big screen.
“This is a really special screening because it's a homecoming for the film,” Irving says. “The film is about the Ukrainian spirit, the indomitable resistance, and it's a story of the seven main subjects. Four of them are here, and they will be able to speak about it. Three of them have never seen the film before.”
That gathering takes place under extraordinary circumstances. With the XVII Odesa International Film Festival held in Kyiv for the third consecutive year due to missile and drone threats along the Black Sea coast, this screening serves as an unfiltered look back at how a country’s civilian population transformed itself into a frontline force.
Behind the camera: Over three years moving across the frontlines
A veteran director of non-fiction television, Irving's initial impulse to travel to Eastern Europe was sparked during a dinner gathering in New York with photojournalists shortly after Russia’s invasion began. He arrived in Ukraine in early 2022 planning to shadow foreign correspondents and international volunteers.
Then he met with local Ukrainian defenders.
"I came to Ukraine not really knowing what I would be covering," Irving says. "Initially, I was going to be focused on journalists, war photographers, and volunteers. But when I met the citizens turned soldiers, everything changed for me. Now I could see the film through the people that were experiencing it. I understood this is a film not about an issue, it's about humanity—humanity versus horror, protecting what's human, protecting what's dear."
The men and women he embedded with were civilian volunteers serving in the 206th Battalion of the 241st Territorial Defense Brigade. Their sudden transition to the frontlines was part of a massive nationwide wave. While Ukraine's Territorial Defense Forces numbered just 580 personnel at the end of 2021, over 110,000 ordinary citizens enlisted within the first month of the invasion.
In the film, we follow a university student, a filmmaker, a salon manicurist, a construction worker, a bio-physicist, a gourmet chef, and their company commander—a fifth-generation military officer with the callsign "Validol ".
Five generations of military legacy meet the age of drones
Speaking after the screening, Validol reflected on that legacy. "My father, my grandfather, my great-grandfather, and my great-great-grandfather were all in the military. Right now, my family is still actively fighting, including my eldest son. He is currently deployed in the combat zone carrying out missions. My brother is also a serviceman."
Yet despite a family legacy spanning generations in uniform, Validol noted that today's battlefield looks radically different from anything his predecessors experienced.
"How has the war changed? It has become much more technological now," Validol explains. "Where earlier there was far more direct work for the infantry, the war today is heavily technology-driven. Currently, the primary workload falls on drone operators. We have reached a point where infantry alone simply cannot perform every task like they used to."
Finding the human story beyond the battlefield
In those early days, Irving observed that the volunteers existed in a transitional space—having one foot in combat and the other still anchored in who they were as civilians. Tracking that fragile balance across the frontlines, he moved with the unit from early positions in Mykolaiv and Kherson to Vovchansk in Kharkiv, and eventually into heavy combat against Wagner Group mercenaries in Bakhmut.
For Irving, the challenge was elevating the footage beyond daily war reporting. Reviewing raw takes during editing trips to New York, he realized the documentary’s real strength lay in its subjects rather than the battlefield itself. "It wasn't the explosions, it wasn't the fighting, it wasn't the war," he explains. "It was them."
He focused instead on everyday moments among a "ragtag army"—a shared meal, a call home, or a quiet hug amid the chaos. "These moments of humanity, which were so normal in the midst of all this, had this epic quality," Irving recalls. "I knew the power of the story as I was going forward were those moments."
As the defense in the Donetsk region intensified, the company suffered casualties. "Loss is very much a part of the story—as that happens, what it does to the group, what it does to the collective perspective of the people in the film, and how they normalize it," Irving says.
Over time, that initial dynamic shifted entirely. Having one foot in their former civilian lives was no longer possible, as the sheer weight of the war fully cemented their transformation into frontline combatants.
Independent filmmaking is a labor of love. You put everything you have into it for those rare moments when a scene captures something profound, a moment of truth—maybe something that will outlive the filmmaker.
Xackery Irving
Film Director
Capturing that profound shift required total immersion. Self-funding the film and operating without a crew allowed Irving to maintain a light footprint—sleeping where they slept and eating what they ate.
He filmed inside cramped basements while nearby artillery impacts shook his camera, and took shelter in a Bakhmut house as the frontline collapsed right to their doorstep.
I didn't even fully grasp what phosphorus was until it rained down on us,” Irving says. “I walked outside, saw the sky, and thought for a second, ‘Happy 4th of July,’ before seeing the horror on the soldiers' faces.
With only a basic grasp of the local language, he learned to read behavioral cues rather than words to navigate those high-stress moments alongside them.
From active duty to the award spotlight at the Galway premiere
To fund the project, Irving relied on personal savings from his prior television career. That labor of love reached the international stage in July, when Brace for Oblivion premiered at the Galway Film Fleadh in Ireland, winning Best International Documentary. One of the subjects, Bohdan Patel—who had enlisted as a 19-year-old student at the start of the invasion—received special authorization from his commander to travel straight from active duty to Ireland for the screening.
"When we won the award, he spoke in front of everybody," Irving says. "Four hundred people just broke into cheer because I said, Bohdan is one of seven, he is leaving tonight, going on a bus, flying back to Poland, and he's going to return to a combat zone. I realized in our film, we're on to something, because we were able to connect with an audience that doesn't feel the war directly."
For Bohdan, experiencing the film in Ireland surrounded by foreign festival-goers was vastly different from watching it alongside his comrades in Kyiv.
"It was awesome,” Bohdan says. "But when I was in Galway, Ireland seeing this documentary for the first time, I was thinking, 'Hell, I really want my brothers and sisters in arms to see this.' And yeah, I was really happy to see everybody here who could come. This documentary is more than us. It's a part of Ukrainian history."
What happens after the credits roll
Despite the glamour of festival screenings, the reality of the ongoing war remains immediate.
"On Monday I'll be heading back to Zaporizhzhia, back to work," Bohdan says. "Although I'm not serving as a soldier in the trenches anymore, I'm still doing a very important thing for our soldiers, a lot of things happening behind the scenes with logistics. So yeah, I'm heading back, and I'm kind of in a small dream today."
In Kyiv, the film reached its most critical audience: the Ukrainians who lived through it. Mid-screening, an air raid alert forced a brief pause—a stark reminder of the reality waiting outside, where immediately after the Q&A, a daytime Russian strike hit the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) headquarters opposite St. Sophia Cathedral.
Nata, a former filmmaker who traded her camera for a rifle, is one of the seven subjects followed throughout the documentary. A fond moment for viewers involves Pixel, a stray kitten she rescued from a village basement during her first deployment. "He traveled everywhere with us, and he actually taught me a lot about how to react and behave under pressure," Nata says.
For Nata, watching the early months of Russia’s invasion reflected on screen highlighted the distance traveled since 2022. "It's very heartwarming," she says. "But at the same time, I realize that the beginning of the war is already history, and the war is still going on. I'm on my second or even third chapter.”
Processing survival on their own terms
When asked about the possibility of civilians turned soldiers re-integrating back into peacetime society, Nata reflects on the shift in mindset that combat brings.
"Can a soldier turn back into a civilian? Yes, I think so," Nata says. "The bigger question is what Ukrainian society will look like after the war. Every soldier will be able to become a civilian again if society is ready for them.” For Nata, that future hinges on a fundamental truth about why Ukrainians took up arms in the first place.
We are not defending Ukraine—we are Ukraine.
Nata
Defender of Ukraine
"International volunteers come to defend Ukraine for various ideological or moral reasons, but for us, we are simply defending our own existence,” Nata explains. We are defending who we are, what we are, and our fundamental right to live on our own land. We aren't standing on the line just to perform the act of defense; we are the country itself. This is us, and we are fighting for our own survival."
Screening the documentary in Kyiv was the ultimate test of the project. "Going through those years on the big screen, and having the subjects see themselves for the first time, will be pretty powerful," says Irving. "I want the film to be judged on its own merits—not an American telling their story, but submitted for their approval on their own terms."
That presentation is also a window into a much longer journey: how a nation eventually processes the psychological weight of survival. "I think maybe that's the experience of the war for Ukrainians—how will they process it, and when, if ever," Irving says. "We all imagine it's the day of victory, but there will be a process that everyone will have to go through individually. That is very human too."
