‘Kyiv is gasping for breath’: Russia’s escalating attacks are upending daily life in the Ukrainian capital. Here’s how residents are coping.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
11:17:50 UTC
20:17:50 KST

‘Kyiv is gasping for breath’: Russia’s escalating attacks are upending daily life in the Ukrainian capital. Here’s how residents are coping.
Russian attacks on Kyiv and the surrounding region intensified in late spring, and since August 27, the only respite has come during a visit to the Ukrainian capital by U.S. presidential envoys. Kyiv residents were able to go a full day without air raid alerts only on September 6. The shift in Russian strike tactics is linked to the Russian army’s effort to exhaust Ukraine’s air defenses. In addition to military warehouses, civilian facilities have also come under attack. One of the new targets has been warehouses in the Kyiv region — likely struck in retaliation for the Ukrainian military’s summer strikes on Ozon and Wildberries warehouses and oil refineries. Daytime air raid alerts paralyze life in the city, while nighttime alerts interrupt the sleep of hundreds of thousands of people. Disrupted logistics have caused some goods to disappear from Kyiv supermarkets. Meduza spoke with Kyiv residents who are trying to live amid constant shelling — and are already preparing for a harsh winter.
‘We saw a fireball that looked like an exploding sun’
Marusya, 42, lives in Borshchahivka
No one in Kyiv sleeps normally these days — except for those on some kind of heavy medication. I take sleeping pills every so often, when it gets unbearable and I just want to get some sleep.
We’ve gotten used to nighttime shelling, but lately they’ve started shelling us during the day too — that’s something new. Along with the familiar buzzing, droning, and explosions, there are now sounds that put you on edge simply because they’re unfamiliar. A kind of rumble with a metallic, almost “galvanized” overtone.
Waking up to an explosion at night is scary: you’re defenseless and relaxed. During the day you keep yourself alert — so something went boom, fine. But the daytime alerts have become nonstop. I didn’t think it would drag on this long. It seemed like there’d be some banging and then it would calm down, but the lull never comes.
I don’t think this is retaliation for the strikes on Wildberries. And even if it is, it’s just a pretext. If there hadn’t been such a pretext, they would have tied it to something else. They’ve probably been stockpiling and gathering up [missiles]. If there’s an urge to pound, they’ll pound regardless.
Overnight on August 21, a friend of mine in Solomianka had a strike hit the building next door. She got lucky: the day before, she and her son had ended up staying over at someone else’s place for the night. The blast blew out the windows in her apartment, knocked the doors off their hinges, and brought down her half-condemned balcony. My friend jokes, “I was already afraid it would fall on someone’s head. Thank God the blast wave tore it off.”
There are plenty of damaged buildings in our neighborhood too [because of the war]: you look around and there’s a chunk missing from one building here, another there. I checked on my map app: the nearest building hit by a major strike is 800 meters (2,625 feet) from mine.
There’s a shelter in the building next door, but I haven’t even gone down there out of curiosity. I don’t see the point. If the building collapses, it’s harder to pull bodies out of a shelter than out of a bed. I don’t understand people who still believe in the “two walls” rule and hang out in hallways. I think if it’s going to hit, it’s going to hit. I especially crack up when I hear on the tram: “The nearest shelter is the underground crossing.” Have you seen that underground crossing in Lukianivka? What kind of “shelter” is that?!
Over the entire course of the full-scale war, my husband and I have left our apartment [for safety] only twice. The first time was at the start of the invasion, and the second was recently, when a Zircon missile was launched at Kyiv. We saw a fireball through the window that looked like an exploding sun, followed by a glow of a different color. We went out into the courtyard, smoked a cigarette each, and went back to sleep.
Putin threatened strikes on our energy infrastructure in response to Volodymyr Zelensky’s statement about strikes on Russian airports. As if the Russians hadn’t been hitting our energy facilities before, only civilians? Right now everyone is anxious, meaning on edge: winter is close, which means there will be more strikes on the power and heat. But that’s expected. It’s not news at all.
I don’t see the point in being afraid — we’ve already been through a lot, and we’ll get through whatever new thing comes. Whatever circumstances we’re given, we’ll figure out how to live with them. My mom keeps pushing to order LED strip lights: she lives alone, and darkness scares her more. I’m just glad my laptop holds a charge for a long time so I can watch movies in the dark.
There’s a sense of mild, general panic. I live near a big mall that closes during air raid alerts. When that happens, the supermarket next door, which stays open, immediately fills up. You go in for some bread, kefir, or ice cream, and there are lines of 20 people at the register with carts piled high.
People are grabbing everything. The other day I wanted to buy some thin vermicelli for chicken broth. But everything cheap had been cleaned out completely. Out of curiosity I went to another store — same story there. I think it’s a combination of two things: people have started stockpiling in anticipation of shortages, and deliveries have already slowed down.
We badly underestimated what we had: peace, stability, and quiet nights. A night without an air raid alert, without any “booms,” has become a bonus. Normal life is starting to feel like a distant memory: “Wait, was that even allowed?” I feel anger, sadness, and resentment over the lost time that could have been good.
I used to make plans: at least once a year, take a trip to the sea without a return ticket. Now I can barely plan for tomorrow. I might guess that I’ll do something, but I don’t promise anyone anything.
‘Death has begun touching our district too’
Oleksyi, 50, lives at Kharkivska station in the Darnytskyi district
The shelling machine has kicked into high gear. It used to happen sporadically, but now we live in a world of brief pauses between attacks.
We’ve really gotten under the Russians’ skin over the past year. First, they’ve come to realize they can’t conquer Ukraine. Out of frustration, they’ve grown vicious and started smashing everything they can. Second, we’ve also become much more active in striking back at them. Our drones are reaching all the way to Yekaterinburg. They’re taking revenge. These actions are unlikely to bring the Russians victory, but they’ll cause Ukrainians a lot of suffering: hunger, a lack of medicine, and logistics problems.
My son just started first grade. First graders aren’t even supposed to have homework, but we sit down and do it anyway: the kids don’t have time to get through the curriculum in class because they spend the whole day running back and forth [to the shelter].
We decided to celebrate the start of the school year as a family at a cafe. But then an air raid alert went off, and we were told, “Finish up quickly and leave.” We also wanted to take our son to a children’s play area known for staying open during alerts. But they called and said, “We’re closing [because of the attack].” We didn’t go: what’s the point of taking a kid there and then sitting outside for hours [waiting for the alert to end]?..
Getting from the left bank to the right bank has been a problem since the start of the war: [the aboveground sections of] the metro close during air raid alerts. In the last couple of weeks, it’s gotten worse. If you live on the left bank and work on the right, or the other way around, you live in total paranoia. When you hear the alert, you’re not afraid of being bombed — you’re afraid you won’t make it to where you need to go again.
For three days in a row, I sat and waited [for a train to run], for hours at a time. It’s especially frustrating when you’re tired in the evening, just want to get home as fast as possible, walk up to the metro — and there’s another alert. Or worse, when you’re already inside the station or on the train and you hear that dreadful voice: “The trains are going to Vydubychi station, please clear the cars.” For thousands of exhausted people, that sounds like a death sentence.
To get home, you end up asking someone [for a ride], because the buses and trolleybuses are packed. And even by car it takes a long time because of the insane crawl of traffic jams.
Sleepless nights are becoming the norm, though your nervous system adapts. Sometimes people ask me how the night went, and I can’t remember. Something explodes, something burns, and your brain just stops registering any of it and keeps sleeping. My kid’s psyche has adjusted too: at night you need to sleep, not be afraid, or you’ll go crazy.
Some coworkers of mine had their homes bombed and have nowhere to live now. Compared to that, the sound of explosions outside our window is just noise. Thank God we’re alive and unhurt.
For a long time, no one in our district was killed. At worst, some nonresidential buildings were damaged. About a year and a half ago, death started to touch us too, little by little: three people died at Slavutych station. And this past spring, a Russian missile tore down an entire section of the building very close to our home. So many people died!
Now there’s no faith that the night will pass quietly. In the evenings, crowds rush to take shelter at Kharkivska station. We don’t go into the metro: there’s often nowhere to sit or lie down, and a direct hit would just bury everyone [since the station isn’t very deep]. There’s not much point to it.
I roughly mapped out the area around our building — figured a two-by-two-kilometer square. My wife and I agreed: if strikes start hitting inside that square, we’ll go to the metro. And if there are deaths nearby, it’s time for my wife and son to leave. In the three years of the war so far, nothing has hit here.
Kyiv is gasping for breath. It’s like a damaged ship barely staying afloat: a couple more torpedoes and it’ll go under. There’s a fear that this winter will be deadly. Right now things aren’t so bad: the power stays on, there’s water. But that could all end in a week or two.
The line between summer and fall feels like a warning shot — the calm period is over. You expect the nightmare to start again any day now: sitting for days without power, and when it comes back, frantically charging power banks. You realize just how vulnerable you are, how dependent on the power plant.
I think this fall will be decisive for our family. I’m afraid no amount of preparation for winter will help us: we simply won’t be able to hold out in the apartment. If wealthy people with powerful generators can keep themselves warm, our family specifically won’t manage without electricity, water, and heat. Most likely, my wife and son will have to wait out this winter outside Kyiv.
As for me, I’ll be left trying to make it through this ordeal and somehow winter over in the city. If not in our own apartment, then we’ll huddle together at friends’ place, wherever it’s warm. I put my trust in God: if it’s His will that I stay alive, I’ll get through this winter. And if not…
‘We maneuver under the shrapnel’
Ivan, 56, lives at Klovska metro station in the Pecherskyi district
The other day I was walking near Ukraina Palace, and I heard a siren, then cannon fire. I stopped — and then there was a piercing howl. A jet-powered drone was flying by, fast, cutting clear across the sky. And then it just tore off toward the southwest! Judging by the sound, it wasn’t shot down — it landed in one piece. This summer alone, the Russians have changed their bombardment patterns three or four times. There’s no chaos here, no scenario where guys down a glass of vodka, go on duty, and go, “Let’s go pound them!” They approach it methodically: they take into account both the body’s circadian rhythms and the rhythms of social life.
The massed strikes come overnight from Friday to Saturday, when people are relaxed, and then again from Monday to Tuesday. The Russians know exactly when a person’s “circuits blow” most reliably: they attack between midnight and 1 a.m., interrupting the first phase of sleep. Then they strike again between 3 and 4 a.m., which breaks up deep sleep. I look at people on public transit — a lot of them are falling asleep standing up.
Air raid alerts often start during rush hour: it throws off the rhythm of the city, and it hits people emotionally if not financially. Time is the most precious resource, and you’re losing it.
Every increase in shelling is also tied to bigger events: the start of [last] heating season, our strikes on their oil refineries and warehouses. Right now the escalation is clearly meant to put pressure ahead of the next round of negotiations and to shape public sentiment the way they want — that’s why they’re hitting businesses.
My family lives in a safer region, while I’m in Kyiv. My daughter is dying to come here, and I tell her, “This isn’t a joke, better not right now.” They recently came to visit and were horrified: they got the full experience of what it’s like to be in an apartment during a barrage.
There haven’t been any direct hits on our neighborhood yet — they’re pounding the perimeter, while for us it’s just the windows rattling and the doors shaking. There’s constant smoke and haze in the air. We’ve even gone down to spend the night in the metro twice. Recently I was about to call my family, and then there was a serious boom. We talked, and just as I hung up, it really let loose! The door blew shut, slamming closed, and I actually ducked, thinking, God forbid, the glass [would shatter into shards].
The supermarket near my house has been picked clean, the shelves are empty — the only thing left was lentils. My neighbor went looking for vegetables and found nothing. I went looking for semolina to make cheese pancakes and had no luck either. But it’s fine, I always keep grains in stock, we’ll get by on porridge.
Public service ads have popped up around the city, with kids on posters declaring: “We are energy independent.” I guess that’s how they’re preparing people for winter, to avoid panic. Looks like I’ll have to buy a power station.
People don’t know where to build their lives, what to hold on to. The world is changing, and right now you need flexibility, the ability to jump from one foothold to the next. It’s good when a person doesn’t stiffen up but adapts instead. As Eisenhower once said, plans are worthless, planning is everything. So we set goals and maneuver under the shrapnel.
‘You’re always waiting: will it hit or not?’
Olena, 37, lives in the Obolonskyi district
It’s gotten harder for me to handle the anxiety: there’s much more unpredictability in the shelling now. There are more strikes, more danger, and life is paralyzed. You’re constantly waiting: will it hit or not?
[Friends of my daughter’s] had a children’s birthday party planned for late August at a mall next to Epicentr. The parents looked at the whole situation and moved the celebration to a less impressive but safer venue.
I work in several districts of the city and in the suburbs. Yesterday I drove past a mall that was [still intact], and today it was already standing there with its windows blown out.
The Nova Poshta logistics center was hit, and package deliveries started getting delayed. My [child’s] class had ordered printed learning materials for school. The supplier received them, we paid — but then a strike hit the warehouse in Dnipro. The supplier had to reorder a reprint, and we had to pay the difference in cost, because the price had gone up.
The destruction of warehouses causes enormous losses for businesses and the economy. I don’t care that I won’t be able to buy myself a new iPhone. What I care about is that prices are rising while my purchasing power is falling, because my salary is in hryvnias, and the hryvnia keeps devaluing.
I haven’t seen an actual food shortage. In late August, people cleared out the supermarket shelves, but supplies were restocked the next day. But our favorite dumplings, which a year ago cost 70 to 90 hryvnias on sale, now cost 190 to 200. I’m afraid that in a week they’ll be up to 300. I need to stock up on cat food too: the pouches have gotten more expensive, and people are panic-buying them.
From what I’ve seen in the news, Ukraine has decided to make the Russians reconsider their behavior by striking their major warehouses. But we don’t produce our own Patriot missiles — we depend entirely on deliveries. I think it’s shortsighted to take steps like that. We got hit with similar retaliatory measures in return. But because of its sheer size, losing these warehouses amounts to something like 10% for our neighboring country. Given Ukraine’s size, our damage is far greater.
The boys are measuring whose is bigger, and somehow I’m the one who suffers for it. I’m not a boy, I don’t have anything to measure, so maybe there’s something about this I just don’t understand. The Russians are going to destroy our energy grid regardless, using whatever pretext they can find. Russia’s rhetoric is harsh enough, and I’m sure they’ve had a target list ready for a long time.
We’re not doing anything special to prepare for this winter — we already prepared for the previous ones. We always keep a basic stock of food, even in peacetime. In 2025 we got a power station, and last winter we got some great sleeping bags from a charitable foundation.
Lately I’ve noticed that people around me have become more irritable and less patient from the stress. My child has long been afraid of loud noises: a motorcycle backfiring, construction equipment, the clatter from a building site. Now my daughter has gotten more anxious. And I myself have switched to fast carbs because of the stress.
I’m tired. I want the boys to make up their minds and sit down at the negotiating table without escalating things further. A human life is more important and more valuable than anything else.
‘I say out loud, “Oh, I’m scared” — and the panic subsides’
Olha, 70, lives in Troieshchyna
Until recently, the circumstances at least allowed for some kind of existence, even a life of sorts, but in the last few days things have gotten really hard. I recently spent about three hours at the clinic and never got to see a doctor: the clinic closed during an air raid alert. There’s no time even to ask a question at the front desk. First a line builds up, and by the time it’s your turn, a new alert is announced.
Getting around the city isn’t any easier. I work from home, but sometimes I need to get to the office. When the metro shuts down, everyone switches to surface transit. You can end up standing at a stop for hours, letting one packed minibus after another go by. Calling a taxi is an option, but the price triples in those moments. It’s a similar story with intercity trains: alerts delay them, so you have to build in six to eight hours of extra time for any trip.
I try to adapt, to have a plan B. I don’t waste energy being annoyed by things I can’t control. I just put my energy toward the task at hand. I didn’t get to see the doctor today — fine, I’ll come back tomorrow, I’ll just bring a folding chair and a book.
I honestly can’t understand this war at all, so I don’t ask myself why the strikes have intensified. I guess they want to terrorize us more, so we’ll be more afraid.
I read the news in small doses: I skim it but don’t get deeply pulled in. My friend doesn’t sleep at night because of the shelling, and afterward she asks, “How did you [spend] that night?” I answer, “Sorry, I was asleep.” She doesn’t understand me.
Once I wanted to be like everyone else and worry along with the rest. The shelling was very heavy, and I dove into my feed. It said a Zircon was inbound. I kept reading: a drone was inbound, then another missile. I don’t really have a clear idea of what a missile actually is — I just know it’s dangerous. I started googling what a “Zircon” and “Shahed” drones are, and my brain just about broke. I could feel panic and fear washing over me. I thought: why did I even read that? So I could sit here shaking and not sleep? It’s not like I can change the Zircon’s flight path anyway.
I decided not to go to the bomb shelter — it’s far away, and I have nowhere to run to anyway. I decided that if anything happens, I’ll just unlock the front door so the blast wave doesn’t jam it shut, and go stand in the hallway. And after that, all that’s left is to say a prayer. Or rather, it just comes on its own: “Lord, help me.” Those words calm and support me.
When I was 55, I went through a hard period in my life, and I got interested in psychology. For the past three years I’ve been part of a therapy group, so I have self-help tools at my disposal. My emergency response in a moment of panic is breathing: inhale for a count of four, hold for six, exhale for eight. I keep my focus on the air entering my lungs.
The “be here now” practice keeps me from spiraling into anxious thoughts. Of course, the body reacts to the sound of explosions, and shock sets in. You can’t reason your way out of fear, so I don’t fight it — I just let the feeling be. Sometimes I say out loud, “Oh, I’m scared, I’m scared.” And when I say it, the panic recedes a little.
I believe that in a dangerous situation, my body will instinctively save me. Last year I was staying at a cottage in the Cherkasy region. And at night, something flew directly overhead. I can’t say exactly what, probably a Shahed. And a helicopter was shooting it down. Then there was the sound of the Shahed falling. But you couldn’t see the drone itself! And I had this feeling it was falling right onto me. In that moment you’re not really aware of what’s happening at all. I instinctively ran into the shower. Later the woman who owned the house told me that, as it turned out, that was the safest spot.
That woman, by the way, follows everything closely and reads all the news. She once told me, “Oh, it’s so great that our guys shelled something over there, such a big fire! They hit it, I’m so happy!” And the next day there was a strike where we were too — a bad one, a lot of people died. I sat down and thought: “God, why is it like this? Now they’re celebrating. What are we [all] doing?!”
I’ve been ready for winter for a while now, given how hard last winter was. But I’m not panicking too much — we’ll take problems as they come. I’m afraid to keep a gas canister in the apartment. But I’ve stocked up on food. Not because prices will keep rising. It’s just that we’re expecting a new addition to the family in February, so I stocked up on powdered milk: what if there’s no milk, like in the nineties? And I really love coffee with milk. At the start of the war there was no milk, and it’s very hard for me to deny myself that pleasure.
I also bought a kilogram each of buckwheat, rice, and pasta; two bottles of oil; five cans of chicken. And about 50 packets of cat food — I can get by on tea alone, but the cat can’t. It came out to two boxes of food.
I’m planning to store up water, both drinking and utility. I got a special valve for the sewage pipe: I’m on the first floor, and last winter, when the building had no water, there were problems. I also have a home composting toilet.
If the heat gets shut off but the power stays on, I’ll warm up with the air conditioner and a space heater. If there’s no power either, I’ve got dry alcohol fuel tablets and an ordinary brick stashed away: you can heat them in the [gas] oven, and they hold heat really well. Hot water bottles saved me last winter too — I have five of them.
And I also dance. Honestly, I danced a lot last winter: it really warms you up and keeps your spirits up. I put on Modern Talking — great, rhythmic music. So I definitely won’t be cold.
‘There’s a nagging feeling that 2022 is coming back’
Mykola (name changed), 41, lives in Irpin, Kyiv region
I installed a Telegram bot called Kontur — it’s AI-based OSINT analytics. It shows where any given Shahed drone or missile currently is and where it’s heading. It’s not a real radar, but the bot at least lets you get a sense of what’s going on.
On average, it shows about 400 drones a day heading toward Kyiv. You can watch them coming in from the direction of Kursk and Bryansk, along the Russian and Belarusian border, heading toward the capital. It literally looks like stones falling from the sky. They just keep falling and falling, the stream never stops.
Thanks to the bot, you can at least roughly gauge the scale of the problem. It gives you the illusion of control. If you don’t track the alerts, it feels like you’re leaving yourself to chance. And when you can see the threat, it somehow feels easier to get through. For instance, when you’re on a train and you check: there’s an alert in Kyiv, and there’s a whole herd of Shaheds over the city. You immediately know the train is going to sit there for hours until the situation is sorted out.
It used to be the regular ones, what we called “mopeds with a propeller stuck in their rear.” And they almost never made it through — except during a major bombardment, when they’d bring together aircraft, ballistic missiles, ship-launched missiles, all that arta [artillery]. To overwhelm our air defenses, they’d launch 400 to 500 Shaheds at us at once, of which maybe 20 would get through. But that’s nothing compared to what’s happening now.
The type of attacking drone itself has changed. It looks like a major shift: the new jet-powered drone reaches its target very fast from the border and is harder to shoot down. If it used to come in pulses — say, one raid, and then it would settle down — now the raid never stops.
I have a nagging feeling that 2022 is coming back. Back then the sky was undefended too: planes would fly in and bomb wherever they wanted. It’s the same thing now, just without people in the cockpits. Small jet-powered aircraft fly in and hit everything indiscriminately.
Analysts say Kyiv is just a trial run, and this way the Russians can terrorize any city. It used to be much calmer in Irpin: everything was flying toward Kyiv, not from our direction. Now they’ve taken up exactly this direction: within a 5-to-10-kilometer (3-to-6-mile) radius of our district, there are strikes constantly.
In the summer I sleep with the windows open and wake up at every explosion. When you jolt awake five or six times a night, it’s obvious you’ll be wiped out the next day. It takes a toll on both your mental and physical health. I have diabetes, and my blood sugar has been running high lately. Any chronic condition flares up when your body doesn’t get to rest properly.
Recently they burned down a warehouse belonging to a general goods retail chain. They’re trying to paralyze the capital, and Irpin is part of Kyiv’s metropolitan area. For Kyiv, our town is essentially just an upscale bedroom suburb. After 2022, it seemed like the worst had already happened here, since Irpin had been so badly burned then. But that view is changing now.
It’s precisely in the metropolitan area that a city’s life-support systems are always located. Store warehouses and hypermarkets around Irpin have suddenly become military targets. No one expected strikes on them. They’re trying to cut off the arteries that feed Kyiv from every direction, in order to terrorize it and drive people out. There’s a total destruction of infrastructure underway, aimed at extinction. They want to strip us of everything: food, water, electricity, gas. And logistics, so that nothing at all can be brought in here. It’s a kind of local genocide.
Some might say these strikes started because of the strikes on Wildberries. I don’t think so. In a war of attrition, strikes like these are one of the inevitable stages. Obviously both sides suffer, we just have fewer resources and less capacity. On top of that, Wildberries is just a trading platform — it’s not responsible for the country’s life-support systems. But here they’re destroying everything indiscriminately: food warehouses, basic enterprises. They burned down a Coca-Cola plant — who was that hurting? They burned down a big warehouse of medicine. And there’s news like this every day: one day it’s a strike on a wine warehouse, the next it’s a candy warehouse — I guess so we won’t get to eat anything sweet.
At the start of the war, people cleared out [store shelves] en masse, and now they’re doing it again. But back then, food warehouses weren’t being bombed, so there was somewhere to make up the shortfall. Now, if logistics aren’t restructured quickly, there won’t be anywhere left to draw from, especially given how many people live in Kyiv’s “human anthills” [densely packed high-rises].
In 2022 I also stocked up, and moths ended up eating half of my supplies. Now I look at it more calmly. And if it comes down to it, there’s the option of moving to a part of the country that’s safer and has more food.
For my apartment I recently bought a more modern, higher-capacity battery that can now power not just the gas boiler but the refrigerator too. But overall… what kind of self-sufficiency can you even talk about when it’s an apartment? If the water’s gone, it’s gone. I don’t feel anything about it anymore — it’s just a fact of life.
We’ll sit under LED lamps for a while, then by candlelight, then start up the generator. What else can you do? The main thing is not to freeze to death. Everything else can be survived. As a neighbor of mine, a soldier from Mariupol who went through Russian captivity, put it: “They didn’t break us in captivity, and they sure as hell won’t break us now.”
People are meant to make this world better, not destroy it. What’s happening now is a great grief and a great evil. You look at the destroyed buildings, and it aches. So much effort went into building them! So many generations wanted to leave something behind for their children. One apartment is someone’s entire life, an entire universe. And all of it gets multiplied by zero. On an unreal scale.
This former Soviet state, Russia — it always leaves scorched earth behind. The country doesn’t build up continuity for itself, and it doesn’t let anyone else build it up either. You can’t live like that.
I’m a design engineer, and I love creating things, I want to build. You pick up a tool, go over to an old machine, fix it, it runs — that’s a good in itself. Or people sit down together and come up with, “Let’s build a kindergarten for our kids, let’s start a business.” That’s also a good — developing, living a normal life instead of stomping around in a swamp. And instead we’re being dragged back into the Stone Age.
I really want all of this to end. I want to create things, not live in constant fear of being killed.

European leaders trying to ‘buy time’ for Kiev with ceasefire calls – Lavrov
European leaders calling for a ceasefire in the Russia-Ukraine conflict are seeking to preserve the government in Kiev in its current aggressive anti-Russian form, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has said.
Even politicians who acknowledge that Kiev cannot militarily retake the former Ukrainian regions that have joined Russia since 2014 and now advocate a truce are pursuing an agenda that threatens Russia and its citizens, the top diplomat said. Speaking in an interview on Tuesday, Lavrov named Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni as examples.
The proposed ceasefire “is also just a way to buy time, as everyone knows,” Lavrov said, adding that Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky “makes no secret of that” as he seeks additional weapons supplies.
According to the Russian minister, the goal of this ploy is to preserve and keep in power “the regime currently ruling in Kiev,” whose defining traits he described as “Nazism, aggressive Russophobia, violations of human rights, language rights and religious freedom.”
As for Europe, it wants to preserve that openly Russophobic and aggressive neo-Nazi regime. It is the European plan. I don’t see how the Russian people can accept this outcome.
Moscow’s objections to freezing the conflict remain unchanged, as does its opposition to proposals to deploy troops from NATO member states in Ukraine following a potential peace deal, Lavrov said.
“Any people in military uniforms and any military facilities will be legitimate [targets] for us, and no scenario under which Ukraine will acquire NATO membership in all but name is acceptable to us,” he stressed.
Lavrov was interviewed in Moscow by Russian-American television host Dimitri Simes and visiting US political commentator Andrew Napolitano, better known as Judge Napolitano, after his former role on the New Jersey Superior Court.

Norway holds traditional funeral for late King Harald
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
11:15:22 UTC
20:15:22 KST

Ilayda Cakirtekin
09 September 2026•Update: 09 September 2026
Norway held a traditional funeral ceremony for the late King Harald V on Wednesday after he died on Aug. 28 at the age of 89.
Oslo's city center was secured, cordoned off and decorated ahead of the procession, which traveled from the Royal Palace to Oslo Cathedral and then to the Palace Church at Akershus Fortress, according to broadcaster NRK.
The procession with King Harald's coffin started at noon from Castle Square, with the royal family following the late king to the church.
Around 1,900 soldiers lined both sides of the procession route, forming a ceremonial corridor.
In total, approximately 3,500 Armed Forces personnel were estimated to be ceremonially represented in Oslo, according to the Norwegian Armed Forces.
The funeral was attended by members of European royal families, heads of state and government officials from several countries.
Swedish King Carl XVI Gustaf and Queen Silvia, Danish King Frederik X and Queen Mary, Spanish King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia, Dutch King Willem-Alexander and Queen Maxima and Belgian King Philippe and Queen Mathilde were among the royal guests.
Prince William of Wales and Princess Anne also attended the funeral.
The ceremony was planned to be held in Oslo Cathedral, which has around 800 seats but can accommodate around 1,000.
The government invited people to a memorial service at Oslo City Hall after the burial.
At the same time, the royal family will hold a private memorial service at Akershus Castle Church, where royal guests and state representatives will be present.
In the afternoon, a reception at the Palace was also planned.

Exclusive: EU lawmakers join pressure to use 200 billion euros in Russian assets to help Ukraine

Exclusive: EU lawmakers join pressure to use 200 billion euros in Russian assets to help Ukraine
BRUSSELS, Belgium — Members of the European Parliament (MEPs) have sent EU leaders an open letter calling for the urgent use of 200 billion euros ($230 billion) of Russian assets to help Ukraine, according to a letter first seen by the Kyiv Independent on Sept. 9.
Swedish MEP Karin Karlsbro, the letter's lead signatory, told the Kyiv Independent that she organized the letter because "Ukraine needs substantial, long-term financing now."
"Utilizing the frozen assets would fundamentally change Europe's ability to finance Ukraine long term. It would be a powerful signal to let (Russian President Vladimir) Putin know that time is not on Russia's side."
The document also underscores the need to use the assets in a way that will protect countries at risk of legal challenge.
The 122 MEPs who signed the letter said they "strongly welcome" an earlier open letter from four EU countries, first reported by the Kyiv Independent, that called on the bloc to revisit the possibility of using Russian assets to support Ukraine.
That push led Karlsbro to believe "we have momentum right now."
"We are now putting renewed pressure on (the European) Council and (the European) Commission to act by gathering strong support from MEPs across the political spectrum and from all over Europe," Karlsbro said.
The MEPs' letter also says that the EU should "ensure that Russia ultimately bears the financial consequences of the destruction it has caused."
The idea of using Russia's assets was discussed by the EU in 2025 but ultimately failed due to Belgian concerns over legal risk, and a lack of solidarity to back Belgium if legal challenges arose.
read also
Belgium remains central to the discussion because 180 billion euros (about $210 billion) of the Russian assets immobilized in the EU are held by the financial clearing house Euroclear, which is based in Belgium, just outside Brussels.
"We deeply regret that in December 2025, the European Council failed to reach an agreement to use these assets for the benefit of Ukraine," reads the MEPs' letter.
The letter also throws its support behind a specific solution intended to reduce the legal risk that would land on Belgium's shoulders.
"The immobilized Russian accounts should be transferred to a new EU instrument acting as a custodian and shouldering all legal obligations to the Central Bank of Russia," the MEPs recommended.
"Belgium shouldn't have to shoulder Europe's responsibility alone," Karlsbro said.
"By bringing the assets under EU control, we would share the risks collectively. This would remove a massive obstacle and should be our first course of action."
EU custodianship of the assets was proposed by Ukraine's Finance Minister Serhii Marchenko in a Sept. 4 interview with Euronews, but a fully developed legal proposal does not yet exist.
The letter reinforces the earlier call made by EU countries for the European Commission to make a formal proposal and urges the European Commission and EU capitals to "act without delay."
"The European Union has repeatedly committed itself to supporting Ukraine for as long as it takes. We now need to ensure that this commitment is backed by the necessary resources," the letter reads.
Karlsbro and a group of other MEPs are also meeting with French President Emmanuel Macron, at the time of writing, to discuss the issue.
France holds 19 billion euros ($22 billion) of Russian assets, second only to Belgium in the EU, and is said to share some of Belgium's concerns.

Drunk Russian Man Sold to Recruiters by Friends, Sent to Fight in Ukraine
A Russian prisoner of war captured in Ukraine said he was enlisted in the Russian military after a drinking session, claiming his companions arranged a contract in his name, collected the associated payment, and left him at a military recruitment office before he was sent to fight in Ukraine’s Sumy region.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The account was shared on Ukraine’s national telethon on September 9 by Vadym Karpiak, spokesperson for Ukraine’s 8th Air Assault Corps, who said the man was among recently captured Russian troops describing how they entered military service.
Karpiak said the prisoner had been drinking with a group in Russia before waking up at a local military enlistment office. According to the prisoner’s account, his drinking companions had an arrangement connected to military recruitment, signed a contract on his behalf, and took the money linked to the enlistment.
The man was subsequently deployed as an assault soldier and sent to attack Ukrainian positions in the Sumy region, Karpiak said.\
The spokesperson said recently contracted soldiers make up a significant share of Russian troops being captured and are often sent to frontline positions shortly after joining the military. In some cases, he said, soldiers receive limited information about their mission and are initially instructed to occupy a position and wait for further orders.
Karpiak also described another account from a Russian POW who said commanders used access to food and water to pressure troops into advancing. According to the prisoner, soldiers who refused to move forward could be left without resupply for days, while supplies were delivered farther ahead of their positions to compel them to advance.
Russia continues relying on new contract recruits to replenish frontline units amid mounting personnel losses. On September 9, Ukraine’s General Staff said Russian forces had suffered more than 1.5 million personnel losses—killed and wounded—since the start of the full-scale invasion, a figure that cannot be independently verified in real time.

Ukrainian Armor Unveils Saigak-1 and Varta-3 Armored Vehicles at MSPO-2026
Ukrainian defense manufacturer Ukrainian Armor presented two new armored vehicles, the Saigak-1 and the Varta-3, at the MSPO-2026 exhibition in Poland, according to a company press release on September 8.
Both vehicles are designed for the safe and rapid transport of security personnel during combat operations, special missions, training, and patrols. According to Ukrainian Armor, the vehicles are adapted for diverse terrains and all seasons, and can also be deployed for disaster relief and technological accident response.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The Saigak-1 features an armored hull with PZSA 3 ballistic protection and STANAG 4569 Level 1 mine protection. Built on an all-wheel-drive chassis with a 240-horsepower diesel engine, the vehicle can reach maximum speeds of 140 km/h and has a range of up to 600 kilometers using an 80-liter fuel tank.
The vehicle accommodates a crew of two and three additional personnel. To enhance safety, the Saigak-1 is equipped with front and rear cameras, an automatic fire suppression system, RunFlat tires, and climate control, Ukrainian Armor reported.
The heavier Varta-3 features PZSA 6 ballistic protection and STANAG 4569 Level 3a/3b mine protection. Powered by a 326-horsepower diesel engine with 1,400 Nm of torque and an automatic transmission, the 4×4 all-wheel-drive vehicle reaches speeds up to 100 km/h and has a gross weight of up to 14,800 kg. It is designed to transport a two-person crew and eight additional personnel.
For combat deployments, the Varta-3 can be equipped with a rotating machine gun platform or a remotely controlled combat module. It also includes mine-resistant seats, communication and navigation systems, video surveillance, an automatic fire suppression system, air filtration and ventilation, and RunFlat tires, according to the manufacturer.
“It has already become a tradition for our company to present new products at the MSPO exhibition in Poland. This year, we are also pleased to present two new armored vehicles. The Varta-3 is an updated and improved version of our Varta-2,” Vladyslav Belbas, General Director of Ukrainian Armor, stated.
“We developed it on the German Mercedes-Benz Unimog chassis. This allowed us not only to reduce the cost of the vehicle but also to improve its driving characteristics and off-road capability,” he continued.
Belbas added: “The Saigak-1 is a pickup-based armored vehicle aimed at replacing standard daily military transport with a more protected vehicle. We aimed to create a solution that combines mobility, practicality, and an additional level of protection for personnel.”
Also unveiled at MSPO 2026, Ukraine is developing a 35-ton tracked infantry fighting vehicle named Pegas, designed by the Kharkiv Morozov Machine Building Design Bureau.
The concept features NATO STANAG 4569 Level 6 frontal armor, an integrated anti-drone electronic warfare system, and the domestic BM Topaz combat module equipped with a 30 mm cannon, anti-tank guided missiles, and a grenade launcher.

Ukraine Hits Russian Rare Su-33 Fighter, Mi-8 Helicopter, and Radars in Massive Black Sea Drone Strike
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
11:14:35 UTC
20:14:35 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Hits Russian Rare Su-33 Fighter, Mi-8 Helicopter, and Radars in Massive Black Sea Drone Strike
Ukrainian drone forces destroyed a rare Russian Su-33 carrier-based fighter, an Mi-8 helicopter, and two radar systems during a wide-ranging overnight operation against Russian military targets around the Black Sea, according to Unmanned Systems Forces Commander Robert “Madyar” Brovdi on September 9.
Brovdi confirmed that Ukrainian forces struck the Russian naval base at Novorossiysk overnight into September 9, claiming damage to several military vessels, including missile carriers.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Farther along the coast in Anapa, Ukrainian drones destroyed a Su-33 fighter and an Mi-8 helicopter, Brovdi said.
The same operation also targeted two Russian radar systems—a Kasta-2E2 and a 92N6 radar.
The Su-33 is a particularly notable loss.
Developed from the Soviet Su-27, the Su-33 is a twin-engine carrier-based air-superiority fighter designed for operations from Russia’s Admiral Kuznetsov aircraft carrier. It features folding wings, reinforced landing gear and an arresting hook for carrier operations.
Unlike Russia’s much larger fleets of land-based Su-30 and Su-35 fighters, the Su-33 exists only in limited numbers. Production ended decades ago, and Russia maintains the remaining aircraft rather than manufacturing replacements.
The fighter was originally intended to defend Russian naval formations from aerial threats and can carry air-to-air missiles as well as a 30mm cannon.
With Admiral Kuznetsov spending years undergoing repairs and modernization, and information circulating that it can even be sold for scrapping, surviving Su-33s have frequently operated from land bases rather than from the carrier for which they were designed.
The overnight operation extended well beyond Anapa and Novorossiysk.
Brovdi said Ukrainian drones struck another 13 vessels belonging to Russia’s so-called shadow fleet in the Black Sea.
According to the commander, Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces have now hit 282 shadow-fleet vessels since July 6.
He also released broader figures covering combat operations between September 1 and 8, saying the Unmanned Systems Forces struck 16,720 Russian targets and inflicted losses on 3,395 Russian troops during the week.
“+16% in September compared with August. The average daily number of enemy personnel destroyed on the line of contact has increased significantly: 411 personnel per day in September compared with an average of 355 per day in August,” Brovdi said.
He attributed the increase partly to Russia concentrating more troops near the front, particularly in the Dobropillia sector of the Donetsk region.
“[Russian forces] increased the concentration of personnel on the front line, primarily in the Dobropillia direction of the Donetsk region, which was also reflected in the destruction results,” Brovdi added.
Earlier, reports emerged that two Russian Su-35S fighter jets collided in mid-air in the Kursk region. The crash resulted in the death of one pilot, while the second pilot managed to survive.

Russian Shahed Drone Strikes Passenger Train in Kharkiv Region, Injuring at Least Seven
A Russian Shahed-type drone struck a passenger train traveling from Kharkiv to Izium on September 9, injuring at least seven people.
This was reported by Oleksandr Pertsovskyi, Chairman of the Board of Ukrzaliznytsia.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Izium City Military Administration, the attack occurred at approximately 10 a.m. at a railway station near the village of Iskra in Ukraine’s Kharkiv region. The drone hit the rear section of the Kharkiv–Izium train, causing a fire.
“The enemy continues to insidiously target passenger trains, and sometimes the time between detecting the threat and the strike is measured in minutes,” Pertsovskyi told Suspilne Kharkiv.
Emergency medical teams were deployed to the scene and were providing assistance to the victims.
Authorities said information on the full consequences of the attack was still being clarified.
The strike comes amid continued Russian attacks on Ukraine’s railway infrastructure and passenger trains. In an earlier attack, Russian drones struck a suburban diesel train in Ukraine’s Sumy region, injuring at least 10 people, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service (DSNS) reported.

As rescuers were working at the scene, Russian forces carried out a second strike on the same location. The Real War Telegram channel described the follow-up attack as a “repeat cynical strike.”
No emergency personnel were injured in the second attack, according to the DSNS. Rescue crews subsequently extinguished the remaining fires at the site.
Russia has also targeted other civilian facilities in recent attacks. On September 8, a Russian attack drone struck the Kyiv office of television channel Wt—Ukraine while journalists were broadcasting live as part of the “United News” telethon.

Enemy state?: Israeli incitement against Qatar intensifies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
11:13:31 UTC
20:13:31 KST

Breadcrumb
As elections near, Israeli incitement against Qatar intensifies
Israeli incitement against Qatar has escalated markedly in recent days, in a development that goes beyond traditional political disputes and raises broader questions about the motives behind the escalation and its implications for Gulf security and the future of regional mediation.
The inciting rhetoric against Qatar is no longer limited to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his ministers or to figures on the far right but also involves prominent opposition figures, including former Israeli Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, who has called for Qatar to be designated as an "enemy state".
The position on Qatar has become part of Israel's domestic political competition as elections are in late October.
The Israeli rhetoric is particularly significant because it comes a year after the Israeli attack on Doha on 9 September 2025. Doha is the capital of a Gulf state that was, at the same time, playing a mediating role between Israel and Hamas, in coordination with the United States and other international and regional parties.
Observers believe that part of the Israeli rhetoric against Qatar can be understood in the context of domestic Israeli politics, where foreign policy often becomes a tool in internal political conflict.
In this context, presenting Qatar as an "adversary" or "threat" can become a means of strengthening hardline political rhetoric and demonstrating the ability to adopt tougher positions towards countries that maintain relations or channels of communication with Hamas.
One of the most serious consequences of this rhetoric lies here: when attacking a sovereign state becomes part of domestic political competition, the boundaries of political rhetoric may gradually expand to include new political, economic or security pressures.
Recent attempts have emerged to portray Qatar as a party to the Israeli war on Gaza or to hold it responsible for crises falling out from the war.
Such claims ignore the nature of Doha's role as a mediator, as well as the nature of its official relations with various parties.
Qatar maintains in its political and diplomatic discourse that it operates openly and through official channels with the states it deals with and that its role as a mediator does not mean adopting the positions of the parties with which it communicates.
In this context, attempts to hold the mediator responsible for the outcomes of the war or the failures of the warring parties raise a political issue, particularly when it concerns matters such as occupation, settlement activity and Israeli security and military policies.
The escalation of Israeli incitement against Qatar, coinciding with the first anniversary of the Israeli attack, gives it a different significance.
Talk of targeting a Gulf state is no longer merely a hypothetical scenario or political rhetoric detached from reality but comes after a military incident targeting the Qatari capital.
Ultimately, the escalation in Israeli rhetoric against Qatar appears to intersect with three main tracks: Israel's domestic political struggle, the repercussions of the war in Gaza, and Gulf concerns about the conflict spilling into its security sphere.
At a time when the region needs more channels of communication and mediators capable of bringing together opposing parties, turning mediation itself into a reason for targeting could lead to precisely the opposite result.
Israel is hostile to peace
Jaber Al-Harmi, editor-in-chief of the Qatari newspaper Al Sharq, told The New Arab that Israel represents a party hostile to anyone seeking to achieve peace, stability and security in the region, and that its establishment has historically been associated with a state of turmoil, chaos and instability in the region.
Al-Harmi added that countries working to promote security, peace and coexistence in the region naturally do not align with Israel's approach and that the positive role played by Qatar, whether through mediation or diplomatic efforts, is not accepted by Israeli political circles.
He pointed out that mediation efforts by Doha to reach a ceasefire in Gaza represent one of the most prominent issues exposing the extent of the divergence between the Qatari position and Israeli positions.
Al-Harmi said that the campaigns of incitement and attempts to distort Qatar's image by the Israeli government and its official figures, as well as some opposition voices, are part of a broader campaign that is not limited to Israel but extends to the United States and various political and media spheres to undermine Qatar's role and attempt to influence its image and international standing.
Such attempts have taken place before, he said, and Qatar confronted them and managed to overcome them.
The current campaigns will not achieve their objectives because Doha does not operate in secret and has nothing to hide. Rather, it acts clearly and openly, in coordination with official authorities in the countries where it is involved in political or diplomatic matters.
Qatar carries out its mediation and diplomatic roles according to a clear vision and through official and public channels, he said.
The nature of its relations and communications with different parties falls within its efforts to address crises and advance dialogue and negotiation.
Domestic calculations
Abdullah Bandar Al-Otaibi, an assistant professor in the Department of International Affairs at Qatar University, said the escalating Israeli incitement against Qatar comes in the context of domestic Israeli calculations and an attempt to export internal crises and shift their consequences onto an external party, as this rhetoric expands to include different parts of Israel's political landscape rather than only the far-right government.
Al-Otaibi told TNA that, politically, the more important point is that Israel's own conduct has become one of the factors contributing to a negative image of Israel internationally, amid the continuation of its operations and violations of the sovereignty of countries in the region, including Syria and Lebanon.
This conduct also comes shortly after the Israeli attack targeting Qatar, which caused casualties, including a member of the Qatari security forces.
According to Al-Otaibi, this attack, along with Israeli operations in other countries, raises a fundamental question about the extent to which Israel is committed to international law and respects the principle of state sovereignty.
He added that the problem lies in reinforcing the perception that there is an exception in the application of international law, with Israel treated as though it were a state above the rules of sovereignty and accountability, allowing violations of the sovereignty of other states to be justified under headings such as national security or security necessities.
This situation threatens not only a particular state but also affects the entire regional and international security and stability system.
Therefore, the issue is not only about Qatar's position towards Israel or political disputes between the two sides, in his view, but about a broader principle concerning the need to apply international law equally, respect state sovereignty and prevent national security from becoming an open-ended justification for violating international rules.
Al-Otaibi noted that, by presenting Qatar as an "enemy", Israel is attempting to convince the Israeli voter that the source of the problems it faces comes from abroad rather than from its own policies and practices.
He said the aim is to create an external enemy that can be held responsible for political, diplomatic and humanitarian repercussions.
He stressed that international rejection of and dissatisfaction with Israel are not the result of campaigns carried out by other countries but a direct result of what he described as aggressive conduct, the war in Gaza and its accompanying humanitarian repercussions and violations, in addition to Israeli policies in the region.
Qatar's soft diplomacy
Sadiq Al-Emari, director-general of the Qatari Press Centre, told TNA that Qatar has become a thorn in the side of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and the right-wing opposition in Israel.
Qatar's soft diplomacy has caused clear annoyance on the Israeli side, he said, adding that this is a source of pride.
He added that Qatar's position in confronting Netanyahu, whom he described as a war criminal, represents an honourable position.
Statements by Netanyahu and opposition figures about targeting Doha in retaliation for its political and diplomatic positions represent further evidence condemning the state terrorism practised by Israel, he said.
Regarding Israeli accusations concerning Qatari aid provided to Palestinians, Al-Emari said claims about how the aid was directed are incorrect.
He noted that Qatari aid was provided directly to Palestinian families, in limited amounts not exceeding $100 per family.
According to him, this amount contributes only to covering a small part of Palestinian families' needs and does not allow it to be converted into funding for the purchase of weapons or military equipment.
He stressed that Qatar is a "state seeking peace" and that it is making continuous diplomatic efforts to establish peace and calm conflicts in the region.
It cannot, under any circumstances, be described as a party seeking to destabilise the region or support violence, he said.
He concluded by stressing that Israeli recognition of the role Qatar has played through its diplomatic and political positions on the Palestinian issue, even when it comes in the context of accusations and criticism, reflects the extent of the influence Qatari diplomacy has come to exert in the region.
Escalating incitement
Omani researcher Abdullah Baabood told TNA the escalating Israeli incitement against Qatar should be taken seriously, particularly because it is no longer limited to figures within Netanyahu's far-right government but is also present in the rhetoric of prominent opposition figures.
This suggests, in his view, that the position towards Qatar is no longer merely a passing political dispute but has, to varying degrees, become part of political competition and internal political conflicts in Israel, particularly as elections approach.
Baabood said it is natural that when an attack on the capital of a sovereign Gulf state becomes something that can be politically celebrated, followed by calls for further political, economic and security pressure on it, this would raise concerns extending beyond Qatar to the rest of the Gulf states.
The paradox, he said, is that Qatar was not a party to the war but played the role of mediator, working in that capacity in coordination with the United States and other parties.
Its channels with Hamas were a key part of efforts to reach a ceasefire and secure the release of Israeli hostages.
Therefore, attacking Qatar for maintaining these channels contains an obvious contradiction: a mediator cannot be asked to perform its role and then be punished because of the tools and channels that make mediation possible, he said.
Baabood added that the issue should not be viewed from a Gulf perspective merely as a Qatari-Israeli dispute.
An attack on the sovereignty of any Gulf Cooperation Council member state, or a threat to repeat such an attack, affects the security of the entire Gulf and raises serious questions about the role of GCC states and the effectiveness of the regional deterrence and protection system.
A precedent that passes without a clear collective response may, over time, become something that can be repeated.
The Omani researcher added that the first anniversary of the attack on Doha should not merely be an occasion to remember what happened but an opportunity to reconsider what can prevent such an attack from being repeated against Qatar or another Gulf state.
What is required at the Gulf level, he said, is a clearer position considering any infringement on the sovereignty of a member state to be an infringement on the collective security of the GCC states and translating this principle into more effective political and security arrangements.

Have we found alien life? Hundreds of scientists weigh in
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
11:13:30 UTC
20:13:30 KST

Have we found alien life? Hundreds of scientists weigh in
- Date:
- September 9, 2026
- Source:
- The Conversation
- Summary:
- Two major alien-life announcements in 2025 generated enormous excitement, but most astrobiologists remained unconvinced. Only 6.6% of surveyed experts thought possible biological molecules on K2-18b probably represented extraterrestrial life, while 15.1% said the same about intriguing mineral patterns in a Martian rock.
- Share:
It may seem like we are on the verge of discovering alien life. In 2025, a press release stated that we have the “strongest hints yet” of extraterrestrial life on the exoplanet K2-18b. And when talking about a collected sample from a rock named “Cheyava Falls” on Mars, NASA Administrator Sean Duffy said this was the “closest we have ever come” to discovering life on the red planet.
Such moments capture the imagination. But they also raise an important question: what do the majority of scientists actually think?
Surprisingly, we usually don’t know. When a scientific controversy or breakthrough dominates headlines, press officers and journalists often quote a handful of experts. These views may be insightful, but they rarely tell us what the wider scientific community thinks. And yet public discussions frequently rely on phrases such as “the science says” or “scientists believe”, as if there were a clear and measurable answer.
In reality, systematic evidence about scientific opinion is often missing. My colleagues and I recently tried to change that in the domain of astrobiology. Shortly after the two major announcements of possible extraterrestrial life in 2025, we surveyed astrobiologists to understand how expert judgment was distributed across the field.
The first case concerned the exoplanet K2-18b. In April 2025, researchers reported possible traces of molecules called dimethyl sulfide and/or dimethyl disulfide. On Earth, these are associated with biological activity. Media coverage was extensive, with many reports framing the finding as an extraordinary advance in the search for alien life.
The second case came in September, when NASA announced that Cheyava Falls appeared to preserve a potential biosignature – so-called “leopard spots” which are mineral rings that on Earth are often formed by microbial activity. Again, headlines, and NASA officials themselves, suggested something momentous.
What scientists actually thought
We surveyed hundreds of astrobiologists from across the global research community, within days of each announcement. We asked a simple question: did scientists think extraterrestrial life had probably been found?
The results revealed a rather cautious picture. For K2-18b, only 6.6% of surveyed astrobiologists agreed that scientists had probably found extraterrestrial life. Nearly two-thirds disagreed, while 28.0% remained neutral. For the Mars case, confidence was higher but still cautious: 15.1% agreed, disagreement fell to 44.6% and neutrality rose to 40.3%.
Looking only at agreement and disagreement, however, misses an important part of the story. The proportion of astrobiologists who strongly disagreed fell dramatically, from 35.1% in the K2-18b case to just 11.1% for Mars. Much of the movement was therefore not from rejection to endorsement, but from strong rejection towards more tentative positions.
In other words, expert opinion moved in structured ways. The shift from K2-18b to Mars was not a simple movement from “no” to “yes”. Instead, the community became more open to the possibility without embracing it outright.
One possible reason is that the two cases involved different kinds of evidence. The K2-18b claim relied on possible atmospheric signatures detected from across interstellar distances, whereas the Martian case concerned a rock that could be studied directly and in much greater detail. At the same time, astrobiologists have long been aware that apparently lifelike features can sometimes arise through non-biological processes. Often, the challenge is not imagining how life could produce a signal, but understanding all the ways nature might produce something similar without life.
Scientific opinion is rarely binary. Public discussion often treats science as though communities either agree or disagree. But the distribution of opinion matters too. Strong agreement, agreement, neutrality, disagreement and strong disagreement can each tell us something different about how a scientific community is responding to a claim.
A large neutral response can indicate several things. Scientists may judge the evidence genuinely inconclusive. They may hold an intermediate level of confidence. Or they may regard a claim as too speculative to endorse or reject decisively. Likewise, movement from strong disagreement towards ordinary disagreement may signal a softening of attitudes even when overall disagreement remains high. Treating scientific opinion as simply “for” or “against” risks flattening these important distinctions.
Beyond extraterrestrial life
The broader lesson extends well beyond extraterrestrial life. In areas such as climate science, pandemics, artificial intelligence or medical research, public conversations frequently invoke scientific consensus.
Sometimes strong agreement genuinely exists. Sometimes it does not. But we often lack systematic ways of measuring what scientists actually think, especially where evidence is emerging or uncertainty remains substantial. Instead, discussions rely heavily on selective quotation, vocal individuals or assumptions about community views.
Efforts to do this more systematically are beginning to emerge. At Durham University, our research group, C-Scope (the Centre for Scientific Community Opinion Polling and Evaluation), studies how expert opinion is distributed and how it changes over time. We are not trying to replace evidence with polling, nor to treat majority opinion as truth. Our aim is to better understand how scientific communities respond to uncertainty.
Scientific knowledge advances through uncertainty, disagreement and gradual revision. If public discussion, and perhaps political will, increasingly turns on claims about what scientists think, we should make more effort to find out.
Story Source:
Materials provided by The Conversation. Original written by Peter Vickers, Professor in Philosophy of Science, Durham University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow and with Ukrainian President Volodomyr Zelensky in Kyiv on the weekend to discuss how to end the war between the two countries. Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The visit to Moscow on Saturday was a diplomatic faux pas, rants journalist Edward Lucas (Lithuania) in Delfi:

“Donald Trump has made his ability to bring wars to a swift end an integral part of his political image. Furthermore, the political calendar is piling on the pressure: the mid-term elections are just around the corner and the presidential election campaign begins about a year from now. ... The more urgently Washington needs results, the more sense it makes for Moscow to play for time, continue the war and wait for the next offer. This is why I would focus less on the number of visits by Witkoff and instead ask what has changed in Putin’s calculations after each of these visits. Abramovich Loses Third Bid to Escape EU Sanctions
At least a functioning channel of communication
This diplomatic initiative must be taken seriously, political scientist Bernardo Ivo Cruz urges in Diário de Noticias (Portugal):
“The EU and Kyiv’s allies have made it clear: only Ukraine will decide the terms for ending the war. This means that we may have to accept a settlement that is acceptable to the Ukrainians but which results in tangible gains for Russia. An imperfect peace that would neither fully restore the justice violated by the aggression nor wholly uphold international law. ... Yet after four and a half years of war, the mere return of a diplomacy capable of engaging with both Moscow and Kyiv must be taken seriously.”
Too early for diplomacy
Diplomacy can only begin once Russia has lost, Le Point (France) argues:
“At this stage there will be no diplomatic solution to this war. Some conflicts end around a negotiating table. But there are others where the negotiating table only comes into play once an imperialist regime has realised that it has lost. That was the case with Germany in 1945. And with Serbia in 1995. And it is exactly what will happen with Russia too: the diplomats will only get to work once the reality of the battlefield has, in one way or another, been acknowledged in the Kremlin’s inner circles. Until then, the winter will be brutal, and we must help Ukraine to hold out.”
A small step in the right direction
Military expert Oleksiy Kopytko (Russia) is optimistic in a Telegram post republished by Echo:
“There is no doubt that the path to genuine agreements will involve heavy-handed pressure. Right now it looks like the US is intent on exerting pressure primarily, or even exclusively, on Ukraine, because the country is heavily dependent on external support. With regard to Russia, only China could assume this role, but Beijing has yet to intervene. ... This round of negotiations will not lead to an immediate end to the war. That would take a miracle. ... But it is a small step in the right direction. I am confident that by winter serious attempts will be made to initiate genuine negotiations leading to a ceasefire.”
Putin’s final bid with Trump
So far Putin’s hopes regarding Trump have been dashed, Gazeta Wyborcza (Poland) concludes:
“Putin and his entourage had hoped that Trump would do for them the job they themselves are unable to do on the front line, and force the Ukrainians to hand over to the Russians what they demand but have been unable to secure despite heavy losses. ... That was their aim at the summit in Anchorage in August 2025, but it failed. ... Trump’s shelf life is coming to an end. It looks as though his fellow Republicans will suffer a defeat in the mid-term elections on 3 November and his hands will be tied by a hostile Congress. ... So if the Kremlin can still get anything out of him, it has to be now.”
No hope without concessions by Zelensky
In a Telegram post republished by Echo, journalist Fyodor Krasheninnikov (Russia) sees the Ukrainian president playing a key role:
“I am wholeheartedly in favour of ending the war as quickly as possible, but in September 2026 there is only one way this will be possible – namely, if Trump’s envoys persuade Zelensky to accept Putin’s humiliating and unjust terms. Should this prove impossible for Zelensky, talks is all there will be. To those who want to jump to conclusions about my stance and ask, ‘Well what do you propose?’ I say: I am not proposing anything. I am merely saying that the war will continue and there are no other options unless Zelensky is prepared to make concessions.”
Russia wants to eliminate the Ukrainian state
All Russia’s demands call into question Ukraine’s very existence, making concessions on Ukraine’s part practically impossible, argues journalist Vitali Portnikov on TSN (Ukraine) :
“Russia has a clear ambition: the elimination of Ukrainian statehood and the expulsion of a large part of the Ukrainian population from the territories in which they live. ... It will not seek a compromise with a nation whose statehood it seeks to eliminate. That is why, since 2014, there has been no alternative but to stand firm against it; there will be no other option in 2026, nor beyond that. ... What is at stake here is nothing less than the right of Ukraine and the Ukrainian people to an independent existence.”

Setback for asset tax plan as BBB threatens to force Senate vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
11:12:35 UTC
20:12:35 KST

Setback for asset tax plan as BBB threatens to force senate vote
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The cabinet’s wealth tax reforms are in jeopardy after the farmers’ party BBB threatened to block them in the senate unless the coalition parties agree to a major overhaul.
MPs voted in favour of a new “box 3” tax on assets earlier this year, but the vote in the senate was postponed amid speculation that the centre-right coalition partners, VVD and CDA, were poised to vote against the plans in the upper house.
The cabinet wants to change the income tax system so that investors and savers are taxed on the growth of their assets each year, a system favoured by D66 and backed by VVD and CDA in the lower house.
But the two parties’ senators want to replace box 3 with a capital gains tax, which would be paid on the actual profit made from selling shares or other assets such as real estate.
Right-wing opposition parties, including the BBB and JA21, also favour this option, meaning the bill in its current form would almost certainly be voted down.
The BBB has said it will force a vote in the upper house unless finance minister Eelco Heinen withdraws the plan altogether, which would mean starting from scratch.
Withdraw or vote
“It can’t be up to the cabinet whether or not we examine a law in the Senate,” BBB senator Bart Kroon told the upper house’s finance committee. “Withdraw it or we’ll put it to the vote.”
Heinen had hoped to amend the bill as part of the current budget settlement so that it could be passed and enacted before 2028.
The finance minister has already torn up the plans once after the proposed new system attracted international criticism amid concern that investors would be forced to sell shares in order to pay tax on unrealised returns.
A new bill would not make it onto the statute book before 2029, costing the Dutch treasury an estimated €3 billion a year in lost revenue in the meantime.
The cabinet has been trying to reform the mechanism since the Supreme Court ruled in 2021 that the current system, which taxes assets based on a notional growth rate, breached European human rights laws.
Since then it has implemented a stopgap system that still taxes assets at a fictional rate but gives savers the option of declaring their actual growth rate instead. They can still pay the fictional rate if it works out lower.
