New science shows we crave both close friends and large networks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:43:40 UTC
19:43:40 KST

Rachel Feltman: For Scientific American’s Science Quickly, I’m Rachel Feltman.
Think about your friends for a second. Do you feel like you have the right number of them? If you feel like you’ve heard that there’s a right answer to this, you’re probably thinking of the work of anthropologist Robin Dunbar, who famously landed on the number five for close friendships and around 150 for less intimate connections. Of course, you probably won’t be shocked to hear that friendship is hard to quantify, and your results may vary wildly.
So why does this matter? We know that having some number of good friends is really beneficial—one 2010 meta-analysis found that people with stronger social relationships are less likely to die in any given period of time—and we also know that many people struggle to form and maintain these connections. In 2023 Pew Research found that 8 percent of American adults claimed to have no close friends at all.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Today’s guest is Jessica Ayers, an assistant professor of psychology at Boise State University. She says that she and her colleagues see a lot of confusion about friendship and how to do it—and not a lot of research aimed at closing the knowledge gap. Their latest study challenges some common assumptions about how humans set out to build their social networks in the first place.
Thank you so much for coming on to chat with us today.
Jessica Ayers: I’m very excited to be here.
Feltman: So you recently worked on a study about friendship. How did the idea for this study come about?
Ayers: Yeah. So when it comes to friendship, one of the strangest things is that we actually know very little about how human friendships function compared to all the other social relationships that we have in our lives: parenting relationships, relationships with other family members, romantic relationships.
Then there’s friendships where everyone is just like, “They’re there, they exist,” but we don’t really know how or why, and that is mind-boggling because there are so many huge benefits associated with having friendships, like healing faster after surgeries. Not having friendships, so experiencing loneliness, can sometimes have the same negative physical impact as smoking.
So there are some really big positive benefits of having friendship, and we don’t really know about them. So the study really came from this idea of, well, you know, some people have a lot of friends; some people don’t have a lot of friends. Some people with a lot of friends are lonely; some people with a lot of friends aren’t lonely.
Where do these different ways of making friendships actually come from, and how does that actually impact how we’re feeling? And so as a graduate student, I was kind of looking into this question with my co-author, Diego Guevara Beltrán, who’s the co-first author with me on this paper, and we were really just interested in trying to understand, like, “How do we get these differences?”
How do we have people with a lot of friendships versus a little friendships? How do we make that decision? And what kinds of other personality factors or other behaviors that we can measure are associated with this preference?
Feltman: Yeah. So how did you go about trying to answer that question?
Ayers: A lot of different ways—so when we’re doing scale construction to come up with a way to actually see, like, is this idea real, can we measure it in the real world, there’s a bunch of different steps you have to go into, and so they’re very technical. We won’t really pay too much attention to them. But basically, we went through this painstaking task of finding the items that actually get at: Do you want a lot of friends? Do you want a little friends? Do you want emotionally close friendships? Is it okay if they’re not as emotionally close?
To show across multiple different samples, these concepts seem to resonate, and they seem to show up in the same way. And then, after we had done that, we started looking at the different personality constructs that are associated with this.
So we found, like, people who want a really wide network of friendships, they also tend to be more extroverted. People who are worried about not having enough emotionally close friendships, sometimes they’re actually more lonely. And so we did five different studies. Most were done in the U.S. The fifth one also contained participants from the Philippines, Egypt and one other one that I can’t remember off the top of my head [Editor’s Note: Brazil] to show that this isn’t just a Western phenomenon.
This seems to be kind of a universal phenomenon. When we’re making friendships, we’re kinda making a decision between “Do we want a quantity versus quality of friendships?” And the really surprising thing about our scale was that it showed us we might actually not be thinking about that in the right terms, or we might not be thinking about it the right way compared to how the research has presented it before.
Because one of the most surprising things that we found in our study was that when people had a wide network of friendships, they could also still want really emotionally close friendships within that wide network.
So while most of the previous research has always relied on this kind of implicit foundation— it’s one or the other: you want a lot of friends, or you want really emotionally close friendships—we found that it’s not quite as clear-cut to those two things.
Feltman: Hmm. Could you unpack for us a little bit, kind of, what the existing paradigm is in terms of how, you know, close friendships versus a lot of friendships work and what your data actually found?
Ayers: So when we think about this idea that there has to be a trade-off in how we make friendships, this comes from a lot of evolutionary biology, looking at human growth, human development, that kind of shows that when humans have these really fundamental goals that they have to achieve, there’s often a trade-off in how they achieve.
So you can think of, like, you grow, and you reach sexual reproduction and sexual maturity earlier. And so there’s a trade-off in there for “How much are you growing? At what point do you make that turn from somatic maintenance to reproductive maintenance?” Another really famous one is this idea that there is a trade-off between the quality and quantity of the children that we have.
And so we see some research in other nonhuman primates looking at how those individuals invest in their children. Some of them invest in only a few children, and they invest very heavily in them, or I should say offspring ’cause they’re not humans, and others will invest or not as heavily in their offspring, but they have so many more of them.
And so the most famous one, when we were thinking about our study in particular, was actually thinking about how people invest in potential romantic partners. Are they investing in short-term relationships, or are they investing in potentially one long-term relationship? And so when we were looking at some of that original data and the original scales used to measure what we call sociosexual orientation, we started thinking about, well, you know, some of these things are actually really similar to friendships, except for friendships have this cool kind of nuance of you don’t just have one friend at a time.
And so when it came to the data, we found that people, they seem to have preferences for both for the extent to which they want a wide network of friends and the extent to which they want emotional closeness within those relationships.
And so the fact that we have both of these things operating at the same time is really cool and interesting because that kind of starts pointing toward how we’re making our social networks, that it’s not just we have to pick only a few number of people and be emotionally close to them, but we can’t have other people that we may go to for other needs, or the flip side—we have a bunch of people, but we’re not close to any of them.
Feltman: So people want both close friends and a wide network of friends, but do they have preferences as to one or the other?
Ayers: We see in the data that people tend to fall on one of the two categories. They have a stronger preference for one or the other, but they still have the preference for the other. But to kind of go one step further beyond that, when we were then looking at some of the things associated with this preference, for example, having this preference for a wide network of friend, you generally tended to have more friends if you had a stronger preference for a wide network of friends.
You had more people that were willing to come and help you, more friends that were willing to come and help you, whereas when you had this preference for this emotional intimacy within your friendships, what we saw was that those people tended to say that they had lower friendship quality in their current friends.
So you can think of it more as like an alarm going off of, like, you don’t have enough people that are satisfying what you need in these friendships.
And so we have this preference for how wide we actually want our networks to be, but we also have this red flag that’s kind of operating in the background of like, hey, like something isn’t going right.
Like maybe you have this preference for this huge network of friends, but that flag is also going off in the back of your head, telling you, “Hey, but none of them are close. None of them will help you if you need them.” You don’t have those strong connections that we know are so important to human social life.
Feltman: What do you think the implications of this are for situations where people don’t feel like they’re really satisfied with the friendships that they have—because, you know, we talk a lot about the loneliness epidemic and how shallow so many friendships feel now that so much of our lives are online.
So what do you think some, like, further questions are here or even takeaways im- immediately?
Ayers: Yeah. So there’s a bunch, and we can go down the rabbit hole, we can put on our tinfoil hats, and I can talk to you about all the ideas I have. But I think the biggest takeaway is that this scale is giving us a way to actually start measuring some of the stuff you’re pointing at: that loneliness, the isolation, “my friendships feel fake, and they feel hollow.”
Because you’re exactly right—research tells us that friendships that are maintained primarily online, they’re not as satisfying as those that are in person and face-to-face. But the world is moving toward “that’s the way we’re maintaining our relationships.”
So what I like to think about is if we can actually start using specifically the preference for emotional closeness within friendships as a way to maybe screen people for, are you actually satisfying your social goals? Are you meeting the correct number of friends that make you feel like you’re satisfied or make you feel like you have people that are there to help you?
And that exactly talks about the loneliness epidemic or leads to the loneliness epidemic kind of solution of being able to point at, like, hey, it’s actually specifically a lack of these positive social interactions with friends that is what’s making you feel lonely.
It’s not that you don’t have friends. It’s not that you’re not good at making friends. It’s the actual interaction, the emotional closeness, all the things that we know we need to have to have satisfying friendships. Like, we now have a way to actually point at it and say, like, “Here. It’s right here.”
Feltman: It seems like, you know, one thing that, that you’re getting at is that lack of perceived emotional intimacy isn’t necessarily something that’s wrong with the friend or the friendship or with, you know, your ability to make friends, but that sometimes we’re not fostering those friendships and doing the kinds of activities that make us feel like we have that emotional intimacy and fulfillment. Could you talk a little bit more about how people who feel like they’re lacking this kind of closeness in their friendships can remedy that?
Ayers: Yeah. So I can give you some speculations ’cause you’re kind of pointing right at the forefront of the research for the things we’re trying to figure out now. So ways that people can remedy that: we know the face-to-face interactions, they are so incredibly important. The best way to maintain a friendship is to have some kind of face-to-face interaction.
But one thing that’s really important to remember and pay attention to is that the ways in which we make friendships are different. We do know that there is a pretty strong sex difference in how men and women make friends, and not saying that, like, men only do this, women only do this—they do both. But we know that there’s a slight sex difference in terms of which direction they’re likely to lean.
Women tend to have what we call face-to-face friendships. They’re more likely to be emotionally close, they’re more likely to talk literally face-to-face, and they’re more likely to interact in one-on-one situations, whereas men’s friendships, they’re more likely to be team-building, activity-oriented interactions.
And so when we’re thinking about like, “Okay, well, how do I get that face-to-face interaction that makes me feel like my relationship is actually fulfilling?” For women, it might be going to a coffee shop and having a talk about what’s going on in their lives, catching up, chitchatting, whatever you wanna call it.
But for men, it might not be going to that same coffee shop and catching up in that way. It might be like, “Hey, there’s a pickup basketball game. Let’s go hang out,” “Oh, my gosh, our favorite sports team’s playing. Let’s go watch it at the local bar”—things that are more activity-based that still allow for that catching up, still allow for the relationship to be strengthened by being face-to-face and with each other but not in the same way.
And I think that’s something that’s really important to remember—is that we, all of us, we have friendships that go both ways. We have friendships that are face-to-face, emotionally close. We have that kind of relational aspect to it, and we also have the ones that are more task-oriented. And it’s not a problem to have one or the other, but you have to know what makes you feel satisfied and fulfilled, so you know how to actually go about making those relationships fit that need for you.
One thing that’s really important, um, to mention here is our studies, they don’t show a sex difference where men and women prefer different parts—or like, it’s not like men want this really wide network; women want this really emotionally close network.
Like, some of the previous research may have suggested or may have kind of had this underlying assumption that because women have these face-to-face relationships, of course they have to be emotionally close; they have to always be looking for that. Men have task-based friendships—of course it has to be something that’s really wide so you can do all the tasks in the world. It doesn’t seem like that’s the case.
Everyone has these preferences. They’re operating under the surface. And so what I think is really interesting is that that kind of points toward “How are we organizing our social networks?”
How are we actually going through and figuring out, like, how many close friends do I have? How many acquaintances do I have? How many people are in my network that I’m friendly with, but I wouldn’t call them a friend? It kind of points toward, like, maybe this is where this different orientation toward making friends is coming from, is this underlying idea of the quantity versus quality of friends we have in that network.
Feltman: Hmm. So I know that this wasn’t the focus of the study exactly, but as someone who researches friendship, do you have any advice for people on how to go about making friends in the first place?
Ayers: Do I have advice? Yes. Not all of it will be perfectly scientifically backed. A lot of it is kind of like my internal speculations about what I think is happening. We know that when people are making friendships, they have to be genuine. Like, when someone is faking a friendship, you can feel it, or when they’re faking social interactions with you, you can feel it.
It feels icky. It feels like this person really is like, there’s just something I can’t put my finger on, but they’re not really interested in me. So we know that if people are trying to make friendships under those kind of situations and under those kind of false pretenses, the friendship isn’t gonna flourish.
Another one is to find shared interests in some way, shape, or form because we know that having that shared common knowledge base as the start of a friendship leads to friendships that can be maintained because there’s always something that you can fall back on to continue talking about building a relationship over.
So that is really important. I wouldn’t necessarily say, like, be open or be willing to go out there to find friends, but also kind of knowing where your niche is—for me, I’m not gonna go to, like, a gym and go look for gym bros because that’s not something that I value in my friendships.
I’m going to look for someone that I can have conversations with, that I can run ideas by, and so I’m more likely to make friends at a coffee shop or a bookshop than I am when I go to the gym. And so knowing what your own preferences are, the things that make you feel satisfied, helps you kind of guide yourself toward the people that are gonna make friends with you long-term.
And then another thing that’s really important is also just remembering that, like, you are bringing something to the table when you’re making friends. Like, you have intrinsic value; you have intrinsic worth. Some of my other research, not related to this stuff but tangentially, shows that, like, we actually really like people as potential friends who are interested in us and wanna know stuff about us.
So, like, you, you bring something to the table. Not only do you wanna know about that person, that person wants to know about you, and you make better friendships when you have that kind of dynamic and you have that understanding going in.
Feltman: Well, thank you so much for coming on to chat with us about this. I will definitely be keeping it in mind as I socialize.
Ayers: Thank you so much for having me.
Feltman: That’s all for today’s episode. We’ll be back on Friday to talk about another aspect of humanity’s friendship problem: how our social lives are changing now that we spend so much of our time talking to machines.

Serbia's President Vucic dissolves parliament, calls snap elections
BELGRADE, Sept 9 - Serbia's President Aleksandar Vucic on Wednesday dissolved parliament and announced snap elections for next month as he seeks to extend his hold on power by running for prime minister.
Vucic, a populist who has been in power as president or prime minister for 12 years, has faced nearly two years of anti-corruption demonstrations triggered by the collapse of a railway station awning in the city of Novi Sad in November 2024 that killed 16 people.
"Were the elections necessary for us if there were no such tensions, if there were no such political conflicts, certainly they would not be necessary," Vucic said in a televised statement. He added that any delay in the election "would threaten the survival of democracy."
He set the election date as October 25, confirming earlier statements on timing. A parliamentary vote was initially scheduled for next year.
Vucic has ruled as prime minister or president since 2014 and held the reins of power in both positions. While he has overseen a chapter of economic development he has faced growing criticism over perceived corruption and authoritarianism.
Still, he commands support from his ruling Serbian Progressive Party which on Saturday nominated him to run for prime minister in the upcoming elections. It is unclear if Vucic will resign from his position as president before the parliamentary election.
The student-led protest movement, which has organised some of Serbia's largest demonstrations in decades, has yet to announce whether it will back a candidate or political bloc in the election.
Rasa Nedeljkov of pollster CRTA said the vote would be a test of support for Vucic after nearly two years of anti-government protests.
"Since 2024 it was clear that elections will be a way for the ruling party to seek legitimacy," Nedeljkov said, while adding that opponents of Vucic faced an uphill battle. REUTERS

The required details were subsequently filled in.According to the GBA, Rao was listed as a voter in Part No-129, Serial No-431 of the 76-Malleshwaram assembly constituency in the 2002 electoral roll.

In view of this, the Booth Level Officer (BLO), without issuing any notice, has recommended inclusion of his name in the final electoral roll, considering him to be a respected person.
Accordingly, necessary action has been initiated to include his name in the final electoral roll," the GBA said.He is currently enrolled as a voter in Part No-59, Serial No-187 of the 157-Malleshwaram assembly constituency under the name 'Prof CN Rao M'. Ukraine reveals ‘game changer’ RAM-2X strike drone
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
11:40:34 BST
19:40:34 KST

Ukrainian defence manufacturer UKRSPECSYSTEMS has publicly identified itself as the maker of the RAM-2X precision-strike uncrewed aerial system, revealing a weapon the firm says has already been used extensively in combat and produced at scale rather than a new developmental design.
The company unveiled RAM-2X under its own name at the MSPO defence exhibition in Kielce, Poland, on 8 September, after previously withholding its involvement for Ukrainian security reasons. UKRSPECSYSTEMS says the system has been manufactured and employed operationally at large scale by Ukraine’s Defence Forces.
Speaking to the UK Defence Journal ahead of the announcement, Rory Chamberlain, Managing Director of UKRSPECSYSTEMS UK, said the company had wanted to discuss the system publicly for some time but had been prevented from doing so by Ukrainian security considerations.
He said those restrictions had now reduced sufficiently to allow UKRSPECSYSTEMS to identify itself as the manufacturer and begin discussing a capability that had previously remained largely hidden behind operational footage and battlefield reports.
Chamberlain told us RAM-2X became fully operational in 2024. Asked what the company meant when it described the system as being used at large scale, he would not provide an exact figure but said the scale was already in the “tens of thousands”, adding that this was a low estimate. On the company’s account, RAM-2X has already been developed, adapted and employed through several years of high-intensity war before the company has been able to put its name publicly alongside the system.
In its formal announcement, Chamberlain said: “RAM-2X isn’t new to the battlefield; what is new today is that we can finally talk about it publicly. It has been developed through combat and continuously improved using feedback from the Ukrainian units operating it.
“What matters is not simply the range or performance of an individual aircraft. RAM-2X demonstrates a different approach to precision strike: matching the effector to the target and generating military effect at a price and scale that can be sustained in war. And when RAM-2X is connected with SHARK-M, the result is much more than two drones. Persistent reconnaissance and precision strike become part of the same operational system – finding, tracking and engaging demanding targets at depth.”
Combat footage opened to public scrutiny
Alongside the reveal, UKRSPECSYSTEMS has opened what it calls the X-Archive, a collection of combat footage the company says was supplied by Ukrainian military units operating RAM systems and cleared for public release. The initial material concentrates on Russian air-defence equipment, with the company saying RAM systems have been credited with strikes against more than 450 air-defence-class targets.
That figure is the company’s own and refers to RAM systems collectively, so it should not be read as confirmation that RAM-2X alone conducted all 450 engagements. UKRSPECSYSTEMS is progressively releasing footage that it says can now be publicly associated with the RAM family after previously circulating without attribution.
Chamberlain also gave the UK Defence Journal additional detail on how the desired effect against such targets has changed during the war. He said RAM-2X had moved from an approach in which attacks could seek a mission kill, disabling a system sufficiently to take it out of the fight, towards one where Ukrainian forces increasingly sought complete destruction. The reason, he explained, was that equipment left damaged on the battlefield could subsequently be used as a decoy, changing the Ukrainian concept of operations.
Chamberlain said: “So now we aim for total kill on all the systems.”
He said SHARK reconnaissance aircraft remain over the area to provide rapid battle damage assessment after an engagement, allowing the unit to establish the effect of the strike.
Dmytro Khasapov, General Director of UKRSPECSYSTEMS, said: “This is not the beginning of RAM-2X’s story. It is simply the first time we are able to tell that story publicly. RAM-2X was developed in Ukraine, through combat, against real targets and in one of the most demanding electronic-warfare environments in the world. When we say combat-proven, we mean evidence, not a marketing claim. That is why, alongside RAM-2X, we are opening the X-Archive so people can see declassified evidence of the system at work.”
Up to 180km range with a 3.5kg warhead
RAM-2X is intended for precision strikes against high-value targets at operational-tactical depth. UKRSPECSYSTEMS gives the aircraft a range of up to 180 kilometres, endurance exceeding two hours and a 3.5kg warhead. According to the company, the system incorporates automatic target lock and tracking, while available options include optical navigation for operations where satellite navigation is denied and AI-based object recognition.
That electronic-warfare resilience is particularly important in Ukraine, where satellite navigation, control links and communications are routinely subjected to jamming and other forms of interference.
Rather than presenting RAM-2X as an isolated aircraft, UKRSPECSYSTEMS is positioning it as part of a broader reconnaissance-strike architecture connecting sensors, communications, ground control, software and effectors.
SHARK-M links reconnaissance directly to strike
A central element of that architecture is the relationship between RAM-2X and the company’s SHARK-M reconnaissance UAS, a pairing UKRSPECSYSTEMS calls the “Killer Duo”. SHARK-M is used for persistent reconnaissance and targeting, while RAM-2X provides the strike component. The company says the reconnaissance aircraft can also act as a communications relay in heavily contested electronic-warfare conditions.
Asked how closely the two aircraft are integrated, Chamberlain told the UK Defence Journal that information is shared automatically between the systems. That matters particularly for attacks at depth because targets may move between initial detection and the arrival of the strike aircraft. Persistent surveillance, he said, allows the target to remain under observation throughout that process.
Chamberlain said: “They’re all automatically shared. So it’s that full integration, and you have to understand that in Ukraine, your targets are often moving, and when we are looking at the deep strike as well, and the time onto target, it’s important that you have ISR with persistence there.”
The company’s wider argument is that shortening the connection between finding a target and attacking it can be as important as the performance of the strike aircraft itself.
Battlefield imagery used to train target recognition
Chamberlain also explained how UKRSPECSYSTEMS is using years of reconnaissance imagery to develop the AI-based object recognition offered with RAM-2X. He said the company’s ISR systems have been observing Russian targets since the beginning of the full-scale invasion, building up imagery as equipment, camouflage and operating practices have changed.
That includes seeing targets in low light, partly hidden by vegetation or otherwise presented differently from a clean reference image. Chamberlain said this material is used to train recognition systems across RAM-2X, SHARK and the company’s wider portfolio.
The approach, he said, allows the recognition tools to be updated as Russian forces adapt their own methods, rather than relying on a static library of target imagery.
More than 1,500 drones produced each month
The scale of UKRSPECSYSTEMS’ wider operation has also increased considerably during the war. Chamberlain told the UK Defence Journal that the company now employs well over 4,000 people and is approaching 5,000, while producing more than 1,500 drones per month across its portfolio.
He declined to disclose the exact mix of aircraft making up that monthly output or how far production exceeded the 1,500 figure, citing operational security. The company says it is also working to much shorter development cycles than those normally associated with conventional defence programmes.
Chamberlain said hardware changes could be introduced approximately every three weeks, while software could be updated around every six weeks, with broader system updates occurring on roughly three-month cycles or faster. He said that pace was necessary because equipment that works effectively on the Ukrainian battlefield cannot be assumed to remain effective indefinitely as enemy tactics, electronic warfare and countermeasures evolve.
UK interest as exports begin to open
The public disclosure of RAM-2X also comes as UKRSPECSYSTEMS begins looking beyond Ukraine, with the gradual easing of Ukrainian defence export restrictions opening opportunities with NATO customers.
Chamberlain told the UK Defence Journal that the company is already seeing British interest and hopes ultimately to offer the capability to the British Army. He said: “So you know the Ukrainian export rules are starting to relax, and with the start of the drone deal, that means the export is open for those NATO customers, and obviously we have the UK showing interest, which is great, and we hope to bring this for the British Army.”
He added that there was also considerable interest elsewhere within NATO.
Commander calls RAM-2X a ‘game changer’
The commander of Ukraine’s 15th “Black Forest” Brigade, using the callsign Sarmat, whose formation has operational experience with the system, told us: “RAM-2X has been a game changer for the Ukrainian battlefield. For destroying HVT targets over 150km RAM-2X is the best.”
The unit price of RAM-2X has not been publicly disclosed, but the UK Defence Journal understands it is priced as a genuine consumable, allowing it to be employed in substantial numbers rather than treated like a scarce, high-end missile. We understand that a successful RAM-2X strike can in some circumstances destroy equipment valued at two to three orders of magnitude more than the cost of the UAV itself, and potentially four orders of magnitude at the upper end.
For context, the UK Defence Journal understands a P-18 Terek radar to be valued at around $3.6 million, an S-400 launcher at approximately $15 million and a Buk-M3 launcher at around $30 million. Those figures do not mean every RAM-2X sortie attacks equipment of that value, but illustrate the economics behind matching comparatively inexpensive precision-strike UAVs against high-value battlefield systems.
The comparison with conventional precision weapons is not exact, though. Different weapons have different ranges, payloads, survivability and target sets, but the underlying concept is to make precision strike affordable enough to be used repeatedly and replenished at wartime scale.
Chamberlain said this ability to change quickly was fundamental to the company’s approach, arguing that equipment has to remain relevant to battlefield conditions rather than simply meeting a fixed specification. He told the UK Defence Journal that UKRSPECSYSTEMS continually adapts its systems as operating conditions change, adding that the evidence of their performance was already visible in combat.
Why this all matters
Asked finally why he was personally so enthusiastic about RAM-2X and the wider UKRSPECSYSTEMS approach, Chamberlain pointed less to any single specification than to the speed at which the system changes with the battlefield. He said: “You know, this is not, dare I say, a snake oil kind of scenario. The images are there. The reality is there.”
Larger changes, he said, come every few months or faster as Ukrainian units encounter new threats, tactics and countermeasures. Chamberlain said: “You have to be relevant on a battlefield to win a war.”
That, perhaps more than the 180km range or the numbers produced, is the point UKRSPECSYSTEMS is trying to make with RAM-2X. The aircraft being shown at MSPO is not a frozen design emerging from a development programme, but a weapon the company describes as shaped by combat, changed by combat and still changing with it.
RAM-2X is being displayed alongside the wider UKRSPECSYSTEMS portfolio at MSPO in Poland from 8 to 11 September, marking the first time the company has been able to publicly connect its name to a strike system that it says has already spent years operating in the war in Ukraine.

Flights were cancelled at Soekarno-Hatta International Airport in the capital Jakarta after volcanic ash spread across western parts of the country.
More than 2,300 domestic and international flights were cancelled nationwide following the eruption, leaving around 340,000 passengers stranded at seven airports.
Authorities later determined that conditions were safe for aviation, and Soekarno-Hatta International Airport and Halim Perdanakusuma Airport, along with three other airports where flights had been suspended following the eruption, resumed operations.

German far right’s ‘remigration’ plans amount to ethnic cleansing, says Merz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:38:56 UTC
19:38:56 KST

BERLIN — German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Wednesday that plans put forward by the far-right Alternative for Germany for a tough migration crackdown would devastate the German economy.
“’Remigration’ is nothing more than a synonym for ethnic cleansing based on origin and skin color,” Merz said during a speech in the Bundestag, in his sharpest attack yet on the surging AfD after a dismal election defeat for his center-right Christian Democratic Union.
“One in six workers in the skilled trades holds a foreign passport. If those who work in Germany are forced to leave the country again because you’re championing ‘remigration’, then the skilled trades in Germany will no longer be able to function. Then not a single nursing home would remain open, and not a single hospital in Germany would continue to operate. Then not a single restaurant could stay in business in Germany. That would be the result of your immigration policy,” he added.
“Remigration” is a far-right concept that can range from deporting people without legal status to the mass removal of immigrants and their descendants. The AfD had dedicated an entire chapter to “immigration and remigration” in its election program for Saxony-Anhalt.
Its lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund — who is also the state’s potential next premier — attended a 2023 meeting at which party figures and far-right extremists discussed “remigration plans” that included the mass deportation of “non-assimilated” German citizens and sparked nationwide protests.
Merz’s comments constitute the harshest condemnation yet of the AfD’s policies and come as the chancellor himself is facing mounting questions over his ability to lead Germany’s weakened coalition government. His dismal approval ratings helped fuel the AfD’s victory in Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday — and contributed to his party losing more than half of its support.
Following the election, Merz and his CDU are searching for a new narrative in their fight against the far right. The AfD, now the most popular party in national polls, has vowed to destroy Merz’s conservatives and seize power nationwide after the next national election, scheduled for 2029.
“You have failed to understand the message that voters in Saxony-Anhalt sent you last Sunday,” said AfD national co-leader Alice Weidel, who spoke before Merz in the Bundestag. “That doesn’t really matter anyway, because your time is up. The people want a change in policy, and they will get it. In the next election, the people will give the AfD — that is, us, the Alternative for Germany — a clear mandate to govern.”
Advertisement
Merz also attacked the AfD over its Russia-friendly positions, accusing the party of ignoring the threat facing Germany.
“We learned this in a whole new dimension on August 4, if not before,” Merz said, referring to the explosive-laden-drone attack on the airport of Leipzig-Halle. “Not a word from you on this, Ms. Weidel … It’s a clear fact — one you’re well aware of — that this attack was planned for months in Russia, was specifically directed against Germany, and that it was only by sheer coincidence that more extensive property damage and personal injury were prevented. Yet you’re laughing it off, ladies and gentlemen. That shows how you think and where you stand.”
He then added that the AfD was helping the Kremlin in its efforts. “Not a word from you about the disinformation campaigns originating in Russia — with your support — that have been attempting for weeks, months, and years to destabilize our country, our society, and our democracy,” he said.
“You are part of this problem we face in Germany, and we will use every means at our disposal to prevent you from continuing down this path,” Merz added.

Teens charged in hate‑fueled arson attacks on ethnic-owned Tallinn food businesses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:36:00 UTC
19:36:00 KST

Teens charged in hate‑fueled arson attacks on ethnic-owned Tallinn food businesses
A 16-year-old boy has been charged with multiple arson and assaults motivated by extremist views, with a 19-year-old also charged over a hammer attack.
The 16-year-old is charged with systematically setting fire, with the use of accelerants, to cars and restaurants, reportedly owned by people of color, and causing over €82,000 in damages, the prosecutor's office said.
The prosecutor says evidence points toward the youth holding extremist views, including on Islam and on immigration, and the people and businesses targeted were maingly from the Bangladeshi, Pakistani and Nigerian communities.
According to the indictment, the teenager repeatedly set fire to cars belonging to ethnic minority people, and also set fire to a kebab kiosk on Akadeemia tee in Mustamäe and a restaurant serving Indian food on nearby Rahumäe tee. He allegedly used lighter fluid or bottles filled with gasoline to do so. At the time of the restaurant fire, a person was inside the building when he set fire to it, meaning a threat to life and well-being.
The acts were not limited to attacks on property. In June, the 16‑year‑old and a 19‑year‑old followed a victim and attacked him using a hammer. The prosecutor's office charged both men with attempted assault causing life‑threatening bodily harm.
"The acts which the young man is accused of were well thought out, planned and committed within a relatively short period of time," said Prosecutor Rita Siniväli. "The evidence collected indicates that his actions were influenced by extremist views, including anti‑Islamic, anti‑Muslim and anti‑immigration narratives."
She added that the young man's views were "expressed in actions directed against specific people and groups. The victims are mainly citizens of Bangladesh, Pakistan and Nigeria who have lived and worked in Estonia for a lengthy time."
Siniväli called it important to see the implications of how the actions can evolve. "A person can hold very extreme or unacceptable views for others. However, a line is drawn where hostile attitudes begin to manifest in crimes directed against other people or their property. In this criminal case, the young man's hostile attitudes did not remain in just thoughts or words, but based on the evidence collected, they manifested themselves in arson and violence and became increasingly dangerous over time."
Vadim Kuperštein, head of the Crimes Against Persons Department of the Northern Prefecture Criminal Bureau, said the cases seemed distinct at first glance but were unifited by the similar circle of victims. "The young people made a conscious effort to avoid being identified and learned to cover their tracks," he said. "Despite this, the police saw commonalities between the cases, identified the young men, and arrested them in June."
According to Kuperštein, neither young man has expressed any remorse. "This is a clear sign that the young men did not act out of momentary emotions, but had specific motives and goals that they were trying to achieve."
He urged parents to be vigilant about the content young people consume. "It is important to react early. The longer a young person is exposed to such information, the more extreme views and beliefs can become entrenched, and it will be much more difficult to change the situation later."
Both young men are currently in custody.

Ebola virus spreads to new DRC health zone, WHO says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:35:25 UTC
19:35:25 KST

The number of health zones affected by Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has risen to 61 across six provinces after the virus spread to the Kayna Health Zone in North Kivu province, the World Health Organization’s Africa office said in a situation report late on Tuesday.
At least 6,686 cases, including 3,226 deaths, have been recorded since the outbreak began in mid-May, according to the report.
WHO said the epidemiological pattern of the Bundibugyo virus strain outbreak was becoming increasingly heterogeneous, with transmission trends diverging across affected provinces and health zones.
“The trends reinforce an increasingly heterogeneous epidemic, with declining transmission in some areas occurring alongside intensification and continued geographic spread elsewhere,” the report said.
The affected provinces are Haut-Uele, Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Bas-Uele and Tshopo.
Ituri remains the main focus of the outbreak, while substantial transmission continues in North Kivu and Haut-Uele and new areas continue to be affected.
WHO also highlighted the rising proportion of deaths occurring within communities.
Between August 31 and September 6, the proportion of confirmed deaths occurring in communities reached 75 percent, up from 56.6 percent two weeks earlier.
The report said persistently high community mortality could reflect several barriers, including delays in detection, notification and transfers to treatment facilities, limited recognition of the illness, transport and geographical challenges, and a lack of community trust.
“This divergence is concerning, as the increase in community deaths alongside the continued decline in treatment facilities deaths indicates that the earlier reduction in overall mortality has not been sustained,” it said.
The government of DRC and health partners last week launched a revised 180-day multisectoral response plan worth $1.3 billion aimed at breaking chains of transmission.
The plan calls for a major expansion of epidemiological surveillance, contact tracing, community engagement, risk communication and logistical capacity, as well as preparedness measures in at-risk provinces.

Srebrenica, Ratko Mladic and what his war crimes tell us about the Gaza genocide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:34:21 UTC
19:34:21 KST

The death of Ratko Mladic, the infamous Bosnian Serb general and convicted war criminal, marks the end of one of the darkest chapters in history.
Yet, his death does not close the window of pain and suffering for thousands of Bosniaks – many of them survivors, some others family members of those killed by the Butcher of Bosnia.
And most of all, Mladic’s death brings into sharp focus the sufferings of Palestinians and the war crimes committed by the state of Israel over the past three years. And the inaction of a world which refuses to see the genocide unfolding right before its eyes.
To understand Mladic - he died in The Hague at the age of 84 while serving a life sentence for his war crimes – we must look back to July 1995, when he led a group of Bosnian Serb soldiers into the town of Srebrenica with the intent to clear it of the non-Serb population.
According to findings by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY), upon entering the town, he declared, “we give this town to Serb people as a gift,” by which he meant to forcibly remove the Bosniaks and Croats from the country.
Later, in the presence of international media, he emphasised the need to eliminate Bosnia’s non-Serb populace, either temporarily or permanently.
Mladic was not just a monstrous general but the chief architect of ethnic cleansing in Bosnia, convicted of many crimes, including genocide, crimes against humanity, and war crimes.
As commander of Bosnian Serb forces, he ordered the siege of UN-declared safe Bosniak areas (Bihac, Gorazde, Srebrenica, Zepa, and Sarajevo), held UN soldiers hostage and blocked the Vance-Owen Peace Plan.
He also masterminded the systematic torture and execution of Bosniaks and Croats in concentration camps such as Omarska, Manjaca, Keretem, and Trnopolje.
Mladic’s role in orchestrating the Srebrenica genocide, in which at least 8,372 Bosniak men and boys were separated from their families, transported, and killed by the Bosnian Serb army, is well documented and was affirmed by both the ICTY and the United Nations.
Despite extensive court proceedings, ICTY findings, and testimonies of survivor witnesses detailing and proving his primary role in the genocide, Mladic remained at large for nearly 16 years, moving to different locations within Serbia.
Eventually, he was detained in northern Serbia, indicted by the international tribunal, and transferred to The Hague. The court found him guilty of at least 11 charges, including two counts for genocide.
But he pleaded guilty to none and brazenly denied the genocide in Srebrenica.
Wounds that never healed
Mladic’s case has been one of the most significant cases before the ICTY.
It raises serious questions about the functioning and capacity of the legal systems, particularly the ICTY and the International Criminal Court (ICC).
What exposes the global judicial system is the fact that the fate of thousands of people who disappeared during war is still unknown.
Hence, the gap between the legal system and survivors’ lived experiences persists, although his capture and trial have marked a major success for the tribunal.
Some survivors of the Bosnian War and relatives of victims of Srebrenica have expressed that they found solace in Mladić’s death, while it hardly mattered to others, as it reawakens their traumatic memories of the war.
Women who endured the worst atrocities, particularly sexual abuse, are still dealing with long-term psychological effects, negatively influencing their lives today.
According to studies, many survivors are still suffering from panic attacks, nightmares, and persistent anxiety because of reliving their traumatic experiences.
A study shows that at least 57 percent of women in Bosnia who have suffered sexual violence during the war continue to meet clinical criteria for post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and are struggling to reconcile with the past events even after decades.
Sexual violence is often employed as a weapon of war, used by perpetrators to take revenge and to punish, terrorise, and humiliate their victims.
In the Bosnian context, such violence was not confined to women and young girls, but young boys and elderly men were also among the worst sufferers, subject to the worst forms of sexual violence.
Many survivors contend that Mladic’s death cannot compensate for the scale of loss and suffering he has orchestrated and therefore offers them no relief.
Lessons for the world
While justice does not necessitate death for each wrongful death, it does demand an end to hatred and an apology, something that is not observed in the case of any convicted war criminal, many of whom instead exhibit deep resentment toward victims.
More than 30 years after the end of the Bosnian war, survivors are still waiting for justice and accountability.
Their experiences and trauma are influenced by both the past events and present situations, especially the denial of genocide.
The rhetoric of genocide denial is so prevalent in the Balkans that it is frequently combined with toxic narratives, such as negationism, revisionism, and triumphalism.
Such narratives get reinforced when convicted war criminals such as Ratko Mladic, whose aim was to create ethnically pure Serbia by eradicating Muslims and Croats, are awarded and glorified.
The horrific atrocities unfolding before our eyes in Gaza bear many similarities to those that occurred in Srebrenica over thirty years ago.
From bombing civilian infrastructure and using rape as a tool of war to blocking humanitarian aid convoys, every single incident is recurring.
Yet, the international community, including the European Union and the United States, stand by in silence and inaction.
In stark reality, what enables the loss of human lives is both the inaction and the injustice of those who can prevent such brutalities.
Thus, the lessons learned from the earlier experiences must not be forgotten or remain confined to history books, commemoration events, or memorial sites; they must instead serve a purpose to stop genocides from happening anywhere on Earth.
The world must act now to uphold international law and human rights and hold perpetrators accountable for their crimes. It will help break the cycle of impunity and vengeance.

====================================================================================================

Durban Conference 25 years on. Mandi Mudarikwa: “It’s up to us all to build the kind of world we want to live in”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:34:00 UTC
19:34:00 KST

The third UN Conference Against Racism, Racial Discrimination, Xenophobia and Related Intolerance in 2001 was a watershed moment for millions across the world. Seven thousand people representing governments and civil society from 170 countries gathered in Durban, South Africa. Led by countries in the Global South, the Durban Conference challenged the idea that human rights is a Western concept, recognized the historical roots of contemporary forms of racism and called on States to repair the lasting consequences of colonialism and slavery. While the US and Israel withdrew from the Conference, the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action were adopted, both of which became foundational documents for the global fight against racism. But with racism still very much alive, we spoke with activists about their struggles and hopes.
My name is Mandi Mudarikwa and I’m a human rights strategic litigator at Amnesty International. My legal career has been about using law and the courts as instruments of justice, accountability, and the advancement and enjoyment of human rights.
Human rights are a promise and a commitment. The promise of equality, freedom of speech, privacy and access to, among others, health and education as well as the commitment to make these rights a reality. Too often, however, these are promises that remain as words on paper. In this context, my work seeks to use strategic and precedent-setting litigation to challenge systemic injustice, shape progressive jurisprudence, and advance human rights standards across diverse legal systems.
Moments of hope
When I think about how far we have come, and all the work that has been done to not only reject but confront racial discrimination, the legacies of colonialism, slavery, and apartheid, I also think of systems that once, in some places, still define people as superior or inferior based on the colour of their skin, their race, ethnicity, descent or national origin, denying their humanity and their rights. But alongside that history, I also think of the moments of hope, solidarity and unity that show us what is possible when we come together in unity to challenge injustice and human rights violations.
 
Despite those efforts contributing, unfortunately those in power have not done enough to dismantle the structures and systems that enable racism, discrimination and xenophobia. Committing to a world that is substantively equal and fair for everyone does not, by itself, undo historic injustices and transform our societies. The adoption of the promise of equality was not enough to undo the systemic underfunding and under-resourcing that resulted from decades of state-sanctioned discrimination. 
We can see this, for example, in schools in many countries that predominantly serve racialized communities. Many continue to be underfunded and under-resourced reflecting inequalities that were not erased simply because discriminatory policies were formally abandoned or condemned. The promise of substantive equality and fairness, therefore, has not yet translated into true substantive equality or the enjoyment of human rights for all.
Dehumanization
Even further, we are witnessing the promise of substantive equality being intentionally challenged and undermined, including through people feeling increasingly emboldened to speak openly about others as inferior simply based on their race, their nationality or their background. Dehumanizing language and ideas have gained momentum and with them, the willingness to openly question whether everyone is truly entitled to the same human rights.
We have witnessed people adopting a zero-sum approach to human rights as though one person’s rights or one group’s progress must come at the expense of another’s. Progress towards racial equality is framed not as expanding rights for everyone, but as chipping away the rights of others. It’s a dangerous way of thinking that intentionally pits people against one another. Instead of recognizing equality as a principle that strengthens the human rights and dignity of everyone, it turns human rights into a competition.
And that is when you begin to see how difficult it is going to be to really leave racism, discrimination and xenophobia in the past. We are not only struggling to dismantle the systems and inequalities that these ideologies created, we are also confronting efforts to revive and legitimize the very ideas that underpin them.
The Durban Declaration
The Durban Declaration came about in response to a conversation about the need for more protections and more concrete and transformative action.  
 
In that moment in 2001, there was almost a global recognition of the need to do away with racism, discrimination and xenophobia because of their impact on access and enjoyment of human rights.  
For me, one of the most important things about both the Declaration and the Programme of Action is that they go beyond condemnation. They provide a plan for action, a commitment to confront the structures, systems and inequalities that allow racism and discrimination to persist.
What we need now is for states to use this plan of action to take clear, concrete actions and turn the promises into reality, to remember why they were made, to defend the progress we have achieved, and to build a world that is fundamentally different from the one we had before.
Strategic litigation
Strategic litigation can be a powerful tool to drive change, and the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action provides an important framework for strategic litigation because it gives us a clear set of principles for challenging racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia and related forms of intolerance. It helps translate international commitments into arguments for accountability, equality and access to rights at the national level.
We saw this in a case whereby Amnesty International intervened in Canada earlier this year where an asylum seeker woman was excluded from access to free childcare, and without childcare, she was unable to work. We supported the case when it went before the Supreme Court of Canada, which ruled that excluding asylum seekers was discriminatory and unconstitutional. It’s a powerful example of how the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action can inform concrete legal change.
But a ruling is only the beginning because strategic litigation does not end when a Court issues its decision. Its real impact depends on implementation. Progress takes time, and one decision on its own may not transform a system. But when combined with others and with advocacy, organizing and other strategies for change, each victory can build on the last and contribute to lasting systemic change. Accordingly, if fully implemented, this decision has the potential to dismantle the compounded effects of the intersection of racism, discrimination, and xenophobia.
My message to young people?
Never forget that we are not equal until we are all equal. Importantly, equality does not happen by chance, nor through passive hope, it requires deliberate action. It calls on each of us to challenge, confront, and dismantle systems upon which inequality and discrimination thrive. So, onwards and forwards: together, with purpose and courage, turning our commitment to substantive equality into meaningful action and creating the world we want to live in; a world where everyone is valued, respected, and substantively equal.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Wednesday denounced the far-right AfD’s call for mass “remigration,” calling it “ethnic cleansing by skin color and origin.”
His comments came in a heated parliamentary exchange with Alternative for Germany (AfD) co-leader Alice Weidel, three days after the party scored a crushing election victory over Merz's center-right CDU in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.
The chancellor took aim at AfD's demand for mass deportations of rejected asylum-seekers and people arriving via irregular channels.
"The word 'remigration' is nothing other than a synonym for ethnic cleansing," Merz said about the AfD's flagship policy.
"Remigration is nothing other than ethnic cleansing by skin color and origin," he added to howls of protest from AfD deputies in the Bundestag.
The AfD took almost 44% of the vote in Sunday's election, against 17% for the CDU.
The AfD, which fell three seats short of an absolute majority, said it was now in talks with other groups and MPs in an effort to form a state government.
The rise of the AfD has unnerved many who feel Germany has a special responsibility to atone for its Nazi past.
Weidel took to the lectern first, declaring that the days of Merz's coalition "are over."
People wanted "a change of course in politics at last, and they don't want 'business as usual,'" she said.
She also denounced the government's immigration policy, saying it had made Germany unsafe.
"German citizens have to live with the daily consequences of mass migration," she said.
"With knife violence every day, attacks on trains and in stations, with run-down and threatening cityscapes."
Hitting back, Merz said the AfD's immigration policy would massively impact the labor market.
"Not a single care home could work operate, not a single hospital, not a single restaurant," he said.
Merz also accused the Moscow-friendly AfD of contributing to what he said were Russian efforts to "destabilize" Germany, following a foiled drone attack at Leipzig airport last month Berlin blamed on Russia.
"There has been nothing from you, Mrs. Weidel, on what happened on Aug. 4 at Leipzig airport," he said. "You are part of the problem we have here in Germany."
Noisy AfD lawmakers who often heckled Merz drew the ire of Parliamentary Speaker Julia Kloeckner.
"We aren't on a football pitch here; save that for the weekend," she said.
"If this kind of behavior happens again, I will have you thrown out."

Finland completes work on 200km fence along border with Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:33:47 UTC
19:33:47 KST

Helsinki says the fence will help protect NATO's longest border as concerns grow over Russian hybrid activity and the potential use of migration to exert pressure on the country.
Finland completed a 200-kilometre security fence along its border with Russia, strengthening NATO’s longest frontier with a country's accused of intensified hybrid attacks on Europe.
The project was launched after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine transformed Finland’s security environment and prompted the country to abandon decades of military non-alignment and join NATO in April 2023.
Later that year, more than 1,300 migrants without visas arrived at Finland’s eastern border. Helsinki accused Moscow of “hybrid warfare” by orchestrating the movement of third-country nationals towards the frontier, a charge the Kremlin denied.
Finland shut its land border with Russia in late 2023. Apart from a brief reopening of two crossings that December, the frontier has remained closed ever since.
“Today, it is calm but tense, and we really don't know about tomorrow,” Interior Minister Mari Rantanen told reporters on Monday at a media event near the Nuijamaa border crossing in south-eastern Finland.
“It can change really rapidly and that is why we need to be very prepared.”
The 4.5-metre-high fence has been built in sections and is equipped with cameras and sensors.
It covers 200 kilometres of Finland’s 1,340-kilometre frontier with Russia, with most of the barrier concentrated in the southeast.
“This is one part of our border security and it is helping us for surveillance, but also keeping people out of Finnish territory if needed,” Rantanen said.
The new fence cost €356 million, with an estimated €2-3 million in annual maintenance costs, according to Finnish border authorities.
Despite rapid advances in drone technology, a physical barrier was still “viewed as the best solution for crowd control,” Border Guard project manager Erkki Matilainen said.
Rantanen said the fence could be extended further and called for greater EU financial support for countries along the bloc’s eastern frontier.
“What we particularly need is EU funding for eastern member states so that projects like this can be financed,” she said.
Last week, Helsinki proposed extending its Border Security Act until the end of 2028.
The legislation allows Finland, under exceptional circumstances, to restrict the reception of asylum applications in limited areas of the border when its sovereignty or national security is deemed to be under threat.
The law has proved controversial, with legal experts warning that it risks breaching Finland’s international human rights obligations and EU law.
Similar barriers have been built elsewhere along NATO and the EU’s eastern flank, as countries bordering Russia and Belarus strengthen their frontiers.

Center Party head: Snap elections a realistic possibility
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:33:00 UTC
19:33:00 KST

Center Party head: Snap elections a realistic possibility
The replacement of ministers just six months before general elections, along with crises in several sectors, is a clear sign that Estonia needs a snap election, Center leader Mihhail Kõlvart told ERR.
Kõlvart said the current government reshuffle, which will see Defense Minister Hanno Pevkur and Energy and Environment Minister Andres Sutt, both of the Reform Party, leave their posts, shows there is nothing left to save in the current governing coalition, not even through a reshuffle.
"It seems to me that the situation within the Reform Party itself is probably not particularly stable at the moment either," Kõlvart said. "If ministers decide not to continue in politics, then they don't see a future. Nor do they see a future for their own party."
Given the coalition's low approval ratings and the scandal in the defense sector, Kõlvart said the reasonable course of action would be to hold a snap election.
"If we look at the situation pragmatically — insofar as politicians are capable of looking at a situation pragmatically at all — we can see crises in key sectors," he said, pointing to defense, education and healthcare, as well as the need for a new political leader for the energy sector.
"Every sector needs a new approach and a fresh start," Kõlvart said.
He added that Defense Minister Hanno Pevkur's departure alone is not enough.
"In my view, the responsibility today is primarily political and extends beyond a single minister. The systemic disorder is not solely a problem of the Ministry of Defense," Kõlvart said.
With public trust in both the government and the Riigikogu at a record low, Kõlvart argued that a snap election is the only way out of the current political crisis.
"The sooner the better, even if it is just three or four months earlier rather than seven months from now," he said. "Then these issues can be addressed systematically, rather than having new ministers come in and spend their time campaigning for the election."
Although the Social Democrats have said they do not support a snap election, Kõlvart said holding one remains a realistic possibility because Estonia currently has a minority government and the opposition has more votes in the Riigikogu than the governing coalition.
"It comes down to political choices," he said. "We have also seen that politicians, including the Social Democrats, can change their minds and quite quickly."
Kõlvart said the Center Party's aim is to demonstrate that there is a genuine need for an early election. He also rejected the argument that there would be insufficient time for proper political debate.
"It seems to me that the argument that a snap election should not be held because we wouldn't have time to organize a debate is not entirely sincere," he said.
Kõlvart argued that voters can already distinguish between parties that genuinely want political change and those that would prefer to wait until the scheduled election in the hope of improving their polling numbers.
"Today, society can judge who genuinely wants change and who says quite openly that because our poll numbers aren't high enough and our competitors' numbers are high, we should wait another six months for the situation to change so that we can win more seats in the Riigikogu," he said.
Turning to the upcoming Riigikogu election, Kõlvart said no one can predict what will happen when voters go to the polls in March. Like every other party, he said, the Center Party's goal is to enter government, while its current level of support also gives it reason to hope it could win the election.
As for potential coalition partners, Kõlvart said governing with the Reform Party could largely be ruled out.
"The Reform Party has had plenty of time to put its vision into practice and show what it can achieve in the economy and in defense," Kõlvart said. "In our view, the Reform Party has failed to deliver. Therefore, our goal would be a coalition in which the Reform Party would not participate for the next four years."

Swiss and French train stations named among best in Europe – with Germany free-falling down rankings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:30:42 UTC
19:30:42 KST

The latest European Railway Station Index ranks the top 60 busiest railway stations in Europe – and there are clear winners and losers.
The latest edition of the European Railway Station Index is out now – and the best major hub on the continent is Switzerland’s Zürich Hbf.
Issued by the Consumer Choice Center, the new ranking evaluated 60 of Europe’s busiest railway stations looking at the percentage of services which are delayed and the average wait time.
It also took into account factors such as the number of in-station services, accessibility options, whether or not the station has free wifi, national and local railway coverage and ticket types.
Switzerland “continues to set the standard for reliability”, with a national punctuality rate of 94.1%. Zürich Hbf came in first place overall, with just 4% of its train services delayed, while Bern Hbf was joint fifth with a delay percentage of 1.8%. Although ranked 14th overall, the most punctual trains departed from Luzern Hbf, which had just 0.3% of its services delayed.
On the flip side, Germany’s performance “continued to deteriorate” compared to previous editions.
Of the bottom 30 stations, 15 are in Germany, and the highest ranked station from the country is Berlin Hbf in 18th, where 61.1% of services are delayed and the average wait time is 20 minutes.
Europe-wide, the average delay rate is 29% – in Germany, it is 49.4%. Similarly, the average wait time on the continent is 8.06 minutes, versus 14.74 minutes in Germany.
Polish stations on the rise
For 2026, 10 new stations joined the ranking thanks to increased passenger numbers.
Two of the top five best performers among these newbies come from Poland: Kraków Główny in first place (ninth overall), and Poznań Główny in third (13th overall).
Consumer Choice Center note that Kraków’s main station boasts direct routes to Warsaw, Zakopane, Łódź, Gdańsk and Katowice domestically, as well as top destinations like Berlin,
Munich, Vienna and Prague elsewhere on the continent.
Kraków Główny is also fully integrated with the Galeria Krakowska shopping centre, giving travellers access to plenty of shops and restaurants. Praise was also lavished on the station for having integrated bus and tram services, written and verbal station announcements, and a first-class lounge.
Looking ahead, Consumer Choice Center points to the ongoing modernisation of the network with a plan for an additional 4,700km of new track “ultimately promises to transform Polish rail into one of the most modern rail networks in Europe”.
Time for a rail escape to Poland, anyone?

1. Zürich Hbf, Switzerland
2. Gare du Nord, Paris, France
3. Amsterdam Centraal, Netherlands
4. Wroclaw Główny, Poland
5= Bern Hbf, Switzerland
5= Gare Montparnasse, Paris, France
7. Gare Saint-Lazare, Paris, France
8. London Bridge, UK
9= Kraków Główny, Poland
9= London St. Pancras Intl., UK

Alibaba sends AI ‘digital employees’ to work in rival apps from ByteDance, Tencent
QoderWake tool now lets users create assistants that can function within office communication platforms from rivals, as well as Alibaba’s
The latest version of the QoderWake tool, launched by Alibaba Cloud on Tuesday, allowed users to generate fully functioning workers using a single-line description of the required role, the company said. These digital workers could then be put to work within any of China’s three major workplace communication platforms: Alibaba’s DingTalk, ByteDance’s Feishu and Tencent’s WeCom.
QoderWake’s digital workers could “operate seamlessly” within the three workplace platforms, autonomously absorbing context from shared documents, calendars and group chats, Alibaba said on Tuesday.
The move reflects how domestic tech giants are aggressively pivoting their costly AI models towards lucrative business-facing applications capable of executing complex enterprise workflows. Meanwhile, they are open to incorporating rival products at the application layer, shifting away from their traditional “walled-garden” approach.
Beyond customised roles, QoderWake also had 10 ready-to-use roles, including product manager, data analyst, user interface designer and front- and back-end developer, the company said. These roles had been fine-tuned using data from top-tier industry teams, allowing them to undertake real-world tasks without requiring additional training, it added.
Since its initial release in April, QoderWake had deployed nearly 100,000 digital employees, executing around 2 million tasks across real-world enterprise scenarios over the past three months, the company said.
