MS NOW Wants to Turn Its Viewers Into a Fandom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

Even if you’re a casual consumer of MS NOW, formerly MSNBC, you know the names: anchors like Chris Hayes, Stephanie Ruhle, and yes, the one and only Rachel Maddow. The network has built a stable of talent who’ve amassed a massive number of casual viewers, plenty of fans … and more than a few obsessives.
Now, the network’s president, Rebecca Kutler, is looking to build that entire audience into something more akin to a fandom—turning casual viewers and fanatics alike, whether on TV or online, into paying members of an MS NOW media universe.
To do it, she’s launching an ambitious subscription program, called the MS NOW Membership, designed to connect MS NOW consumers much more directly to the Hayeses and Maddows of the world. Sure, plenty of news providers now offer subscriptions, WIRED included (and by the way, you can subscribe here). But what struck me about Kutler and Co.’s efforts was both their methodical approach—they surveyed 18,000 people before landing on a final offering—and their resolute focus on MS NOW’s deep bench of talent as the locus of their paid program. In a world where influencers are the new newscasters, and linear TV is in an inevitable decline, MS NOW is diving directly into the breach: applying the influencer playbook to build a sustainable business that’s future-proofed … at least until the next great audience pivot.
I caught up with Kutler at WIRED’s New York studios, just days before MS NOW’s subscription launch. We talked about turning TV talent into fandom magnets, beating Fox, and whether media consolidation is actually good news for the network.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
KATIE DRUMMOND: Rebecca, thank you so much for being here today. Start by telling me when you joined MSNBC. What’s the timeline?
REBECCA KUTLER: I think it was right before the midterms in 2022. I had grown up at CNN. I spent more than 20 years there. I left earlier in 2022, and some folks that I knew and really respected reached out from then MSNBC, and they talked about one of those jobs that has a lot of running room and is a little ambiguous, but in the best way. I thought, “Yeah, let's check it out.” I started at MSNBC, now MS NOW, running their digital businesses, basically all their nonlinear businesses.
It gave me a real opportunity to learn the place, but also think about what are the missed opportunities that we could take advantage of in the next few years.
At some point in your tenure, you took on the whole thing.
Yes.
What were those big challenges that you identified when you looked at the whole portfolio and thought to yourself, “What are we going to do here?”
One of the things that immediately struck me when I came over was the fandom.
I had worked in other newsrooms. I have friends who work in other newsrooms. I love the news and love what we do, but I had never worked at a place where the audience really sees themselves as fans, with a deep connection to talent.
When I joined MS, it was also at the same time Jen Psaki joined, and we had known each other a little from a previous life. So we went out into the field together and did a few pretty straightforward field reporting pieces. And I've walked through airports over my career with a lot of different anchors and newspeople, but I’ve never had the experience of walking through with Jen and seeing the [attention she got]. That's why she was a great fit for MS. She’s someone people were behind and were rooting for, and had a deep connection with.
When you think about Rachel Maddow and how she lands. You’re very close to this industry. If you talk to anyone in publishing and ask them where they would ideally like to debut their book, I think most of them would say The Rachel Maddow Show. There’s a reason for that: The audience loyalty and engagement with Rachel has been proven over decades.
It’s funny, when she shares a WIRED story on social media, the traffic to that story and the engagement on her social media around WIRED is crazy. I can tell you firsthand looking at the analytics, you can feel it.
I want to ask you more about talent in a minute, but that brings me to this Membership program you're launching. I'm going to read from the press release, which I very rarely do. You will offer “new opportunities for members to interact directly with the brand’s trusted journalists, exclusive community features to engage with each other, a new roster of contributors and experts, original creator content, new verticals that explore how news and politics impacts everyday life, and 24/7 access to livestreams and television programming.”
In layman’s terms, if someone’s a MS NOW viewer, they watch it on TV sometimes, they see it on social media, what should they expect from this? What are they getting that they’re not already getting by having cable TV?
I want to answer your question directly, but I just don’t want to assume your audience is the MS NOW audience. So if you'll allow me 30 seconds …
Give us your best pitch.
We launched as a new brand about a year ago. People traditionally see us as this cable channel, and that's great. We have a huge cable audience. We're actually right now the number two most-watched basic cable channel.
Who's number one?
Fox.
I see. OK. We might talk more about that later.
But that’s just one piece of our business. We have, right now, a digital business before we even launch what we're launching this week, that has more uniques than places like Axios, Politico, The Atlantic. People spend more time with us digitally than places like the Washington Post and NPR.
And on YouTube, we have been quite efficient at building out our presence in that space. We get more clicks on YouTube than ABC News, NBC News, and CBS News combined.
I say all of that to say we are starting from a position of strength. What we are excited about, and why we're launching this product, is all those digital things I just mentioned, we don't have a way to catch all those people if they’re not going to be watching cable.
Got it.
It’s taking our current superfans who watch us on linear and giving them more. So what are they going to get? They're going to get direct access to our talent. Seven days a week at noon and at 6:00 pm, if you are a member of the MS NOW community, you can hop on and directly interact with one of our anchors or one of our reporters.
On Monday it’s going to be Rachel Maddow, and then you go through the week. You're going to hear from Michael Steele, you’re going to hear from Jen Psaki, you're going to hear from Reverend Al Sharpton. You’re going to hear from the people that you know and love from watching them on MS NOW and have the opportunity to ask them your question directly, and not just interact with our talent, but also interact with each other.
When we started this process around a year and a half ago, we didn’t just sit in a conference room and think, “Hmm, let’s make another commodity news app.” Because let's be honest, a lot of that already exists. What we did was actually start from a place of product research. We went out to 18,000 people. We did surveys, we did in-person interviews, and we spent time taking that research and getting to where we are this week.
What I most want people to know is, what you see this week will look vastly different six months from now and a year from now if we're doing our jobs right. What we need to do is build and learn and test and add investment and expand where we need to, but not really think that we’re going to get it all right on day one, but give ourselves that latitude.
Is the goal to pull linear viewers onto digital, or is it to better engage the digital audience, or both?
It's both. All those people consuming us on YouTube, on digital, on social, in audio, 90 percent of those people do not regularly consume us on linear television. So a big function of this product is to say, “Hey, you’re watching YouTube videos all the time of Lawrence O'Donnell. Maybe you’re not someone who's going to be a cable subscriber. But can you come join our community in another capacity? Can we create a product that entices you to be part of an MS NOW community, even if you're someone who's reluctant to become a cable customer?”
I would say that, for the average person, if you ask them, “Fox News, MS NOW, who do those networks reach?” I would say Fox News reaches Republicans, and that’s who has it on TV, that's who’s going to that website. I would say MS NOW reaches progressives, Democrats, left-leaning people. Is that a stated goal for you, or do you want that tent to be bigger?
Is the audience for MS NOW different from the audience for Fox? Of course it is. There's probably a small amount of overlap, but not a lot, and that's OK.
For example, when I think forward to election night, I gotta say, I think there’s nowhere I'd rather hang out on election night than at our table with Rachel and Nicolle [Wallace] and Lawrence and Chris [Hayes] and Michael [Steele] and everyone.
What we try to do is be smart, respect our audience, and be a fun place, and a place where, again, Michael Steele is a big part of our election night. He was chairman of the Republican National Committee.
Right.
We have a broad range of views, but I think they all fall under that pro-democracy banner.
Are you competitive? Do you want to beat Fox? Do you want to see that number one?
Look, I am a pretty competitive person. I just see who our competition is as wider than that typical cable landscape.
I want to build a great product right now and have a large membership community, and I want to make sure that we are competing on every battleground.
That is yes, absolutely on cable, yes on digital, yes on YouTube, yes in audio. I think that because of the life that this brand lived under previous ownership, there were times when our wings were clipped a little from a business perspective, and that wasn't—if I was sitting in the seats of the leadership team at NBC, I might have made the same decisions.
When you’re working for the very large, very successful companies that NBCUniversal and Comcast are, they need to look at the whole company and figure out where best to invest their dollars. So what they did makes sense for them. But now we're lucky to be a part of Versant, and Versant has several pieces of their portfolio that generate a lot of cash.
What is Versant, for those who may not know?
Versant is the spinoff, so a spinout, of NBCUniversal. For folks that weren't following along day by day, around a year ago, NBCUniversal spun out a series of businesses. Those include what is now MS NOW, CNBC, brands like E!—you know, Live from the Red Carpet—and then golf.
We are now part of a company that is incentivized to invest the money that we earn as MS NOW back into MS NOW. We're just no longer part of a company that has to invest in theme parks and other things that, for that company, made a lot of sense.
I don’t think it’s a secret that cable news audiences are declining, and I’m going to ask this in the bluntest possible way: That’s an older audience, so what do you do when they die?
I am not blind to the long-term challenges. That’s why we are investing in digital. But do I think the cable business right now for MS NOW is quite healthy? I do.
Our average viewer watches nine hours a week.
That is a lot of MS NOW.
Do I wake up in a panic in the middle of the night? No. Do I know there are long-term challenges? Yes.
What do you wake up at night worrying about? Working in media and journalism is hard. It's a hard business, and these are really difficult transformations to try to undertake, and to undertake successfully. What's the hardest part of this for you right now?
What I wake up angsty about sometimes is I know we have this guest or that guest coming up, but how can we upgrade? How can we make it better? What is the better question? What is the better way in?
I might be old-school when I say this, but I think content always wins. Every single race.
I want to ask more about talent. You do have some real fandom magnets. I think one of the biggest challenges in publishing today, especially on digital, is that it is so noisy. There is so much competition. It’s not just news, but it’s everything on someone's Instagram feed. How do you encourage your journalists, your talent, to break through that in a digital context?
I'll just pick on Chris Hayes for a minute here. Because there’s almost no time that I talk to Chris Hayes that I don’t then hang up the phone or walk out of his office and think to myself, “That guy’s brain is huge.”
I think that’s the answer to the question of how do you break through? Every brand and every place in the media has to figure out what their breakthrough is. Look, there's people who want to break through by showing cat videos all day. People want to break through by writing outrageous headlines that aren’t really based in facts.
Yes.
Where I want MS NOW to break through is being brainiacs, is coming to the table with something that is intellectually interesting, that is showing me something or teaching me something or adding value to a news story in a way I hadn’t thought about it before, of drawing on their experience, decades of experience working in the room, being in the room where it happened.
What has the experience been like of transitioning some of the more TV-comfortable talent that you have, who are accustomed to doing a cable news show, and saying to them, “Now you do these interactive sessions with our audience, now you do TikTok, now you participate in these other parts of the ecosystem”?
One of my rules is: don’t do anything that feels weird for you. What I mean by that is, if you in your own life don’t use TikTok, I don’t recommend trying to become a TikToker. It’s going to land weird. We’ve seen it. So what I have encouraged our shows, our hosts, everyone in the MS NOW family, to do is don’t try to be everywhere. Don’t try to be everything.
I mean, a great example, Symone Sanders [Townsend] is fantastic at TikTok and Instagram because she grew up in those spaces and knows those audiences. That might not be the same for Lawrence O’Donnell. Lawrence O’Donnell is a huge hit on YouTube.
What has Trump 2.0 been like over there? Have you seen an audience bump? Have you seen fatigue? The challenge with the story of Trump 2.0 is that there are a thousand stories a day. How are you thinking about reaching your audience in a way that can grab them and hold them?
What I want our audience to know is that we are who we are, and we’re proud of who we are, and you can come to us on any platform at any time and trust that you are getting our best reporting and our best analysis without fear.
We haven’t talked about it yet, but as part of the spinoff, we had to build our own newsroom. What we tried to do is build our newsroom knowing the moment. We’re not trying to be commodity news. We’re trying to build an absolutely kickass DC newsroom, and I think we’ve done that.
MS NOW is one of the very few media brands in growth mode right now. It's impressive.
I'm curious about your take on the possibility of a merger between Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery, which would place CNN and CBS News under one owner. Would that consolidation be good for you? Does this help you even if the broader implications can be troubling?
In a functioning healthy democracy, you need a very healthy free and fair press. So I am rooting for better, stronger newsrooms. I worked most of my career at CNN, and while they might be technically a competitor or rival now, the world is a better place with a stronger CNN.

Ukraine Unveils RK-2PZ Surface-to-Air Missile Based on Barrier Anti-Tank Missile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:28:21 UTC
19:28:21 KST

- Category
- Defense Tech
Ukraine Unveils RK-2PZ Surface-to-Air Missile Based on Barrier Anti-Tank Missile
Ukraine’s state defense conglomerate Ukroboronprom has unveiled a new anti-aircraft missile designed for upgraded Strela-10 surface-to-air missile systems and the new Desna air defense system, Militarnyi reported from the MSPO defense exhibition in Poland on September 8.
The new RK-2PZ surface-to-air missile was developed on the basis of the Barrier anti-tank guided missile, itself a modification of the R-2 missile family.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The RK-2PZ has a caliber of 130 mm and carries a 6.1-kilogram warhead. The missile itself weighs 28.9 kilograms, while its total weight in the launch container reaches 47 kilograms.
After receiving target designation, the operator selects a target for automatic tracking using a control panel and either the television or thermal imaging channel of the system’s optical targeting station.
Once launched from its container, the missile is guided toward the target using a laser guidance system. As it approaches, a proximity sensor is activated to initiate the high-explosive fragmentation warhead. In the event of a direct hit, a contact sensor triggers the warhead.
The RK-2PZ is intended for use with upgraded Strela-10 air defense systems, also known as Ryf. The modernized system retains the original Strela-10’s MT-LB tracked chassis, launcher rotation mechanism, and operator station.
The Ryf underwent its first live-fire tests in December 2021.
The missile is also intended for the new Desna air defense system. Unlike the upgraded Strela-10 platform, Desna is a newly developed launcher module for RK-2PZ missiles that will be mounted on a chassis that has not yet been publicly demonstrated.
According to Militarnyi, detailed performance specifications for both the RK-2PZ missile and the Desna air defense system have not been publicly disclosed.
During the exhibition, Ukraine has also revealed the launcher for its Koral surface-to-air missile for the first time, showcasing an upgraded system intended to engage both conventional aerial threats and ballistic targets.

Ukraine Revives Osa Air Defense Systems With New Domestically Made RK-19 Missile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:27:56 UTC
19:27:56 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Revives Osa Air Defense Systems With New Domestically Made RK-19 Missile
Ukraine has developed a new domestically produced surface-to-air missile designed to replace Soviet 9M33-series interceptors used by the Osa-AKM short-range air defense system.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Militarnyi on September 8, the RK-19 missile was displayed at Ukraine’s defense industry stand during the MSPO defense exhibition in Poland, where its intended role and key technical specifications were disclosed publicly.
The RK-19 can engage aerial targets at ranges of up to 10 kilometers and altitudes of up to 5 kilometers. Its maximum flight speed is listed at 600 meters per second, exceeding the roughly 500-meter-per-second maximum speed of the Soviet 9M33M3 missile it is intended to replace.
Like the original Osa ammunition, the Ukrainian missile uses radio-command guidance. The RK-19 carries a 14.3-kilogram warhead, while the missile and its launch container have a combined weight of 163 kilograms. The container measures 3,255 mm in length, 320 mm in width, and 303 mm in height.
The missile was first shown publicly in April 2026 during a video address by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy marking Ukraine’s Gunsmith Day. At the time, its specific launch platform had not been officially detailed.
The latest presentation confirms that the RK-19 was developed as a replacement for the Soviet-made 9M33 family used by the Osa-AKM, potentially allowing Ukraine to keep the existing air defense systems operational without relying on dwindling stocks of Soviet missiles.
The Osa-AKM is a mobile, short-range surface-to-air missile system designed to protect troops and infrastructure from aircraft and cruise missiles. Each combat vehicle carries six 9M33M3 missiles and can engage targets at ranges of up to 10 kilometers and altitudes of up to 5 kilometers.
Ukraine has operated Osa systems extensively during Russia’s full-scale invasion, including against Russian drones and cruise missiles. However, stocks of compatible Soviet-produced interceptors have declined during the war, limiting the intensity with which the systems can be employed.
Earlier, Ukraine unveiled the launcher for its domestically developed Koral surface-to-air missile, a significantly redesigned interceptor intended to engage both conventional aerial threats and ballistic targets. The latest version weighs about 450 kilograms, carries a 36-kilogram warhead, and uses inertial navigation, radio-command correction, and an active radar seeker.

Russia’s military personnel losses since the start of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine have surpassed 1.5 million killed and wounded, according to figures released by the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine on September 9.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The General Staff said Russian forces lost another 1,480 personnel on September 8, bringing Ukraine’s estimate of total Russian personnel losses since February 2022 to 1,500,870.
“This is the largest loss in a single war suffered by the Russian army since World War II,” the General Staff said, adding that the figure exceeds the combined losses of the Soviet and Russian armies in all wars and armed conflicts of the second half of the 20th and early 21st centuries.

The 1.5 million figure represents cumulative battlefield personnel losses reported by Ukraine and includes both Russian troops killed and wounded. Moscow does not publish comprehensive figures that can be directly compared with Ukraine’s running estimate, and the total cannot be independently verified in real time.
Ukraine has published daily estimates of Russian personnel and equipment losses throughout the full-scale invasion, updating its figures as new battlefield information becomes available.
Meanwhile, Russia is preparing to mobilize up to 600,000 additional troops through 2027, according to Ukrainian military intelligence chief Oleh Ivashchenko. Russia’s military spending hits a record 44% of its budget
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:27:05 UTC
19:27:05 KST

- Russia's military spending hit a record 44% of federal budget outlays in the first half of 2026, economist Janis Kluge calculated from Finance Ministry data.
- Classified spending, mostly military-related, already exceeded 8.4 trillion rubles after six months against a full-year budget target of 11.6 trillion rubles.
Russia spent a record 44% of its federal budget on the military in the first half of 2026, according to calculations published by Janis Kluge, a research fellow at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs, based on data from Russia’s Finance Ministry.
Direct military spending totaled 10.7 trillion rubles, about $125 billion at current exchange rates, for the first six months of the year, Kluge found, a 30% increase over the same period in 2025. That spending equaled 10.5% of Russia’s gross domestic product for the first half of the year and 57.3% of federal budget revenue, meaning more than half of every ruble the government collected in taxes and other income went toward the war.
Kluge’s data shows classified spending, budget lines the Kremlin does not disclose in detail, driving much of the increase. Russia’s 2026 budget law set a full-year target of 11.6 trillion rubles for classified spending, but the government had already spent more than 8.4 trillion rubles on those hidden categories after just six months, putting the full year on pace to blow well past its own budgeted figure. Russian budget documents indicate that roughly 85% of classified spending goes to military needs, based on figures Kluge has cited from earlier quarters this year.
The military’s share of the federal budget has climbed steadily since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in February 2022. Kluge’s tracker, which compares the first half of each year going back to 2018, shows military spending at 24.5% of federal budget outlays in the first half of that pre-war year, dropping to around 20% in 2020 and 2021, then rising sharply to 29.6% in the first half of 2023, 36.6% in 2024, and 39.3% in 2025 before reaching the current 43.8% figure for 2026. Open, publicly itemized military spending has held relatively steady over that same stretch, hovering between roughly 11% and 15% of the budget each year.
Nearly all of the growth has come from the classified category, which has gone from a modest supplement to open spending before the war to now making up close to two-thirds of the total military budget.
Total direct budgetary military spending since the start of the full-scale invasion now stands at 57.1 trillion rubles, or roughly $666 billion, according to Kluge’s calculations. That figure covers only formal federal budget line items and does not include off-budget costs such as regional government spending on recruitment bonuses and compensation payments to the families of killed and wounded soldiers, costs Kluge has tracked separately in other analyses of Russia’s regional budgets.
The first quarter of 2026 alone saw military spending reach 5.9 trillion rubles, itself a record at the time and up 30% from the first quarter of 2025, driven largely by a 43% jump in classified spending during that period compared with a year earlier. Kluge has since raised a technical question about the scale of that first-quarter jump, noting that Russian federal spending patterns showed unusually low classified outlays at the end of 2025 and that December 2025 budget spending overall fell sharply from a year earlier.
That pattern, he has suggested, could mean the Finance Ministry deferred some spending originally planned for 2025 into 2026, in part to avoid missing the deficit target the government had publicly committed to for last year.
The spending surge has come as Russia’s oil and gas revenue, historically the backbone of its federal budget, has weakened. Kluge’s first-quarter data showed oil and gas revenue falling 45% year over year, a decline tied to Western sanctions on Russian energy exports and a stronger ruble that reduces the ruble value of oil sold in dollars.
Non-oil and gas revenue rose about 7% over the same period, but not enough to offset the shortfall, leaving military spending equivalent to roughly two-thirds of total federal budget revenue in the first quarter, by Kluge’s calculation. Bloomberg has separately reported that Russian finance officials have privately told President Vladimir Putin that current war spending levels are becoming unaffordable.
Kluge’s calculations rely on published Russian Finance Ministry budget execution data, which the ministry continues to release on a regular schedule even as it withholds detail on how classified funds are ultimately spent. He has cautioned that spending patterns typically ease in the second and third quarters of the year compared with the first, meaning the full-year share of GDP devoted to the military could land lower than a straight-line projection from Q1 alone would suggest, even as the absolute ruble totals keep setting records.

EU reiterates Israeli settlements illegal under intl' law, calls them obstacle to 2-state solution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:26:04 UTC
19:26:04 KST

Melike Pala
09 September 2026•Update: 09 September 2026
The European Union reiterated its longstanding position that Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories are illegal under international law, saying they constitute an obstacle to peace and the viability of a two-state solution.
"We take note of the announcement of eight member states – together with the UK, Canada, Iceland and Norway – to impose national restrictions on trade with illegal settlements," Anouar El Anouni, the EU Commission spokesman for foreign affairs, told Anadolu.
"The EU's longstanding position is clear: settlements are illegal under international law. They constitute an obstacle to peace and to the viability of the two-state solution," he added.
The bloc considers Israeli settlements established in the occupied Palestinian territory after June 1967 to be illegal, he said.
"Goods originating from Israeli settlements in territories that came under Israeli administration since June 1967 are not entitled to benefit from any preferential tariff treatment," El Anouni noted.
His remarks came after 11 European countries — France, the UK, Denmark, Spain, Finland, Ireland, Iceland, Norway, Poland, Portugal and Sweden — as well as Canada announced their intention to impose national restrictions on trade with Israeli settlements.
The countries also said they would support European restrictions on such trade.
In a joint declaration, the countries said the situation in the occupied West Bank is "rapidly deteriorating," citing unprecedented levels of occupiers' violence and continued settlement expansion.
"We firmly oppose any action resulting in the annexation of Palestinian land and the forced displacement of Palestinian populations," they said.
The countries called on Israel to immediately halt the expansion of settlements and civilian administrative powers in the occupied West Bank.
They also urged accountability for occupiers responsible for violence and called for investigations into allegations involving Israeli forces.
Growing calls to EU
There are growing calls in Europe for the EU to go beyond measures targeting settlement goods and take broader action in its trade relations with Israel.
Several European governments, lawmakers, and civil society groups have called on the EU to suspend or restrict trade arrangements with Israel, arguing that the bloc should use its economic relationship with Israel as leverage to address settlement expansion and the treatment of Palestinians.
The calls have also focused on the EU-Israel Association Agreement, which provides the framework for bilateral trade relations and grants preferential treatment to certain goods.
Supporters of stronger measures have argued that the agreement should be reviewed or suspended in response to Israel's policies in the occupied Palestinian territory and the wider conflict.
However, EU-wide trade measures require agreement among member states, and divisions between EU countries have so far complicated efforts to adopt a common position.
While the EU has not yet imposed a general import ban on products originating from illegal Israeli settlements, it excludes such products from trade preferences under the EU-Israel Association Agreement and continues to assess options for broader trade measures.

Breadcrumb
John Malkovich bails on Israel performance following backlash, blames 'fake quotes'
John Malkovich has cancelled a planned visit to Israel amid online backlash, with the Hollywood actor blaming fabricated quotes attributed to him in Israeli media.
The 72-year-old actor had planned to travel to Tel Aviv in April 2027 for a one-off performance of The Music Critic, a satirical stage show that has toured dozens of countries around the world since 2021.
But in a statement on Tuesday, Malkovich announced he would no longer travel to the country after he was quoted praising Israel in local media.
An article published by The Jerusalem Post over the weekend quoted the actor as saying he was "thrilled to return to Israel" and expressing "strong closeness and solidarity" with Israeli people.
The announcement was met with backlash online, where social media users slammed the Oscar-winning actor's decision to travel to the country.
"I was made aware of an article which appeared in The Hollywood Reporter (first published in The Jerusalem Post) announcing a date in Tel Aviv, Israel, for a performance of a piece called 'The Music Critic,'" Malkovich said in a statement to Hollywood media.
"A PR company hired by the Israeli promoter drafted a quote for the article that was attributed to me, though I never made the statements that were quoted, nor was I consulted before they were printed. I did not utter these phrases, and they most certainly are not approved by me, nor do they reflect my feelings," he continued.
"The fact that they were printed as direct quotes from me is unacceptable and untenable. For this reason, I have decided I cannot participate in the Tel Aviv performance."
Malkovich has visited Israel several times during his decades-long career, once in 2008 as a guest of honour at the Jerusalem Film Festival and again in 2013 to perform The Infernal Comedy: Confessions of a Serial Killer at the Eilat International Chamber Music Festival and the Tel Aviv Museum of Art.
The visit had looked to be a rare show of public support for Israel from a major figure in Hollywood, where a cultural boycott has gathered pace in response to the genocide in Gaza and escalating violence in the occupied West Bank.
Thousands of actors, directors and film workers in 2025 vowed to cut ties with the Israeli film industry, which the Film Workers for Palestine said was "implicated in genocide and apartheid against the Palestinian people".

Finland says GNSS jamming, wind caused Ukrainian drones to enter its airspace in spring
HELSINKI, Sept 9 - Four Ukrainian military drones found in Finland in March and April were diverted from their intended route by satellite navigation interference in combination with wind, Finnish police and border guards said on Wednesday.
Finland and nearby Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania have seen a string of recent incidents where Ukrainian drones aimed at Russia have strayed into their airspace.
• "The investigation established that the UAVs (Unmanned Aerial Vehicles) originated in Ukraine and formed part of Ukraine's countermeasures in response to Russia's war of aggression," the Finnish Border Guard said in a statement.
• "The UAVs had not, however, been targeted at Finland; instead, they were thrown off course by strong GNSS (Global Navigation Satellite System) jamming detected in the eastern Gulf of Finland at the time, combined with the prevailing weather conditions," it added.
• The agencies said the prosecutor had closed the investigations into the incidents, having found no grounds to pursue criminal liability.
• The agencies said all four drones had carried explosives. No injuries or property damage were reported in connection with the crashes. REUTERS

'One in six attacks': Israel was most targeted nation by hacktivism campaigns in first half of 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:22:05 UTC
19:22:05 KST

Israel was the world’s top target for hacktivist attacks in the first half of 2026, with one in six attacks targeting the Jewish state, the Radware H1 2026 Global Threat Report revealed on Wednesday.
Hacktivist attacks are carried out by non-state actors, often sponsored by states but not officially part of their organization, against selected countries for geopolitical reasons.
According to the report, Israel absorbed 16% of all the hacktivist campaigns, with 784 recorded reports of attacks; the United States was second with 8%, and the United Kingdom was third, while many European countries supporting Ukraine in the war against Russia absorbed a significant number of secondary attacks.
The report noted that a spike in attacks of this style was recorded during the US and Israel war against Iran, after hacktivist attacks hit a record low during the first months of the year.
In comparison to previous years, the first half of 2026 has been one of the periods with the lowest number of hack attacks recorded, with the peak of hacktivism attacks being reached after the October 7 massacre and the beginning of the Israel-Hamas War, the report said.
“The most significant finding is not merely that Israel once again ranks first but that the gap between it and the other countries continues to widen,” Ron Meyran, vice president of Cyber Intelligence at Radware, said.
“The digital arena has become an inseparable part of every military conflict, and the campaign against Iran demonstrated how quickly dozens of groups can mobilize and act against organizations in Israel,” Meyran added.
Most hacktivist groups active in the first half of the year were from the pro-Russia, anti-Western collective, with 85% of such attacks claimed by groups in the collective, the report added. The most active group was NoName057, which accounted for almost 40% of the attacks.
Targeting infrastructure, autonomous systems
It also noted that the attacks centered on infrastructure, with the main targets being industrial facilities that provide essential services and whose disruption could pressure public officials.
According to the findings, 37% of the attacks targeted governmental institutions, while other targets were against manufacturing services (8%), business (7%), hospitality (6%), and the financial sector (5%).
In terms of the services targeted, the main objective was to disrupt autonomous system numbers (ASNs); the main companies affected by those attacks were Microsoft (22%), Amazon Web Services (13%), and Google Cloud Platform (7%).
Secondary targets included several European hosting providers, notably Hetzner Online (8.4%), because their infrastructure is key to supporting Ukrainian and Israeli networks, such as uPress, Radware, Hosting Ukraine, and Cellcom.

6 potato pancake recipes that everyone can make
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
13:21:43 EEST
19:21:43 KST

6 potato pancake recipes that everyone can make
Kyiv • UNN
UNN presents six potato pancake recipes: classic, with meat, cheese, mushrooms, liver, and without flour or eggs.
Deruny are a simple potato dish that can be diversified with various fillings and additional ingredients. UNN has compiled the top 6 best recipes, among which there is an option to suit every taste.
Classic deruny
Ingredients:
-  potatoes - 1 kg; 
-  onions - 2; 
-  eggs - 2; 
-  flour - 30 g; 
-  garlic - 2 cloves; 
-  salt - to taste; 
-  ground black pepper - to taste; 
-  oil - for frying. 
Preparation:
Peel the potatoes and grate them. Add the grated onion and squeeze out the excess liquid.
Add the minced garlic, eggs, flour, salt, and pepper. Mix thoroughly.
Heat a frying pan with oil. Spoon the potato mixture into the pan, forming small pancakes.
Fry the deruny for 3-4 minutes on each side until golden brown.
Serve hot with sour cream.
Deruny with meat filling
Ingredients:
-  potatoes - 1 kg; 
-  onion - 1 large; 
-  eggs - 2; 
-  flour - 4 tbsp.; 
-  ground meat - 400 g; 
-  salt - to taste; 
-  pepper - to taste; 
-  oil - for frying. 
Preparation:
Peel the potatoes, grate them on a fine grater, and squeeze out the excess liquid.
Grate the onion on a fine grater as well.
Mix the potatoes and onion, then add the eggs, flour, salt, and pepper.
Prepare the ground meat in advance. Chicken can be used raw, while beef or pork is recommended to be fried beforehand until partially cooked.
Spoon the potato mixture onto a preheated frying pan. Place some ground meat in the center and cover it with another layer of potatoes.
Fry over medium heat for approximately 4 minutes on each side.
Place the finished deruny on a paper towel.
Deruny with cheese
Ingredients:
-  potatoes - 1 kg; 
-  onion - 1; 
-  eggs - 2; 
-  flour - 50 g; 
-  hard or semi-hard cheese - 100 g; 
-  garlic - 2 cloves; 
-  salt - to taste; 
-  ground black pepper - to taste; 
-  oil - for frying. 
Preparation:
Squeeze the grated potatoes and onion to remove the excess liquid, leaving the starch.
Add the grated cheese, eggs, flour, minced garlic, salt, and pepper.
Mix all the ingredients.
Spoon the mixture into a preheated frying pan with oil.
Fry for 3-4 minutes on each side.
Deruny with mushrooms
Ingredients:
-  potatoes - 1 kg; 
-  onions - 2; 
-  eggs - 2; 
-  flour - 100 g; 
-  sour cream - 150 g; 
-  champignons or seasonal mushrooms - 300 g; 
-  salt - to taste; 
-  ground black pepper - to taste; 
-  oil - for frying. 
Preparation:
Grate the potatoes and onions on a fine grater.
Add the flour, sour cream, salt, and pepper, and mix.
Add the eggs and mix well again.
Cut the mushrooms into small pieces and fry them.
Add the mushrooms to the potato mixture.
Fry the deruny in a preheated frying pan with oil on both sides until golden brown.
Serve with sour cream or yogurt sauce.
Liver deruny
Ingredients:
-  chicken liver - 300 g; 
-  onion - 1; 
-  carrot - 1; 
-  potato - 1; 
-  sour cream - 2 tbsp.; 
-  egg - 1; 
-  flour - 3 tbsp.; 
-  salt - 1 tsp.; 
-  black pepper - ½ tsp.; 
-  dried garlic - ½ tsp.; 
-  oil - for frying. 
Preparation:
Finely chop the liver.
Add the chopped onion, grated carrot, and potato.
Add the egg, salt, pepper, and dried garlic.
Add the flour and sour cream, and mix.
Heat a frying pan with oil.
Spoon the mixture into the pan, forming deruny.
Fry on both sides until browned.
Deruny without flour or eggs
Ingredients:
-  potatoes - 700 g; 
-  sunflower oil -60 ml; 
-  butter - 15 g; 
-  salt - 1 tsp.; 
-  ground black pepper - to taste. 
Preparation:
Peel the potatoes and grate them on a coarse grater.
Cover them with cold water and rinse several times until the water becomes almost clear.
Drain the potatoes in a colander and squeeze them thoroughly through a clean towel. The mixture should remain as dry as possible.
Add the salt and pepper immediately before frying.
Heat a wide frying pan, then add the oil and butter.
Add the potatoes in small portions and form thin deruny.
Fry over medium heat for 4-5 minutes on each side.
Place the finished deruny on a paper towel and serve hot with sour cream, yogurt sauce, or fresh herbs.

19:17:04 KST

MOSCOW, September 9. /TASS/. Pressure from imported products, including those from China and Kazakhstan, on the Russian rolled steel market persists, although the overall situation remains stable and predictable. At the same time, competition in the finished products segment has intensified due to an influx of low-quality products, Director of Severstal Distribution (part of Severstal) Viktor Romanovsky told reporters.
"If we talk about import pressure on the Russian market, it still persists," Romanovsky said in response to a question about competition from Chinese and Kazakh imports. He added that some local players had redirected their volumes to other markets, but their share was not large enough to significantly reduce the overall pressure.
According to Romanovsky, the situation is more challenging in the finished products segment. "If we talk about competition in finished products, the situation here has definitely not improved and may even have worsened," he said. Romanovsky stressed that despite efforts by Russian producers and their customers to reduce costs and improve efficiency, large volumes of low-quality products continue to enter the market.
"And customers whose purchasing power is declining often choose price over quality, sometimes disregarding the quality characteristics of the product itself," Romanovsky added, explaining the reasons for increased competition in this segment.
Last summer, Severstal CEO Alexander Shevelev said that rising steel imports into Russia were increasing the market's sensitivity, although imports were not yet particularly painful for Russian steelmakers. Severstal is analyzing the situation and does not rule out initiating anti-dumping duties.
Severstal is a vertically integrated mining and steel company and one of Russia's largest steel producers. The company's key asset is the Cherepovets Steel Mill, which has an annual production capacity of around 12 mln metric tons of steel. Severstal's largest shareholder is Alexey Mordashov, who owns approximately 77.03% of the company's shares.

Google to invest €13bn in Finnish AI data centres, its biggest European push yet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:16:43 UTC
19:16:43 KST

Google will spend at least €13 billion on data centres and digital infrastructure in Finland over the next two years, its largest single investment in Europe, in a bet on the country's cheap power and climate.
Helsinki has landed the biggest cheque Google has written anywhere in Europe
The company announced on Wednesday that a €13 billion investment will fund data centres and supporting infrastructure across four municipalities, along with clean energy projects and funds dedicated to local biodiversity, education, research and workforce development.
The facilities in Hamina, Kajaani, Muhos and Vaala will power a range of Google services, among them its Gemini chatbot. The company described the decision as "a testament to Finland's leadership in responsibly building AI infrastructure."
Construction is expected across 2027 and 2028, and the firm estimates the investment will add €3.6 billion a year to Finland's GDP while supporting more than 37,000 jobs, roughly 16,000 of them in construction.
Once the building stops, Google projects the sites will sustain around 7,000 jobs annually, spanning technical and facility roles, equipment suppliers, as well as the shops, restaurants and services used by those workers and their families.
Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo welcomed the announcement in Google's statement.
"Google's decision is a clear testament to our strengths. The value of the data economy extends far beyond direct investment into spurring innovation, research and development," Orpo said, adding that closer collaboration would "deliver lasting benefits for both parties."
Why Finland
The appeal to invest in Finland is rooted in its cold climate.
Data centres generate enormous heat and consume vast quantities of electricity, and Finland offers a cold climate that reduces cooling costs alongside relatively cheap and stable power from nuclear plants, wind and hydro.
That combination has produced a boom, with dozens of data centres already under construction across the country.
Google's own presence dates back to 2009, when it bought a disused paper mill in the coastal city of Hamina and converted it, expanding steadily since.
For Orpo's right-wing government, attracting this kind of investment has also been a priority, especially since Finnish elections will take place in April of next year.
Finland is contending with record unemployment and weak growth, and the data economy has become one of the few sectors offering the prospect of substantial investment and job creation.

Poor condition of Baltic Sea behind flounder population slump
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:15:00 UTC
19:15:00 KST

Poor condition of Baltic Sea behind flounder population slump
Although fishers attribute the low abundance of flounder to the spread of an invasive species, a fisheries scientist says the cause is the Baltic Sea's poor hydrological conditions.
According to Taavi Suitsberg, chairman of the NGO Lääne County Coastal Fisheries Association and a professional fisherman, fishers believe the decline in flounder numbers is due to the invasive round goby, which competes with native fish species for food and reproduces more quickly.
At the same time, Suitsberg said the growing number of gobies is a double-edged sword for fishers. Although they are said to be crowding out flounder species, gobies are themselves edible fish and serve as food for larger fish.
However, Suitsberg acknowledged that he could not say exactly why flounder numbers are declining and that fishers had also learned about the possible impact of the invasive species from scientists.
Redik Eschbaum, head of the coastal fisheries working group at the University of Tartu's Estonian Marine Institute's Department of Fish Biology and Fisheries, said aquatic ecosystems are so complex that it is difficult to pinpoint a single cause for a species' decline.
However, Eschbaum confirmed that a lack of food cannot be the direct cause, as researchers have not found emaciated flounder. Flounder numbers were also already low before the round goby became widespread, all of which points to hydrological conditions as the cause.
According to Eschbaum, cod are in an even worse situation than flounder. Like flounder, their spawning depends on inflows of saltwater. Cod fishing is banned altogether in the Baltic Sea.
One thing flounder and cod have in common is pelagic eggs, meaning their eggs float freely in the water rather than sticking to underwater plants or objects. These species spawn in deeper, saltier layers of water where their eggs also develop.
Eschbaum said there are two possible reasons why spawning has become more difficult for these species. First, decomposing algae on the seabed may be leaving too little oxygen there.
Another possibility is that climate change has altered wind patterns. "Saltwater inflows are no longer as extensive and don't occur at the same time of year as they used to. But the fish have no way of anticipating that," Eschbaum said.
Eschbaum said that historically, two types of flounder were distinguished in the Baltic Sea: deepwater-spawning flounder and coastal-spawning flounder. It was later discovered, however, that they are two entirely separate species.
Although Baltic Sea flounder are a good example of rapid evolution, the two species have adapted differently. Coastal-spawning flounder, for example, are faring somewhat better, although they too would benefit from saltier water.
Although Eschbaum said flounder numbers are not expected to increase in the near future, the species cannot be considered endangered.

Ukraine's KORT unveils Hunter Killer line of mid- and long-range attack drones – photos
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09

Ukraine's KORT unveils Hunter Killer line of mid- and long-range attack drones – photos
KORT, a Ukrainian drone and component manufacturer, has unveiled its Hunter Killer line of UAVs, comprising mid- and long-range one-way attack drones.
Source: Ukrainska Pravda at the MSPO-2026 exhibition in Poland
Details: The unveiled line includes aircraft of various types with warheads weighing between three and 70 kg.
A KORT representative told Ukrainska Pravda: "We currently have four versions of aircraft with different modifications and different warheads on display. We are also working on larger long-range attack drones and mid-range attack drones equipped with pusher engines, meaning the propeller is located at the rear of the drone. This change in the design is being made at the request of the military to increase the chances of hitting armoured targets."
The mid-range strike line starts with the Hunter Killer 3. This fixed-wing drone was developed based on the Ardea reconnaissance drone. The company is presenting three versions of the Hunter Killer 3 with take-off weights of 10, 10.5 and 14 kg.
Depending on the modification, the aircraft can remain airborne for 60 to 140 minutes and cover distances of 100 to 250 km. Its warhead weighs 3 kg. Radio communications or Starlink are used for control. The drones are also equipped with thermal imaging cameras and an automatic navigation system.
The more advanced line consists of the Hunter Killer S, 10M, 15S, 15M, 15 and 20 models. They can be used as either mid-range or long-range attack drones.
The Hunter Killer S, 10M, 15S and 15M are mid-range attack drones. They have a stated range of up to 300 km and can carry a warhead weighing up to 15 kg. The models differ in fuselage design and communications systems. The Hunter Killer S and Hunter Killer 15S use Starlink, while the other models in this group are equipped with radio communications.
The Hunter Killer 15 and 20 are long-range attack drones. According to the company, they can cover up to 700 km and carry a warhead weighing up to 10 kg. The models also have different fuselage designs.
The most advanced models in the line, the Hunter Killer 50S and 70, are at the final testing stage. The Hunter Killer 50S is a mid-range attack drone with a 60-kg warhead and a range of up to 600 km. The Hunter Killer 70 is a long-range attack drone with a 50-kg warhead and a range of up to 1,200 km. The company is also developing a 70-kg warhead.
The two latest models are distinguished by interchangeable wings that allow the range to be extended by increasing the wing area. The fuselage remains unchanged.
The long-range strike versions of the Hunter Killer drones are also equipped with an eight-channel CRPA antenna manufactured by KORT. It is designed to ensure the aircraft can navigate in conditions of electronic warfare.
Earlier, at the MSPO exhibition in Poland, Ukraine also presented, for the first time, an anti-aircraft missile for the Osa surface-to-air missile system as well as a new version of the Vilkha missile.

Republicans tie midterm hopes to Trump at Dallas convention despite political risks
DALLAS, Sept 9 - Republicans kicked off their first-ever midterm convention in Dallas on Wednesday, betting that President Donald Trump can energize core supporters and help the party hold onto its congressional majorities despite his unpopularity.
The two-day gathering underscores the extent to which Republicans are tethering their fortunes to Trump and serves as a showcase for their strategy ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.
The event is so centered on the president that Republican National Committee Chairman Joe Gruters has informally dubbed it "Trumpapalooza," a nod to the popular Lollapalooza music festival.
Many Republicans in competitive House and Senate races skipped the convention, underscoring concerns within the party that Trump's appeal to loyal supporters may not be enough to overcome broader voter dissatisfaction over inflation and the war on Iran.
About 30 minutes before the program was set to begin, a steady stream of guests moved through the 21,000-seat American Airlines Center, while hundreds more waited outside.
The stakes are high. With the elections less than two months away, Republicans face the prospect of losing control of at least one chamber of Congress, with public polling showing Democrats more motivated to vote.
"Republicans are delivering freedom, opportunity, security and common sense," Gruters said from the stage as the program got under way. "Democrats are being overtaken by radical socialists, driving their party further and further from the values that make America great."
With no official party business on the agenda, the gathering resembled a Trump campaign rally more than a traditional party convention, which is held every four years to nominate presidential and vice presidential candidates.
Trump will speak both nights, delivering the keynote address on Wednesday and then offering the last word after Vice President JD Vance speaks on Thursday evening. In his remarks, Gruters described Trump as the "greatest president" in U.S. history and the "greatest Republican messenger of our lifetime."
RNC spokesman Rick Gorka said the party expects to fill the arena with officials, donors, activists and members of the public, after opening the gathering to the public through a free ticket lottery. Organizers took the unusual step as some party insiders privately worried attendance could fall short of expectations.
At least 16 candidates in competitive House and Senate races were scheduled to speak, according to the RNC's schedule. Those staying away include Representative Tom Barrett of Michigan and Senator Susan Collins of Maine, both facing strong Democratic challengers this fall.
Matthew Wilson, a political science professor at Southern Methodist University, said some Republican candidates may fear the convention will be "more a celebration of Trump" than an effort to boost their chances.
"Trump has always cared more about 'brand Trump' than about the Republican Party," Wilson said. "I think that's why there's some wariness from their standpoint about being a visible presence at this event."
That critique echoes a broader complaint from Trump's opponents, who say he has spent much of the summer burnishing his legacy through construction projects in Washington, rather than addressing Americans' concerns about rising living costs.
A CHANCE TO RALLY THE BASE
The convention will face stiff competition for viewers with the start of the NFL season, with opening night coinciding with a Super Bowl rematch between the New England Patriots and Seattle Seahawks and Thursday's program overlapping with a matchup between the San Francisco 49ers and Los Angeles Rams.
Still, after months of negative headlines over the Iran war and inflation, many Republicans see the gathering as their best chance to promote candidates, draw contrasts with Democrats on affordability, immigration and healthcare, and energize a Republican electorate expressing less enthusiasm about voting than Democrats, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll.
Trump cabinet members who will address the gathering include Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, whose comments are likely to be closely watched amid concerns about the growing U.S. debt and high cost of living.
One notable absence from the published list of speakers is Senate Majority Leader John Thune, who has publicly clashed with Trump over the Senate's failure to advance the SAVE America Act, a voting restrictions bill championed by the president. Thune will be at the convention, however, and will meet with donors and candidates, a person familiar with the matter said.
According to the program outline, speakers will cast Democrats as too far left while touting Trump's domestic record, including the administration's efforts to restrict immigration and lower drug prices and a 2025 tax-and-spending package that eliminated taxes on tips and Social Security benefits.
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is dispatching four Democratic lawmakers to Dallas as part of the party's counter-programming effort.
"Americans are drowning in the failed Republican economy," Jeffries said in a statement. "Rather than taking a single step to lower costs, MAGA extremists are partying with their super-rich donors in Dallas."
By holding the event in Texas, Republicans are drawing attention to one of the midterms' highest-profile races: the U.S. Senate contest between Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton and Democratic state Representative James Talarico. Paxton, a fiercely loyal Trump ally, was scheduled to speak on Wednesday. REUTERS

FACTBOX – BRICS summit in India: Who’s attending and what’s on the agenda
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:10:49 UTC
19:10:49 KST

- Leaders from across Asia, Africa, Middle East, Latin America expected to attend including China's Xi, Russia's Putin and Iran's Pezeshkian
- Agenda could include Iran-US conflict, de-dollarization, India-China relations
BRICS leaders will gather in the Indian capital New Delhi this weekend for a two-day summit as the expanded grouping seeks to strengthen its role in global political and economic affairs.
The 18th edition of the BRICS Leaders’ Summit, scheduled for Sept. 12-13 and hosted by Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, will bring leaders together from across Asia, Africa, the Middle East and Latin America.
Who is attending?
Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian are among the leaders expected to attend.
South African President Cyril Ramaphosa, Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko, Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto are also expected to be there.
The expanded BRICS membership comprises Brazil, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Iran, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa and the United Arab Emirates.
The group has also partner countries, including Belarus, Bolivia, Kazakhstan, Cuba, Malaysia, Nigeria, Thailand, Uganda, Uzbekistan and Vietnam joining the framework.
Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim, Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul and Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed are also expected to attend.
Cuba, Nigeria and Uzbekistan are likely to be represented by their presidents, Miguel Diaz-Canel, Bola Tinubu and Shavkat Mirziyoyev, respectively.
United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres is also expected to attend.
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva is expected to be represented by Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira, while the UAE is expected to send Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan in place of President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan.
Agenda and key points
The agenda is generally expected to focus on trade, development financing and reform of global institutions.
However, the summit comes amid the conflict between Iran and the US, and its broader impact on the global economy, including an energy crisis that has particularly affected Asia. The issue is therefore likely to emerge as a major point of discussion among members.
Iran may push for a summit declaration reflecting its position on the conflict, while the organization requires full consensus to reach an agreement.
The summit could also provide an important backdrop for India and China’s complex relationship.
If Chinese President Xi attends, it would be his first visit to India since his 2019 informal summit with Prime Minister Modi.
The two countries are among the world’s largest economies and are major BRICS members, but their relationship continues to be shaped by unresolved border and sovereignty disputes.
Eerishika Pankaj of Australia’s Lowy Institute has described BRICS and the India-China strategic dialogue as institutional mechanisms that allow the two sides to maintain communication despite their differences.
“Cooperation and unresolved sovereignty disputes coexist,” Pankaj wrote, arguing that BRICS should be viewed as a means of maintaining dialogue rather than evidence that India and China have resolved their disagreements.
Beyond bilateral issues, BRICS is also expected to address reform of global institutions, an issue the bloc has repeatedly raised in relation to institutions such as the UN, IMF and World Bank.
De-dollarization
Another key area of BRICS cooperation has been the use of national currencies in trade and finance, reflecting efforts by members to reduce their dependence on the US dollar.
Egyptian Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly said last year that BRICS member states were increasingly adopting local-currency settlements in bilateral financial transactions as part of a broader strategy to reduce reliance on foreign currencies and strengthen economic cooperation within the group.
However, despite discussions about expanding local-currency settlements in trade, members have stopped short of establishing a common BRICS currency.
The New Development Bank, the bloc’s multilateral development bank, has also made local-currency financing a strategic priority.
According to its 2024 report, 43.5% of its approvals that year were denominated in member countries’ currencies, primarily the South African rand and Chinese yuan.
A short history of BRICS
As these leaders gather in New Delhi, their meeting underscores the bloc’s dramatic expansion since its creation in 2006.
BRIC was formalized at a meeting of foreign ministers on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York in 2006, bringing together Brazil, Russia, India and China.
The first leaders’ summit of the then BRIC was held in Yekaterinburg, Russia, in 2009.
South Africa joined in 2010, transforming BRIC into BRICS. The grouping subsequently underwent another major expansion, bringing in countries from the Middle East and Africa and, most recently, Indonesia.
According to figures cited by BRICS, the grouping now represents about 49.5% of the world’s population, 40% of global GDP and 26% of global trade.
BRICS describes itself as a platform for consultation and cooperation on global and regional issues, including international political and economic governance.
The last BRICS summit was held in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, in 2025 while China is due to host the 2027 summit.

More schools close in Indonesia as haze worsens
Schools in Palembang switch to remote learning as haze from forest and peatland fires pushes air pollution to unhealthy levels
Schools in the capital of Indonesia’s South Sumatra province switched to remote learning on Wednesday as worsening haze from forest and peatland fires pushed air pollution to unhealthy levels, adding to disruptions that had already affected more than 1.4 million students across the country, officials said.
Indonesia has been plagued by forest and land fires for decades but an intensifying El Nino pattern and a prolonged dry season made the impact of the fires especially dire this year. Toxic haze and smoke have spread far beyond Indonesia’s borders in Southeast Asia, creating a regional health crisis.
The smoke has drifted as far as the Philippines, more than 800km (500 miles) away, and breached Malaysia’s emergency-level threshold, forcing authorities to declare an emergency last week in a town in Sarawak state on Borneo Island.
In Palembang, the capital city of South Sumatra province, schools from kindergarten to junior high were ordered to start conducting classes online on Wednesday under an emergency measure.
Mayor Ratu Dewa said the thickening smoke posed health risks to children, including acute respiratory infections.
“Students’ health and safety remained the government’s priority,” Dewa said. Teachers were also asked to avoid excessive assignments during the period of remote learning, he added.
The policy, affecting more than 250,000 students at 1,030 schools in Palembang, would be reviewed regularly, and in-person classes will resume once conditions improve, he said.

Kiev wants advance Patriot shipments against unbought missiles
Ukraine wants its Western donors to supply highly sought-after Patriot interceptors from their own stockpiles, which would be replenished later with 1,000 missiles that Kiev plans to purchase with EU money.
The unorthodox proposal was outlined on Tuesday by Ukrainian Defense Minister Evgeny Khmara during a video call with Western arms donors. It comes amid a global shortage of US-made weapons, with Ukraine competing for supplies against numerous other countries while arguing that its need to intercept Russian ballistic missiles should take priority.
Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky previously sought to secure 300 Patriot interceptors for the upcoming winter. His reported effort to impress US President Donald Trump with long-range strikes on Russian refineries and e-commerce warehouses has produced no clear results.
The attacks were allegedly intended to persuade Trump to approve additional Patriot supplies. Kiev also overspent Western donor funds while pursuing the strategy and has a $27 billion military budget deficit.
Speaking to members of the Ukraine Defense Contact Group, Khmara said his country is contracting 1,000 Patriot missiles “through the EU loan,” but acknowledged that the purchase does not resolve the immediate shortage.
“The majority of these missiles will only start to be shipped in the coming years, which is why we ask that you supply us the missiles from your stockpiles today in exchange for future improved missiles from our contracts,” he said.
German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said at the same meeting that Berlin is working to provide additional Patriot interceptors of the older PAC-2 model from its own stocks, along with air-to-air missiles that Ukraine uses against Russian drones and cruise missiles, including from Western-donated F-16 fighter jets.
Western Europe’s purse remains open for Kiev
The meeting, co-chaired by Pistorius and British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting, coincided with announcements from both the EU and the UK regarding their respective aid programs.

The British government pledged a £100 million ($136 million) “winter air defense package,” with the money slated to be spent on US-made weapons through NATO’s Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) program.
Trump’s mediation efforts renewed
Trump has sought to distance the US from the Ukraine conflict, arguing that European NATO members should bear more of the burden of the prolonged hostilities with Russia. RIVARO Holding has completed the acquisition of a 49.99% stake in AS Rīgas starptautiskā autoosta, becoming the largest shareholder of Riga International Bus Station. The transaction was financed with a loan from Signet Bank AS, while the new owners plan to make additional investments in the development of the bus station. The new shareholder plans to focus on the continued development of the existing infrastructure and improving the quality of passenger services.
At the first stage, priority areas and improvements will be identified that will have the most immediate impact on passengers’ everyday experience, including ticketing systems, digital services and information screens. Riga Bus Station will continue operating at its current location. RIVARO Holding does not plan to demolish the existing bus station or change its purpose; the focus will remain on developing the facility and improving its operation for passengers.
“For a bus station with more than 60 years of history, modernisation is a strategic necessity. At the same time, decisions of this scale need to be considered in the broader context of the city’s development, and no shareholder can make such decisions alone: the Rail Baltica infrastructure, railway hub, Central Market and Riga’s historic centre are all located nearby. This requires a coordinated approach involving all relevant stakeholders. While discussions on long-term development solutions continue, we will focus on what can be done now and what passengers will be able to appreciate in the near future: making ticket purchases faster and more convenient, making information about platforms and service changes clearer, facilitating transfers and providing a higher-quality environment at the bus station,” says Vasily Serdyukov, Member of the Board of SIA RIVARO Holding.
According to the new shareholder, ticket prices are not directly determined by the owner of the bus station: fares for regional routes are approved by the state, while prices for international services are set by carriers. “The bus station generates revenue when it is convenient, accessible to passengers and in demand. That is precisely where our interest lies,” says Vasily Serdyukov.

Top EU court throws out Orban-era attempt to block funds for Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:09:19 UTC
19:09:19 KST

Editor's Note: This article has been updated with comments from the European Union Spokesperson for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy.
The EU's Court of Justice on Sept. 9 dismissed a legal challenge filed by former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban intended to prevent money linked to frozen Russian assets from being spent on the EU's military aid to Ukraine.
EU countries agreed in EU 2024 to bankroll some military assistance for Ukraine using the interest generated on Russian government assets that have been "frozen" within the EU since Moscow launched its 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Orban's Hungary in August 2025 sought to challenge the legality of the procedure that provided for the European Peace Facility — an EU instrument for providing security assistance to partner countries — to support Ukraine in this way.
However, the Luxembourg-based Court of Justice has thrown out the action as "it does not fall within the jurisdiction of the EU judicature."
"We welcome the judgement of the General Court, which confirmed the limits of judicial review in Common Foreign and Security Policy," Christian Wigand, EU Spokesperson for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy, told the Kyiv Independent.
"The decision of the European Peace Facility Committee concerned the Union's strategic or political choices and therefore fell outside the Court's jurisdiction under its case-law. This judgment means that the support already granted to Ukraine has not been called into question."
Agreements concluded by EU member states under the EU's Common Foreign and Security Policy (CFSP) generally do not fall within the court's remit.
The European Peace Facility is generally funded by direct contributions from EU countries and was established to help prevent conflict and provide non-lethal aid.
Its scope was expanded in light of the full-scale invasion to provide direct lethal aid to Ukraine, and it has provided Kyiv with 11.1 billion euros ($13 billion) of support since 2022.
However, Orban undermined the peace facility's effectiveness not only through legal challenges but also by blocking the reimbursement mechanism for EU countries purchasing equipment for Ukraine.
That issue has remained blocked even after Orban was voted out of office in April 2026, because of differences of opinion over how much to reimburse old contributions versus provide fresh support to Ukraine.
However, the EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said at a meeting of EU defense ministers on Sept. 1 that agreement was close.
"I think it's very clear that there is a determination to unlock the European Peace Facility, and that's something that we will work on very closely," Kallas said.
The current Hungarian prime minister, Peter Magyar, has not spoken about the European Peace Facility case but has adopted a more constructive approach to relations with the EU since taking office in May.
While Magyar has repeatedly ruled out his country providing direct military assistance to Ukraine, he has affirmed Kyiv's right to defend itself and signaled Budapest would not obstruct assistance from other EU members.

Israel tells UK to close East Jerusalem consulate within 30 days
Israel announced it would close the consulate after UK said it was imposing sanctions on illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank.
Israel has told the United Kingdom to close its consulate in occupied East Jerusalem within 30 days, according to reports, after the British government announced sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
Israel informed the UK of the timeline for the closure and said British diplomats working at the consulate will also lose their diplomatic status in 30 days, the Reuters news agency reported on Wednesday, citing two Israeli officials and two sources familiar with the matter.
UK staff on a US-led Gaza coordination mission, along with those in Ramallah, must also leave within seven days, Reuters reported, citing one Israeli official and the two other sources. Al Jazeera has approached the UK’s Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO) for confirmation of the reports.
This follows a series of retaliatory measures by Israel in response to the UK, France and Canada announcing sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements on Tuesday.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar confirmed the UK would be dropped from the Gaza mission and that several UK MPs, including former Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn, would be barred from entering Israel.
He also said Israel would close the UK’s consulate in occupied East Jerusalem.
“The British move is morally distorted, and constitutes blatant interference in the affairs of a sovereign state and its electoral process,” Saar said, referring to Israeli elections next month that could see Netanyahu unseated.
UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said on Wednesday he regretted Israel’s decision, but said he was not surprised.
“We weighed the costs and benefits of acting … and we thought we simply could not stand by because we feared Israeli action,” he told the BBC.
Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir said he had appealed to Netanyahu for the closure of the consulate as “Israel’s resolute response to British audacity”, accusing it of operating on behalf of the Palestinian Authority (PA).
Miliband on Tuesday told lawmakers that, in addition to banning imports of goods from Israeli settlements in the West Bank, the UK would also take measures against companies and individuals providing services to settlements, including “construction, infrastructure, financing, or real estate”.
France and Canada also said they would ban the import of products from Israeli settlements, while nine other countries, including Denmark and Portugal, endorsed the British action.
France also has a consulate in occupied East Jerusalem accredited to the PA.
The UK, France and Canada were among countries that in 2025 formally recognised the State of Palestine and have previously imposed sanctions on settlements and Israeli ministers over accusations of inciting violence against Palestinians.
Israel’s government was due to meet on Wednesday to discuss its response to the other countries that signed the UK statement.
