The war in the Gulf will have to end in compromise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:09:04 UTC
19:09:04 KST

The war in the Gulf will have to end in compromise
The US and Israel have not achieved their original objectives, Iran has not surrendered and the costs are spreading across the region.
The current Gulf war does not look like other wars. Conflicts, whether short or prolonged, usually end in one of two ways. Either one side achieves a decisive victory over the other, typically followed by the signing of a surrender agreement and the imposition of the victor’s terms on the defeated party, as happened in the first and second world wars, both of which ended in Allied victory. Or such wars end in a settlement based on the principle of “no victor and no vanquished”, with each side throwing the full extent of its military capabilities into battle against the other. Both sides are exhausted without either achieving a decisive result, at which point they move to end the fighting and reach a settlement that takes their interests into account. The war then ends almost as though it had never begun, apart from the human and material losses it caused.
One example is the Iran-Iraq war, which lasted eight years without either Iran or Iraq achieving its objectives. Iraq did not liberate Arabistan, and Iran did not succeed in overthrowing Iraq’s Baath Party regime.
Looking at America’s modern wars, the truth is that it has not won any of them. It may not have been defeated, but it did not achieve the objectives for which those wars were fought. The image of the helicopter evacuations from Saigon remains vivid, as does the historic scene at Kabul airport, when America’s allies clung desperately to a lifeline, to no avail.
In the Vietnam War, the Americans lost nearly 60,000 military personnel. The result was an agreement in Paris to end the war and provide the United States with a way out, amid a clear Vietnamese victory. The Americans withdrew from Vietnam and the country was unified on Vietnamese terms.
The same was true of the US war in Afghanistan. Thousands of tonnes of bombs were dropped on the country, only for the United States to withdraw suddenly and chaotically, in scenes that resembled an escape from disaster. Then there was the US invasion of Iraq, where the war seemed almost to have been fought on Iran’s behalf. What Tehran had been unable to achieve during the eight-year war, America achieved for it by handing Iraq over to Iran. America may lose wars, but it does not learn from them before starting another.
Today, the current Gulf war is strange and falls outside both of these familiar patterns. Last year, we were surprised by a US-Israeli war on Iran that lasted a little less than two weeks, with the aim of eliminating Iran’s nuclear programme. Yet it suddenly stopped. US warships departed, and Israeli aircraft left the skies above Tehran without dropping their payloads, following a decision by the US president. Both sides claimed victory, despite the fact that the objective of the war had not been achieved.
Things remained unchanged for months before the war suddenly resumed. At the time, the Americans and Iranians were engaged in negotiations mediated by Oman, and talks between the parties were supposed to resume just one day after the start of massive military operations: relentless bombardment from US warships and Israeli aircraft flying around the clock over Iranian cities.
The second surprise was that this war, too, stopped without warning, ushering in a period of threats that fighting would resume: US and Israeli threats met by Iranian threats, and an intermittent war in which an American strike is answered by an Iranian one, and so on. Israel, the occupying state, has meanwhile been kept out of this contest of wills.
This, then, is not a war like other wars. It resembles a cockfight. Nor is it being fought according to the principle of “no victor and no vanquished”. Both sides continue to claim that they possess the will and the ability to fight.
On the battlefield, every American strike is met by an Iranian strike, even if the Iranian response has less impact. But this means that the Iranians have not surrendered, that their resolve has not weakened and that they still retain a relative capacity to confront their adversary.
Turning to President Trump’s decision to maintain the blockade on Iran and tighten the economic sanctions he has described as devastating and unprecedented, it is worth remembering that sanctions have been imposed on Iran for more than 40 years.
This invites comparison with the sanctions and blockade imposed on Iraq after its invasion of Kuwait, which led to the deaths of hundreds of thousands amid shortages of food and medicine and impoverished Iraqis to the point that they sold their most valuable possessions simply to meet the costs of everyday life.
The blockade and sanctions therefore had an enormous impact on the lives of Iraqis. But is Iran’s situation comparable with Iraq’s? I believe it is entirely different, and the comparison is inaccurate. Iran is several times the size of Iraq. Iraq was surrounded by countries hostile to its political regime, including Iran and Syria. Its only lifeline was Jordan, which was itself constrained at the port of Aqaba to prevent any breach of the blockade.
Iran’s situation is different. It has extensive borders with several countries, including Pakistan, Afghanistan, Turkmenistan, Azerbaijan and Iraq. There is no clear hostility between Iran and these states that would lead them to tighten the blockade or adhere rigidly to US sanctions. Iraq, in fact, amounts to an open border through which Iran can obtain whatever it needs.
More importantly still, Iran has a coastline of roughly 700 kilometres on the Caspian Sea, which opens onto several countries, most notably Russia, which shares the sea with Iran and maintains good relations with Tehran. For this reason, I do not believe that the blockade and sanctions, however severe they become, will force the Iranians to back down or surrender.
In my view, if the Iranians were given a choice between surrender and fighting another war, they might choose war. They still appear to possess a degree of strength and perhaps the ability to rebuild their capabilities as well.
In conclusion, the objectives behind this US-Israeli war on Iran were to end Iran’s nuclear programme, eliminate its missile system or at least limit its range, and overthrow the regime. None of these three objectives has been achieved. It is true that the supreme leader and many Iranian leaders have been killed, that large parts of the country’s infrastructure have been destroyed and that Iran’s military capabilities have been weakened. Despite all this, the current Iranian leadership has become more hardline than its predecessors.
What is striking is the issue of freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz. It was not a direct cause of the outbreak of war, but it has become one of its consequences. It is almost as though the US-Israeli objectives of the war had been achieved, even though they have not. Restoring freedom of navigation through the strait has now become the urgent priority, in order to prevent a global rise in oil prices and avert a worldwide recession and financial and economic crisis. As a result, all efforts are now focused on this issue, while discussion of the original reasons for the war has receded.
Finally, mediation efforts must intensify, with other influential powers such as Europe and China joining the commendable efforts already being made by Pakistan, Oman and Qatar. Their involvement could give mediation greater weight, perhaps influencing the parties to the conflict and bringing them towards a compromise that safeguards everyone’s interests, ensures the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, spares the world a financial and economic crisis, and protects Arab states from bombardment and violations of their security and national sovereignty, even though they are not parties to this war.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

Ash-covered shoes and a president in crisis: A Reuters reporter remembers 9/11
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:07:39 UTC
19:07:39 KST

Ash-covered shoes and a president in crisis: A Reuters reporter remembers 9/11
WASHINGTON, Sept 9 - President George W. Bush was jogging around a Florida golf course before dawn when I first saw him on September 11, 2001.
As one of two Reuters correspondents traveling with Bush that day, I was covering what was expected to be a routine event with schoolchildren to promote his education policies. He had been president of the United States less than eight months.
Within hours, the untested Bush was confronting the worst attack on American soil since Pearl Harbor in 1941.
The tragedy unfolded as Bush visited the Emma E. Booker Elementary School in Sarasota, Florida. As the president was meeting staff and students, I was in a nearby press center set up for reporters. We watched a live television broadcast showing smoke pouring from one of the World Trade Center twin towers in New York. It had been hit by a plane in what we initially assumed was an accident. Then, as we watched, a second plane struck.
Bush was at the school, reading to children. Cameras captured the shocked look on his face as a White House aide entered the classroom and whispered to him about the second plane, saying "America is under attack."
By the end of the week, Bush would show a range of emotions as he came to grips with events that marked a turning point in his presidency and in American life — horror and anger at the attacks, grief and tears for the victims, and defiant promises to make those responsible pay.
The former president, now 80, plans to attend a ceremony on Friday to mark the 25th anniversary of the attacks at Ground Zero in New York. On Wednesday evening, he will share his reflections on the anniversary at his presidential library in Dallas, while 16 artworks he has painted reflecting the courage and sacrifice of that day will be on display.
"It became evident ... that the world had changed," Bush would later tell CBS's "60 Minutes II."
Bush spent the rest of his presidency working to prevent another such attack. The hijackings exposed security vulnerabilities, spurring increased safety measures at airports and public buildings. His administration drew fire for the harsh interrogation tactics used on some Islamic militant suspects, and his 2003 invasion of Iraq was seen by many as a costly mistake.
The former president declined an interview request from Reuters for this story.
SCRAMBLING TO PROTECT THE PRESIDENT
A quarter century later, the memories remain vivid.
In the immediate aftermath of the hijacked plane attacks, there was a scramble to protect the president. As Bush was whisked away to Air Force One to leave Florida, the scale of the crisis was becoming clear.
The World Trade Center towers collapsed, leading to the deaths of about 3,000 people. A third plane plowed into the Pentagon, killing 64 people on the plane and 125 in the building. A fourth plane slammed into a field in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, after passengers fought back against the hijackers, and all 44 people on board died.
Panic gripped Washington. Plumes of smoke from the Pentagon prompted fears of car bombs. The White House was evacuated, with the Secret Service telling female staffers to take off their heels and run.
Bush spent the day flying across the country on Air Force One, first to Barksdale Air Force Base in Louisiana and then to Offutt Air Force Base in Nebraska. Later, he was to push for improved communications equipment on Air Force One after he had trouble staying in touch with the White House as he flew around the country.
In Nebraska, he entered an underground bunker to hold a teleconference briefing with top national security aides and Vice President Dick Cheney.
Eager to return to Washington, Bush arrived back at the White House late that afternoon. That night he gave an Oval Office address.
"The pictures of airplanes flying into buildings, fires burning, huge structures collapsing, have filled us with disbelief, terrible sadness, and a quiet, unyielding anger," Bush said.
Meanwhile, along with much of the White House press corps, I was still stranded in Florida, unable to fly anywhere as all air travel had been shut down. As president of the White House Correspondents' Association at the time, I helped push for our return home, and we finally took a chartered bus back to the capital.
After a 14-hour drive, our first view of Washington was the smoking gash in the Pentagon.
On September 14, I traveled with Bush to Ground Zero. The towers were still burning, the smell evident miles away. As Bush walked around the ravaged site with then-Mayor Rudy Giuliani, there were worries that some surrounding buildings had weakened to the point of collapse.
A thick layer of ash lay everywhere, on sidewalks, streets and on the shoulders of weary firefighters.
Standing on the remains of a firetruck, Bush told emergency crews that the United States was now at war with Islamic militants.
"I can hear you! I can hear you! The rest of the world hears you! And the people who knocked these buildings down will hear all of us soon!" he said through a bullhorn.
The shoes I wore that day were covered with ash and soot. When I got back home, I put them in a plastic bag and stowed them in a closet.
Twenty-five years later, there they remain. Too ruined to wear, too dear to throw away. REUTERS

How France fell in love with Céline Dion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:07:24 UTC

How France fell in love with Céline Dion
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on:
Two years after her dazzling performance atop the Eiffel Tower for the 2024 Olympic Games in Paris, Céline Dion is back in the French capital for a series of sold-out concerts – and fans are over the moon. Some 500,000 people are expected to attend the concerts.
In the Paris suburb of Nanterre, dozens of fans took part in a karaoke event organised by the city, hoping to win the last remaining tickets. “It takes me right back to my childhood,” said one fan who has been listening to the singer for four decades. For another fan, the Canadian singer is the true Queen of Pop: “I’d rather go and see Céline than Beyoncé or Lady Gaga. I love them too, but Céline is on another level!”
Another of her biggest admirers has made a career out of being Céline. Sébastien Costic has imitated Dion across Europe for the past 30 years. A former primary school teacher, when he performs, he has the full Céline look: custom-made accessories, gowns, wigs and high heels. Since the announcement of Céline’s comeback, bookings for his tribute shows have doubled.
For Costic, Dion holds a very special place in the hearts of French people: “Today, you almost forget that she isn’t French. You feel like she’s one of us (...) because she’s so close to people – in her attitude, her popularity, and through the songs she’s shared with the world. She has also helped people around the world discover the French language.”
After being diagnosed with a rare and debilitating neurological condition, Dion was forced to put her career on hold in early 2020. Then, against all odds, she made a surprise appearance on the Eiffel Tower during the Paris Olympic Games. Her resilience was celebrated around the world.
“D’eux”: A turning point
In 1994, Céline Dion teamed up with popular French song-writer Jean-Jacques Goldman for the album D’eux. Their partnership struck the right chord: around 11 million copies were sold, making it the best-selling French-language album of all time. Co-producer Erick Benzi explains in this edition of France in Focus that, “In the United States, a singer’s voice is often used as an instrument. In France, we’re more into storytelling”.
Dion rethought the way she sang. It took her “roughly ten seconds” to understand that in French, she didn’t need to push every single note, Benzi recalls. As a result, Céline recorded three songs in one day, instead of one. Her extraordinary efficiency earned her the nickname OVNI or “Objet Vocal Non Identifié (Unidentified Vocal Object, a play on words of the acronym OVNI which stands for Objet Volant Non Identifié – the equivalent of UFO in English).
A star who keeps it real
Céline Dion’s voice is not the only reason for her vast success. She has won audiences over with her generosity and her genuine connection with fans. “She’s incredibly sincere. She doesn’t act like she’s a star”, says Thérèse Zaydman, adding “Céline Dion is the youngest of 14 children. Her parents didn’t have much money. When she was little, she slept in the drawer of a dresser! So I think she’s stayed true to her roots.”
Céline has never shied away from sharing the challenges she has faced in life: the death of her husband, René Angélil, her personal struggles and, in 2022, her diagnosis with stiff-person syndrome.
Two years later, her surprise appearance on the Eiffel Tower, where she performed “L’Hymne à l’amour”, moved the entire nation. Today, fans are counting down the days until they can finally see their idol on stage: the international superstar who calls France her second "chez moi”.

Aktif Bank becomes first Turkish bank to join China's global yuan payment system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:06:28 UTC
19:06:28 KST

Aktif Bank has become the first Turkish bank to join China’s Cross-Border Interbank Payment System (CIPS), marking a step towards expanding financial ties between Türkiye and China.
The agreement was signed on the sidelines of the China International Fair for Investment and Trade (CIFIT). CIPS facilitates international payments and settlements in Chinese yuan, potentially reducing the time and costs associated with traditional multi-currency conversions.
The bank plans to make CIPS payments available through its digital banking platform, allowing small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) as well as larger companies to conduct yuan-denominated transactions more efficiently.
Growing yuan use creates new opportunities
Aktif Bank General Manager Aysegul Adaca Ogan said CIPS, developed by the People’s Bank of China, has expanded significantly over the past five years and now serves more than 1,800 participating banks.
She said yuan-denominated payments accounted for 28 percent of China’s foreign trade volume, worth around $6 trillion, over the past five years, while trade between Türkiye and China doubled from $25 billion to $50 billion over the same period.
“With rising yuan payments in Chinese foreign trade and the growing demand for yuan payment systems in Türkiye, joining this platform has been a viable opportunity for us,” Ogan said.
Aktif Bank targets wider global payment corridors
Ogan said the bank aims to expand its international payment network beyond Europe and the Americas, with China becoming an important part of its long-term strategy.
“We have over 1,300 banks worldwide, and we want to expand our corridor to include regions like China after Europe and the Americas, after closely monitoring opportunities in the Chinese market,” she said.
Ogan added that Aktif Bank’s participation in CIFIT as the only Turkish bank represented an important step in strengthening its presence in the Chinese market.

Chinese authorities have officially confirmed that all 33 missing Latvian nationals had been in China and have no information indicating that the travellers crossed the border back into Nepal, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MFA) told LETA.
According to the MFA, this means that the Latvian nationals were most likely on the Tibetan side of the Himalayas when the catastrophic floods and mudslides struck. Chinese authorities have also asked Latvia to provide DNA samples for comparison.
It was previously reported that belongings belonging to the travellers had been found on the Chinese side near the border crossing. The MFA is currently determining whether the items will be photographed and whether the images will be made available for identification. Meanwhile, Red Cross DNA experts are expected to arrive in Nepal this week to speed up and facilitate the comparison of samples.
MFA Consular Department representative Jurģis Barkāns, who is currently in Nepal, is also exploring options for transporting to Latvia the travellers’ belongings left behind at hotels.
The MFA noted that the amount of belongings must first be established
and it must be determined whether the items can be identified. Arrangements could then be made with transport companies to bring them to Latvia.
The MFA stressed that not all relatives have received or fully understood the information sent last week regarding the necessary steps and formalities. Relatives have been sent a detailed explanation compiling information from the Ministry of Welfare, Ministry of Justice, Latvian Association of Local and Regional Governments, and Ministry of Education and Science. On Wednesday, the Ministry of Justice will hold a meeting with relatives to explain the information provided and answer their questions.
The MFA is also asking relatives who are not currently on the ministry’s contact list but believe they should receive information directly to get in touch. The ministry stressed that it is currently important for all relatives to obtain a certificate confirming the travellers’ status as missing persons. The Latvian nationals have been placed on an international missing persons list, and relatives need the relevant certificate to complete other formalities.
The Chancery of the President of Latvia has also asked the MFA to contact the Ombudsman, who is prepared, where possible, to advise both the ministry and the relatives of the missing people.
Information about this option has been sent to the relatives.
As previously reported, the collapse of a glacier on the 26th of August triggered a flow of ice debris, causing water and mud to surge from a glacial lake and resulting in widespread destruction in Nepal and China. As of the 3rd of September, the confirmed death toll had reached 1,252, while another 4,216 people were considered missing.
A large group of Latvian tourists organised by yoga enthusiasts from Yantra was also near the epicentre of the disaster, while a smaller number of Latvian tourists were in the disaster zone as part of a group organised by the local company Mighty Himalayan Trek. The MFA is aware that three Latvian residents who were in the region at the time were not affected by the flood-triggered mudslide in Nepal, while 33 are currently considered missing.

The 23-year-old man who was arrested at the Brussels South railway station with a loaded Kalashnikov last week says that he came into possession of the military grade weapon by chance and had come to Belgium to sell it. The man appeared before the Brussels magistrates’ court today.
Suspect found with Kalashnikov at Brussels South says he stole the weapon ‘by chance’
“My client came into possession of the weapon in the Lille area of France,” his lawyer Benoit Lemal told the court. “Whilst moving house, he saw a car left unlocked and unattended. He took the opportunity to steal a bag from the vehicle. To his great surprise, he found a weapon inside the bag.”
According to Lemal, the suspect, a man in his twenties, then decided to travel to Belgium to sell the weapon. “He had heard through the grapevine that such a weapon could easily be sold in Belgium and that he could make money that way. He is not part of a criminal organisation, as the public prosecutor’s office claims,” the lawyer insisted.
No plea for release
The court is deciding whether to confirm the suspect’s detention. “I have not, in any case, requested his release,” said lawyer Lemal. “I shall defer to the presiding judge’s judgement.”
A second suspect, also in his twenties, appeared before the court this morning too. “According to the public prosecutor’s office, my client is a member of a criminal organisation involved in arms trafficking, but he denies this,” his lawyer Mustapha El Hajjami says. The fifth season of Fauda has arrived on Netflix worldwide, bringing the hit Israeli series into territory shaped directly by the October 7 massacre and its aftermath.

The season begins several years after the attack, with Doron and other members of the unit struggling with what happened before being drawn into a hunt for terrorists who escaped to Europe.

After airing in Israel, the show has attracted viewers in Germany and has also been sold for broadcast in France.
Together, the selections show how Israeli television and film continue to draw on the country’s security challenges, social divisions and recent history, while increasingly finding audiences far beyond Israel.

Over 20,000 olim made Aliyah to Israel from 100 countries in past year, data shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:03:30 UTC
19:03:30 KST

More than 20,000 new immigrants arrived in Israel during the Jewish year 5786 (September 23, 2025 to September 3, 2026), coming from over 100 different countries worldwide, according to a new data report released by the Aliyah and Integration Ministry and the Jewish Agency.
The breakdown of the Aliyah figures released on Tuesday for the past year shows that Russia topped the charts with 5,685 olim (immigrants to Israel) arriving in Israel, followed by 4,364 from France, 3,333 from the United States, and 975 from the United Kingdom.
Additionally, 797 olim came from Ukraine, 491 from Belarus, 440 from Canada, 247 from Australia, 243 from Argentina, 241 from Georgia, 210 from South Africa, 210 from Germany, and 200 from Brazil.
Olim of all age groups
The data also showed that 35% of the olim were people aged 18-35, reflecting significant growth in Israeli society and the economy.
According to the data report, many of these young immigrants were physicians and professionals in in-demand fields. Some 24% of the olim are children and youth up to age 17, who have now been integrated into the Israeli education system. An additional 18% are aged 36-50, 9% are aged 51-60, 5% are aged 61-65, and 10% are 66 or older.
The two oldest olim this year were both 102 years old at the time of their arrival in the country – one from Russia and one from France. The youngest was a two-week-old infant who arrived with his family from Mexico.
Where are Olim making their start?
About 31% of all olim this year settled in communities north of Hadera or south of Ashdod. Specifically, 3,862 olim (about 20% of the total) settled from Hadera northward, while 2,247 (about 11%) settled from Ashdod southward.
Tel Aviv attracted the largest number of new olim this year, with 2,762 newcomers, followed by Netanya (2,224), Jerusalem (2,134), Haifa (1,504), Ra’anana (1,042), Bat Yam (957), Ashdod (846), Beit Shemesh (680), Ashkelon (534), and Rishon LeZion (450). Nahariya, the northernmost city on the list, absorbed 307 olim, while Eilat, the southernmost, welcomed 132.
'The essence of Zionism'
Reflecting the year’s data, the Aliyah and Integration Ministry and the Jewish Agency touched on the Diasporas connection to the Jewish state, stating in the report, “Even in a year marked by a challenging security situation, thousands of Jews from every corner of the globe chose to make aliyah to Israel, build their homes there, and raise their children there – a choice that reflects the deep and enduring connection between world Jewry and the State of Israel.”
Maj.-Gen. (res.) Doron Almog, chairman of the Jewish Agency, commented on the Aliyah numbers during a challenging year, stating that they represent “the essence of Zionism.”
“Aliyah is the strongest response to every challenge we face; it serves as a growth engine that contributes to strengthening the State of Israel,” Almog said.
Aliyah and Integration Minister Ofir Sofer emphasized, “Every oleh who arrives strengthens society, the economy, and the resilience of the country, and aliyah is a central component of its future.”

Israeli student grades dropping sharply, initial national evaluation report confirms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:03:29 UTC
19:03:29 KST

Israeli students have seen a major drop in grades and performance, according to an initial, not yet formally verified, report by the National Authority for Measurement and Evaluation in Education (known by its Hebrew acronym, RAMA), confirmed on Tuesday.
Education Minister Yoav Kisch released the RAMA report after the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) published the international Program for International Student Assessment (PISA) results on Tuesday, with officials describing the findings as a "catastrophic event on a historic scale."
According to RAMA's initial findings, which the Education Ministry emphasized were not final, only 3% of 9th-grade students were considered to be fully fulfilling the ministry's requirements in their science and technology education programs, with another 16% considered "near" full requirement fulfillment.
The number of students fully fulfilling the Education Ministry's requirements was higher in 6th-grade English (36%), mathematics (37%), and Hebrew (20%).
These results were consistent with the PISA results, in which, compared with the previous PISA tests in 2022, Israeli students fell eight places in science, seven in reading, and six in mathematics.
Across all three subjects, Israel's 2025 PISA results were the lowest ever recorded for the country.
Kisch attempts to delay RAMA release showcasing tenure failures
Every three years, RAMA and the Education Ministry publish a detailed national analysis simultaneously with, or close to, the OECD's official publication.
But long after the organization had granted media representatives full access to the data, and despite the publication being known about and scheduled years in advance, Kisch's representatives and officials from the measurement authority still had not managed to "complete the necessary coordination regarding the format of publication."
In other words, while Kisch could not prevent the publication of the embarrassing report, which presents his tenure as a failure, he tried to delay it until the last moment and held a media "briefing" at the exact time the report was released.
According to KAN News, several weeks ago Kisch requested that the RAMA report not be published on the same day as the PISA results.
Kisch published the results that day regardless, KAN reported, after the government's legal advisor said he did not have the authority to withhold the findings and after RAMA told him it intended to publish the results that day.
KAN also cited the Education Ministry as saying that the RAMA findings "are under external professional review in light of the claims raised by the ministry."
Yuval Bagno contributed to this report.

Microsoft Store returns to Syria as US restrictions on country ease
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:03:27 UTC
19:03:27 KST

DAMASCUS - Users in Syria have begun regaining access to the Microsoft Store in recent days without the need for virtual private networks (VPNs), marking a new development after years of restrictions that limited Syrians’ access to a range of digital services provided by US technology companies.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
Users inside Syria said they were able to open the store through Syrian internet connections, browse apps and games, download and install them, and update software directly. Previously, accessing the service often required a VPN or a connection routed through networks outside the country.
Access, however, does not yet appear to be universal. Other users said the store remains blocked for them or that they are still unable to access some of its services, suggesting that availability may be rolling out gradually or could vary depending on internet service providers or account settings.
Microsoft has not yet issued an official statement explaining the apparent restoration of access in Syria or why availability continues to differ among users.
The development is significant beyond access to an app store. For years, Syrians faced restrictions on US-based digital products and services due to sanctions and other controls on business and technology services provided to the country.
Syrian users, technology companies, and software developers often relied on technical workarounds to bypass geographic restrictions and access certain platforms, while other services remained entirely or partially unavailable.
US policy toward Syria undergoes transformation
The change comes as US policy toward Syria undergoes a broader transformation, with Washington easing or removing a number of restrictions previously imposed on the country. Those changes have opened the way for international companies to reassess which products and services they can legally provide to users in Syria.
So far, however, Microsoft has not publicly linked the apparent restoration of Microsoft Store access directly to those policy changes. It therefore remains unclear whether the shift in US policy is the immediate reason for the service's availability.
The return of the Microsoft Store also does not necessarily mean that all Microsoft products and services are now available in Syria. Certain subscriptions, payments, cloud products, and other services may be subject to separate rules and restrictions.
Still, the ability of some Syrians to access the Microsoft Store without using a VPN represents another indication that part of the digital isolation the country experienced for years may be beginning to recede.
The extent of that shift could become clearer in the coming weeks, particularly if Microsoft expands access to additional services and other major US technology companies take similar steps to restore their products and platforms for users in Syria.

Netanyahu to sue Haaretz, UAE won't deny MbZ 7 Oct. warning
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:03:23 UTC
19:03:23 KST

Breadcrumb
Netanyahu to sue Haaretz, UAE says 'no comment' on MbZ 7 October warning
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced on Wednesday plans to sue Haaretz over its report that UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed warned him of an imminent Hamas-led attack before 7 October 2023, while Abu Dhabi stopped short of denying the claim.
Netanyahu said he would file a libel lawsuit against the Israeli newspaper, journalist Shlomi Eldar and "other parties" over the investigation, which alleged that Mohammed bin Zayed personally warned him around a week and a half before the Hamas-led attack.
Meanwhile, the UAE foreign ministry said it does not comment on "media stories or speculation regarding conversations between government leaders", without explicitly denying that the call took place.
The ministry added that UAE and Israeli government bodies have maintained "open and direct channels of communication" since relations were established more than five years ago.
"When necessary, all relevant intelligence information has been, and continues to be, communicated between the relevant bodies," it said.
The response was described by Israel's public broadcaster Kan as ambiguous, with the outlet noting that it did not contain an explicit denial of the report.
Kan also reported that Netanyahu had sought a denial from the UAE following the Haaretz investigation.
Netanyahu's office has categorically rejected the account, saying no warning had been delivered to the prime minister by the UAE before 7 October.
On Wednesday, however, Israeli newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper cited a senior Middle Eastern intelligence official as saying Abu Dhabi had indeed passed Israel a warning about the possibility of a "large and imminent operation" by Hamas.
The unnamed official, described as having detailed knowledge of the covert relationship between Israel and the UAE and contacts before 7 October, said the information came from a "very reliable" source and was treated with "great seriousness" by Emirati officials.
According to the report, the warning reached Israel "a short time" before the Hamas-led attack and indicated that something could happen "very soon", although it did not include a specific date.
The official declined to say whether the intelligence explicitly referred to then-Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar or how the warning was passed to Israel.
He also refused to confirm whether Mohammed bin Zayed personally telephoned Netanyahu about the intelligence.
Yedioth said the official’s account nevertheless corroborated at least part of the original Haaretz report.
Netanyahu threatens legal action
Announcing the planned lawsuit on Wednesday, Netanyahu said the Prime Minister’s Office, National Security Council and military secretariat had thoroughly examined records from the period and found no trace of the alleged call.
He said diplomatic calls between himself and Mohammed bin Zayed are conducted through an unusual secure system in which an Emirati representative arrives at the Prime Minister's Office with a dedicated encrypted device.
Netanyahu said investigators had checked both his call records and records of entries to his office during the relevant period and found no record of an Emirati representative entering.
"There is no possibility of entering the Prime Minister’s Office without documentation and registration by the security authorities on site," Netanyahu said.
Haaretz said it stood by its reporting.
Yedioth, however, reported further details about the highly secretive communications between the two leaders, saying their calls are not conducted through Israeli communications systems.
According to the newspaper, an Emirati intelligence representative brings a new phone to Netanyahu's office with a dedicated application installed on it whenever a call is arranged.
The device is handed to Netanyahu before the representative leaves the room, after which Mohammed bin Zayed calls. The phone is destroyed immediately after the conversation, according to the report.
Kan similarly reported that an Emirati representative personally brings Netanyahu a dedicated phone for calls with the UAE president.
Sources who spoke to the broadcaster said Mohammed bin Zayed had himself subsequently told several senior figures about the alleged conversation.
Senior Israeli officials were surprised by the reported call, Kan said, with some only learning of it following the Haaretz investigation.
Haaretz reported on Tuesday, citing three senior foreign sources, that Mohammed bin Zayed called Netanyahu in the final days of September 2023 and warned him that Sinwar was planning a major operation against Israel.
The newspaper said the call lasted around 45 minutes and that the UAE leader feared the expected action could cause bloodshed, destabilise the region and damage the Abraham Accords.
Netanyahu reportedly responded "relatively calmly", saying he believed Hamas intended to act in the occupied West Bank and assuring Mohammed bin Zayed that Israel was prepared for all scenarios.
The investigation alleged that Netanyahu did not pass the warning on to Israel’s security chiefs.

Son of Israel’s US envoy among four fallen soldiers honored in new pre-army program
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:03:18 UTC
19:03:18 KST

A new pre-military preparatory program established in memory of four IDF reservists killed together in Gaza in November 2023 is set to open in northern Israel, the Ma’ase Center and Welfare and Social Affairs Ministry announced.
“The Four” program will operate in Eliad in the Golan Heights and is intended for young adults aged 18 to 20 from traditional, religious, and haredi backgrounds who are preparing for military or national-civic service.
The program commemorates Maj. (res.) Moshe Yedidyah Leiter, Sgt.-Maj. (res.) Yossi Hershkovitz, Master Sgt. (res.) Sergey Shmerkin, and Master Sgt. (res.) Matan Meir.
Leiter was the son of Yechiel Leiter, Israel’s ambassador to the United States.
The four men served in the 551st Brigade’s 697th Battalion and were killed on November 10, 2023, when a booby-trapped tunnel shaft exploded near a mosque in the Beit Hanoun area of northern Gaza.
The 10-month program was established by the Ma’ase Center’s Nitzotz network of preparatory programs together with the Welfare and Social Affairs Ministry.
Organizers said it would combine preparation for military or national service with leadership training, physical fitness, field exercises, agricultural work, and volunteering in northern communities.
Preparing young Israelis for service
Participants will receive guidance ahead of enlistment, including help navigating recruitment and placement procedures, alongside personal mentoring designed to strengthen discipline, self-confidence and independent living skills.
The program will also include navigation exercises, hikes, and other field activities, as well as classes focusing on Israeli identity, leadership, and Israeli society.
Its location in the Golan Heights is intended to give participants a role in supporting northern communities and agriculture following years of disruption caused by the war.
“We want to raise a generation that does not only ask, ‘What does the country give me?’ but first and foremost asks, ‘What can I give to the country?’” said Yaakov Hershkovitz, Yossi Hershkovitz’s father.
“After October 7, we all understand more than ever that Israel’s security rests on people who are willing to take responsibility, get up, and act,” he said.
Hershkovitz said that the program sought to develop the values that the four soldiers represented, including responsibility, leadership, volunteering, and commitment to Israeli society.
“Service in the IDF begins long before enlistment day,” he said. “It begins with values, responsibility, love of the land, the ability to lead [and] volunteer, [the ability to] cope with difficulty and, above all, to be a person who sees those around them.”
Program aimed at youth seeking a path to meaningful service
Liz David, director of the Residential Care Division at the Welfare and Social Affairs Ministry, said that the initiative would provide a supportive framework for at-risk young adults who wanted to enlist in the IDF and become more integrated into Israeli society.
She said the program would preserve the four soldiers’ legacy through “camaraderie, giving, responsibility, and love of the land.”
Dina Bar Hama, head of the Nitzotz preparatory programs at Ma’ase Center, said the initiative had emerged from the families’ desire to turn the loss of the four men into a long-term educational project.
“The Four Preparatory Program was born out of pain, alongside the choice to grow from it and nurture the leaders of the younger generation,” Bar Hama said.
She said participants would be taught values associated with Leiter, Hershkovitz, Shmerkin, and Meir, including responsibility, commitment, contribution to society, and camaraderie.
Hershkovitz, 44, was the principal of the ORT Pelech boys’ school in Jerusalem and had previously worked as a Jewish educator in the United States. Meir, 38, was a television producer best known for his work on the Israeli series Fauda. Leiter, 39, was a reserve company commander, paramedic, and medical student. Shmerkin, 32, was a reservist from Kiryat Shmona.
The program will join Ma’ase Center’s existing Nitzotz network, which focuses on preparing young Israelis for military and national service, and helping them develop the skills they need for employment and adult life.

İzmir celebrates 104 years since liberation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:03:00 UTC
19:03:00 KST

Izmir celebrates the 104th anniversary of its liberation. (AA Photo)
The western province of İzmir marked the 104th anniversary of its liberation from occupation on Sept. 9 with a series of ceremonies and festivities, drawing citizens from across the city.
The commemorations began in the early hours with a large-scale march, featuring a 350-meter-long Turkish flag carried through the streets. Residents gathered along the route, waving national flags as the city came together to mark the historic anniversary.
The celebrations were attended by senior political figures, district mayors, representatives of political parties and leaders of various civil society organizations.
İzmir Mayor Cemil Tugay, Governor Süleyman Elban and Aegean Army and Garrison Commander Gen. Zorlu Topaloğlu paid tribute to the founder of modern Türkiye, Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, by laying a wreath at his monument.
Addressing the crowd, Tugay said İzmir’s history was inseparable from Türkiye’s struggle for independence.
“İzmir is the name of that great struggle, from the first shot fired to victory and the pursuit of a fully independent Türkiye. İzmir is the city of liberation, the city of foundation and the city of the Republic,” Tugay said.
“On the 104th anniversary of our liberation, we are once again standing side by side, gathered in the squares with our flags in our hands and carrying that same immense sense of pride,” he added.
Tugay described Sept. 9 as a symbol of a nation’s determination to live under its own flag and on its own homeland after years of suffering, struggle and longing.
“On the 104th anniversary of our liberation, we once again share that pride and keep that determination alive together, beneath the same sky and under the crescent-and-starred flag,” he said.
The liberation of İzmir on Sept. 9, 1922, represented a decisive turning point in the Turkish War of Independence and brought the years-long occupation of western Anatolia to an end. The withdrawal of Greek forces followed their defeat in a series of battles as Turkish troops advanced westward.
Türkiye’s commemorations of the final phase of the independence struggle have been continuing for more than two weeks, beginning with the Battle of Dumlupınar on Aug. 26, 1922, which took place across several provinces in western Türkiye.
The conclusion of the battle on Aug. 30 is commemorated annually as Victory Day, a national holiday in Türkiye.
The Turkish offensive that followed Dumlupınar rapidly pushed Greek forces out of western Anatolia. Turkish troops entered İzmir on Sept. 9, with the final Greek forces subsequently leaving Turkish territory.
Afyonkarahisar, one of the key fronts of the War of Independence, has likewise hosted a weeklong program of ceremonies and events commemorating the anniversary.
The Turkish War of Independence began after Allied forces occupied parts of the Ottoman Empire in the aftermath of World War I. The ensuing national struggle, led by Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, ultimately resulted in the establishment of the Republic of Türkiye in 1923.
President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan on Sept. 9 marked the occasion, paying tribute to the heroes of Türkiye’s War of Independence.
“I commemorate with mercy and gratitude all our heroes, particularly Gazi Mustafa Kemal, who led our National Struggle to a great victory,” Erdoğan said in a social media post.
The president also congratulated İzmir on the anniversary and sent his greetings to the city’s residents.

Which Document Proves Indian Citizenship? There Isn’t 1 Answer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:02:00 UTC
19:02:00 KST

In August 2026, two former Indian bureaucrats faced a challenge they never expected: they were asked to prove their Indian citizenship.
Navdeep Suri was India’s ambassador to the UAE and Egypt, while Ramesh Chander had served as ambassador to Belarus, among their other assignments. However, amid the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of the electoral roll, their names were missing from the 2003 voter list, which is being considered as the baseline of the last “pure roll.”
Their names are missing from the 2003 roll because they were serving India abroad at that time. But the voter roll revision mechanism flagged them as suspected doubtful citizens. They were told that ordinary identity documents like Aadhaar and Voter ID will not do; they will have to support their claim with more solid documents like passports, birth certificates or old land records.
The government has said the ongoing SIR is nothing but a routine electoral roll revision process, but in a country where no single document serves as proof of citizenship — and citizenship is essential for voting rights — the electoral roll revision has led to a rush for a range of documents, from birth and school-leaving certificates to land records.
Many applied for passports even though they have no plan for travelling abroad, only because they considered a passport to be unquestionable proof of citizenship.
However, a Ministry of External Affairs official said in June that an Indian passport is a “travel document” and not itself a document of Indian citizenship and that it had never been regarded as conclusive proof of citizenship.
Others have contested this claim, citing how the government’s own material on Overseas Citizens of India (OCI) says that an Indian passport is given only to an Indian citizen.
In any case, only about 7 percent of India’s population currently holds a passport, meaning the very document many now treat as the gold standard is one most citizens have never needed and don’t have.
As recent statements by different ministers and government officials, as well as court rulings, reveal, there is no single document that alone can prove one’s Indian citizenship. It is not an issue as long as one’s citizenship is not challenged. However, as soon as one’s citizenship is challenged, the burden of proof lies on that person.
The Citizenship Act recognizes citizenship principally through birth, descent, registration, naturalization and incorporation of territory. People belonging to the last three categories usually have citizenship certificates. However, for people belonging to the first two categories — who form the overwhelming majority of Indians — citizenship has to be proved through other documents.
According to a Q & A on a government website, “citizenship can be proved by any documents related to date and place of birth.” The government has not yet clearly notified any specific document. However, it has repeatedly rejected common identity documents like Aadhaar, PAN (tax ID), voter ID, driving license, ration cards and bank records as proof of citizenship.
Recently, a Calcutta High Court ruling said that possession of a voter card, Aadhaar card, bank account documents and PAN card does not automatically constitute conclusive proof of Indian citizenship.
A Guwahati High Court order in 2022 had echoed a similar view: there is not a single document that can prove the citizenship of a person. Documents, including passport, ration card and voter ID, can constitute supporting evidence, but citizenship had to be assessed from the totality of evidence.
Recent government policies indicate that the government is increasing emphasis on birth certificates; they are being made mandatory in several aspects like admission in educational institutes and for driving licenses. The Union government has tightened rules for delayed registration of birth certificates, prioritizing integrity of the document for its importance in official purposes, including identity and citizenship-related documentation.
Over the past year and a half, when thousands, mostly Bengali-speaking Muslims, were detained in different states as suspected illegal Bangladeshi migrants, the police had mostly insisted on passports, birth certificates or school leaving certificates
The citizenship screening drive to ensure a voter roll free from illegal foreigners has led to problems due to multiple factors. Many people, especially of an older generation and from the marginalized sections of society, do not possess land records, birth certificates or school-leaving certificates.
Birth certificate possession has risen sharply for the younger generation, but remains genuinely rare for the old. The national birth registration rate was just 56.2 percent as recently as 2000 and had reached only 84.9 percent by 2017. National Family Health Survey data shows only 26.9 percent of children under five had a birth certificate in 2005-06. As registration systems improved, this share more than doubled to 62.3 percent by 2015-16.
All this means a meaningful share of adults, particularly those born before the early 2000s, have no registered record of their own birth.
Similarly, Census 2011 data put literacy among Indians aged 60 and above at just 28 percent for women and 59 percent for men nationally. This rate is lower in rural areas.
Taken together, the electoral roll revision process imposes a heavy burden of proof on older, poorer and rural Indians — the population least likely to have the paper trail the government now demands. This is why there is widespread apprehension that the voter roll revision may end up disenfranchising millions of Indians.
Given that recent months have seen a series of deportations, including wrongful ones, the disenfranchised will have reason to feel anxious about greater harassment.

‘The land had its own stories.’
A common narrative among European settlers was that the lands they occupied were empty and, therefore, free to claim. This assumption, imposed across many colonies, severed Indigenous peoples from places to which they held deep cultural and spiritual ties. Central Australia was no exception: the doctrine of ‘terra nullius’, used to justify British claims over Australia, treated the land as if it belonged to no one, disregarding the long histories of Aboriginal communities who had been living there for tens of thousands of years.
For this short documentary, the British artist Patrick Waterhouse collaborated with the Warlukurlangu art centre to revisit that history by intervening in official colonial documents and maps. Working for several years with Warlpiri artists from Yuendumu and Nyirripi, he invited them to respond to these archival materials through their own visual languages. The film captures the collaborative process, the conversations prompted by these documents and the striking works that emerge: pieces in which colonial cartography intersects with Indigenous knowledge and art.

Scientists thought “intensive parenting” was driving down birth rates. They found the exact opposite.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:00:50 UTC
19:00:50 KST

New research suggests that adopting highly demanding, child-centered parenting attitudes is associated with a stronger desire to have children. Rather than deterring people from starting or expanding families, subscribing to these ideals appears to go hand in hand with wanting to become a parent. The findings were published in the Journal of Marriage and Family.
Over the past few decades, a cultural shift has transformed how many people approach raising kids. This approach, known as intensive parenting, is a style where childrearing is viewed as an emotionally absorbing, labor-intensive, and financially demanding project. Parents are expected to place their children’s needs above their own and constantly provide stimulating activities to boost their social and cognitive development.
At the same time, birth rates have been steadily declining in many high-income nations. In Sweden, the total fertility rate dropped to an all-time low of 1.45 children per woman in 2023. Similar trends are visible across the Nordic region. For instance, a 2021 study of Finnish adults indicated that younger generations are increasingly preferring to remain childless.
“We have known for some years now that we are witnessing an unprecedented and unexplained decline in fertility,” study author Sunnee Billingsley, a professor of sociology at Stockholm University, told PsyPost. “Fewer people are entering parenthood and/or they are having fewer children overall. This is even the case in Sweden, where family policies have long been believed to hold fertility levels stable and at a high level in relation to other wealthy countries.”
Because traditional economic models suggest that rising costs reduce demand, some scholars have speculated that the heavy time and financial burdens of modern parenting are driving this fertility decline. The assumption is that people are either opting out of parenthood entirely or stopping at fewer children because they feel they cannot meet these high standards.
“When I thought about what has changed since 2010, when the fertility decline began, the shift in parenting culture caught my attention,” Billingsley said. “It seemed to me that the increased time, energy, financial, and emotional investment in children could lead to fertility decline.”
The research, led by Billingsley, aimed to test whether this assumption holds true using specific survey data. Measuring these beliefs can be complicated. For example, a 2022 study in the United States found that parents do not always adopt every aspect of the intensive parenting ideal, but rather combine different expectations in unique ways. The research team wanted to see how these varied, multidimensional attitudes directly related to individuals’ childbearing plans in a country known for strong social support.
To explore this, the researchers analyzed data from the 2021 Swedish Generations and Gender Survey. Their sample included 3,397 Swedish men and women. The women were aged 18 to 40, and the men were aged 18 to 45. The researchers excluded individuals who were currently pregnant or who reported that they were physically unable to have children.
Participants answered questions about their short-term and long-term childbearing plans. They indicated whether they intended to stay childfree, postpone parenthood, or stop having children if they were already parents. The survey also included six questions measuring intensive parenting attitudes. Participants rated their agreement with statements such as “children’s needs should come before their parents'” and “child rearing is the most demanding job in the world.”
Using a statistical technique, the researchers grouped participants into five categories based on their overall attitude profiles. These groups ranged from those who strongly endorsed intensive parenting to those who actively rejected it. The researchers then mapped these profiles against the participants’ fertility intentions.
In the study sample, 24.6 percent of childless respondents intended to remain childfree. The researchers originally expected that strong intensive parenting attitudes would increase this likelihood. Instead, the results pointed in the opposite direction.
People who held strong or moderate intensive parenting attitudes were actually between 20 and 26 absolute percentage points less likely to want to stay childfree compared to those who rejected intensive parenting ideas. Even respondents who held mixed or neutral views were less likely to want to remain childfree than the reject group.
A similar pattern emerged for parents deciding whether to expand their families. Among respondents who already had two or more children, 86.8 percent intended to stop having kids. However, those with strong intensive parenting attitudes were 14 percentage points less likely to intend to stop than the group that rejected these attitudes. This indicates that people with demanding parenting ideals were more open to having a third or higher-order child.
The researchers found no consistent link between these attitudes and the intention to simply delay having children. Childless women did not show statistically different intentions to postpone parenthood based on their attitude profiles. There was a slight indication that some men with strong attitudes were less likely to want to postpone, but the overall pattern did not clearly support the idea that intensive parenting drives people to put off starting a family.
Overall, the findings suggest that intensive parenting attitudes and the desire for children act as a package deal. Rather than scaring people away, embracing the heavy demands of modern parenting aligns with a commitment to family building. The authors note that this might reflect anticipatory socialization, a process where people who already want children naturally start absorbing the dominant parenting culture around them.
“We cannot assume that the widespread decline is due to people being resistant to parenting demands in today’s intensive parenting culture,” Billingsley explained.
“Intensive parenting norms are widespread and have made parenting more challenging,” she said. “It is very surprising that it does not seem to lead to resistance to enter parenthood. The way it seems to work is that people who are thinking about having a child also seem to be getting on board with what that requires nowadays. We call this the package deal. Those who reject the norms are also those who are seem to reject the idea of having children.”
Another explanation is that children provide a pathway for individuals to gain social esteem. If raising a successful child is viewed as a personal achievement and a reflection of good morals, people who highly value this intensive approach may be more motivated to have children to fulfill that social role.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The study relies on cross-sectional data, meaning the survey captured a single snapshot in time. This prevents the researchers from determining a strict sequence of events or verifying that attitudes directly cause specific family plans.
The survey also had a relatively low response rate. Although the researchers applied statistical weights to adjust for underrepresented groups, the findings might not perfectly capture the views of the entire population. Additionally, the questionnaire only included six items to measure intensive parenting, leaving out other dimensions of the ideology.
The Swedish context itself is another factor to consider, as the country offers robust institutional support for parents, including subsidized childcare and generous paid parental leave for both mothers and fathers. “Sweden is a unique case because of the relatively strong support families receive in the form of well-paid parental leave to fully cover infant care, job security, and a family-friendly social and work environment,” Billingsley noted.
“In addition, women have more support from their partners in the day-to-day business of childrearing compared to other non-Nordic contexts,” she added. “This means that men and women in Sweden may be uniquely able to adhere to intensive parenting norms and have a child than in other parts of the world. Whether the surprising relationship we uncovered in Sweden is generalizable is unknown. There is little research documenting patterns such as this elsewhere.”
Because these policies might buffer the potential negative impacts of intensive parenting, the relationship between these attitudes and fertility might look different in countries with weaker social safety nets. Future research will aim to address these gaps by expanding the scope of the data.
“The focus so far has been on childbearing plans in Sweden and we now have the data to look at whether these plans were realized and actual childbirth,” Billingsley said. “There is also new data allowing us to explore the intensive parenting and fertility intentions relationship across a range of countries in Europe, which will allow us to know whether the relationship is robust across different contexts.”
The study, “Are Intensive Parenting Attitudes a Deterrent to Childbearing?,” was authored by Sunnee Billingsley, Stefanie Mollborn, and Gerda Neyer.

how interior design evolves to meet new human behaviors and shifting habits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:00:39 UTC
19:00:39 KST

Shifting daily routines, remote work, and changing social habits are reshaping how we experience interior architecture. Traditional boundaries across homes, hotels, hospitals, offices and schools are dissolving to support multifaceted lives. Whether a compact apartment floor plan shifts to accommodate working from home, or a public destination merges dining with quiet retreat, spaces are being asked to accommodate different uses, experiences, and ways of interacting.
As Cheryl Durst, CEO of the International Interior Design Association and an iF DESIGN AWARD juror, notes, designers are moving away from traditional labels to focus on how people actually occupy space. Eight 2026 iF DESIGN AWARD-winning projects across Italy, Japan, Taiwan, South Korea, China, and Brazil showcase this shift through reconfigurable interiors, hybrid public hubs, and interactive objects.
Samba Shelving Unit by Maya Arquitetura | all images courtesy of iF DESIGN AWARD
IF DESIGN AWARD 2026 RECIPIENTS CHAMPION USER-LED ENVIRONMENTS
Recognized by theiF DESIGN AWARD 2026, designers such as DAIKYO, Yuko Nagayama and Associates, Yule Space, JFR Studio, Anna Maya, and Martinelli Luce with HABITS share a core spatial ethos: architecture should not dictate human behavior. Instead of expecting people to fit into fixed architectural layouts, these designers build space around individual behavior. Their work positions human experience, emotional well-being, and adaptability at the very center of the design process, letting users adjust their environments as daily needs change.
Forest Book Loft by Taiwanese studio Yule Space
DYNAMIC FLOOR PLANS, IMMERSIVE RETREATS, AND RESPONSIVE OBJECTS
The Grammoluce lamp, created by Martinelli Luce in collaboration with HABITS, turns lighting control into an intuitive, physical tactile experience. Instead of relying on digital switches or conventional dimmers, users adjust illumination by placing weighted objects directly onto the lamp’s elastic membrane. Adding weight stretches the surface and increases light output, turning an invisible atmospheric adjustment into a visible, tactile dialogue between the object and the person using it.
Grammoluce lamp, created by Martinelli Luce in collaboration with HABITS
In the Forest Book Loft, Taiwanese studio Yule Space blurs the lines between retail, hospitality, and residential retreats. Uniting a bookstore, a restaurant, and guest lodging inside a restrained, exposed-concrete frame, the design uses expansive glazed openings to pull the surrounding landscape straight into the interior. Literature, local gastronomy, and nature come together in a singular spatial narrative that constantly shifts with daylight and changing seasons, showing how multi-programmatic spaces can create deeper connections to place.
Forest Book Loft by Taiwanese studio Yule Space
The Saerodowon Pop-up & Dining space reimagines brand experience by transforming the mythical Korean paradise of Mureungdowon into a physical escape. Designed for sugar-free soju brand Saero, the interior uses layered, mountain-like exterior silhouettes and quiet wooden pavilion structures to guide visitors on a sequential journey. As guests move deeper into the space, the intense rhythm of the city fades away, leaving behind an atmosphere tailored for quiet exploration, eating, drinking, and togetherness where architecture itself sets the emotional stage.
Saerodowon Pop-up & Dining, designed by OOB Company
The Relation Wall, developed by DAIKYO in collaboration with Yuko Nagayama and Associates alongside further team members of the Relation Wall Project, addresses the limitations of the classic Japanese open-plan ‘LDK’ (living, dining, kitchen) model. Recognizing that open spaces can lack privacy as life evolves, the studio designed a movable partition system engineered with high-performance sound insulation and variable translucency. By adjusting these panels, occupants can effortlessly switch between wide-open communal spaces and quiet, acoustically isolated sanctuaries, allowing the architecture to continuously mirror changing family dynamics.
Relation Wall, developed by DAIKYO in collaboration with Yuko Nagayama and Associates alongside further team members of the Relation Wall Project
With HyperTank, JFR Studio takes spatial storytelling into total immersion, demonstrating how physical interiors can merge with digital environments. The entertainment and education complex is designed as a futuristic cosmic voyage where visitors pass through boarding concourses, interactive transit chambers, and personal hibernation pods. High-resolution LED screens, dynamic soundscapes, and tailored lighting simulate cosmic phenomena like solar flares and nebulae, proving that modern interiors can serve as active narrative journeys rather than passive containers.
HyperTank by JFR Studio
Addressing the changing role of the office, JAM BASE at Grand Green Osaka redefines the workplace around unscripted human encounters. Bringing together a diverse mix of entities — from corporations and startups to government agencies, educational institutions, and artists — the hub’s coworking and communal areas are specifically designed to spark interaction among different fields. Guided by three core principles — Midori (nature), Yohaku (open space), and Gocha-Gocha (lively mixing) — the architecture uses overlapping pathways to turn physical density into a continuous catalyst for unexpected collaboration.
JAM BASE by surDL and Nikken Sekkei Ltd
On an object scale, the Samba Shelving Unit by Brazilian architect Anna Maya brings dynamic movement directly into everyday furniture. Built from modular circular components that can be added, shifted, or completely reassembled, the shelving system mirrors the fluid, improvisational rhythm of Brazilian samba. By rejecting a static final form, the design invites the owner to become an active collaborator in shaping their own interior landscape as storage needs evolve over time.
Samba Shelving Unit by Maya Arquitetura
The Modular Home by Studio Doruk Bicer flips the conventional rulebook of micro-living by proving that small footprints do not require static sacrifices. Enclosed within just 49 square meters, its reconfigurable modules move and adjust to serve shifting daily routines. Integrated smart technology enables the architecture to extend, letting a single footprint transition between living, working, and resting areas. Instead of forcing residents to compromise their habits to fit a rigid plan, the room transforms around human activity.

Conversion therapy still practised in Switzerland, report finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09

19:00:22 KST

Conversion therapy still practised in Switzerland, report finds
A report published on Tuesday by the Intercantonal Centre for Information on Beliefs (CIC) confirms that conversion therapy is being practised in religious and spiritual settings in the cantons of Geneva and Vaud. The report also includes testimonies from victims of these practices.
The report says conversion therapy can cause profound and lasting harm, in some cases leading to suicide. Eighteen people who had been subjected to attempts to change their sexual orientation or gender identity gave first-hand accounts to the CIC.
More
Seven graphics showing how LGBTIQ+ people are doing in Switzerland
The authors of the study highlight what they describe as a destructive psychological mechanism. “The process at work is one that intensifies feelings of guilt. Many victims already carry a sense of guilt linked to their sexual orientation, which is further reinforced when attempts to change it fail,” they explain. The failure of those attempts is often interpreted as a lack of faith or personal weakness.
The investigation, carried out between 2023 and 2026, was based on 41 interviews, observations and an analysis of numerous documents. “Our study clearly shows that practices aimed at changing or suppressing emotional and sexual orientation or gender identity do exist in the cantons of Vaud and Geneva,” says Manéli Farahmand, the centre’s research director.
Prevalence of practices in Christian circles
These practices are rarely described as conversion therapy. They exist on a spectrum, ranging from structured programmes to less visible and more informal forms. They include prayer sessions involving the laying on of hands, guided readings, exorcism sessions and even so-called energy healing.
More
Switzerland’s queer community fears rollback of LGBTIQ+ rights
All of these approaches are based on the belief that heterosexuality and the gender binary are the natural or divine norms. As a result, any identity that falls outside those norms is treated as a “disorder” or a “wound”.
The study found that these practices are most prevalent in certain Christian groups, including Evangelicals, traditionalist Catholics and Charismatic Christians, largely reflecting Switzerland’s religious landscape. Similar practices were also identified within New Age and holistic spirituality contexts.
Support for the victims
In light of the findings, the CIC is developing awareness-raising resources. “Recognising that these practices exist inevitably raises the question of how best to support those affected by them,” the research team concluded.
+ Swiss government backs federal ban on conversion therapy
Legally, the cantons of Neuchâtel, Valais and Vaud have already banned conversion therapy. A draft bill is currently under consideration in Geneva. There is still no federal legislation in place, but the Swiss government has expressed its willingness to introduce it. The issue now lies with the Senate.

How Silk Road as East-West melting pot turns Central Asia into culinary destination

Unknown Publisher

How Silk Road as East-West melting pot turns Central Asia into culinary destination
Far more than a simple trade route, ancient network was a vibrant hub of cultural exchange that shaped modern culinary landscape, say scholars
Imagine it is the height of the Tang dynasty (618–690, 705–907), and the imperial court awaits a gift of pure opulence.
The exotic luxury would not have been a golden statue or precious gem; those were easy enough for high royalty to procure. Rather, it was a humble peach, specifically, the “golden peach of Samarkand,” which symbolised the allure and mystery of a faraway land.
Originating in what is modern-day Uzbekistan, the luscious peach shows how food spread along the Silk Road and how Central Asia often served as a centre for cultural blending, particularly in spreading ingredients both East and West.
“In many ways, Central Asia is a forgotten land, and few people in East Asia or Europe are familiar with the many names of prominent empires that rose and fell in this vast region,” said Dr Robert N. Spengler III, the director of the Paleoethnobotany Laboratories at the Max Planck Institute for the Science of Human History in Germany.
He pointed out that Central Asia sat at the crossroads of the Silk Road, and that foods like rice, chicken, and melons came from China, while items like wheat, lentils, cattle, and fava beans spread from Southwest Asia. All of them travelled through Central Asia.

Republicans kick off ‘midterm convention’ to overcome Trump unpopularity

2026-09-09

19:00:06 KST

Republicans are gathering in Texas on Wednesday for a rare “midterm convention”, as they attempt to convince Americans to vote for a party led by a deeply unpopular president who has overseen inflation and led the US into an increasingly unpopular war.
Donald Trump will dominate the two-day convention, appearing both nights as the GOP works to cling to control of the House of Representatives in November. Republicans plan to put the president at the center of the event, a bold strategy given his approval rating is hovering at about 38%, while accusing the Democratic party of being socialist and out of touch with Americans.

Less than two months out from the midterm elections, the Republican party faces a serious battle to retain its slender control of the House, while Democrats are increasingly hopeful they could pick up Senate seats. Winning either would put the Democratic party in position to stymie Trump’s aims during his final two years in office.
The convention represents perhaps Republicans’ final opportunity to make a large-scale, high-profile pitch to Americans. Whether voters buy that is a different matter, given costs, including gas prices, have risen during Trump’s presidency. Forecasters give Republicans a slim chance of holding on to the House, in particular, and some members of Congress have been keen to distance themselves from the event. Several Republican members of Congress said they will skip it entirely.

He also alleged that Trump’s efforts to enact restriction on mail-in voting amount to a promise to end fair elections in the future.
“If Democrats don’t win, if they don’t win in this election, we may not have other elections,” Pritzker said. “Or certainly we’re going to have future elections, every single one of which will be rigged.”
Hakeem Jeffries, the House minority leader, said a contingent of Democrats on Thursday will “counter the falsehoods and extremism” on display in American Airlines Center.
Republicans facing close re-election bids have proved particularly likely to dodge the event, mindful that their Democratic opponents are looking for any opportunity to tie them to Trump. Tom Barrett, facing a close re-election fight in Michigan, and Zach Nunn, locked in a tight race in Iowa, are among those who have said they won’t be in Texas, and on Thursday Axios reported that “only about 100 lawmakers and candidates are expected to attend.”
As well as risking association with Trump, there was the issue of cost. Multiple reports have suggested that House Republicans were being asked to donate at least $25,000 to the party to get a ticket.
Among the few who are confirmed to be attending are JD Vance and the former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt, along with Ken Paxton, the Republican candidate for Senate in Texas who is polling neck-and-neck with Democrat James Talarico in a state that hasn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1988.
There are signs too, that enthusiasm is low among the rank and file. The RNC announced in mid-August that Americans could apply for tickets to attend the event, suggesting that applicants would enter a lottery, and only a lucky few would be granted access.
Yet on Friday, days before the event was due to begin, applications for tickets were instantly being granted on an RNC sign-up page, suggesting the event was not yet at capacity.
Should the attendance be lacklustre, it will be a clear indictment of Trump himself, given RNC marketing materials in the buildup had made it clear it was the president’s show. Indeed, some messages billed the event as “Trump’s midterm convention” – ditching the term ‘Republican’ altogether – while every press release has been at pains to stress Trump will be there both nights.
Trump himself was bullish about the convention in a podcast interview last week, telling the Texas lieutenant governor, Dan Patrick: “It’s going to be big stuff.”

  Chris Hippensteel contributed to reporting
