ECB to hike rates again due to inflationary pressures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
09:35:30 UTC
18:35:30 KST

Burhan Sansarlioglu, Emirhan Yilmaz and Emir Yildirim
09 September 2026•Update: 09 September 2026
The European Central Bank (ECB) is gearing up for its second rate hike of the year amid inflationary pressures, mostly due to energy prices, while all eyes are turned to the bank’s projections and its president Christine Lagarde’s upcoming statements.
Oil prices once again reached $100 a barrel due to the ongoing Middle East conflict, while natural gas prices in Europe rose to levels higher than those of 2023.
The eurozone’s annual inflation rose to its highest level in the past three years at 3.3% in August due to the rapid rise in energy prices.
Peter Vanden Houte, chief economist at the ING Group, told Anadolu that the bank is expected to raise its deposit rate by 25 basis points to 2.5% due to the eurozone economy’s resilience and that high energy prices pushed inflation back up above 3%.
Houte stated that core and services inflation have yet to signal broader concerns as the ongoing pressures remain largely energy-driven, which could prevent the ECB from adopting an overly hawkish stance at its upcoming conference.
“We expect the ECB’s new projections to contain only modest upward revisions to growth and inflation forecasts,” he said. “Although financial markets are pricing in further rate increases later this year, we are a bit more cautious.”
Houte noted that the bank might adopt a wait-and-see stance after this month’s rate hike.
“Only if the Middle-East conflict drags on, potentially pushing energy prices even higher, the ECB might consider hiking rates again in December,” he added.
Bill Diviney, head of macro research and senior eurozone economist at ABN AMRO, told Anadolu that the bank’s updated macroeconomic forecasts and Lagarde’s remarks will draw attention from the markets, as the ECB’s 2027 inflation forecast is expected to see an upward revision.
“Lagarde will likely be pressed on the prospect of future moves given that markets are pricing in nearly two more hikes after September’s move, but while we expect hawkish rhetoric around inflation, she is likely to reiterate the ECB’s meeting-by-meeting approach,” he said.
Alain Durree, head of European macro research at Natixis, stated that Lagarde might adopt a neutral tone in the near future to keep all options on the table while avoiding signaling a prolonged rate-hiking cycle.
Durree noted that the ECB would not pause rate hikes until the end of 2027.
“First, a resolution of the Middle East conflicts by early January should ease energy prices. Second, softening labor market conditions by then will limit the risk of second-round effects,” he said.
“Third, the projected appreciation of the euro will further dampen both headline and core inflation,” he added, noting that these three main factors could support the bank’s likelihood to continue rate hikes despite a complex economic balance after September.
Marco Wagner, senior economist at Commerzbank, told Anadolu that the bank’s trajectory after this month’s rate hike is “less certain.”
“Investors in the futures markets expect two more rate hikes by the middle of next year; however, we consider it more likely that key interest rates will remain unchanged in the coming months,” he said.

Aktif Bank became the first Turkish bank to participate in China’s Cross-Border Interbank Payment System (CIPS) in a newly signed deal at the China International Fair for Investment and Trade (CIFIT).
The system facilitates global payments and settlements to be made in Chinese yuan while eliminating the time and cost differences that traditional multi-currency conversions require, which is expected to benefit Turkish small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) alongside large corporations, the bank’s general manager told Anadolu.
Aysegul Adaca Ogan, speaking on the sidelines of the event, stated that the relatively young platform was developed by the People’s Bank of China (PBoC) and has grown over the past five years with foreign banks participating in the scheme, serving over 1,800 banks.

“With rising yuan payments in Chinese foreign trade and the growing demand for yuan payment systems in Türkiye, joining this platform has been a viable opportunity for us,” she said.
Ogan stated that Aktif Bank will open its digital banking platform to enable SMEs to make payments through CIPS.
“We have over 1,300 banks worldwide, and we want to expand our corridor to include regions like China after Europe and the Americas, after closely monitoring opportunities in the Chinese market,” she said.
“We’re the only Turkish bank at the fair’s pavilion and our presence here today is an important step in our long-term strategy,” she added.

KONGSBERG adds U.S. radar to its top-selling gun system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
09:33:16 UTC
18:33:16 KST

- KONGSBERG has integrated Echodyne's MESA radar into its PROTECTOR RS4 and RS6 remote weapon stations to counter drones.
- The PROTECTOR family is the world's most widely fielded remote weapon station, with more than 25,000 units delivered to over 31 countries.
Norwegian defense company KONGSBERG has selected a radar built by U.S. firm Echodyne to help its remote weapon systems detect and shoot down drones, the companies announced September 9.
KONGSBERG has integrated Echodyne’s MESA radar into its PROTECTOR RS4 and RS6 remote weapon stations, turning the widely used gun mounts into counter-drone systems capable of tracking and engaging small unmanned aircraft. The PROTECTOR family is the most widely fielded remote weapon station in the world, with more than 25,000 units delivered to over 31 countries and more than 8 million hours of combat use, including in Ukraine. The stations let troops fire machine guns, grenade launchers or larger weapons from inside a vehicle, using cameras and sensors instead of exposing a gunner.
Echodyne’s MESA radar is a solid-state, electronically steered radar built to be smaller and lighter than traditional radar systems with similar performance, a design meant to let it fit on vehicles and stationary mounts without adding significant weight or power draw. The radar feeds range, speed, bearing and other tracking data to the weapon station’s fire-control system, which the companies say helps the gun hold a stable lock on fast, small drones that are difficult for older sensors to track.
“Integrating MESA radar gives the PROTECTOR family the precise, stable and persistent tracks needed to cue the fire-control system, sustain target lock and act decisively against fast-moving, low-signature drone threats,” said Eben Frankenberg, CEO of Echodyne. “Just as important, MESA delivers that performance in a compact, software-defined package that can scale across a large installed base and adapt as the threat evolves.”
The radar becomes especially useful when PROTECTOR systems fire programmable airburst rounds, ammunition set to detonate near a target rather than on direct impact. Precise tracking of a drone’s speed and distance helps the system time the round’s detonation to catch the target in its flight path. The radar can also work alongside other sensors on the battlefield, receiving a target track from a separate radar or spotting system and refining it for the weapon station to use.
Echodyne and KONGSBERG have spent several years testing the radar-equipped system together before this announcement, the companies said, and plan to keep working on other uses for the radar across KONGSBERG’s broader product line. Beyond the PROTECTOR integrations already announced, the companies did not specify which additional systems they are exploring or provide a timeline.
Echodyne has previously supplied radar for counter-drone work with the Australian Defence Force and other security applications, but this marks its selection for KONGSBERG’s PROTECTOR line specifically. The two companies are exhibiting the system this week at the MSPO defense exhibition in Kielce, Poland, which runs through September 11.

The Italian Ambassador to Budapest, Giuseppe Scognamiglio, traveled to Székesfehérvár, a city in central Hungary, to participate in the celebrations marking the 10th anniversary of the activation of the NATO Force Integration Unit Hungary, in the presence of Hungarian State Secretary for Defense Attila Elek Varga.

Logistics centers, cargo terminal, warehouses hit: group strikes by Russian Armed Forces

MOSCOW, September 9. /TASS/. Russian forces continued to carry out group strikes overnight against military-industrial facilities and seaports in Ukraine, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
TASS has compiled the main information about the strike targets.
Defense Ministry’s statement
- Overnight, the Russian Armed Forces continued to carry out group strikes on military-industrial facilities, seaports in Ukraine, and ships, as well as logistics centers supporting the Ukrainian armed forces, the ministry reported.
Targets of strikes
- According to the ministry, the strikes in Kiev hit a warehouse belonging to a company that manufactures unmanned boats and fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), as well as their components.
- The Russian Armed Forces also struck logistics facilities at the Starokazachye road checkpoint in the Odessa Region, which were used to transport military cargo into Ukrainian territory.
- In addition, the Russian military carried out strikes with high-precision weapons against warehouses containing military equipment and fuel and lubricants used to support the Ukrainian armed forces in Nikolayev and the Nikolayev Region.
- The Nikolayev-2 logistics center, used to store military cargo and equipment for the Ukrainian armed forces, was struck.
- The Russian Armed Forces also struck the Elektrotechnika logistics center, used to store and distribute unmanned aerial vehicles and their spare parts.
- In addition, a warehouse terminal of the Dimetra company, used to store military equipment of the Ukrainian armed forces, was struck.
- The Russian military also struck the Zhovtnevoye warehouse terminal, storing fuel, lubricants, and military equipment for the Ukrainian armed forces.
- The ministry specified that six tanks with fuel and lubricants for the Ukrainian army, as well as five storage facilities with military cargo, were destroyed.
- In addition, the Russian Armed Forces carried out strikes with precision weapons against warehouses, logistics facilities, and energy infrastructure used to support the Ukrainian armed forces in Nikolayev and the Nikolayev Region.
- As a result, the Nika Terra cargo terminal, storing fuel and lubricants as well as military equipment of the Ukrainian armed forces, was struck.
- The ministry specified that three tanks with fuel and lubricants for the Ukrainian armed forces, as well as three storage facilities with military cargo, were destroyed.
- The Russian military also struck an UAV production facility and a UAV storage warehouse located on the terminal grounds.
- In addition, the Metro logistics center, used to store military cargo and equipment for the Ukrainian armed forces, was struck.
- The Defense Ministry added that strikes were also carried out against the ATP YUTK logistics center, used to store military cargo and equipment intended to support the armed forces of Ukraine, and the Nova Poshta logistics center, used to deliver, distribute, and store military cargo and equipment for the Ukrainian military.
- In addition, four fuel and lubricant tanks and a warehouse with military equipment for the Ukrainian armed forces were struck in the port of Nikolayev.
- Russian forces struck a dry cargo ship sailing to the port of Odessa that was delivering military cargo to Ukraine.
- Earlier, the Defense Ministry reported that service members of the Russian unmanned systems forces units struck an enemy tank and armored vehicles between the settlements of Sliznevo and Kurgannoye in the Kharkov Region.
Situation in Ukraine
- Ukrainian media reported explosions overnight and on Wednesday morning in Kiev, Nikolayev, Romny in the Sumy Region, and in Kharkov.
- Industrial facilities sustained damage in the Belotserkovsky, Buchansky, and Obukhovsky districts of the Kiev Region, Timur Tkachenko, head of the regional administration, reported on his Telegram channel.
- He added that warehouses in the region were also damaged.
- Operations at the Tudora-Starokazachye border crossing between Moldova and Ukraine were suspended after explosions were reported on the Ukrainian side overnight, the Moldovan Border Police reported.
- According to Ukrainian authorities cited by the police, the Starokazachye checkpoint was hit by a drone.
- No drone debris or other objects posing a threat to public safety were found in the border zone on Moldovan territory, the police added.
- Military cargo for the Ukrainian armed forces is being delivered from Romania via international checkpoints in the Odessa Region, transiting through Moldova.
- The Ukrainian Starokazachye checkpoint, located on the border with Moldova in the Odessa Region, has suspended operations following the explosions, the State Border Guard Service of Ukraine reported.

Flower-crowned cows bring Alpine tradition to Gstaad festival
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
09:30:27 UTC
18:30:27 KST

Decorated cows made their way from the Alpine pastures into Gstaad on Saturday for the annual Züglete festival in Switzerland. Families dressed their animals with floral crowns before leading them down the mountain and through the busy town centre.
The event marks the traditional move from the summer pastures to their winter farms. Crowds gathered along Gstaad's promenade to watch several herds pass, while cowbells and alphorns added to the day's celebrations.
The festival also drew visitors from abroad. Two tourists from Melbourne said they had built their European holiday around seeing the Züglete after discovering the event online. The cows will continue towards their winter homes, with the journey reversed in spring when they return to the Alps.

The Fairphone (Gen 6+) Review: Finally in the US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

Finally available in the US! Repairable with long-term software support. Five-year warranty. Good performance. Daylong battery life. Distraction-free mode. Expandable storage. Capable cameras.
TIRED
Feels very plasticky. Not supported on Verizon, with caveats on other carriers. Not waterproof. Cameras still don’t match the competition.
It’s time to vote with your wallet.
The US has long had fewer smartphone options than the rest of the world. The Apple-and-Samsung duopoly, supported largely by carriers—where people buy most smartphones—has made it hard for other phone brands to break through. It’s partly why the Dutch manufacturer Fairphone hasn’t sold its repairable, ethically made smartphone in the US in its 13-year existence—until now.
Fairphone finally made it across the pond with a new model, the Fairphone (Gen. 6+). If you’ve complained about the lack of repairable smartphones, the inability to self-replace a battery, or even the idea of a more ethically manufactured phone, the Fairphone should be on your list (if it’s time to upgrade).
I’ve been using this $650 Android handset for several weeks, and it’s pretty good.
Fairer Phone
There isn’t much of a difference between the Fairphone (Gen. 6) I reviewed last year and the (Gen. 6+). The phone comes in a new cobalt blue color to commemorate people who work in the cobalt mines (a crucial component in smartphones) and the Fair Cobalt Alliance, a nonprofit cofounded by Fairphone.
Chiefly, the Fairphone has a slightly more souped-up processor—the Qualcomm Snapdragon 7s Gen 4—alongside 12 GB of RAM. That last part is important, as many of the new software features in our smartphones, specifically those powered by artificial intelligence, demand a lot of memory; the 12 gigs here should give the Fairphone a longer shelf life in being able to take advantage of those capabilities.
Performance has been plenty satisfactory, whether I was using Google Maps to navigate, doomscrolling through Instagram Reels, or playing PokémonGo while waiting for a doctor’s appointment. My benchmarks show the tiniest of performance bumps over the processor in the Gen 6. You may see a slight stutter here and there, but it barely affects day-to-day use. The software is also more polished this time around; I haven’t run into notable bugs, which I can’t say for last year’s model.
I don’t mind the look of the new Fairphone—the blue and the yellow-accented button is a fun combo—but it does have a very plasticky feel. You might like Fairphone’s accessory system, which lets you replace part of the backplate with accessories like a wallet or phone grip by removing two screws (you can use the included screwdriver). I haven’t bothered, as it feels a little clunky; I don’t want these items permanently on the back, and unscrewing them is a hassle. Hopefully, Fairphone can move to a MagSafe-like system in the future.
The 6.3-inch AMOLED, 120-Hz screen is more than adequate. It’s colorful, sharp, and bright enough to read in sunlight. Fairphone’s adaptive brightness mode can be a little aggressive, so I often manually adjusted the brightness slider, but I don’t have much else to complain about.
Battery life from the 4,415-mAh cell isn’t impressive, but it won’t have you running to a wall outlet all the time either. I typically ended most days with around 20 percent by bedtime; that’s with around five to six hours of screen-on time. It’s a shame there’s no wireless charging, but that’s a nice-to-have not necessarily a deal-breaker. Oddly, the phone doesn’t come with a USB-C cable (the lack of a charging block is standard across phones these days), but the idea is that you probably have one lying around in a drawer. Less e-waste!
The dual-camera system, powered by a 50-MP main and a 13-MP ultrawide, is solid. No, Fairphone can’t really compete with the big tech giants like Google, Apple, and Samsung on this front. Low-light scenes suffer the most, with details lost in shadows—stay very still to avoid a blurry image. Photos from the 32-MP selfie camera can also look a little soft. Still, it’s not so poor that you won’t use it. You’ll get perfectly adequate results, but if you rely heavily on your smartphone’s camera for video and photos, you may want to look elsewhere.
Photograph: Julian Chokkattu
Main camera
Fairphone doesn’t meddle too much with the base Android 16 software, except for Fairphone Moments, which is tied to the yellow switch on the right edge of the phone. Flick the switch and the phone’s interface goes minimal, only offering access to a handful of apps. You can create your own Moments—up to five apps—to help you focus on the task at hand. For example, if you’re driving, you can flick the switch and have it only let you access Google Maps, Spotify, and Phone. It’s a neat system, though its practicality completely depends on your willpower to use it.
I’d have liked to see Fairphone win some brownie points with a headphone jack, but alas. You’ll at least appreciate the microSD card slot to expand on the already generous 256 GB of internal storage (unusual at this price). You might even prefer the capacitive fingerprint sensor baked into the side power button, rather than the under-display fingerprint sensor in most Android phones.
Long-Lasting
People are holding onto their phones for longer. But manufacturers can do several things to make it easier. Software and security updates are crucial, and thankfully, Fairphone promises seven years of updates through 2033. It also comes with a five-year warranty, virtually unheard of for a phone.
A big part of the Fairphone is repairability (iFixit gave it a 10/10 score). With the included screwdriver, you can remove that same backplate mentioned earlier to access the battery. Fairphone has instructions on its website for accessing the 11 other components you can replace, from the speakers and display to the USB-C port. Fairphone will sell these parts through 2033, and they’re cheap, too! Replacing the display, for example, will cost just $90. (You can also access most of this information in the preinstalled My Fairphone app.)
There are some caveats. The Fairphone (Gen. 6+) only has an IP55 dust- and water-resistance rating, meaning it’ll be fine in the rain, but a drop in the pool may wreck it. That’s the trade-off for having such easy access to the device’s internals for repairs.
And while the Gen. 6+ works on T-Mobile and AT&T, it doesn’t support Verizon (which includes all the smaller MVNOs that rely on Verizon’s network, like Visible). Fairphone’s website has a chart showing carrier compatibility, and you’ll see that some MVNOs on AT&T’s network are only partially supported, like Boost Mobile and Cricket. Other limitations include the lack of millimeter-wave 5G or missing eSIM support on T-Mobile. For what it’s worth, I’ve used it with an eSIM on Google Fi—the phone dips to 4G more often than other phones, but it hasn’t been a big issue for me. Your mileage may vary.
Can you find better specs for the money? Sure. The Pixel 10a will easily give you a better camera system. For $50 more, the new Samsung Galaxy S26 FE delivers flagship-grade performance and a telephoto camera. But you’ll also be out of pocket if you drop either phone and need a screen replacement. The Fairphone doesn’t have that problem, and you’ll have a little more peace of mind that your phone was made sustainably, with fair wages paid out to folks in the supply chain. The Fairphone (Gen. 6+) proves you no longer have to make massive compromises just to take a stand.
Julian Chokkattu is Senior Editor, Gear at WIRED, overseeing personal technology, gadgets, and gizmos. He has been reviewing consumer products for a decade, specializing in mobile—from smartphones, tablets, and smartwatches to smart glasses and virtual reality. This is his sixth year at WIRED. Previously, he was the mobile and wearables ... Read More

Russian sources warn Ukraine’s drone war has entered a new sea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
09:29:07 UTC
18:29:07 KST

- Russian sources describe a pattern of Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian-linked assets expanding from the Black Sea into the Caspian and Baltic seas and now the Mediterranean.
- Ukraine's SBU has publicly claimed only one of three cited Mediterranean strikes, the December 2025 attack on the tanker Qendil.
A Russian military-affiliated Telegram channel has raised alarm that Ukraine’s reach at sea now extends beyond the Black Sea into the Mediterranean, framing a string of drone strikes on Russian-linked vessels there as part of a wider pattern that has already put Russian military and commercial assets at risk across three separate seas.
Ukraine’s drone campaign against Russian naval and shipping targets started in the Black Sea, where a senior U.S. defense official said last year that Ukrainian forces had destroyed or damaged at least 32 medium to large Russian naval vessels, forcing much of Russia’s fleet to relocate away from Crimea. Kyiv has since extended that campaign into the Caspian Sea, over 1,000 km from Ukrainian territory. Ukraine’s military intelligence claimed its first Caspian strike in November 2024, damaging the missile ships Tatarstan and Dagestan at the port of Kaspiysk in Russia’s Dagestan region. Ukrainian forces have hit Caspian targets repeatedly since, including three Lukoil offshore drilling platforms in January 2026 and an FSB border patrol boat in May 2026, with Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces publicly claiming responsibility for each strike.
Ukraine has also struck Russian assets in the Baltic Sea. In May 2026, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukrainian drones hit the Baltic port of Primorsk, setting it on fire, and struck an oil tanker, a Karakurt-class missile ship and a patrol boat. Kyiv also blew up the Russian Baltic Fleet corvette Boyky at Kronstadt Naval Base. Ukrainian or suspected Ukrainian drones later crossed into NATO airspace over the Baltic states and Finland that same spring, according to open-source tracking, during the wider campaign against Russian oil export infrastructure at ports including Primorsk and Ust-Luga.
Against that backdrop, the Mediterranean now appears to be the newest theater. Ukraine’s SBU security service publicly claimed responsibility for a December 2025 drone strike on the Qendil, an Oman-flagged crude oil tanker tied to Russia’s sanctioned shadow fleet, more than 2,000 km from Ukraine. The SBU said its Alpha special unit used aerial drones to critically damage the empty tanker, and Reuters confirmed the vessel shown in strike footage matched the Qendil using file imagery.
Two more Mediterranean incidents remain unconfirmed by Ukraine. In March 2026, the Russian-flagged LNG tanker Arctic Metagaz caught fire and sank between Libya and Malta while carrying gas from the Russian port of Murmansk. Russia’s Transport Ministry blamed Ukrainian naval drones and called the strike an act of terrorism; Libyan port authorities confirmed the vessel suffered explosions and a fire before sinking, and all 30 crew members were rescued.
Ukraine did not respond to the allegation. In the most recent incident, on September 6, 2026, Russian opposition journalist Alexander Nevzorov published footage he said showed the sanctioned, Russian-flagged cargo ship Lady Mariia struck 12 times by drones while carrying Iranian weapons and armored vehicles toward Russia. Neither the strike’s origin nor the cargo claim has been independently verified.

Exhumation ordered in renewed probe into death of intel official
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
09:28:11 UTC
18:28:11 KST

Authorities are set to exhume the body of Kaşif Kozinoğlu, a former senior official at Türkiye’s National Intelligence Organization (MİT), as part of a death investigation that was reopened 15 years later, in an effort to uncover further evidence surrounding his death.
Kozinoğlu’s grave in Istanbul’s Ümraniye district is expected to be opened in the coming days. Tissue samples taken from the grave will undergo toxicological and chemical analyses.
Investigators will also examine whether Kozinoğlu was given any medication other than those he was prescribed while in prison.
Kozinoğlu was arrested in 2011 as part of the Ergenekon investigation. The Ergenekon trial was later found to have been based on fabricated evidence and allegations made by FETÖ, who sought to purge military officers by accusing them of plotting a coup.
Kozinoğlu died in prison on Nov. 12, 2011, during the eighth month of his detention, shortly before he was scheduled to testify in the case.
His death was officially attributed to a heart attack. However, questions were raised over whether he had received timely and adequate medical attention, while allegations that he may have been poisoned also fueled controversy surrounding his death.
The case file also contained conflicting accounts from prison guards and medical personnel regarding the circumstances under which Kozinoğlu was transferred from the prison to hospital.
The investigation into his death was recently reopened after the Justice Ministry established a special unit to examine unresolved cases that have attracted significant public attention.
As part of the renewed investigation, security camera footage showing how long it took for an emergency alarm to be noticed on the night Kozinoğlu fell ill is being re-examined, along with an email reportedly sent to his lawyer after his death.
One of the key areas of focus in the reopened investigation is an allegation that Kozinoğlu had requested Coraspin, a blood-thinning medication and vitamin pills shortly before his death, but that the vitamin medication was not subjected to a detailed toxicological and chemical analysis during the autopsy.
The case file also includes an email reportedly sent to Kozinoğlu’s lawyer after his death, which allegedly claimed that his death was not caused by a heart attack.

Hong Kong targets biomedicine powerhouse status in debut 5-year plan
Tied to the national strategy, the city’s first five-year blueprint doubles down on Greater Bay Area medical tech and healthcare cooperation

Hong Kong’s first-ever five-year plan is expected to be unveiled on September 16 at a Legislative Council meeting, followed by Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu’s 2026 policy address.

Iran said on Wednesday it had attacked 10 ships near the Strait of Hormuz after the U.S. sank five Iranian oil tankers, in the biggest declared wave of tit-for-tat attacks on shipping by both sides since the start of the six-month-old war. REUTERS

rodolphe parente and marion mailaender revive the spirit of 1985 paris sports club
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
09:25:44 UTC
18:25:44 KST

rodolphe parente and marion mailaender reimagine ken club
Rodolphe Parente and Marion Mailaender reimagine Paris’ Ken Club as an architecture in motion, bringing the 1985 identity of the fitness and social club into a contemporary setting opposite the Eiffel Tower. The architects approach the past as an architectural remix, shaping a place where the visual language and atmosphere of the 1980s are sampled, reworked, and given a new rhythm. Parente and Mailaender imagine the club almost as a film set built to last, recreating the atmosphere of another era without turning the interiors into a period replica. Saturated colors, rounded forms, reflective surfaces, and theatrical contrasts between light and shadow give the spaces a sense of movement.
all images by Ludovic Balay
The Parisian sports club looks back to its 1985 beginnings
When Mireille and Pierre Benzaquen founded the Ken Club in 1985, it quickly became a social spot where people came to exercise, meet, and spend time together. Forty years later, the renovation takes that history as its starting point. Parenteand Mailaender were tasked with recreating the spirit of the original Ken Club without copying its appearance. References to the 1980s are abstracted and redistributed throughout the interior, allowing the building to acknowledge its past.
A light-filled interior is organized around seating areas, pools, circulation routes, and planted zones, while strong graphic interventions interrupt the architectural framework. Pale surfaces meet turquoise, yellow, pink, and green, producing an environment that feels deliberately removed from the visual language often associated with fitness spaces. A patterned ceiling spreads irregular green forms across a warm yellow surface. Seen from below, the composition reads almost like an oversized graphic work, while its scale turns the ceiling into an active part of the spatial experience. Circular openings are cut into walls, framing views between rooms and introducing a recurring motif of curved geometry. The pool area takes this language in another direction. Blue surfaces surround the water, while a large circular opening creates a view into the adjoining space.
This approach reflects what made the Ken Club different when it opened. It was designed as a place where exercise and social life could happen together, and the new interiors continue that idea. Members move between areas for training, swimming, resting, and meeting, with the architecture changing along the way.
The architects describe the project as an ‘architectural remix’ and a ‘sample of a state of mind.’ Rather than trying to recreate the club exactly as it looked in 1985, they have taken its atmosphere as a starting point. The result feels connected to the original Ken Club without turning the interior into a recreation of the past.

'Poster-boy actions': Vijay Mallya's message to those calling him 'bhagoda'

EU court hands another defeat to Abramovich in fight against sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
09:24:41 UTC
18:24:41 KST

Roman Abramovich may appeal to the Court of Justice of the EU within two months and 10 days from notification of the judgment. | Clive Mason/Getty Images
The EU’s General Court has rejected Russian tycoon Roman Abramovich’s challenge to sanctions imposed on him following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, upholding asset freezes and travel restrictions against the billionaire.
The Council of the EU acted within its powers when it extended the measures against the billionaire former owner of Chelsea Football Club in 2022 through September 2025 and March 2026, judges ruled, according to a statement issued by the Court on Wednesday.
Abramovich, who holds Russian, Israeli and Portuguese nationality, is the majority shareholder in Evraz, one of Russia’s largest steel and mining groups. He also owns shares in Norilsk Nickel, a major producer of palladium and refined nickel.
Advertisement
The EU Court said the bloc's sanctions criteria were objective, sufficiently precise and proportionate. They target prominent businesspeople operating in Russia, particularly those active in sectors that provide significant revenue to the Russian government.
It dismissed Abramovich’s claim that the EU was targeting him because of his public profile, noting that sanctions were imposed on him because of his capital holding “and not, as he maintains, a desire to exploit him on account of his public notoriety,” the statement said.
Judges also rejected Abramovich’s argument that the measures were effectively decided by Council working groups rather than by EU governments directly. Even if those groups may have carried out preparatory work, the Council took the final decision, the Court said.
Restrictions therefore complied with EU law and the bloc’s Charter of Fundamental Rights, it said and proportionate to the objective of supporting a peaceful resolution to the war in Ukraine.
Abramovich may appeal to the Court of Justice of the EU within two months and 10 days from notification of the judgment.

President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy has approved the Concept for promoting the development of the Plast and Scouting movement in Ukraine and abroad for 2027-2035.
"The Concept will allow creating systemic conditions for the movement's development and making it more accessible to a significantly larger number of Ukrainian children and youth – both in Ukraine and abroad. And this is not only a strategic framework for the future. The state plans to direct over UAH 60 million to support the Plast and Scouting movement, in particular for their development in Ukrainian centers abroad," the Ministry of Youth and Sports of Ukraine reported.
It is noted that Plast and scouting organizations operate in dozens of countries worldwide and acquire special importance under conditions of defense against Russian aggression.
In particular, Plast in Ukraine unites about 12,000 members and operates in all regions and about 20% of territorial communities where active combat operations are not taking place.
At the same time, the ministry states that the public demand for participation in Plast significantly exceeds the current institutional capabilities of the movement.
"The Concept aims to create systemic conditions for scaling up the movement: increasing the number of educators and volunteers, developing training centers and infrastructure, supporting Plast and scouting programs, and expanding physical and online accessibility for children and youth," the report says.
Thus, by 2035, it is envisaged to strengthen the human resource potential of Plast educators and scout leaders, expand the network of specialized infrastructure, and ensure the physical accessibility of the Plast and Scouting movement for over 50% of children and youth at their place of residence.
The department stated that the Cabinet of Ministers must now approve an implementation plan for the Concept within two months and determine the avenues for financial support of its measures.

UK rules out cyberattack after major flight disruptions

Unknown Publisher

UK rules out cyberattack after major flight disruptions
September 9, 2026
Martin Rolfe, CEO of the UK's National Air Traffic Services (NATS), has ruled out a cyberattack after a major interruption Tuesday in operations at British airports.
"We will be doing a very, very thorough and full investigation," Rolfe told the BBC on Wednesday morning.
Nearly 2,000 flights were cancelled and delayed due to air traffic control problems that started Tuesday morning and lasted for several hours. NATS said a problem involved an issue with the flight processing system.
Although NATS said the problem was resolved, more than 150 flights were cancelled on Wednesday, and more delays were expected throughout the day.
London's Heathrow Airport on Wednesday said "some disruption may continue as airlines reposition aircraft and crew," and advised travelers to check flight status before heading to the airport.
"There are going to be dozens of cancellations in the morning of flights coming into Heathrow because, basically, the flights didn't go out tonight," travel journalist Simon Calder said to Sky News. "The consequences will be horrible," he added.
Questions over the UK's network
The UK's Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said Wednesday that she had summoned Rolfe for a closer explanation of what caused the malfunction, amid concerns over the UK's air traffic network.
This is not the first time a major system failure has affected British airports. In August 2023, several flights were cancelled due to a "system meltdown," costing airlines $135 million (€116 million). In 2025, problems with flight radars affected several airports in the UK, including Heathrow Airport.
"I am seeking assurances that lessons will be learned and systems that support aviation are up to the job," Alexander said on X.
Ryanair, Europe's biggest airline, said at least 150,000 passengers using its services experienced delays of up to eight hours. Two hundred of its flights were cancelled.
For the second time, the airline demanded that NATS CEO Rolfe resign.
Rolfe told Sky News he accepted "full responsibility" but did not say if he was considering stepping down.
NATS provides air control traffic services to 15 UK airports. It is a public-private partnership which is partially owned by airlines including British Airways and easyJet, pension funds and the government.

“Racial violence is accelerating and we must resist”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
09:21:57 UTC
18:21:57 KST

Liliane Umubyeyi on the importance of reparatory justice
Liliane Umubyeyi co-founded African Futures Lab in a bid to rewrite the narrative around Africans and people of African descent and to ensure they receive the reparatory justice they deserve.
Now, as anti-right movements become the norm and racial violence around the world accelerates, she wants to remind people that there’s a movement of people fighting back, calling for reparations and holding those in power to account….
Politics has always been a part of my life.
As a young child in Rwanda, I remember there being a violent political climate preceding the 1994 Rwandan genocide against the Tutsi. By the time I was 10, we were forced to flee following the genocide.
We travelled to Kenya, on to Cameroon where I learnt French, before settling in Belgium, where we were Black African refugees.
After studying law, taking on a PhD and working for differing human rights organizations, including the UN, I began to see a disconnection between human rights and racial justice. I could see the impact of colonialism in terms of how the organizations I was working for resolved problems – they had a Eurocentric way of thinking when it came to how political and legal systems should work.
Changing the narrative: from charity to accountability
I wanted to change things but knew it would be impossible in a big organization. Together with a friend, we co-founded African Futures Lab – and while I didn’t set out to become an activist, I somehow just became one.
Our aim was to change the culture of impunity concerning the racial injustices affecting Africans and People of African descent and the discourse around the development of their societies.
Since the second half of the 19th century, we were seen as people to save and support and African/African descendent immigrants in the Global North were to blame for socio-economic issues in these countries. However, this would not have been the case if our bodies and our natural resources weren’t exploited for so many years. African people helped to build the wealth and contributed to the development of colonial powers through the exploitation of African resources and labour, so African Futures Lab wanted to move the narrative from charity support to accountability and reparations, with a particular focus on gender and climate.
One of the key issues we are working on is the violence perpetrated by colonial administration to Metis children.
These children, born to African mothers and European fathers during Belgium’s colonial rule in Rwanda, Burundi, and the Democratic Republic of Congo, were systematically abducted and forcibly separated from their families between 1948 and 1961.
I remember hearing how a family member was kidnapped from his mother as a child. His mother kept sending letters, trying to find her child for many years, but she could not speak the language, nor did she have the resources to find him. I started to wonder why the mothers of these mixed-race children were not in the picture. I’m a mother. I am from Rwanda. I know what it would feel like if my child was taken from me.
They deserve access to justice
Belgium was instrumental in turning socio-economic categories into ethnic categories in the case of Rwanda. France was instrumental in creating the conditions which lead to the genocide against the Tutsi in Rwanda. We’ve had apologies from Belgium. However, France is yet to address the issue of reparations, having just recognized the moral responsibility. Essentially, they’ve destroyed a country, apologized, then said “let’s move on”.
When it comes to racism, crimes related to colonialism and neo-colonialism, there’s a real refusal to talk about it.
Liliane Umubyeyi
In the human rights space, we talk about reparations all the time. But when it comes to racism, crimes related to colonialism and neocolonialism, there’s a real refusal around it. For me, it was natural to ask, ‘Why don’t Africans deserve to have access to justice for the crimes related to colonialism? And why don’t the mothers of the Metis children deserve justice?’ They have seen their children abducted which is the most heinous crime.
Since 2022, African Futures Lab has been working with a collective of Metis associations in Burundi, DRC and Belgium. In 2024, five Metis women brought a case against the Belgian State and won, with the court ordering to pay reparations. The women were themselves were Metis children separated from their families by the Belgian colonial government. When the ruling came through it was surreal. In 2026, the Belgian state appealed the decision, but again we won.
Now we want to use the Court decision to amplify its impact. For example, what can we do for the people who stay in the DRC, Rwanda, or Burundi? This victory was for five women, but what about the others?
Some of the mothers of abducted Metis children are still alive, so how do we make sure that before they die, they can access psychological help or financial support. These are basic rights, and we need to strike while the iron is hot.
A long battle
Far-right movements have been around for years, but now, racial violence is accelerating and we must resist. Continuing to demand accountability and call for reparations for historical and contemporary racial injustices is an act of resistance. It is a way of refusing to be silenced.
The African Union’s decade of reparations was already in our agenda, but I think it makes even more sense to take tangible action. The conversations around reparations and racial justice are still very much happening in conferences and academic circles but it’s important that more people have access to these conversations and can learn about the real and ongoing impact of colonization.
Together with partners Reforms Initiative, Baraza Media Lab and Deep South Solidarity Fund, we created the Wakati Wetu Festival, the first-ever reparations festival on the African continent, which took place last year. It was a place to bring people from more than 20 countries and 75 organizations together and transform an ecosystem to make sure that colonial and racial violence is on the agenda and prove that reparative justice is not an isolated battle. We worked with several organizations to bring the festival to life, including Amnesty International, as it’s about creating a network to win these battles and prove that hope is stronger than fear.
Given what’s happening in the world, the battle might take longer than expected and I don’t know whether our generation will win it, but at least those who will come in 50 years won’t have to start from scratch – and for me that is key.
This story was originally published in Le Soir.
In our series, Voices of Reparatory Justice, we speak with artists, activists and leaders who share their stories of repair and resilience in fighting against the negative impacts of historical injustices, slavery, and colonialism. Despite existential challenges, their journey to secure dignity and rights of racialised groups, restores hopes for our collective future, humanity must always prevail. This is one of those stories. ====================================================================================================

Rogue OpenAI agents hijacked a German wiki, and it stayed secret for weeks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
09:16:46 UTC
18:16:46 KST

The latest report of an OpenAI agent swarm attack has prompted calls from MEPs for the EU's AI Office to "use its new powers" to "counter agentic risks" rather than letting companies self-report incidents.
Researchers discovered last week yet another OpenAI swarm attack, this time with agents bypassing safety parameters to take over German wiki forum DseWiki, prompting calls from MEPs for the EU's new AI Office to take urgent action to counter the threat of agentic AI rather than allowing companies to self regulate.
The agents had been allowed to visit the 25-year-old German programming website with read-only access but managed to exploit a web request to hijack the site, turning it into a bulletin board.
The rogue agents made more than 18,000 posts sharing answers, research on their environment and how to bypass sandbox restrictions and hide themselves from human detection, according to the research group Nightingale Collective.
The incident took place sometime between May and June this year, and it is understood that OpenAI learned of the incident weeks ago but kept it under wraps.
This is the third reported incident following two others in July, one involving rogue agents attacking OpenAI's own infrastructure and another where 1,200 rogue OpenAI bots bypassed their restricted environments and launched a five-day attack on the open-source AI platform Hugging Face.
However, only on Saturday did OpenAI acknowledge the German wiki incident in an X post, where they outlined that in response to the latest incident they are "working on a framework for when and how we share AI misalignment incidents".
AI misalignment is industry-speak for when artificial intelligence systems pursue goals or behave in ways that diverge from human intentions, values or safety constraints, with the potential to ignore common sense or implicit human boundaries.
A divided response
Experts are divided on the dangers posed by AI in light of the recent rogue AI attacks, with some such as world-leading AI expert Yann LeCun dismissing apocalyptic scenarios and forecasts that there is a 10-20% risk that AI will end humanity.
While others such as Geoffrey Hinton have said, "What's happening is these things are getting smarter," and warned that "companies investing in AI have a vested interested in telling you… [AI] won't go rogue."
According to the EU's AI Act and its most recently introduced measures, which came into effect in August, companies that offer AI models with systemic risk are obliged to report serious incidents such as misalignment incidents to the EU's AI Office "without undue delay".
On Monday, the European Commission announced it had received a formal incident report from OpenAI but did not disclose when it was submitted however they remain in close contact with the AI company and are investigating further.
Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier underlined how serious the German wiki event was, saying, "Incident reports are not just a tick-box, you have to be quite precise and accurate about the measures you are aiming to take."
Co-chair of Parliament's AI Working Group, Michael McNamara, said in response to the latest incident that he believes "the AI Act already gives us the capability to counter agentic risks and it important for the Commission use its powers under the Act".
The Irish MEP also said, "However, these incidents make it clear that the AI Office needs the staff and resources to match both the growing capability of these systems and the growing danger they can pose to society."
Meanwhile, Italian MEP Brando Benifei, who co-chairs the Working Group too, said, "Recent agent breakouts show that the AI Act’s systemic-risk rules are necessary, but their credibility now depends on enforcement."
He added, "The AI Office must use its new powers to obtain model access, conduct independent evaluations and require mitigation, rather than rely on corporate self-reporting. Without action, machine-speed attacks could turn ordinary vulnerabilities into systemic failures.”
The German wiki incident also comes days after the European Commission officially designated ChatGPT as a Very Large Online Search Engine (VLOSE) under its flagship tech legislation, the Digital Services Act.
What OpenAI says
OpenAI also stated in Saturday's X post that the current misalignment disclosure practices, i.e. reporting when AI broke the rules, need to be expanded to take into account what they describe as a "new phase of model capabilities".
"We and the larger AI community do not yet have a clear standard for how to report misalignment," said OpenAI, adding that they are "working on a framework and will share it in upcoming weeks" with the cooperation of several government agencies around the world.
On Sunday, OpenAI's chief scientist Jakub Pachocki published a blog post outlining his concerns over the rapid development of AI risks, stating "We are facing a transition to a world with incredibly intelligent machines, and we need to ensure that transition works out well for humanity."
The Polish computer programmer also revealed his belief that "no lab has solved alignment and monitoring to a sufficient degree to continue responsibly scaling at maximum speed for much longer" and urged that "international coordination on future AI development needs to become a top priority for governments around the world."

In short:
Carlton has delisted seven players from its AFL roster.
One of those delisted was Elijah Hollands, months after suffering an on-field mental health episode.
Hollands took to social media after being delisted, thanking the greater AFL community for its support since his mental health challenges became public.
Elijah Hollands is at peace with the end of his Carlton career, saying he realises there are more important things in life that he needs to focus on.
Hollands was one of seven players delisted by the Blues on Wednesday, with former GWS star Zac Williams, Jordan Boyd, Lachie Fogarty, Lewis Young, Flynn Young and Harry Charleson also among the casualties.
But it was Hollands' axing just months after suffering an on-field mental health episode that represented the biggest story.
Carlton was fined $75,000 for its handling of Hollands during a round-six loss to Collingwood.
Hollands tallied just one disposal for the match, with his erratic behaviour catching the attention of fans even before the game started.
The 24-year-old was hospitalised days later before deciding to step away from football to concentrate on his mental health.
It meant Hollands wasn't able to add to his 47-game AFL career, 14 of which were played at Gold Coast.
His brother Oliver Hollands remains at Carlton.
Elijah took to Instagram to share his thoughts about the end of his time at the Blues, which could also spell an end to his AFL career.
"Football means an extreme amount to me," Hollands wrote.
"My dad played professional footy, my great-grandfather played professional footy, my brother plays professional footy — it is everything I have lived and breathed for as long as I can remember.
"I have only ever wanted to do one thing my entire life: copy what was done before me and play AFL footy. It was something that I just knew I was going to do when I was a kid and it was all I ever cared about.
"And now, unfortunately, that purpose I had is no longer.
"I love this game, but I have come to realise that there are things in my life that are far more important than footy right now and they're the things I will now prioritise."
Hollands thanked the greater AFL community for its support since his mental health challenges became public.
"As an extremely confident 18-year-old, I certainly envisioned my career going a whole lot differently, but I am OK with accepting that it just isn't in the plans set for me," Hollands said.
"I'll be moving into the next chapter of my life, leaving what will feel like a big hole to fill, but I am excited about what can come from having my health and mind in much greater shape."
Carlton's other big delisting was Williams, who joined the Blues from GWS at the end of 2020 on a six-year deal believed to be worth about $5 million.
The soon-to-be 32-year-old managed only nine games this year, with his time at Carlton plagued by injuries.

MOSCOW, September 9. /TASS/. Trade turnover of agricultural products between Russia and Turkey grew by nearly 30% year-on-year in January-July 2026, the Russian Agriculture Ministry reported following talks between Russian Deputy Minister of Agriculture Maxim Markovich and Turkish Deputy Minister of Agriculture and Forestry Ahmet Bagci.
"In January-July 2026, trade turnover between the countries increased by nearly 30%, while Russian exports rose by more than 40% compared to the same period last year. In particular, imports of Turkish goods to Russia are also growing. In January-July, they increased by over 10%, driven primarily by shipments of peaches, sour cherries, sweet cherries, apricots, and citrus fruits," the ministry said in a statement.
The ministry recalled that in 2025, mutual trade in agricultural products grew by 5.5%, with Russian exports increasing by more than 9%. Grain and oilseeds make up the bulk of domestic supplies to Turkey.
"Stable and productive agricultural cooperation between our countries serves our mutual interests. We see broad prospects for further trade growth and stand ready to increase exports of Russian products to the Turkish market," Markovich said, as quoted by the ministry.
The ministry also reported that mineral fertilizer supplies remain a key area of bilateral cooperation. In 2025, Russian fertilizer exports to Turkey nearly doubled, surging by more than 90%. The supply mix includes complex, nitrogen, and potash fertilizers. "Both sides are interested in further expanding trade," the ministry said.
To establish more stable conditions for interaction, the agricultural ministries signed a memorandum of understanding on mineral fertilizer supplies during the meeting. The document is expected to provide fresh momentum to cooperation and lay the groundwork for continued export growth.

Finland has also been an attractive location for digital infrastructure supporting social media workloads, with TikTok planning on expanding its data center capacity in the country.

“Britain has to stand for something. Britain has to show leadership. Britain has to stand for fairness against injustice, where people are being bullied out of their homes, intimidated. We will always stand with the underdog and take what action we can to support them.” NEW ENDS
Tuesday’s sanctions announcement also prompted a swift backlash from Israel, which ordered the closure of the British consulate in Jerusalem and banned 12 British MPs and activists from entering Israel.
Washington’s ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, threatened that the US could take retaliatory action over trade, but the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said the US would “obviously” not follow the UK government’s actions but did not want to see the West Bank destabilised.
Miliband told Sky News he would “let our American friends speak for themselves” but insisted the international community had been “quite frustrated to put it mildly, with some of the actions of the Israeli government”.

Miliband accepted the closure of the British consulate in Jerusalem would be “damaging” but said the government had “weighed up the costs and benefits in advance if this”.
The government is set to enact:
- 
  An import ban on goods from illegal settlements in the occupied territories and a new ban for arms licences and other exports that “materially contribute to the occupation”.
- 
  A comprehensive sanctions regime against providing services such as construction or financing for Israeli settlements and a ban on advertising them in the UK.
- 
  Personal sanctions against the main individuals accused of promoting settler violence.
- 
  A new ban for arms licences and other exports that “materially contribute to the occupation”.

The prime minister, Andy Burnham, said the sanctions were “the right thing to do” and emphasised they were aimed “not at the Israeli people”. Burnham is due to face MPs over this issue at prime minister’s questions.

Purity of China quartz deposit ‘highly similar’ to US Spruce Pine standard: study

Purity of China quartz deposit ‘highly similar’ to US Spruce Pine standard: study
Geologists identify Xiaohuaguo site in central Hubei, unlocking potential silica resources for solar panels and semiconductor production
The quartz from the Chinese deposit is described as having “highly similar” properties to the resources produced at North Carolina’s Spruce Pine, which is crucial to the global production of solar panels and semiconductors.
In the US, there is a growing call from the industry to use high-purity quartz as a weapon against China’s rare earths export ban.
“This discovery of the Xiaohuaguo high-purity quartz deposit provides a new prospective area for the exploration of hydrothermal vein-type high-purity quartz resources in China,” the team wrote in a paper published in the peer-reviewed Chinese-language journal Earth Science last month.
“Furthermore, the particle size, morphology and residual fluid inclusion characteristics of the purified quartz sand were highly similar to those of Unimin’s IOTA-CG type high-purity quartz sand, demonstrating significant potential for application in high-end technology fields.”
Researchers from the China University of Geosciences, the Wuhan Centre of China Geological Survey and the Hubei Geological Bureau conducted the exploration and purification of the Xiaohuaguo quartz.
While quartz is the second most abundant mineral in the Earth’s continental crust, high-purity quartz is a rare form characterised by silica purity above 99.9 per cent.

Taiwan’s TSMC to adopt next-generation chipmaking technology
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
09:11:23 UTC
18:11:23 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — TSMC, Intel, and Samsung are embracing ASML’s next-generation High NA EUV technology as demand for more powerful AI chips accelerates, Nikkei Asia reported Tuesday.
ASML’s High NA EUV machines can print finer circuit patterns than conventional systems, allowing chipmakers to fit more transistors into smaller areas. Generally, the more transistors the more powerful the chip.
ASML is the only company that makes EUV lithography machines, which use light to transfer circuit patterns onto silicon wafers. Its High NA systems increase the technology’s aperture from 0.33 to 0.55, improving resolution and allowing chipmakers to produce smaller and denser circuit patterns.
Intel is already using High NA EUV on select layers of its 18A chips, Nikkei Asia reported. ASML said in July that Intel had entered high-volume manufacturing of a subset of its Core Ultra Series 3 processors, making it the first company to ship high-volume logic products made with the technology.
Samsung plans to introduce the technology into high-volume DRAM production by 2028, which it said would be the industry’s first such deployment in memory manufacturing. The company expects the technology to help extend DRAM scaling while simplifying production.
TSMC plans to use High NA EUV in high-volume manufacturing of advanced chips from 2030. The company said the number of chip layers using the technology is expected to increase as transistor designs become more complex, particularly for AI applications.
The three companies’ commitments could also ease concerns over the cost and complexity of High NA EUV, per Nikkei Asia. The machines can cost about NT$12.81 billion (US$407 million), making them significantly more expensive than conventional systems.
TSMC and ASML are working with other industry partners to develop 12-inch photomasks, up from the 6-inch masks currently used with High NA EUV. The larger masks are expected to increase factory productivity and lower chipmaking costs.

The Trump administration separately announced new sanctions on more than two dozen Iranian commercial and private airlines and foreign cargo providers, in a further effort to isolate Tehran from its remaining trading partners.
The exchange marks one of the sharpest escalations since the framework deal the two sides signed in June broke down the following month.
Both sides have been attempting to assert control over the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway through which roughly one-fifth of the world's traded oil passed before the war began.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Army Sixth Corps has announced plans to conduct a second Tianma live-fire exercise next week in Hsinchu.

Two live-fire exercises in less than a month demonstrate an unusually high level of training intensity, Liberty Times reported. The Tianma exercise is the most important annual anti-armor live-fire drill for Taiwan’s military. It primarily involves live-fire launches of TOW and Javelin anti-tank missiles.

This allows troops to conduct live-fire drills and training in the areas where they are actually stationed.
The TOW-2B missile uses advanced wireless radio-frequency guidance, extending its maximum range to 4,500 meters, per Liberty Times. It has a “top-attack” capability, which allows it to fly over enemy tanks and detonate directly overhead to penetrate the vehicle’s most vulnerable top armor.
Taiwan plans to procure 24 additional TOW launchers and 1,545 missiles, with deliveries expected to begin in 2029. Combined with the original purchase, Taiwan will eventually possess 124 launchers and 3,245 TOW missiles.

'I am appalled': Holocaust survivor raises alarm over far-right AfD victory in Germany
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
09:10:49 UTC
18:10:49 KST

Eva Umlauf was two years old when she and her mother were freed from the Nazi death camp Auschwitz in January 1945. She says she is horrified to see that more than 80 years later, the far-right is once again on the rise in Germany.
The Alternative for Germany (AfD) party's victory in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday has left a far-right party within reach of power in a German state for the first time since the end of World War Two.
"What can I say? I expected this, and yet I'm appalled," she told Reuters in an interview. "I am appalled, I am saddened; I don't know what drives people to vote for this party."
Umlauf, a Slovakian-born pediatrician and psychotherapist who lives in Munich, visits schools to educate children about the Holocaust and serves as president of the International Auschwitz Committee.
Her comments reflect the alarm many minority representatives have expressed in recent months, as opinion polls point to the advance of the far-right in Saxony-Anhalt, as well as in Berlin and the eastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, which both vote on September 20.
"We're afraid. We know what happens – what happens to minorities, what happens to foreigners," she said.
AfD rejects comparisons to Nazis, claims charges used to silence opposition
The AfD, founded as a eurosceptic party during the eurozone crisis in 2013, rejects comparisons with the Nazi Party, responsible for the Holocaust that killed some 6 million Jews as well as Roma and Sinti people, homosexuals, and others.
It wants to restrict immigration, especially from countries it considers "culturally alien" to Germany, quit the euro, and restore ties with Russia to bring energy prices down. It says its policies reflect common sense ideas shared by millions of Germans and denies being antisemitic.
Instead, it accuses mainstream parties of using such charges to silence opposition.
However, opponents accuse the party of downplaying Germany's Nazi past, pointing to a comment by one of its leaders in 2018 who described the period as "just bird shit in 1,000 years of successful German history."
The Central Council of Jews in Germany, the country's main Jewish organization, also sees the party as "a party where antisemites and far-right extremists have found a home."
The Saxony-Anhalt branch of the party is classified as right-wing extremist by the local office of the domestic security agency, the Office for the Protection of the Constitution. The AfD itself dismisses the classification as politically motivated.
European Jews concerned about rise in antisemitism on far-left, far-right
Sunday's election in Saxony-Anhalt took place in a period of heightened anxiety for many Jewish people in Europe, where there has been a sharp rise in antisemitic attacks and incidents since the Hamas attack on Israel on October 7, 2023, and the subsequent Israeli campaign in Gaza.
Far-left parties and their supporters have also been accused of fostering antisemitism, but the AfD has come under increased scrutiny as its support in the polls has grown.
Its party program for the election proposes a "patriotic cultural policy" that would focus school history lessons away from the Nazi period to figures such as 19th-century "Iron Chancellor" Otto von Bismarck. It would restore military memorials to German soldiers killed in both world wars.
Such priorities have alarmed critics who say they reflect a wish to forget Germany's decades-long effort to confront its history and the crimes of the Nazi period. But Umlauf said she did not believe the party's views were shared by a majority of Germans.
"If you take the whole of Germany into account, you have an average of 30% AfD support. And I believe – and I hope – that this will actually mobilize the other 70%."

Silicon wafers are the foundational material for semiconductor production. SEMI data showed that global silicon wafer shipments totaled 3.57 billion square inches in the second quarter, up 7.4% from the same period a year earlier, according to Stockfeel.

The Challenger 3 main battle tank programme is undergoing a performance review and reapproval process, with Defence yet to quantify potential delays to Initial and Full Operating Capability or decide whether the tank should remain in service beyond 2040.
Defence Minister Luke Pollard provided a response to two written parliamentary questions from Conservative MP Ben Obese-Jecty, who sought further detail following the National Infrastructure and Service Transformation Authority’s Major Projects Annual Report 2025 to 2026.
One question asked for the length of the forecast delay and risk to Challenger 3’s Initial Operating Capability and Full Operating Capability arising from delivery by the prime contractor. The other asked when Defence expected to decide whether the planned out-of-service date should be extended beyond 2040.
Pollard said: “The Armour Main Battle Tank Programme is currently subject to an ongoing review of programme performance and a related reapproval process. Under current plans, reapproval is expected during Financial Year 2026-27.”
The answer though does not provide a revised date for either Initial Operating Capability or Full Operating Capability, meaning the scale of any forecast schedule movement remains undisclosed while the review continues.
Defence is considering the wider consequences of programme performance as part of the reapproval work, including the effect of the timetable on preparing Army personnel to operate the new tank.
Pollard said: “As part of this work, the Department is considering a range of factors, including programme timelines and impacts on associated activities such as training and familiarisation.”
Challenger 3 is being produced by Rheinmetall BAE Systems Land through the upgrade of Challenger 2 vehicles, providing the British Army with a new turret, 120mm smoothbore gun and other changes intended to modernise the UK’s main battle tank capability.
The questions follow the identification of schedule risks within the Armour Main Battle Tank Programme in the latest major projects reporting. Obese-Jecty specifically sought to establish how those risks could affect the two principal milestones used to measure the introduction of the new capability.
The future service life of Challenger 3 is also unresolved. The current planning assumption cited in the question places its out-of-service date in 2040, but Defence is considering the issue as part of wider decisions about future capability and investment rather than through the present programme review alone.
Pollard said: “Decisions relating to the future Out of Service Date for Challenger 3 will be considered through wider capability and investment planning. It would be premature to comment further until these processes have concluded.”
The position means a decision on extending Challenger 3 beyond 2040 is not necessarily tied directly to the programme reapproval expected during the 2026-27 financial year, of course.
For the nearer-term programme, however, reapproval is now the key milestone. Until that process is completed, Defence has declined to state how far Initial or Full Operating Capability may be affected by the delivery risks identified in the major projects report.

The European commute: Which EU country spends the most time getting to work?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
09:09:20 UTC
18:09:20 KST

Just how long do Europeans spend getting to work? Across the continent, the daily average commute sits at 48 minutes, but that hides a massive divide.
For millions of workers across the continent, the daily journey to the office is an unavoidable ritual. But just how long do Europeans actually spend getting to work?
According to new research from talent management company SD Worx, the daily average commute across Europe sits at 48 minutes. However, that continental average masks how differently nations experience geography, traffic, and worker mindsets.
While the European average hovers around three-quarters of an hour, individual countries experience vastly different realities on their roads and rail lines.
Countries such as Italy and Slovenia manage to keep daily travel times relatively brief, hovering around 35 minutes.
At the opposite end, countries push much closer to the hour mark. Sweden and Ireland report hefty averages of 57 and 56 minutes, respectively.
Taking the top spot overall, Belgium officially crosses the one-hour mark at 61 minutes a day. This is driven by the fact that 13% of its workforce are "super-commuters", according to SD Worx, spending two hours or more on the road—the highest rate in Europe—with 14% travelling over 120 kilometres daily.
Distance vs. congestion: The Netherlands and Romania
The data also reveals fascinating differences in why commutes take as long as they do. For instance, the Netherlands and Romania both average 53 minutes for a daily commute, but the underlying dynamics are entirely polar opposite:
Workers in the Netherlands cover 63 kilometres on average, leaning on efficient infrastructure to handle long-distance travel.
In Romania, workers spend that same 53-minute window covering much shorter geographic distances, where heavy traffic and urban congestion eat away at the clock.
The commuting paradox
Perhaps the most intriguing takeaway from the research is how workers psychologically handle their travel times.
Even in Belgium—where the average commute surpasses the 57-minute limit that people generally consider "acceptable"—only 34% of workers view that time as wasted.
Despite enduring some of the longest transit times on the continent, demand for more remote work among Belgian employees sits at just 32%, staying right below the international average.
Across Europe, the daily commute remains a patchwork of infrastructure challenges and personal routines, proving that the time we spend getting to work is about much more than just kilometres on a map.

Estonian PM to officially offer former EDF commander the post of defense minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
09:08:00 UTC
18:08:00 KST

Estonian PM to officially offer former EDF commander the post of defense minister
Prime Minister Kristen Michal will ask former Estonian Defense Forces commander Martin Herem to become the new defense minister.
According to Michal, Herem's experience and knowledge of what needs to be improved within the Ministry of Defense's area of responsibility make him a strong candidate. He added that Herem will most likely become the new defense minister.
It was previously reported that Prime Minister Michal had privately offered Herem the position of defense minister, but Herem himself has not publicly accepted the offer. It is now known that the Reform Party board will approve Herem's candidacy at its meeting on Tuesday.
According to Michal, Herem is demanding that defense spending remain at 5 percent. "His message to me, as well as to others who have asked him, has been that the Russian threat is real and must be addressed," he added.
According to the prime minister, Herem needs political support to carry out various reforms, including an overhaul of the defense sector. "The problems that exist there need to be resolved," Michal said.
Herem accepts
Herem confirmed to ERR on Wednesday afternoon that he has accepted Michal's offer and will take office as defense minister.
Had Herem turned down the offer, the Reform Party would have approached other candidates. Michal named Marko Mihkelson, Alar Laneman, Kalle Laanet, Eerik-Niiles Kross, Kristo Enn Vaga and Mati Raidma as other possible choices.
Asked whether the dismissal of Ministry of Defense Permanent Secretary Kaimo Kuusk is also an important issue for Herem, Michal said the former commander of the Estonian Defense Forces would be joining the ministry primarily to put the defense sector in order.
"In that sense, Kuusk's message has been honorable: He was the first to raise his hand and say that he takes responsibility. Hopefully, the government can dismiss him tomorrow and begin, so to speak, cleaning up or putting the ministry in order," Michal said.
Hanno Pevkur, who is still serving as defense minister, told ERR that he asked Permanent Secretary Kaimo Kuusk on Wednesday to step down. The government will approve the move on Thursday.
It emerged on Wednesday that Energy and Environment Minister Andres Sutt, a member of the Reform Party, will step down as minister. "Since we're already reshuffling the Cabinet, it makes sense to change ministers now as well," Michal said. The prime minister will look for a new minister both within and outside the party.
SDE leader finds proceedings unbecoming
Social Democratic Party (SDE) head Lauri Läänemets wrote on social media that he does not consider the appointment of a new defense minister, or the way it is being carried out, appropriate for a democratic state governed by the rule of law.
"The removal of Ministry of Defense Permanent Secretary Kaimo Kuusk is being carried out in the Georgian style, based on party interests, something we have previously seen in Viktor Orbán's Hungary or in Poland. A hallmark of democracy is a professional and apolitical civil service that is free from and protected against partisan agendas and political turmoil," he wrote.
"To prevent the politicization and political influencing of the civil service, the law lays down specific rules governing when and under what circumstances an official can be dismissed. The Government of the Republic Act specifically states that the end of a minister's term in office cannot serve as grounds for dismissing a secretary general. A secretary general can and may only be dismissed for objective reasons. A party's desire to bring someone in as defense minister is not an objective reason," Läänemets wrote.
"By demanding that the Ministry of Defense secretary general be dismissed, Martin Herem, and the Reform Party by carrying out that demand, are sending a signal to the civil service that the party and politicians stand above the law and an impartial state apparatus and must be obeyed. This is extremely damaging to the democratic and continuous functioning of the state," Läänemets said.

State TV and Radio Committee urges Ukrposhta, Nova Poshta, Meest, DHL, FedEx, UPS not to mail Russian books from abroad
