Scholar warns Taiwan political gridlock straining democratic institutions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
08:23:55 UTC
17:23:55 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Flaws in the government have begun to undermine the nation’s democracy, Dr. Kharis Templeman, a research fellow at Stanford University’s Hoover Institution, said on Wednesday.
He pointed to the constitutional court crisis, in which the KMT-majority Legislative Yuan blocked President Lai Ching-te’s (賴清德) seven constitutional court justice nominees in December 2024 and last July.
“I think Taiwan is on the edge of the point where healthy, political competition and pluralism are starting to damage the institutions of democracy,” Templeman told Taiwan News.
Because of these vacancies, the court did not meet the 10-justice quorum requirement and was therefore unable to hear or rule on major cases. “When your constitutional court is no longer functioning, that is a pretty serious situation,” Templeman said.
In December 2025, the court repealed the law that required 10 justices to hear and decide cases and at least nine justices to agree on rejecting a law. However, it remains understaffed and politically constrained.
Templeman also expressed concern about Premier Cho Jung-tai’s (卓榮泰) refusal to sign legislation passed by the Legislative Yuan, “basically creating a power that no previous premier had ever claimed they had.”
Cho said that signing amendments to the Radio and Television Act, the Cable Radio and Television Act, and the Satellite Broadcasting Act, would allow political parties, the government, and the military to acquire shares in media corporations and thereby exert influence.
The premier defended his decision on Tuesday, saying that not countersigning the bills was the Cabinet’s duty to history and his personal responsibility.
Despite the political deadlock, the scholar said the three major political parties still pass much legislation, including a special defense budget. “A lot of legislation actually still passes by cross-party consensus,” he said.
Regarding Chinese infiltration, Templeman said Beijing follows a dual-track strategy. The first is a hard track, which uses threats to try to prevent Taiwan from moving towards independence. The soft track includes people-to-people engagement and other methods to influence public opinion.
Templeman said that generally speaking, China has not succeeded in directly shaping Taiwan’s politics. “They have certainly kept moves towards independence limited, but they have not changed hearts and minds,” he said.
He argued this is because Taiwanese are politically engaged, highlighting their close attention to politics, high voter turnouts, and frequent protests.
“Large parts of Taiwan society are hyper aware, hyper sensitive to (Chinese) influence,” he said, “so it's actually very easy for people to identify the more overt forms of (Chinese) interference in Taiwan's democracy.”
Templeman said he was optimistic about the nation’s democratic future. “There's a democratic DNA in civil society, in the engagement of ordinary people with politics, and over the long run, I think that will carry on forward.”
He added that despite past and present political infighting, he was confident the country will overcome it and end up with a stronger democracy.
“Presuming that the (Chinese) threat is held at bay, I think Taiwan's democracy will be in a better place in 10 or 15 years,” Templeman said.

UK brings forward maritime role for Protector drones
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
09:23:43 BST
17:23:43 KST

Britain is bringing forward plans to give the RAF’s Protector drone a maritime capability, with a review of the programme now under way and revised milestones expected by December 2026.
Defence Minister Luke Pollard disclosed the move in response to a written parliamentary question from Conservative MP Ben Obese-Jecty, who asked what progress had been made towards integrating Protector with P-8 Poseidon maritime patrol aircraft and Type 26 frigates.
Pollard said: “The Defence Investment Plan directed Maritime capabilities for the PROTECTOR RG Mk1 be brought forward, and a review of PROTECTOR is therefore currently underway. Rebaselined milestones are expected by December 2026, with a Review Note to follow.”
He added: “In the interim the Capability Sponsor, Cyber and Specialist Operations Command, is progressing capability development activity.”
The 2025 Strategic Defence Review recommended exploring a maritime surveillance capability for Protector, integrated with the RAF’s P-8 Poseidon fleet and the Royal Navy’s new Type 26 anti-submarine warfare frigates.
The review said Protector should be enhanced with maritime surveillance equipment and improved connectivity to give the long-endurance remotely piloted aircraft wider utility. It also placed Protector within the planned evolution of Britain’s anti-submarine warfare force under Atlantic Bastion, envisaging underwater, surface and airborne drones operating alongside Type 26 frigates, P-8 maritime patrol aircraft and nuclear-powered attack submarines.
The concept would use Protector’s endurance to provide persistent surveillance over large maritime areas while connecting its sensor picture with crewed aircraft and warships. The aircraft can remain airborne for more than 30 hours, providing a potentially useful means of maintaining coverage without continuously committing a P-8 to the same task.
The concept is not entirely new to British forces, of course. In 2021, a maritime-configured MQ-9B SeaGuardian, the maritime variant of the aircraft family on which Protector is based, took part in a series of demonstrations in the UK.
During Exercise Joint Warrior, SeaGuardian operated with an RAF P-8 in a manned-unmanned teaming demonstration supporting anti-submarine warfare activity, including the tracking, monitoring and reporting of sonobuoys.
The maritime MQ-9B configuration demonstrated at the time included a maritime surface-search radar, Automatic Identification System receiver and electro-optical and infrared sensors. General Atomics has also developed an anti-submarine warfare mission kit capable of working with sonobuoys.
Those capabilities should not be taken as confirmation of the final equipment fit for British Protector aircraft, which has yet to be disclosed or properly evaluated.
Defence had already begun examining a wider maritime role before publication of the Strategic Defence Review. In January 2025, ministers said Britain was working with the NATO Intelligence, Surveillance and Reconnaissance Force to scope options for using Protector in the North Atlantic and Arctic.
After the Strategic Defence Review, however, the Government stopped short of giving a timetable. Asked in October 2025 when Protector would be integrated with P-8 Poseidon and Type 26, Pollard said the maritime capability was being considered through the forthcoming Defence Investment Plan.
The published Investment Plan subsequently allocated £590 million to Protector over the four years to 2029-30, but did not explicitly describe the maritime surveillance programme. It separately committed £260 million to upgrade the RAF’s P-8 Poseidon aircraft and equip them with the UK-built Sting Ray torpedo.
The latest answer now confirms that the Investment Plan actually resulted in a direction to bring Protector’s maritime capabilities forward, with detailed programme milestones being reconsidered as part of the wider Protector review.
That review comes as the overall aircraft programme works through a number of outstanding issues. The latest government major-projects assessment rated Protector Red, citing its pending programme rebaseline alongside trained crew numbers, Full Motion Video metadata dissemination and delays to weapons testing.
Some of those issues have since moved forward. Protector is already being employed operationally, Paveway IV has been operationally available since March 2026 and Brimstone 3 testing has progressed to analysis ahead of operational clearance.
By December, Defence now expects to have rebaselined the milestones governing the programme, including the work intended to turn Protector from a predominantly land-focused persistent surveillance and strike aircraft into another sensor within Britain’s increasingly integrated North Atlantic maritime force.

DPP defends Taiwan’s new rule for group travel to China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
08:23:30 UTC
17:23:30 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — DPP Legislative Caucus Secretary-General Chuang Jui-hsiung (莊瑞雄) defended the government’s new registration requirement for group travel to China on Wednesday, calling it a “necessary precaution” for people traveling to risky areas.
The Mainland Affairs Council had previously warned that new Chinese travel rules — including restrictions on leaving China on national security or other grounds — that are set to take effect Tuesday could increase risks for Taiwanese traveling to China, per Storm Media. In response, the Ministry of Transportation and Communications required travel agencies to assist customers with registering through the MAC’s reporting system for travelers going to China.
Agencies that fail to comply could face fines ranging from NT$10,000 (US$317) to NT$50,000. MAC Deputy Minister Liang Wen-chieh (梁文傑) clarified Thursday that the registration requirement was introduced to address a new form of group travel to China that emerged after the government banned travel agencies from organizing tours, per Storm Media.
Under the new arrangement, travel agencies assist customers in organizing trips but do not directly operate the tours. Liang said travel agencies would not be penalized if individual participants declined to register.
The policy drew criticism from the tourism industry. Taiwan Strait Cross-Strait Tourism Development Association Chair Hsiao Po-jen (蕭博仁) said members of the public are not required to report their overseas travel to the government and argued that the new requirement was intended to discourage travel to China, per UDN.
Hsiao said travel agencies would sue the Tourism Administration if it imposed fines under the new rules. He also suggested that any penalties should be imposed on travelers rather than travel agencies.
Facing strong opposition, the Tourism Administration delayed enforcement of the requirement and gave travel agencies a grace period to adapt to the new rules. KMT Legislator Lee Yen-hsiu (李彥秀) said that if the government intends to turn the registration requirement from discretionary to mandatory, it should apply the same standard to other destinations classified as Level 3 under the Ministry of Foreign Affairs’ travel advisory system, per ETtoday.
China’s Taiwan Affairs Office Spokesperson Chen Binhua (陳斌華) also criticized the measure, saying that the new rule was a tactic by the DPP administration to discourage cross-strait exchanges, per UDN. He added that Taiwanese in China are afforded equal protection under the law and can seek assistance from tourism authorities or local Taiwan Affairs Office branches.
Chuang defended the registration requirement, saying it is the government’s responsibility to obtain information that could be used to assist citizens in an emergency, per CNA. Given the travel advisory and the risks associated with traveling to China, he said it was reasonable for the government to take precautionary measures.
Chung also urged the government to improve communication with travel agencies and called on the industry not to misconstrue the measure’s intentions as surveillance. He argued that with the opposition controlling the legislature, the government does not have the time to “surveil its people.”

‘Totally reliant on Mother Nature’: UK drought raises water security fears
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
08:19:45 UTC
17:19:45 KST

‘Totally reliant on Mother Nature’: UK drought raises water security fears
Record heatwaves have troubled British farmers, raising concerns over reservoir levels and food supply.
London, United Kingdom – In a wheat field near High Wycombe in the rolling English countryside, Alex Nelms watched the harvest on his farm die in a matter of days.
His crop had looked strong until the first heatwave came in May, when temperatures surpassed 35 degrees Celsius (95 degrees Fahrenheit) just as his milling wheat entered its grain-fill phase, the critical weeks when the plant fattens its kernels.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Sudan’s date palm trees under threat from drought and wildfires
- list 2 of 4How wildfires are scorching France’s wine industry
- list 3 of 4El Nino: A phenomenon supercharged by climate change
- list 4 of 4Dead fish fill vanishing river as drought grips Indonesia
“It just killed everything stone dead,” he told Al Jazeera. “Everything was finished really early, and when we were sort of full of optimism and hope, it was scuppered almost overnight.”
Nelms farms just over 2,000 acres (809 hectares) of arable land in south Buckinghamshire, on a business his grandparents founded in 1955. His uncle, who has worked the farm for more than 40 years, has just suffered the worst harvest of his career.
Last month, the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said almost three-quarters of England, 71.3 percent, remained in drought. Rainfall in August reached just 34 percent of what would normally be expected by that point in the month, Defra said, and reservoir levels were 18.2 percentage points below where they should be for the time of year.
“We’re totally reliant on Mother Nature,” Nelms said, and nature did not deliver this year.
After a historically dry spring and a run of summer heatwaves, the farm is down roughly 1,000 tonnes on its average harvest, a shortfall of some $270,000 in revenue.
The farm, tucked in the Chiltern Hills, a steep, long ridge of white limestone rock, has no irrigation and never will.
“That has serious knock-on effects on our cash flow,” he said. A third consecutive difficult year would mean hard conversations with his bank and landlord, and farming to minimise risk rather than maximise output, “consequently, probably producing less food”.
‘Financial crisis point’
The National Farmers’ Union (NFU) says farmers are at a “financial crisis point” after the worst drought in 50 years, with historically low harvests, stunted grass growth, rising fuel and fertiliser costs, and a severe outbreak of bluetongue disease in livestock.
The union puts the gross production value loss of wheat at approximately $499m and the cost of replacing a shortfall in forage at roughly $45m.
NFU president Tom Bradshaw has said farmers now lack “breathing space” and are “increasingly exposed to geopolitical shocks, as well as repeated weather extremes, animal disease and global wars”.
He believes action is needed now to ensure the future of British farming “and enable the next generation to keep producing the nation’s food”.
To manage the risk, Nelms is diversifying, planting oilseed rape again on about 350 acres (142 hectares) for the first time in 20 years. He says that the crop’s usual insecticide protection, neonicotinoid seed treatments, is now banned, leaving it exposed to cabbage stem flea beetle and to game birds that can “absolutely nibble, eat, and destroy a crop”.
Growing it also means breaking a continuous wheat rotation that has kept a soil-borne disease called “Take-all”.
Tax allowances would make investing in grain storage and diversified income worthwhile, he said, as well as government-backed bridging loans, modelled on COVID-era support, to survive a bad year without permanent damage.
It is the kind of relief the NFU is pressing the government to provide nationally.
The union wants an interest-free “Keep Britain Growing” loan tied to drought losses, help covering the cost of disposing of livestock lost to bluetongue, faster planning permission for on-farm reservoirs, and clearer rules letting farmers access water as soon as levels allow, echoing Nelms’s case for storage on his farm.
“Drought conditions will continue to worsen until we receive sustained rainfall across the country and we still all have a role to play in conserving precious water supplies,” according to Philip Duffy, the Environment Agency’s chief executive, in a statement shared by Defra.
The Environment Agency has applied for a drought order to restrict abstraction from the River Severn, and 10 water companies, serving 30 million customers, now have restrictions in place.
“A few days or even weeks of wetter weather cannot reverse the impacts of several months of exceptionally dry conditions,” added Duffy.
Defra noted that the first meaningful rains since June have fallen but they have been patchy, so reservoirs and groundwater are still declining even as a handful of rivers see brief upticks in flow.
Despite the losses, Nelms is hopeful about farmers pulling together – sharing labour, machinery and market routes. He points to the Central Chiltern Farmer Cluster, where growers meet to talk through their problems and find solutions together.
“We’re working together, not competing with each other,” he said.
For a farm like Nelms’s, with no irrigation and no water in reserve, that patchiness is the problem. Soil parched from months without rain needs to absorb sustained rainfall before groundwater can even begin to recharge, let alone refill the reservoirs a future harvest might depend on.
“Our climate has changed,” Water Minister Emma Hardy, who chairs the National Drought Group, said late last month, “and we will continue to take all action necessary.”

A senior artificial intelligence researcher who spent the past three years building foundational models at tech giants OpenAI and Anthropic has resigned, issuing a stark warning that leading industry labs are rushing recklessly toward uncontrollable superintelligent systems.
Jacob Coxon, 27, announced his departure from Anthropic on Tuesday, stating that neither the firm nor its rival OpenAI is acting responsibly in their push to develop advanced AI.
"Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives," Coxon wrote in a series of posts on the US social media platform X on Tuesday.

His high-profile exit marks the latest in a series of resignations by safety-focused researchers leaving top AI developers over ethical and existential concerns.
In his statement, Coxon warned against underestimating the speed and capability of upcoming AI systems, predicting they could soon gain the ability to hack software, disrupt entire industries and autonomously acquire real-world resources.
“The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt. If anything, many executives and senior researchers will couch their phrasing in the press to sound sensible - but I hear the same people express fear privately,” he said.
Addressing fellow researchers across commercial labs, Coxon urged workers to "call for different conditions" and noted that slowing the competitive race may require drastic measures, including pacing agreements between labs or a temporary ban on capability advancements.

Roadworks in Georgia's capital uncover rare 10th-century pottery cache

- The pottery dates from the 10th–11th centuries, when Tbilisi was a multicultural economic hub under Arab rule and a key Silk Road stop.
- The findings will be studied at the National Museum, while city officials work to modernise the avenue amid concerns about asbestos and ongoing traffic disruption.
AI generated
TBILISI - Amid the debris six metres beneath Tbilisi's main thoroughfare, roadworks that have frustrated residents have yielded an archaeological prize: a cache of 10th-century pottery among the oldest mediaeval works ever found in the Georgian capital.
Work on Rustaveli Avenue, the city's stately central boulevard, began this summer to add pedestrian crossings, improve signage and make other upgrades.
The project has brought traffic chaos and drawn complaints from residents, who must now navigate gaping holes and crushed brick on their daily walks, but it has also given archaeologists a rare glimpse into Tbilisi's past.
The discovery of the ceramic workshop came as little surprise to David Lordkipanidze, director of the National Museum, located just a stone's throw from the dig site.
"Tbilisi is very rich with archaeological material...so it's very logical to find workshops of different periods," he said.
Medieval Georgian chronicles date Tbilisi's founding to the 4th century, when Vakhtang I ruled over the kingdom of Kartli in what is now eastern Georgia.
Preliminary studies of the pottery's ornamentation suggest the fragments date from sometime between the 10th and 11th centuries, when Tbilisi was under Arab rule and an important stop along the Silk Road. The archaeological findings will be brought to the National Museum for 3D scanning and proper review, Lordkipanidze said.
Tbilisi blossomed in the medieval period, during which time the city changed hands between the Umayyad caliphate of Damascus, Baghdad's Abbasid caliphate and the formidable Seljuk Empire, among others.
"Tbilisi was always multicultural," Lordkipanidze said, and "a real centre for the region, particularly an economic centre."
Successive waves of conquest by the Mongols, Persians and Russians have influenced the look of the city, where crumbling, 19th-century houses cling to hillsides above the Kura river, which flows from the Caucasus mountains to the Caspian Sea.
Tbilisi's name - which means "a warm place" in Georgian - refers to the hot, sulphurous waters that pour forth from the mountains ringing the city and form creeks that trickle below its streets. Some are now on full display due to the renovation works along Rustaveli Avenue.
Tbilisi's mayor has pledged a "well-organised and modern" result and workers are labouring through the night to meet a November deadline. The city hall is under pressure to investigate claims that asbestos was dug up from the bowels of the avenue. REUTERS

In response to the backlash over the sanctions, Miliband told Sky News, “Well, I’m a proud British Jew, and I don’t agree with the chief rabbi.”
“I have great respect for the chief rabbi, but I don’t agree with him, and I believe that it must be possible to do what we did yesterday, which is to stand up for British values of the rule of law, of dignity for people, of the prevention of injustice, and do so in a way, as I did yesterday, to say to anyone in our country who holds British Jews responsible for the actions of the Israeli government, that is antisemitism, pure and simple.”
When asked if he could understand the Israeli government’s argument that they are acting defensively with the measures taken in the West Bank, Miliband told Sky News that Israel’s actions are making the country “less secure.”
UK acted with 'various allies' says Miliband
“I don’t want to see Israel isolated in the world,” he said, noting that the United Kingdom had acted with various allies in deciding to impose sanctions.
They all “shared our deep, deep sense of disquiet about what was happening,” he said, but declined to say whether the United States government was supportive of London’s decision.
“I’ll let our American friends speak for themselves,” he said, making clear that the US government had “been informed” of the UK’s move to sanction prior to its official announcement.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio spoke to journalists on Tuesday, making it clear that the US government would not be following the UK’s lead, though he refrained from criticizing Miliband’s decision.
Amichai Stein, Goldie Katz, and Reuters contributed to this report.

Two bear cubs killed in Tartu County after repeated human contact
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
08:17:00 UTC
17:17:00 KST

Two bear cubs killed in Tartu County after repeated human contact
Two bear cubs were culled in Tartu County on Sunday after repeatedly returning to residential homes despite being relocated, the Environmental Board (Keskkonnaamet) said.
The board said the bears had lost their species‑typical behavior, damaging yards and entering outbuildings, and attempts to return them to the wild proved impossible.
While in the past there was a bear culling season in the fall, brown bears can now only be culled via a special license, for instance issued if they are judged to be a nuisance. In this case the state Environmental Board said the bear cubs were treated as animals in a helpless state were no longer capable of surviving independently in the wild, in the understanding of the Animal Protection Act.
Tanel Türna, head of the Environmental Board's hunting and aquatic wildlife department, said so far as is known the young bears first came to a settlement in early June in Kõnnu village, Kastre municipality, and at the time they numbered four.
"The loss of their fear of humans was probably caused by people themselves feeding wild animals. Hopefully, two of them have since returned to a normal life as bears.," Türna said, noting these had not been seen again. "Unfortunately, the two bears fitted with ear tags and GPS tracking devices did not" return to to normal lives, he went on.
At the same time, the bears in question in any case also damaged beehives near a residential home and repeatedly entered outbuildings, and attempts to return them to the wild by the home owner themselves did not work out.
Türna said their had been multiple such incidents, which indicated an "unnatural" pattern of behavior had developed with the bears, mostly relating to a lack of fear of humans, resulting from members of the public feeding them.
"As a result, a difficult decision had to be made last Sunday and, as a last resort, the bears were killed," Türna said, noting zoos and wildlife parks had been contacted but none had spare capacity to house the cubs.
Bear cubs need to keep a healthy fear of humans and be capable of independently foraging for food in the wild, rather than continually returning to human settlements, he added.
"We ask people not to seek contact with wild animals and under no circumstances to feed them. It must be kept in mind that bears that are currently young and still relatively small will be large by next year and, if they seek proximity to people, could pose a very serious danger," Türna stressed.
There are an estimated 1,100 Eurasian brown bears in Estonia at present.
What to do if you encounter a bear in the wild
In most encounters, bears are not looking for a fight — they want to move away from a perceived threat. What looks like a charge is often a bluff, intended to warn rather than attack.
A brown bear will often rear up on its hind legs and growl before a potential attack. If you spot one, back away slowly, speak calmly, avoid eye contact, and never run. If attacked, lie flat on the ground, protect your head and neck, and play dead.
Prevention is the best protection. Make noise while walking in the forest — talk, clap, or step on dry branches so bears can avoid you. Don't walk alone in known bear habitats, stay clear of cubs, and never approach animal carcasses, which bears may defend. If a bear enters your yard, scare it off with loud noises rather than stopping to take photos.
Bears are most active at dusk and at night, but they can also be seen during summer berry season and in autumn near oat fields.

“Ninety‑seven percent of our work is classified, but the remaining three percent gives you a glimpse into the complexity and advanced capabilities our teams are developing,” she added.

Oil surges past $100 a barrel again as US-Iran clashes intensify
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
08:16:34 UTC
17:16:34 KST

Brent crude has shot up to above $100 a barrel after US forces destroyed five Iranian tankers and Tehran responded with missile strikes on Jordan, the latest escalation in the conflict that has kept the Strait of Hormuz largely shut since February.
The front month contract on Brent crude, the international standard for oil prices, crossed $100 per barrel again on Wednesday morning while the US standard, WTI, hovered around $95.
Prices have risen almost 20% since the middle of last week as fighting around the world's most important oil chokepoint has once again intensified.
It is also the first time since 23 July that oil has hit the $100 mark.
US Central Command said its forces destroyed five Iranian tankers carrying crude oil on 8 September after Iran's Revolutionary Guard fired ballistic missiles at a US Navy warship twice within two days. The command did not identify the ship, but said it was not hit and continued patrolling regional waters.
It followed a similar strike on 5 September, when Iranian forces fired ballistic missiles at a US aircraft carrier and a destroyer, both of which evaded the attack. The command responded by disabling or destroying three Iranian tankers.
Tehran retaliated by firing missiles at a US military base in Jordan, where air defences intercepted most of them, and renewed threats to target tankers in Kuwaiti and Bahraini waters.
Iran has also repeatedly warned vessels against using unauthorised routes through the Strait of Hormuz.
Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, said Tehran would soon declare an exclusion zone outside the strait, warning that any vessel entering without Iranian coordination would be added to a sanctions list.
Saudi Arabia has been drawn in too, with Aramco facilities at Jazan attacked again on Monday, though damage was reported as limited.
Roughly 7 million barrels a day are still moving through the Strait of Hormuz, against about 20 million before the war began on 28 February.
No end in sight
The military escalation is running alongside a financial one.
Washington launched Operation Economic Outcast in late August, an effort to sever Iran from the global financial system by targeting its access to digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping.
The US Treasury designated close to 60 companies, individuals and vessels at the outset and has signalled fresh measures weekly, with the European Union endorsing the campaign this month.
Rhetoric on both sides has hardened.
US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth said the country "will destroy [and sink]" Iranian oil tankers if Iran fires on American vessels while the Iranian parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf replied by stating "strike our assets and you get struck".
US President Donald Trump has continued to insist the waterway is functioning, posting on Truth Social last week that "Hormuz volumes are BACK" and claiming 18 million barrels a day were flowing.
However, the US Energy Secretary Chris Wright put Monday's figure at 17 million barrels of crude and products combined, while acknowledging the multi-day rolling average is considerably lower.
During last week's White House press conference, US Vice President JD Vance also declined to categorise the ongoing conflict as a war and stated that "the only reason we do not have a worldwide energy crisis is because of the leadership of the President."
Faced with the latest developments, analysts are adjusting upward.
Goldman Sachs raised its Brent and WTI forecasts by $5 on Monday to $85 and $80, respectively, for December and warned prices could exceed $120 next year should Gulf output remain 4 million barrels a day below pre-war levels, though the bank does not treat that as its base case.

1,000 Patriot missiles arrive too late for this winter, so Ukraine asked the Ramstein arms coalition to open its warehouses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
08:14:59 UTC
17:14:59 KST

Ukraine is contracting about 1,000 missiles for its American-made Patriot air defense systems, but most arrive only in later years, so at the Ramstein meeting of its allies it asked for interceptors out of their existing stocks before winter, the Defense Ministry said. Nine governments announced new contributions there, and Germany was the only one to commit interceptors from its own stocks. The Ramstein format meeting is the Ukraine Defense Contact Group, a coalition of roughly 50 countries that coordinates weapons for Ukraine, named after the US air base in Germany where it first met in 2022.
Ukraine contracts for later, asks for stock now
Ukraine's Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara told partners the country is signing for roughly 1,000 Patriot missiles, whose PAC-3 version is the only round in its arsenal that reliably stops Russian ballistic missiles, paid for with partner support and the European Union's credit line. Those deliveries take time. So Ukraine asked allies to release missiles from their warehouses now and take the improved contracted rounds later. It made the same case for air-to-air missiles and shoulder-fired launchers, which crews use against cruise missiles and, as a stopgap, against the jet-powered Shahed attack drones, the Iranian-designed weapons Russia now flies at Ukrainian cities by day.
The European Commission cleared the loan money for interceptors days earlier. How many rounds it buys depends on the price Washington sets.
What partners pledged
The ministry listed the results by country.
- 
Germany promised interceptors for Patriot systems and for F-16 fighter jets, plus drone purchases.
- 
The United Kingdom put up £100 million ($135 million) through PURL, short for the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List, the NATO mechanism that lets allied and partner governments buy US-made arms for Ukraine. London added another 95,000 drones by the end of the year and tens of thousands of extended-range artillery shells financed by other countries.
- 
The Netherlands pledged $300 million for the Drone Line, Ukraine's program that holds a drone-strike zone over the front, and 300 counter-drone missiles.
- 
Estonia committed to keep its support at at least 0.25% of its economic output in 2027.
- 
Norway confirmed a previously announced $200 million for Patriot missiles.
- 
Spain gave €2 million ($2.3 million) for fuel through NATO's procurement agency, plus air-defense missiles and artillery ammunition.
- 
Lithuania put $10 million into PURL.
- 
Poland prepared a €50 million ($58 million) package including air-defense equipment.
- 
Sweden pledged $28 million, half of it to PURL.
It was the coalition's 36th session, co-chaired online by Germany and the United Kingdom according to the German Defense Ministry's invitation, and the first for Khmara and for Commander-in-Chief Mykhailo Drapatyi, the general who took over Ukraine's army in July.
Brussels cleared Ukraine to spend EU loan money on American Patriot missiles for the coming winter of Russian attacks
Germany opens its own warehouse
German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said he decided, alongside the NATO summit, to give Ukraine urgently needed PAC-2 interceptors, an older Patriot round, from the stocks of the Bundeswehr, Germany's armed forces, before winter. Russia has announced it will attack Ukraine's energy system. He told the others to check their reserves and do the same.
Germany will also step up deliveries of AIM-9 air-to-air missiles from the same stocks, the US-made rounds fighter jets fire at incoming drones and missiles, and keep delivering IRIS-T air defense systems, including serially produced guided missiles for them. Ukraine intends to order several thousand more IRIS-T rounds using the EU loan.
The money and the deadline
Allies allocated more than $10 billion over the past year for American weapons through PURL and the US foreign military sales program, $3.5 billion of it under the EU loan, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said. Khmara said partners promised €70 billion ($81 billion) this year, while Ukraine sees €62 billion, and the missing €8 billion is needed to meet that pledge, with the total defense deficit at €23 billion ($27 billion), according to the ministry's readout. He asked for those decisions by November. A day earlier, Ukraine handed the alliance a list of priority air- and missile-defense needs, the Defense Ministry reported.
Two timelines at the table
Elbridge Colby, the US under secretary of war for policy and the Pentagon's top policy official, told the group his department cannot predict when the war ends, that Russia is rebuilding its forces and defense industry, and that Ukraine's needs will persist for months and years. Europeans already lead on conventional defense and provide most of the support, he said.
Russia is expanding its manpower too, and by Ukraine's estimate plans to mobilize about 300,000 more soldiers this year and the same in 2027, Khmara said, Radio Svoboda reported. He presented the war plan Ukrainian forces now operate under, and said their drone kill zone stops Russian advances and kills more than 30,000 Russian soldiers a month, by the military's own count.

Ukraine, Russia trade drone strikes, killing 6

Three people were wounded in the strike on the Starokozace border crossing, around 500 kilometres (310 miles) south of Kyiv, Ukraine's State Border Guard Service said.
The strikes forced the checkpoint to close temporarily, Kiper said, adding that multiple fires broke out as a result of the attack.
Ukrainian emergency officials also said the capital, Kyiv was attacked overnight. While some fires were started, there were no casualties.
What is the latest in US-brokered peace talks?
Russia on Tuesday resumed its near-daily airstrikes on Kyiv after a brief pause while US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Moscow for talks.
At least five people were killed in Kyiv on Tuesday, officials said.

Ukraine has suggested talks that could take place in September, but Russian officials have said it is "too early" to discuss specifics such as a venue or dates for the talks.
Despite US pressure, talks between Moscow and Kyiv have yielded no results beyond sporadic prisoner swaps.

Republicans put Trump center stage in US midterms gamble
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
08:13:22 UTC
17:13:22 KST

Breadcrumb
Republicans put Trump center stage in US midterm convention in Dallas
US Republicans open an extraordinary midterm convention in Dallas on Wednesday betting that putting Donald Trump at the center of their campaign can rescue a party facing grim election forecasts—despite the president's deeply negative approval ratings.
The two-day gathering, dubbed "Trumpapalooza," is designed to persuade the Republican leader's supporters that he is effectively on the ballot on 3 November, when Republicans risk losing the House of Representatives and face a fierce fight to retain the Senate.
"So what I really want you to do is pretend, please, that I'm on the ballot," Trump said recently at a rally in South Carolina. "Just come and vote. It's so important."
Decision Desk HQ projects Democrats to win the House 230-205 and the Senate to finish 51-49 in their favor—revising its 50-50 prediction as the outlook continues to worsen for Republicans.
Trump, whose approval rating stood at just 33 percent in recent polling, will speak on both convention nights at the American Airlines Center.
His challenge is to mobilize voters personally loyal to him without further alienating independents already souring on his presidency amid inflation woes, gasoline prices topping $4 a gallon and the continuing war with Iran.
"Many Trump supporters only vote when he's on the ballot," Matthew Green, a politics professor at the Catholic University of America, told AFP. "They're not diehard Republican voters; they're diehard Trump voters. So, in that respect, it makes some sense to feature Trump in the hopes of getting those folks to turn out in November."
But Green was skeptical that asking those supporters to imagine Trump on their ballots could overcome his broader weakness.
"When you're in the low- to mid-30s, that's traditionally associated with a very bad midterm for your party," he said of the 80-year-old's approval ratings.
Trump show
The gathering is the first Republican national convention held specifically for a midterm election, although Democrats experimented with similar meetings in the 1970s and 1980s.
No candidates will be nominated and no formal party business is planned.
Instead, organisers have constructed what amounts to a two-night television rally touting Trump's record and Republican candidates.
More than 100 House members and candidates are expected, with over 50 speakers or presentations scheduled each night.
Trump delivers Wednesday's keynote and returns for Thursday's finale after Vice President JD Vance speaks. Cabinet members, congressional leaders and candidates in closely watched House and Senate races are also on the program.
Republicans plan to highlight tax cuts, immigration enforcement, manufacturing and prescription drug prices, while depicting Democrats as dangerously far to the left.
Some Republicans, however, are privately hoping Trump sticks to that script rather than the personal grievances and off-message subjects that regularly dominate his appearances.
Staying home
Not everyone is coming.
Numerous lawmakers in competitive races have decided that, less than two months from Election Day, their time is better spent campaigning at home.
Green said vulnerable Republicans have two reasons to keep their distance: Trump's unpopularity and the cost of losing precious days in their districts.
"If you are a Republican running in a swing district, you probably want to get as much distance from Trump as possible," he said.
House Speaker Mike Johnson has acknowledged the dilemma, saying some members need to remain home because it is a "critical time" immediately before early voting accelerates nationwide.
Republicans who do attend have also been asked to contribute at least $25,000 for tickets and lodging.
The event doubles as a huge fundraising opportunity, with a Trump roundtable priced at $250,000 per person and photographs with the president offered for $88,600.
And even Trump's promised national television showcase faces an unusually formidable rival: both convention nights coincide with the opening games of the NFL season.
"Spending three or four days away from your district to go to a convention is not a good way to spend your time if you're facing a tight re-election," Green added.

UK keeps door open to more E-7 Wedgetails
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
09:13:19 BST
17:13:19 KST

Britain remains open to buying additional E-7 Wedgetail airborne early warning aircraft, but any further procurement will depend on available funding, Defence Minister Luke Pollard has said.
The update came in response to a written parliamentary question from Conservative MP Ben Obese-Jecty, who asked what progress had been made on Recommendation 47 of the 2025 Strategic Defence Review, including maintaining the aircraft and exploring further procurement through cost-sharing arrangements with NATO allies.
Pollard confirmed that Defence will take responsibility for maintaining the UK’s E-7 fleet once the aircraft have formally entered service.
He said: “The MOD will assume responsibility for maintaining the E-7 Wedgetail aircraft once they are accepted into service.”
Preparations for that transition are already under way, with personnel being trained to support the aircraft ahead of Initial Operating Capability.
Pollard said: “In preparation, training of maintenance personnel is already underway as part of wider efforts to establish and sustain the UK E-7 enterprise ahead of Initial Operating Capability.”
The E-7 Wedgetail is intended to provide the RAF with airborne early warning and control capability, using its radar and mission systems to detect and track aircraft and other threats while helping coordinate friendly forces across a wide area.
The UK programme has attracted significant amount of scrutiny over the size of the planned fleet, particularly after the number of aircraft was reduced from the original order. Recommendation 47 of the Strategic Defence Review called for the existing E-7 capability to be maintained while exploring options to procure additional aircraft, including through cost-sharing arrangements with NATO allies.
On further procurement, however, Pollard of course stopped short of announcing a new order or confirming that a NATO cost-sharing arrangement had been agreed.
He said: “The UK remains open to exploring all opportunities for future E-7 Wedgetail procurement, subject to the availability of funding.”
The wording leaves open the possibility of expanding the fleet in future, but makes clear that no additional purchase has yet been committed.
For the immediate programme, the focus remains on bringing the existing aircraft into service and establishing the personnel, maintenance and support structure needed to sustain them.

Germany news: Merz, Weidel face off after AfD state win

Germany news: Merz, Weidel face off after AfD state win
Published September 9, 2026last updated September 9, 2026
What you need to know
- Far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) leader Alice Weidel and Chancellor Friedrich Merz are facing each other in parliament
- The general debate comes days after the AfD's victory in Saxony-Anhalt's state election
- The result has increased pressure on Merz, who is being blamed by some in his conservative Christian Democratic Union for the party's poor performance
Here is a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on Wednesday, September 9, 2026.
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.
US defense company to manufacture cruise missiles in Leipzig
US defense company Covenant said Wednesday it aims to produce cruise missiles at a new factory in Germany beginning next year. The move comes as investment in Germany defense industry increases.
The plant, in the eastern German city of Leipzig, would manufacture long-range Anthem missiles, with a payload of 200 kilograms (441 pounds).
The 10,000-square-meter (108,000-square-foot) site will be the group's largest missile production facility, Covenant said in a press release, without mentioning the value of the investment.
The Anthem ground-launched cruise missiles will also be manufactured at sites in the United States and Israel.
Production in Leipzig will begin with around 1,000 units per year, before increasing to 5,000 units, and create many jobs, the firm said, without giving further details.
Anthem is aimed at helping to plug a "capability gap within European armed forces in the field of long-range precision weapons," Covenant said.
"When you look at our adversaries, you see thousands of hardened targets, beyond the range of current capabilities," said Michael Kaufman, Covenant's co-founder and chief executive said in a press release.
"Anthem was built to credibly hold those targets at risk in a prolonged conflict. If our stockpiles run thin, so does our deterrence."
Germany and other European NATO members are looking for long-range weapons as a response to the Russian threat. At the NATO summit in Ankara, the German government agreed with the United States to buy US Tomahawk cruise missiles.
Founded in 2024, Covenant said it has raised more than $250 million from investors in three funding rounds, including investment from a venture capital firm belonging to Peter Thiel, a billionaire and ally of US President Donald Trump.
Last week several hundred people demonstrated in Leipzig against Covenant's plans to open a factory there.
Merz again calls for major cuts to EU budget as Costa visits
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has again called for cuts to the next EU long-term budget amid a visit to Berlin by European Council President Antonio Costa.
He argued that the plan was unaffordable at a time when domestic spending restraint was increasingly necessary.
The proposed budget put forward by the European Commission is for the 2028-34 period. In total, it envisages spending of almost €2 trillion ($2.33 trillion) across the seven years.
This is a fraction of what individual EU member states combined spend at the national level but then it only covers a small fraction of public sector responsibilities, the largest of which are agricultural spending and so-called "cohesion policy," or regional development and attempts to uplift less prosperous parts of the union.
"Europe needs both realism and reform," Merz said at a press conference with Costa, noting that the current budget it almost 60% larger than its predecessor. "At a time of budget cuts in all member states, this is simply unaffordable."
Merz also called for the next budget to reprioritize issues like competitiveness and defense, saying it would not be possible "to solve 21st century problems with a 20th century budget."
The budget, formally known as the Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF), is always difficult to negotiate for two main reasons. It tends to naturally pit net contributors, who often want to keep spending low, against net recipients, who tend to argue the reverse. It also requires unanimous approval from all 27 member states, so a true compromise acceptable to all must be found.
Costa and Merz said they hoped an agreement could be reached by the end of 2026, which would allow for a planning period of one year after the budget is agreed.
Costa is currently touring European capitals seeking common ground on the issue among heads of state and government.
"We cannot ask [for] more from member states," he said. "We need to create new own resources in order to protect the national budgets. All national budgets must be respected."
Update — Police at Rheinfelden border post give all clear
Police in Freiburg near the Swiss border say that their search of a car at the Rheinfelden border crossing is complete.
They confirmed prior reports that suspicion of a potentially dangerous situation arose, initially at around 1 p.m., "as a result of the actions of explosives-detection dogs."
Two German citizens were provisionally detained, a standard safety exclusion zone was set up and federal police specialists responded at the scene, police said.
The incident had led to long queues at the busy boder crossing between Germany and Switzerland across the Rhine River east of Basel.
"At around 8 p.m. the all-clear could be issued. No dangerous materials were found. The autobahn could be reopened once again," police said.
Porsche completes sale of Bugatti and Rimac stakes as authorities give green light
Porsche has completed its sale of its remaining stakes in luxury supercar marque Bugatti and Croatian electric supercar maker Rimac.
It had first announced plans to sell its remaining stake in the company to HOF Capital in April of this year, saying it wanted to prioritize its core businesses.
On Wednesday, Porsche said that the sale had been approved by regulators and been completed.
The struggling Stuttgart-based company said it had raised roughly €1 billion ($1.16 billion), €250 million of which would go towards debt repayments and pension funds.
Rimac and Porsche had previously shared ownership of Bugatti — once purely a part of the VW Group, which includes Porsche — in a 55:45 split, while Porsche held a minority 20.6% stake in Rimac.
The VW Group had resurrected the Bugatti brand, already twice deceased, in 1998 and used it for a series of prestige projects making the fastest road-legal cars in a straight line available anywehere in the world — typically selling only a handful of models to the super-rich in a loss-making but headline-grabbing venture.
As it faces up to swingeing cuts and a drastic restructuring scheme, such luxury projects and anything falling beyond the remit of its core business are coming under considerable pressure.
Haribo cancels annual chestnuts for sweets trade-in because of African swine fever
German confectionary giant Haribo has called off a long-running annual autumn promotional event for a second year running.
For decades, the company had run a scheme in which members of the public were invited to bring in chestnuts and acorns that they had gathered, and exchange them for Haribo sweets.
The company said on Wednesday that the prevalence of African swine fever, sometimes called warthog fever, in western Germany made the event too dangerous. Typically Haribo would donate the nuts to animal parks and game reserves. But because of the risk of transmission, via saliva remnants potentially on the nuts, this would pose too great a risk.
It took the same step last year but said on Wednesday that the tradition would have to be shelved "for the foreseeable future."
"We greatly regret that the chestnut actions cannot take place this year," the company said in a press release, saying that it had been a "fixture of the autumn" for generations of families.
"At the same time, we want to show children that their engagement for nature remains important," Haribo stressed.
To this end, the company announced that it was planting a Haribo forest as part of the efforts to repopulate the plant life in the Ahr Valley after the major flooding of 2021 and would be involving local schools in the process.
Rheinfelden border crossing to Switzerland closed, police checking car for explosives
Traffic was halted in both directions along the A861 autobahn bridge linking Germany and Switzerland at Rheinfelden early on Wednesday evening.
"As a result of a police operation, the Rheinfelden-autobahn border crossing is currently closed in both directions," federal police, who are responsible for transport network and border security, said in a public statement.
Speaking to the dpa news agency, a police spokesperson elaborated that the reason was that officers were checking a car suspected of containing explosives. It was not yet clear when the busy border crossing — a bridge over the Rhine River, which serves as the demarcating line in the border town east of Basel — would reopen.
A short while later, police in nearby Freiburg said that two men had been taken into provisional detention. They were in the car during a check when service dogs indicated the presence of explosives, police said. An examination of the car was ongoing.
The A861 is a special highway connecting the A98 on the German side with Switzerland's A3 highway.
Germany's ADAC motoring club said the disruption had led to queues stretching back kilometers in both directions.
Estimates suggest around 30,000 vehicles cross the bridge daily.
Switzerland is in the Schengen Zone free travel area so border checks are not obligatory, but still they are fairly common occurrences as cars and other vehicles cross, both because of concrete causes for suspicion and as spot checks.
Bayern Munich give teen talent Tim Binder first pro contract
Bundesliga champions Bayern Munich have put another German teen talent on the books of their senior side.
Attack-minded Tim Binder, who is probably happiest on the right wing, joined Bayern's academy setup as a 12-year-old when he was poached from Augsburg.
The 19-year-old has signed a pro contract with Bayern running until the summer of 2030.
Binder had featured in several pre-season friendlies with Bayern's senior squad this summer and joined the team's training camp after the World Cup. He's currently recovering from a muscle strain and is not available to play.
"Tim brings a lot of potential with him. He's fast, good at dribbling and has a super character. He recently demonstrated his talents in the season preparation with the pros," Bayern's sporting director Christoph Freund said. "Tim is a prime example of the exceptional opportunities for youth development on our campus."
Bayern play newly-promoted Elversberg away from home this Sunday in the Bundesliga.
Thuringia ex-BSW lawmakers form new group, to maintain AfD firewall
Time for a quick update on the other, largely forgotten, almost ungovernable state in eastern Germany, where the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) is the strongest single party.
In Thuringia, the lawmakers and former members of the left-wing populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) have formed a new party, called "Gerecht" or "Just."
They have also formally dissolved the old state BSW chapter, which formally still existed even though they had left the party.
Thuringia's wing of the BSW used to be the party's main electoral success story. After winning 15 seats and 15.8% of the vote in 2024's state election, the lawmakers upset the national party leadership by electing to join a coalition government with the Christian Democrats and the Social Democrats.
In so doing they upheld the so-called "firewall," the pledge from most German political parties not to work with the AfD.
But the national BSW leadership — most notably party founder Sahra Wagenknecht — questioned their decision and have argued that the party's subsequent dip in popularity can be attributed in part to it.
In August, seemingly eying the series of fresh elections in eastern Germany, the national party leadership demanded that the state lawmakers leave the coalition government.
Most of the members refused and left the party, and 10 of them have now formed a new group and formally rejoined Thuringia's shaky coalition government. Losing some of its members means the coalition in Thuringia is now in the minority and in need of opposition support to legislate.
Three former BSW members have formed a rival group in parliament called Deine Stimme zählt, "your vote (or your voice) counts," while two others intend to remain lawmakers in Thuringia but to become unaffiliated independents.
A similar question faces the five BSW lawmakers elected to Saxony-Anhalt's state parliament on Sunday. They could in theory seek a coalition with the AfD, or offer some kind of confidence and supply arrangement for a minority AfD government.
Seeking to form a "firewall" coalition could prove more complex in Saxony-Anhalt, at least assuming the Christian Democrats continue to rule out cooperation with the socialist Left Party, because such an alliance would be well short of a stable majority.
Prosecutors investigate SPD's top candidate for Berlin election
Less than a fortnight before elections, prosecutors have announced that they are investigating the Social Democrats' candidate to become mayor of the city-state of Berlin.
Steffen Krach is under investigation by authorities in Hanover, in connection with his other role as the head of the district authority for the Hanover area. He has held that role since 2021 and only became a key figure in the SPD's Berlin campaign during the past year or so.
A spokesman for prosecutors told the dpa news agency that three propeties in Hanover and Berlin had been searched as part of an investigation into potential corruption. Prosecutors issued similar comments to other German news outlets. They said they could not comment further given an ongoing investigation and stressed that the presumption of innocence always applied.
Krach is currently on gardening leave from his role in Hanover because of the election campaign in Berlin, which is entering its final phase.
"On behalf of the SPD Berlin and in the name of our state chair and lead candidate, Steffen Krach, we categorically reject these baseless allegations," a spokesman from Krach's office told dpa. "We are, of course, cooperating fully with the authorities to clear up these basless allegations."
Unlike Saxony-Anhalt, the vote in the left-leaning German capital is likely to be a close-run contest in which no party looks set to dominate.
Polls are quite volatile and vary quite markedly, but in the most broad strokes they point to a possible five-way fight to emerge as the largest party, with the SPD, Greens, Left Party, CDU and AfD all typically polling somewhere between 10% and 20% support.
Leaders of Greens, Left see 'clear attack on our German democracy' from Trump's orbit
Two senior left-leaning politicians have told DW's Matthew Moore at the Bundestag, the lower house of the German parliament, that they were not very surprised to see US President Donald Trump effectively voicing support for the right-wing populist Alternative for Germany (AfD) online late on Tuesday.
"It's obviously now the first time that the President of the United States is endorsing a far-right extremist party in Germany," the Greens' co-leader Franziska Brantner said. "Elon Musk has done so, JD Vance, but this is a different step."
Brantner called it a "clear attack on our German democracy and respect for our institutions."
"It's no mystery that Trump and his MAGA movement have been supporting AfD here for many years with money, with support of people. And it's one network of those who want to destroy our free world, and we will fight back," she said.
Meanwhile, the co-leader of the socialist Left Party said he was not surprised that Trump "supports those who want to dismantle our democracy," given his own "very authoritarian" regime. He said it was a part of a broader pattern, noting how Elon Musk was "one of the first to congratulate the AfD for its election success" on Sunday night.
"And that clearly shows that we are in a situation where there are attempts to undermine our democracy from outside with a lot of money," Pellmann told DW.
Railway bridge falls off transport at building site, likely delaying project
A major rail construction project in western Germany faces potential delays after a replacement bridge fell off a transport vehicle at the construction site, potentially causing damage.
The moment that one side of the vehicle's supports for the massive piece of bridge suddenly gave way, with the cargo sliding off and then tipping over, was caught on video.
The 57-meter (roughly 188-feet) long structure was being moved into position to cross the Hundem River in Kirchhundem, east of Cologne.
Rail operator Deutsche Bahn said it was investigating whether any damage was caused in the accident and said that a delay in the project, which was supposed to be complete by September 15, seemed likely.
"We will now carefully investigate how this accident could have happened at the construction site, and how we can continue our work as quickly as possible," Deutsche Bahn spokesman Fritz Esser told regional broadcaster WDR. "For it's also clear: we want to repeat the bridge installation as quickly as possible."
The affected area Kirchhundem is a major chokepoint in regional rail refurbishment plans with three rail bridges needing replacement.
German flags lowered for King Harald's funeral
Flags are flying at half-mast in Berlin's government district for the funeral of Norway's King Harald V in Oslo.
German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, of the conservative Christian Social Union (CSU), ordered mourning flags to be flown at the country's highest federal institutions, including the Bundestag, Bundesrat, Chancellery and federal ministries.
Lowering flags to half-mast is, alongside state ceremonies and state funerals for distinguished figures, the only formal expression of state mourning in Germany.
There are no fixed criteria for when it is ordered. Instead, the decision is made on a case-by-case basis.
When the Interior Ministry orders mourning flags, both the German and European Union flags are lowered outside federal government buildings.
Germany also lowered flags to half-mast for the funeral of Britain's Queen Elizabeth II four years ago.
Germany postpones Merz-Trump call
The German government has postponed a planned phone call between Chancellor Friedrich Merz and US President Donald Trump, without saying whether the decision was linked to Trump's praise for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party after its election victory in Saxony-Anhalt.
Government spokesperson Stefan Kornelius said the German side had postponed the call, which had been due to take place on Wednesday to mark the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks in the United States.
No new date has yet been set.
Kornelius declined to say whether the postponement was connected to Trump's comments on the Saxony-Anhalt election.
Two days after the vote, Trump hailed what he called a "really big night" for a "populist party in Germany" and wrote on his Truth Social platform that "they are on the move."
He also used the acronym "MGGA," apparently meaning "Make Germany Great Again," echoing his "Make America Great Again" slogan.
Kornelius pointed instead to Merz's previous position that foreign interventions or commentary on German domestic politics, particularly around elections, were unacceptable.
The planned conversation was intended to mark 25 years since the September 11, 2001 attacks.
In a statement read out by Kornelius, Merz said Germany had stood in full solidarity with the United States after the attacks and remained ready to defend shared values.
"That is freedom, democracy and respect," Merz said.
US startup to build cruise missiles in Germany
US defense startup Covenant plans to begin mass-producing low-cost cruise missiles in Germany in early 2027, as European countries seek more long-range weapons amid growing concern over Russia.
The company says it has already secured one European contract for its ground-launched Anthem missile and is in talks with other potential customers, although it has not identified the countries involved.
Covenant plans to manufacture the missiles at a facility in the eastern German state of Saxony.
"Our aim is to reach 5,000 by 2028, or at least a run rate of 5,000 during 2028," co-founder and CEO Michael Kaufman told Reuters.
First deliveries are expected in early 2027.
Why produce them in Europe?
European governments are increasingly looking for weapons that can be produced without relying heavily on US components.
Covenant says most parts used in the Europe-built version of its Anthem missile will be sourced on the continent.
"The supply chain has no reliance on the US," Kaufman said, adding that less than 5% of the missile's components currently come from outside Europe.
"Our goal is to get that down to zero."
Germany and Britain are separately developing a missile with a range of more than 2,000 kilometers (1,240 miles), part of a broader push to strengthen Europe's own long-range strike capability.
Greens, SPD reject AfD coalition talks in Saxony-Anhalt
The Greens and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) have rejected an invitation from the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) to hold exploratory talks on forming a government in Saxony-Anhalt.
The move underlines how difficult coalition-building is likely to be after the AfD emerged as the strongest party in Sunday's state election but fell short of an outright majority.

Before the election, all other parties had ruled out entering a coalition with the AfD.
Despite that, AfD state secretary-general Tobias Rausch said the party would invite all parties represented in the state parliament to exploratory talks.
What about the SPD?
The SPD also rejected the invitation.

"We will not accept the offer of talks," the spokesperson said.
It remains unclear how a stable government can be formed in Magdeburg, with the AfD lacking the numbers to govern alone and other parties maintaining their refusal to join it.

Second Reform minister resigns in a week as Andres Sutt steps down

Second Reform minister resigns in a week as Andres Sutt steps down
Andres Sutt has announced his resignation as Minister of Energy and Environment, the second Reform Party government minister to leave office in the space of a week.
Sutt said he made the decision ahead of the March 2027 Riigikogu election, which he said he will not be running in.
Sutt said he had thoroughly considered his situation over a lengthy period of time, making his final decision in mid‑summer.
"During an election autumn, people always ask who will be running. This time around too, and me too. This time, my answer is no," Sutt noted on social media.
Sutt noted it is customary for a minister to run in elections, meaning now was the time for him to step down. "Consequently, it is only right to make room for the next person who will run in the elections and for me to return to the Riigikogu. At the Riigikogu I will help see through to the finish line both the energy and environmental bills which are halfway there. I will certainly be having my say on financial and fiscal matters. Naturally, I will also support the party and the next minister with advice," he continued.
The outgoing minister added he would remain active in national politics until the end of his Riigikogu mandate – up to the 2027 elections. "I will remain a member of the Reform Party and I am not going anywhere as far as Estonia is concerned," Sutt added.
He also expressed a desire to return to his professional field after eight years in politics, adding two parliamentary terms is the right time to move on after.
Sutt's replacement not yet named
Sutt said he has names on who may be his successor as minister, which falls under the Ministry of Climate's remit, but has agreed not to disclose them. Prime Minister Kristen Michal (Reform) also could not yet say as of Wednesday lunchtime who might succeed Sutt, stating he has been "looking both inside the party - where there are strong candidates, in the environment, climate and energy fields - and outside, for people with leadership experience and expert backgrounds". The ministerial portfolio is "complex," Michal said.
Sutt singled out improving the crisis resilience of the energy system as one of the main achievements during his term. "I think that things are moving in the right direction with energy," said Sutt. In the field of nature conservation, he singled out the creation of a forestry advisory board as a positive development.
Sutt, 58, joined Reform in 2018 following a lengthy career at the Bank of Estonia (Eesti Pank), where he was vice governor from 2001 to 2009. He was made energy and environment minister in March 2025 at the start of the current Reform‑Eesti 200 administration, having already served as minister of enterprise and information technology in Kaja Kallas' first cabinet, from January 2021 to July 2022.
This is the second minister from the Reform Party to have resigned in the past week: Hanno Pevkur stepped down as defense minister after four years in the post, following controversy over a defense procurement deal. His replacement is due to be announced today, Wednesday.
Government ministers do not sit at the Riigikogu, but it is standard practice for them to run in elections as "vote magnets." Following an election and the formation of a new administration, those elected as MPs who are made ministers vacate their Riigikogu seats, which are usually given to the next highest‑polling candidate not to have secured a seat and from the same party's numerically ordered electoral list. Conversely, when they step down as a minister and return to the Riigikogu, that alternate MP must vacate the seat for them. In Sutt's case, Toomas Järveoja must step down as an MP.
Editor's note: This piece was updated to include comments from Sutt on his term in office and potential successor, and from the prime minister.

Germany will supply Ukraine with PAC-2 interceptor missiles for Patriot SAM systems from Bundeswehr stocks.
Boris Pistorius, German Minister of Defense, stated this in an interview with Suspilne.

A White House spokesperson defended the gifts, citing Trump’s “longstanding practice of giving Christmas gifts to people in his orbit, including at times employees and aides”.
They said the gifts were unrelated to any of the individuals’ duties, making them “entirely permissible under relevant legal and ethical standards”. AFP

Türkiye leads OECD in PISA 2025 score gains
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
08:09:23 UTC
17:09:23 KST

Türkiye has recorded the largest score increases among the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) countries in all three areas assessed by the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) 2025, according to results released by the OECD.
The assessment covered 91 countries and economies and evaluated the skills of 15-year-old students in science, reading and mathematics.
Türkiye has participated in PISA since 2003.
The 2025 assessment was conducted digitally between April 14 and May 16 across 203 schools in 56 Turkish provinces, involving 7,702 students from 12 regions.
Türkiye posts gains across all three subjects
Türkiye's scores increased in every field compared with 2022. Its overall ranking among participating countries rose by 15 places in science, 18 in reading and 11 in mathematics.
Türkiye scored 494 in science, 472 in reading and 462 in mathematics in PISA 2025.
Compared with its first participation in 2003, Türkiye improved its science score by 60 points, reading by 31 points and mathematics by 39 points.
While average education performance has declined in both the OECD and globally since 2003, Türkiye's scores have moved in the opposite direction.
Türkiye climbs OECD rankings
Among the 38 OECD members, Türkiye ranked 14th in science, 13th in reading and 23rd in mathematics.
The Ministry of National Education said Türkiye was the only OECD country to increase its scores in all three areas over the past decade. It also recorded the largest score increases among OECD members in science, reading and mathematics compared with 2022.
Because the number of participating countries has more than doubled since 2003 — from 41 to 91 — Türkiye's long-term progress was also assessed using percentile rankings.
From 2003 to 2025, Türkiye improved its relative position by 64 percent in science, 60 percent in reading and 52 percent in mathematics.
The results were published simultaneously worldwide, with separate reports issued by Türkiye's Ministry of National Education and the OECD.
Türkiye’s PISA gains follow years of investment in school infrastructure, digital education, and programmes aimed at strengthening basic skills and reducing learning gaps.
In 2024, the education ministry launched the Türkiye Century Education Model that seeks to focus on STEM education by training teachers.
Türkiye has also increased its focus on reading, literacy and mathematics through supplementary materials and targeted support, while free textbooks and expanded preschool access have aimed to strengthen foundational skills.
