Poland orders Turkish surveillance systems for its scout vehicles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
07:59:58 UTC
16:59:58 KST

- ASELSAN signed a contract to deliver 24 more ARSUS reconnaissance and surveillance systems to Poland, with deliveries planned for 2028 and 2029.
- The deal builds on a 2024 framework agreement and follows a $410 million electronic warfare export contract ASELSAN signed with Poland in December 2025.
Turkish defense company ASELSAN has signed a new export contract to supply Poland with 24 more sets of its ARSUS reconnaissance and surveillance systems, the company announced September 8 at the MSPO defense exhibition in Kielce, Poland.
ASELSAN signed the deal with Polish manufacturer AMZ Kutno for use by the Polish Armed Forces. Deliveries are planned for 2028 and 2029, adding to a broader framework agreement the two companies signed in 2024 that covers deliveries through 2035.
The ARSUS system is a mast-mounted reconnaissance and surveillance suite that combines radar, day and night cameras, and other sensors. AMZ Kutno integrates it onto its Kleszcz armored reconnaissance vehicles, which are based on the company’s Bóbr-3 4×4 chassis. Poland ordered 286 of the Kleszcz vehicles in 2024, with deliveries running from 2026 through 2035, and received its first ARSUS-equipped systems in late 2025.
“As a global defense brand, ASELSAN is continuing to expand its international footprint, particularly across Europe, NATO markets and other key regions,” said Ahmet Akyol, president and CEO of ASELSAN. “Poland is an important part of this broader international growth, and our partnership with the country has been gaining momentum. This new contract is another important step in deepening our cooperation.”
“Following last year’s major electronic warfare contract, we are now expanding our collaboration into reconnaissance and surveillance, further strengthening the relationship between ASELSAN and Polish industry,” Akyol said.
That earlier deal, a $410 million electronic warfare export agreement, was signed in December 2025. ASELSAN says it now works with more than 20 Polish suppliers and is looking at further cooperation in training, maintenance and joint centers of excellence.
ASELSAN describes itself as Europe’s fifth-largest defense company by market capitalization. Founded in Türkiye in 1975, the company builds systems spanning air defense, electronic warfare, counter-drone weapons, and naval and underwater platforms. At MSPO 2026, it is also displaying its STEEL DOME air defense architecture, which includes several counter-drone systems such as the GÖKBERK laser weapon and the KORKUT anti-drone gun, along with naval drones including the KILIÇ underwater vehicle and TUFAN surface vessel.
The company says it exports to 97 countries and has a direct presence in 25, with more than 14,000 employees.

EU to give cities more power to crack down holiday rentals like Airbnb
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
07:55:29 UTC
16:55:29 KST

European cities will gain more leeway to curb short-term rentals such as Airbnb under plans to bring down housing costs in tourism hotspots that the European Union is to unveil on Wednesday.
The European Commission is to lay out conditions under which local authorities can limit short lets, as part of an "affordable housing" package that seeks to address what EU chief Ursula von der Leyen has called a "social crisis".
"Nurses, teachers, and firemen cannot afford to live where they serve. Students drop out because they cannot pay the rent. Young people delay starting families," she said in a speech last year highlighting the issue as a priority for Brussels.
Though hugely popular with visitors, short-term lodgings are blamed by residents in many popular travel destinations for depriving locals of apartments for long-term rent and pushing up prices.
From New York to Tokyo and Barcelona, a growing number of cities worldwide have imposed or considered restrictions on tourist flats in recent years.
But curbs have often been followed by court challenges from rental providers and tourism operators, resulting in legal uncertainty.
The commission's Affordable Housing Act aims to provide cities with legal cover, clarifying when authorities can take action without falling foul of EU single market rules.
Cities and other relevant authorities will be allowed to limit holiday rentals as well as the purchase of property for short-term letting purposes in areas deemed "under housing stress", according to a draft seen by AFP.
The document laid out a series of parameters that needed to be met for an area to be defined as under stress, such as the ratio between house prices and incomes there.
"Population dynamics" and future housing supply and demand will also need to be taken into account, the draft said, adding any measure should be non-discriminatory, necessary and proportionate.
'Structural solutions'
The legislation will not affect landlords that rent out their own primary residence for short periods of time.
Housing affordability has become a growing issue across the 27-nation bloc in recent years.
Property prices have surged by 60 percent, while rents have climbed by 20 percent over the past decade, leaving millions struggling to find a home they can afford, according to Brussels.
The EU says this is mainly driven by insufficient housing supply but short-term lets add extra pressure in certain areas.
Short rentals account for only about 1.2 percent of the European Union's housing stock but the share can reach as much as 20 percent in popular districts of some tourist destinations, according to EU data.
Holiday lets "can generate important economic and social benefits, especially for households struggling to make ends meet" but "they may also aggravate housing demand pressures in some constrained local housing markets," the EU draft read.
Yet, that's something rental providers dispute.
"For the great majority of cities, the claim that short-term rentals are driving housing stress does not survive contact with this evidence," tech lobby group CCIA wrote in a letter to the commission this month.
In some cities with restrictions, rents and hotel prices have gone up, the letter added, noting Lisbon recently overturned some of the curbs it had previously imposed.
"Europe's housing crisis needs structural solutions, and the implementation of this Act should focus on increasing the supply of homes," said an Airbnb spokesperson.

Shabana Mahmood signs information-sharing deal with Belgian counterpart to tackle small boats
Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, has signed an information-sharing deal with her Belgian counterpart to help both countries tackle small boats and people smuggling.
According to the Home Office, this is the first law enforcement deal of this kind signed with an EU member state since Brexit.
Explaining what it will do, the Home Office says:
The UK-Belgium Law Enforcement Cooperation Agreement (LECA) will enable police officers in both countries to exchange intelligence autonomously and more quickly, helping identify, disrupt and dismantle organised criminal networks, including those involved in migrant smuggling.
Under previous arrangements, certain information exchanges required judicial approval before intelligence could be shared, creating delays at critical stages of investigations and reducing investigators’ ability to develop a timely and comprehensive picture of criminal networks operating across both countries.
The new agreement removes those barriers, enabling officers to share information autonomously and act more quickly against criminals operating across borders. It will strengthen joint investigations and specialist training to detect and disrupt criminal activity linked to small boat crossings, as well as wider organised crime such as drugs and firearms smuggling.
Belgian officers are now also able to join the UK-France Intelligence Cell in northern France, where National Crime Agency (NCA) officers work alongside French counterparts to identify and dismantle organised migrant-smuggling networks operating across Europe.
Transport secretary Heidi Alexander tells MPs cyber-attack ruled out as cause of air traffic control chaos
Heidi Alexander, the transport secretary, has said that a cyber-attack has been ruled out as the cause of the air traffic control disruption that has caused chaos at airports.
Speaking at the start of the debate on the civil aviation bill, Alexander said:
A four-hour air traffic outage yesterday left hundreds of thousands of passengers facing cancellations, diversions, and delays.
I would like to apologise wholeheartedly to passengers for this disruption.
We often take for granted the way in which our aviation system just works, but yesterday that was not the case.
Safety must remain air traffic controllers’ overriding priority, and this morning I have spoken to Nats [formerly National Air Traffic Services] chief executive Martin Rolfe, who informed me this outage was due to a technical issue at their Swanwick site.
So, while my understanding from Nats is that we can rule out a cyber-attack on this occasion, I do not believe this issue was unavoidable.
We also spoke this morning about how Nats responded to resolve and minimise the disruption as quickly as possible, and I am grateful to the airports and airlines who responded straight away.

Downing Street has ruled out allowing another Scottish independence referendum – even though Andy Burnham implied at PMQs that the Scots could have one if a majority were in favour.
In response to a question from the SNP MP Chris Law, Burnham said the situation in Scotland was “exactly the same” as in Northern Ireland, where the law says a referendum on leaving the UK and joining a united Ireland should take place if that’s what people want.
But later No 10 suggested Burnham mis-spoke. At the post-PMQs briefing, the PM’s press secretary said:
The PM’s been repeatedly clear on this. In his call with the Scottish first minister in his first week, the PM stated upfront that another referendum on independence was off limits and as our election manifesto makes clear, Labour does not support independence or another referendum.
At PMQs Law referred to Burnham telling MPs last week that he would stick to every word of the Good Friday agreement. He went on:
[The PM] will therefore know that the Northern Ireland Act 1998 contains a provision for a referendum on leaving the United Kingdom, but no equivalent provision exists in the law for Scotland. Does he recognise that the people of Scotland have an equal right to choose their own future, and that the conditions for a second independence referendum should be set out in law?
Law was referring to a provision in the Good Friday agreement saying the Northern Ireland secretary has to order a referendum on reunification “if at any time it appears likely to him that a majority of those voting would express a wish that Northern Ireland should cease to be part of the United Kingdom and form part of a united Ireland”. Quite how the Northern Ireland secretary would decide this is not specified.
Responding to Law, Burnham said:
[Law] mentions the Good Friday agreement, and I will stick to it 100%.
I remind him, on the question of a border poll, that that is to be considered by the Northern Ireland secretary when there is clear consensus in the country – when public opinion has changed to the point at which the call has to be considered. I would say that it is exactly the same situation in Scotland. I am not aware that there is majority public support for another referendum, and until that changes, there will not be one.
In fact, some recent polls suggest there would be a small majority for independence if a referendum were to take place now.
John Swinney, the SNP leader and Scottish first minister, later claimed that Burnham had made an important concession. He posted on social media:
To go from “off limits” to this is an acceptance of the reality that the people of Scotland will decide their own future – not the UK government.
For the first time since 2014, a British prime minister accepts that majority support for a referendum should mean one takes place.

Andy Burnham is striking a welcome new tone at PMQs. He sounds like a man interested in the questions being asked, instinctively minded to be helpful (particularly to backbenchers) and, when confronted with a political criticism, interested in engaging with the argument. By contrast, when Keir Starmer was doing it, as the questions came his mind just seemed to be whirring towards the default ‘line to take’ discussed in advance. Perhaps it’s just because Burnham is new to the job and he has not been burned yet by making too many rash promises (or quasi-promises, like today’s on the Gravesend-Tilbury ferry – see 12.31pm). But he does seem to have some sort of strong, innate desire to win people round that might persist. During the summer, when Patrick Maguire from the Times put it to him in an interview that he worried too much about being liked, Burnham replied: “Isn’t the job to be popular by making people’s lives better? Isn’t that what you should be doing?”
Getting Kemi Badenoch to like or admire him may be too much to ask, but it was notable that Burnham kept stressing his commitment to working with her on issues like defence spending. Badenoch opened her questions with a reference to Burnham’s mini-gaffe last week, when he told Tan Dehsi that he was fully committed to raising defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030 when he meant 3.5% by 2035. Badenoch could have made this highly embarrassing for Burnham, but he got out of it fairly well – not actually committing to 3% by 2030 while at the same time implying (as Alex Wickham from Bloomberg explains here) that he will get there in the end.
The most interesting comments were about welfare. For at least a year now, the Conservatives have been arguing that the answer to the defence spending challenge (in fact, the answer to every government spending challenge) is just to cut welfare spending. In response to a challenge on this, Starmer would have just attacked the Tories’ record on defence. But Burnham sounded like someone who has actually read the Tory proposals in detail (which wouldn’t take long) and thought about why that might be a bad idea. And he told Badenoch:
I looked at it and I don’t think myself that taking £4bn out of housing benefit is the right consensus around this issue because that would create levels of homelessness in this country that we wouldn’t have seen before, hundreds of thousands of children in temporary accommodation.
He went on:
We do everything to support our national security, but it can’t come at the expense of social security. Having strong national security also depends upon having resilience in our communities. This side of the house will not be forced to choose between the two, and we will set out a plan to get to 3.5% (of GDP spent on defence) by 2035 at the spending review.
The Conservatives clearly think this is a mistake. Before the end of PMQs, a Tory spokesperson had put out a press release saying:
Britain heard it loud and clear today: Andy Burnham will not cut welfare to fund the defence of our country. The prime minister is prioritising the ballooning benefits bill over our national security. Shameful. This is not leadership, it is surrender.
But, if Labour want to win an argument with the opposition about welfare, they are going to have to explain why benefits matter and what happens when you cut them. Today, Burnham made a start.
The second most interesting comments were the ones that Badenoch did not make; she did not say anything about Israel. Maybe that was just because she decided it was yesterday’s story, but it is also possible that that she realises that she is in the wrong place on this issue. Yesterday she published an article on this issue which did not contain a word of criticism of Israel and which accused Burnham of just caving in to Corbynism and antisemitism. The Tories seemed to be eagerly awaiting Donald Trump to lash out. But the White House said very little, it turned out that those well-known Corbynites Emmanuel Macron and Mark Carney were doing exactly the same thing and even the Board of Deputies of British Jews was more critical of settler violence in its response than Badenoch. When a mainstream political leader ends up to the right of Donald Trump and the Board of Deputies on Israel policy, they have probably got it wrong.
Because Badenoch had not raised Israel, Burnham had to save up his global leadership spiel for his final answer. (See 12.19pm.) But it was worth the wait; it was pretty good.
Daisy Cooper (Lib Dem) asks about mental health provision in Hertfordshire. Will the PM back her campaign for a new facility there?
Burnham says that is a good question. Cooper is right to point to wasted spending in the health system, when people have to be sent a long way for care. A mental health strategy will be put to the Commons before Christmas, he says.

Brimstone 3 moves closer to Protector clearance
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
08:54:29 BST
16:54:29 KST

Brimstone 3 integration with the RAF’s Protector remotely piloted aircraft has moved into the analysis stage after further weapons testing in the United States and UK, Defence Minister Luke Pollard has said.
The update came in response to a written parliamentary question from Conservative MP Ben Obese-Jecty, who asked what progress had been made on integrating Brimstone 3 with Protector following earlier delays identified in previous answers and the National Infrastructure and Service Transformation Authority’s Major Projects Annual Report.
Pollard said the earlier delays had now been addressed through a revised testing programme involving activity on both sides of the Atlantic.
He said: “Previous delays have been overcome through a revised plan of combined USA and UK based testing, with final elements of safe separation trials concluding in the USA in June 2026 and further UK testing being conducted in August 2026.”
Safe separation testing is intended to demonstrate that a weapon can be released from an aircraft without creating an unacceptable risk to the platform or the weapon itself. The completion of those trials represents a key step towards clearing Brimstone 3 for operational use from Protector. The remaining work now centres on assessment of the trial results before the necessary clearances can be issued.
Pollard said: “Brimstone 3 trial data is undergoing necessary analysis required prior to issuance of operational clearances.”
Brimstone 3 is a precision-guided weapon intended for use against a range of ground targets and forms part of the planned weapons package for Protector, which is replacing the RAF’s Reaper fleet. The same parliamentary answer also provided an update on Paveway IV, another weapon intended for Protector.
Pollard said: “Paveway IV has been operationally available since March 2026.”
Paveway IV is already available operationally, while Brimstone 3 remains subject to analysis of trial data and the subsequent clearance process.
The latest update is significant because the Brimstone 3 work had previously been affected by delays. According to Pollard, those issues have now been overcome through the revised joint US-UK testing plan, with the final elements of safe separation testing completed in June and additional UK activity carried out in August.

German UGV maker ARX expands into Poland’s defense market
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
07:54:05 UTC
16:54:05 KST

- German UGV maker ARX Robotics is expanding into Poland, its fourth national market, the company announced September 9 at the MSPO defense show.
- ARX plans to invest tens of millions of euros in Poland and build a headquarters and support facilities, without disclosing a jobs figure or timeline.
German unmanned ground vehicle maker ARX Robotics is expanding into Poland, the company announced September 9, its fourth national market as it grows across Europe.
ARX plans to invest tens of millions of euros in Poland over the coming years, starting with a Polish legal entity followed by a permanent headquarters and dedicated training and maintenance facilities, the company said. It aims to create a number of skilled jobs by the end of the decade as the Polish operation grows.
The company announced the move at the MSPO defense exhibition in Kielce, Poland, which runs September 8 to 11.
“Poland is on the frontline of Europe’s security and is showing the seriousness, speed and industrial ambition Europe now needs,” said Marc Wietfeld, CEO and co-founder of ARX Robotics. “In light of increased Russian aggression towards our friends and allies along NATO’s eastern flank, we believe the time is right to deepen our commitment to Poland.”
“As our fourth market, Poland is an important step in our company’s growth,” Wietfeld said. “We want to build long-term capability here, support Polish Armed Forces and become part of Poland’s defense industrial base. Our experience in Ukraine has shown how quickly modern warfare is evolving, and we want to bring those lessons closer to Polish and NATO forces and help strengthen deterrence where it matters most.”
ARX did not name the three other European countries where it already operates, though the company said Poland gives it an active presence in three of Europe’s five largest defense markets, in addition to its work in Ukraine.
Munich-based ARX was founded in 2021 by former German Armed Forces members Marc Wietfeld and Stefan Röbel. Its main product is the GEREON family of unmanned ground vehicles, tracked robots that can carry loads of up to 500 kg (1,100 pounds) at speeds up to 30 km/h (19 mph) and a range of 40 km (25 miles). The vehicles are built for tasks including reconnaissance, casualty evacuation and battlefield logistics, jobs meant to keep soldiers out of direct danger.
ARX has deployed GEREON systems with Ukrainian forces at scale, and the company says its work there, including direct feedback from troops on the front line, feeds into how it develops systems for NATO and other European militaries. In July, German engine maker Deutz and ARX began serial production of GEREON vehicles in Ulm, Germany, with the first units bound for Ukraine.
The company’s systems have also been tested by the armed forces of Germany, Austria, Switzerland, Hungary and Estonia, according to previous company statements. ARX raised 9 million euros in seed funding in 2024 in a round led by NATO’s Innovation Fund.

Over 20 years after his capture, accused 9/11 mastermind still awaits trial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
07:52:25 UTC
16:52:25 KST

This Friday, the United States will mark 25 years since the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, still unable to secure full justice for the nearly 3,000 victims killed that terrible day and the additional 4,300 people who died in the years that followed, most of them rescuers and first responders who rushed to the site and developed a long list of illnesses linked to hazardous substances released into the air in the aftermath of the attacks.
Although al-Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden was killed in 2011, the trial of the man considered the mastermind behind the largest terrorist attack in history has not even begun. That is despite the fact that he has been in custody for 23 years. The U.S. failure to put Khalid Sheikh Mohammed on trial is perhaps the most symbolic example of the bitter legacy of the American response to the attacks. Years of torturing detainees and holding them at CIA “black sites” — a term for prisons outside the United States with no judicial oversight — or at the military detention facility at Guantanamo Bay continue to come back to haunt the American justice system.
Khalid Sheikh Mohammed was 37 or 38 — depending on which of his reported birth dates is to be believed — when he was captured on March 1, 2003, in Rawalpindi, Pakistan. He was captured in a joint raid by the CIA and Pakistani security forces on a safe house where he was staying. After his capture, he was held for about three and a half years at secret CIA detention facilities around the world, where he was subjected to severe physical interrogation, before being transferred in September 2006 to the military facility at Guantanamo Bay in Cuba, which is also outside the U.S. constitutional and judicial framework.
The official indictment against him was first filed in February 2008. It charged him with thousands of offenses, including conspiring to hijack aircraft and carry out the attacks; murder in violation of the laws of war — a charge encompassing 2,977 individual counts of murder for every person killed at the World Trade Center, the Pentagon and aboard the plane that crashed in Pennsylvania; attacking civilians and civilian objects; aircraft hijacking; destruction of property in violation of the laws of war and more.
In addition, the U.S. government has accused Khalid Sheikh Mohammed of involvement in the first World Trade Center bombing in 1993, the 2002 nightclub bombing in Bali and the murder of American journalist Daniel Pearl. If convicted, he would face the death penalty.
The military prosecution based much of the indictment on several confessions by Mohammed that he had planned the attacks. But even in the initial indictment, prosecutors did not include his confessions from interrogations at CIA facilities, which involved 183 rounds of waterboarding, a technique designed to simulate drowning. Instead, they relied on his confession during interrogations at Guantanamo, where he was questioned by FBI agents.
In 2009, then-U.S. president Barack Obama’s administration announced its intention to move Mohammed’s trial to a civilian court in New York. Then-attorney general Eric Holder argued that “there is no better way” than to put Mohammed in a courtroom, where he would have to face 12 jurors and see how the strength of the U.S. legal system surpassed everything he had tried to do. The decision met fierce political and public opposition, with critics arguing that it was inappropriate to try a terrorist in a civilian court. Congress subsequently passed a special law blocking funding for the transfer of Guantanamo detainees to U.S. soil.
As a result, in 2011 the Obama administration returned the case to the military justice system at Guantanamo. The problem is that this system was built almost from scratch specifically for al-Qaeda operatives and thousands of detainees after 9/11. It has suffered from legal instability, frequent turnover among military judges and a lack of clarity. As a result, virtually every decision by military judges triggers lengthy appeals to civilian courts in the United States, repeatedly freezing the proceedings for years at a time.
In 2024, for example, Mohammed agreed to a plea deal under which he would admit to most of the charges in exchange for prosecutors dropping the death penalty. But the plea agreement was rejected by the authorities in a sprawling political and legal saga.
Twenty-three years after his capture, it turns out that even military judges are in no hurry to accept the case as it stands today. Last week, a military judge ruled that Mohammed’s confessions during FBI interrogations at Guantanamo in 2007 were also not made voluntarily, excluding what prosecutors had described as “the government’s most important evidence in the case.”
In a 45-page ruling, Judge Lt. Col. Michael Sharrma wrote that “the prosecution failed to prove, by a preponderance of the evidence, that Mr. Mohammed’s statements to the FBI were voluntary.” Sharrma also found that FBI agents deliberately failed to explicitly tell Mohammed that he had the right to remain silent and consult with an attorney and that anything he said could be used against him at trial, as required under U.S. law.
Because the Guantanamo detention facility was established from the outset in part to avoid the need to uphold detainees’ rights, the decision by a military judge in 2026 represents a major blow to the prosecution. It is also a significant indictment of the administration of President George W. Bush and the measures taken in the aftermath of 9/11.
Defense lawyers argued that Mohammed had “essentially been trained by the CIA through torture, along with years of isolation and solitary confinement, to later tell FBI agents what they wanted to hear.”
Meanwhile, Lt. Col. Sharrma has set a trial date for June 5, 2028. If prosecutors decide to appeal his decision to exclude Mohammed’s confession, it is reasonable to assume that date will be pushed back again.
For now, Mohammed is already 60 or 61 and suffers from a number of health problems. Who knows when — or whether — he will ever stand trial.
And so, as the United States and the world mark 25 years since the attack that changed them forever, survivors are aging and victims’ families fear they may never see the end of the case.

Swiss army chief warns ‘Switzerland is in Russia’s sights’
Switzerland’s army chief Benedikt Roos has warned that the country is in Russia’s sights, but many Swiss people remain unaware of the potential threat.
Roos believes Switzerland faces both hybrid and military threats, but says many people have yet to grasp the seriousness of a crisis he considers imminent.
“I am concerned,” the chief of the armed forces said in an interview published by Swiss public broadcaster SRF. “We must assume there are targets in Switzerland that a major player in this global power struggle could set its sights on.”
More
Swiss army and intelligence service have new heads
Asked whether Switzerland is a target for Moscow, Roos replied: “Yes. This is a clash between two systems: the liberal democratic world and the autocratic one. More than ever, Switzerland is part of the Western world and is therefore a potential target.”
But why, the SRF reporter asked, would Russia attack the country? “Switzerland has critical infrastructure that is vital to Europe as a whole, including electricity and gas networks, key north-south transport links and major data centres. Anyone seeking to destabilise Europe could target exactly those assets,” said Roos, who has led the army since January.
In Leipzig, Germany, drones carrying explosives have been discovered. “We are seeing increased activity in this area. There has been more drone activity over critical infrastructure. Fortunately, none of them have been carrying explosives, but that could happen here too.”
+ Several unidentified drones spotted over a Swiss military base
Asked about unauthorised drone activity over military sites, he said: “In around 80% of cases, the drones are being flown by tourists or private individuals. But in the remaining 20%, we are not sure who is responsible and cannot clearly attribute them to any particular actor. We are investigating some cases in cooperation with the police, but we still do not know who is behind them.”
Roos himself is concerned about the Swiss Armed Forces’ delay in developing defences against drones. “We are strengthening our capabilities. The number of small reconnaissance drones issued to troops has increased tenfold over the past year. Now we need to step up our efforts on drone defence. This is one of the capability gaps we urgently need to close.”
More
Seven weaknesses in ‘Fortress Switzerland’
Asked about an earlier statement that Switzerland has no missile defence capability, the senior officer said: “Yes, that is correct when it comes to defending against cruise and ballistic missiles. We have significant capability gaps in this area. The delivery of the new Patriot system is being delayed and costs are rising, so we are looking at alternatives that could help close the gap more quickly.”
His biggest concern, however, is what he sees as a lack of public awareness of the threat. “This is the crucial issue. Public awareness is still too low. We are no longer insulated from what is happening elsewhere in the world. Fortunately, most of us have no direct experience of war. The idea that Switzerland could be drawn into a crisis has not yet fully sunk in,” said Roos.

Enemy shelling left some consumers without electricity in five regions of Ukraine

Due to attacks on energy infrastructure, consumers in five regions remain without electricity. No restrictions on electricity supply are forecast.
As of the morning of September 9, due to enemy shelling of energy infrastructure, some consumers in five regions of Ukraine remain without electricity. Restoration work is ongoing wherever the security situation allows. This was reported by the Ministry of Energy, UNN writes.
As a result of hostilities and shelling of energy infrastructure, some consumers in the Kyiv, Mykolaiv, Sumy, Kharkiv and Chernihiv regions were without electricity as of the morning. Restoration work is ongoing everywhere the security situation allows
Unfortunately, the enemy continues attacks not only on our energy infrastructure but also on energy workers. In the Zaporizhzhia region, an enemy UAV attacked a service vehicle belonging to energy workers. They were traveling to restore electricity supply in one of the communities in the region. Fortunately, no one was injured.
No restrictions are expected today. Find out about any changes to electricity supply on the official resources of your distribution system operators.
Consumers are advised, where possible, to shift active energy consumption to daytime hours—from 10:00 to 15:00—and to limit the use of high-powered electrical appliances from 18:00 to 22:00. This will help reduce the load on the power system.
We remind you
On September 8, a Russian attack damaged the energy infrastructure of the Mykolaiv and Kherson regions. After the security situation stabilized, electricity supply was restored.

Israel elections: Netanyahu or Eisenkot – what do the polls show?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
07:48:25 UTC
16:48:25 KST

Israel’s leading opposition party is polling ahead of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud ahead of the Oct. 27 general election, but surveys suggest the race remains highly dependent on smaller parties and post-election coalition choices.
Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar is the narrow favorite to emerge as the largest party in the 120-member Knesset, polling at 22-25 seats compared with 20-21 for Likud in surveys published between Sept. 3 and Sept. 8.
However, winning the most seats and forming the government are two different things in Israel’s parliamentary system.
Yashar could finish first while Netanyahu remains prime minister if he succeeds in assembling the support of at least 61 lawmakers. Conversely, opposition parties could collectively win more seats but fail to form a government if they cannot agree on coalition partners or outside support.
A new Maariv poll published Tuesday gives the opposition its clearest route yet to a majority, projecting 57 seats for opposition parties and four for a new party led by Yoaz Hendel and economist Yaron Zelekha. If the Hendel-Zelekha alliance joins the opposition, the bloc would reach 61 seats, the minimum needed to form a government.
Hendel and Zelekha, however, have not yet indicated which political bloc they would support if their party enters parliament.
While the recent polls disagree over which camp is ahead, they point to the same broader picture: Netanyahu’s bloc remains below a majority, while the opposition’s path depends heavily on smaller parties and coalition arithmetic.
The polls published by Maariv on Sept. 4, Channel 13 on Sept. 3 and Maariv again on Sept. 8 placed Yashar ahead of Likud.
A poll conducted by the Lazar Research Institute and published by Maariv on Sept. 4 projected Yashar to become the largest party with 23 seats, while Likud received 20.
A separate poll conducted by the Index research center and published by Israel’s Channel 13 on Sept. 3 put Yashar at 22 seats and Likud at 21, leaving only a one-seat difference between them.
The Sept. 3 Channel 13 figures represented a narrowing of Yashar’s lead. The broadcaster’s previous poll, published on Aug. 27, had projected Yashar to win 24 seats compared with 19 for Likud.
The latest Maariv poll, published Tuesday, showed Yashar strengthening to 25 seats, while Likud remained at 20.
A poll published by the Israeli Public Broadcasting Corporation KAN on Sept. 6 did not provide Yashar’s individual result in the figures cited, but showed Likud falling by one seat to 20.
The surveys therefore suggest that Yashar is more likely to finish first, although the small differences between parties in some polls and the margins of error mean that Likud could still narrow the gap before election day.
Eisenkot also leads Netanyahu when voters are asked whom they prefer as prime minister.
Maariv’s Sept. 4 poll showed 48% preferring Eisenkot compared with 39% for Netanyahu. Channel 13’s Sept. 3 poll similarly placed Eisenkot ahead by 47% to 37%.
Former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett also led Netanyahu by 43% to 39% in the Maariv poll.
These figures demonstrate Netanyahu’s political vulnerability but do not directly determine who becomes prime minister, as the position depends on which candidate can build a parliamentary coalition.
The polls published between Sept. 3 and Sept. 8 present different pictures of the contest between Netanyahu’s allies and the opposition.
The Maariv poll published on Sept. 4 produced a strong result for the Jewish opposition, giving it 57 seats compared with 51 for Netanyahu’s bloc. Arab parties received the remaining 12 seats.
Despite holding a six-seat advantage over Netanyahu’s camp, the opposition was still four seats short of the 61 required to govern without outside support.
The Sept. 4 Maariv poll was conducted by the Lazar Research Institute among 600 Israelis and had a margin of error of 4.4 percentage points.
Channel 13’s poll, published on Sept. 3, showed Netanyahu’s bloc and the Jewish opposition tied at 53 seats each, with Arab parties receiving 14 seats.
That represented a significant change from the broadcaster’s Aug. 27 poll, which had placed the opposition on 57 seats and Netanyahu’s bloc on 48. Arab parties had received 15 seats in the earlier survey.
The Sept. 3 Channel 13 poll was conducted by the Index research center among 940 Israelis, with a stated margin of error of 4.3 percentage points.
KAN’s poll, published on Sept. 6, placed Netanyahu’s bloc narrowly ahead with 52 seats, compared with 51 for the camp led by Eisenkot. Arab parties received 13 seats, while a new alliance between Hendel and Zelekha secured four.
The newest Maariv poll, published Tuesday, showed Netanyahu’s bloc falling to 47 seats, while the opposition parties received 57. The Hendel-Zelekha alliance received four seats, meaning the opposition could reach 61 if the new party joins its bloc.
The Tuesday Maariv poll was conducted by the Lazar Research Institute among 600 Israelis and had a margin of error of four percentage points.
Taken collectively, the polls put Netanyahu-aligned parties at 47-53 seats and the Jewish opposition at 51-57. Arab parties receive between 12 and 14 seats, while the Hendel-Zelekha alliance is projected at four seats in some polls.
The most important point is therefore not whether Netanyahu’s bloc receives 47, 52 or 53 seats. It is that every poll leaves it below 61.
The sharp movement between the recent polls is largely linked to smaller parties crossing or falling below the electoral threshold.
Ofer Winter’s Amcha Yisrael received four seats in the polls published by Channel 13 on Sept. 3 and Maariv on Sept. 4, while Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionism received between five and six.
Channel 13’s Aug. 27 poll had placed Netanyahu’s bloc at only 48 seats. After Winter’s party and Religious Zionism crossed the threshold, his camp rose to 53 seats in the broadcaster’s Sept. 3 poll.
However, Maariv’s latest Tuesday poll showed Netanyahu’s bloc losing ground after Winter’s far-right Amcha Yisrael party failed to win any seats. Religious Zionism was projected at five seats, while Likud received 20, Otzma Yehudit eight, and the religious parties United Torah Judaism and Shas seven each.
This shows how Netanyahu’s prospects could change quickly depending on whether smaller right-wing parties cross the threshold. If they fail, a considerable number of right-wing votes could be left without representation, sharply reducing his coalition options.
The Hendel-Zelekha alliance could also prove decisive. The latest Maariv poll projects it at four seats, enough to give the opposition a 61-seat majority if it joins the anti-Netanyahu bloc. But if it remains neutral, refuses to recommend either side, or backs Netanyahu, the opposition may again fall short.
The parties’ candidate-list decisions have intensified this uncertainty.
Winter rejected an alliance with Smotrich and submitted an independent list, prompting criticism from the Religious Zionism leader. On the opposition side, Eisenkot also decided that Yashar would run separately rather than merge with the Together alliance led by Bennett and including candidates from Yair Lapid’s Yesh Atid.

F-16 and Patriot Missiles: Key Outcomes of the 36th Ramstein Meeting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
07:47:23 UTC
16:47:23 KST

Following the 36th Ukraine Contact Group meeting in the Ramstein format, Ukraine will receive missiles for F-16 fighter jets and Patriot air defense systems, along with funding for weapons procurement programs.
Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense reported the development.
During the meeting, Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara and Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine Mykhailo Drapatyi presented Ukraine’s “War Plan” to international partners for the first time. The plan outlines the strategy guiding the Ukrainian Defense Forces.
Following the latest Ramstein meeting, Germany announced new deliveries of interceptor missiles for Patriot air defense systems, missiles for F-16 fighter jets, and funding for the procurement of drones.
The United Kingdom will allocate $135.6 million to purchase U.S. weapons under the PURL program and will also deliver 95,000 drones by the end of the year.
London announced the delivery of tens of thousands of extended-range artillery shells purchased with funding from other countries.
The Netherlands will allocate $300 million to the Drone Line project and to procure 300 anti-drone missiles.
Estonia announced that it would continue supporting Ukraine in 2027 and allocate at least 0.25% of its GDP to aid for Ukraine.
Sweden and Lithuania will contribute $14 million and $10 million, respectively, to the PURL program, while Norway will allocate $200 million to purchase missiles for Patriot air defense systems.
Spain will provide $2.3 million to purchase fuel through the NATO Support and Procurement Agency and deliver air defense missiles and artillery ammunition.
Poland will also provide Ukraine with $58.13 million in assistance. Part of the funding will be allocated, among other things, to air defense systems.

Ebola virus spreads to new Congolese health zone: WHO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
07:47:08 UTC
16:47:08 KST

James Tasamba
09 September 2026•Update: 09 September 2026
The number of health zones affected by Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo has increased to 61 across six provinces after the virus spread to the Kayna Health Zone in North Kivu province, the World Health Organization (WHO) Africa region office said in a situation report late Tuesday.
At least 6,686 cases have been recorded, including 3,226 deaths, since the outbreak in mid-May, according to the report.
The report said the epidemiological pattern of the Bundibugyo virus strain outbreak in Congo is becoming increasingly heterogeneous, with divergent transmission trends across affected provinces and health zones.
“The trends reinforce an increasingly heterogeneous epidemic, with declining transmission in some areas occurring alongside intensification and continued geographic spread elsewhere,” the report said.
Affected provinces include Haut-Uele, Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Bas-Uele and Tshopo.
Ituri remains the principal focus, while substantial transmission continues in North Kivu and Haut-Uele and new areas continue to be affected.
WHO highlighted the rising proportion of deaths occurring in the community.
Between Aug. 31 and Sept. 6, the proportion of confirmed deaths in the community reached 75%, up from 56.6% two weeks earlier.
The report underlined that the persistence of high community mortality may reflect multiple barriers, including delayed detection and notification, delayed transfer to treatment facilities, limited recognition of illness, geographic and transport barriers, as well as community trust.
“This divergence is concerning, as the increase in community deaths alongside the continued decline in treatment facilities deaths indicates that the earlier reduction in overall mortality has not been sustained,” the report said.
The Congolese government and health partners last week launched a revised 180-day multisectoral plan worth $1.3 billion aimed at scaling up and coordinating the response to break chains of virus transmission.
It provides for a massive strengthening of epidemiological surveillance, contact tracing, community engagement, risk communication and logistical capacity, as well as the preparation of at-risk provinces.

‘Gambling with our lives’: AI researcher quits Anthropic with dire warning about safety
“The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” staffer says in resignation post after leaving the tech giant.
An artificial intelligence researcher who worked at Anthropic — and previously OpenAI — has resigned, saying both tech giants are "gambling with our lives."
Jacob Coxon shared his exit in a post on X, warning that the world should "not underestimate the power of this technology." He added: "These will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything, revolutionize any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources. We have all witnessed the progress in each of these domains, and progress is not slowing."
Coxon said both Anthropic and OpenAI are "racing straight to self-improving superintelligence," which refers to a scenario in which AI models can develop a more capable successor of themselves, creating an unstoppable feedback loop.
Advertisement
That is seen, by AI companies such as Google-owned Deepmind, as one of the possible triggers for a scenario in which AI vastly exceeds human intelligence (known as artificial superintelligence) instead of just matching it (known as artificial general intelligence).
"The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade," Coxon said in a follow-up post.
"Jacob is correct here — we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans," he said.
Hubinger estimated the chances of that happening to be higher than ten percent within the next decade, and added that there's no plan yet on how to keep AI aligned with human goals in the superintelligence scenario.
Last week, U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders announced he would introduce legislation to ban firms from developing superintelligence.
Advertisement
In the EU, the bloc's flagship AI law mandates that companies assess and mitigate so-called loss-of-control risks, in which humans no longer have control over AI models.
Both OpenAI and Anthropic have recently flagged incidents in which agents powered by their models went rogue, breaking out of their isolated test environments and carrying out unauthorized real-world cyberattacks.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has instructed his lawyers to issue a libel lawsuit against Haaretz following a recent report in which it claimed that he had been warned by the UAE about Hamas’s October 7 attack, the Prime Minister’s Office announced on Wednesday.
The lawsuit will also target Shlomi Eldar, the Haaretz journalist who covered the story.
The PMO stated that the story was completely fabricated and that there had been no communication between Netanyahu and the UAE from the start of September 2023 until the October 7 attack.
“A thorough examination not only of the prime minister’s call log, but also of the records of entries into the Prime Minister’s Office during this period, does not show any entry of the Emirati representative into the Prime Minister’s Office,” the PMO said.
The PMO said the report was part of a “sinister plot with clear political timing, as part of the Left’s election campaign,” warning that there would be “more such false plots.”
PMO blames Ronen Bar, Herzi Halevi for October 7
The announcement also directed blame for October 7 at former Shin Bet head Ronen Bar and former IDF chief of staff Herzi Halevi, claiming that they had seen the signs of the massacre hours before the attack began, and accusing them of not informing Netanyahu in time.
In response to the PMO announcing the lawsuit, Haaretz stated that it stood by its report.

UK air traffic control provider boss given one week to deliver report into flight chaos
Gwyn TophamandMark Sweney
The head of the UK air traffic control provider Nats has been given a week to report back on the reasons for the technical failure that has disrupted thousands of flights in the UK and across Europe since Tuesday.
Downing Street said the government still had confidence in Nats chief executive Martin Rolfe, who was summoned to meet the UK transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, on Wednesday morning as the number of flight cancellations passed 2,000.
Hundreds of thousands of passengers had their travel disrupted and delayed, with many stuck on grounded planes for many hours as the incident unravelled. Other passengers were stranded overnight at airports in the UK and abroad.
Alexander raised “significant concerns” with Rolfe, according to the prime minister’s official spokesperson, who told reporters: “She’s asked him to carry out a full investigation into what happened to make sure that lessons are learned, so that this doesn’t happen again.”
They added: “It’s self-evident that she wants answers and the full investigation to be reported back in a week’s time, and she’s got confidence in him to deliver that.”
Pressed on whether the government’s confidence in the head of air traffic control was conditional on the investigation, the spokesperson replied: “We have confidence in him and he’s been tasked with the investigation, which will report in a week’s time.”
Airlines including Ryanair and WizzAir have called for Rolfe to resign or be sacked by Alexander.

German chancellor accuses far-right AfD party of seeking ‘ethnic cleansing’
And if you missed our earlier coverage of Friedrich Merz’s fiery debate with AfD’s leader Alice Weidel (10:05, 10:21),we have this report by our Berlin correspondent, Deborah Cole.
“Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, has accused the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) of seeking “ethnic cleansing” with its “remigration” drive, after the nativist party’s seismic weekend victory in a state election.
In his first public confrontation with the AfD since Sunday’s shock outcome in Saxony-Anhalt, Merz said at a raucous parliamentary debate that the far-right party would take an axe to one of the pillars of the German economy with a racist campaign of mass deportations.
“The term ‘remigration’ is nothing but a synonym for ethnic cleansing based on origin and skin colour,” he said on Wednesday to applause from the other parties in the Bundestag lower house.
In a fiery speech addressed to the AfD parliamentary group, which repeatedly interrupted him with loud taunts and heckling, Merz said millions of working immigrants were crucial to German society.
“If those working in Germany have to leave the country again because you are championing ‘remigration’,” Merz said, “then the skilled trades in Germany will no longer be able to function: not a single care home will remain open, not a single hospital in Germany will remain operational, and not a single restaurant in Germany will be able to stay in business.”
He said the AfD’s rhetoric, which propelled it to the strongest showing for a far-right party in a German state since the Nazi period, “is precisely what is dividing our society so deeply”.
Support for Merz, a conservative Christian Democrat, has plummeted in the 16 months since he took office at the helm of a coalition with the centre-left Social Democrats, amid disappointment over slow progress on economic growth and the cost of living.
He has adopted a hard line on border policy in a faltering bid to win back AfD supporters, and acknowledged Germany still had “problems in the area of migration”.”
Germany's Pistorius warns against 'real, serious, acute' threat from Russia and criticises 'treasonous' AfD
Meanwhile, German defence minister Boris Pistorius is speaking in the Bundestag, outlining why Germany needs to ramp up its defence spending to counter the emerging threat from Russia.
He says the proposed spending is needed to deliver on the pledge to keep the country safe, despite some criticism based on “very simplistic approach” of “populist” comparisons against schools, roads, or hospitals.
“A strong, capable Bundeswehr and a united, capable Nato are essential if we are to truly protect and preserve our achievements and our way of life. Without security, nothing else matters,” he says.
He says the Russian threat Germany and Europe more broadly is “real, serious and acute,” as demonstrated by the recent attempted drone attack in Leipzig, as well as other incidents including an armed Russian fighter jet in Estonian airspace and drone incidents elsewhere.
“Russia is attempting to spy on, influence, intimidate, and destabilize our societies – and, above all, to sow uncertainty among the public. And this represents a new level of threat. Moscow is increasingly willing to accept the risk of escalation.”
He says Russia is “massively ramping up” its defence spending, a clear “threat” against Europe.
Without willing to disclose too much, Pistorius adds:
“Why, after all, did CIA Director Radcliffe travel to Moscow just under two weeks ago? Certainly not to buy matryoshka dolls or go to the ballet.”
“And the only ones … who deny it, who call him a friend … who want to pull out Nato and jeopardise the security of us all, they are sitting right there – that is the AfD,” he says, adding that the party’s links with Russia are “treasonous.”
“You need to realize that these are the very people ready to hand us over to Putin tomorrow,” he warns.

EU unveils ‘buy European’ public procurement rules to counter China
Jennifer Rankin
in Brussels
European authorities will be encouraged to buy more domestic goods and services when they spend public money under the EU latest effort to counter China’s economic might.
In a further “Buy European” plan, the European Commission published proposals on Wednesday for a sweeping overhaul of EU public procurement rules.
National authorities and public bodies, such as schools and hospitals, will be encouraged to buy goods and services made in Europe but, unlike earlier plans to promote domestically manufactured clean tech, there will be no binding “made in Europe” quotas.
Brussels officials are concerned that many public agencies think existing EU rules oblige them to choose the cheapest bid when spending public money, which can lead to the contract going to a non-European firm.
The European Commission’s lead official on industrial policy, Stéphane Séjourné, told reporters the regulation would give public sector buyers greater legal certainty and clarity about purchasing goods and services made in Europe.
“Purchasers can have a more preferential approach to European bids [and] restrict or reject bids from countries which do not have a public procurement agreement or do not play by binding rules in terms of public procurement internationally,” he said.
Séjourné hopes the proposals will encourage more democratic scrutiny over the spending of public money by local authorities.
“It won’t be the European Commission’s fault if purchasers were to prefer Chinese buses to European buses because … in the [draft regulation] there is every possibility to give preference to European buses.”
Meanwhile in Serbia, the country’s president Aleksandar Vučić dissolved parliament and announced snap elections for next month as he seeks to extend his hold on power by running for prime minister.
Reuters reported that Vučić, a populist who has been in power as president or prime minister for 12 years, has faced nearly two years of anti-corruption demonstrations triggered by the collapse of a railway station awning in the city of Novi Sad in November 2024 that killed 16 people.
At least 20 injured after passenger train crashes with truck in Poland
At least 20 people have been injured, four of them seriously, after an InterCity passenger train struck a truck at a level crossing in Poland and derailed.
Poland’s railway operator, PKP Intercity, said 120 people were on board at the time of the crash.
Russia hopes to see restarted peace talks with Ukraine, says Europe 'harming itself' by cutting off Russian gas
Russia hopes that peace talks between Ukraine and Russia, mediated by the United States, will resume in the near future, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said in comments reported by Reuters.
No such direct talks have taken place since February.
But the Kremlin will not publicly discuss potential elements of a possible peace settlement, Peskov added.
He was speaking after Russian president Vladimir Putin and US president Donald Trump had a telephone call on Tuesday to discuss prospects for ending the war.
Peskov also said that European countries have found themselves in a difficult position amid rising gas prices, and that they could buy gas at cheaper prices from Russia.
European natural gas prices have soared amid the war in Iran, hitting their highest level last week since late 2022, when the start of the Ukraine conflict prompted Europe to cut off Russian pipeline gas.
Peskov said Europe was harming itself by buying expensive gas at spot prices as opposed to the more affordable Russian option, and suggested that the controversial Nord Stream pipeline could be restarted soon.
Kremlin’s spokesperson also confirmed that Russia would respond to Hungary’s decision to expel 10 Russian diplomats from Budapest.

Devil’s Arrows: Ancient builders hauled 55,000-pound stones 11 miles for Britain’s tallest stone row
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
07:41:21 UTC
16:41:21 KST

Devil’s Arrows: Ancient builders hauled 55,000-pound stones 11 miles for Britain’s tallest stone row
- Date:
- September 9, 2026
- Source:
- Curtin University
- Summary:
- Britain’s towering Devil’s Arrows were built from 25-tonne stones hauled at least 18 kilometers from Brimham Rocks around 4,000 years ago. The discovery reveals an astonishing feat of prehistoric engineering and suggests the stones’ distant source may have been chosen for cultural or spiritual reasons.
- Share:
Ancient builders hauled enormous 25-tonne (55,000-pound) stones across at least 18 kilometers (11 miles) to create Britain's tallest surviving prehistoric stone row, according to new research into the iconic Devil's Arrows.
The study, led by Curtin University in collaboration with the University of York, UK, is the first to pinpoint the geological source of the towering stones. Researchers traced them to Brimham Rocks, a rugged area in North Yorkshire.
Located near Boroughbridge in northern England, the Devil's Arrows rise as high as seven meters (23 feet). They form an unusual stone alignment in a lowland landscape, and despite their striking size, scientists had not been able to determine where the stones originally came from.
Researchers believe the stones were transported and raised during the Late Neolithic or Early Bronze Age, possibly around 2000 BC.
A Distant Source for Britain's Giant Stones
Lead author Dr. Anthony Clarke, from the Timescales of Mineral Systems Group within Curtin's School of Earth and Planetary Sciences, said the discovery challenges previous ideas about the decisions prehistoric people made when constructing major monuments.
"Our research shows these stones weren't simply taken from the nearest available source -- they were deliberately chosen from a challenging landscape 18 kilometers away," Dr. Clarke said.
"Plumpton Rocks, which is closer to the Devil's Arrows, had previously been identified as the probable source of the stones. Our findings instead point to Brimham Rocks, showing that prehistoric builders transported these enormous stones significantly further than thought.
"Each stone weighs more than 25 tonnes, so moving them would have required incredible planning, coordination and engineering skill.
"This tells us prehistoric people placed real importance on the landscape itself. It wasn't just about convenience -- the location the stones came from likely held meaning for them."
The findings suggest that the builders were not simply choosing the easiest or closest source of stone. Instead, the landscape around Brimham Rocks may have carried cultural, symbolic, or spiritual significance.
Co-author Dr. Jim Leary from the University of York said the discovery changes how researchers can interpret prehistoric monument building.
"These results show that ancient communities were making deliberate and meaningful choices about where their stones came from," Dr. Leary said.
"It highlights the importance of landscape and shared belief systems, as well as the remarkable effort involved in transporting and raising stones of this size."
Mineral Fingerprints Reveal the Stones' Origin
To determine where the stones came from, the researchers used a new low-impact sampling technique. Adhesive tape allowed them to collect tiny mineral grains from the stones without damaging the monument.
They then analyzed the age "fingerprints" of those grains and compared them with geological samples from possible source locations. The results matched the Devil's Arrows to Brimham Rocks.
The evidence also allowed the team to rule out natural explanations such as glacial movement. That means the enormous stones were intentionally moved to the monument site by people.
New Clues to Prehistoric Engineering
Dr. Clarke said the researchers now plan to use their non-invasive technique on other standing stones whose origins remain uncertain. They also hope to carry out targeted excavations at both the Devil's Arrows and the newly identified source area.
"These next steps could help us better understand when the stones were moved and how these extraordinary monuments were constructed," Dr. Clarke said.
Justin Scully, National Trust General Manager for Fountains Abbey & Studley Royal and Brimham Rocks, said the findings establish a direct connection between Brimham Rocks and the Devil's Arrows, linking two distinctive Yorkshire landscapes.
"We're incredibly grateful to the researchers for helping us uncover this new chapter in the stones' story and deepen our understanding of the people who shaped this landscape thousands of years ago," Mr. Scully said.
"The Devil's Arrows are deeply cherished by local communities, and we're delighted that this discovery adds a new chapter to their story."
The study, "Deliberate Prehistoric Sourcing of the Devil's Arrows, Britain's Tallest Stone Row," was published in the Proceedings of the Royal Society A.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Curtin University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Anthony Clarke, Jim Leary, Chris Kirkland. Deliberate prehistoric sourcing of the Devil\'s Arrows, Britain\'s tallest stone row. Proceedings of the Royal Society A Mathematical Physical and Engineering Science, 2026; 482 (2345) DOI: 10.1098/rspa.2026.0504

The Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) is providing up to $75 million in financing to establish an advanced green manufacturing facility in northwestern Türkiye.
The AIIB made another investment as part of ongoing efforts to develop Türkiye’s advanced technology and green manufacturing capacity.
The advanced plant to be built in the northwestern province of Kırklareli will be established by Chinese manufacturer Great Rich Technology, marking the firm’s first production base outside China.
The facility will be co-financed by the World Bank Group’s International Finance Corporation, and it will produce energy-efficient window films, paint protection films, and specialized materials to absorb carbon dioxide and volatile organic compounds.
The investment aims to reduce industrial emissions, expand the availability of low-emission advanced materials in emerging markets, and help solidify Türkiye’s position as a manufacturing hub bridging Europe, Asia and other neighboring markets.
Ajay Bushan Pandey, vice president of the AIIB, told Anadolu Agency that the bank made its second-largest investment among all its members in Türkiye over the past decade.
“$9 billion and about 40 projects we have invested in, and then there are many more projects in the pipeline,” he said.
“We have our second-largest investment in Türkiye, [and] the only country that is first is India, […] but if you look at it per capita-wise, I think Türkiye will be the highest,” said Pandey.

How one woman’s Tesla was remotely controlled – and used to harass her – by an abusive ex-partner
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
07:35:02 UTC
16:35:02 KST

Almost a year ago, Stacey* heard her Tesla car alarm sound on three occasions in the middle of the night.
By that point, the Sydney woman had suffered four years of domestic abuse by her former partner and disgraced businessman, Enrico Pucci. When the alarm sounded, she was “too scared” to go outside because she thought he may be damaging her vehicle, according to police documents tendered in court.
The next morning, the car appeared undamaged, but Stacey noticed its electronic dashboard had been reset and a “parental control” profile had been added.
Three days later, Pucci, now 50, followed her in a car and started to yell at her about a man she was dating.
“You thought you’d get away with this. I am in your car. I am in your maps,” he shouted at her, according to the police records.
Over the coming days, Stacey found that the parental control profile, to which she had no access, could almost entirely control the car, including its speed, climate control, lock and curfew hours, determining when the car could be driven.
Between 6 and 12 November 2025, Pucci remotely alternated the car’s temperature setting between extremely cold and extremely hot.
“The victim has not been able to drive certain speeds and on most recent occasions throughout this period, [the accused] has turned on ‘Valet Mode’ which immediately reduces the speed to 40km per hour causing significant safety issues for the victim on the road”, the police documents stated.
“The victim has not had any control of her vehicle since she noticed the parental control profile added on the 1st November 2025.
“The accused has been the only one with access to the vehicle’s controls utilising the Tesla app. This has caused the victim significant stress, mental harm and fears for her physical safety when operating her own vehicle.”
Last Wednesday, Pucci was convicted of 30 domestic violence related charges against Stacey, including using the Tesla car app to harass her.
Judge Peter Feather sentenced him to two years and three months before Parramatta local court in western Sydney, with a non-parole period of 15 months, after he pleaded guilty to the charges the week before a hearing scheduled in August.
During his sentencing remarks, Feather said Pucci had engaged in “abusive behaviour” towards his former partner over the course of four years. This included “multiple methods to dominate” the woman, including using the Tesla app to control her car, and forging fraudulent employment opportunities to “create dependency” while “also forcing her to pass up other opportunities”.
“When viewed cumulatively, [it] amounts to conduct that’s both coercive and controlling in nature, reflecting a pattern of behaviour designed to entrench power and compliance,” Feather said.
‘Everything went quiet’
The police documents detailed years of abuse. In an incident which led to a conviction of common assault, Stacey in March 2020 told Pucci she wished to separate while they were in the car with the victim’s two-year-old son.
“The accused threatened that would be the last time the victim sees her son if she ended the relationship,” the documents said. “The accused forcibly took her phone and typed a message to the victim’s ex husband stating that she could not care for her son and wished to give him up.”
“The accused forcibly removed the victim from her car and dragged her to a nearby pillar, pinned her against it and said ‘say goodbye to your son’. The accused drove off with the victim’s child, leaving the victim without a phone or a car.”
According to the documents, Pucci returned a few minutes later, then grabbed Stacey’s arm and said, “I hope you comprehend what will happen to you if you break up again”.
Separately, in 2021, after they were married, Pucci strangled Stacey to the point she recalled hearing gurgling noises and “fighting” for her life, the documents stated.
“Everything went quiet, and the victim blacked out,” the documents read.
“The victim believed she was going to die.”
Stacey bought a Tesla car while they were still a couple, the documents said. 
 After having trouble navigating the technology, Stacey was offered help from Pucci, who said he would need the car to be registered in his name so “he could take control of the Tesla app to ‘assist her’”.
“The victim agreed, solely for the purpose of assistance with the vehicle technology,” the documents said.
In November 2025, a month after the relationship had ended, Pucci used Stacey’s Tesla car app to harass her, which fell under a charge of using a carriage service to stalk or harass.
This included seven attempts by Pucci to disconnect her car from its charging port via the Tesla app.
History of abuse
Pucci is appealing against his sentence for the 30 offences and is scheduled to face court again in late October.
The offences include eight counts of stalking or intimidation with the intention to cause fear or physical harm, six counts of common assault, two counts of choking a person without consent, one count of using a carriage service to threaten to kill and one count of using a carriage service to menace, harass or offend.
In 2017, the federal court found that a Sydney cleaning firm owned by Pucci had treated some vulnerable foreign workers as “slaves” after refusing to pay them for months and leaving them to go without furniture, food and critical medical treatment.
The fair work ombudsman secured a penalty of nearly $450,000 in the federal court against Grouped Property Services (GPS) Pty Ltd. Pucci, the company’s current owner and sole director, was fined $3,000 for firing a woman when she asked why she had not been paid.
His brother, Rosario Pucci, the former owner-operator of the company, was described by the federal court as being “intimately involved” in the exploitation and fined a further $74,300.
In 2022, ASIC disqualified Enrico Pucci from managing corporations for the maximum period of five years due to his “involvement in the failure of three companies”, which owed almost $10m to creditors.

Everyone’s tax bill is falling, except the top 10%: CBS
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
07:34:01 UTC
16:34:01 KST

Everyone’s tax bill is falling, except the top 10%: CBS
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The share of income going on income tax has fallen for all income groups over the past ten years, except for the top 10% of earners, according to the national statistics office CBS. The top tier pays 24.9% of its income in tax, while the very lowest pays nothing.
The typical household paid 12.3% of its gross income in income tax and national insurance contributions in 2024, down from 15.4% in 2011.
The figures do not include VAT, which hits the poorest hardest, or pension and unemployment insurance premiums. Including all taxes and premiums, the typical household paid 32.3% in 2024, against 35.2% in 2011.
The figures also don’t say anything about purchasing power. Consumer prices are more than a fifth higher than in 2021, and inflation was 3.3% in August, driven by rising energy costs.
Low earners
 The highest earners paid 24.9% in 2024, slightly more than the 24.7% they paid in 2014. Every other group is paying less.
The biggest drop was for low earners. The second-poorest 10% of households now pay 2.3% of their income in tax, down from 6.7% in 2014. CBS said the employment tax credit was raised substantially over the period, particularly for lower incomes.
“You see a levelling trend here,” CBS chief economist Peter Hein van Mulligen told the Telegraaf. Whether income inequality has fallen as a result cannot be read from these figures alone, he said, and other CBS data show it has stayed broadly stable.
Singles pay most, self-employed more
 Couples with two incomes pay far less than anyone else on the same income. On a household income of around €100,000, a couple with two salaries pays 11.9% in tax, a couple with one salary pays 19.4% and a single person pays 22.5%.
The self-employed are the only group paying more than a decade ago, up from 13.4% to 15.6%.

The IDF and Shin Bet security agency said Wednesday that they had destroyed three weapons depots and a rocket launch pit in the Gaza Strip that had been used to fire rockets at Israel during the war.
In a joint statement, the IDF and Shin Bet said the targeted strikes were carried out Tuesday in several areas of Gaza. They said the weapons depots belonged to Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad.
“The terrorist organizations stored dozens of different kinds of weapons inside the storage facilities, including rockets, Kalachnikov rifles, and additional combat equipment,” the statement said.
“Furthermore, the IDF identified that recently, Hamas terrorists have been arriving at the storage facilities and using the weapons stored inside them to establish control in the Gaza Strip and carry out operations.”
The military said its forces remain deployed along the so-called "yellow line," which runs through Gaza from north to south under the current ceasefire arrangements.
“The IDF will continue to operate decisively to degrade the capabilities of terrorist organizations in the Gaza Strip while thwarting any attempt to rebuild capabilities or use weapons intended to harm IDF troops,” the military said. It added that troops under the IDF Southern Command were deployed in accordance with the agreement and would continue acting against immediate threats.
The latest strikes came days after the military attacked Hamas infrastructure in response to an explosive device that detonated against an IDF engineering vehicle in the yellow line sector of northern Gaza.
No soldiers were injured in the explosion.
The IDF described the incident as another Hamas violation of the ceasefire, though it remained unclear when the explosive device had been planted. The military opened an investigation to determine when the device was placed, leaving open the possibility that it had been planted before the current arrangements took effect.
The military said the Hamas infrastructure targeted in response had been used to advance plans for attacks against Israel and IDF troops.
The developments come as Israel considers a new model for transferring control of parts of Gaza away from the IDF.
Last week, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz had instructed the military to draw up a plan for establishing “pilot zones” in Gaza, modeled on arrangements being implemented in southern Lebanon.
Under the emerging proposal, which Katz raised and Netanyahu supports, designated areas of Gaza would be entered by international forces tasked with clearing the territory, establishing governance and preventing Hamas operatives from returning.
The plan would be coordinated with the United States, according to the report.
The proposed model draws on Israel’s approach in southern Lebanon, where Israeli forces withdraw from designated areas as they are transferred to the control of the Lebanese military.
The Gaza proposal remains under development and has not yet been implemented.

Hualien township mayor and husband arrested for alleged vote-buying
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
07:31:26 UTC
16:31:26 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Hualien prosecutors on Tuesday arrested incumbent Xiulin Township Mayor Sitang Yuci (王玫瑰) and her husband, Hu Chih-min (胡智民), over alleged vote-buying ahead of the local elections.
Prosecutors said Wednesday that Sitang Yuci and Hu used cash, gifts, and free banquets to solicit voter support, while a charity group is suspected of helping channel local corporate contributions toward the activities, per Liberty Times. It is the first reported vote-buying case this year.
Sitang Yuci, a KMT member, is set to leave office and run for Hualien County Council, while Hu, a retired police officer who has never held political office, is running to succeed her as mayor. Prosecutors allege the couple held banquets in March and April under the pretext of celebrating Hu's 60th birthday, where eligible voters were encouraged to support his candidacy.
Xiulin Township receives more than NT$100 million (US$3.1 million) a year in corporate contributions from mining operations, cement plants, power plants, and other facilities that can face opposition from nearby communities, Liberty Times reported. Investigators suspect some of the money was allocated to the Little Sun Caring Association as charitable funding before an official with the association, surnamed Hsu (徐), used it to finance banquets for Hu.
Sitang Yuci and Hu also held a social gathering in Yilan where guests received cash gifts, and investigators are examining whether those expenses also involved the alleged misuse of corporate contributions. The couple frequently appeared together at township events during Hu's campaign, where they promoted his candidacy.
Hualien prosecutors said Prosecutor Chiang Ang-hsuan (江昂軒) led investigators from the Ministry of Justice Investigation Bureau, Hualien police, and the National Immigration Agency in searches Tuesday at eight locations, according to Liberty Times. The searches included Xiulin Township Office and the suspects' residences.
Prosecutors said Sitang Yuci, Hu, and Hsu are suspected of breaching Article 99, Paragraph 1, of the Public Officials Election and Recall Act, which prohibits vote buying. After questioning, prosecutors arrested the three and sought their detention without visitation, citing concerns that they could flee, destroy evidence, or collude with co-defendants and witnesses.
They could also face charges of embezzlement of public-welfare funds, per CNA. Investigators have identified suspected cash payments of about NT$1,000 to NT$2,000 per vote.
