Turkish apparel industry calls for creation of ‘production hubs’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
06:11:33 UTC
15:11:33 KST

Türkiye’s ready-to-wear industry has called for the establishment of regional production hubs to help reverse market contraction and declining employment in the sector.
Turkish Clothing Manufacturers’ Association (TGSD) Co-Chair Toygar Narbay said the industry needs a new and integrated industrial policy that brings together production, exports, employment, financing, technology and branding under a common objective.
“As large companies shrink, our production scale, skilled workforce and supply chain have also weakened,” Narbay said.
Narbay proposed the creation of production basins under Turkish capital and management along a corridor stretching across Syria, northern Iraq and Azerbaijan.
He said such production hubs could help attract cost-sensitive orders, make better use of idle machinery and increase utilization of Türkiye’s textile and supporting industries, ultimately lowering costs.
“Through these production basins, we can secure cost-sensitive orders, reactivate idle machinery and fill domestic textile and supplier capacities,” Narbay said.
According to Narbay, Syria alone could generate 250,000 jobs and provide annual export capacity of $5 billion in the medium term.
Assessing the impact of ongoing conflict in the Middle East on the industry, Narbay said Türkiye’s ready-to-wear exports fell 2 percent in January-August, while textile exports rose 1 percent during the same period.
He also noted that capacity reductions in the Far East caused by the energy crisis had redirected some orders to Türkiye.
“While demand has contracted by around 10 percent in the United States and Europe, the contraction in Turkey has remained at 2 percent, indicating that orders are continuing to come to Türkiye,” Narbay said.

The music of the Bulgarian band Ostava has always managed to capture the pulse of society, addressing pressing issues in a poetic way. We hear this once again in their latest single, “Kurshumi” (Bullets) from the album “Sartse/Vina” — a story about disappointment, time and the journey back to each other. The music and lyrics were written by Georgi Georgiev, the band’s guitarist and vocalist, who, together with Svilen Noev, is one of Ostava’s songwriters. His original idea was for the song to be slower, which is why its tempo gradually builds throughout. During rehearsals, however, Ostava’s drummer Dani suggested a beat that was twice as fast. This helped shape the song’s final indie-alternative sound.
The message was inspired by the major social protests that took place recently and by the disappointment caused by empty political promises. But, as Zhoro explains, there is more to it:
PHOTO Facebook / Ostava
“The lyrics also have a very personal dimension. They talk about these disappointments, but also about how we emerge stronger from them because we don’t allow the empty words that are aggressively thrown at us every day to hit us. Sometimes we try to move forward, and all of this just passes us by. Basically, salvation lies in love, as the song says.”
PHOTO YouTube / ostavaofficial
The premiere of the video for “Bullets” comes just days before Ostava’s traditional autumn concert, with which the band celebrates its birthday. This year, the concert will take place on September 9 at Maimunarnika in Borisova Garden in Sofia, with the young band Scarlet taking the stage before them. Three days later, on September 12, Ostava will give another concert, this time at Orpheus Open Air Cinema in Plovdiv. With these two major open-air concerts, the band will bid farewell to the summer.

Biden admin. was unaware of any UAE Oct. 7 massacre warning to Israel, sources tell 'Post'

06:09:37 UTC
15:09:37 KST

The Biden administration was not aware of any specific warning from the United Arab Emirates before the October 7 massacre that Hamas was planning a major terror attack, two sources familiar with the details told The Jerusalem Post on Wednesday.
Even in the period after the massacre, Biden administration officials did not hear that the UAE had issued a specific warning, the sources said.
The fact that the Biden administration was not aware that a warning was issued does not mean the UAE did not convey a message to Israeli leadership. However, it is reasonable to assume that if a significant warning had been issued, the Biden administration would have learned of it from the Emiratis, either before the massacre or, certainly, afterward.
Comments come in reaction to Haaretz report that MBZ warned Netanyahu of upcoming terror attack possibility
The comments follow a report initially published by Haaretz on Tuesday, stating that UAE President Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan (MBZ) had spoken with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu over a week before the massacre for approximately 45 minutes.
During the conversation, MBZ reportedly said that Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar was planning a “major move” against Israel. He is said to have expressed concern that the incident could lead to bloodshed, destabilize the region, and even undermine the Abraham Accords.
The report also claimed that then-CIA director William Burns heard from MBZ that the latter had tried to convey to Netanyahu that “something is about to explode” in the region.
However, a source familiar with the details told the Post that MBZ spoke with Burns after October 7, and told him that, in a discussion he had with Netanyahu before October 7, he had conveyed a “general warning about the volatile situation on the ground” — meaning that it was not a specific warning about an impending war or anything of that nature.
Biden admin. denies report that UAE warned US about October 7
Despite these claims, Biden administration officials were not aware of any such specific warning.
In one instance, former secretary of state Antony Blinken outright denied a quote that was attributed to him in the Haaretz article.
"For the record, this is false. Complete fiction," he wrote in a post on X/Twitter with a screenshot of his quote.
Haaretz reported that Blinken spoke with Qatari Emir al-Thani, who informed him that he had offered to negotiate a quick deal.
“There are hundreds of hostages in Gaza, and among them, in my estimation, dozens of civilians. They need to be released now," al-Thani told Blinken, as quoted by Haaretz.
"I offered the Israelis to mediate a quick deal for their release, but they are not interested.”
The report claims that Blinken responded: “Let’s wait,” and added, “I will speak with Netanyahu personally.”
The former secretary of state also reportedly told the Qatari emir he would travel to Israel within three days of the conversation.
“Right now, the situation is complex,” Blinken said, as quoted by Haaretz. “Israel is still under attack, and there’s no one to talk to. We will wait three days.”
Notably, the UAE did warn senior US and Israeli officials that Israeli actions and rhetoric were “putting regional stability at risk” in the period leading up to the massacre.
Senior UAE advisor warned Israel against political decisions contradicting Abraham Accords in 2023
In March 2023, UAE businessman Khaldoon al-Mubarak, a senior advisor to MBZ, traveled to Israel and conveyed a message to senior Israeli officials: “The direction in which the government is heading is in complete contradiction to the Abraham Accords, and ... some politicians are even encouraging violence.”
“This runs contrary to the spirit of the agreements and the current conduct and puts regional stability at risk,” Mubarak said at the time.
The UAE’s Foreign Ministry stated on Tuesday that “the UAE’s engagement since October 7 has consistently been aimed at de-escalation, regional stability, and preventing violence,” adding: “Officials in the UAE and Israel have maintained open and direct lines of communication since the beginning of relations more than five years ago. Whenever necessary, all relevant intelligence has been and continues to be shared between the relevant parties.”

Ukraine Unveils New Air Defense Missile to Replace Soviet Osa-AKM Stocks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
06:09:03 UTC
15:09:03 KST

Ukraine has unveiled a new domestically produced air defense missile designed to replace dwindling Soviet-era ammunition for its Osa-AKM systems, according to Ukrainian media.
The RK-19 missile, developed by Ukraine’s state defense industry and displayed at the MSPO defense exhibition in Poland, is designed to replace the Soviet 9M33-series missiles currently used by Ukraine’s Osa-AKM air defense systems, Militarnyi reported.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The missile was first publicly revealed in April 2026 in a video address by President Volodymyr Zelensky marking Ukraine’s Day of the Defense Industry Worker.
The RK-19 can intercept aerial targets at distances of up to 10 kilometers (6 miles) and altitudes of up to 5 kilometers (3 miles). It has a maximum speed of 600 meters per second (1,968 feet per second) and uses a radio-command guidance system similar to that of the Soviet missiles it is intended to replace.
The missile and its launch container weigh 163 kilograms (359 pounds) combined, while the warhead weighs 14.3 kilograms (31.5 pounds).
Filling a Soviet-era gap
The Osa-AKM is a Soviet-designed, all-weather surface-to-air missile system used by Ukraine to protect troops and critical infrastructure from aircraft and cruise missiles.
Each Osa-AKM launcher carries six 9M33M3 missiles. Those missiles can engage targets at ranges of up to 10 kilometers (6 miles) and altitudes of up to 5 kilometers (3 miles), with a maximum speed of around 500 meters per second (1,640 feet per second).
How Russia Is Trying to Paralyze Kyiv Without Occupying It
The development of the RK-19 comes as Ukraine faces a growing shortage of air defense ammunition.
Zelenskyy said in August that deliveries of air defense missiles had fallen threefold compared with 2025, with the decline extending beyond the summer to earlier months of the year.
Ukraine has increasingly turned to domestic production and cheaper interception technologies as it seeks to conserve scarce air defense missiles.
Brave1 defense-tech developers, for example, have recently demonstrated technology designed to intercept Russia’s Bundel drone-missiles at a substantially lower cost than the incoming weapons.
The RK-19 could provide Ukraine with a domestically produced replacement for a key Soviet-era air defense munition while reducing reliance on dwindling stocks of 9M33-series missiles.

CSO to celebrate 200th anniversary on world stages
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
06:03:23 UTC
15:03:23 KST

The Presidential Symphony Orchestra (CSO) will take Türkiye’s cultural and artistic heritage to some of the world’s most prestigious stages as it celebrates its 200th anniversary.
Culture and Tourism Minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy announced the orchestra’s international concert program in a social media post, saying the CSO, whose history dates back to 1826, would showcase Türkiye’s rich artistic heritage through the universal language of music.
The orchestra’s international journey will culminate with a concert at New York’s Carnegie Hall on Sept. 21, 2027.
“Since 1826, our CSO, which has shaped our country’s musical heritage, will present concerts in Bucharest, Prague, Vienna and New York, introducing Türkiye’s rich artistic heritage to the world through the universal language of music,” Ersoy said.
“This special journey will culminate on Sept. 21, 2027, at New York’s Carnegie Hall, one of the iconic venues of classical music.”
Ersoy also congratulated CSO chief conductor Cemi’i Can Deliorman and the orchestra’s musicians, wishing them success at their international performances.
The CSO’s 200th anniversary international program will begin in Bucharest with a concert at the Bucharest National Opera House on Nov. 3, 2026.
Conducted by Bujor Hoinic, the concert will be held to mark Republic Day and will feature Ferit Tüzün’s “Turkish Capriccio,” Mozart’s Piano Concerto No. 20 and Hoinic’s symphonic poem “Angora.”
The CSO will begin its European tour in March 2027 under Deliorman.
The orchestra will perform at the Dvořák Hall of Prague’s Rudolfinum on March 29 and at Vienna Konzerthaus on March 31.
The tour’s soloist will be Mischa Maisky, one of the leading cellists of his generation
.
The program will include Tüzün’s “Nasreddin Hodja Suite,” Antonín Dvořák’s Cello Concerto and Dmitri Shostakovich’s Symphony No. 10.
The Prague concert will carry particular significance as it will take place at the Dvořák Hall and feature one of the Czech composer’s best-known works.
The CSO will also perform the European tour program in Ankara on March 26.
The international program will conclude with the orchestra’s Carnegie Hall concert on Sept. 21, 2027.
Deliorman will conduct the concert at the New York venue, regarded as one of the world’s most prominent stages for classical music. Details of the program will be announced in the coming months.
The CSO will also host leading international conductors and soloists in Ankara during its 200th anniversary season.
The season will feature a repertoire and lineup of artists comparable to those presented at major concert halls in the world’s leading cultural capitals, giving audiences in Ankara the opportunity to hear internationally acclaimed conductors and soloists.

Archaeology reveals new clues about Süleyman’s final campaign
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
06:03:06 UTC
15:03:06 KST

Research in 2024 and 2025 found Ottoman-era artifacts scattered across 80 hectares, shedding light on the settlement known as Turbek.
Archaeological research near Szigetvar Castle in Hungary, where Ottoman Sultan Süleyman the Magnificent led his final military campaign, has revealed that the settlement around his presumed place of death was larger than previously thought.
Research by the University of Pecs in 2024 and 2025 found Ottoman-era artifacts scattered across approximately 80 hectares, shedding light on the settlement known as Turbek.
The findings indicate that Turbek was not only more extensive than earlier estimates suggested but also prosperous.
Süleyman left Istanbul on May 1, 1566, to lead his 13th and final military campaign. His imperial tent was erected on a hill overlooking Szigetvar Castle. He died there during the night of Sept. 6-7, 1566, while Ottoman forces were besieging the fortress.
Historical sources say his death was concealed from the army to protect morale and ensure the peaceful accession of his son, Selim II. His internal organs were reportedly buried at the encampment, while his body was taken to Istanbul about 42 days later.
On Selim II’s orders, a tomb was built at the site where Süleyman was believed to have died. The site later became an important pilgrimage center, with a mosque, dervish lodge, guesthouse and guard barracks nearby. A civilian settlement gradually developed around the complex and became known as Turbek.
The settlement was destroyed after Ottoman rule ended, and its location was eventually forgotten.
An interdisciplinary team led by Professor Norbert Pap of the University of Pecs examined historical documents, maps and land records. Researchers concluded that the complex stood on Vineyard Hill in the Turbek-Zsibot area, about 4.2 kilometers northeast of Szigetvar Castle.
During the 2024-2025 research, Turkish and Hungarian researchers conducted surface studies and geophysical surveys across the wider area.
They discovered ceramics, coins, jewelry, Ottoman metalwork, painted glass and porcelain fragments. A rare 16th-century gold coin and a silver coin from the Crimean Khanate were also found.
Researchers said the findings demonstrate that the Ottoman settlement extended well beyond the central tomb complex.

105 square meters of mosaics unearthed at Pompeiopolis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
06:02:42 UTC
15:02:42 KST

Conservation work on the mosaics has been completed, with measures taken to preserve their current condition. (AA Photo)
Culture and Tourism Minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy has announced significant findings at the ancient city of Pompeiopolis in the Black Sea province of Kastamonu, where archaeologists have unearthed about 105 square meters of well-preserved fourth-century A.D. floor mosaics and a marble head depicting Eros from the late second century A.D.
Ersoy said in a social media post that excavation, documentation and conservation works were continuing at the ancient site, one of the major centers of the Paphlagonia region during the Roman Imperial period.
“During our work in the central nave of the basilica, we uncovered approximately 105 square meters of floor mosaics dating to the fourth century A.D., consisting of geometric compositions and in very good condition,” Ersoy said.
He noted that the mosaic flooring in the central nave had not yet been fully uncovered.
“Our excavations are continuing. Let us also announce another important find from our 2026 works: an Eros head dating to the second half of the second century A.D.,” he said.
The first construction phase of the basilica is also believed to date to the second half of the second century A.D., around A.D. 150-160, based on its architectural features, stratigraphic evidence and archaeological finds.
The structure underwent significant architectural and functional changes in later periods, according to the ministry.
The Eros head, found in the basilica’s pastophorion area during the 2026 excavations, is also dated to the second half of the second century A.D. The find provides new information about the artistic and cultural environment of Pompeiopolis during the Roman Imperial period.
Pompeiopolis became an episcopal center in the fifth century A.D., highlighting the city’s religious and administrative importance during Late Antiquity.
Architectural modifications, decorative elements and floor mosaics in the basilica also indicate that its later phase was linked to the Christianization of the city and its growing importance as an episcopal center.
Conservation work on the mosaics uncovered during the 2026 excavations has been completed, with measures taken to preserve their current condition. Excavations are continuing to reveal the remaining sections of the mosaic flooring in the central nave.
The ongoing excavation and conservation work is expected to provide a more detailed understanding of the basilica’s architectural and functional transformation from the Roman Imperial period through Late Antiquity, while further uncovering and documenting its mosaic floors.
The findings, including the Eros head, architectural elements from Late Antiquity and the floor mosaics, are contributing to a broader understanding of Pompeiopolis’ urban and religious history.

Historic Yedikule gardens set for revival after 100 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
06:02:21 UTC
15:02:21 KST

At the foot of Istanbul’s historic land walls, centuries-old urban farming traditions are being revived as the İsmailpaşa Garden in Yedikule prepares to return to cultivation after roughly a century.
The approximately 20,000-square-meter site is being restored for agricultural production by Fatih Municipality, with plans to grow crops historically associated with the area, including Yedikule lettuce and Swiss chard.
The project is set to bring the soil back into production and also preserve traditional cultivation practices and the agricultural knowledge passed down through generations.
Agricultural plots around the fortifications played a role in supplying the city with food from the Byzantine period onward, while Yedikule and its surroundings became one of Istanbul’s important garden districts during the Ottoman era.
Ottoman records illustrate the scale of this agricultural belt. A 1733 record lists 77 gardens stretching along the land walls from Yedikule to Ayvansaray, with more than 300 gardeners working across them.
The gardens produced vegetables and fruits including cabbage, leeks, onions, garlic, pumpkins, carrots, cucumbers and melons, making the green belt an integral part of the city’s everyday food supply as well as its landscape.
The İsmailpaşa Garden itself has left traces in historical records. According to Fatih Municipality’s 2025 Activity Report, the site appears on 19th-century Ottoman maps, while foundation records identify the relevant parcel as a bostan, or cultivated garden.
The revival project also places emphasis on protecting the site’s historical character. In June, Fatih Mayor Mehmet Ergün Turan met at the garden with Harvard University historian Cemal Kafadar, representatives of the Yedikule Gardeners Association and local gardeners. Discussions focused on preserving the area’s historical and natural fabric, sustaining traditional cultivation and strengthening its connection with public life.

UK flight disruption continues as Turkish Airlines issues warning
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
06:01:59 UTC
15:01:59 KST

Delayed passengers wait and queue with their luggage at Terminal 3 of London Heathrow airport, west of London on Sept. 8, 2026, following major disruption due an issue affecting the NATS air traffic control systems.(Photo by Henry NICHOLLS / AFP)
Turkish Airlines has warned passengers of possible delays and cancellations as British airports struggle to clear a backlog caused by a failure in the country’s air traffic control system.
“Some of our flights arriving in and departing from the United Kingdom may experience delays and cancellations,” the carrier said.
Passengers were advised to check their flight status through the TK Assistant application or the airline’s website.
The warning came as 177 flights scheduled for Sept. 9 were cancelled across Britain, nearly all of them at London’s Heathrow Airport, according to aircraft tracking website Flightradar24.
About 1,300 flights to and from British airports were cancelled the previous day after a fault in the flight processing system operated by National Air Traffic Services, or NATS.
NATS said the technical problem had been resolved but warned that the aviation network would need time to recover.
“This has been a very complex recovery and has created difficulties for the whole aviation network,” it said, apologizing for the disruption and urging passengers to check with their airlines.
Heathrow resumed departures late on Sept. 8 but warned that disruption would continue.
Gatwick, Birmingham, Liverpool and Edinburgh were also affected, while dozens of flights were cancelled at Dublin Airport in Ireland.
British Airways said the disruption had affected tens of thousands of customers and would have a significant knock-on effect on its operations.
Ryanair said more than 65,000 of its passengers had been affected and renewed its call for NATS chief executive Martin Rolfe to be dismissed.
Rolfe accepted “full responsibility” for the failure but declined to say whether he was considering resigning.
British Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander was due to meet Rolfe on Sept. 9. She said she was seeking assurances that lessons would be learned and that the systems supporting the country’s aviation network were fit for purpose.
Britain’s worst air traffic system failure in recent years occurred in 2023, when delays and cancellations affected more than 700,000 passengers.

Norway bids final farewell to King Harald V as 'grandfather' of the nation's casket leaves palace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
06:00:20 UTC
15:00:20 KST

Norway's royal family, led by new King Haakon VIII, foreign royals, heads of state and dignitaries took part in the procession to Oslo's Lutheran cathedral on foot.
Norway bid farewell to King Harald V on Wednesday, as crowds lined the streets of Oslo and foreign royals and world leaders gathered for the funeral of the long-serving monarch.
A 21-gun salute rang out over the Norwegian capital as the funeral procession made its way from the Royal Palace to Oslo Cathedral.
Harald’s son, the new King Haakon VIII, and other senior royals walked behind the coffin, which was draped in the red Norwegian royal standard. Harald’s widow, Queen Sonja, and Haakon’s wife, Queen Mette-Marit, followed by car.
Norwegian officials and foreign dignitaries joined the procession, including the monarchs of Sweden, Denmark, Spain, the Netherlands, Belgium, Luxembourg, Monaco and Jordan.
Britain’s Prince William and Japan’s Crown Prince Akishino were also present, alongside political leaders from more than 20 countries, including Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
High security
At the end of the religious service, four F-35 fighter jets flew over the cathedral in a "missing man" formation, as the casket was taken to the Akershus Castle chapel.
There it will be lowered into the crypt of the royal mausoleum, next to Harald's parents and grandparents.
He will be laid to rest in a $2 million (€1.7 million) sarcophagus whose design remains secret.
Once the burial is completed, flags across the country, which were lowered to half-mast after Harald's death, will once again be raised and church bells will ring for an hour.
Norway's police force has mobilised nearly 3,000 officers in what it has described as "one of the biggest operations" in its history.
Some 3,500 soldiers have also been deployed, while exceptional airspace restrictions have been imposed over much of the eastern part of the country.
Until his death, Harald, who ascended the throne in 1991, was the oldest reigning monarch in Europe.
Despite mounting health issues in his later years, he had always ruled out abdicating and was extremely popular among Norwegians.
Embodying an open and tolerant Norway, he made a deep impression by celebrating diversity in a 2016 speech marking the 25th anniversary of his reign.
"Norwegians are girls who love girls, boys who love boys, and girls and boys who love each other," he said, adding: "Norwegians believe in God, Allah, the Universe and nothing."
Reinvigorated monarchy
Thousands of Norwegians filed past the king's casket in the past week, some waiting in line for hours.
The square in front of the palace has been covered with flowers, drawings and candles.
"He was the grandfather of the nation," said Gunn Johnsen, 81, speaking to the AFP news agency on Tuesday, explaining that she took an hour-long train ride to pay her last respects.
"Generous, inclusive, kind," added her friend Vigdis Simonsen, 64.
Near the University of Oslo, a large billboard displayed a photo of a smiling Harald with the inscription "Thank you for everything."
Almost 72% of Norwegians said they support the monarchy, up by eight percentage points from a previous survey in May, in an opinion poll conducted after the king's death and published last week.
Support had dropped to its lowest level in February, when 60% said they were in favour of maintaining the monarchy while 27% were not.
At the time, the royal family was embroiled in a series of scandals that damaged its image.
Mette-Marit in particular was under heavy criticism for her past ties to the late convicted American sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and her son's legal troubles.
While Haakon VIII, 53, is very popular, opinions on the new queen remain deeply divided.

However, the elderly couple opted not to grant her forgiveness.

Reform UK says migrant deal was ratified by far-right National Rally president
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
06:00:02 UTC
15:00:02 KST

Reform UK has insisted its deal with France’s far-right National Rally to return migrants back across the Channel was fully approved by the party and signed off by its president, Jordan Bardella, amid a furious backlash in France.
The agreement unveiled on Friday between Nigel Farage and Bardella, who is the 30-year-old protege of presidential candidate Marine Le Pen, appeared to directly contradict Le Pen’s long-held policy of refusing to accept the return of those who arrive in the UK in small boats from France.
Le Pen was pressed for her position by journalists from France TV, the state broadcaster, on Monday. Le Pen declined to comment, saying she would talk about the issue soon, but at a time of her choosing.
In 2021, Le Pen said she wanted a rewriting of border agreements for the UK to specifically send people arriving on boats back to their countries of origin, instead of returning them to France.
Since the agreement, Bardella has come under fire from political parties in France for signing the deal, with Benjamin Haddad, the Europe minister, criticising Bardella for “submission” that was “against our interests and sovereignty”.
Some French media have questioned whether Bardella was duped by Reform, querying whether the French translation accurately conveyed the meaning by Farage that the National Rally (RN) was prepared to accept any migrants back who travel by small boat.
However, a Reform spokesperson said it was “signed off by both Bardella and the presidential team”, that the policy was included in the French version as well as the English, and it could “confirm both parties are fully on board”.
Until the summer, Bardella had been considered as a potential replacement for Le Pen in next spring’s presidential election but will now run as her future prime minister. In July, when a Paris appeal court upheld Le Pen’s conviction for embezzling European parliament funds, her ban from running for office was reduced, allowing her to stand.
Farage has kept Le Pen at arm’s length, while having cultivated good relations with Bardella over the past year, but he is rumoured to be planning to meet her later in the autumn.
He previously rejected the idea of a tie-up in 2014 in the European parliament when he accused Le Pen’s party of having a history of “prejudice and antisemitism”, which she said was slander. Last week, Farage said he would not have done a deal with the party when led by Jean-Marie Le Pen, Marine’s father, a convicted Holocaust denier who co-founded the Front National in 1972. Le Pen expelled her father from the party in 2015. Farage praised her, saying she had got rid of “extreme elements”.
At the heart of the row in France is the wording of the document Farage brought out for Bardella to sign with him on stage in Birmingham, calling it a memorandum of understanding.
Both texts, presented side by side in English and French, state that, if Farage and Bardella become prime ministers of their respective countries, the UK will intercept boats launched from the French coast, and that France will return people onboard to their countries of origin.
But the English text carried an extra phrase saying “France will ordinarily accept these persons” who would then be returned to their home country. This appeared to show that Bardella was promising to accept returned persons in France, which contradicts the long-held position of RN.
France TV said RN denied any controversy, saying the text was only a declaration of intention that would be refined at a later point. Speaking in Italy over the weekend, Bardella suggested his party in government would prevent migrants from reaching France by much tougher border controls, resulting in the numbers crossing to the UK being much lower.
However, RN’s opponents were critical of Bardella for signing a memorandum on immigration on stage with Farage.
The MP, Sacha Houlié, an ally of the centre-left would-be presidential candidate, Raphael Glucksmann, wrote on X about what he called “a miserable episode where the whole of France could see Mr Bardella used as a doormat by the English far-right.” He told the RN: “You claim to be patriots, you’re cowards.”
Gabriel Attal, the former centrist prime minister and presidential candidate, wrote on X: “To applause from his party members, Nigel Farage made Jordan Bardella sign a memorandum to ensure that all migrants intercepted in the Channel are sent back to France. Either Jordan Bardella doesn’t understand English or he is shamefully weak when it comes to defending French interests. And I think he does understand English.”
Édouard Philippe, a former prime minister and centre-right candidate, said it was an example of hypocrisy and division in Bardella’s party. Philippe said it looked like Bardella found it difficult to stand up to Farage in order to “protect French interests”.
Xavier Bertrand, the rightwing head of the northern Hauts-de-France region, wrote on X that in agreeing that France alone would take responsibility for returning people to their home countries, Bardella was “reducing France to the status of Britain’s subcontractor.”
Chris Philp, the Conservative shadow home secretary, said: “Reform UK’s deal with Jordan Bardella is a complete farce … Time and again, Reform prove they are fundamentally unserious with grand claims for the cameras, with none of the detail or hard work that might survive actual scrutiny.”

Apple unveils folding iPhone Duo as new CEO takes center stage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
06:00:02 UTC
15:00:02 KST

Apple has unveiled the iPhone Duo, the company’s first foldable phone and the most significant change to the iPhone since the smartphone’s introduction in 2007.
The nearly $2,000 device takes inspiration from iPads’ wide screens and combines them with the portability and camera features of iPhones. When opened, it is the company’s largest phone display and thinnest phone. The Duo opens and closes like a passport to double its screen size.
“iPhone Duo brings an entirely new design while preserving everything you love from an iPhone,” said John Ternus, the company’s new chief executive. “It feels effortless to use and it makes new experiences possible.”
The phone will start at $1,999 and be available on 23 October.
The product release event, titled “Surprise and Shine”, began at 10am Pacific Standard Time on Apple’s campus in Cupertino, California, south of San Francisco.
“I started the day with an intelligent personal hub and why there’s no product in the world that is better to be that hub than iPhone,” Ternus said. “We think the best way to achieve that is with a foldable design. Others have created foldables that just feel like two phones stuck together … scrolling through vertical content feels compromised.”
While competitors have released foldable smartphones since the late 2010s, the new model is a first for the iPhone maker, and its rollout serves as the first big test for Ternus, who assumed the role on 1 September. He claimed the Duo “will redefine the experience of using a foldable phone”.
Apple reportedly began testing prototypes of its folding iPhone display in early 2021 – though at the time there were no plans for its launch, according to a Bloomberg report.
The company started the event with its more routine announcements, including the new iPhone 18 Pro, which starts at $1,199, and 18 Pro Max models, which start at $1,299. Apple emphasized the AI-enabled features that will be integrated throughout the phone. Called Siri AI, the company said it will be able to tap into third-party apps and already works with over 300,000 apps.
Among the many AI-related features available on the new iPhones will be a novel mechanism that fingerprints an image and identifies as captured by an iPhone’s camera – not generated by AI. The feature, called Apple Reference Image, will act as a “digital negative”, as one Apple executive described it, and serve as proof that the the original image was not AI-generated.
Both new iPhones also represent a “massive leap” in battery life, executives said – the iPhone 18 Pro Max will have 45 hours of battery life and the iPhone 18 pro will have 36 hours of battery life.
Though the foldable iPhone took center stage on Wednesday in California, overall demand for foldable phones makes up only a small sliver of overall mobile device sales. Customers’ interest in standard iPhones, by contrast, remains high, as evidenced in Apple’s most recent robust earnings.
The company also unveiled new iterations of some of its other product offerings at its events and over the next few months, including updates to its Apple Watch and AirPods lines.
The company announced the fifth generation of its AirPods headphones, describing them as 50% more noise cancelling than AirPods 4 and sporting five hours of battery life. The latest iteration starts at $129.
The company also introduced its latest watches, Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, pitching them as some of the most advanced and accurate wearable devices to support health and fitness goals.
The updated watch will include several new AI features, including “Health Age”, which analyzes heart health, sleep, mental wellbeing, movement health, metabolic health, hearing and nutrition and measures how users stack up to their chronological age.
The watch will also include “audio intelligence”, meant to enable your watch to record ambient conversations throughout the day and take notes, producing a transcript of what someone said 15 seconds earlier in case you missed it. At the end of the day, a watch user can review a summary of their day, called a “Siri Recap”. The company said these recordings are stored on the device and anything that is collected is end-to-end encrypted.
Ternus took the stage as CEO for the first time, marking the beginning of his tenure as the head of Apple, replacing the outgoing CEO, Tim Cook. In a note to employees on his first day, Ternus said that he was excited about “the incredible products already in the works and the ones we haven’t even imagined”.
“I’m honored to be stepping into this role at what is truly the greatest company in the world, and I am so excited about everything we have in store,” Ternus wrote in his letter. “We have a huge launch next week that’s going to be phenomenal. Thanks for everything you’ve all done to make it possible.”

Polanski calls for report on ecosystem collapse to be published in full

Zack Polanski has challenged Andy Burnham’s government to publish an unredacted version of an explosive report by the UK’s spy chiefs that found the collapse of overseas ecosystems would have catastrophic consequences for the UK’s national security.
The Green party leader in England said the prime minister should come clean about the scale and impact of the climate and nature crisis and called on the government to publish in full the report that warns the UK faces devastating security consequences.
Speaking at the Wild Summit event in Bristol on Wednesday, Polanski asked the prime minister: “Will you tell the truth – and release the full unredacted report from the joint intelligence chiefs? Or will you keep hiding the truth from the public?”
The Guardian revealed last year that the report paints a devastating picture of severe food shortages, price rises, migration, political destabilisation and possible war, resulting from the collapse of ecosystems, fuelled by the human-induced climate crisis and over-exploitation.
A redacted 14-page version, including some of the report’s findings, was published in January but the government has repeatedly refused to publish the full version, despite repeated freedom of information requests from journalists and calls from MPs.
Polanski, who is expected to be the Green party candidate in the upcoming byelection in Holborn and St Pancras, argued that the extreme weather experienced by much of the UK this summer should be a wake-up call for ministers.
“It was a bleak preview of what is to come if we continue to allow the greed of corporations to come above the survival of our natural world – and all that relies on it. This must mark a turning point. Where we say: no more loss, no more quieting of birdsong, no more steady trickling of sewage and poison into our waters.”
The report by the joint intelligence committee and other government departments, revealed by the Guardian last October, shows that the UK will face catastrophic consequences from the collapse of key ecosystems in other countries. These include the Amazon rainforest, which scientists fear is reaching a “tipping point” triggered by deforestation and rising temperatures, which would turn the ecosystem from a huge absorber of carbon dioxide into a net source of carbon.
Food shortages would be almost certain to result from the decline of ecosystems overseas, the report found, as would a big increase in global migration, with the potential to fuel unrest. Among the most alarming findings was that armed conflict, which includes nuclear war, was also a potential consequence.
The report was due to be published at an event last October, attended by King Charles, in the Natural History Museum. However, at the last minute the publication was pulled, at the behest of Downing Street.
In an interview with the Guardian after his speech, Polanski said the Green party would introduce a nature, biodiversity and national security bill to make climate adaptation “fundamental to everything we do”. The party would also seek to appoint a climate resilience minister whose principal job would be to address problems such as extreme heat, surface-water flooding and wildfires.
Polanski reiterated a commitment to introduce a basic income for farmers to “ensure those producing the food we rely on are paid properly for their work”.
“We know farmers have had wrecked harvest after wrecked harvest. Their crops are struggling and on top of that you’ve got supermarkets where the bosses are taking record bonuses while fleecing farmers,” he said.
Simultaneously on Wednesday, in a letter to Burnham, a coalition of green groups has warned that national security, public health and economic growth are at risk without urgent action to restore nature.
The UK has a legally binding target to restore 30% of nature by 2030. This target, which was set by more than 100 countries during Cop15 negotiations in Montreal in 2022, is considered the minimum restoration needed to halt and reverse the global decline in nature. The UK is currently on track to miss this target, with a recent plan to reach this target in England condemned as “pathetic” and “completely insufficient”.
“Your government has diplomatic and legal obligations to halt the decline of wildlife and protect 30% of the land and sea for nature by 2030 … On the current path the UK will miss those targets,” the groups warn the prime minister in the letter.
The letter also highlights that two-thirds of the UK’s protected nature sites need “urgent repair”, with many of these sites neglected or damaged by intensive industry, pollution and the climate crisis. The groups warn this leaves communities and businesses exposed to flooding, drought, wildfires and pollution. This warning comes as new research finds that about £2bn a year needs to be invested in protected nature sites – up from roughly £1.1bn today – to restore them by 2042. The groups are calling for more funding, stronger laws and decisive enforcement to “stop the abuses that are hollowing out our natural world”.
A Labour spokesperson said: “This is the first government to take seriously the risks that climate change and nature loss pose to our food security, economic resilience, and national security.
“We’re taking decisive action, including launching the UK’s first taskforce on the national security and resilience risks of climate change and nature loss, investing in nature recovery at home and abroad, and delivering the largest nature-friendly farming budget in history.”

UK datacentres will create just 25% of jobs predicted by tech sector, analysis finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
06:00:00 UTC
15:00:00 KST

Datacentres in the UK will create just a quarter of the jobs predicted by the tech sector, while consuming vast amounts of energy, according to new research.
Environmental thinktank Verdant predicts that all the datacentres currently planned are likely to directly employ 10,400 workers – compared with the more than 40,000 cited in projections by the industry lobby group TechUK.
Labour has defended the rapid rollout of AI datacentres in the face of growing public scepticism, amid concerns about their demand for water and energy. The government has also echoed TechUK’s claims about job creation.
Verdant’s analysis is based on 20 projects for which data on staffing levels are publicly available, including via planning applications, company accounts and press releases – as well as international comparisons.
It says the datacentres that have already been built have directly created fewer than 4,400 jobs – about 8.6 jobs for each megawatt of energy they consume, against the 43.7 jobs claimed in TechUK’s projections.
Verdant also argues that the many future projects currently at the planning stage are on a far larger scale, and so likely to be much less job-intensive – perhaps creating as few as 1.6 permanent positions per megawatt.
Its analysis focuses on the permanent workers needed to maintain and operate datacentres, setting aside the much larger number of temporary construction jobs needed to build them.
James Meadway, the thinktank’s co-director, said: “We’re being rushed into supporting a frantic pace of datacentre buildout on very flimsy economic grounds.
“Clearly artificial intelligence and related technologies have great potential. But vast new datacentres arrive at significant real costs to local communities and even our climate ambitions, and their use case has to be made by the government and industry – rather than assuming we can build first and then work out why we did later.”
To underline the resource intensity of the vast data warehouses, Verdant compared the 8.6 jobs they currently create per megawatt of power used with about 400 in a car plant and more than 3,600 in a hospital or health facility.
The government rejected this comparison, and questioned Verdant’s methodology. A spokesperson said: “This report relies on a deeply misleading jobs-per-megawatt metric, makes false comparisons with hospitals and schools, and appears to confuse electricity capacity with actual consumption. More seriously, it discounts the wider economic value of compute [computing capacity] and the national security and sovereignty case for building critical digital infrastructure in Britain.”
Verdant said it had based its calculations on the electricity capacity that tech firms claim they need – which could still crowd out alternative plans, even if the completed datacentres don’t end up using all the capacity.
Labour has classified AI datacentres as critical national infrastructure in an attempt to speed up the planning process, and Andy Burnham has underlined his backing for the sector by appointing AI minister Kanishka Narayan to his cabinet.
Narayan has advocated a rapid increase in datacentres, partly on grounds of national sovereignty. He told the Times last month: “The British public is very clear that it wants strong defence. It wants strong, sovereign capability, it doesn’t just want foreign billionaires to own things that matter to our lives. If we’re being true to those British values, it is impossible to achieve that without building a sovereign level of datacentre capacity in this country.”
By contrast, the Green party in England has called for a moratorium on building datacentres, while there have been protests in Scotland, amid claims that massive projects are being rushed through.
Zack Polanski, the party’s leader in England, said: “The government is planning to steamroller local opposition so private companies can build datacentres – but it can’t explain what the benefits are.
‘“England and Wales are still facing drought after our hottest summer ever, but these datacentres are set to be given priority access to water. Meanwhile, this latest research suggests far fewer jobs may actually be created in constructing and staffing them than the government claims.”
In response to the Green party’s call for a “pause”, a government spokesperson insisted that it would “simply send investment and good jobs abroad, while leaving Britain dependent on overseas computing for the processing of sensitive health and defence data”.
A spokesperson for TechUK said: “Our estimates that the UK datacentre industry supports 43,500 jobs, and could support 40,000 more by 2035, are built on a published methodology using industry data and standard economic impact assessment techniques. The figures were built transparently from the best available industry data at the time, and we are confident they remain a reasonable estimate of the sector’s employment contribution.”

'The Kingdom strongly supports the non-proliferation of weapons,' Trump pushes for Saudi nuclear deal in letter
The agreement, which was reportedly submitted August 24, opens the door to peaceful nuclear cooperation between Washington and Riyadh, including the transfer of reactors, equipment, and technology
US President Donald Trump reportedly sent a letter to House Speaker Mike Johnson on August 24, transmitting some of the text of the Agreement for Cooperation Between the Government of the United States and the Government of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia Concerning Peaceful Uses of Nuclear Energy. Trump also transmitted his written approval, authorization, and determination concerning the agreement, along with an unclassified Nuclear Proliferation Assessment Statement.
According to the communication, the agreement provides a comprehensive framework for peaceful nuclear cooperation based on mutual commitment to nonproliferation, permitting the transfer of material and equipment, including reactors, components, and information for peaceful nuclear purposes. It would also allow the transfer of sensitive nuclear technology to support a joint enrichment and conversion study, or upon written agreement of both parties, though it does not permit the transfer of restricted data.
Any special fissionable material transferred would be limited to low-enriched uranium, aside from small quantities for use as samples, standards, detectors, or targets.
The agreement has a 30-year term but can be terminated by either party with at least one year's written notice. Key nonproliferation conditions and controls would remain in effect after termination or expiration for as long as any covered material, equipment, or components remain in either party's territory or jurisdiction, until the parties agree such items are no longer relevant to nuclear safeguards.
Suggested articles
Trump's communication states that Saudi Arabia "strongly supports the nonproliferation of weapons of mass destruction" and has reiterated its commitment to nonproliferation. It noted the kingdom is a party to the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons and has a Comprehensive Safeguards Agreement with the International Atomic Energy Agency.
Trump said he considered the views of relevant departments and agencies and determined the agreement's performance "will promote, and will not constitute an unreasonable risk to, the common defense and security," and has approved and authorized its execution.
The administration said it is prepared to begin consultations with the Senate Foreign Relations and House Foreign Affairs committees, with a 30-day continuous session review to be followed by a 60-day review period.

Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis said Greece remained open to dialogue on maritime boundaries in the Aegean and eastern Mediterranean but would continue to defend its positions.
Mitsotakis spoke after an informal summit with Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi and Greek Cypriot leader Nikos Christodoulides in Egypt’s El Alamein on Sept. 8.
“Stability, however, in no way implies concession or acceptance of a fait accompli,” he said.
He said cooperation between Greece, Egypt and Greek Cyprus was not directed against any country and sought to promote stability and prosperity in the region.
Mitsotakis cited the 2020 agreement between Greece and Egypt on the partial delimitation of their exclusive economic zones as an example of how maritime boundaries could be settled through dialogue and respect for international law.
Türkiye rejected the agreement as “null and void” when it was signed, saying the area concerned lay within its continental shelf and that the deal violated Libya’s rights.
On Cyprus, Mitsotakis reiterated support for a settlement within the U.N. framework and in accordance with Security Council resolutions.
He also backed efforts by the U.N. secretary-general and his personal envoy to restart negotiations.
Türkiye supports a two-state settlement based on the sovereign equality and equal international status of Turkish Cypriots.
Mitsotakis said Greece would launch initiatives on freedom of navigation during its presidency of the U.N. Security Council in October.
He stressed the need to protect passage through critical shipping routes, including the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb, under international law.
Energy cooperation also featured in the talks. Mitsotakis reaffirmed support for the planned GREGY electricity link between Egypt and Greece, intended to carry renewable power from Egypt to Europe.
He also outlined the potential for gas from fields off Cyprus to be liquefied in Egypt and shipped through Greek terminals at Revithoussa and Alexandroupoli for onward supply to European markets.
On Gaza, Mitsotakis reiterated support for a two-state solution and called for implementation of the second phase of the ceasefire plan and the disarmament of Hamas.
The leaders also discussed Lebanon and Libya.
Mitsotakis backed Libya’s unity and a Libyan-led political process under U.N. auspices, free from foreign interference.
He also called for a reduction in irregular migration from eastern Libya to Greece.

UAE bets on US AI as Gulf emerges as battleground in US-China tech race - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
05:58:36 UTC
14:58:36 KST

- i24NEWS
- International
- UAE bets on US AI as Gulf emerges as battleground in US-China tech race
UAE bets on US AI as Gulf emerges as battleground in US-China tech race
The UAE is not trying to compete directly with the United States in developing the most advanced AI models or chips. Instead, its ambition is to build the infrastructure needed to power the technology
The United States and China are emerging as the two dominant powers in artificial intelligence — and countries around the world may soon have to decide which technological ecosystem they want to belong to.
For the United Arab Emirates, that choice has already been made.
According to political and AI analyst Obaid AlZaabi, the UAE has chosen Washington as it races to establish itself as a major AI hub for the Middle East and beyond.
“There are only a few actors in the AI race,” AlZaabi said. “Those are the US and China. And in the Middle East there are only two players really, which are the UAE and Israel.”
The UAE is not trying to compete directly with the United States in developing the most advanced AI models or chips. Instead, its ambition is to build the infrastructure needed to power the technology.
AlZaabi points to the UAE’s energy resources, capital and growing computing infrastructure as key advantages. “The UAE aims to take all the compute from West Asia, North Africa, East Africa, Central Asia, the subcontinent and the Balkans as the major hub for compute,” he said.
The strategy relies heavily on access to advanced chips, however — an area where the US maintains a dominant position. “In the AI game, the US has a dominant position,” AlZaabi said. “They hold all the chips. They have the agents, the models, they have the chip production.”
That technological advantage is increasingly becoming a geopolitical tool.
AlZaabi says the UAE previously maintained close relationships with both Washington and Beijing, but that the strategic importance of AI has made neutrality more difficult.
Suggested articles
“The UAE was very close to the US and China,” he said. “But the US has made it clear: if you want to be part of the AI revolution, you have to do it with them exclusively. So the UAE had to pick — and we picked the United States.”
AlZaabi believes that choice could become increasingly important as the US-China technology rivalry expands beyond individual AI models and into the infrastructure supporting them.
He points to competing satellite systems as an early example of a broader technological divide, arguing that countries could eventually find themselves operating within separate US- and China-led technology ecosystems.
“It’s no longer a question of what’s going to happen,” he said. “We know what’s going to happen. The US and China will have their own two sovereign AIs.”
For countries caught between the two powers, he argues, remaining outside either system could carry a high cost. “If you don’t work with them, you will be in a very weak situation,” AlZaabi said. “You’ll basically not have a space.”
For the UAE, the objective is therefore not simply to import American AI, but to secure a stake in the infrastructure behind it. “The UAE could be described as buying into the order,” AlZaabi said. “But… the UAE is contributing in such a way that it’s taking ownership — and let’s say equity — in the system.”
Ultimately, he sees the UAE becoming a regional hub for American AI.
“The UAE is building the energy infrastructure, the compute infrastructure and the political infrastructure to be the hub for American AI in Asia and the Middle East,” he said.
For Abu Dhabi, the bet is that computing power will become a strategic resource on the scale of the infrastructure that transformed the Gulf’s economy in previous generations.
And as the competition between Washington and Beijing intensifies, the UAE may be betting not only on AI itself — but on choosing the right side of the emerging technological divide.

Datasel: Our information puts value of RKIK contracts at over €150 million
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
05:58:00 UTC
14:58:00 KST

Datasel: Our information puts value of RKIK contracts at over €150 million
Datasel is calling on the Estonian Center for Defense Investments (RKIK) to hold talks, as the goods were manufactured and delivered and allegations concerning their quality remain disputed, a Datasel spokesperson said in a written statement.
"Our message is simple: Datasel had the capacity and access to the supply chain needed to fulfill these contracts. The goods were manufactured, inspected and delivered or made available for pickup and subsequent allegations concerning quality and the termination of the contract remain disputed. No court or arbitration tribunal has yet ruled on these issues," the statement said.
The statement explained that behind the contract numbers are engineers, factory teams and specialized suppliers who committed their time, materials and capital in good faith. However, goods sitting in warehouses generate additional costs and Datasel believes a better solution would be to complete the work safely and transparently rather than allow a resolvable commercial dispute to turn into years of litigation.
According to Datasel, public discussion has portrayed the matter as involving just a single €70 million contract, but the company said this is not the case.
"The National Audit Office reported €71.6 million in disputed procurement volume across all suppliers and a €59.8 million advance payment to the largest supplier. Former Defense Minister Hanno Pevkur separately described the amount specifically associated with Datasel as approximately €60 million. Datasel's contract and accounting records show that its contracts with RKIK were worth more than €150 million, of which advance payments received amounted to approximately €59 million, while goods delivered and invoiced were worth approximately €58 million," the spokesperson wrote.
According to the spokesperson, RKIK and Datasel exchanged inquiries, written proposals, technical information and contract terms over a period of several months, while Datasel disclosed its supply chain, manufacturing sources, countries of origin, product locations and technical capabilities. The final contracts were preceded by a pre-purchase agreement and RKIK representatives visited the relevant manufacturing facilities before placing the order and conducted additional inspections during the contract period.
"RKIK has subsequently said that its current team cannot find documentation showing how the initial contact with Datasel was established or how the company was selected. This apparent gap in RKIK's records management is not evidence that Datasel concealed information or that the subsequent months of negotiations and inspections did not take place," the spokesperson said.
"Datasel is an Italian defense industry supplier founded in 2005. Its technical foundation is built on the experience and industry network of founder and continuing technical collaborator Sandro Pazzini whose previous work at established European defense companies included major, high-value programs. Datasel was acquired by Neco Defence Munitions in 2024, adding industrial resources and the broader group's expertise in metallurgy, casting, precision engineering and high-precision machining," the statement said in its description of the company.
Datasel: A website is not a credible indicator of industrial capacity
Datasel says it operates as a supplier, manufacturer and integrator through established manufacturing partners, including experienced ammunition component manufacturers that are active in the industry and also supply other European defense customers.
"This networked model is common in the modern defense industry. A company's website or historical employee headcount is not a reliable indicator of the industrial capacity available through its contracted supply chain. Datasel has fulfilled contracts worth more than €110 million and, since its acquisition by Neco Defence Munitions, has several orders of a similar nature pending," the statement said.
The claim that Datasel did not deliver anything is contradicted by public information, the statement said, adding that former minister Pevkur confirmed that deliveries had taken place and that tens of millions of euros worth of material was stored at a warehouse in Europe where ministry auditors and internal control staff physically inspected it.
"Under the contracts, several batches were presented for inspection. RKIK representatives inspected the relevant batches and authorized them for shipment. The goods were then picked up or made available for pickup. Datasel also made substantial advance payments to manufacturing partners, continued procuring materials and maintained inventory and supplier commitments related to the orders. Manufacturing, inspection, release, acceptance and final delivery to Estonia are separate stages and reporting should not reduce them to a single claim that nothing was delivered," Datasel's press representative wrote.
Datasel: RKIK announced contract termination before communicating its concerns
Datasel disputes allegations of quality issues.
"According to our records from the time, the specific concerns now being made public were not formally raised until weeks after RKIK had issued notices terminating the contracts. This sequence of events matters: allegations raised later cannot, without evidence, establish that a demonstrated quality defect was the actual reason for the earlier termination of the contracts — rather, they appear to be a justification sought after the fact," the statement said.
According to Datasel, a proper technical claim should identify the defective batch, the contractual specification, the sampling and testing method, the experts' findings, the written notice and an opportunity to remedy the defect. None of these issues has been finally adjudicated by a court or arbitration tribunal. Datasel said it will submit complete, dated documentation in the relevant proceedings, including inspection reports, correspondence, delivery records and termination notices.
"Without admitting that any product delivered was noncompliant, Datasel remains prepared to honor the agreed warranty. Any genuine noncompliance that is properly identified, documented and raised within the warranty period will be investigated and, if confirmed, the product will be repaired or replaced in accordance with the contract," the company said.
RKIK has acknowledged that the expiration of the external funding window was a reason for terminating the contract. Datasel asked RKIK to inspect additional finished goods and according to the company, RKIK did not participate in those inspections after the relevant EU funding or authorization window had closed.
"A funding deadline is not, in itself, evidence of improper performance by a supplier. Nor does it erase goods already manufactured, costs already incurred, warranty procedures or damages resulting from the termination of the contract," the statement said.
RKIK's assertion that Datasel's counterclaim may be "tactical" is speculative, according to the company, particularly since RKIK has also acknowledged that it has not reviewed the underlying documents.
"Datasel's claims are based on contracts, correspondence, inspection and delivery records, advance payments to suppliers, inventories and evidence of damages. These materials will be submitted to the competent Estonian court and to international arbitration, rather than debated through selective public comments."
Datasel wants to restore RKIK contracts
Without prejudice to the company's claims and legal position, Datasel is asking RKIK to immediately enter into good-faith discussions aimed at reinstating the contracts or reaching an equivalent structured agreement to complete them. Datasel is prepared to engage its supply chain, present the remaining goods for inspection in accordance with the contracts, address any properly documented warranty issues and fulfill its remaining obligations within a mutually agreed and commercially reasonable timeframe.
"This proposal is made without any admission of breach of contract, delay, liability or noncompliance. Any resolution would also require corresponding funding, approvals, inspection, acceptance, transportation arrangements and payment terms on the buyer's part," a Datasel representative wrote.
The statement also addressed journalists, asking them to examine the matter fairly.
"We are not asking the media to adjudicate a legal dispute or take sides. We are asking that the chronology, the deliveries and the available path toward a resolution receive the same scrutiny as the allegations. If Estonia needs ammunition and Datasel remains ready to supply it, a serious discussion about completing the contract should not be ruled out from the outset."
Datasel said it is prepared to complete the contract.
"If the ammunition is needed and Datasel remains ready to complete delivery, the Estonian public deserves to know why the door to fulfilling the contract remains closed. We are ready to sit down at the table, listen and do our part to finish what was started."
It emerged last Wednesday that Estonia sought to buy shells for Ukraine and paid a total of €70 million in advance to Indian businessmen, who own the company, who had reportedly never sold a single shell before. RKIK terminated the contract and claims the company only delivered an incomplete shipment of low-quality components.

As SDF disband in Syria, Kurds ponder how to secure their rights
After the SDF and PKK in Turkiye dissolved, Kurdish experts express concern if their rights will be won through democratic means.
Erbil, Iraq – The merger of the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) into the government forces last month has sparked a debate among many Kurds in Syria as well as in neighbouring Iraq and Turkiye about the future of their rights.
Though Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa has promised constitutional protection for Kurdish language and political rights, analysts question if the decision to drop the “armed struggle” will imperil the struggle to secure Kurdish rights and identity.
“We want this day to be the beginning of a true transition from the battlefields to the fields of construction, and from the era of weapons to the era of peace,” SDF leader Mazloum Abdi (also known as Mazloum Kobani) said from the presidential palace in Damascus late last month.
Abdi said an “important page” had been turned in Syria’s history.
While some Kurdish politicians hail the integration as a door for the Kurds to participate in building the new Syria and to demand their rights through the constitution, others consider the step a result of Turkish and US pressure.
Turkiye has calculated close ties with the Syrian government, which came to power after Bashar al-Assad was toppled in December 2024, and has attacked Kurdish fighters along its border with Syria in the past. Although the US helped form the SDF in 2015, it threw its weight behind the al-Sharaa government.
The US-backed SDF, which was formed to fight the ISIL (ISIS) group, controlled Syria’s northeast, home to most of the country’s Kurdish population, for more than a decade. But earlier this year, the government forces took over northern Syria in a swift military push. After months of talks, the SDF was disbanded, and the Kurdish-led Autonomous administration was dissolved.
Talal Mohammed, the head of the Kurdistan Democratic Peace Party in Syria, believes such developments are a turning point in the course of the Kurdish issue.
“This represents an opportunity for the Kurds to be partners in building a democratic Syria,” Muhammad told Al Jazeera. “We already had a self-administration, a military force, but we did not have any international or regional recognition,” he said.
“The coming phase requires uniting the Kurdish ranks and working to attain all our rights … in the new constitution,” he said.
But Mohammad warns that Turkiye is pushing to end the issue of armed Kurdish groups.
Turkiye considers the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK), which led a decades-long armed rebellion, and its affiliates in Syria, Iraq and Iran as “terrorist” groups. Ankara accuse them of launching attacks to destabilise the region through separatist violence.
The PKK decided to dissolve in May 2025 and end the armed conflict. The move came months after jailed PKK leader Abdullah Ocalan urged the group to lay down its arms in a bid to end the conflict, which has killed thousands. Turkish government welcomed the move.
Ankara views the People’s Protection Units (YPG), which led the SDF, as a “terrorist” group and an arm of the PKK inside Syria.
Mohammad explains that the PKK is the most important Kurdish group in the entire region, and it affects the file of the Kurds in Syria. “Ending the SDF and the PKK was a Turkish dream and a major Turkish project,” he said.
No guarantees
Other Kurdish politicians suggest that the peace initiative in Turkiye and the SDF’s integration in Syria will empower the Kurds and maintain their rights.
Perwin Yousef, the co-chair of the Democratic Union Party (PYD), a branch of the PKK in Syria, rejects that the integration is a setback.
“We did not feel any disappointment, and our project continues, and we will continue to work to obtain all our rights through political understandings and agreements within the new Syrian constitution, and our struggle will continue,” Yousef told Al Jazeera.
But she also acknowledges that there are no guarantees so far for the national, political, and cultural rights of the Kurds. These issues, Yousef says, could derail any agreement.
“There are no guarantees for the Kurds so far … we want to guarantee cultural rights and recognition of the Kurdish language as an official language, in addition to the political rights of the Kurdish people, and to be partners in decision-making within the Syrian state,” she said.
The Kurds are an ethnic group of people Indigenous to the Mesopotamian plains and nearby highlands, which today stretch across southeastern Turkiye, northeastern Syria, northern Iraq, northwestern Iran and southwestern Armenia. The Kurdish population is concentrated in these areas, where the Kurdish groups have aspired to establish an independent Kurdish state.
“The Kurds have long talked of reuniting their people in a greater Kurdistan,” Joost Hiltermann, a special adviser to the International Crisis Group, wrote in a paper back in 2016.
“These different national populations have discovered over time that what sets them apart may be more significant than what they have in common: differences in dialect, tribal affiliation, leadership, ideology, historical experience,” he wrote.
Kurdish academic Sarbast Nabi, a professor of political philosophy at Koya University in the semiautonomous Kurdish region of northern Iraq, believes the latest deals between the PKK and the SDF with Turkish and Syrian governments will hinder Kurdish aspirations.
“The SDF found itself compelled to take this decision, which is a decision subject to the Turkish will, because Turkiye holds Abdullah Ocalan,” Nebi explained. “Therefore, this decision is neither Syrian nor Kurdish, but rather it is an expression of a Turkish will,” he said.
“What happened in Syria serves Turkish national security … it worked to marginalise the Kurdish issue, amid perceptions within the Trump administration of winning Turkiye to its side,” he argues.
”The Kurdish issue became a victim of the pressure exerted by the Turkish lobby, while the Kurds in Syria became a tool in the hands of the Kurdistan Workers’ Party … At present, there are no independent discourses for the Kurds in any part of Kurdistan,” he said, referring to the Kurdish region straddling Syria, Iraq, Turkiye and Iran.
A forced choice?
Many Kurds argue that regional and international powers have their own national interests and schemes, and they have used the Kurds for their own agenda and dumped them when their geopolitical utility was over.
Muhammad Amin Penjweny, an expert on the political affairs of the PKK and Turkish politics, argues that Kurdish groups need to be pragmatic after the decline of Western support, especially after the fall of al-Assad’s government.
“What the SDF did through integration with the Syrian forces is not a failure, but rather a victory, because it had no other solution after the withdrawal of American and French forces … leaving it alone without military or political protection in the face of Turkiye and Syria,” he explained.
“It is true that the SDF was a large military force against ISIS, with American assistance, but after the fall of al-Assad the equation changed,” he said, adding that the Kurds had ”no other option” but to integrate into the Syrian army.
Despite the fanfare and what appears to be a ”success”, mistrust and scepticism within Kurdish circles remain high, and the fate of Ocalan could be a decisive factor.
PKK leaders have warned from their stronghold in the mountainous region of northern Iraq to halt the peace process with Turkiye unless democratic reforms are implemented.
“As a gesture of goodwill, the Kurdistan Workers’ Party burned its weapons, but the party will not hand over its weapons until after the release of Abdullah Ocalan and his comrades held in Turkish prisons,” Penjweny said.
“The Kurdish dream of establishing a Kurdish state still stands. There is an American, French, and British position that holds that the Treaty of Lausanne, concluded in the last century, did not lead to stability in the region,” he said, adding that the Kurds were a victim of this treaty over the past hundred years. The 1923 Treaty of Lausanne, signed by Turkiye and allied powers, divided the Kurdish areas across four different countries.
Sentiments across Kurdish populations in Syria, Iraq and Turkiye differ due to multiple factors. In Iraq, Kurds enjoy the most rights in the region, where their rights are protected by the constitution established after the US-led invasion and the toppling of President Saddam Hussein in 2003. The Kurdistan Regional Government is the official ruling body in the semi-autonomous Kurdish region.
”What was achieved by Syrian Kurds is better than what they had under Assad. For Iraq, independence or the creation of a Kurdish state is far fetched because Kurdish semi-autonomous region is legal and recognised by the constitution,” said Soran Ali, a Kurdish writer based in Iraq.
But some Kurds in Turkiye have a very pessimistic outlook about the future of the community.
“The Kurdish dream is gone because of the SDF, PKK, Iraq and Iran,” Ahmed Kani, a nationalist Kurdish researcher in Turkiye, told Al Jazeera.
”As long as Turkiye is a strong state, the Kurds in the four parts of Kurdistan will not be able to achieve their dream of statehood,” he told Al Jazeera.
