Chinese scientists find a hidden atomic structure that unlocks methane
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
05:33:42 UTC
14:33:42 KST

Chinese scientists find a hidden atomic structure that unlocks methane
- Date:
- September 9, 2026
- Source:
- Dalian Institute of Chemical Physics, Chinese Academy Sciences
- Summary:
- Scientists found that a tiny atomic structure that forms on nickel oxide during methane conversion is more effective than the metallic nickel long believed to drive the reaction. The discovery allowed a low-nickel catalyst to rival one containing 10 times more metal, potentially opening the door to cheaper and more efficient industrial catalysts.
- Share:
Partial oxidation of methane (POM) is considered a promising industrial method for producing syngas, a mixture commonly used to make fuels and chemicals. For years, scientists have assumed that metallic nickel (Ni) nanoparticles serve as the main active centers that drive this reaction. However, there has been an important unresolved question. The metallic Ni observed after a reaction may simply form when nickel oxide is reduced by syngas at high temperatures, rather than representing the species that actually performs the catalysis.
Nickel can change both its oxidation state and its atomic arrangement under the high-temperature redox conditions involved in POM. Until now, these changes have been difficult to track in detail, making it challenging to determine the true structure responsible for the reaction.
A Hidden Active Structure Forms During the Reaction
In a recent study published in Nature Catalysis, researchers found that highly active structures can form in situ when the surface of NiO reconstructs during POM. The results reveal the atomic-scale source of the catalytic activity and show why it is important to observe catalysts while they are operating under realistic reaction conditions.
The research was led by Profs. Tao Zhang, Aiqin Wang and Xiaoyan Liu from the Dalian Institute of Chemical Physics (DICP) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS), together with Prof. Wei Liu from DICP, Prof. Tao Yang from Xi'an Jiaotong University, and Prof. Graham J. Hutchings from Cardiff University.
To investigate the process, the team created a Ni/Al2O3 catalyst containing only 0.8 wt% Ni using a microemulsion method. Despite its relatively low nickel content, the catalyst performed strongly during POM. It converted 92% of the methane, while CO and H2 selectivities reached 87.0%, with the H2/CO molar ratio remaining stable at about 2.0.
High Performance With Much Less Nickel
One of the most striking findings was that almost no metallic Ni could be detected in the catalyst after the reaction. Even so, its overall performance was comparable to that of an 8.0 wt% Ni/Al2O3 catalyst produced through impregnation, despite containing only one tenth as much nickel.
The low-loading catalyst also performed far better than another 0.8 wt% Ni/Al2O3 material prepared using the same impregnation method. Under identical conditions, that catalyst did not effectively carry out POM and instead showed only methane combustion activity.
The researchers also observed that metallic Ni nanoparticles present at the beginning of the reaction were quickly oxidized into the NiO phase under POM conditions. Yet NiO alone was not enough. A pre-formed pure-phase NiO catalyst showed no POM activity and instead catalyzed only the complete oxidation of methane.
Atomic Reconstruction Reveals the True Active Site
A closer examination revealed what was actually happening on the catalyst surface. During the reaction, the researchers captured the in situ formation of a reconstructed [Ni1O4Ni4] structural unit on the NiO(100) surface.
DFT calculations indicated that this newly formed motif makes it much easier to break the C-H bonds in methane, one of the key steps in activating the molecule. The calculated activation barrier was only 12.5 kcal·mol-1.
That barrier was far lower than the value calculated for the intact NiO(100) surface (38.5 kcal·mol-1) and also below the barrier for the metallic Ni(111) surface (15.7 kcal·mol-1). This substantial kinetic advantage strongly supports the conclusion that the reconstructed structure is the true active center responsible for POM.
Together, the experimental observations and theoretical calculations show that catalytic activity does not come simply from metallic nickel or ordinary nickel oxide. Instead, it emerges from a specific atomic structure that forms dynamically while the reaction is taking place.
"Our study highlights the critical role of in situ characterization in identifying dynamic active structures under reaction conditions," said Prof. Liu. "Dynamic reconstruction enables low-loading catalysts to achieve high performance, offering new opportunities for the rational design of efficient catalysts while reducing reliance on high metal loadings."
Story Source:
Materials provided by Dalian Institute of Chemical Physics, Chinese Academy Sciences. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Yuanlong Tan, Qiao Zhao, Chen Liang, Chaobin Zeng, Hongwen Guo, Fengyuan Liu, Guang Xian Pei, James Hayward, Jingyuan Ma, Han Zhao, Xiao Yan Liu, Wei Liu, Tao Yang, Aiqin Wang, Graham J. Hutchings, Tao Zhang. In situ generation of active motifs on Ni/Al2O3 during partial oxidation of methane to syngas. Nature Catalysis, 2026; 9 (8): 848 DOI: 10.1038/s41929-026-01580-1

====================================================================================================

Where do PSG rank among Europe's greatest dynasties?
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
06:30:53 BST
14:30:53 KST

Real Madrid? Ajax? Liverpool? Ranking Europe's greatest football dynasties
- Published
Some find success sweet but fleeting, others spend years building to the pinnacle, and then there are those whose lasting glory evolves into a dynasty.
Paris St-Germain begin their Champions League campaign on Wednesday hoping to enter that bracket, attempting to become continental champions for a third successive season.
To mark this, we're looking at how the Parisians compare to those clubs who have enjoyed the most dominant eras in European competition.
Some will point out that football existed before the European Champion Clubs' Cup began in 1955 - so apologies to Stan Cullis' 'world-champion' Wolves outfit and the Mitropa Cup's early Vienna heavyweights.
However, this top 10 debate is centred around winning European football's grandest prize.
10. Paris St-Germain 2024-
OK, straight in with the current champions, because this is a dynasty in the making.
PSG have had a lacklustre start to the season - they always do this, don't they? However, you wouldn't bet against Luis Enrique's slick side adding a third successive European crown come next summer.
The Parisians have been France's most dominant force since the arrival of Qatar Sports Investments 15 years ago, but it took a change of approach for the holy grail of continental success to arrive.
"It's the end of the glitter," professed president Nasser Al-Khelaifi after years of lavish spending, ushering out the "flashy, bling-bling" era.
Instead, Enrique arrived in 2023 intent on building a coherent team. There was still significant investment, but on younger players who could be moulded by his philosophy and discipline while given room to flourish.
The result was two scintillating Champions League triumphs.
9. Inter Milan 1963-65
Talking of discipline. Helenio Herrera, the Argentine-born defender reared in Casablanca and Paris, had already traversed the dugouts of Atletico Madrid, Malaga, Deportivo and Barcelona before landing in Milan in 1960.
Herrera set about implementing his tactical brand of catenaccio at San Siro - one he insisted is misremembered as being more defensive than it actually was - and developing a ruthless counter-attacking team known as 'Grande Inter'.
Winning the Scudetto in 1962-63, Herrera's outfit became the first to lift the European Cup without losing a game the following season as Sandro Mazzola netted twice against Real Madrid in the final.
The Italians defended their crown the following year, despite losing their semi-final first leg at Anfield, edging Benfica in the final. It was the Portuguese giants' second final defeat in three seasons. Some may say they were cursed...
8. Benfica 1960-62
The story goes that Bela Guttmann, fresh from winning the title with Porto, rocked up at Benfica, sacked all the senior players and promoted a talented bunch of youth team players instead.
Those promising youngsters won the title and then went all the way in the European Cup, beating Barcelona in the 1961 final.
That summer, a teenage Eusebio also joined Guttmann's squad and steered them to European glory once more, seeing off Tottenham Hotspur in the semi-final before beating the great Real Madrid in the competition's showpiece.
The legendary Ferenc Puskas scored a first-half hat-trick for the Spaniards, but Eusebio netted twice after the interval to seal Benfica a second successive crown.
Guttmann, buoyed by his remarkable success, left the club after not being offered the pay rise he felt he deserved and the curse the Hungarian boss supposedly put on the club - that they would not win another European trophy for 100 years - has become fable.
Whether the often-disputed story is true or not, the Lisbon giants have not landed another since - losing eight European finals, including three in the 1960s.
7. Bayern Munich 1973-76
This was Bayern's coming of age. Emerging from what was a fiercely competitive West German football scene, the Bavarians - promoted to the Bundesliga less than a decade earlier - were able to establish themselves as heavyweights in Europe.
With a backbone of goalkeeper Sepp Maier, marauding sweeper Franz Beckenbauer and the prolific Gerd Muller, and fresh off West Germany winning the 1974 World Cup, Bayern clinched three on the bounce, despite their domestic form dipping.
In fact, Beckenbauer said Bayern were past their peak after the first European Cup win over Atletico Madrid, but experience carried them through big games.
They beat Leeds in a controversial final in Paris, and then saw off Saint-Etienne the following year.
6. Barcelona 2008-12
The teams above make the list for their trophy-winning spells. Pep Guardiola's Barcelona were European champions twice in three years - losing to Jose Mourinho's treble-winning Inter in between - but their dynasty was built on more than silverware.
Guardiola only spent four seasons at Barcelona, but it was an era-defining tenure, the Catalan giants pioneering a brand of football that would be celebrated and copied the world over.
Perhaps the real success of a team is in its legacy. Guardiola's tiki-taka Barcelona built around La Masia graduates Xavi, Andres Iniesta, Sergio Busquets and, of course, Lionel Messi still resonates more than a decade since he left.
5. AC Milan 1988-1995
Where does this particular Milan dynasty start and end? It was fuelled, of course, by Silvio Berlusconi, who saved the club from bankruptcy in 1986 and appointed the up-and-coming Arrigo Sacchi as boss.
You could argue it continued until a Champions League final defeat by a young Ajax side in 1995. In between, the Rossoneri won back-to-back European Cups in 1989 and '90, then thrashed Cruyff's Barcelona 'Dream Team' in 1994 after defeat in the final the previous season.
In fact, the only campaigns in which Milan did not reach the final were after their quarter-final second leg was abandoned because of floodlight failure while trailing Marseille in 1991. The Serie A giants' refusal to re-enter the pitch for the final minutes of that one also led to them being banned the following year.
From Sacchi to Fabio Capello, through the brilliant Dutch trio of Ruud Gullit, Marco van Basten and Frank Rijkaard to homegrown stars Franco Baresi, Paolo Maldini and Alessandro Costacurta - the Italian core remaining from that 1989 triumph to the defeat by Ajax six years later - Milan were a phenomenal force.
4. Liverpool 1976-1984
In an era of English dominance on the continent, winning seven of eight European Cups between 1977 and 1984, Liverpool's 'Boot Room' boys led the way.
The Reds won four of those, Nottingham Forest - who could argue they also deserve a spot on the list - went back-to-back and Aston Villa completed the haul.
Liverpool's European pedigree really began when Bill Shankly's side won the Uefa Cup in 1973, the Reds doing it again three years later under Shankly's former assistant Bob Paisley.
Paisley was able to deliver the biggest prize of all the following season in Rome and, after Kenny Dalglish was brought in to replace Hamburg-bound Kevin Keegan, retained the European Cup at Wembley against Club Brugge in 1978 - the Scottish forward netting the winner.
Three years later, after Brian Clough took Forest to the top, Liverpool were European champions again when Alan Kennedy's goal downed Real Madrid in Paris.
Perhaps most impressive is how the Anfield outfit were able to maintain that success through a series of managers. The line of succession from Shankly to Paisley then landed on Joe Fagan, who was in charge when they beat Roma - in Rome - in '84. That was before the Heysel disaster, and defeat by Juventus, the following year.
3. Real Madrid 2013-18
Atletico fans look away now. Two finals in three years and twice Diego Simeone's side ran into their Madrid rivals, losing in agonising fashion in both 2014 and 2016.
The second of those also sparked a three-year winning run for the most successful club in European Cup history.
Real Madrid's formula was seemingly simple: construct a team of the world's best players - spearheaded by Cristiano Ronaldo - and stick a legendary former star in charge.
Zinedine Zidane's new-era galacticos just felt inevitable - they always found a way to win, becoming the first club in the Champions League era not only to retain the trophy but to lift three in a row.
After downing Atletico in the first of the three-peat, they beat Juventus and then Liverpool - the latter remembered for Gareth Bale's cameo, Loris Karius' blunders and Sergio Ramos leaving his mark on Mo Salah.
2. Ajax 1968-73
Similar to Guardiola's Barcelona, the influence of this Ajax side was seen far beyond the trophy cabinet. The lineage of their philosophy - via Johan Cruyff - survives through several of the clubs on this list, from Catalonia to Paris.
Rinus Michels was the pioneer, taking Ajax from the threat of relegation to the most dominant side in Europe, losing the 1969 final to AC Milan but returning to win it for the first time two years later with their swaggering brand of Total Football.
Michels left for Barcelona on the back of that success, though Stefan Kovacs was able to retain the trophy the following year and then add a third successive European crown to Ajax's pile with an impressive run that included knocking out Bayern Munich, Real Madrid and then Juventus in the final.
Cruyff, about to win the second of his three Ballon d'Ors, followed Michels to Barcelona and Ajax's dynasty began to fall apart. The legacy, however, remains.
1. Real Madrid 1955-60
When it comes to dominance, no one compares to the Real Madrid side who stormed to five successive European Cup triumphs after the competition began in 1955.
With the tournament in its infancy, it was perhaps not considered as imperative by certain nations compared to how Champions League participation dominates clubs' thoughts today, but Real Madrid's style and success helped to alter perceptions.
Alfredo Di Stefano, already a world star by the time Real beat Reims in the inaugural final, was an integral part of the Spanish giants' success, the legendary Paco Gento likewise a stalwart (he also won a sixth European Cup in 1966).
Then, in 1958, Madrid added Hungarian genius Ferenc Puskas following his two-year ban for refusing to return to Budapest after the revolution in 1956.
Puskas was 31 when he joined, but scored 35 goals in 39 European Cup games for Real Madrid, including four in the 7-3 win over Frankfurt at Hampden in the 1960 final. Di Stefano grabbed the other three as Madrid made it five on the spin.

  - Published8 June
  - Published28 August

The Russian exception: Why Moscow still has a role in Europe’s ITER fusion project despite EU sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
05:30:23 UTC
14:30:23 KST

EU-Russia tensions collide with decades of scientific cooperation at ITER, the world’s largest nuclear fusion experiment. As fusion becomes a strategic EU priority, Brussels faces a dilemma over its continued reliance on Russian expertise and technology.
The European Union and Russia are geopolitical adversaries, with Russia under sweeping EU sanctions and its ties with the bloc severely curtailed.
Yet inside one of the largest international scientific collaborations in history — and the world’s largest nuclear fusion experiment — the two remain linked by a partnership forged decades ago and built to endure for generations.
While Brussels steps up pressure on Moscow over its war in Ukraine and hybrid attacks, Russian engineers and their European counterparts continue to work together on an international project called the “International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor” (ITER), an experimental nuclear fusion machine that seeks to harness the fusion of hydrogen nuclei to generate vast amounts of energy.
Last Monday, the EU’s Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen visited ITER in Cadarache, France, calling the fusion device “key for our decarbonisation and energy independence goals.”
PF1 poloidal field coil and gyrotrons
Launched in 2007, ITER is a fusion machine currently under construction and the result of a collaboration among 33 nations, including Russia, China, the United States and the European Union.
The project aims to demonstrate the potential of fusion as a viable low-carbon energy source, which could contribute to the EU’s goal of achieving climate neutrality by 2050. According to ITER’s website, Europe bears “the largest portion of construction costs,” accounting for 45.6 percent.
However, while Brussels has steadily reduced its dependency on Russian energy, excluded Russian public institutions out of EU research cooperation and funding and banned Russian funding to European research organisations in response to Russia's invasion of Ukraine, Russia has never been expelled from ITER, whose rules stipulate that no member can be removed.
Instead, Russia remains a 9.1% contributor to the project and the country still provides crucial scientists and technology.
"The Russian Federation is an ITER member and participates through its Domestic Agency, Project Center ITER,” an ITER spokesperson told Euronews. “All ITER-related activities are conducted in accordance with the applicable legal and regulatory requirements.”
Beyond financing, Russia plays a crucial role in supplying a range of highly specialised components, including the PF1 poloidal field coil, which is used to shape and control the fusion plasma.
It also provides gyrotrons, which are powerful devices that generate high-frequency electromagnetic waves used to heat plasma in fusion reactors. Other components include “equipment supporting the power supply protection of the superconducting magnets,” and “vacuum vessel upper ports,” according to the spokesperson.
A major EU investment
Russia’s contribution takes on added significance as nuclear fusion has become a major EU investment priority. Brussels is set to unveil its own fusion strategy, after recently announcing €330 million to accelerate the sector and support nuclear technologies and skills.
The strategy, which has been delayed by one year, is expected to address governance, regulatory clarity and international cooperation with Europe’s central role in ITER at its core. Asked whether Russia’s participation in the ITER nuclear fusion programme had caused diplomatic delays among member states in reaching agreement on the future of the strategy, the European Commission has yet to respond.
But a Council document assessing nuclear energy, including ITER, dated 9 July and seen by Euronews carefully avoided any reference to Russia.
Instead, it made clear that the EU shall “continue collaboration with the ITER Organisation and partners on ITER-related activities.”
Russia’s Science Minister visits ITER
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the EU suspended Russia’s participation in flagship research programs like Horizon Europe, Horizon 2020 as well as Euratom and Erasmus Plus.
Other major European scientific institutions like the world-renowned physics research center CERN suspended Russia’s Observer status in 2022 and made clear it would “not engage in new collaborations with the Russian Federation.”
But despite the broader freeze in scientific ties, ITER signed a cooperation agreement in June with Russia’s Kurchatov Institute covering scientific information exchange, research programs and training.
Russian and European officials have also continued high-level contacts around the project. In July, Russian Science Minister Valery Falkov visited the ITER site in France, accompanied by a large delegation.
Supporters of ITER’s collaboration with Russia argue that the project is a decades-long endeavour requiring specialised knowledge, huge industrial supply chains and international collaboration. In addition, the project was designed on the assumption that scientific cooperation could survive political changes.
"The poloidal field coil system, for example, includes contributions from Europe, Russia and China, requiring components and technologies from different national supply chains to be integrated into a single machine system," ITER's spokesperson said.
Alongside their commitment to ITER, several countries are conducting national initiatives to develop the knowledge and technologies needed to operate nuclear fusion systems over the next two decades.
Recent research from the European Parliament suggests that progress in technological development since ITER's foundation in 2007 "might pave the way for the technology to be ready for industrial use in the second half of the century".
Science can’t 'trump geopolitics'
But the issue of the EU’s reliance on Russia over nuclear fusion and ITER has raised concerns in Brussels.
In 2025, three MEPs asked EU Commissioner Jørgensen in a written question whether the EU plans to “phase-out dependence on Russian participation in ITER.”
In a public letter, Jørgensen replied that ITER's founding rules don't allow members to be kicked out, only for members to withdraw voluntarily.
For Andrea Wechsler, one of the signatories of the letter, the Commission's response "did not provide a convincing political strategy for dealing with Russia's continued participation in the governance and technological ecosystem of ITER."
"I believe the Commission should reassess the issue and explain how these new forms of institutional cooperation are consistent with the EU's broader policy towards Russia," she told Euronews. "We need a comprehensive security and strategic review of Russia's involvement in ITER and a clear plan to ensure that no new technological dependencies are created."
The concern is also shared by some NGOs. Sehila Gonzalez de Vicente, global director of fusion energy at climate NGO Clean Air Task Force, argued that international cooperation has been central to fusion energy's progress, but that may no longer occur on the same global scale.
"(Scientific) collaboration is likely to become more concentrated among trusted allies and partners, while countries and companies seek to protect commercially sensitive technologies and maintain a competitive advantage in the emerging fusion industry," Gonzalez de Vicente told Euronews.
While Wechsler said she opposes the “isolation of Russian researchers, students or scientists”, she maintained that the scientific nature of strategic technology cooperation should not make it geopolitically neutral.
"I would not interpret the continuation of the project as evidence of a consensus that science should simply trump geopolitics," she added.
The European Commission didn't reply to a Euronews request in time for publication.

Daniel Libeskind Awarded the 2026 Praemium Imperiale for Architecture
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
05:30:00 UTC
14:30:00 KST

The Praemium Imperiale is a global arts prize that recognizes exceptional achievements in architecture, painting, sculpture, music, and theater or film. The award has been presented annually since 1988 by the Japan Art Association, with one postponement in 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic. Previous laureates include Portuguese architect Eduardo Souto de Moura, Japanese architect and humanitarian Shigeru Ban, and Burkinabé-German architect Francis Kéré, recognized by the association as professionals "who transcend national and ethnic boundaries, embodying the culture and arts of our time." This year, the laureate in the architecture category is Polish-American architect Daniel Libeskind, co-founder of Studio Libeskind, known for the design of the Jewish Museum in Berlin and the World Trade Center Master Plan in New York City.
On Tuesday, September 8, the 2026 Praemium Imperiale laureates were announced in Paris, Rome, Berlin, New York, London, and Tokyo. The Japan Art Association considers architecture a form of art, recognizing Libeskind's work alongside Cate Blanchett's in theater and film, Jenny Holzer's in painting, Andy Goldsworthy's in sculpture, and Herbert Blomstedt's in music. The five laureates are recognized for their personal achievements as well as their contributions to "enriching the global community," and each receives an honorarium of 15 million yen and a testimonial letter. They will be presented with a medal at an awards ceremony in Tokyo on October 28, 2026.
Alongside the recognition, the Association offers a perspective on Libeskind's career and achievements. The architect and urban designer is "celebrated for his ability to evoke cultural memory through emotionally resonant and original architecture" and his "lifelong engagement with music, philosophy, and literature." The Association highlights his binational background as a Polish immigrant in the United States, and his early achievements as a musician before switching to architecture. As an architectural designer, it points to Libeskind's sensitivity to sound and physical experience, and his steady commitment to hand-drawn design, balancing risk with a respect for history. Among his current works, the organization cites Studio Libeskind's broad range of projects, including museums, concert halls, convention centers, university buildings, hotels, retail complexes, and residential towers; the ongoing Albert Einstein Discovery Center in Ulm, Germany; and his 2018 book, Edge of Order, about his design philosophy and creative journey.
Related Article
"I Wanted to Look at Places in a New Three-Dimensional Way": In Conversation with Daniel Libeskind
Libeskind has also been awarded the Goethe Medal, the Hiroshima Art Prize, the Dresden Peace Prize, and the European Civil Rights Prize of the Sinti and Roma. His firm's latest projects include a new high-density residential development in Seoul, South Korea, designed in collaboration with HJ Design Partners and Seoul-based SAMOO Architects & Engineers. The Daechi Ssangyong 1 Redevelopment Project replaces an existing five-building, 630-unit complex in Daechi-dong, Gangnam-gu, with six new residential towers up to 49 stories tall and nearly 1,000 housing units. The firm is also designing a mixed-use building of over 20,000 m², featuring a green wall and incorporating bio-sourced materials, to transform the Issy-les-Moulineaux station area in Paris, adjacent to the future Line 15 station of the Grand Paris Express, and is renovating the Boerentoren, an Art Deco tower and one of Europe's earliest skyscrapers, located in the heart of Antwerp, Belgium.

Teams typically comprising a medical officer, assistant medical officer, nurses and other health staff travel by helicopter or small aircraft on scheduled monthly or bi‑monthly rotations to villages and longhouses.

Killer mosquitoes: As the climate changes, African diseases are spreading to Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
05:23:31 UTC
14:23:31 KST

In 2026, an extreme heatwave caused 10,000 deaths across just five European countries. Another consequence is the spread of infections previously uncommon in on the continent. In France, a case of dengue fever has been confirmed, and in Berlin, three residents were diagnosed with infections caused by bacteria that live in brackish water after being infected on Germany’s Baltic coast, which warmed unusually quickly this year. Climate change is altering the conditions under which pathogens spread, expanding the areas where they can thrive and extending the transmission season. The risk maps that doctors, laboratories, and public health authorities have relied on for decades are becoming outdated ever more rapidly. Medical professionals will have to be retrained, new guidelines drawn up, and laboratory diagnostics overhauled to prevent outbreaks of diseases that until recently were considered exotic.
A new map of infectious diseases
For decades, European healthcare systems operated on the assumption that infectious diseases existed within clearly defined geographic boundaries. Diseases considered endemic to Africa and Asia were generally associated with overseas travel — disease surveillance, medical training, diagnostics, and prevention were all built around this assumption.
That geographic divide is becoming increasingly unreliable. International trade and transport are bringing invasive species into new territories, while rising temperatures make it easier for them to become established in new areas while simultaneously extending their active season. One striking example is the Asian tiger mosquito (Aedes albopictus), which can transmit dengue, chikungunya, and Zika viruses. By June 2025, established populations had been recorded in 16 EU/EEA countries and 369 regions, up from 114 a decade earlier.
Meanwhile, the geographic range of other infections is expanding. In 2024, Europe recorded 1,436 locally acquired cases of West Nile virus infection. The main vectors in Europe are Culex mosquitoes, while birds serve as the virus’s natural reservoir. Rising temperatures and a longer mosquito season create conditions for more intensive transmission and an expansion of areas at risk.
Malaria in the north: risk or reality?
Fortunately, an outbreak of a non-endemic infection does not automatically lead to an epidemic. Malaria is a case in point.
Although Anopheles mosquitoes — the vectors that transmit the malaria parasite — are widespread in Europe (where the climate is becoming increasingly favorable to them), sustained local malaria transmission has not become established on the continent. Instead, almost all detected cases remain imported.
Sustained local malaria transmission has not become established on the continent; almost all detected cases remain imported
In 2022, EU/EEA countries reported 6,131 confirmed cases of malaria, and of the 5,375 cases with a known place of infection, 99.8% were associated with travel, while just 13 are believed to have been acquired within the EU. Eight of those were linked to infected mosquitoes introduced from abroad, mainly at airports; two occurred in healthcare settings; and the source of infection could not be established in the remaining three. Thus, these cases did not indicate the emergence of a sustained chain of transmission through local Anopheles populations.
For such transmission to take hold, several conditions must coincide: prolonged warm weather, a large population of mosquito vectors, an infected person from whom local mosquitoes can acquire the parasite, and a subsequent “human–mosquito–human” chain of transmission that is not interrupted through timely diagnosis, treatment, and vector control.
Climate change does not guarantee an epidemic — it merely makes the conditions for one more favorable. The spread of infections that are atypical for a given region depends to a large extent on the effectiveness of disease surveillance, the speed of diagnosis, access to treatment, and the effectiveness of vector control.
A blind spot in diagnosis
Accurate and timely diagnosis is the foundation of effective medical care, and to achieve this, it is crucial that doctors order the right test for each patient. A hospital may have extensive laboratory capabilities, but unless a doctor suspects a particular infection and orders the appropriate test, diagnosis — and, thus, the necessary response — may be delayed.
An Italian doctor treating a patient with fever, headache, and muscle pain is unlikely to suspect dengue or West Nile fever unless the patient has recently traveled abroad. But under the current circumstances, local transmission can no longer be ruled out. The Italian National Institute of Health recommends considering the possibility of arboviral infections not only when a patient has recently traveled abroad, but also when the pathogen is known to be circulating within the country.
European states differ in how quickly they are adapting to the changing infectious-disease landscape. According to the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC), countries and regions vary in their levels of surveillance, laboratory preparedness, and experience with local arbovirus transmission. Diagnostic protocols, the sharing of up-to-date epidemiological information, and doctors’ clinical awareness do not always keep pace with the changing situation.
A single missed case will not necessarily lead to an epidemic, but it can delay the detection of a local outbreak and the implementation of public health measures. As long as the source of infection remains unknown, an established mosquito population can continue transmitting the virus to other people, meaning early detection is essential not only for the patient, but also for timely epidemiological investigation and vector control.
A new disease calendar
Climate change is altering not only the geography of infectious diseases but also when the risk of infection emerges. A striking example is non-cholera Vibrio bacteria, which thrive particularly well when water temperatures exceed 20°C and salinity is between 0.5% and 2.5%. This makes the relatively low-salinity Baltic Sea, especially its shallow, rapidly warming waters, particularly vulnerable.
In 2026, Berlin's State Office for Health and Social Affairs (LaGeSo) linked the unusually early appearance of vibriosis cases to the early warming of coastal waters. What matters is not only where conditions are suitable, but also when the water reaches the critical temperature threshold and how long the warm period lasts.
A similar shift is occurring with mosquito-borne infections. Earlier warming triggers vector activity sooner, a warm autumn extends the transmission season, and a mild winter makes it easier for some mosquitoes and their eggs to survive. Within the right temperature range, the time required for a virus to develop inside a mosquito also decreases. The ECDC notes that mosquito-borne disease transmission seasons in Europe are becoming longer and more intense.
Mosquito-borne disease transmission seasons in Europe are becoming longer and more intense
As a result, the infectious-disease season is becoming a moving window rather than a fixed period, and public health surveillance professionals must increasingly track actual weather and environmental conditions rather than relying on the old calendar.
Climate threats to health: heat and allergies
Climate change affects human health in many ways. Extreme heat is rarely recorded in statistics simply as “heatstroke.” More often, its effects are indirect — aggravating cardiovascular, respiratory, kidney, and other diseases while increasing the risk of death among vulnerable people. Researchers therefore use measures such as heat-related mortality and excess mortality to assess its impact.
According to Lancet Countdown, heat was associated with an average of 546,000 deaths per year between 2012 and 2021. This estimate includes both the direct and indirect effects of exposure to high temperatures.
In the spring of 2026, extreme heat in India and Pakistan affected hundreds of millions of people, with temperatures exceeding 46°C in some places. According to an assessment by World Weather Attribution, human-induced climate change roughly tripled the likelihood of such a 15-day heatwave.
Limited reporting of deaths and illnesses makes it particularly difficult to assess the health impact of heat in Africa. At the same time, healthcare facilities are already facing a growing burden: during the extreme heat of 2024, the WHO assisted hospitals in Mali that were overwhelmed by patients suffering from heat-related illnesses.
Climate change is also shifting the biological calendar of plant life. Between 2015 and 2024, birch, alder, and olive pollen seasons in Europe began one to two weeks earlier than they had between 1991 and 2000. In some regions, both the length of the season and the amount of airborne pollen increased as well.
The scale of these changes varies by plant species, climate, and region. Temperature affects the timing of flowering, while humidity, precipitation, air pollution, and atmospheric carbon dioxide levels influence pollen production and allergenicity. As a result, people in different parts of Europe experience allergy seasons that vary in both timing and intensity. Monitoring systems, doctors, and patients therefore increasingly need to rely on real-time pollen data, while cities must take the allergenicity of plant species into account when planning urban greenery.
Plans are in place, but the money is lacking
The impact of climate change on public health has gradually made its way onto the WHO agenda. In the organization's 2025–2028 General Programme of Work, addressing the health impacts of climate change is listed first among its six strategic objectives. The 2026–2027 budget also provides for the development of climate-resilient health systems via vulnerability assessments, national adaptation plans, and specialist training.
In March 2026, the WHO was accredited by the Green Climate Fund, a move that will allow the organization to help countries develop health-related projects and secure funding to protect public health. The actual amount of funding will depend on the preparation and approval of specific proposals.
However, the gap between political commitments and available resources remains enormous. According to the WHO, health projects receive about 2% of the overall funding allocated to climate adaptation. When all climate finance distributed by international banks and funds is taken into account, the share going to health is just 0.5%.
By comparison, the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) estimates that developing countries will need between $310 billion and $365 billion a year by 2035 to protect themselves against the impacts of climate change. Yet in 2023, international public funding for such measures amounted to just $26 billion.
By 2035, developing countries will need between $310 billion and $365 billion a year to protect themselves against the impacts of climate change
Climate threats, then, are already firmly embedded in strategies and budget documents, but recognition of the problem still far outpaces the funding commitments being made to address it.
Real-time medicine
Adapting healthcare to a changing climate means moving from static, historical maps of infectious diseases to dynamic risk assessments. Health data need to be analyzed alongside meteorological and veterinary surveillance, while mosquito populations and other disease vectors must be monitored year-round.
For doctors to respond effectively to emerging threats, this information must reach them quickly. Health systems need automatic alerts about local transmission, regularly updated diagnostic protocols, and access to PCR and serological testing beyond major medical centers. The same principle applies to allergies, with pollen monitoring accompanied by timely warnings for patients.
Heat-health action plans should specify in advance which weather conditions trigger protective measures, who issues the appropriate warnings, how hospitals and social services adjust their operations, who assists older people and other vulnerable groups, and how the response is funded. This is the approach recommended in the WHO’s 2026 guidance: clearly defined roles, early-warning systems, measurable actions, and adequate resources.
And of course, every strategy needs a budget, clearly assigned responsibilities, and measurable performance indicators. Otherwise, recommendations will remain on paper, while healthcare services continue to respond only after a threat has already become too obvious to miss.

AfD state election win worries most Germans: Poll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
05:23:00 UTC
14:23:00 KST

People protest and hold placards during a rally called by the organizations Campact and Fridays for Future named "Time to Act: Stop the AfD!" at the Brandenburg Gate in Berlin on Sept. 7, 2026, one day after regional elections in the eastern federal state of Saxony-Anhalt. (Photo by John MACDOUGALL / AFP)
Nearly two-thirds of German voters are concerned about the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party’s victory in Saxony-Anhalt’s state election, a nationwide poll showed.
The Infratest dimap survey for public broadcaster ARD found that 64 percent were worried about the result, while 24 percent welcomed it. Researchers surveyed 1,051 eligible voters across Germany on Sept. 7.
However, 51 percent said other parties should engage more with the AfD in political work. The question did not specifically address coalition agreements.
Respondents were divided over whether the AfD’s lead candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, should be elected state premier, with 45 percent in favor and 48 percent opposed.
According to official results, the AfD won 43.8 percent of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt on Sept. 6, more than doubling its 20.8 percent share in 2021.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU) fell to 17.2 percent from 37.1 percent.
The AfD secured 39 of the 83 seats in the state parliament, three short of an outright majority.
The result has left the state facing difficult coalition arithmetic.
Germany’s mainstream parties have long ruled out cooperation with the AfD under the political “firewall” intended to keep the far right out of government.
Forming a majority without the AfD would require all five other parties represented in parliament to work together.
Trump hails AfD's record win
In another development, U.S. President Donald Trump praised AfD after the record result, attributing its rise to opposition to the country’s immigration policies.
“Wow! The Populist Party in Germany just had a really big night,” Trump said on Sept. 8 in a post on his Truth Social platform.
“They finally got tired of the absolutely horrible Immigration rules and regulations which have hurt Germany so badly. THEY ARE ON THE RISE, and not going to take it anymore! MGGA!!!” he added, using an abbreviation for “Make Germany Great Again.”

Russian forces shot down 596 Ukrainian drones during the night, the defence ministry said on Wednesday, with strikes killing at least four people in Novorossiysk in the southern Krasnodar region.

Talks in Norway
Meanwhile, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy arrived in Norway on Tuesday, the eve of the funeral of King Harald V, in a visit that will also allow talks with Oslo on air-defence support.
Zelenskyy met Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre on Tuesday evening, the premier's office said in a statement.
"We will discuss continued support for Ukraine. The main issue is strengthening air defence and assistance in other areas that are important for getting through the winter," Zelenskyy said in a post on X.
The Ukrainian leader said he and his wife would "express our gratitude to Norway at the farewell ceremony for His Majesty King Harald V", who died last month aged 89 and will be buried in Oslo later on Wednesday.
"Ukraine has a critical need for air defence systems and other forms of military support and it is preparing to face a difficult winter," Støre’s office said.
"The talks will focus in particular on how Norwegian military and civilian assistance can best meet Ukraine's current needs," it added.
No press briefing is planned for security reasons.
"Our weak point is anti-ballistic capabilities. We will grow stronger. I will have meetings in both Norway and Canada," Zelenskyy said on Sunday.
"We must develop our own Ukrainian anti-ballistic system".
Norway is one of the main providers of military and civilian aid to Kyiv following Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Earlier on Tuesday, the UK announced it was committing £100 million (€116 million) to boost Ukraine's air defence capabilities this winter, including with Patriot missiles.
The UK will also supply "air defence interceptors, large-calibre artillery rounds and drones" as part of the contribution to a NATO programme supporting Kyiv, the defence ministry said in a statement.
The Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) was established in 2022 by the US Department of Defence and NATO.
More than 20 countries have invested billions of dollars in the programme which aims to ensure a predictable flow of lethal and non-lethal support for Ukraine, with military hardware purchased mainly from the US.

The ‘veg-only’ gatekeepers  of urban housing in India
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
05:22:31 UTC
14:22:31 KST

A real estate agent posted a video promoting a high-value flat in Tardeo — priced at around Rs 6.5 crore — attached to a ‘veg-only’ condition. The clip went viral, then triggered criticism from political parties and social media users, after which the agent apologised.
Shreepati Arcade at Nana Chowk, south Mumbai, entered the city’s imagination in 2002 as an engineering and real-estate milestone: at 45 floors and around 161 metres, it was then the tallest occupied residential tower in India. Yet, the detail that has outlasted the height record is not architectural. It is social. The tower’s developer, R C Chaturvedi, has said that the apartments were sold only to vegetarian families, primarily from Jain, Marwari, and Sindhi communities, and that a handful of interested non-vegetarian buyers from a minority community were asked to step aside in the name of establishing a “vegetarian society”.“It became the USP for selling the flats,” recollects Chaturvedi. “We realised that most of the clients showing interest were vegetarians. There were only four clients from a minority community, all non-vegetarians, who were keen to buy the apartments in the tower. But we requested them and explained to them that this would be a vegetarian society. They respected our decision.”More than two decades later, the building’s identity as a veg-only zone remains intact. The story is not so much an aberration as an example of a longrunning Mumbai pattern: housing societies and neighbourhoods as spaces where personal preference, community power, and public claims of equality are continually negotiated, and often contested.
Food, friction… flashpoints
Few issues make that friction as visible as food. Vegetarianism can be a matter of individual taste, but in many communities, it is also a marker of ritual practice and group identity. In Mumbai’s property market, it has periodically become a screening device — sometimes openly stated, sometimes silently enforced — determining who can live where, and at what cost.A recent controversy illustrates how contemporary marketing can amplify an old practice. A real estate agent posted a video promoting a high-value flat in Tardeo — priced at around Rs 6.5 crore — attached to a ‘veg-only’ condition. The clip went viral, then triggered criticism from political parties and social media users, after which the agent apologised. The speed of the backlash made the episode seem like a new flashpoint, but property market observers know how veg-only buildings, and clusters have existed for decades. The difference today is that the condition is more easily recorded, shared, and debated publicly, rather than remaining an informal understanding between brokers and resident committees.
Changing localities
Mumbai’s “vegetarian clusters” have historical roots that are partly demographic and partly economic. Localities like Walkeshwar and Babulnath in south Mumbai, and parts of Ghatkopar on the eastern suburbs are often cited as areas where communities observing strict vegetarianism have consolidated over time.Upscale South Mumbai areas of Walkeshwar and Nepean Sea Road are even said to have no non-veg restaurants anywhere. Jashwant Mehta, a Walkeshwar resident, said some housing societies there have Jain temples and are home only to vegetarians. “In fact, demand and prices in such societies are higher than in buildings with better amenities,” he said.A Malabar Hill resident said that in some housing societies, where the majority is vegetarian, it is informally understood that the sale of flats is only to vegetarian families. “However, such conditions are not put in writing. This practice is prevalent in many areas of Mumbai,” the resident said.Some of this clustering followed familiar urban patterns: groups migrated for trade and employment, relied on community networks for housing and finance, and preferred to live near places of worship and businesses aligned with their customs. Once a neighbourhood acquired a reputation — whether for Jain temples, specific festival calendars, or food norms — successive waves of residents reinforced the same identity, making it harder for outsiders to enter even without any explicit written rule.Notably, the practice is not limited to enclaves stereotyped as ‘Gujarati’ or ‘Jain’. Even traditionally Marathi stronghold areas like Dadar, Lalbaug, and Kalachowki have housing projects that cater exclusively to vegetarian communities.
The insidious veg ‘logic’
There are multiple motives behind insisting on vegetarian-only residency, and they do not all carry the same weight. Some residents argue from the standpoint of religious discipline, ritual purity, and sensory comfort: they do not want the smell of meat in corridors, the possibility of cooking odours entering ventilation shafts, or shared spaces being used for non-vegetarian catering. Others frame it as a lifestyle choice akin to rules about noise, pets, or smoking. In this view, a building is shared environment, and residents can seek neighbours with compatible habits.But the same rule can also operate as a proxy for excluding particular communities. A property agent said vegetarianism is sometimes insisted upon to keep out members of minority communities, many of whom are presumed to be meat-eaters.The conflict sharpens in buildings with shared facilities, because common spaces force residents to negotiate collective norms. Many larger complexes now include community halls, clubhouses, banquet spaces, and sometimes society-run cafeterias or in-house restaurants. Architect Moayyed Fatehi describes a common arrangement: a residential complex may be multicommunal and harmonious on the surface, yet impose parameters on food in shared spaces.Fatehi’s own example from a luxury complex in Worli, Central Mumbai, indicates how these rules can be designed as a compromise: residents are free to cook and eat what they like inside their private flats, but society-controlled kitchens and banquet facilities remain veg-only. “Non-veg food cannot be cooked in the common banquet hall, but it can be served if you get it from outside,” he said.
Societies’ gatekeepers
Developers, too, play a role in shaping these norms. Many do not impose strict dietary restrictions, because it narrows the buyer pool and complicates sales. Yet, reports suggest some have begun reserving one wing or a couple of floors within a larger complex for vegetarians, a move that transforms social preference into a physical partition.Brokers and agents become key intermediaries in this ecosystem, because they accumulate informal knowledge about which buildings will reject which buyers. Over time, many learn to pre-filter enquiries. If they believe a society will object to minority communities, single women, bachelors, or openly nonvegetarian tenants, they may avoid showing those listings to those clients in the first place. This creates a parallel property market, where the burden falls on excluded groups: higher search costs, repeated rejections, more time spent negotiating, and sometimes a “minority premium” in the form of higher rents or prices in the smaller set of buildings willing to accept them.
The legal angle
The legal picture remains contested. One approach, said housinglaw specialists like advocate Anil Harish, treats a housing society as an association of like-minded members. Under this reasoning, people may choose to contract with those who share their norms, and a society may regulate collective life much as it might regulate commercial use of apartments, structural alterations, or other activities affecting neighbours. From that vantage point, a vegetarian-only condition is defended as an expression of freedom of association and contractual choice.The opposing approach holds that cooperative housing societies are not purely private clubs; they are quasi-public institutions managing essential urban resources — housing and neighbourhood access — within a framework meant to be open and non-discriminatory.A 2005 Supreme Court judgment — Zoroastrian Cooperative Housing Society Ltd vs District Registrar, Cooperative Societies (Urban) — is the leading case on the issue. The Zoroastrian Society bylaws restricting membership exclusively to members of the Parsi community, was challenged when a Parsi member sought to transfer his plot to a non-Parsi builder. “The apex court reversed the lower court order and upheld the validity of the society’s by-law. It held that there was nothing in the Gujarat Cooperative Societies Act, 1961 or Rules that precluded a society from restricting membership to persons of a particular community, persuasion or belief. The society’s “community-based membership restriction was upheld”, and the attempt to force admission/transfer contrary to the bylaws did not succeed.But advocate Vinod Sampat has argued that open membership is foundational: societies cannot discriminate on grounds of caste, creed, religion, or sex, and restrictions that prevent someone from buying a flat violate fundamental rights tied to residence and equality. “Article 15 of the Constitution prohibits discrimination by the state, and arbitrary exclusion by private bodies/societies violating public policy,” he said.“A housing society’s role is strictly administrative, limited to clearing dues and recording transfers. They cannot superimpose discriminatory rules or reject valid sale deeds,” Sampat pointed out, adding that many restrictions imposed by office-bearers amount to an abuse of power. This argument treats discriminatory gatekeeping as an unlawful barrier to equal participation in city life.
Pan-India phenomenon
Veg-only societies span regions and cities, reinforced by kinship and community ties and promoted by a preference for dietary common ground among neighbours. So, in Kolkata, with its love of machher jhol and kosha mangsho, several buildings and societies have quietly remained as vegetarian enclaves, shaped largely by Gujarati, Jain and Marwari communities. In South Kolkata’s Bhowanipore, the constituency now represented by CM Suvendu Adhikari and formerly by ex-CM Mamata Banerjee, the coming together of veg-only societies occurred over the decades.Till the mid-20th century, Bhowanipore was mainly an upper-middle class Bengali neighbourhood with a sizeable Sikh presence. Decades of migration and clustering have made veg-only societies a common feature so much so that some properties in Bhowanipore are sold or rented only to families that follow a strict vegetarian diet.Same is the story in Hyderabad. Cosmopolitan on the outside, conservative in pockets, the Telangana capital is well used to landlords in some traditional neighbourhoods preferring to rent out their homes only to vegetarian tenants.While Hyderabad’s western corridor, particularly Gachibowli, Hi-tech city, Kondapur, Nallagandal and Tellapur, has a relatively fluid rental market where food habits rarely become a major consideration, the situation is different in older neighbourhoods like Lingampally in Kacheguda, Chikkadpally, Badichowdi, Gujarati Galli, Gowliguda, Chappal Bazaar, etc.
“Our main objective is to keep our property clean and maintain its sanctity. We do not want nonvegetarian food to affect the atmosphere or purity of our home. Ultimately, we give the property based on trust, as we cannot keep monitoring what tenants buy, order or bring into the house,” said a landlord in Chikkadpally.So, Shreepati Arcade’s veg-only identity — once marketed as a unique selling proposition — now sits within a larger story: a reminder that a city’s skyline does not just reflect wealth and engineering, but also the boundaries — sometimes visible, often invisible — that residents draw around belonging.(With inputs from Sudipto Das & Sunny Baski)

TASHKENT, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- Chinese technology is driving industrial transformation and injecting strong momentum into economic development in Uzbekistan's Namangan Region, Governor Shavkat Abdurazakov has said.
In a recent interview with Xinhua, Abdurazakov said that Namangan is deepening practical cooperation with China across the board, with more than 70 joint projects underway in infrastructure, construction materials, green energy and other key sectors.
Agriculture and textiles are among Namangan Region's pillar industries. Its capital, Namangan city, known as the "city of flowers," is one of Uzbekistan's major exporters of finished textile products.
Abdurazakov said that scaling up the adoption of agricultural technology and advancing agro-industrialization remain top priorities for the region's development.
In recent years, Namangan Region has widely adopted cotton cultivation techniques, improved seeds and specialized fertilizers from China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, resulting in a substantial increase in cotton yields per hectare, he said. "This represents a major breakthrough in our agricultural sector."
Local farms are expanding the cultivation of lavender and other high-value aromatic crops, extending the agricultural supply chain into pharmaceuticals, perfumery and eco-tourism, he added.
On industrial and infrastructure cooperation, Abdurazakov said the first unit of a 500-megawatt solar power project, constructed by a Chinese enterprise in the region, was successfully connected to the grid in December 2024.
The project has significantly alleviated power shortages in local industrial zones, he noted.
Highlighting Namangan's strategic position connecting Tashkent, Uzbekistan's capital, with the densely populated Fergana Valley in Central Asia, Abdurazakov emphasized the region's active integration into regional connectivity initiatives, particularly the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway.
"The railway will not only expand Namangan's export footprint but also facilitate its integration into the broader regional market of the Fergana Valley," he said.
Abdurazakov said that Chinese enterprises have brought cutting-edge technologies and valuable development experience to Namangan while creating jobs for local people.
Namangan looks forward to further deepening cooperation with Chinese companies and local authorities to share development opportunities and achieve mutual benefits, the governor added. ■

How Russia Is Trying to Paralyze Kyiv Without Occupying It
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
05:17:00 UTC
14:17:00 KST

Russia failed to capture Kyiv in 2022. It is now trying to dictate how the city sleeps, travels, and works.
The latest attack began early on Tuesday, Sept. 8, just hours after the expiration of a three-day pause in strikes on Kyiv and Moscow, which was observed during the visit of US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff. Russian missiles and drones killed three people and wounded 16, according to Ukrainian officials. The strike damaged at least 14 high-rise buildings, a dormitory, a school, a clinic, and multiple warehouses.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“The moment the US president’s peace envoys left, Putin launched another massive, horrific attack against Kyiv,” Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said.
Attacks are spread across the entire day
For much of the war, Kyiv’s air-raid routine followed a grim but predictable rhythm: Russian drones arrived at night, missiles struck before dawn, and the city dusted itself off to restart in the morning.
Russia is now deploying smaller groups of drones throughout the day and night. Many are jet-powered models that travel faster and are significantly harder to intercept than the propeller-driven Shahed drones used earlier in the war.
Kyiv Post documented more than 100 jet-powered drones approaching Kyiv during one 12-hour period.
Russia launched more than 2,800 jet-powered drones against Ukraine in August, averaging roughly 90 a day, according to Ukrainian Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat. Their use increased fivefold in July compared with June.
Rutte: Civilian Deaths in Ukraine Highest Since May 2022 as Aid Delays Cost Lives
During one four-day stretch in late August, Russia launched nearly 1,500 drones, more than half of them jet-powered. Kyiv and the surrounding region faced attacks for five consecutive days, disrupting commutes and preventing metro trains from crossing the Dnipro River during alerts.
Between Aug. 27 and Sept. 1, Kyiv endured more than 60 air-raid alerts totaling 52 hours. The city spent more than two full days under alert within a six-day period.
The Institute for the Study of War (ISW) assessed that Russia had not necessarily increased the total number of drones used in each campaign. Instead, Moscow was distributing a comparable number across more hours to maximize fatigue and economic disruption.
A single drone approaching Kyiv can trigger citywide sirens, interrupt transit, and send workers into shelters. Once the all-clear sounds, another group can repeat the cycle.
The economic target is time
Every alert carries an economic cost. Beyond physical destruction, the sirens mean delayed workers, interrupted production, closed stores, suspended deliveries, and disrupted public transport. Schools move children into shelters, while medical and emergency crews must continue operating under the threat of additional strikes.
Russia is also targeting the logistics that keep Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities supplied.
Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi estimated in late August that Russian strikes had destroyed roughly 90% of the food-logistics capacity operated by major retail chains, contributing to temporary shortages of milk, sugar, fruit, and vegetables in Kyiv supermarkets.
The attacks have hit Nova Poshta sorting centers, supermarket distribution facilities, and warehouses storing books and consumer goods. Russian strikes have also hit food-storage facilities in Odesa and destroyed Epicentr hypermarkets.
“They are hitting civilian businesses, food warehouses, hypermarkets, postal terminals, warehouses where books are stored,” Interior Minister Ivan Vyhivskyi said.
In August, air alerts consumed 21.8% of scheduled operating hours for Ukrainian shopping centers. In practical terms, malls lost more than one out of every five hours in which they were supposed to operate.
The government’s response shows the scale of the problem. Ukraine is introducing a two-level alert system:
- Yellow alerts will indicate drone threats. Businesses may remain open if employees and customers have access to shelters. Authorities have recommended keeping Kyiv’s metro fully operational.
- Red alerts will indicate missile threats, including ballistic missiles and large combined attacks. Businesses must stop operating and people must move to shelters.
“The economy must continue to function, taxes must flow into the budget and people must receive their salaries,” Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi said.
Kyiv is also reducing its curfew and adjusting transport rules to limit the economic damage caused by prolonged alerts.
A modern siege logic
Kyiv is not facing a physical siege comparable to the capital of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Sarajevo. During the Bosnian War, Sarajevo was encircled and subjected to 1,425 days of shelling and sniper fire in a campaign that international courts found was intended to terrorize civilians.
Kyiv remains connected to the rest of Ukraine. Goods, weapons and people continue to move. Russian artillery does not surround the capital.
The similarity lies in the use of sustained danger to control civilian life. Russia cannot erect checkpoints around Kyiv, but it can use air-raid alerts to interrupt movement. It cannot physically close every factory, but it can force repeated work stoppages. It cannot occupy the capital, but it can make normal life dependent on when the next drone is launched.
The three-day pause for Witkoff and Kushner demonstrated how selectively that pressure can be applied. Russia and Ukraine agreed not to attack each other’s capitals during the envoys’ visit, but Putin continued to reject a broader ceasefire and insisted on Russia’s existing territorial demands.
The diplomatic pause protected the capitals during the talks but did not protect civilians elsewhere or stop fighting along the front.
Beyond psychological warfare
Civilian exhaustion is only one effect of the campaign. Continuous drone waves also force Ukrainian air-defense crews to work extended shifts, leaving less time to rest, relocate, and repair equipment.
By combining comparatively inexpensive drones with ballistic and cruise missiles, Russia forces Ukraine to decide when to use its most capable and limited interceptors. Patriot systems are essential for stopping ballistic missiles but cannot be used economically against every drone probing Kyiv’s airspace.
Defending the capital also creates a strategic trade-off. Radars, launchers, and interceptors assigned to Kyiv cannot simultaneously defend power stations, airfields, weapons factories, and other Ukrainian cities.
Russia therefore imposes costs even when most of its drones are intercepted. Ukraine must expend ammunition, keep crews constantly active, and defend a growing number of potential targets. The strikes also demonstrate that Kyiv’s political and security institutions remain targets.
For example, on Sept. 4, a Russian drone struck the Security Service of Ukraine headquarters in central Kyiv. President Volodymyr Zelensky said the drone had been directed towards the office of acting Security Service (SBU) chief Oleksandr Poklad.
Preparing for a winter war
Witkoff and Kushner arrived in Kyiv after more than three hours of talks with Putin in Moscow. They described their discussions with Zelensky as substantive and said there had been “significant progress” toward restarting trilateral negotiations, although no dates or venues were announced.
The central dispute remains unchanged. Russia demands that Ukraine surrender territory it still controls in Donbas. Kyiv refuses, while battlefield analysis indicates that Russia could require years to capture the rest of the Donetsk Oblast at its current rate of advance.
Zelensky is preparing for the possibility that the war will continue into winter. During the Kyiv talks, he requested a winter package covering air defense, energy support, and access to US liquefied natural gas.
“If the war continues in the winter, we strongly count on the winter package,” Zelensky said. However, the US delegation announced no new Patriot batteries. Ukraine recently received a small number of Patriot interceptors, while Britain has pledged additional air-defense assistance.
Neither measure eliminates the shortage.
Ukraine needs separate production tracks for drones and ballistic missiles. Zelensky said 67 Ukrainian companies were working on systems capable of intercepting jet-powered drones, although only three to five had demonstrated results.
Ukraine has also sought US permission to manufacture anti-ballistic systems and interceptors. In July, President Donald Trump said that Washington would license Ukrainian production of Patriot interceptors, but he later appeared to reverse that position.
However, on Sept. 2, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that licensing negotiations remained underway.
Even if an agreement is reached, experts estimate that establishing production would take at least a year.
The goal is friction, not collapse
The campaign does not have to force Kyiv to capitulate to impose strategic costs. Its immediate effect is to make daily life slower, less reliable, and more expensive.
When trains stop, warehouses burn, stores close, and workers spend hours in shelters, Russia inflicts damage without advancing on the ground. By forcing Ukraine to expend interceptors and concentrate air defenses around the capital, Moscow reduces the resources available to protect other cities, infrastructure and the front.
The aerial campaign has already killed civilians, disrupted transport, damaged commercial logistics, and forced Ukraine to redesign its warning system.
Countering it will require more than Patriot missiles. Ukraine needs cheaper anti-drone interceptors, dispersed warehouses, alternative transit routes, more shelters, and geographically precise alerts that prevent one drone from shutting down a city of millions.

On Wednesday, the Transport Administration will install a new bidirectional speed‑camera cabin at kilometer 78.6 of the Risti–Virtsu–Kuivastu–Kuressaare road, in Liiva village, Muhu municipality. Its purpose is to help ensure compliance with the 40 km/h speed limit and make road crossing safer for pedestrians.
The cabin will be installed facing the Virtsu–Kuressaare direction, allowing vehicle speed to be measured in both directions. The camera will not begin measuring speed immediately at the new location. First, the necessary configuration work will be carried out and traffic management will be adjusted to the new solution. The Transport Administration will inform road users when the speed camera begins operating.
In May 2025, a child was killed in a traffic accident in Liiva village after being struck by a truck trailer.
There are currently 68 speed‑camera cabins on Estonia's state roads, six of which can measure speed in both directions. The Transport Administration has 34 measurement systems for use in the cabins, which are relocated between different cabins as needed.
The Transport Administration noted that stationary speed cameras help reduce speeding in high‑risk locations and thereby reduce the likelihood of traffic accidents and their possible consequences. They also help monitor driver behavior, the agency added.

Possible massacre and cannibalism 7,000 years ago uncovered in Granada
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
05:14:07 UTC
14:14:07 KST

Analysis of nearly 1,000 bones found in three caves in Granada shows that cannibalism was a recurring Neolithic practice, with signs of collective violence, possible rituals and skulls turned into containers.
Three caves in Granada reveal that cannibalism was a recurrent practice during the Neolithic in the south of the Iberian Peninsula. The analysis of nearly 1,000 human remains found at Malalmuerzo, Carigüela and Majólicas has made it possible to date these assemblages for the first time and determine that acts of cannibalism took place in different periods and social contexts.
One of the most striking cases is Malalmuerzo, where researchers suggest that the cave may have been the scene of an episode of collective violence followed by acts of cannibalism around 5000 BC.
More than half a century after these sites became key references for the study of prehistoric cannibalism, an international team has re-examined the remains using radiocarbon dating and new taphonomic analysis techniques.
The results indicate that Neolithic cannibalism in the Iberian Peninsula was not an isolated phenomenon, but a practice that recurred at different times and under varying social circumstances, in line with evidence documented in other regions of Europe.
The research, published in the 'Journal of Archaeological Science', involved universities and research centres in Spain, Austria, Brazil and Argentina.
Cannibalism in three Granada caves with different contexts
The team examined nearly 1,000 human remains from the three caves in search of evidence of deliberate manipulation. The researchers studied cut marks, fractures and tooth marks under the microscope and combined statistical analyses, machine learning and direct radiocarbon dating to determine how and when the bones were modified.
Although all three sites show evidence linked to cannibalism, such as cut marks, cooking and bite marks, each tells a different story. Malalmuerzo shows signs of violence; Carigüela reveals the recurrence of these practices and a distinctive treatment of skulls; and Majólicas points to possible ritual practices.
For decades, prehistoric cannibalism tended to be interpreted as a homogeneous phenomenon. However, the new study shows that practices that appear similar may reflect different social realities and that their meaning needs to be analysed by jointly considering chronology, the archaeological context and the evidence preserved in the bones.
This is how Antonio Rodríguez-Hidalgo, Ramón y Cajal researcher at the Institute of Archaeology of Mérida and one of the study’s authors, explains it.
A possible massacre followed by cannibalism at Malalmuerzo
The Malalmuerzo cave offers one of the most striking findings of the research. The remains point to a possible episode of collective violence around 5000 BC, involving individuals of different ages whose bodies were subsequently consumed.
In Carigüela, the new dates indicate several episodes of cannibalism throughout the Neolithic. Among the most unusual discoveries are two skulls that were modified so they could be used as containers.
The most recent episode is documented at Majólicas, around 3800 BC, and does not appear to be linked to a violent context. Some bones stained red, probably with cinnabar, point to possible ritual practices.
Neolithic cannibalism was recurrent in Europe
The three Granada sites fit into a broader pattern observed in Europe. Cannibalism during the Neolithic would not have been a continuous practice, but a phenomenon that appears concentrated in specific periods and regions.
Anthropophagic practices are particularly concentrated in three phases: the late 6th millennium BC, the mid-5th millennium BC and the late 3rd millennium BC, the last already in the Bronze Age.
Although the researchers have not identified a single cause that explains all these episodes, they believe they may be linked to changes in social organisation, relations between different groups and the way in which death and violence were understood.
New techniques reveal secrets of remains excavated decades ago
The research also highlights the scientific value of historical archaeological collections and shows how new techniques can provide unprecedented information on material excavated decades ago.
Among the authors is Miguel C. Botella, then director of the Laboratory of Forensic Archaeology at the University of Granada, whose work was crucial to the study of these remains.
"His work helped establish Malalmuerzo, Carigüela and Majólicas as benchmark sites for the study of cannibalism in Europe’s late Prehistory," concludes Francesc Marginedas.
