Call of corruption: What you should know about Ukraine’s billion-dollar scam industry milked by Zelensky’s government
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
05:13:27 UTC
14:13:27 KST

Call of corruption: What you should know about Ukraine’s billion-dollar scam industry milked by Zelensky’s government
Ukraine’s enormous and toxic scam-call industry has suddenly been put under unprecedented pressure from forces Vladimir Zelensky cannot control.
Zelensky’s prosecutor general, Ruslan Kravchenko, tendered his resignation after Western-backed investigators accused his own chief cybercrime prosecutor of extorting protection money from scamsters, allegedly on behalf of his chief. Kravchenko has nevertheless insisted he stepped down for political reasons.
Ukraine’s industrial-scale scam-call network preys on the weak, robbing vulnerable people of their life savings and in some cases pushing them into violent crime. But the competition is literally cut-throat and explosive, and is believed to be behind a recent bomb attack linked to Ukrainian agents in Monaco.
How big is Ukraine’s scam-call industry?
Scam-calling rapidly developed between 2014 and 2016 in Ukraine. The keys to its swift growth were corruption in law enforcement, global technological advances in transborder communications and e-banking, and the abundant labor force.
The Geneva-based NGO Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC) estimated in April that the industry generates $1 billion a month and employs 60,000 people.
Who do Ukraine’s scam-call centers target?
One of Ukraine’s specifics is that young men defrauding Russian pensioners can rationalize their actions as fulfilling their patriotic duty without going to the front line.
Moscow perceives the crime business as a national security threat, claiming it works hand in glove with intelligence agencies. Russian authorities have reported dozens of cases in which a fraud victim was enticed to carry out criminal activity, from firebombing rail equipment to bringing a disguised explosive device to the office of a law enforcement agency.
However, true criminals go where the money is. Last year, GI-TOC estimated that half of victims of Ukrainian offices were Russian, but now reportedly 80% of them focus on Western nations.
How are Ukraine’s scam centers run?
Basically, they are the modern incarnation of telemarketing fraud, known as “boiler rooms” in English criminal slang. Ukrainian “offices” have their own “cold callers” – criminals who search for potential victims, “closers” – more skilled manipulators who actually defraud their marks, “floor managers” to oversee each individual operation, and “drops” who exfiltrate stolen money. In fact, most Ukrainian terms are borrowed.
Who owns and protects Ukraine’s scam-call industry?
The criminal networks normally run in regular office spaces, each with its own IT support to spoof phone numbers and grease the digital cogs and wheels. Larger offices have dedicated HR, accountants, security, and marketing.
Many of the centers pay bribes to officials, though there is a dispute over how compromised the government is. Western media tend to say paying off local police gives you a tip of an impending raid ordered from Kiev.
But Ukrainian media – and last week’s allegations – suggest a top-to-bottom network rife with infighting, hostile takeovers, and selective enforcement of the law.
Who works at Ukraine’s scam centers?
The workers are overwhelmingly young people in their late teens and early twenties, most of them male, aimless in life and with a taste for making quick cash, according to industry insiders.
“They are convinced that scamming people is better than enduring mockery working as a cashier,” a scam office tech guy told Ukrainskaya Pravda for an exposé it published. “For them it’s a small-time alluring crime.”
Why does the West allow its citizens to be targeted by Ukrainian scammers?
European law enforcement agencies are limited by the fact that their governments are determined to support the government in Kiev to keep the war with Russia rolling.
However, earlier this year, Ukrainian media reported that Western pressure reached a point where a major crackdown was imminent. Zelensky’s messaging aligned with the narrative.
Why has Ukraine’s profitable and connected scam-call center industry been targeted?
Zelensky sent a law to the Ukrainian parliament in early September, seeking tougher punishments for fraudsters.
Some Ukrainian media argued that Zelensky ordered the clampdown to pre-empt the latest scandal, initiated by Western-backed anti-corruption agencies. Last year he tried and failed to place the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU) and the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO) under the Prosecutor General’s Office.
The same agencies are chasing down multiple, multimillion corruption schemes linked to Zelensky’s inner circle that you can read about in RT’s ‘State of Corruption’ series.
In short, officials close to Ukraine’s leader have been accused of taking over $100 million in kickbacks from Ukraine’s energy industry, laundering millions to secure bail for a former energy minister, creaming millions from a missile and drone maker that was originally a TV production company run by Zelensky’s business partners, and running a system of vote-buying in parliament.
What impact has the sudden clampdown on Ukraine’s scam-call centers had?
Between January and mid-July, law enforcement reportedly took out over 2,000 jobs in the scam industry. But in just a single week in August, officials reportedly raided 95 scam offices where some 1,794 scammers were employed.
While the now-departed Kravchenko boasted of the results, NABU surveillance of his cybercrime underling, Sergey Kropiva, who the agency has accused of running a nationwide protection racket, reveals it was a PR exercise.
“We are not bending over backwards,” he allegedly told an accomplice. “We are dragging our heels, hitting ten of them [fraud offices] a week… The important thing is good media coverage of all this s**t.”
Ukrainian media say as of early August there were roughly 2,000 offices in Ukraine, each employing dozens or even hundreds of people and half of them paying protection money to corrupt officials.
According to Zerkalo Nedeli, the bribes amounted to roughly $240 million per year, 15% of which found its way to the Prosecutor General’s Office in Kiev.
Kravchenko is widely seen as having upped the ante following his appointment by Zelensky in 2025, triggering an industry-wide turf war. His downfall was described in the press with a crime-slang saying: “The cat got ruined by his own greed.”
If prosecutors creamed 15%, who has been taking the other 85%?
Corrupt officials are reportedly scattered throughout the Ukrainian government, from the border guard service, to Ukraine’s financial regulator, to national police, to secret services.
People at the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) and the military intelligence agency HUR are allegedly on the take. The firefights in Kiev in which the two services engaged last week were described by some outlets as a conflict for scam proceeds.
There were claims in the Ukrainian press that scam money not only lines the pockets of security officials, but also generates off-the-books funding for their operation, not unlike the CIA did under President Ronald Reagan, when it sold weapons to Iran to fuel right-wing Contras insurgents in South America. The CIA reportedly overhauled both the SBU and HUR after the 2014 coup in Kiev.
What kind of risks are the Ukrainian heads of scam-schemes prepared to take?
One of Kropiva’s recorded conversations linked the ongoing semi-crackdown with “that guy in Bali.”
The reference was apparently to the kidnaping of two Ukrainian citizens in the Indonesian island province that took place in February. One of them escaped, while the other was held for ransom and later dismembered.
The victims were identified by the media as Igor Komarov and Yermak Petrovsky, the sons of suspected career crime bosses who were allegedly working together in the fraud business. The horrific torture video of Komarov was national news in Ukraine.
The bombing of exiled businessman Vadim Ermolaev and members of his family in Monaco in June was organized by a duo of HUR and SBU agents, according to Ukrainian investigators.
Ermolaev’s son Artur was previously sentenced to a suspended term in Estonia for running scam-call centers that victimized Estonian citizens to the tune of $114 million. There was speculation that the bombing attack was a warning for the father to stay away from the industry.
Meanwhile, Kropiva himself was quite brazen in his managerial role, bragging that he can “screw everyone in the law enforcement” and do what he wants, the recordings show. His alleged accomplice and girlfriend complained when he told her to remove Instagram photos proving her lavish lifestyle.
She came to her bail hearings wearing what journalists recognized as a $3,400 Saint Laurent jacket, which probably didn’t help her case.

Delay tactic or genuine solution? Carbon capture under fire again as EU invests in ‘unproven’ technology
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
05:12:12 UTC
14:12:12 KST

Carbon capture and storage has been found to be “technically uncertain and very high cost”.
CO2 emitted by a fertiliser factory in the Netherlands will be stored underneath the seabed in Norway, in what the owners are calling the “largest commercial carbon capture and storage (CCS) project in Europe”.
At an opening ceremony this week, the ammonia and fertiliser plant announced that it will capture 800,000 tonnes of CO2 a year then liquefy it to be sent by ship to Norway.
Having funded the project, the European Commission was keen to promote its investment – with the Commissioner for Climate, Net Zero and Clean Growth attending the inauguration alongside the Prime Ministers of both countries.
While the Commission says the Sluiskil plant, run by Norwegian chemical company Yara, is a “strategic investment”, opponents say it is “risking billions in taxpayers’ money to fund a dangerous distraction that delays climate action”.
As one of the most divisive topics in climate action, we look into the facts about carbon capture and how the EU came to be funding this experimental technology.
What is carbon capture and storage?
Carbon capture and storage (CCS) refers to technologies designed to prevent CO2 from entering the atmosphere in the first place and/or to remove it after it has been emitted.
As is done at the Sluiskil plant, most projects use a liquid to chemically remove the CO2 emitted from the production process, where it is then compressed into a liquid-like state and transported typically through a pipeline to a storage site. At that point, it’s either stored deep underground or is transformed into things like building materials or synthetic fuel. In the case of the latter, this technology is referred to as CCUS, where the ‘U’ stands for utilisation.
As of February 2026, there were 75 operational CCS projects around the world, according to climate change publication Carbon Brief. Almost all of them are at fossil-fuel extraction and processing sites, according to the IEA’s database. Together, these projects capture 62.5 million tonnes of CO2 (MtCO2) each year. This is equivalent to 0.2 per cent of total global emissions in 2025.
While Yara’s chief executive, Svein Tore Holsether, said in a statement, “The carbon capture facility in Sluiskil proves that large-scale industrial decarbonisation is possible today”, the cumulative emissions saved are a very, very tiny drop in the ocean.
US non-profit the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA) has conducted in-depth research into CCS. Their Energy Finance Analyst, Andrew Reid, says: “Despite the political and financial support that has been pointed to CCS over the past three to four years, it remains technically uncertain, very high cost, and reliant upon huge subsidies to move from feasibility to construction and operation.”
CCS: To help the fossil fuel industry to extract and sell more oil and gas
To understand its uses, it’s important to understand where carbon technology originates from. According to Carbon Brief, it “was originally rolled out at US and Canadian oil wells in the early 1970s as a way to achieve “enhanced oil recovery”. This involves injecting captured CO2 into depleted wells – a process that stores the gas, but also helps to extract more oil.” This is by far the most significant use for carbon capture worldwide, with three-quarters of it used for this purpose.
This means that “the majority of CO2 that is both captured and used today helps the fossil-fuel industry to extract and sell more oil and gas,” according to Carbon Brief.
How did the EU end up funding carbon capture and storage?
One of the arguments against CCS, which campaigners have been making for years, is that it is a way for polluters to keep polluting, rather than emitting less of the gases which are heating up the planet at alarming rates.
“All capture and storage projects suffer from the same problem: they distract attention and resources from cutting emissions at source and give polluting industries like fertiliser production a pass to keep on polluting,” says Rachel Kennerley, Senior International Carbon Capture Campaigner at the Center for International Environmental Law (CIEL).
Belén Balanyá, researcher and campaigner at Corporate Europe Observatory (CEO), has been tracking the lobbying efforts of the fossil fuel industry for 25 years. She has recently focussed on lobbying by the CCS industry. The outcomes of annual COP climate talks are known to be influenced by lobbyists representing industry. Balanyá found that around 500 CCS lobbyists were at COP29 in 2024. A year earlier, at COP28, CCS proponents (largely tied to fossil fuel industries) scored a significant win with the endorsement of “abatement and removal technologies” in the agreement.
Referring to fossil fuel industries, Balanyá says, “You look at what’s on the agenda and it’s always escape hatches to stay in business,” she tells Euronews Green. “It’s where they move when they’ve been forced to – when there’s more knowledge and more acceptance about climate change and their role and that they have to decarbonise.”
CCS being endorsed in a COP agreement may have contributed to its legitimacy in political circles within the EU. The CCUS Forum (now the Industrial Carbon Management (ICM) Forum), set up by the European Commission in 2021, is an annual event with working groups that feed directly into EU policymaking. CEO found that every group has been co-chaired by the fossil fuel industry or associated organisations.
A newly released report from the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) details the risks of overshooting 1.5°C of warming and how we can limit them. It assessed what it called Carbon Dioxide Removal and found that many issues remain with the technology, such as whether it can scale sustainably (due to costs, land and energy use), whether it would actually keep CO2 out of the atmosphere permanently and who’s responsible for regulation and leaks.
CCS: Good or bad?
Wherever commentators stand on CCS, there is some agreement that for some industries, the technology can be useful. Yara’s project targets emissions from ammonia production which “provides a relatively concentrated CO2 stream, making this one of the more straightforward industrial applications of carbon capture rather than an example of the very hardest emissions to abate,” according to Domien Vangenechten, Programme Lead in Clean Economy at E3G.
“The lesson should therefore not be that Europe needs CCS everywhere, but that we should pragmatically deploy it where it can cut substantial emissions today.”

Getting those steps in does reduce the risk of early death. But it is also the pace that matters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
05:09:14 UTC
14:09:14 KST

It is not only the number of steps per day but also the walking pace that matters for lowering the risk of early death, according to new research.
It is both: the number of steps and the walking pace that count against all-cause and cardiovascular disease mortality, a new study published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine found. This means different combinations of the number of daily steps and walking pace can be associated with a lower risk of early death.
“Our findings inform flexible step-based pathways to lower mortality risk for middle-aged and older adults, particularly those with barriers to increasing daily step counts or stepping intensity,” researchers said, highlighting that most of the studies did not look at the association of different combinations of daily step counts and stepping intensity with mortality risk.
The researchers analysed activity-tracker data from middle-aged participants in the UK Biobank, who wore a device for seven days between 2013 and 2015.
After looking at wearable device data from 64,743 participants aged 40 to 69 years who took from less than 5,000 to over 10,000 steps per day at different paces researchers found that taking between 7,500 to 10,000 steps per day showed the biggest reduction in early death irresponsible of the pace.
In the meantime, a brisker pace for at least 30 minutes every day – taking 90 steps per minute – was also associated with a lower risk of death from any cause, irrespective of how many steps were taken.
“Regardless of total daily step counts, maintaining higher walking cadence maybe a promising target for preventing premature mortality,” researchers said.
For those living a sedentary lifestyle with less than 5,000 steps per day, “increasing stepping pace may substantially lower all-cause and cardiovascular disease mortality risk,” researchers said. In the meantime, those who prefer to walk slower can benefit from taking more steps instead.

Liberal Michigan rabbis and other Jewish leaders are calling on the Democratic Party to agree to a list of “nonnegotiable” principles about Jewish safety and Israel as the party’s US Senate candidate in the state, Abdul El-Sayed, seeks to make inroads with Jewish voters.
The campaign, backed by a progressive Zionist group, comes as a different subset of Michigan Jewish leaders are urging their community to reject El-Sayed outright and instead vote for his Republican opponent, former US Rep. Mike Rogers.
“I think he has the potential to be an amazing, visionary leader in the state of Michigan and in this country,” Rabbi Josh Whinston, who heads the Reform Temple Beth Emeth in Ann Arbor and has met privately with El-Sayed, said Monday about the Democratic candidate during a press conference. “But his vision needs to be more inclusive.”
Whinston was one of more than a dozen Jewish clergy who signed “Nonnegotiable Michigan,” the open letter. It does not directly address El-Sayed by name but outlines five principles its signers say “leaders who want our votes” must demonstrate.
The letter lists five “nonnegotiables”:
“Jewish safety — including for Zionist Jews — in Michigan and across America”;
“Our right to define our own Jewish identities”;
“Jewish sovereignty in Israel”;
“Welcoming our full participation in American political life”; and
“An affirmative vision for a better future in the Middle East.”
The “Nonnegotiable” campaign is backed by Zioness Action Fund, a registered 501(c)4 associated with the advocacy group Zioness, which bills itself as “Unabashedly progressive. Unapologetically Zionist.” Past Zioness actions have put pressure on progressive spaces to become more welcoming of Zionism as the progressive movement has sharply turned against Israel.
The initial signatories number 16, most of whom are Reform and Conservative rabbis and cantors serving congregations in the state. The initiative was spearheaded by Whinston and Rabbi Aaron Starr, of the Conservative Congregation Shaarey Zedek in Southfield, a Detroit suburb. Starr is also president of the Michigan Board of Rabbis.
“We realized we were all having this same experience of our members coming to us and saying, ‘Rabbi, what should I do?’” Starr told the Jewish Telegraphic Agency about the letter’s origins.
At the press conference, Starr compared the relationship between Jews and political parties to a marriage. “I would advise against a couple getting married if they can’t ensure each other’s safety and can’t honor each other’s identity,” he said.
It remains relatively rare for Jewish spiritual leaders to directly involve themselves in electoral politics, though a large coalition of thousands of rabbis signed onto a letter opposing “rising anti-Zionism” shortly before the election last year of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, a harsh critic of Israel.
The latest letter comes as Michigan’s Jewish community of around 100,000 has been put in the national spotlight in a crucial election for deciding control of the Senate. In late August, El-Sayed, a strident Israel critic who has questioned its future as a Jewish state, apologized to Jewish Democrats for his past comments about the Temple Israel attack in West Bloomfield Township earlier this year. El-Sayed had said of the attacker, who lost family in an Israeli strike in Lebanon, “Hurt people hurt people,” triggering backlash from the Jewish community.
The candidate has also been meeting with Jewish voters and leaders, and recently told JTA that “safety” is the top concern he hears from them. His campaign intends to hire a Jewish liaison, sources have told JTA.
El-Sayed has not budged on other issues of concern to Jewish voters, including his reticence to back a two-state solution that would specifically recognize Jewish sovereignty — though he has said he would be open to the possibility if Israelis and Palestinians jointly agreed on it.
Letter was in the works since before El-Sayed's apology, petition's leader says
The petition’s leaders told JTA their letter had been in the works since before El-Sayed’s apology, and said he needs to do more. “It took on another level of meaning after his quote-unquote ‘apology,’ which was really only a partial apology,” Starr said.
Following one of El-Sayed’s apologies, Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel, who is Jewish, urged the same room of Jewish Democrats ”to place the needs of the world above even our own self-interest and, yes, even our own survival.” Invoking Queen Esther and “Jewish values,” Nessel’s remarks have since been criticized by Jews across the spectrum and spurred renewed debate over the role of Jewish interests in the broader political conversation.
In contrast to Nessel, and to the rival letter urging a Rogers vote, the “Nonnegotiable” campaign does not endorse a candidate. Instead, it argues that Democratic leaders should make clear to Jews that they agree with what the letter defines as central Jewish concerns.
“Every constituency must occasionally remind its party that support is earned, not owed,” the letter states. “This is a good faith effort to make our needs unmistakably clear, and to invite any candidate seeking public office — now or in the future — to engage, listen, learn, and grow.”
Spokespeople for the El-Sayed campaign and for the Michigan Democratic Party did not immediately return JTA requests for comment.
Starr said the values articulated in the letter go beyond El-Sayed: Jews, he told JTA, also have “an eye to 2028.”

Pilots considered aborting landing after touchdown in Miami cargo crash, NTSB says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
05:01:15 UTC
14:01:15 KST

The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) said on Tuesday that evidence recovered from a flight data recorder suggested the pilots of an Amazon Prime Air cargo plane involved in a deadly crash considered aborting the landing after the aircraft touched down.
The 32-year-old Boeing 767 operated by Miami-based 21 Air overran the runway by some 1,300 feet (396 m) and crashed into two vehicles, killing five people and injuring five others on Sunday.
NTSB Chair Jennifer Homendy told reporters that investigators would interview both of the pilots on Wednesday and then release details from the cockpit voice recorder.
The NTSB said 30 seconds before the end of the flight data recording, the nose landing gear and right main landing gear touched down on the runway at a speed of 158 knots (181 mph), while 19 seconds before the end of the recording, the left main landing gear touched down at a speed of 134 knots.
A few seconds later, the brakes were released, and the throttles were increased to values consistent with go-around thrust, indicating a late attempt to abort the landing and get back in the air.
But 11 seconds before the end of the recording, throttles were reduced to idle power, and brakes were reapplied. The final ground speed was 65 knots at the end of the recording.
The NTSB said there was no indication in the recorded data that speed brakes or thrust reversers were deployed to help slow the plane.
32 investigators examining case
Homendy is leading a team of 32 investigators at Miami International Airport. She said the NTSB was able to reopen one of the two runways closed since the accident to allow for departures from an easterly direction late on Tuesday.
The Amazon cargo plane was on its third flight of the day, coming from San Juan, Puerto Rico. It had flown from Cincinnati to Miami and from Miami to San Juan earlier on Sunday before the crash at 1:53 p.m. EDT (1753 GMT).
The captain, 55, received his type rating for the 767 in May and has 7,145 hours of flight time, while the first officer, 37, received his type rating for the 767 in April 2025 and has 2,655 flying hours, the NTSB said.

China needs monkeys: lab animal shortage could hinder biotech growth
As fundraising and out-licensing deals in China grow, so does demand for monkeys and other primates for testing
China’s biotechnology market has “significantly” driven up the demand for primate experimental models as the market recovers, tightening the supply of laboratory monkeys, according to a leading biotech firm.
Primate experiments typically use monkeys and other non-human species to test the safety and efficacy of a drug under development before clinical trials on humans.
Over US$110 billion worth of Chinese-developed drug candidates were traded in 81 out-licensing deals in the first half of the year, equivalent to 80 per cent of the full-year value in 2025, data from China’s National Medical Products Administration showed.
Joinn added that the price increase resulted from the tightened supply of non-human primates for experimental use in China, as their breeding rate has remained relatively stable.

US Rep. Chris Pappas swiftly defeated progressive opponent Karishma Manzur in a Democratic Senate primary in New Hampshire on Tuesday, capping off one of several races in which criticism of Israel and AIPAC became prominent talking points.

'We’ve got to turn the page on Donald Trump’s reckless leadership'

Having secured the Democratic nomination, Pappas is seeking to fill the seat of three-term Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, who is not seeking reelection this year. As he and Manzur spoke to the press during the final weeks of the campaign, their messaging often included condemnations of Israeli leadership.
New Hampshire Democrats chose Pappas, a four-term congressman, as their Senate nominee at a time when their party is hoping to take control of both houses of Congress. Why a 50% harvest collapse won't leave shelves short of Champagne
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
05:00:51 UTC
14:00:51 KST

France’s Champagne region is facing an extraordinary harvest collapse. Yet consumers should not expect the number of bottles reaching shops to halve — at least not yet.
The reason is that this year’s harvest does not determine how many bottles can be sold immediately. Champagne takes several years to make, and producers hold substantial stocks and reserve wines from earlier harvests to help maintain supply when a crop is poor.
And across France, wine production is expected to reflect a very poor harvest this year. According to preliminary estimates from Agreste, the French Agriculture Ministry’s statistics office, overall wine production is to fall to 3.39 billion litres in 2026.
That would be 6% less than in 2025 and 28% below the 4.72 billion litres produced in 2023.
If confirmed, it would also be France’s smallest wine crop since 1957, when output stood at 3.25 billion litres, according to the International Organisation of Vine and Wine.
The decline partly reflects a 2.5% reduction in the area of French vineyards in production. But drought and repeated heatwaves have had the greater effect by reducing the amount of wine produced from each hectare.
“Evidence strongly suggests that heat and drought, through lower yields per hectare, are the dominant explanation for this year’s exceptionally low harvest,” Jean-Marie Cardebat, Professor at Bordeaux University and affiliated to INSEEC Business School, told Euronews Business.
The regional figures support this. Some of the steepest falls are in areas where relatively few vineyards have been removed.
Bordeaux and Languedoc-Roussillon, where large areas of vines have been uprooted, are expected to produce 10% and 5% more wine respectively than in 2025, although both remain below their recent averages.
Why has Champagne been hit so badly?
Wine production from this year’s harvest in the Champagne region is forecast to fall by 48%, from 2.57 million hectolitres in 2025 to 1.34 million this year.
For wine carrying the Champagne protected designation, the fall is slightly steeper. Output is expected to drop by 49% to 1.24 million hectolitres, 47% below the five-year average.
However, these figures refer to wine made from grapes harvested this year. Not the number of bottles of Champagne to be sold.
After Champagne, the worst affected regions are Jura, where production is forecast to fall by 36%, and Bourgogne-Beaujolais, where it is expected to decline by 33%. Losses for Burgundy Pinot Noir exceed 50%, according to Agreste.
In Champagne, harvesting began in mid-August and the grapes reached exceptional ripeness. But frost in the Aisne, hail and drought since March severely reduced the crop. The average weight of grape bunches fell to its lowest level in 20 years.
Will fewer bottles of Champagne be sold?
The crop damage is severe, particularly for individual growers. But a 49% fall in wine produced from this year’s grapes does not mean the supply of finished Champagne will immediately fall by the same amount.
Before the full scale of the damage was clear, the industry had set the amount of the 2026 harvest that could be sold at 8,800 kilograms of grapes per hectare. That was only around 2% below the 9,000 kg/ha limit set in 2025 and reflected weaker demand and the need to manage stocks.
The actual harvest is now expected to average no more than around 7,000 kg/ha, according to the Syndicat Général des Vignerons de la Champagne. That would be the lowest level since the 1980s.
Growers who fail to reach the permitted level cannot make up the missing grapes. Champagne houses, however, can soften the impact by drawing on wines held in reserve.
“Champagne has lost roughly half of a normal harvest, but this will not translate into an immediate 50% fall in sales because producers can draw on extensive stocks and reserve wines,” Professor Cardebat said.
He called the production loss “extremely significant”, adding that the lost production was “equivalent to approximately 140 million 75-centilitre bottles”.
This represents about €2.7bn in potential commercial value, according to the professor, based on the average turnover generated per bottle shipped in 2025.
However, he stressed that this was not an estimate of immediate revenue losses because producers can draw on substantial stocks and reserve wines.
Professor Cardebat described the situation as “a major production and productivity shock”, adding that the longer-term risk would arise if very small harvests became recurrent.
“Then stocks would decline, costs would rise, and Champagne could eventually become less able to supply all its markets,” Professor Cardebat told Euronews Business.
A smaller harvest is not entirely bad news - yet
Overall, the smaller harvest is not expected to have an immediate significant impact on wine producers’ revenue.
According to Professor Cardebat, the greater economic concern is the accumulation of poor harvests. “This will be the third consecutive very small French harvest,” he said, adding that many producers were already financially fragile because demand had weakened while the costs of energy, labour, machinery and financing had risen.
Lower yields also mean that producers must spread many of their costs across fewer bottles, pushing up the cost of each one and squeezing profits. Even if stocks delay the impact on revenue, another poor harvest could further weaken cash flow and producers’ ability to invest.
Producers also risk losing shelf space if they cannot supply retailers consistently. If Champagne shortages persisted, competitors such as Prosecco and Crémant could gain ground among shops and consumers.
However, France has also been struggling with excess supplies of some wines, particularly red wine, as consumption declines. A temporarily smaller harvest can help reduce stocks and bring supply closer to demand without permanently removing more vineyards.
According to Professor Cardebat, this creates a paradox: "Economically, lower productivity is bad for producers, but lower aggregate supply can help rebalance a market suffering from excess production".
He also added that the regions suffering the largest shock from bad weather conditions this year are not those facing the greatest structural financial risk. Champagne benefits from a powerful global brand, relatively high margins and its reserve system.
According to Professor Cardebat, the bigger structural risks were in Bordeaux, the South-West and parts of Languedoc-Roussillon, where producers have faced weak demand, low prices and vineyard removals. Those relying heavily on red wine are generally more exposed than producers of white or sparkling wine.
The Champagne harvest is therefore the most dramatic part of France’s 2026 wine story, but not necessarily its greatest financial crisis. Its reserves should keep bottles moving for now. The test will come if harvests of this size stop being exceptional.

Privacy screens and sculpted headrests: What's new in premium economy?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
05:00:13 UTC
14:00:13 KST

Premium economy is getting an upgrade as airlines make flying more private, comfortable and luxurious – just without the hefty business class price tag.
If you, like me, prefer to maximise your travel budget for on-ground experiences rather than flight fares, but are on the taller side and do like a bit of extra leg room (plus an excuse to splurge just a little bit), premium economy can be a happy medium between a standard economy fare and business or first class.
And the perks of premium economy travel doesn’t start and end in the sky. Think more generous baggage allowances (at least compared to economy), speedier check-in and not having to wait as long to board.
Now it seems airlines are betting that more passengers are willing to pay slightly more for this middle ground, with a new wave of offerings set to make the premium economy cabin more private, spacious and, perhaps, more luxurious.
From privacy screens and sculpted headrests to sleep pods and cozy slippers, here’s what’s on the horizon for premium economy class passengers.
Emirates’ privacy screens
This month, Emirates unveiled what it says is the “world’s first electric premium economy seat with full-height privacy screen”.
The Dubai-based airline's latest offering will be rolled out on its Airbus A350 aircraft, with a 2-3-2 configuration across 28 seats.
Passengers will be able to raise and lower the divider using the seat controls. They can also adjust their seating position with the control unit.
And for those who like to keep their phone charged in the sky, Emirates is also introducing wireless charging facilities to its premium economy cabins.
American adds more premium economy seats
Also in September, American Airlines launched its first retrofitted Boeing 777-300ER into commercial service, featuring 44 premium economy seats and being deployed on some of the carrier’s long-haul routes.
The redesigned seats come with sculpted headrests, adjusted calf and foot rests, wireless charging and both USB-C and AC power.
American, which has recently announced a number of new European flights for next summer, also rolled out 30 extra leg room seats as part of its Main Cabin Extra offering. Here, passengers can watch hundreds of titles as part of its inflight entertainment and enjoy free high-speed wifi if they are an AAdvantage member.
Lufthansa’s culinary upgrades and cozy slippers
As part of its “Future Onboard Experiences” initiative, stylised as FOX, Lufthansa introduced revamped in-flight offerings in May, coinciding with the 100th anniversary since it was founded.
Lufthansa’s upgrade to the premium economy cabin included revamped dining options, such as a business class-level appetizer offering and three hot main meals to choose from, with a side of toasty bread. The meal is rounded off with pastries or a slice of cake.
For extra comfort, the premium economy cabin also provides passengers with “cozy” slippers.
TAP Air Portugal introduces premium economy cabin
In June, TAP Air Portugal launched its premium economy offering on select fleets.
Branded “Economy Prime”, the cabin class is only available on the carrier’s long-haul flights. There are 12 seats in total, with four seats per row, however, passengers will always have the seat next to them left empty.
When it comes to in-flight dining, there’s a choice of two hot dishes, followed by a snack served before reaching the destination.
Economy Prime travellers are also given an amenities kit and can enjoy a selection of films and series on the carrier’s 13-inch HD screens.
On ground, passengers benefit from premium check-in, fast track, premium boarding and priority baggage, as well as an allowance of one 10kg cabin bag and two 23kg checked bags.
Divided into two fare options, Prime and Top Prime, the latter adds flexibility, giving passengers the option to change or refund their ticket, at no added cost.
Wizz Air's unique spin on premium economy
Hungarian low-cost carrier Wizz Air launched “Wizz Class” earlier this year. The premium add-on gives passengers a seat in the first row, with a choice of window or aisle, while the middle seat is kept empty for extra space.
Other perks include extra leg room seats, priority boarding, two items of cabin baggage, plus a snack and soft drink onboard.
The service is available for purchase on selected flights to and from Budapest, Bucharest Otopeni, London Luton, London Gatwick, Rome Fiumicino, and Warsaw.
Air New Zealand’s world-first sleep pods
Air New Zealand is set to give passengers a chance to lie down mid-air with its Skynest sleep pods, which it says would be a world first.
Skynest will make its debut on the carrier’s ultra long-haul flights between New York and Auckland starting in late December, where up to six premium (and standard) economy travellers at a time can swap their seat for a bed.
Passengers can book a four-hour session to “recharge in comfort” in their own private pod, which comes with a privacy curtain, ambient lighting, USB charging outlets and personal stowage.
The sessions are priced from NZ$495 (€250.45), which includes an appropriately named “Nestcessities” kit containing earplugs and an eye mask, because if you’re willing to pay extra to sleep at 35,000 feet above sea level, you may as well make yourself as comfortable as possible.

In praise of the bitter: Alexina Anatole’s recipes for tahini panzanella and curried corn farinata
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
05:00:02 UTC
14:00:02 KST

Bitterness has long had an image problem: is it delicious or disgusting? Here’s another contradiction: though bitterness seems as if it should sit alongside hot, pungent flavours such as mustard and horseradish, in reality it cools more than it builds. In Ayurvedic cooking, for instance, bitter ingredients are valued for their ability to refresh and rebalance, and those are qualities that run through both of today’s dishes, from the elegant bitterness of tahini in the panzanella to the clean bite of grapefruit in the dipping sauce for the farinata.
Tahini panzanella (pictured top)
Prep 10 min
Cook 25 min, plus resting
Serves 2-4
500g large tomatoes, eg, beef, oxheart or monterosa
1 tsp flaky sea salt
  ½ small garlic clove
  1 tbsp sherry vinegar, or red-wine vinegar
  1 tbsp pomegranate molasses
  1 small red onion, peeled and very thinly sliced
½ tbsp capers, finely chopped, or nonpareilles, which are already petite enough
½ tbsp sesame seeds, lightly toasted
Basil leaves, to garnish
 For the croutons
125g sourdough, crusts on, torn into rough pieces
2 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
  ½ tsp flaky sea salt
For the tahini dressing
2 tbsp tahini
1 tbsp lemon juice
  1 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
  ¼ tsp fine sea salt
Heat the oven to 220C (200C fan)/425F/gas 7. Chop the tomatoes into haphazard, chunky pieces and put them in a colander set over a bowl. Toss with the flaky salt and leave to drain for 10–15 minutes.
Meanwhile, spread the bread pieces on a baking tray, toss with the olive oil and salt, then bake for 10 minutes, until golden. In a bowl, grate the garlic into the tablespoon of sherry vinegar, to help take the edge off.
Make the tahini dressing by whisking the tahini, lemon juice, olive oil and salt, then gradually add about two tablespoons of ice-cold water until the mix is the consistency of double cream (the amount of water will depend on the thickness of the tahini).
Transfer the drained tomatoes to a serving bowl and stir in the pomegranate molasses, sliced red onion and capers. Add the sherry vinegar and garlic mix, and the croutons, and toss thoroughly. Stir through the tahini dressing, then leave for five to 10 minutes, so the croutons soften a little. Serve garnished with the toasted sesame seeds and basil leaves.
Curried corn farinata with grapefruit dipping sauce
Prep 10 min
Rest 15 min
Cook 40 min
Serves 3-4 as a light lunch
For the farinata
100g chickpea flour
  ½ tsp ground turmeric
  ½ tsp garlic powder/granules
  ½ tsp fine sea salt
1 tsp cumin seeds, toasted
1 tsp coriander seeds, toasted
  4 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
75g tinned sweetcorn, drained, or frozen and defrosted
3 spring onions, finely sliced
Mint leaves, to serve
For the grapefruit dipping sauce
4 tbsp fresh red grapefruit juice (from about 1 grapefruit)
1 tbsp rice vinegar
  1 tsp caster sugar
  1 red chilli, finely chopped (seeds and all, if you like things spicy)
In a large jug, combine the chickpea flour, turmeric, garlic powder or granules and salt. Gradually whisk in 230ml cold water, ensuring there are no lumps, then leave to rest for 15 minutes.
Heat the oven to 230C (210C fan)/450F/gas 8. Roughly crush the cumin and coriander seeds, until broken up but not fully ground.
Make the dipping sauce by mixing all the ingredients in a small bowl.
Place a 20cm nonstick, ovenproof frying pan on a medium-high heat. Once hot, add three tablespoons of olive oil and leave to heat for a minute. Meanwhile, whisk the last tablespoon of oil into the batter.
Add the crushed spices to the pan, let them sizzle lightly in the oil for 30 seconds, then pour the batter into the centre – it should sizzle. Sprinkle over the corn and spring onions, then bake for 25 minutes, until golden and crisp around the edges. Remove, leave to sit for a minute, then turn out on to a board. Cut into wedges and serve at once with the dipping sauce and mint leaves.
- 
  Alexina Anatole is the author of the Small Wins Substack and Sweet: the Secret to the Best Desserts, published by Square Peg at £27. To order a copy for £24.30, go to guardianbookshop.com.

Burnham urged to tackle inequality with policies including wealth tax
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
05:00:01 UTC
14:00:01 KST

Andy Burnham should tackle inequality in the UK by introducing a wealth tax, universal free personal social care and bringing gas and electricity networks under public ownership, according to a report from more than a dozen influential thinkers.
In the lead-up to the first budget of the chancellor, John Healey, this autumn, the Compass thinktank has collated 70 policy options from 15 leftwing thinkers that they argue would deliver on the prime minister’s promise to end 40 years of neoliberalism.
Introducing the report, Ending Business as Usual, Michael Jacobs, a former adviser to Gordon Brown, and Neal Lawson, director of Compass and a close friend of Burnham, praise what they call the prime minister’s “invaluable aura of authenticity”.
However, they warn that while he has ambitious plans “there is no guarantee that he will be given any longer to deliver results than his immediate predecessor”. The authors argue that it is “simply not the case that a British government can no longer govern from the left of centre”.
Among the policy proposals, which the organisation states is “a menu of policy options, not a manifesto”, are a £50,000 cap on political donations, the abolition of the House of Lords and an immediate cost of living package.
The plans also include a raft of far-reaching tax policies, including the introduction of a wealth tax on net assets of more than £10m, which would raise about £24bn a year, according to Caitlin Boswell from Tax Justice UK.
Other mooted policy ideas include equalising capital gains tax with income tax, which would raise a further £11.3bn a year – enough “to fund the building of 90,000 new social homes”. The Institute for Fiscal Studies has argued such a move would risk lowering total tax revenue and investment, and lead wealthy individuals to move their money or leave the country.
The essay also calls for what it describes as the “regressive, outdated and unfair” council tax as well as stamp duty to be replaced with a proportional property tax, noting such a move would result in 23% of households – concentrated in London and the south-east – paying more.
“If the new Labour government is serious about rebuilding public confidence and delivering material improvements to people’s lives, it must be prepared to address one of the structural causes of inequality: a tax system that favours wealth over work,” writes Boswell.
Suggested social policy changes in England include introducing free personal social care, paid for by a surcharge on income tax rates for people aged over 40, and a contribution from housing wealth. Sebastian Rees, from the Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR) argues that personal care needs, such as washing, dressing and eating should be covered by the state with accommodation or ordinary living costs, remaining the responsibility of the individual and their family, a model currently in place in Scotland.
Stating that a 1% surcharge on income tax for the over-40s would raise between £8bn and £9bn, it also argues that care costs could be secured against a property and recovered after sale or death. This would “would allow housing wealth to contribute to the cost of reform without requiring people to sell their home when they first need care,” says Rees. Elsewhere, the report calls for universal free childcare, which it argues would “boost the economy, support children’s development, help families and promote gender equality”.
Chris Hayes, from Common Wealth, calls for government-owned companies to be put in charge of running energy networks, as well as the setting up of regional energy boards, while the director of politics at Green Alliance, Holly Brazier Tope, argues for a climate resilience standard for critical infrastructure.
Michael Jacobs, professor of political economy at the University of Sheffield, said Burnham and his chancellor must resist pressure to conform to the “moderation and orthodoxy” that he argues ended the tenures of Keir Starmer and Rachel Reeves.
“There are a wealth of alternatives,” he says. “As Burnham knows, the public is disillusioned with politics and angry with their politicians. He does not have long to prove to voters that, when he says he wants to end business as usual, he means it.”

Europeans want a united Europe but question whether it can get there, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
05:00:01 UTC
14:00:01 KST

Europeans overwhelmingly want a strong, united and independent Europe but question whether it can get there, according to a study that suggests a continent-wide crisis of confidence is creating fertile ground for far-right narratives of decline.
The report, based on 5,800 interviews in France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Poland and the UK and analysis of the way Europe is discussed in the politics and media of 15 countries, paints a picture of an ambitious but disillusioned public.
It found that 68% of respondents spoke about Europe in terms of a “general deterioration or loss of normality”, compared with just 12% who said they viewed the present moment as a time of “European awakening and renewal”.
Many recognised the major challenges facing Europe, including war (43%), economic pressures (33%) and the need for greater international autonomy (29%). But 74% said Europe was not dealing well with them, and 56% believed its future was “in danger”.
The problem is not lack of ambition: an overwhelming 73% of respondents harbour a strong European vision of unity and political integration (35%), peace and security (28%) or prosperity (19%), while only 13% hope for “less Europe” or EU dissolution.
For many, said the study’s author, Paweł Zerka, a senior fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations (ECFR) thinktank, the problem was “not that they’ve stopped wanting a stronger Europe, but that they no longer believe it’s achievable”.
The result, Zerka added, was an “imagination gap. People can picture the kind of Europe they want, but struggle to imagine a credible path from where it is today to where they want it to be. These are matters of policy, not just communication.”
A week before the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, is due to deliver her annual “state of the union” address in Brussels, Zerka said the evidence suggested the bloc needed “fewer grand promises” and more “proof of trajectory”.
The study cites dozens of conversations with Europeans. “I’m regularly relieved I live in Europe. It’s not perfect and some things are going in the wrong direction, but no region in the world is safer, freer and more democratic,” one German said.
However, while he identified the climate crisis and far-right parties as the continent’s greatest challenges, he said they were not being tackled effectively. “Elections focus too much on the here and now, and not enough on the future,” he said.
The respondent said he would like Europe in 20 years’ time to be “free, democratic, sustainable, less indebted, politically further to the left [and] peaceful”. Asked whether he thought that was likely to happen, he said: “No.”
The study classed Europe’s voters in four categories. The Positives (19%) are staunch pro-Europeans who view current crises as a catalyst for a stronger, more integrated union. The Negatives (39%) believe Europe’s best days are behind it.
Almost half of people in France, Germany and Italy – and almost all who voted for radical-right parties such as Germany’s AfD, France’s RN, the Dutch PVV and Reform UK – were Negatives, with 83% speaking of Europe in terms of loss and decline.
The Disconnected (12%) are generally apathetic voters for whom EU integration is distant background noise, and the Uncertain (31%) share pro-European values but doubt the continent’s ability to act decisively, keep citizens safe or uphold its values.
Almost a third (32%) of respondents across all countries surveyed mentioned “Europe’s slowness” in their responses. As one young Polish citizen, born in the 2000s, put it bluntly: “The EU fundamentally discusses a lot, but does nothing.”
The bloc’s failure to stand its ground when confronted by powerful actors was also a recurring theme, mentioned by almost a third (30%) of all respondents, with the EU’s recent tariff concessions to Donald Trump a particularly humiliating symbol.
Zerka said the Uncertain group was key to the future trajectory of Europe. “Leaders tend to preach to the Positives or bow down to the Negatives,” he said, but it “is among the ‘uncertain’ where belief in Europe’s future remains up for grabs.”
Unlike hardened Eurosceptics, Uncertain voters retain a strong emotional attachment to the European project, the report argues, but are alienated by institutional inertia, bureaucratic slowness and perceived geopolitical weakness.
Winning back those doubters would require politicians to demonstrate that collective European action can solve tangible domestic crises, from energy security and defence to climate change and the cost of living crisis, Zerka said.

====================================================================================================

European democracies are running out of time to turn away from the abyss | Rafael Behr
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
05:00:01 UTC
14:00:01 KST

Not all that long ago, Europe was a beacon of liberal idealism. One memoir recalls it as an era “comfortably saturated with confidence in the unfailing and binding power of tolerance and conciliation”. The economic system seemed obviously preferable to barbarous alternatives. “People honestly believed that the divergencies and the boundaries between nations and sects would gradually melt away into a common humanity,” the author added.
Those words could describe the spirit of globalisation at the turn of the millennium. They were written in the 1930s by Stefan Zweig, reflecting on the optimism of late 19th-century Vienna from the perspective of a Jewish émigré whose world had been destroyed by murderous nationalism. Zweig took his own life in 1942. He never saw fascism defeated. He couldn’t have imagined a renaissance of liberalism in the second half of the 20th century so complete as to attain a pitch of complacency rivalling the one he remembered from his childhood.
Now momentum is with the nationalists again. Victory for the Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) in the region of Saxony-Anhalt over the weekend is not the biggest electoral prize won by a far-right party in Europe in recent years, but it is one of the most shocking because it is Germany. No country had more to learn from history if it wanted to immunise its democracy against extremism. None pursued a more systematic programme of inoculation. The word for it is Vergangenheitsbewältigung – hard to say and tricky to translate, meaning roughly coming to terms with a shameful past.
There is no excuse of ignorance about the AfD’s rise. It is a knowing repudiation of atonement. The party flirts with Nazi imagery and embraces racist definitions of nationhood, seeking to deport Germans whose credentials it sees as biologically improper. It is extreme enough to induce squeamishness in Marine Le Pen, leader of France’s far-right National Rally (RN). She has spent years carefully cultivating respectability and is leading the polls ahead of next year’s presidential election. She doesn’t want to jeopardise her mainstream credentials by association with the unambiguous extreme.
That is less of an impediment across the Atlantic. Elon Musk is an AfD fan, deploying his control of X to boost the party’s campaign messages. Last year, the US vice-president, JD Vance, met Alice Weidel, AfD co-leader, during a visit to Munich. There was no space in his diary for Olaf Scholz, then the German chancellor. Clearly, the AfD meets the criteria for endorsement set out in Donald Trump’s national security strategy, which pledges support for “patriotic resistance” movements committed to halting the “civilisational erasure” of Europe by immigration.
In Britain, Nigel Farage could once have assumed entitlement to that status as an early and enthusiastic cheerleader for Trump. But in the competition for Maga accolades, Reform UK has lost ground to parties and people even further to the right – Rupert Lowe’s Restore Britain; ultra-nationalist agitator Tommy Robinson; pretty much anyone who can muster a mob of blackshirts or a passing troll who catches Musk’s eye posting racist conspiracy theories online.
It would be absurd if it wasn’t so effective. “We never fall into the same abyss twice,” writes Éric Vuillard, the French novelist. “But we fall in the same way, in a mixture of ridicule and dread.”
The reach and pungency of the US right, drenched in white supremacism, interferes with Farage’s old strategy of banking far-right support and feinting moderation to make gains in the mainstream. Chasing credibility with fanatical racists in an international digital arena makes it hard to reassure a domestic analogue audience that he should be allowed near Downing Street.
The tension shows in Farage’s attitude to the AfD. He spoke at a rally for it in 2017. Now he describes it as a “mixed bag” of a party, whose cultural stances are “utterly respectable and decent” but whose enthusiasm for dictators is “very difficult”.
Farage has called AfD support for Vladimir Putin “hard to understand”. It can’t be that far beyond comprehension for a man who, in 2014, described the Russian president as the world leader he most admired, albeit “as an operator, not a human being”.
If Farage needs further insight into what might motivate a Kremlin fellow traveller, he could reach out to Reform’s former leader in Wales, Nathan Gill, who is serving a prison sentence for accepting bribes to make pro-Russian speeches in the European parliament when he was a Brexit party MEP.
Proximity to the Moscow line is a fairly reliable measure of fanaticism and venality on the spectrum from far-right to even further-right politics in Europe and the US. The same applies on the left, where a credulous appetite for Russian propaganda endures decades after the demise of Soviet ideology.
Thankfully, there is not much of a market in British politics for openly pandering to Putin. That is one reason why Trump is also unpopular, although opinion polls suggest he is viewed more favourably by Reform supporters than the wider public. Farage has stopped boasting of his White House connections, perhaps because they have dried up, or maybe because sycophantic flapping around a foreign tyrant, even an American one, doesn’t project strength in a wannabe prime minister.
It is striking how little the Reform leader has to say about the rest of the world and Britain’s place in it. The topic was hardly mentioned at the party’s annual conference last week.
There was a theatrical appearance by Jordan Bardella, the young Le Pen protege and likely prime minister if she wins the presidency. He signed a legally meaningless “deal” with Farage on stopping small-boat traffic across the Channel and was immediately criticised back home for selling out to the UK. The likelihood of a French far-right government taking in more migrants as a policy favour to the UK is close to zero. Having xenophobic nationalists setting the agenda in Paris and London wouldn’t make relations easier, no matter what ideological amity they now claim.
As the architect of Brexit, Farage is one of the most consequential politicians of his generation, but he can’t plausibly claim it as an achievement, even when addressing an auditorium of loyal fans. They know it has failed as well as everyone else.
Farage probably misses the simplicity of his old crusade against Brussels. He might envy nationalist counterparts on the continent, who get to rail against liberal Europeanism while enjoying the economic and strategic privileges afforded by EU membership. They don’t have to explain why it’s so cold on the outside. They play the Eurosceptic game, mobilising the same resentments, targeting the same scapegoats, but modifying the demands in recognition that Farage’s victory was pyrrhic. It doesn’t pay to actually leave. The ambition is to capture the European project, not destroy it, although it amounts to the same thing if the transformation happens through connivance with Maga ideology and Kremlin money.
This doesn’t have to be Europe’s destiny. Nationalists do not form a monolithic bloc. The essence of their creed militates against cross-border partnership. Their egos generate more rivalries than alliances. Their selfishness sabotages deals. Countervailing forces can be mustered. There is no law of history that says a height of liberal optimism must be followed by an equivalent fall into chaos. The “binding power of tolerance and conciliation” was not defeated in the 20th century and it won’t be suffocated in this one either. We see the abyss. We can pass without plunging to the bottom.
- 
  Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnist

Birdwatch: the avian equivalent of a catwalk model, blue cranes are under threat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
05:00:01 UTC
14:00:01 KST

Few birds are quite as elegant as the blue crane. As I watched a pair feeding alongside a busy road in South Africa, against the rather incongruous backdrop of a herd of cows, I was struck by their sheer beauty. With a slender body, curved neck, long legs, elongated tail plumes and a subtle, dove-grey plumage, this bird really is the avian equivalent of a catwalk model.
But not all is well for the blue crane. It has the smallest global range of any of the world’s 15 crane species: apart from an isolated population in Namibia, almost all are found in South Africa, where it is celebrated as the national bird.
Once common and widespread, blue crane numbers have fallen steadily over the past 50 years, and today between only 25,000 and 46,000 individuals remain in the wild. If the downward trend continues, this species faces a genuine risk of extinction.
The reasons for the decline are tediously predictable. As a grassland specialist, when intensive farming takes over, the food supply is inevitably reduced. A lethal cocktail of threats, including illegal poisoning, disturbance, habitat loss and the climate crisis – which this year brought unseasonably early rains followed by drought – mean that its future is far from rosy.
But as I watched these beautiful birds, I could forget about their plight for a few moments and quietly rejoice in their exquisite grace.

Rental prices in Lithuania keep rising, with no sign of relief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

Rents in Lithuania have risen among the fastest in the EU over the past 15 years, with only Estonia recording a larger increase, according to Eurostat data.
Estate agents say the profile of the ideal tenant has remained largely unchanged for years. Single women are considered the easiest tenants to place, while people with young children or pets face a much harder time finding a home.
There are fewer flats available than people looking to rent, pushing prices up year after year. Autumn is the worst time to look for a property, as an influx of students into the major cities drives rents to their highest levels.
“In December and January, rents will ease by 5 to 10%. In the longer term, prices are still rising by at least 5 to 7% a year. They are not rising as sharply as sale prices. We have to acknowledge that sale prices are actually increasing by 12 to 15% a year,” says Marius Čiulada, an estate agent at Ober-Haus.
Eurostat data shows that rents in Lithuania more than doubled over the 15 years from 2010, rising by 177%. However, SEB bank economist Tadas Povilauskas says incomes have risen at a similarly rapid pace.
“We stand out in the European Union for the pace of growth, whether you look at 10 or 15 years. Rents and people’s incomes are still very closely linked. We are also among the leaders in terms of house price growth, and the two are closely related,” he explains.
At present, renting a flat of around 40 sq m in Vilnius costs about €600 a month on average. Prices are somewhat lower in other major cities.
“In Kaunas and Klaipėda, they are about 15-20% cheaper, respectively. Kaunas is slightly cheaper, while Klaipėda is another 10% cheaper. Kaunas attracts a lot of exchange students and has a large influx of students from abroad, so there is also quite a lot of co-living [a housing model in which residents have private rooms but share some facilities],” says an Ober-Haus estate agent.
Another trend is visible in Vilnius and the surrounding area: there is a particularly acute shortage of larger rental houses, which are sought mainly by families returning to Lithuania from abroad.
“It is no secret that there are many German brigade personnel with families, and that market is certainly very favourable to landlords when it comes to house rental prices,” says Justina Zabarauskienė, an estate agent at Capital.
Rents are expected to fall slightly in the near future, as is usual when the heating season begins. But economist Tadas Povilauskas says rental prices will continue to rise in the future, as people’s incomes increase as well.

‘It’s like a death sentence’ says British widow facing deportation from Sweden
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

A 78-year-old British widow facing deportation over from Sweden over Brexit has said she feels she is facing a “death sentence” just hours before she was due to be removed from the country.
“I just want this nightmare to go away before I die,” says Joyce Thomas. “It is dragging me down. I am really not the same person I was. This has taken years. I just feel sick,” she adds as she packs her bags.
Thomas, a retired nurse, who has lived in Sweden for 22 years, was given four weeks to leave the country in August, separating her from her son, grandchildren, large network of friends, her church and her husband’s grave.
Her husband, Gwynne, died in 2023 of cancer. It was on a trip back from the UK in 2022, when they visited their second son in Brighton, that they first learned they should have made a formal application to stay in Sweden after Brexit.
Her subsequent application to stay in the country in 2023 missed the official deadline but she said her husband who looked after all the household administration, had previously been told there was nothing the couple needed to do after Brexit.
She was first told to leave the country in November and after an appeal received the news in August that the administrative court in Luleå upheld Sweden’s migration agency decision that she could not stay.
The migration agency says that simply not knowing she had to apply to stay by the cutoff date at the end of 2021 was not a “reasonable ground” for staying in the country.
So Thomas had little choice on Monday: she got up at 6am to thoroughly clean her flat, cook for supporters that night, and pack her bags for the UK.
Then, late on Monday evening, she was advised that she could stay pending a late application by a lawyer for a review of the removal order.
However, her plight remains the same with the threat of a deportation merely in abeyance.
“I am very stressed,” she says kneeling over two suitcases beside Tia, a collie lent to her for company in the past few weeks by a friend.
“I just want this nightmare to go before I die. I need a peaceful life at my time of life. This is what I want. I just want to get up and be normal,” says Thomas.
Thomas is one of hundreds, potentially thousands of Britons who have either been told to leave voluntarily or removed forcibly through deportation since Brexit.
Last week the migration agency confirmed it had already deported 458 including one 34-year-old who had been in the country since he was 10. Another British businessman was taken into detention last week in Stockholm to be deported.
“I just wish one of those people [in the authorities] had parents in my situation. I think they would think twice because it is the worst think they can do to a human being,” says Thomas.
She appealed to the European Commission and the Swedish government to intervene not just for her but for all the British citizens who have simply made “a mistake” because they did not know Sweden required a formal application to remain after Brexit.
“Please, please can you hear us. We have done nothing wrong. We are not criminals,” she says. “People here are suffering mentally, physically.
“It is cruel. It is inhumane. They must read the papers to know that I am really low. I just feel sick.”
No British minister has said anything about Britons being deported from Sweden since the controversy erupted, apart from the former business secretary Peter Kyle who appealed to the Swedish government on behalf of Thomas’s son, who lives in the constituency next to his.
Her local MP, Håkan Svenneling, raised her case in the Swedish parliament, claiming the controversy is damaging relations between the EU and the UK, while the opposition Centre party has vowed to offer a repreive to Britons with new laws if it gets into power after Sunday’s general election.
She says she has been a brilliant “actor” and gives people the impression she is coping but that is far from the truth.
“This waiting month by month, year by year is like a death sentence. That is how I feel because I am not getting a clear answer [about my future] and I am in limbo all the time.
“At the start of this I was ready to take my life because I was so depressed. I am coping now with a lot of help from good people but it is still hard. Inside I am not coping at all.”
Sweden is among 13 countries, along with the UK, that opted for a “constitutive” system requiring citizens to formally apply to remain in the country. Others, like Spain, opted for a less onerous “declaratory” system requiring registration in the country, something many Britons would already have done at their town hall.
But campaigners at Brits in Sweden say countless British citizens were either given no information or incorrect information about what to do after Brexit by the authorities.
“All I did was make a mistake, a mistake,” says Thomas. “Even with a parking fine they give you notice if you have not paid the fine; why didn’t they tell us we had to apply, and send us a reminder? We got nothing, never mind a reminder.”
The migration agency has said it had no mandate to contact British citizens on the population register to tell them what to do.
Under the withdrawal agreement late applications for permits to remain resident after Brexit were permitted as long as there were “reasonable grounds”.
On Friday the Swedish migration agency told the Guardian it had “no indication” that Sweden had in any way interpreted the withdrawal agreement in an extreme manner or differently from other member states. “The Swedish migration agency has applied applicable law, and there has been an opportunity to appeal rejection decisions,” it said.

Can Ukraine’s newly shown Koral become home-built answer to Patriot? Expert evaluates system displayed at Poland’s MSPO expo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

Ukraine's newly shown Koral missile could become a home-built answer to the Patriot in addition to the "Freya" project. However, the system has yet to prove it can stop Russian ballistic missiles, Ivan Kyrychevsky, an arms expert at Defense Express and a soldier in the 413th REID regiment of the Unmanned Systems Forces, said on a YouTube broadcast.
Currently, the PAC-3 version of the Patriot is the only weapon in Ukraine's arsenal that reliably stops Russia's maneuvering Iskander ballistic missiles, and its interceptors are scarce, costly, and rationed for Ukraine by the US.
But in the podcast, Kyrychevsky places Koral, on the data available so far, at roughly the older PAC-2 level. A PAC-2-class interceptor can handle aircraft and simpler ballistic targets, yet it is not the ideal tool against the fast, maneuvering Iskander and Kinzhal that do the most damage. That leaves Koral a hedge against dependence, not a replacement.
The missile sits a tier below Patriot
Kyrychevsky based the judgment on photos released at the expo. The Koral missile lacks the gas-dynamic surfaces that would let it maneuver in flight, he said, and it carries a different warhead from the "hit-to-kill" round on the PAC-3. He did not treat that as disqualifying.
"We are in a situation where we do not just need means against ballistics, but means of at least some technological level," he said.
Cost tilts Ukraine toward its own missile
The economics push in the same direction. A PAC-3 interceptor runs about $10 million for export, and Kyrychevsky noted that even the US Army finds the missiles expensive to spend at the rate the fighting around Iran has demanded.
"We are better off building our own analog of the Patriot, even a mediocre one, than staying dependent on the regularity of external deliveries," he believes.
Winter still hinges on the Patriot
For all that, Kyrychevsky was blunt about the near term. Koral still needs to be tested against Russian ballistic missiles, even experimentally, to confirm its claimed performance, and power cuts at the plants that build it could slow production.
“My assessment for now is roughly this: hopefully, we’ll be able to put the ‘Koral’ to the test against Russian ballistic missiles on an experimental basis," he said.
This winter, he said, Ukraine will need Patriot interceptors regardless of whether it develops its own. Work on Koral began in 2016, and the system was first shown in 2021, a fast pace for a weapon of its kind, and a separate European project, Freya, is advancing on a parallel track.
In July, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Ukraine, in cooperation with other European countries, was working on an anti-ballistic missile defense system called “Freya". It is intended to serve as a cheaper and more widely deployable alternative to Patriot air defense systems.
Zelenskyy noted that, in theory, Ukraine could develop “Freya” on its own, but doing so would take significantly more time — potentially years. The system would require not only a missile and launcher, but also radars, command-and-control systems, and many other components. Even with European partners, the process will not be quick.

Aircraft tracking website FlightRadar24 said 177 flights scheduled for Wednesday had already been axed, following 1,300 cancellations to and from UK airports on Tuesday.
Nearly all the flights cancelled on Wednesday were at Britain's busiest airport Heathrow in London, FlightRadar24 wrote on X.
The National Air Traffic Services (NATS) said late on Tuesday it was still working to resolve disruption following a "system issue."
"Work is continuing to assist airlines and airports recover from today's disruption," NATS posted on X.
"This has been a very complex recovery and has created difficulties for the whole aviation network, from which it will take time to recover."
Heathrow said late on Tuesday that departures had resumed, after the "technical issue" forced the airport to suspend arrivals the same day.
But it warned that "disruption is expected to continue," asking passengers in an X post to check with their airline before travelling to the airport.
NATS said earlier it had "resolved" the glitch that caused the disruption and was "working as hard as possible to clear the backlog of flights."
"We know this is hugely frustrating and apologise unreservedly," the organisation wrote on X.
Tuesday's chaos follow a technical glitch in July last year that saw scores of flights to and from the UK cancelled, prompting anger from airline chiefs.

Irish budget carrier Ryanair said more than 65,000 of its passengers had been disrupted and it had cancelled more than 50 flights.
Arsenal, due to play Napoli in the Champions League in the southern Italian city on Wednesday, were forced to cancel a news conference ahead of the match after the team's flight was delayed.
British Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said on X she was "seeking assurances that lessons will be learned and systems that support aviation are up to the job."
But Ryanair COO Neal McMahon repeated his calls for NATS chief executive Martin Rolfe to be fired, accusing him of having again "failed UK travellers."
"Enough is enough, it's time for the UK government to intervene...and put somebody in charge who can do the job."
