Croatia on wheels: the great Adriatic motorhome route
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
04:00:35 UTC
13:00:35 KST

On a 25-day road trip we travel along a coastline of striking contrasts, from Roman cities and Venetian towns to pebble beaches, islands and roads overlooking some of Europe's most spectacular scenery.
Travelling by motorhome lets you move at the pace of the landscape and stop in places that would probably never make it onto a conventional itinerary.
We set off from Rovinj, in the north of the Istrian peninsula, heading for Dubrovnik at the southernmost tip of the country. Along the way you pass a succession of historic towns, national parks, fishing villages, fortresses and islands, with the Adriatic as a constant backdrop.
But travelling Croatia on four wheels is not always straightforward. The coastal road is, in places, narrow and winding. And you cannot park the motorhome just anywhere: you have to rely on campsites and authorised areas, which are sometimes a long way from the historic centres and, on occasions, charge eye-watering prices.
In high season, especially in July and August, the problem only gets worse. That is why spring, early summer or autumn can be a better time to set off on this route.
Istria: Croatia's most Italian side
The journey begins in Rovinj, one of Istria's must-visit towns. Its historic centre of narrow, cobbled streets stands on what was once an island and is dominated by the church of St Euphemia. Colourful facades, the harbour and the small islands scattered just off the coast make the town one of the most recognisable sights on the Croatian Adriatic.
Further south lies Pula, at the southern tip of Istria. The city combines crystal-clear waters with one of Croatia's greatest Roman legacies. Pula Arena, built in the first century AD, is one of the six largest surviving Roman amphitheatres in the world. Today its stands host concerts, festivals and shows, weaving antiquity into contemporary cultural life.
A tour of Pula also takes in the Arch of the Sergii on the main street, the Gate of Hercules and the Kaštel fortress. This 17th-century Venetian castle stands on a hilltop and offers sweeping views over the harbour and the city's rooftops.
Istria stands apart from the rest of the Croatian coast. The heart-shaped peninsula is divided between Croatia, Slovenia and Italy and retains a strong Italian influence. Its green hills, vineyards, olive groves, forests and medieval hill towns have earned it the nickname 'the Tuscany of the Adriatic'. Inland, hilltop towns such as Motovun command the views. However, the lack of suitable facilities for motorhomes forced us to leave it off our itinerary.
From the elegance of Opatija to the lakes of Plitvice
After covering much of Istria, our next stop was Opatija, very different from the rest of the coast. Here grand villas, historic hotels and gardens dominate, all steeped in Austro-Hungarian elegance. For decades it was one of the favourite retreats of the Austro-Hungarian aristocracy, drawn by its spas and mild climate.
The Lungomare, a seafront promenade of around ten kilometres, runs along the coast past villas, small coves and crystal-clear waters. The best way to enjoy it is to stroll slowly and stop in the various little nooks for a swim. It is also worth continuing as far as Volosko, a charming old fishing village.
From Opatija you can continue south along the coastal road beneath the Velebit mountains, in one of the most spectacular stretches of the journey. In our case we chose the motorway to reach Nin, near Zadar. There the scenery changes once again.
The compact historic centre of Nin sits on a tiny island surrounded by lagoons. The town preserves some of the oldest traces of Croatian history and its 9th-century Church of the Holy Cross is one of its main landmarks. It is traditionally known as the smallest cathedral in the world. Nin is also known for its sandy beaches, therapeutic mud and salt pans.
In Zadar, motorhomes have a harder time finding somewhere to park, but the visit is well worth the effort. Amid Roman and medieval remains, the seafront concentrates two of its main attractions: the Sea Organ, which turns the movement of the waves into sound through pipes installed beneath the stone steps, and the Greeting to the Sun, a circle of solar panels that lights up at dusk.
Sunset is Zadar's calling card. The phrase attributed to Alfred Hitchcock, who described it as the most beautiful in the world, has become part of the city's tourist lore. From here we left the blue of the Adriatic behind for a day to plunge into the greenery of Plitvice Lakes National Park.
Its 16 lakes, arranged in tiers at different levels and linked by rivers and waterfalls, form one of Croatia's most breathtaking natural landscapes. A UNESCO World Heritage Site, the park is the perfect counterpoint to the coast.
You explore it along footpaths and wooden boardwalks, with electric boats and internal vehicles used on some routes. The great waterfall, Veliki Slap, rises to about 78 metres and is the highest in Croatia. Although the turquoise water and the heat may tempt you in, swimming in the lakes is forbidden.
Šibenik, Trogir and the heart of Dalmatia
Back on the coast we reach Šibenik, a city of white stone, alleyways, staircases and small squares. St James's Cathedral, a World Heritage Site, was built entirely of stone and features an unusual frieze of 71 sculpted human heads, each one different. About 50 kilometres further on lies Trogir, a small island town that feels like Dalmatia in miniature.
The best thing to do is to lose yourself in its narrow stone streets before continuing to Split, the urban heart of the region. Split grew up around the vast palace of the Emperor Diocletian, built more than 1,700 years ago. Today its ancient walls, passageways and chambers form a living city centre where homes, shops, restaurants and cafe terraces all rub shoulders.
Its harbour is also one of the main gateways to the Adriatic islands, with ferries and catamarans to Brač, Hvar, Šolta and Vis. In high season passenger traffic is frantic and ticket prices can be steep. Croatia has more than 1,200 islands, although only around 60 are inhabited. On our trip we visited Korčula, Lopud and Lokrum, the latter just off Dubrovnik's old town and known for its small saltwater lake, the Dead Sea.
The Makarska Riviera and the Pelješac peninsula
Leaving Split, the road once again hugs the Adriatic and one of the most scenic sections of the journey begins: the Makarska Riviera. On one side lies the sea; on the other, the sheer Biokovo mountains. The distance between mountain and coast is minimal, and the bends offer some of the finest viewpoints on the road to Dubrovnik. Before reaching the walled city, we turn off towards the Pelješac peninsula.
Ston is one of its big surprises: a small town protected by a wall that climbs up the hillside, considered one of the most impressive defensive systems in Europe. Mali Ston Bay is famous for its oysters. Eating them freshly opened, raw and with a squeeze of lemon is one of the region's must-try food experiences.
After a stop at Prapratno beach, we continued to Orebić to board a boat to the island of Korčula. Its old town is laid out like a fishbone, a design intended to encourage air circulation and protect the streets from the winds. Korčula claims to be the birthplace of Marco Polo and his figure appears all over the town. Walls, towers and stone buildings recall centuries of Venetian rule.
Before leaving Pelješac, Žuljana offers a quieter reward: crystal-clear waters, mountains and coves with a distinctly Mediterranean feel. One useful tip for enjoying the sea: Croatian beaches are, with few exceptions, pebbly rather than sandy. It is worth bringing mats or airbeds, as locals do, and not forgetting water shoes.
Dubrovnik: The grand finale
The road to Dubrovnik marks the transition from a laid-back Croatia to its main tourist hotspot. After one last bend, the walled city comes into view, one of the most iconic sights on the Adriatic.
In high season thousands of visitors throng Stradun, the main thoroughfare, stopping at every corner to take photos. The city walls, cathedral and narrow lanes of the old town can be seen in a day, although spending three days lets you explore at a gentler pace and add a boat trip to one of the islands. A good option is to explore Dubrovnik at sunset, when many day-trippers have already left.
From Rovinj to Dubrovnik, Croatia changes face time and again. Istria brings its Italian heritage; Dalmatia, its stone-built cities and islands; Plitvice, its forests and waterfalls; and Dubrovnik, the great historical stage facing the sea. That variety, packed into a relatively compact coastline, explains why Croatia now competes with Europe's heavyweight tourist destinations and still offers far more than just sun and sea.

A European Central Bank rate hike is all but certain, the reasoning less so
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
04:00:01 UTC
13:00:01 KST

The European Central Bank is all but certain to raise interest rates on Thursday, with investors pricing the move at near-total probability, but the decision is more awkward than the numbers suggest as inflation is being driven almost entirely by energy with underlying pressures actually easing.
Frankfurt will almost certainly move on Thursday.
Market odds put a quarter-point hike at close to certainty, which would lift the European Central Bank's deposit rate from 2.25% to 2.5%.
What makes this a difficult call is not whether the ECB acts, but why, and whether the reasoning survives contact with the data.
The path here has been compressed as the ECB raised rates on 11 June for the first time in three years, lifting the deposit rate from 2% to 2.25% in response to the energy shock from the Iran war, and then held rates in July while Christine Lagarde pointed hawkishly towards September.
August's inflation figures removed any remaining doubt with eurozone inflation hitting 3.3%, up from 2.9% in July and the highest since September 2023, as energy inflation surged to 14.3% from 10.3%.
The inflation is not spreading
Look beneath the headline inflation and the picture inverts.
Core inflation, which strips out energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, actually fell to 2.4% from 2.5%. Services inflation, the component most closely tied to wages and domestic demand, dropped to 3% from 3.3%.
In other words, there is still little evidence that expensive energy is feeding through into everything else. That is what economists mean by "second-round effects", and their absence is the strongest argument against tightening.
The ECB's own research also supports the distinction.
In a paper published on Tuesday, ECB economists found that adverse energy supply factors, driven by geopolitical tensions, accounted for around 90% of the rise in energy inflation between January and May.
"This time the energy supply shock dominates, while demand and public policy stimulus have minor roles," the economists wrote, adding that "these differences are key to explaining why monetary policy responses differ."
The 2021-22 surge, by contrast, came from "a combination of large and unprecedented supply and demand-side factors," which is why the ECB then "raised interest rates forcefully and persistently" rather than gradually.
The national spread across the EU further underlines how uneven this is.
August inflation ran at 4.5% in Spain, 2.9% in Germany and 2.7% in France, three economies facing the same energy shock with very different results, all governed by one interest rate.
Economic growth is the other complication.
The eurozone has proved more resilient than expected, which ING attributes partly to luck, partly to Asian competitors suffering more from the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and partly to fiscal stimulus. However, resilience does not mean the growth could not, or should not, accelerate.
ING characterises Thursday's expected move as "another insurance rate hike", or "a dovish rate hike," noting that even at 2.5% the deposit rate sits within the range the ECB itself considers neutral.
Going further would mean deciding restrictive policy is required, which would be a different judgement entirely.
Everyone is looking to hike at the same time
The ECB is not acting alone, and that matters for the euro.
The Federal Reserve meets on 15 and 16 September, with Chair Kevin Warsh having used his first Jackson Hole address to argue that financial conditions are not restrictive and underlying inflation has not improved.
Investors had put the odds of a US hike at roughly one in three before those remarks, but now price a 60% chance the Fed hikes the target range from 3.5%-3.75% to 3.75%-4%.
The Bank of Japan follows on 17 and 18 September, with markets pricing an 80% to 90% chance of a move to 1.25%.
On the other hand, the Bank of England is expected to hold rates at 3.75% on 17 September as it currently maintains a much higher interest rate than the rest.
If the Fed were to hike while the ECB held, the dollar would strengthen against the euro and that would cut both ways for Frankfurt.
A weaker euro makes European exports more competitive, but it also makes imports dearer, and since oil and gas are priced in dollars, it would push up precisely the energy costs driving the inflation problem in the first place.
Overall, we can assume a September rate hike is a done deal for the ECB but we can also project that it won't solve the central bank's current dilemma of raising borrowing costs against an inflation it cannot reach, while withdrawing support an economy could still use.

From Oculus to Orbit: The Symbolism of the Circle in Architecture
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
04:00:00 UTC
13:00:00 KST

Throughout the history of architecture, the circle has been associated with multiple meanings—from the cosmic geometry of ancient temples and the oculus of classical buildings to the rose windows of Gothic cathedrals and the portholes of ships. However, in the 20th century, the circle acquired a new cultural meaning. As aviation, space exploration, and technological innovation transformed the way society imagined the future, circular forms began to evoke machines, spacecraft, capsules, and even new forms of habitation.
The use of circular geometry has endured over the centuries, acquiring new meanings and symbolizing new codes. To begin, we need only look back to the Roman Pantheon, which has been admired and studied for more than two millennia because of the monumental scale of its dome and its celestial geometry. Originally commissioned by Marcus Agrippa, it was inaugurated in 27 BCE. However, after a fire in 80 CE, its reconstruction was undertaken by Emperor Domitian. The building would burn again in 110 CE, and this time its new design was commissioned by Emperor Hadrian.
Conceived as a massive drum crowned by a dome, its interior creates a space bathed in natural light entering through a 9-meter-wide oculus, illuminating alternating triangular and rounded altars that define the perimeter of the room. The sphere established an analogy with the heavens, contained within the Pantheon's concrete walls. The cosmic implications of this geometry honored the gods and the heavens through its symbolic design while simultaneously glorifying the Roman Empire itself.
Related Article
Circular Openings: From Boats to Contemporary Architecture
Unlike the Roman oculus, the rose window in medieval architecture emerged around 1135, when Abbot Suger decided to begin construction of the new monumental entrance to the Abbey Church of Saint-Denis. As the Metropolitan Museum of Art explains in "The Royal Abbey of Saint-Denis in the Time of Abbot Suger (1122–1151)," the rose window was positioned below the crenellations and was the first known example of the element being integrated into the design of a church's western façade, although it would eventually become a defining feature of Gothic architecture. At Saint-Denis, the rose window opened onto an upper central chapel on the western side of the structure, from which it could also be seen from the eastern choir. A circular solar disk of this type was incorporated into the western apse wall of Worms, another of the Rhenish imperial basilicas. There, it framed the emperor when he sat on his throne at the western end of the nave.
But how did the circle in architecture eventually become associated with navigation, machinery, engineering, and mobility? As Colin Bisset explains, in the 16th century, King Henry VIII of England ordered the installation of new cannons on his warships. Because they were too large to be positioned at the bow or stern, openings had to be created along the sides of the ships to accommodate them. The French word porte, meaning door or opening, was used to describe these apertures until they eventually became known as portholes.
As circular openings cut into the exterior walls of ships, industrial chambers, aircraft, buildings, and even some spacecraft, portholes are commonly associated with naval construction, providing light and ventilation to interior spaces while being designed to withstand harsh marine environments. In architecture, however, the term refers more broadly to circular windows.
Unlike square openings, circular apertures offer greater structural integrity, which is why passenger ships can be equipped with portholes without compromising their structural stability or buoyancy. This also makes them ideal for applications exposed to extreme external pressure, which is why they are frequently found in submarines and space stations. In such cases, conventional glass can be replaced with high-tech, pressure-resistant materials such as acrylic or quartz.
Portholes gained wider popularity during the Art Deco period, and Le Corbusier's 1923 book Toward an Architecture encouraged architects to look to ships for design inspiration. In it, he developed the concept of the house as a "machine for living" and introduced the Modulor. Among the French architects who embraced round windows were Georges-Henri Pingusson, who used them during the 1920s, and Jean Prouvé, who incorporated them into the design of his prefabricated "Tropical House."
Clorindo Testa, meanwhile, built model ships from a very young age, and his passion for them would later be reflected in the design of the Naval Hospital in Buenos Aires. Designed around 1970 in collaboration with Héctor Lacarra and Juan Genoud, the building's formal appearance recalls a warship, with round windows arranged like the portholes of a vessel and even a rooftop water tank resembling a ship's control tower. However, this is not the only one of his works to feature portholes. The Mariano Moreno National Library, for example, combines large glazed openings with smaller windows—including portholes, square, and rectangular openings—creating different framed views of the exterior.
Thus, the early 20th century saw the circle acquire a new cultural meaning as Futurist architects began to conceive of buildings as dynamic, technological environments rather than static compositions. In 1914, Italian architect and urban planner Antonio Sant'Elia wrote the Manifesto of Futurist Architecture, emphasizing the movement's general principles and, among other ideas, proclaiming:
 "That Futurist architecture is the architecture of calculation, of audacious temerity and simplicity; the architecture of reinforced concrete, iron, glass, cardboard, textile fiber, and all substitutes for wood, stone, and brick, which make it possible to achieve maximum elasticity and lightness…"
In fact, films such as Jacques Tati's Mon Oncle satirized windows by making them resemble eyes, while highlighting the contrasts between two worlds, two ways of living, and two different ways of understanding the city and architecture in the late 1950s. While one world reflected a form of modernity fueled by futuristic optimism, the other represented the traditional city. As circular windows became associated with machines and technological spaces, they gradually acquired a futuristic meaning. Their aesthetic evolved throughout the 1920s and 1940s, reaching new heights during the Space Age of the 1950s through the 1970s.
As a renowned Futurist committed to developing innovative solutions to humanity's problems, Buckminster Fuller became a pioneer of sustainable design and renewable energy and later participated in Habitat I, the United Nations' first conference on human settlements. Around 1920, Fuller sought to create a self-sufficient, sustainable single-family home—the living machine of the future. Although the Dymaxion House was never built, its design demonstrated groundbreaking and influential innovations in prefabrication and sustainability. The house would not only have been exemplary in terms of self-sufficiency, but could also have been mass-produced, flat-packed, and shipped around the world. Its potential could have helped address the postwar housing shortage through the incorporation of new materials, sustainable technologies, and simplified assembly and mass-production processes.
However, in an era of rapid technological advances and groundbreaking achievements, the Space Age aesthetic transformed the modern worldview, leaving an indelible mark on architecture and interior design. The circle became increasingly associated with spacecraft, submarines, aircraft, and capsules, and as journeys beyond Earth's atmosphere began to be imagined, architecture responded by proposing new forms of habitation. Experimental architects and collectives such as Archigram challenged conventional notions of the building, the house, and the city, seeking to connect technology with human life and encourage new perspectives on the architectural profession.
For example, the Bolwoningen community in the Dutch city of Den Bosch emerged from a relatively unknown architectural experiment led by Dries Kreijkamp, who sought to introduce a new morphological solution for housing and establish a new residential typology. Built in 1984, this group of spherical houses with round windows challenged existing paradigms by experimenting with new ways of inhabiting space. Beyond the sustainable advantages offered by spherical structures in terms of assembly and prefabrication, as well as their low energy consumption and ease of maintenance, Kreijkamp argued that round forms represent the most organic form of living: "We live on a sphere, we are born out of a sphere…why not live in a sphere?"
Just as Archigram believed that life was moving at such a rapid pace that it became necessary to rethink new and diverse ways of inhabiting space, many contemporary architects are now reconsidering how they conceive and design architecture in response to today's context and users' needs. From the sacred and cosmic to the technological and futuristic, the symbolic meaning of the circle has continuously evolved throughout history, becoming integrated into the visual language of Futurism and speculative architecture through its associations with machines, vehicles, and the exploration of new worlds.
Architects, designers, and artists have progressively reinterpreted this ancient geometric form as a symbol of technological progress and life beyond conventional architectural boundaries. But does it still carry the same futuristic connotations today? Contemporary architecture continues to incorporate circular windows, cylindrical volumes, domes, and capsule-like spaces, but their symbolism has evolved. What was once associated with technological optimism and space exploration now evokes ideas of resilience, ecological systems, circular economies, alternative forms of habitation, and even a renewed relationship with the natural environment.
This article is part of the ArchDaily Topic: The Lure of Escapism in Architecture and Alternative Worlds. And, as always, at ArchDaily we welcome the contributions of our readers; if you want to submit an article or project, contact us.

Dark energy debunked? Cosmic acceleration may be an illusion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
03:59:08 UTC
12:59:08 KST

Dark energy debunked? Cosmic acceleration may be an illusion
- Date:
- September 8, 2026
- Source:
- University of Oxford
- Summary:
- A new analysis of more than 1,700 supernovae is questioning whether the universe is really accelerating at all. After accounting for the ages of the stars that produce these explosions, researchers found signs that cosmic expansion may actually be slowing. They also argue that the apparent acceleration changes with direction, which would be difficult to explain with dark energy. Other cosmologists dispute the conclusion, setting up a major test for upcoming observatories.
- Share:
A new analysis led by researchers at the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research, Mumbai, together with Professor Subir Sarkar of the University of Oxford, is challenging one of the central ideas in modern cosmology: that the universe is expanding at an accelerating rate because of "dark energy" associated with the quantum vacuum.
Their letter, published in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, argues that the evidence for cosmic acceleration may not be as strong as widely assumed. The conclusion is disputed. In the same issue of the journal, a separate paper co-authored by Professor Maria Vincenzi, also at the University of Oxford, concludes that observations continue to support an accelerating universe.
Reexamining More Than 1,700 Supernovae
Professor Sarkar, from Oxford's Rudolf Peierls Centre for Theoretical Physics, worked with Animesh Sah and Mohamed Rameez of the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research in India to revisit one of cosmology's most important collections of observational data. Their analysis focused on Pantheon+, a dataset containing observations of more than 1,700 Type Ia supernovae.
For more than 25 years, astronomers have relied on these exploding stars to track how the universe has expanded over time. Measurements of Type Ia supernovae were central to the discovery that the expansion of the universe appears to be speeding up, a breakthrough recognized with the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics.
The researchers examined the Pantheon+ observations while including a recently proposed correction related to the ages of the stars that eventually produce Type Ia supernova explosions. They also investigated whether the apparent acceleration looks the same in every direction, as the standard cosmological model assumes.
"There is increasing evidence that the brightness of Type Ia supernovae depends on the age of the stars they come from," said Professor Subir Sarkar of Oxford's Rudolf Peierls Centre for Theoretical Physics, a co-author of the study. "If this effect is not accounted for, it can lead to the erroneous conclusion that the expansion rate is accelerating."
A Universe That May Be Slowing Down
Once the researchers applied the stellar age correction, they found that the observations no longer favored a universe undergoing uniform acceleration. Their analysis instead indicates that, overall, cosmic expansion may be slowing rather than speeding up.
The team also examined whether the apparent acceleration could be anisotropic. In other words, they asked whether the effect varies depending on the direction in which it is measured. Such a result would conflict with the standard cosmological assumption that the universe behaves similarly in every direction on large scales.
Sarkar and his colleagues argue that if the apparent acceleration is directional, dark energy could not be responsible for it. In their interpretation, an effect produced by the quantum vacuum should not vary from one direction to another.
"We found that the inferred acceleration is directed mainly along the direction that we are moving locally, as indicated by the hotspot in the cosmic microwave background, and dies away with distance," explains Professor Sarkar. "This is unaffected by the correction to the supernova brightness - so rejects dark energy independently of whether the correction is applied or not. The correction turns the isotropic component into a deceleration - which again rules out dark energy."
Cosmologists Remain Divided
The findings challenge the prevailing view that the universe continues to expand at an accelerating rate, the conclusion associated with the Nobel Prize-winning discovery announced more than two decades ago.
However, other researchers examining the same broader question have reached a different conclusion. A paper published in the same journal issue and co-authored by Professor Maria Vincenzi of the University of Oxford argues that the available evidence still supports ongoing cosmic acceleration.
She comments: "The lead authors of our study are world experts in understanding how the environments of Type Ia supernovae affect cosmological measurements with more than a decade of experience in both supernova astrophysics and galaxy evolution. Our recent findings provide further confidence in the cosmological framework that has emerged over the past three decades and allow the research community to focus on one of the biggest unanswered questions in physics: the nature of dark energy itself."
Rubin Observatory Could Help Settle the Debate
Both interpretations will soon face a much larger observational test. Data from the Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) are expected to provide measurements of hundreds of thousands of supernovae.
That enormous new sample should give cosmologists a powerful opportunity to test whether the universe is truly accelerating, whether the apparent effect varies with direction, and what role, if any, dark energy plays in shaping the expansion of the cosmos.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Oxford. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal References:
- Animesh Sah, Mohamed Rameez, Subir Sarkar. Pantheon supernovae corrected for progenitor age indicate the universe is decelerating. Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, 2026; 549 (3) DOI: 10.1093/mnras/stag844
- Phil Wiseman, Brodie Popovic, Mark Sullivan, Adam G Riess, Dan Scolnic, Rebecca C Chen, Tamara M Davis, Lluís Galbany, Isobel M Hook, Saurabh W Jha, Lisa Kelsey, Yukei S Murakami, Mickaël Rigault, Benjamin M Rose, Brian Schmidt, Mat Smith, Maria Vincenzi. Still accelerating: type Ia supernova cosmology is robust to host galaxy age evolution. Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, 2026; 549 (3) DOI: 10.1093/mnras/stag797

But the two single-seat F-16Cs, numbered 6727 and 6728, apparently did not leave Hawaii, with witnesses saying they taxied towards the runway before returning to the apron.

Neither the US side nor Taiwan’s air force has publicly explained why the aircraft have been held up for so long, fuelling speculation among military and aviation enthusiasts that technical problems might have emerged.

US pursues deportees abroad for hundreds of millions in unpaid fines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
03:54:00 UTC
12:54:00 KST

US pursues deportees abroad for hundreds of millions in unpaid fines
- The US government is hiring private firms to recover over US$423 million in fines from more than 66,300 deported migrants in Mexico, Honduras, and Guatemala.
- Legal and practical challenges exist, as deportees may lack resources or access to US payment systems, and foreign governments like Mexico are not involved.
- The fines are part of a broader Trump-era strategy to penalise immigrants, with potential effects on future immigration cases and ongoing efforts to enforce payments.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – The Trump administration is hiring private contractors to track down deported migrants who it claims owe the US government hundreds of millions of dollars in unpaid penalties, a move that will test how far its immigration crackdown can reach across borders.
US Customs and Border Protection says it is trying to recover about US$423 million (S$534.92 million) in fines and fees from more than 66,300 people who have been removed from the US.
In August, the agency agreed to pay as much as US$36 million to four firms to find people in Mexico, Honduras and Guatemala it claims are in arrears, according to a notice posted on a government procurement website.
The initiative marks a striking expansion of US President Donald Trump’s immigration enforcement efforts that would extend the government’s power over people it has already expelled from the US.
However, collecting could be challenging.
It’s unclear whether the US can legally require people who have been removed from the country to pay.
The contract notice doesn’t explain how the US could compel payments or what role, if any, the governments of Mexico, Honduras and Guatemala would have.
Mexico’s immigration agency said that it’s not involved in the initiative.
“It’s beyond the responsibilities of the Mexican government, for which reason the country’s authorities in the National Institute of Migration do not participate or have knowledge of it,” the agency said in response to questions on Sept 8.
It’s also far from certain whether deportees would be able to pay what the US says they owe.
Many may have limited resources or lack access to a US bank account, which is required to pay the fines, according to payment methods described in federal documents.
In past cases, the US has threatened that unpaid fines could affect future immigration cases.
The contractors may photograph homes or obtain utility bills, employment records or court papers to locate deportees and establish their ability to pay, according to the contract documents.
CBP awarded the two-year contracts in August to Global Recovery Group, The Baptiste Group, Caduceus Inc and Response AI Solutions, according to federal records.
Each agreement has a maximum value of US$9 million.
The companies didn’t respond to requests for comment.
The amount CBP is trying to collect represents only a small portion of the larger pool of penalties imposed by the US Department of Homeland Security.
From Trump’s return to office on Jan 20, 2025, through July 16, 2026, Immigration and Customs Enforcement, DHS’s enforcement arm, issued more than 103,000 civil fines totalling more than US$84 billion, according to DHS.
By July 16, the government had collected just US$1.2 million.
“Our message is clear: Illegal aliens in the country unlawfully should leave now or face consequences – including financial penalties,” DHS said in a statement.
The fines are based in part on a provision of a 1996 immigration law that allows the government to impose daily penalties on certain people who refuse to leave after being ordered deported.
The authority was rarely used until Trump’s first term, when his administration sent large bills to immigrant families.
The previous administration of President Joe Biden ended that effort in 2021, saying it had proved ineffective and diverted resources from other enforcement priorities.
Trump has now revived the penalties on a far broader scale.
Some immigrants can be fined nearly US$1,000 for every day they remain in the country after being ordered to leave.
Charges can accumulate into the hundreds of thousands, or even millions, of dollars.
US$1 million bills
The fines are part of a wider strategy intended to make remaining in the US increasingly difficult and expensive.
The administration has filed lawsuits to collect unpaid penalties, seized tax refunds and withheld money from wages.
Some immigrants still pursuing legal claims to remain in the US have received bills of US$1 million or more.
At the same time, the government is offering incentives to people who agree to leave.
Immigrants who register through CBP Home, a mobile-phone application used to arrange voluntary departures, can receive paid travel and cash-in-hand from the government.
Homeland Security has said certain outstanding fines may also be forgiven.
Some deportees are already receiving bills.
Mexican citizens deported in 2026 have received collection letters from CBP at their addresses in Mexico, said Juan Cuellar Torres, director of advocacy at the Kino Border Initiative, a humanitarian organisation that works along the US-Mexico border.
The fines, typically about US$250, came with a warning that interest could accrue if they were not paid, he said.
The notices also warned that unpaid debts could be considered in future US immigration proceedings, a potentially significant consequence for deportees who later want to apply for a visa or seek permission to return.
They also warned the debts could be turned over to a private collection agency.
David Leopold, an immigration lawyer in Cleveland, called the overseas effort unnecessarily punitive.
“Going into these countries and pursuing folks who have been deported is just one more step in terrorising people for no reason,” Leopold said. “It’s icing on the cake of cruelty.” BLOOMBERG

Diplomat rejects US allegations of Chinese companies copying US AI technology
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
03:52:43 UTC
12:52:43 KST

WASHINGTON, September 9. /TASS/. Beijing strongly rejects US allegations that Chinese companies use knowledge distillation to copy US artificial intelligence (AI) products, Liu Chang, spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Washington, told TASS.
"The US side’s hyping of the so-called ‘distillation’ concept is a deliberate attack on China’s development and progress in the AI industry. China firmly rejects it," he emphasized, commenting on allegations by US law enforcement and intelligence agencies that "China-based artificial intelligence companies are conducting systematic extraction of proprietary functionalities and capabilities of US AI companies’ models through industrial-scale knowledge distillation campaigns."
In AI, knowledge distillation is a machine learning technique in which a large, complex model is used to train a smaller model.
"We urge the US to respect facts, discard bias, stop its containment on China’s sci-tech development and choose the course of action conducive to sci-tech exchanges and cooperation between China and the US," Liu pointed out. "China opposes politicizing and instrumentalizing trade and tech issues. Such actions will only stifle global AI advances and serve no one’s interests," he added.
The Chinese Embassy spokesperson noted that "the development of AI in China comes from greater self-reliance and strength in science and technology". According to Liu, all countries should contribute to social progress and the common welfare of the international community while developing AI.

Russia’s New Jet Drones With Chinese Engines Challenge Ukraine’s Defenses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
03:51:32 UTC
12:51:32 KST

Flying at heights of several kilometers and close to the speed of a commercial aircraft, Moscow’s new long-range jet-powered drones are causing havoc among Kyiv’s overt-stretched air defenses.
In recent weeks Moscow has been launching waves of the attack drones at the Ukrainian capital, paralyzing the city with near constant air alerts.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Sunday slammed the “horror that’s been happening in the sky these past few days” in response to Russian leader Vladimir Putin’s new , and vowed a response.
The new drones pose a challenge to Ukraine’s previously effective and low-cost anti-drone defense shield, that was hastily developed following Russia’s 2022 invasion.
Ukraine has quickly become a world leader in drone defense and has struck deals with several Western and Middle Eastern countries to share its technology.
However, its network of drone interceptors – which had been shooting down the vast majority of Russia’s more conventional drones, powered by internal combustion engines and propellers – faces a more challenging task against the new jet-powered devices.
Experts say they are fitted with Chinese-made aircraft-style mini jet engines and can fly five kilometers in the air at speeds of 400-600 kilometers (250-370 miles) per hour – up to three times the speed of previous versions based on Iran’s Shahed drones.
Rutte: Civilian Deaths in Ukraine Highest Since May 2022 as Aid Delays Cost Lives
The latest model is larger, six meters (20 feet) long with a 5.5 meter (18 feet) wingspan , and a warhead containing up to 90 kilograms (200 pounds) of explosives, nearly double the payload of earlier versions.
Such an altitude and speed puts them out of range for Ukraine’s current fleet of interceptors and “wipes out the progress we had made in the fight,” Ukrainian military expert Sergii Zgurets told AFP.
In terms of air defense, analysts say the new drones more closely resemble cruise missiles than conventional drones.
Russia is estimated to have launched around 2,800 of the jet-powered drones in August, up from 1,500 in July and just a few hundred in June.
A Ukrainian Air Force spokesman said around 60% are destroyed, compared with more than 90% of slower, lower-flying drones.
Kyiv brought to a standstill
The new attacks come with Kyiv already under strain following a sharp increase in Russian ballistic missile strikes, which have killed dozens since the start of the summer.
On Friday, a jet-powered drone struck the headquarters of Ukraine’s security services in the historic center of Kyiv, a highly symbolic hit carried out in broad daylight.
Ukraine accused Russia of using the strike to disrupt the weekend visit of US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner to Moscow and Kyiv as they sought to revive stalled peace talks.
The wave of attacks has, at times, brought Kyiv to a near-standstill, with up to a dozen air alerts ringing out every day.
During alerts, many businesses and institutions close and the metro service is restricted, causing road gridlock and forcing people onto the streets.
Many schools, which returned from summer break last week, have announced a switch to remote learning.
The disruption to social and economic life has become so severe that authorities announced a rare relaxation of security protocols to allow the city of around three million people to keep functioning.
Ukraine races to develop a response
Kyiv officials have faced criticism for failing to anticipate the threat.
Analysts say Russia began producing jet-powered drones 18 months ago and can now manufacture around 3,000 a month.
Moscow “has a window of opportunity with these jet drones,” Ukrainian blogger Nikolaevsky Vaniok, who is close to the country’s air defense community and followed by more than 2.6 million people on Telegram, told AFP.
In response to the increased threat, Zelensky convened his military cabinet last week to accelerate production of faster interceptor drones.
Prototypes already exist and work is underway “to bring this new weapon up to the required level of efficiency,” he said.
One major Ukrainian arms company producing interceptors for conventional drones said it was “actively working on a solution.”
Zgurets, head of the Defense Express analysis center, argued that Ukraine needs a broader response combining aviation, surface-to-air systems, electronic warfare and more strikes against launch and production sites inside Russia.
“The Russians have gained an edge in this technological cycle,” he said, warning it could take “up to six months” for Ukraine to develop effective countermeasures.

China's inflation edges up, signaling sustained recovery in domestic demand
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
11:42:26 CST
12:42:26 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- China's price levels continued their moderate recovery in August, reflecting sustained improvement in domestic demand under supportive policy measures.
Data released by the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) on Wednesday showed the consumer price index (CPI) rose 0.4 percent month on month in August, reversing three consecutive months of decline, while the year-on-year gain accelerated from 0.5 percent to 0.8 percent.
NBS statistician Dong Lijuan attributed the uptick to several factors: rising energy prices, seasonal increases in food prices, continued gains in travel services during the summer holiday period, and higher prices for smartphones and computers driven by the surging demand for computing power.
Core CPI, which strips out food and energy prices, edged up to 1 percent year on year from 0.9 percent the previous month.
Factory-gate prices also sent encouraging signals. The producer price index (PPI) rose 0.4 percent month on month in August, swinging from a 0.7 percent decline the previous month, while the year-on-year gain widened to 3.8 percent.
The NBS cited the pass-through effect of rising global commodity prices and stronger demand in some sectors driven by domestic industrial upgrading. ■

Feature: Protecting the last citadels: Chinese, French heritage guardians join hands
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
11:41:50 CST
12:41:50 KST

This photo taken in 2025 shows an old house after restoration in Yunshan Tun of Anshun City, southwest China's Guizhou Province. (Xinhua)
GUIYANG, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- In a mountain village in southwest China, a group of French students, entrepreneurs and architects traded in desks and studios for construction tools this summer. Working alongside local craftsmen, they removed old roof tiles, cleared damaged walls and hauled heavy timber beams to help restore centuries-old homes.
For nearly a decade, international volunteers have been a familiar presence each summer in the ancient village of Yunshan Tun in Anshun City, Guizhou Province. This historic site, marked by 600-year-old military fortresses, is home to a cluster of stone citadels known as Tunpu.
For more than 10 years, 429 volunteers from China, France, Greece, Britain, Norway, Belgium, Australia, Germany and other countries have joined conservation workcamps for the old houses, including 98 foreign volunteers, said Yue Jian, a Guizhou architect and organizer of the camps along with REMPART, a French heritage conservation volunteer network.
They stay two weeks or more in each camp, working side by side with local craftsmen and construction teams on demanding physical tasks and gaining hands-on experience in rare traditional craft skills. Fifty French volunteers have participated in the Tunpu workcamp. Among this year's participants was 25-year-old Fatoumata Camara, a student at France's National Institute of Oriental Languages and Civilisations, who returned to China this August for her second conservation experience.
"I had heard from previous French volunteers that this was one of the longest-running workcamps between France and China. Knowing that so many people had been part of it over the years made me want to contribute too," she said, describing the experience as "understanding China's history in places where people still live and where traditions are still alive."
Prior to her arrival, Camara had assumed traditional houses in southern China would be predominantly wooden. Instead, she found extensive use of stone walls combined with wooden structures, an architectural legacy of the region's military history.
Yunshan Tun is part of Guizhou's distinctive Tunpu settlements, a cluster of military fortress villages dating back about six centuries. Built during the Ming Dynasty (1368-1644), the garrisons housed troops, cultivated farmland and guarded China's southwestern frontier. Most of the settlements are concentrated around Anshun, less than 100 km from the provincial capital Guiyang. The extensive use of stone has earned the area a reputation as a "kingdom of stone."
The house Camara helped restore covers 128 square meters across two floors and stands on the site of a Ming Dynasty military outpost. "It showed me how far a long-term heritage conservation project can go and how much a village can be transformed over time," she said.
FROM FRENCH CITADELS TO GUIZHOU HOMES
In the past decades, broad cooperation between Chinese and French institutions has taken international conservators to repair ancient structures -- temples, walls and houses -- not only in Guizhou, but also at various sites including those in Shanxi's Pingyao and in Fujian. The Pingyao workcamp has been included in the UNESCO World Heritage Volunteers initiative. In Guizhou, the program has helped repair 13 centuries-old houses.
Yue Jian, who initiated the volunteer project in Tunpu villages in 2014, visited the stone citadels in the 1990s when he was still a student of architecture. Fascinated by the local approach to building in harmony with the terrain, Yue developed a deep commitment to preserving these historic structures. He followed advice from Ruan Yisan, a renowned Chinese expert on the preservation of historic cities, to work as a volunteer first in France.
"I discovered that heritage preservation did not have to be the exclusive domain of experts and professional institutions. Ordinary young people could also participate, working under professional guidance while learning about architecture and traditional craftsmanship," he said.
Back in Guizhou, he began exploring ways to adapt this approach to rural China. "The French workcamps often focus on large medieval castles, while traditional villages in Guizhou consist of numerous smaller residences, each with different owners and users," he said. Yue treats the whole village as "one large castle," with each traditional house forming part of it.
In French villages, volunteers learned traditional stone-cutting and masonry techniques in restoring medieval stone castles damaged by war. In Guizhou's Tunpu villages, French participants have followed local carpenters to learn traditional timber-frame construction and use indigenous tools such as ink lines, hand planes and chisels to work on wooden columns and joints. "We went to France to learn stonework, and they came to Guizhou to learn woodworking," Yue said.
For participants like Camara, the restoration did not attempt to freeze the village in the past, but aimed to create a balance between preserving the old and bringing in something new that could attract visitors and support the village. "Conservation is not only about making a place beautiful for visitors, but making sure that people living in these historic places have standards of comfort and hygiene," she said.
The workcamp also offered activities in local traditional arts, such as Tunpu opera, batik and wooden mask carving. "I've learnt much more than just restoration techniques. They showed me how incredibly diverse China is. Every region has its own traditions, cuisine, and landscape," she said.
The current repair project, funded by an architecture firm in Shanghai, is scheduled to be completed in August next year.
Local conservation efforts are also increasing. The Anshun city culture and tourism authorities have invested more than 230 million yuan (about 34 million U.S. dollars) in restoring 27 key heritage sites in Tunpu villages and used three-dimensional scanning to digitally document 1,187 immovable cultural heritage sites and 307 items of intangible cultural heritage, forming a digital resource database for Tunpu culture.
DEEP CULTURAL PULL
Marie-Georges Pagel-Brousse, president of REMPART, has traveled to China 15 times, but one particular encounter with a Guizhou foreman was the most memorable. At a workcamp in Xijiang Miao Village in Guizhou in 2019, a local craftsman showed how China's ancestral techniques can help reduce the use of electric power tools. "Guizhou's traditional joinery and carpentry techniques became a lesson for French volunteers. Here traditions have fortunately not vanished; they remain vital, especially where craft know-how is concerned," she said.
For Pagel-Brousse, the workcamps have also demonstrated the value of public participation in heritage conservation. "The presence of volunteers can sometimes encourage local people to rediscover the value of traditions that have become part of their everyday lives," she said.
"The volunteers gain exposure to different yet inspiring working approaches, and develop deep respect for local masters who command their techniques to perfection. Chinese architecture is so impressive and remarkable that it leaves a lasting, uplifting impression," she said.
"The French people I know who have been to China feel a strong pull towards this country and its culture. They travel such a long distance because they are eager to learn, to meet others and to share with people from different backgrounds. None have ever left disappointed," she added.
After the construction team finishes and heads out, it's up to the local people to keep looking after the old houses, Yue said. "Repairing historic houses represents merely the initial stage. Finding ways for them to remain part of modern life poses a new issue to address," he said.
Guizhou has carried out systematic surveys of the remains of military and residential settlements with preliminary documentation completed for more than 300 Tunpu villages, covering their history, customs and cultural practices. The scope of conservation has also expanded from individual houses to entire village layouts, traditional craftsmanship, intangible cultural heritage and the everyday lives of residents.
Some restored houses have become tour venues, heritage workshops, cafes and homestays. During the 2025 Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day holiday period, a peak travel season, five major Tunpu scenic areas in Anshun received more than 1.4 million tourists, generating tourism revenue of over 69 million yuan.
Camara noticed the change during her stay. Many old houses have returned to use as homestays, restaurants and cultural spaces. Modern sanitary facilities coexist with traditional architecture, while residents continue to live in the village and traditional costumes and festivals remain part of local life.
"Through these workcamps, French participants come to understand that China is simultaneously highly modern while remaining deeply attached to its traditions, craftsmanship, heritage and inter-generational transmission," Pagel-Brousse said.
"These projects help us understand one another better, gain greater appreciation for a country and its people, and move beyond stereotypes, prejudice and negative perceptions," she said. ■
Chinese and French volunteers learn about conservation of fortress in Yunshan Tun of Anshun City, southwest China's Guizhou Province, Aug. 2, 2026. (Xinhua)

China's PPI up 3.8 pct in August
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
11:41:43 CST
12:41:43 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- China's producer price index (PPI), which measures costs for goods at the factory gate, went up 3.8 percent year on year in August, the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) said Wednesday.
On a month-on-month basis, the PPI reversed a 0.7-percent decline in July to rise 0.4 percent in August, NBS data showed.
Explaining the month-on-month movement, NBS statistician Dong Lijuan said imported price pressures, particularly higher international crude oil and nonferrous metal prices, pushed up prices in some domestic industries, while industrial transformation and upgrading boosted demand and prices in some emerging sectors.
Seasonal factors also played a role, with stronger summer demand for electricity and coal lifting prices in related sectors, while high temperatures and rainfall weighed on construction activity and prices in related industries.
Wednesday's data also showed that China's consumer price index, a key gauge of inflation, rose 0.8 percent year on year in August. ■

US turning Australia into military base – Guardian
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
03:35:34 UTC
12:35:34 KST

US turning Australia into military base – Guardian
The US is turning Australia into a forward base for potential military operations in the Pacific, with American forces and defense contractors controlling or having access to roughly two-thirds of the country’s military facilities, The Guardian reported on Sunday.
Citing data compiled by the Nautilus Institute for Security and Sustainability, the newspaper identified 110 facilities across Australia with some form of US military or corporate presence out of 168 surveyed.
The US military directly controls 17 facilities, including the Pine Gap intelligence complex in central Australia, which plays a major role in US surveillance and military operations. The facility tracks missile launches, intercepts communications and provides targeting information for American forces around the world.
Other installations include a naval communications station in Western Australia used to communicate with submerged US submarines and RAAF Base Tindal in the north, which is being expanded to accommodate nuclear-capable B-52 Stratofortress bombers.
“These aircraft are able to land on Australian soil carrying nuclear weapons. The US government won’t tell Australia if and when they are. The Australian government won’t ask,” The Guardian wrote.
Beyond the facilities it directly controls, the US military has access to dozens of Australian installations, while American defense contractors, including Lockheed Martin and Northrop Grumman, operate at others. According to the Nautilus data, 41 of the 168 facilities surveyed have no significant US presence, while the status of another 17 remains unresolved.
The American footprint is also expanding. In June, AFP reported that the US was preparing to establish a permanent stockpile of battle-ready weapons, ammunition, and equipment for the Marine Corps in Australia, with the facility expected to reach full capacity by 2028.
“Over more than a decade, the United States has been preparing the capacity for high-tempo warfighting operations with China, springboarding from Australia,” Richard Tanter, the author of the Nautilus database, told The Guardian.
“From a Chinese perspective, Australia is not so much hosting US bases on its territory, it’s a US base in its own right… Australia is a serious piece of real estate in the US warfighting machine,” added Tanter, an honorary professorial fellow at the University of Melbourne.
Canberra maintains that the growing American presence strengthens Australia’s security. Defense Minister Richard Marles said in June that the expanding US footprint was important both for building the country’s military capabilities and for its national security.
Marles also argued that the US presence helped counter what he described as China’s “very significant military buildup” in the region.
Former Australian Defense Minister Christopher Pyne has similarly said the 2021 AUKUS pact between Australia, the US, and UK goes beyond Canberra’s acquisition of nuclear-powered submarines. He described the arrangement as establishing “a new United States submarine base in the Indian Ocean” that would provide Washington with a “massive strategic advantage.”
Tanter criticized Canberra’s approach, calling it “a massive institutional failure in Australia, a kind of learned incapacity at a political, parliamentary and bureaucratic level.”

The state cricket body of NSW is disappointed Cricket Australia has announced plans to seek private investment in the Big Bash.
Cricket NSW says private investment threatens the ability of state bodies to invest in the sport at the grassroots level.
On Tuesday, Cricket Australia announced it would seek private investment into Australia's franchise T20 leagues, beginning with the sale of the Melbourne Renegades.
The decision to introduce private investment into the Big Bash leagues risks leaving cricket in Australia "strategically and financially worse off", according to Cricket NSW.
On Tuesday, Cricket Australia announced it would seek private investment into Australia's franchise T20 leagues, beginning with the sale of the Melbourne Renegades.
The announcement came following months of speculation about whether private investment was the right move for CA, and the game in Australia more broadly.
Ahead of Tuesday's announcement, it was reported that state cricket bodies in NSW and Queensland were opposed to the plan which included exploring sell-offs of 49 per cent stakes in BBL franchises.
On Wednesday, Cricket NSW in a statement said it was disappointed Cricket Australia had pushed forward with the decision to seek private investment without having all stakeholders on board with the process.
"Cricket NSW is disappointed by Cricket Australia's decision to proceed with introducing private investment into the Big Bash leagues without alignment across Australian cricket," the statement read.
"This decision risks leaving cricket in NSW and Australia strategically and financially worse off, with direct consequences for our ability to invest in grassroots cricket.
"We see our role at Cricket NSW, alongside Cricket Australia and all states, as custodians of our game. Our purpose is to inspire everyone to play and love cricket. This starts with growing participation in our sport, ultimately producing great players for our W/BBL clubs, NSW and Australia.
"The profits from our successful and healthy Big Bash clubs – the Sydney Sixers and Sydney Thunder – are reinvested into growing participation in cricket."
Cricket NSW owns the Sydney Sixers and Sydney Thunder franchises.
It said it feared the private investment model would threaten its ability to invest in growing the sport, especially at the grassroots level.
"Yesterday’s announcement threatens this system. The redistribution of profits to external investors reduces our ability to invest in community cricket, creating long-term impacts at all levels," Cricket NSW said.
"The Cricket NSW board is also disappointed by the process leading to this decision.
"We have raised concerns directly with Cricket Australia, proposed an alternative pathway to strengthen the Big Bash, and highlighted significant risks within the proposal, informed by high-quality external advice."
On Tuesday, Cricket Australia chair Mike Baird said the introduction of private investment into the Big Bash would result in greater investment in the sport at all levels.
"By opening the door to private investment in the Big Bash leagues, Cricket Australia is taking a deliberate step to strengthen and secure the long-term future of the game, accelerate growth and ensuring we can keep investing in community cricket and grassroots participation, domestic and international pathways and the elite level," he said.
"This is a significant decision that has involved an enormous amount of analysis, discussion and collaboration over many months. I'd like to thank all involved as we move to what we believe is the best way to secure cricket's future in this country, strengthen the Big Bash and protect our standing on the global stage."
Cricket Australia is hopeful that the Melbourne Renegades franchise will play the 2027/28 season under new ownership.

New Apple CEO to face first test with foldable iPhone launch
- Apple will unveil a foldable iPhone called iPhone Ultra at its Sept 9 event, marking the first major launch under new CEO John Ternus.
- The foldable iPhone will feature a compact design with a smaller external display and a larger unfolding screen, priced around US$2,000.
- Despite supply chain challenges and rising costs, Apple is expected to capture a significant share of the small foldable smartphone market and introduce AI-powered Siri improvements.
AI generated
SAN FRANCISCO – Apple is expected to unveil a slew of new and updated devices, including a long-rumoured foldable iPhone, when it holds its annual late-summer hardware event on Sept 9 in Cupertino, California.
It will also be the first major event under new chief executive John Ternus, who took over from outgoing CEO Tim Cook on Sept 1.
Ternus, 51, joined Apple’s design team in 2001 and worked his way up to leading the engineering teams behind Apple’s entire product lineup, including the iPhones that generate most of the company’s revenue.
The event, which Ternus promised would be “phenomenal” in his first company-wide e-mail as CEO last week, will kick off at 10am local time (1am on Sept 10 in Singapore).
The tech giant is expected to finally reveal a long-awaited foldable iPhone, currently rumoured to be called the iPhone Ultra, which will start at US$2,000 (S$2,530), according to reports.
Like Samsung’s foldable smartphones, Apple’s device will have a smaller external display when closed and a much larger screen that unfolds when the phone is opened.
The format essentially combines the portability of a smartphone with the larger display of a tablet, offering users a larger screen without carrying a tablet-sized device.
The foldable will be a test for Apple, which has not launched a breakout hit since the AirPods 10 years ago.
Samsung launched the industry’s first mainstream foldable smartphone, the Galaxy Fold, in 2019. The South Korean company released an updated model, the Galaxy Z Fold, in 2025 at a starting price of US$2,000.
Foldable smartphones make up a tiny fraction of the market, at less than 2 per cent of global shipments, but Apple could take 31 percent of that demand by the end of the year and reach 40 per cent by 2027, according to research firm IDC.
“Apple’s foldable iPhone is very likely to shift the competitive dynamics both in China and global markets,” IDC research associate Kiranjeet Kaur told AFP.
The foldable iPhone’s release comes as demand for powerful chips amid the artificial intelligence (AI) boom has created a supply chain crunch, pushing prices higher across industries.
As a result, smartphone shipments will decline by more than 16 percent this year while the average cost jumps more than 27 per cent, according to IDC.
“Foldable phones are not immune to the memory supply shortages, but the relative impact is lower considering these phones are already priced in the higher-range,” Kaur said.
In what would be a first for Apple, it is unclear whether the company will launch a new entry-level iPhone this year.
According to various reports, the company might only unveil two higher-end versions of its next series: the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max. A more affordable base version, the iPhone 18, might not launch until 2027.
The foldable Ultra will be around the size of a passport when closed and have only two camera lenses, a regular and an ultra-wide lens, according to Bloomberg.
An improved version of Siri, powered by AI, will be integrated into many of the new devices announced, which could include watches, AirPods, an Apple TV box and the HomePod mini.
The company might also launch a 7-inch device with a screen meant to act as a smart home hub, Bloomberg reported, though it is unclear whether that will be unveiled Wednesday or later in 2026. AFP

Inflation on the mainland picks up in August
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
03:16:28 UTC
12:16:28 KST

The nation's price levels continued their moderate recovery in August, reflecting sustained improvement in domestic demand under supportive policy measures.
Data released by the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) on Wednesday showed the consumer price index (CPI) rose 0.4 percent month on month in August, reversing three straight months of decline, while the year-on-year gain accelerated from 0.5 percent to 0.8 percent.
NBS statistician Dong Lijuan attributed the uptick to several factors: rising energy prices, seasonal increases in food prices, continued gains in travel services during the summer holiday period, and higher prices for smartphones and computers driven by the surging demand for computing power.
Core CPI, which strips out food and energy prices, edged up to one percent year on year from 0.9 percent the previous month.
Factory-gate prices also sent encouraging signals. The producer price index rose 0.4 percent month on month in August, swinging from a 0.7 percent decline the previous month.
The year-on-year gain widened to 3.8 percent, faster than July's 3.5 percent and topped the 3.6 percent forecast by analysts. (Xinhua/AFP)

Laura Gamba

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio delivered a scathing critique of former Colombian President Gustavo Petro on Tuesday during a visit to Colombia, saying President Abelardo De La Espriella’s new administration had inherited a nation crippled by “a series of disasters” stemming from the previous four years of governance.
Speaking alongside De La Espriella in the coastal city of Barranquilla following a high-level bilateral summit, Rubio framed the visit as a historic reset after what he characterized as an anomalous and fractured chapter in relations between Washington and Bogota.
“We have a lot of work to do, because unfortunately, this administration has inherited a series of disasters and poor decisions that were made,” he told reporters.
“To a certain extent, we felt the same way when we took office a year and a half ago. But you are dealing with the mistakes of the past four years, and you have to fix them.”
The rebuke underscored a sweeping geopolitical realignment under De La Espriella, who has rapidly moved to reverse the core pillars of Petro’s administration by aligning Bogota with Washington’s strategic priorities on security, trade and regional defense.
“This high-level meeting confirms, through concrete actions and unwavering determination, that the strategic alliance between Colombia and the United States is stronger than ever,” De La Espriella declared.
Security dominated the summit agenda, culminating in the framework of the newly minted "Barranquilla Accords." De La Espriella signaled his intent to re-establish Colombia as the US’s primary partner in hemispheric security. The initiative aims to upgrade the Colombian Armed Forces’ capabilities across advanced aviation, air defense, radar networks, drones, cyber defense and special forces operations.
Rubio signaled immediate US backing for the initiative, emphasizing that strengthening Colombian security directly protects American national interests.
“Without security, a country cannot progress, and the security threats facing Colombia are the same ones we face in the United States -- the same networks, the same criminal groups,” he said.
In a total departure from Petro’s progressive drug policies, De La Espriella announced an aggressive escalation of the offensive against drug trafficking and transnational cartels.
“We are going to start fumigating. We are going after the laboratories, the precursors, the routes, the drug kingpins and the narco-terrorist armed organizations,” he said, confirming a return to aerial eradication.
He added that his administration will prioritize prosecuting money launderers, seizing illicit assets and expanding judicial and financial intelligence sharing with US agencies.
Prior to the joint statements, Colombian Foreign Minister Omar Bula and Rubio formalized the shift by signing a strategic memorandum of understanding designed to secure supply chains for critical minerals and rare earth elements.

Playing politics with security: Jerusalem must review UK privileges amidst sanctions - editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
03:13:51 UTC
12:13:51 KST

Political signals have consequences.
London has already imposed sanctions on Israeli ministers, restricted arms exports, suspended trade negotiations, and recognized a Palestinian state. The settlement ban adds another layer to a relationship that Britain simultaneously insists remains strategically important.
That contradiction was unusually visible on Tuesday. British ministers stressed that Israel remains an important security partner and that intelligence and security cooperation should continue. Miliband himself emphasized Britain’s continuing relationship with Israel even as he announced the new policy.
Yet only a day earlier, UN special rapporteur Francesca Albanese called on Britain to go considerably further and progressively suspend intelligence cooperation with Israel.
Britain should reject that suggestion unequivocally. Israeli intelligence has helped protect British lives. The most striking known example came in 2015, when MI5 uncovered roughly three and a half tons of ammonium nitrate stored by Hezbollah in northwest London. Israeli officials later said the Mossad had provided the intelligence that led British authorities to the cache.
Intel cooperation usually not publicly visible, but entirely vital
For years, the British public knew almost nothing about the operation. An Intelligence and Security Committee report finally disclosed details in 2025, describing Hezbollah’s stockpile as a contingency for a possible future attack.
Such cooperation is rarely visible precisely because intelligence relationships are supposed to remain quiet.
Tuesday supplied another reminder of why the partnership matters. On the same day Britain announced its measures against settlements, it introduced tougher sanctions against Iran, expanding financial, trade, and aviation restrictions designed to constrain Tehran’s nuclear program and hostile activities.
Iran threatens Israel directly. It has also plotted against dissidents and Jewish targets on European soil, supported Hezbollah and other terrorist organizations, and repeatedly challenged Western interests.
Britain and Israel therefore have genuine strategic interests in common even when their governments disagree sharply.
UK should feel consequences of its decisions
Israel should respond to the settlement ban. Diplomatic relations require reciprocity, and London cannot assume that it will absorb each new punitive measure without consequence. Jerusalem can review discretionary British access and privileges, reconsider aspects of diplomatic cooperation and make clear that partnership works in both directions.
Calls to dismantle intelligence cooperation, however, would be a mistake.
The information exchanged between British and Israeli agencies does not belong to Ed Miliband, Benjamin Netanyahu, or any particular government. It exists to prevent terrorist attacks, disrupt Iranian operations, and protect citizens.
There is also a message here for London.
Britain cannot continually narrow its political relationship with Israel while assuming that the most valuable elements of the strategic relationship exist on autopilot. Allies can disagree, sometimes bitterly. They also have to recognize what they stand to lose when disagreement becomes a systematic downgrading of the relationship.
Britain has chosen a “reset.” It should make certain that, in trying to punish Israel over the West Bank, it does not weaken an alliance that has helped keep British citizens safe.
