US bans Canadian alcohol, motorcycles and dairy products as trade spat escalates
The US and Canada escalated a bitter trade dispute on Tuesday, with Washington imposing new import bans on Canadian alcohol, motorcycles and dairy products as Ottawa's retaliatory tariffs on US goods took effect.
The United States banned a broad swath of Canadian alcoholic beverages, motorcycles and dairy products from import on Tuesday, sharply escalating an already acrimonious trade spat.
The import bans, which go into effect on September 29 and were published on the White House's website, came after Canada's own retaliatory tariffs on US goods took effect after midnight on Tuesday.
Those Canadian levies themselves followed 50 percent tariffs that the United States imposed on some $20 billion of Canadian goods last month, after several rounds of negotiations collapsed.
The breakdown has widened a rift between the longtime allies, who have blamed each other for the failed talks, spurred Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney to urge a further shift away from Canada's biggest trading partner, and cast doubt on the viability of the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement.
"We have everything we need to pivot and prosper," Carney said on Tuesday in a video posted on YouTube.
Read moreCanada's counter-tariffs take effect on several US goods as trade war reignites
"That pivot will come at a cost. There's always a cost to action. But it doesn't come close to the cost of standing still," he said.
The US bans appeared to cover most alcohol products, including beer and various types of wine, whisky, bourbon, rum, vodka, vermouth, tequila, mezcal, and brandy. The dairy ban covers whey protein, invert molasses, cane molasses and non-alcoholic beer, per notices on the White House's website.
In addition to the import bans, various cheese products were added to a list of products subject to a 50 percent tariff, but not banned outright. Some paper, aluminium, wood, furniture, lighting and other products were also added to the list.
A US official said President Donald Trump's pre-existing threat to increase tariffs on Canadian autos from 25 to 50 percent on January 1 remained in effect. The official added that US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer had spoken with Dominic LeBlanc, Canada's minister responsible for bilateral US trade, over the past couple of days, and the pair were expected to speak again in the coming days to see if there was an alternative path for the two countries.

In a social media post on Tuesday night, LeBlanc criticised the latest US measures and said he was in contact with Greer regarding a path forward.
"As has been the case for the last 18 months, our first priority remains on protecting and supporting Canadian workers, farmers, families, and businesses from these unjustified actions," he wrote.
Ottawa strikes back
Ottawa's retaliatory measures, which in turn provoked Washington's move on Tuesday night, were designed to put economic and political pressure on Washington, Canadian government officials said.
Those counter-tariffs cover some $20 billion of US goods, with duties ranging from 15 to 50 percent across products from steel and furniture to clothing and electronics, and are expected to hit sectors in some competitive states such as Michigan and Ohio, ahead of US midterm elections in November.
While the tariffs affect a small amount of exports compared with total trade between the US and Canada, some analysts worry the standoff could destabilise the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement, the free-trade pact that succeeded NAFTA. Together they have underpinned commerce across North America for decades.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom, a 2028 presidential hopeful, ventured farther than ever in his criticisms of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, in a weekend interview that delved into the Democratic Party’s relationship with Israel.
“I think it’s overwhelmingly opposed to the current regime in Israel,” Newsom said of the party, in a PBS NewsHour interview with Amna Nawaz.
Pressed by Nawaz on divisions among his colleagues on Israel, Newsom denied that the subject is “even controversial anymore,” stressing that “the condemnation of what Bibi Netanyahu’s doing is almost universal.” The governor slammed the Israeli military’s conduct in Gaza and condemned the settler violence that has expanded in the West Bank.
“We want a democratic and secure Israel, and we want a secure and democratic Palestinian state as well right next door,” Newsom said, adding that Netanyahu has proved counterproductive to achieving a two-state solution.
Though he repeatedly maintained that Democrats are not divided on Israel, the governor acknowledged that “some of the language” by fellow Democrats “has been weaponized.” Certain “aspects of rhetoric” from individual candidates, he added, are on “the spectrum of concern,” Newsom said.
A number of candidates from the party’s far left place most if not all of the blame on Israel for a war in Gaza that has resulted in tens of thousands of Palestinian deaths. and downplay the role of Hamas in launching the war with the Oct. 7, 2023 raid inside Israel in which 1,200 people were killed and more than 250 were abducted.
Newsom’s rhetoric is in step with party moderates who are critical of the Israeli government but who call for a secure Israel, reject Hamas, and resist pressure from the left to call Israel’s actions “genocide.”
Newsome nonetheless insisted that the party is unified on the issue. “But I think universally, everyone agrees, even if you don’t think it’s genocide, that it’s been a moral catastrophe,” he said of the war in Gaza. “The vast majority of us also agree about the atrocities on Oct. 7th and how horrific and unacceptable it was, and the terrorism that was perpetrated by Hamas.”
Newsom among many US politicians to visit Israel
Newsom was among the many US politicians to visit Israel in October 2023, meeting with survivors and families impacted by the attacks.
During a March book tour, Newsom sparked a backlash when he said that some people were referring to Israel “appropriately as sort of an apartheid state.” He quickly walked back these remarks, telling Politico that he had used the term “in the context of the direction that Bibi is going.”
“I revere the state of Israel,” he declared at the time.
The governor warned, however, that if Netanyahu proceeds in the direction of West Bank annexation, apartheid could become “a word you may hear others use.”
In addition to amplifying his condemnation of Netanyahu this weekend, Newsom also addressed the fact that fewer Democrats are accepting funds from political action committees affiliated with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, the pro-Israel lobbying group.
As for Newsom himself, Track AIPAC, an organization that compiles Federal Election Commission data to flag pro-Israel campaign contributions, did not log any such donations to the likely presidential candidate. But the group did flag him as “pro-Israel.”
“It’s a minority of Democrats that are accepting AIPAC,” the governor said, noting a “dramatic change” over the last couple of years.
“The vast majority of Democrats I talk to, even Democrats in the past that have in the past have taken AIPAC money, are pledging not to now,” Newsom added. “That’s more of a mainstream position, interestingly, within the Democratic Party.”

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Former Taipei Mayor and TPP founder Ko Wen-je (柯文哲) appeared before the High Court on Tuesday as his appeal against a 17-year prison sentence entered its second stage, with the court initially focusing on alleged misuse of political donations.
Ko denied wrongdoing and maintained his not-guilty plea. Prosecutors, meanwhile, argued that the sentence imposed in the first trial was too lenient and asked the High Court to overturn parts of the ruling and impose heavier penalties, per CNA.
The High Court divided the case into three parts to prepare the appeal. Tuesday's hearing focused on the political-donation allegations involving Ko, former campaign officials Lee Wen-tsung (李文宗) and Lee Wen-chuan (李文娟), and Muko Co.
Prosecutors alleged that Ko and Lee Wen-tsung used NT$1 million (US$31,760) in political donations to invest in a commercial media venture associated with producer Chiu Fu-sheng (邱復生). They argued that political donations cannot legally be used for commercial investment and that the district court was wrong to acquit the defendants on this part of the case, per PTS.
Prosecutors also challenged the first-instance findings concerning money transferred through Muko. According to the Taipei District Court's March judgment, Ko, Lee Wen-tsung, and Lee Wen-chuan jointly misappropriated NT$62 million from the political-donation account.
The court found that NT$15 million was transferred to Muko under the guise of payments for the authorization of Ko's image rights, after which NT$4.5 million was transferred from Muko to Ko's personal account as image-rights fees.
Ko's lawyer Cheng Shen-yuan (鄭深元) asked the High Court to livestream the proceedings, arguing that the court's evidence examination and legal arguments should be publicly broadcast.
Prosecutors submitted 428 pages of statements and other evidence in support of their appeal. The court said the first phase would involve determining the scope of the appeals and reviewing the evidence before moving into substantive arguments.
Lee Wen-tsung denied the charges, including allegations that money from the Chung Wang Foundation was improperly used to pay campaign-office employees. He argued that the campaign organization had to employ staff and pay their salaries. Lee Wen-chuan also denied the charges, per TVBS.
Tuanmu Cheng (端木正), who was accused of falsifying accounting documents, changed his plea to guilty in the second instance. He asked the court for leniency, including a sentence that could be commuted to a fine or suspended, and said he was willing to contribute his professional expertise through community service, per NewTalk.
Muko also appealed the first-instance order to confiscate more than NT$56.84 million in alleged illicit gains. Its lawyer argued that the company itself had not been indicted but had nevertheless been ordered to forfeit the money.
The High Court scheduled further hearings for Lee Wen-tsung and Lee Wen-chuan on Oct. 19, Duan on Nov. 5, and Ko on Nov. 16.
TPP Chair Huang Kuo-chang (黃國昌), speaking to reporters after the hearing, said there was no substantive debate as the prosecutor outlined the scope of the appeal and the evidence they will provide. He said preparations for this part of the criminal proceedings will likely be conducted three times, per PTS.
Ko's March 26 first-instance sentence totaled 17 years in prison and six years of civil rights deprivation. The Taipei District Court sentenced him to 13 years for accepting a bribe in connection with the Core Pacific City case, as well as additional prison terms for misappropriation of public funds and breach of trust. The sentences were to be served concurrently.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s benchmark stock index moved lower on Tuesday as investors took profits in several major sectors.
The Taiwan Stock Exchange Capitalization Weighted Index (TAIEX) closed down 220.49 points, or 0.47%, at 47,105.78. Turnover fell to NT$876.7 billion (US$27.8 billion), compared with NT$940 billion the previous session, according to Taiwan Index Plus and CTEE.
Among the index’s most heavily weighted stocks, TSMC was the only gainer. The chipmaker ended up 0.41% at NT$2,470.
MediaTek fell 1.05% to NT$4,710, while Foxconn declined 1.76% to NT$251.50. Delta Electronics dropped 2.43% to NT$1,805, and ASE fell 0.48% to NT$618, according to Anue.
Robot and automation stocks, which had posted strong gains in recent weeks on interest surrounding the Taiwan Automation Intelligence and Robot Show, faced profit-taking as their share prices had already reflected positive factors. Solomon Technology lost 4.58%, Hiwin Technologies declined 3.98%, and Airtac International Group fell 2.55%, according to Sinotrade.
Passive component stocks also faced selling pressure despite strong fundamentals and record-high August revenue reported by industry leader Yageo. Yageo fell 3.74%, Holy Stone Enterprise declined 3.11%, and Walsin Technology lost 1.39%.
Probe card makers were among the few sectors to buck the broader market’s decline. WinWay Technology rose to its daily limit-up of NT$7,700.
Mpi gained 5.56%, while Chunghwa Precision Test Technology rose 4.32%. A probe card tests individual chips on a wafer before packaging, allowing manufacturers to identify defective chips and reduce production waste and costs, according to Business Next.
Semiconductor intellectual property stocks were relatively resilient, benefiting from accelerated orders from major cloud service providers for their own chip designs. The trend is expected to continue, with revenue from IP licensing and chip development services being recognized ahead of schedule. M31 rose 6.57%, while Global Unichip gained 0.42%.
Memory chip manufacturers gained, with Winbond Electronics rising 4.44%, Nanya Technology advancing 2.71%, and Macronix International climbing 1.2%. The sector continues to benefit from strong AI server demand, which has led major memory chipmakers to shift production capacity toward high-end DDR5 and high-bandwidth memory. This has tightened supply and driven higher contract prices for standard DRAM and NAND flash.
Biomedical stocks attracted attention as companies released strong August revenue figures. Energenesis Biomedical, Handa Pharmaceuticals, and NaviFus hit their daily limits, while InnoCare Optoelectronics, PharmaEssentia, VizionFocus, and Obi Pharma moved higher.
Investors also turned to financial stocks, which are often viewed as more stable during periods of market volatility. E Sun Financial Holding rose 4.59%, TS Financial Holding gained 4.14%, and CTBC Financial Holding added 1.19%.
E Sun High Tech Fund manager Lin Che-yu (林哲宇) said investors will be watching companies’ August revenue figures as they are released throughout the week. He said the monthly and quarterly moving averages should provide support if the market enters a period of consolidation, as both are trending upward and could encourage buying when the market pulls back, according to CTEE.
Lin recommended taking profits in sectors that have gained significantly in the short term while buying on dips in sectors with stronger earnings prospects. He favored optical communications, advanced substrates, and mature semiconductor processes, where valuations have pulled back.

China’s factory-gate price growth picks up in August as Iran war fuels energy volatility
Producer price index rises 3.8 per cent, beating economists’ projections amid war-driven oil surge and weak domestic demand
China’s factory-gate price growth accelerated in August, while consumer inflation picked up again, amid volatile energy and commodity costs linked to the US-Israel war on Iran.
The producer price index rose 3.8 per cent year on year last month, up from 3.5 per cent in July, according to data released by the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) on Wednesday.
The reading beat a 3.6 per cent projection from economists polled by financial data provider Wind.
Meanwhile, the consumer price index (CPI), a crucial gauge of inflation, rose 0.8 per cent year on year, rebounding after two months of slower growth. That figure improved upon July’s 0.5 per cent rate and was broadly in line with Wind’s projection of a 0.78 per cent rise.
“Rising international prices for crude oil and non-ferrous metals drove up prices in related domestic sectors,” said Dong Lijuan, a senior NBS statistician.
Dong noted that coal mining prices surged 26.6 per cent year on year in August, while non-ferrous metal processing rose 20.8 per cent. Prices in the oil and gas extraction industry climbed 10.5 per cent.

Iran says captured US underwater drone in Strait of Hormuz
Pentagon plays down the seizure, saying it was an older unmanned vehicle that had malfunctioned
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said on Tuesday it had captured a US uncrewed submarine at the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz, offering a rare glimpse into how underwater drones are being used in military operations.
Iranian state media said the vessel was a Dive-LD, a large autonomous underwater vehicle built by California defence firm Anduril. The 5.8-metre (19-foot) submersible can carry out missions including mine countermeasures, seabed mapping, intelligence gathering and the inspection of underwater infrastructure such as cables and pipelines, the company has said.
“We trapped one of the most modern, intelligent and unmanned submarines of the terrorist American army at the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz. This submersible is equipped with the latest technologies,” the Revolutionary Guards Navy said in a statement carried by Iranian state media.
In response, a Pentagon spokesperson said an underwater drone had “malfunctioned more than a day ago”.
“It was surveying regional waters in support of ongoing operations. The defective drone was an older model that neither collected sensitive data nor carried any classified sonar or radar equipment,” the spokesperson said.
Anduril confirmed the loss of one of its vessels, but played down the significance of the incident.

US judge dismisses suit by British anti-disinformation activist against deporting him
WASHINGTON, Sept 8 - A federal judge in New York dismissed a lawsuit by British anti-disinformation campaigner Imran Ahmed that challenged the Trump administration's ability to detain and deport him.
U.S. District Judge Loretta Preska in Manhattan said on Tuesday that while Ahmed "very well may have valid causes of action," she was required to conclude under a recent appellate court ruling that she lacked jurisdiction to hear his free speech and due process claims under the U.S. Constitution.
Preska's ruling opens the door to Ahmed's detention, but the judge said she would leave the earlier restraining order in effect for five business days to allow Ahmed time to pursue an appeal.
President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown and his administration's use of visa and green card revocations have faced legal challenges that have divided U.S. courts.
Late last year, a U.S. judge temporarily blocked the Trump administration from detaining Ahmed, after the U.S. permanent resident sued officials over an entry ban for his role in what Washington alleges is online censorship.
Washington had imposed visa bans last year on Ahmed and four Europeans, accusing them of working to censor freedom of speech or unfairly target U.S. tech giants with burdensome regulation.
Ahmed, the 47-year-old CEO of the U.S.-based Center for Countering Digital Hate, lives in Washington. He says his wife and child are both U.S. citizens. He did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
A federal judge in July blocked the Trump administration from enforcing the policy that targeted foreign nationals who study disinformation and hate speech on social media for visa denials and deportation.
Legal permanent residents, known as green card holders, do not need a visa to remain in the U.S., but the Trump administration has attempted to deport some over their political views, such as participation in pro-Palestinian protests against U.S. ally Israel's war in Gaza.
Trump has cast such voices as "anti-American" and as foreign policy threats. Advocates have raised free speech and due process concerns and said the Trump administration is punishing such people for criticism of the U.S. government.
The Trump administration has also initiated probes against some activists and rights advocates and sanctioned some international judges. REUTERS

France, South Korea concerned about mutual military support between Russia and North Korea -- Macron
French President Emmanuel Macron said this after talks with President of the Republic of Korea Lee Jae Myung in Paris, according to a Ukrinform correspondent.
“We share a common position in the face of today’s crises. We note North Korea’s increasingly open and active support for Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine, as well as the assistance Pyongyang receives in return for developing its own military programs,” Macron said.
According to him, France and South Korea share a vision of an international order based on international law and the UN system and intend to deepen coordination on security and stability.
The South Korean president, for his part, highlighted France’s role in European efforts aimed at ending Russia’s war.
“France plays a central role in uniting efforts and mobilizing capabilities at the European level to bring an end to the war in Ukraine and restore peace. Korea is also providing Ukraine with support in many areas. We are pleased to join the international community in efforts to establish peace and rebuild Ukraine,” Lee Jae Myung said.
Macron also stressed that the two countries seek to strengthen strategic autonomy, defense cooperation, and interaction in the fields of technology and energy.
“This will help strengthen our sovereignty and independence, cooperate on the basis of mutual respect, and avoid becoming dependent on any major power as a ‘vassal.’ French–Korean relations best embody this ‘coalition of independent states’ in which we believe,” the French president said.
Macron also reaffirmed France’s unwavering support for peace and stability on the Korean Peninsula.
Among the practical steps to strengthen defense cooperation, the French president mentioned the Pégase air mission, which is due to make a stop in the Republic of Korea in the coming days. According to him, the mission demonstrates the parties’ intention to conduct regular strategic exercises, develop industrial cooperation in defense equipment, exchange information, and improve the interoperability of their armed forces.
The situation in the Middle East and ensuring freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz were also discussed by the two leaders.
“In April, I took part in an international summit devoted to the Strait of Hormuz to reaffirm Korea’s readiness to contribute to stability in the region and ensure freedom of navigation along maritime routes. Korea and France will continue to develop close cooperation to guarantee freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz and the security of global supply chains,” Lee Jae Myung said.
Macron, for his part, recalled that France and South Korea, together with the United Kingdom, had launched coordination to establish a special international mission of an exclusively peaceful nature to restore navigation through the Strait of Hormuz. According to him, the possibility of deploying such a multinational mission continues to be “intensively explored.”
As previously reported by Ukrinform, military cooperation between Moscow and Pyongyang , including the supply of ballistic missiles and personnel from North Korea, directly violates UN Security Council resolutions and prolongs the war against Ukraine.

Revisiting Chopper Read reveals a time when the manosphere was on TV
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
02:25:59 UTC
11:25:59 KST

analysis
Most of us remember Chopper Read as a loveable bogan, but revisiting his story is eye-opening
To say that we're currently living through an era of backlash seems bleedingly obvious.
The cigar-smoking, private-jet flaunting, women-hating influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate were arrested in Miami in July on British charges of rape, trafficking for sexual exploitation and offences related to indecent images of a child.
Pauline Hanson called domestic violence a "two-way street" and referred to family violence leave as "holiday leave". And an education report found that female school teachers are being subjected to intimidation and sexual harassment from male students in a culture some described as "toxic masculinity".
In the aftermath of #metoo — a time that witnessed a global outpouring of women's stories of sexual violence as well as popular and political discussion on its causes and remedies — regressive gender norms are again having a renaissance.
And who better represents this than the Tate brothers with their fantasies of masculine physical prowess, financial affluence, emotional repression and garden-variety misogyny?
Andrew tells us that women should be men's domestic or sexual servants and the reporting by journalist Heidi Blake in The New Yorker into the most recent sexual allegations argues that this is not mere rhetoric. Date night with Andrew involved strangulation, being beaten unconscious and rape. He denies this and claims he "loves women".
While it's hard to disagree with the idea that there's been an almighty swing against feminism by men of a younger generation, the problem with framing our current moment as simply "backlash" is that it limits our collective memory to 2017 when #metoo went global.
The manosphere was once bigger
If we go back a few decades earlier to the 1990s and early 2000s we find something much worse than the manosphere: the manosphere writ large as national culture.
This is conservative, Howard-era Australia.
Rather than the Andrew Tates of the world ferreting away in a dark and grubby corner of the internet preying on pimply teenaged boys, they're on our national television giving public service announcements on domestic violence and drink driving, they're ambling into the offices of the ABC where they're adored as great Australian raconteurs, they have advice columns in national newspapers, they write best-selling autobiographies and audiences rush to their comedy shows to hear unfiltered racism, sexism and homophobia, normalised as larrikin culture.
What's my evidence for this? Research I recently did for ABC history podcast The Dead Can't Sue into Chopper Read, a man who transformed from criminal into beloved folk legend and who was elevated to the pantheon of national heroes in the period following his prison release in the 1990s until his death in 2013.
Today most of us remember Chopper as that laughable boganical figure with a handlebar moustache, an inky gallery of tattoos on his hulking, mutilated body, Miami Vice-style glasses and a penchant for tossing enemies into cement mixers — at least this was what he claimed in a notorious interview with Elle McFeast.
But revisiting his writing and his life-story today is like rewatching a beloved childhood film only to find that Aladdin is an Orientalist hellscape and Molly Ringwald ended up with a sex-pest in Sixteen Candles.
Leaving aside the fact that Chopper stole almost all of his stories of being a fearsome stand-over man from other prisoners in Pentridge, the model of masculinity that he represented, and that Australians lapped up at the time, bears a lot in common with the Tate brothers.
A similar brand of masculinity
Firstly, they both grew up in the bleached atmospheres of dread that permeate a physically and psychologically abusive family.
Like the Tate brothers who believe that their father's physical beatings made men of them, Chopper too claims in his autobiography that he loved his dad and "he belted the hell out of me as a child right up until I fought him back at the age of 15".
Being a man meant emotional repression and physical aggression, which, like the Tate brothers, led Chopper to bare-knuckle fighting.
Both Chopper and the Tate bros promote a model of masculinity based on physical power which sees its most benign forms in gym culture — all share a commitment to working out to maintain a muscular, indomitable masculine physique — and its most terrifying forms in intimate violence.
The Tates are currently facing 59 offences in the UK related to sexual violence.
Chopper was never charged but his first wife Mary-Ann Hodge has written of the nightmare of living with a domestically abusive man.
"He'd get wild with me about something, hold me down on the floor and hogtie my arms behind my back. Then he'd bash me around the head," she told journalist Rochelle Jackson.
More publicly, Chopper was shamelessly racist, much like the Tates.
In his autobiography he says that he grew up hating "all Asians", but claims that this is not "real racism, just part of the rough as guts Australian sense of humour, part of the Aussie culture and attitude".
And he was right, at least for a large part of Australian society in the 1990s and early 2000s. People flocked to his shows, his autobiography remains one of Australia's best-selling books, he released a rap album and the media adored him. And yes, he was asked to do Public Service Announcements on domestic violence and drink driving.
We don't often think of the 1990s and early 2000s as an historical era. But like any moment in time, it was crosscut with intimations of the future and residues of the past.
In the life of Chopper we see both: he was born of a culture that has long elevated toxic forms of masculinity to a proud national tradition and a future that draws on this tradition to create its new masculinist monsters.
Perhaps the most uplifting part of this story is that today we have a rich vocabulary to understand and call out the behaviour of today's Choppers, to confine them to grubby corners of the internet or prison, if they're found guilty.

Colby warned that Russia is “reconstituting its forces and its defense-industrial capacity,” requiring allies to prepare for a “protracted conflict” and Ukrainian needs lasting “months and years ahead.”
Washington also placed greater long-term responsibility on Europe, describing the transition toward European allies taking the lead in conventional defense as already underway.
“Support for Ukraine contributes to Europe’s security,” Colby told the nearly 50-country virtual meeting. “Words are not enough. Real money and industrial capacity must be put to work.”
Patriot gap exposed
Ukraine intercepted 31 of 32 cruise missiles in Russia’s latest mass attack, but newly appointed Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara warned that ballistic missiles remain far harder to stop.
Russia’s New Jet Drones With Chinese Engines Challenge Ukraine’s Defenses
“The situation with ballistics is much more difficult. And that difficulty is precisely down to the lack of Patriot missiles,” Khmara told allies.
Moscow is well aware of that vulnerability and is trying to exploit it to exhaust Ukraine’s air defenses, economy and society.
Kyiv is contracting roughly 1,000 Patriot missiles with partner support and EU financing, but most will begin arriving only in future years.
That delay is prompting Ukraine to ask allies for interceptors from existing stocks now, with replacements to come later from future deliveries.
Germany urges allies to release missiles from stocks
Germany answered Kyiv’s call by pledging PAC-2 Patriot interceptors from Bundeswehr stocks and urging other allies to follow.
“If in doubt, decide in favor of Ukraine,” German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius told the Contact Group.
Pistorius warned that Moscow’s ambitions extend beyond Ukraine, pointing to the explosive-drone incident at Leipzig Airport as part of Russia’s wider effort to weaken support for Kyiv.
Instead, he argued, Russia’s “ruthless and irresponsible behavior” was only strengthening Germany’s resolve to back Ukraine.
Berlin is also increasing AIM-9 air-to-air missile deliveries from Bundeswehr stocks, continuing IRIS-T supplies and backing Ukraine’s City Dome project to shield cities against Russian drones and missiles.
UK adds $135 million winter air-defense package
The United Kingdom separately announced a £100 million ($135 million) contribution through NATO’s Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) to accelerate air-defense deliveries before winter.
Britain’s Defense Secretary Wes Streeting stressed that London’s backing for Kyiv would remain firm as diplomatic efforts continue.
“Hopefully it’s been very evident to everyone on this call, the unshakable and unwavering commitment that our Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, and I, and our entire country feel to Ukraine, to its people and to its government as they fight on the front line not just for Ukrainian freedom and democracy, but for all of our freedom and democracy,” Streeting told the meeting.
Britain has pledged more than 120,000 drones to Ukraine this year, with over 25,000 already delivered and thousands more expected before winter.
The UK also delivered its one-millionth large-caliber artillery round in July, with further ammunition supported by Germany, Denmark, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Norway and Sweden.
$27 billion funding gap
Ukraine faces a €23 billion ($27 billion) defense funding gap, with much of it needed to sustain drone supplies through early 2027.
Drones account for up to 90% of Ukraine’s battlefield success, Khmara said, urging allies to decide on funding by November.
Partners have committed about €62 billion of the €70 billion pledged in Ankara, leaving an €8 billion shortfall.
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte pressed governments to increase support, warning that civilian deaths in Ukraine are now at their highest level since May 2022.
“Delays simply cost human lives,” Rutte said.
Russia’s aerial arsenal is also evolving, with increased use of North Korean missiles and jet-powered drones, he warned.
Kyiv: Russia preparing 300,000 more troops
Moscow is preparing to mobilize around 300,000 additional personnel on top of ongoing recruitment, with the buildup expected to continue into 2027.
Kyiv plans to counter Russia’s numerical advantage with technology and speed.
“Our answer is smart technology and speed,” Khmara said.
Ukraine has built what he called a “drone kill zone,” slowing Russian advances and inflicting losses on more than 30,000 Russian troops each month.
‘Winter is coming’
Winter preparedness remained the central emergency throughout the meeting.
“Since Russia is only advancing very slowly at the front line, it is trying to destroy Ukraine’s economic base and critical infrastructure by air raids on port installations, power plants and other civilian targets,” Pistorius said.
He warned that Russian attacks are likely to intensify as temperatures fall.
“Ukraine is racing against time. It requires us to act resolutely and immediately. Together, we must take the right measures to increase Ukraine’s resilience.”
“Ukraine is racing against time,” Pistorius warned. “Preparing Ukraine for winter is of the highest priority, and it requires us to act resolutely and immediately.”

Cristian Volpato's Socceroos future in Football Australia's hands after failed cocaine test
In short:
Young Socceroos player Cristian Volpato has been handed a fine by NSW Police after a secondary test confirmed a positive roadside test for cocaine.
Volpato has maintained his innocence over the failed drugs test when he spoke to Football Australia (FA) staff, insisting that he never knowingly ingested the substance.
What's next?
It is unclear whether he will face any disciplinary action from the FA, with friendlies against Brazil and the Asian Cup being held over the next six months.
Cristian Volpato's immediate availability for the Socceroos rests in the hands of Football Australia after NSW Police confirmed the World Cup star had tested positive for cocaine on a secondary test.
Volpato was pulled over by police on Sydney's Anzac Bridge on July 24 and returned a positive roadside reading for cocaine.
The 22-year-old then underwent independent testing at a private clinic, where it was claimed he returned a negative reading.
But Volpato was then sent for a secondary oral fluid test by police, which again confirmed a positive result for cocaine.
"On Tuesday 1 September 2026, a 22-year-old man was issued a Traffic Infringement Notice for drive motor vehicle with illicit drug present in oral fluid," NSW Police told AAP.
Volpato, who will face no further action, was handed a $722 fine as a result of the second positive test.
The Sassuolo forward had been pulled over by police after driving at 109 kilometres per hour in a 60km/h zone.
The Sydney-born youngster was a late inclusion for the Socceroos' World Cup campaign after switching his international allegiance from Italy to Australia on the eve of the tournament.
Volpato has maintained his innocence over the failed drugs test when he spoke to Football Australia (FA) staff, insisting that he never knowingly ingested the substance.
He also undertook a test when he returned to Italy which was negative, his club side, Sassuolo, said.
In a statement provided to AAP, Football Australia (FA) said: "Football Australia has been made aware of information concerning a reported secondary oral test result relating to one of our players. We are currently seeking independent verification.
"The matter is being managed in accordance with Football Australia's established protocols. To protect the integrity of this process and ensure procedural fairness, we will not comment further."
But the positive reading on Volpato's secondary police test could have major ramifications for his availability heading into January's Asian Cup.
Sources have told AAP that Volpato could be hauled before FA's disciplinary and ethics committee, where the sport's governing body has the power to suspend him from national team action.
The closest comparable case to Volpato's is that of A-League Women goalkeeper Teresa Morrissey, who tested positive for cannabis while driving.
Morrissey claimed the cannabis had been used for medicinal purposes, but was still slugged with a three-game ban by FA last year, which the goalkeeper's legal team had argued was disproportionate with her public profile.
Volpato's off-field indiscretion attracted headlines in Australia and in Italy, where he plays in Serie A.
He has played three games for Sassuolo this season, but failed to finish their last game against Bologna because of a suspected hamstring injury.
Socceroos coach Tony Popovic would not be drawn on whether he would pick Volpato for this month's friendlies with Brazil when he spoke at a press conference in Sydney on Tuesday.
"I don't know exactly the details of what happened and it would be wrong to speculate on what happened," Popovic told reporters.
"These young men, things happen and you can get caught for something we have to look into.
"There is a process that's playing out at the moment and we need to follow that process.
"When that is played out as it should, [only] then I can really comment on that."

US Supreme Court rejects Missouri bid to reactivate GOP-backed voting map
Unknown

US Supreme Court rejects Missouri bid to reactivate GOP-backed voting map
A separate federal court ruling, however, contradicts the Supreme Court judgement, leaving the map up in the air.
The United States Supreme Court has declined to reinstate a Republican-backed congressional map in Missouri, leaving in place an older map for November’s midterm elections.
On Tuesday, Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who handles emergency matters from Missouri, rejected the state’s request to put the new map into effect. He did not refer the case to the full nine-member court nor explain his decision.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3US judge blocks Trump’s latest effort to limit birthright citizenship
- list 2 of 3US Congress rejects constitutional amendment to restrict Supreme Court size
- list 3 of 3Missouri Supreme Court blocks Trump-backed map from November’s midterms
The decision is a setback for President Donald Trump and his Republican Party, which had backed the redistricting effort as part of a broader push to improve their electoral chances.
The new Republican-backed map would have given the party a better chance of winning an extra seat in the US House of Representatives by carving up Missouri’s Democratic-leaning 5th congressional district.
But the outcome of the legal battle remains unclear.
In the hours after Justice Kavanaugh’s decision, a federal court in Missouri temporarily blocked the older congressional map from being used.
That decision by US District Judge Stephen Clark, a Trump appointee, requires Missouri to use the new Republican-backed map for the November midterms.
His order will remain in effect for 14 days while courts consider the dispute. Opponents of the new map have already filed an appeal.
Tuesday’s contrasting court decisions are likely to boost confusion in Missouri, with less than two months to go before the midterm race.
The dispute centers on a congressional map approved by Missouri Republicans in 2025. Missouri joined several other right-leaning states, including Texas, in heeding Trump’s call to redraw their congressional districts to favour Republican candidates.
The new boundaries would have broken up the 5th congressional district, currently held by Democrat Emanuel Cleaver. The district includes much of Kansas City, but the new map would have seen parts of the older district shifted into neighbouring Republican-held districts.
Opponents of the partisan redistricting effort, however, gathered hundreds of thousands of signatures to force the new map to be put up for a vote.
That triggered the ongoing legal battle. Missouri’s Republican officials refused to accept the petition as legal, sparking a lawsuit.
The Missouri Supreme Court unanimously ruled last week that voters must approve the Republican-backed map in a statewide referendum before it can be used.
Kavanaugh’s decision on Tuesday would have allowed last week’s decision to stand. But Clark’s subsequent ruling has added another layer of uncertainty to the issue.
Also complicating the legal dynamics of the case is the fact that Missouri has already held its party primaries using the Republican-backed map.
Opponents of the map argue that Republican officials intentionally dismissed the referendum petition shortly before the primary, with no time to appeal.
Missouri’s Republican attorney general, Catherine Hanaway, argued that reverting to the older map would interfere with the election process, given that the primary was decided with the new map.
Hanaway also said the state “is prepared to follow and comply with” the Clark’s Tuesday order, which she said “binds the state to using” the new congressional districts.
At stake is Republican control over the US House. Republicans hold a narrow majority of 219 positions in the 435-seat chamber, including one right-leaning independent.
Democrats hold 214 seats, meaning the race for control of the chamber is likely to come down to a handful of elections.
As a result of Trump’s mid-decade redistricting push, Republicans improved their chances in roughly 16 districts across the country, including Cleaver’s seat in Missouri. Democrats, meanwhile, have gained an advantage in six districts.

four-level white platform stands as a collective throne at the western edge of greece
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
02:10:03 UTC
11:10:03 KST

Stepped Platform composes a Collective Viewpoint on Othoni
Developed during the Ionian Lab 2026 residency on Othoni, at the western edge of Greece, Dimitris Kontodimos’ West/End (For those who made it this far) takes the form of a four-level white platform positioned toward the open western horizon. The work begins with the island’s ancient association with the name Othronos, interpreted as ‘the throne.’ Rather than reproducing the throne as a singular seat of authority, Kontodimos expands it into a structure designed to be occupied collectively. Measuring 2.5 × 2.5 × 1.25 meters, the installation was built on site by the artist over two to three days from 22 mm MDF panels, which he measured, cut, and assembled himself. Part sculpture, part seating structure and part viewing platform, West/End was conceived from the outset to be used. Visitors can climb onto its stepped levels, sit together and face the sea. In doing so, the work transforms an otherwise unbuilt point in the landscape into a temporary place for collective observation.
West/End Connects Othoni’s Horizon with Histories of Migration
The work’s orientation is central to the project. In Greek, the word for west, dysi, derives from the ancient verb ‘dyo,’ to sink or submerge, referring to the movement of the sun as it disappears beneath the horizon. On Othoni, direction and ending become physically intertwined: the structure faces the setting sun, the edge of the land and the expanse beyond it. For Kontodimos, however, the West is also more than a geographic direction. The island’s history of migration informed the development of the work, introducing another reading of the horizon as a destination associated with departure, possibility, security and prosperity. The sculpture turns this political and cultural imaginary into a bodily experience: where one sits determines what one faces.
The subtitle, For those who made it this far, extends the ambiguity. ‘Making it’ can describe both the act of reaching a place and the idea of having succeeded once there. Rather than offering a monument to arrival, West/End creates a temporary collective throne from which the promise of elsewhere can be observed. The installation is ephemeral and will remain on Othoni until September 2026. ‘People had already found their own way to use it. Climbing up, sitting, facing west. No one needed to be told what it was for. They stayed until the sun was gone, then a little longer,’ mentions the artist.

French centrists struggle to find unity candidate as extremes surge in polls
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Gabriel Attal talks to Edouard Philippe during a meeting of French centrist Renaissance party, in Saint-Denis, France on April 6, 2025. | Thomas Samson/AFP via Getty Images
PARIS — Senior representatives for France’s feuding centrist presidential candidates are sitting down for lunch Wednesday to figure out who is best placed to take on Marine Le Pen in the spring 2027 election race to replace Emmanuel Macron.
But a compromise that could save the political center from being crushed by the extremes doesn’t look like it’s on the menu.
Supporters of Gabriel Attal and Edouard Philippe, two of Macron’s former prime ministers courting similar voters, are growing increasingly anxious that the duo’s internecine duel will drag on so long that it will damage the centrist camp’s chances.
Advertisement
Without a strong candidate from the center, their fear is that the election will slide inexorably into a clash between two anti-NATO euroskeptics who frighten financial markets: Le Pen on the far right and Jean-Luc Mélenchon on the far left.
The presidential election goes to a runoff if no one secures more than 50 percent of the vote. Le Pen appears all but certain to nab one of those spots given her polling numbers, but Mélenchon’s strong start to the campaign means he could well score ahead of Philippe and secure a spot in the second round.
Playing the long game
Despite the pressure to find a real challenger to Le Pen, the squabbling centrists hardly appear in a hurry to resolve their differences.
Attal, who trails Philippe in the polls, has in recent days tried to frame Philippe as out of touch. Asked about the remarks, Philippe responded that candidates sharing the center ground should direct their attacks against the extremes.
Attal’s campaign director Franck Riester told a small group of reporters Tuesday he doesn’t expect a resolution before February. Philippe said in an interview Tuesday he didn’t think a single candidate would emerge before next year.
Instead, Wednesday’s lunch — the latest in a series of regular parleys among the centrists — will be a moment to “air grievances,” according to Riester.
Advertisement
“We will continue to discuss the campaign, ways to avoid inflicting irreparable damage [on each other], and agree on a code of conduct,” he said.
Attal and his advisers started organizing the meetings in the spring, after Philippe launched his campaign but before Attal’s announcement, to ensure the centrist bloc remained united. But the encounters have been marred by disagreements over how to rally around a single champion.
A lawmaker from Philippe’s party, Horizons, concurred that Tuesday’s meeting would not lead to a breakthrough.
Marine Le Pen is seen at Roland Garros in Paris on Aug. 27, 2026. | Mael Ghazi/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images
“We are going because we are polite but we’ve never believed in it,” said the MP, who was, like others quoted in this story, granted anonymity to speak candidly.
Yet Philippe on Tuesday said that like-minded rivals should again meet in early November to chart a path forward. Attal quickly shot back that Philippe is duplicating his own initiative, while Bruno Retailleau, the leader of the conservative Les Républicains, said he won’t attend a meeting of “Macronists.”
Ruinous infighting
While polls suggest Philippe is among the best-placed candidates to mount a serious challenge to Le Pen, the plethora of hopefuls in the political center is allowing the two anti-establishment candidates to dominate the public discourse on everything from banning the hijab to writing off massive chunks of French debt.
Advertisement
One former centrist minister said that “internal competition” between Philippe and Attal, who are the closest ideologically, could end up destroying a centrist bloc that already faces an uphill battle given voter dissatisfaction with Macron’s presidency.
“The risk is that the winner ends up ruling over a wasteland,” said the former minister.
Given the increasing difficulties in reaching an agreement with Attal’s camp, some Philippe supporters are hoping for an alliance with the once-dominant Les Républicains, which Philippe once belonged to. Retailleau, the party’s candidate, is trailing Attal and Philippe in the polls.
But an alliance there too seems elusive. Retailleau last week said he would keep on campaigning “until victory.”

In Germany, Merz’s center-left partners rebel after far-right rout
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

In Germany, Merz’s center-left partners rebel after far-right rout
The SPD’s strategic pivot is likely to deepen Merz’s myriad challenges as questions mount over his ability to lead Germany’s relatively weak coalition government.
From left: Markus Söder, Friedrich Merz, Bärbel Bas and Lars Klingbeil. They're pictured in Berlin after coalition consultations on July 2, 2026. | Tobias Schwarz/AFP via Getty Images
BERLIN — Friedrich Merz’s center-left coalition partners increasingly see themselves facing a stark choice: Turn against the reform course they’ve struck with the chancellor or risk sinking with him.
Following the conservatives’ stinging defeat to the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday — a loss driven in great part by dissatisfaction with Merz and his party, the Christian Democratic Union — there are early signs the Social Democratic Party is turning against the series of reforms it has agreed to push through with the unpopular chancellor.
The SPD’s pivot is likely to deepen Merz’s myriad challenges as questions mount over his ability to lead Germany’s relatively weak coalition government. Merz has acknowledged that his dismal approval ratings helped fuel the AfD’s victory in Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday, but argues that the answer is to press ahead with his reform agenda while doing a better job of explaining its necessity to voters.
Advertisement
That’s not the conclusion his center-left coalition partners have drawn: They argue the problem isn’t one of messaging but of substance.
“The path the federal government has taken with its reform plans has caused particular uncertainty,” Rasha Nasr, an SPD lawmaker in the Bundestag, told POLITICO’s Berlin Playbook Podcast. “It’s very important now that, unlike others in the coalition, we don’t just push this through. The people of Saxony-Anhalt have told us very clearly: ‘This far and no further,’” she added.
Merz has staked his chancellorship on tackling economic and welfare reforms that previous governments deemed too politically difficult, even branding himself the “reform chancellor.” His agenda includes raising the retirement age to shore up the pension system, cutting some health-insurance benefits to curb rising premiums and making it harder for workers to take sick leave in an effort to boost growth.
Tim Klüssendorf, who has said there are reform measures that need to be addressed, is seen at a press conference after an Social Democratic Party leadership meeting in Berlin in March 2026. | John Macdougall/AFP via Getty Images
Until now, the SPD under the leadership of Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil has advanced the reform drive, portraying itself as willing to undertake the tough choices needed to restore Germany’s economy while fighting inside the coalition to resist conservative excesses.
But given Merz’s growing troubles — and rising questions about the durability of the coalition government — the party’s calculus appears to have changed. The shift also comes ahead of two additional state elections on Sept. 20 in which the SPD is hoping to score at least one much-needed win.
Klingbeil signaled a course change already on the night of the Saxony-Anhalt election. The result provides “a reason to reflect on policies here in Berlin and on the federal government’s reform agenda,” Klingbeil told public broadcaster ZDF as votes were still being counted. “And rest assured, that’s exactly what we’ll do.”
Advertisement
The open disagreement prompted the chancellor to discuss divisions between the coalition parties with SPD leaders Klingbeil and Bärbel Bas on Monday via phone, according to a senior government official who was granted anonymity to discuss internal matters.
SPD hopes for redemption
Given its own political weakness, the SPD is very unlikely to pull the plug on the current coalition — a move that would trigger new elections while its poll numbers are scraping historic lows. The party is currently polling at around 12 percent, 4.4 percentage points below its share of the vote in the 2025 federal election, which was its worst result in well over a century.
But the recent signals from SPD leaders suggest they are looking ahead to their own political survival as Merz’s chancellorship grows increasingly precarious.
Manuela Schwesig, the SPD premier of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania who has been able to cut into the Alternative for Germany’s lead in the eastern state, campaigns in Lützow on Aug. 21, 2026. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images
It also comes as the SPD sees a rare glimmer of hope for an election boon that could restore some of the party’s battered political standing.
In the eastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania ahead of a Sept. 20 election, the SPD’s incumbent premier, Manuela Schwesig, is polling a strong second behind the AfD. Under Schwesig — who ranks among Germany’s most well-liked politicians, according to surveys — the SPD has been able to cut into the far right’s lead in recent weeks.
An SPD victory in the state — or even a serious challenge to the AfD’s lead — could give the beleaguered center-left party a desperately needed political boost.
Advertisement
But what’s more significant for Germany’s coalition is the way Schwesig has at least in part attained her popularity: by railing against Merz’s reform drive, depicting the overhauls as harsh and unjust.
“Yes, we need social reforms, the welfare state must be stabilized, and labor costs must not rise,” she told Welt TV on Monday. “But it is unacceptable that, of all people, those who work the hardest and contribute the most are the ones bearing the heaviest burden. Many people also perceive this as unfair. And that is why it is important to change course here.”
Should the SPD congeal around Schwesig and her criticisms, it’s likely to further complicate Merz’s ability to govern and pass legislation that satisfies his increasingly restive conservative faction.
‘Unwavering determination’
Already, disagreements between the SPD and Merz’s conservatives are spilling into the open.
SPD politicians are questioning the coalition’s previously agreed plan to make it harder for workers to take sick days, a measure that sparked public outrage and, for many, reinforced Merz’s image as lacking empathy with regular people. SPD politicians have also called for renewed state subsidies to lower fuel prices — a proposal Merz’s CDU rejects as too expensive.
“Clearly, when it comes to specific measures, there are certainly issues we need to address this fall,” Tim Klüssendorf, the SPD’s general secretary, said of the reforms on German television this week. “Take, for example, pensions, long-term care, and health care, but also the question of whether we’re finally going to do something about these gas prices, including through regulatory measures. These are certainly the measures that must now be put on the table as a direct consequence of the election results.”
Advertisement
Merz, for his part, is sticking to his line that people would agree to his reforms if they better understood their importance.
“This is about nothing more and nothing less than the future of our country and the opportunities for our children and grandchildren,” he said Monday. “And we must not squander them. That is why my determination to continue on the path of reform remains unwavering.”

New CEO, foldable iPhone, AI: Apple faces a pivotal keynote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
01:55:58 UTC
10:55:58 KST

Washington, DC — Apple heads into its September 9 keynote with a new CEO, a potentially transformative new iPhone and growing pressure to prove it can turn its artificial-intelligence ambitions into products consumers actually want.
The event will be John Ternus' first major product launch since taking over as Apple CEO from Tim Cook on September 1, ending Cook's 15-year tenure at the helm. Ternus, a longtime Apple hardware engineer, now faces one of his first major tests in the job as the company prepares to unveil its latest products.
The biggest expected reveal is Apple's first foldable iPhone, a device that would mark the company's entry into a category pioneered by rivals such as Samsung.
Reports suggest the phone could carry a price tag of around $2,000 or more, putting it firmly in Apple's premium tier and testing how much consumers are willing to pay for a new form factor.
But the keynote is about more than hardware.
Apple's AI strategy will be closely watched, particularly the company's efforts to overhaul Siri and make its AI capabilities more useful in everyday interactions.
The company has faced criticism for delays to some of its promised AI features, making the next stage of Apple Intelligence an important test of whether Apple can close the gap with rivals such as Google and OpenAI.
Here is what to expect from Apple's September 9 keynote:
John Ternus' first major product launch
Ternus became Apple's CEO on September 1, succeeding Cook after 15 years. He joined Apple in 2001 and rose through the hardware engineering ranks, eventually becoming the company's senior vice president of hardware engineering.
He is the first product engineer to lead Apple, according to the Financial Times.
That background makes the timing of his first major keynote particularly significant. Rather than inheriting a company in the middle of a quiet transition, Ternus is taking the stage as Apple prepares to introduce one of its most significant new hardware categories in years.
The question is whether Ternus can maintain the operational discipline associated with the Cook era while giving Apple a convincing new direction in hardware and AI.
A foldable iPhone
The foldable iPhone is expected to be the headline announcement.
Apple has stayed out of the foldable-phone market while Samsung and other manufacturers have spent years developing the technology.
The expected device would therefore represent Apple's first major entry into a category that has remained relatively small but could receive a significant boost from Apple's arrival.
Reports suggest the device could cost more than $2,000, although the final price has not been confirmed. The phone is also expected to sit at the high end of Apple's lineup rather than replace its conventional iPhone models.
For Apple, the challenge will be to make the technology feel less like a novelty and more like an obvious evolution of the iPhone.
The next test for Siri and Apple Intelligence
AI could prove just as important as the hardware.
Apple has spent the past two years positioning Apple Intelligence as a major part of its future, but delays to some of its most ambitious Siri upgrades have raised questions about whether the company is moving quickly enough to keep pace with competitors.
The revamped Siri is therefore likely to attract intense attention. Apple does not necessarily need to announce an entirely new AI product.
The more important question is whether it can demonstrate AI features that are useful, reliable and deeply integrated into the devices people already use.
Reports suggest the new Siri will rely partly on technology from Google, underscoring the pressure Apple faces as it tries to strengthen its position in the AI race.
What else to expect
Alongside the foldable iPhone, Apple is expected to unveil new high-end iPhone models, including the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max.
New Apple Watch models and AirPods are also expected to feature in the event, although Apple has not confirmed the products ahead of the keynote.
That leaves Ternus with a particularly consequential debut. Apple's latest keynote is not simply the launch of another iPhone generation.
It is the first major public showcase of the company under its new CEO, with a foldable iPhone and AI strategy likely to provide the clearest early clues about where Apple is headed next.

Pilots tried to abort landing seconds before deadly Amazon cargo plane crash that killed five
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
01:53:52 UTC
10:53:52 KST

Officials in Florida on Tuesday said evidence collected from Saturday’s Amazon cargo plane crash at Miami international airport suggests the pilots considered aborting the flight’s landing before it crashed and killed five people on the ground.
At a press conference on Tuesday evening, officials from the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) released data from the plane’s “black box” flight data recorder, which was recovered from the wreckage on Monday, indicating pilots initiated a “go-around”, or aborted landing, seconds before impact.
The NTSB said that 30 seconds before the end of the flight data recording, the nose landing gear and right main landing gear touched down, while 19 seconds before the end of the recording, the left main landing gear touched down.
A few seconds later, the brakes were released and the throttles were increased to values consistent with go-around thrust.
The NTSB added there was no indication in the recorded data that speed brakes or thrust reversers were deployed.
Jennifer Homendy, the NTSB chair, said the pilots will be interviewed on Wednesday, and details from the cockpit voice recorder will be released publicly after that interview.
The NTSB will be conducting further analysis on the flight data and other available evidence to determine the cause of the accident, officials said.
Earlier Tuesday, officials identified the five people killed on Saturday – and said two more remained hospitalized in critical condition.
At a morning news conference, the Miami-Dade sheriff, Rosie Cordero-Stutz, also said both pilots of the Amazon Prime Air Boeing 767, which careered off the end of the airport’s runway and struck at least two vehicles, were released from the hospital after treatment.
The aircrew, whom she did not name, were the only two people onboard.
The sheriff identified Rolando Aleman Leon, 55; Yoel Rodriguez Narajo, 53; Julio C Pineda, 75; Carlos Acosta Fajardo, 53; and Javierkys Reyes Quevedo, 47, as those killed on the ground.
All five dead and the two people most seriously hurt – men aged 79 and 32 – were in a Ford Econoline van that was hit by the aircraft, operated by the all-cargo airline 21 Air llc under contract to Amazon, while it landed after a flight from San Juan, Puerto Rico, and crashed through fencing on to a roadway.
The victims killed were employees of Professional Ocean Service Corporation, an aircraft contract cleaning company, which released a statement on Tuesday paying tribute to its dead workers.
“Our employees are far more than the people who work beside us each day, they are family, and they are deeply loved,” the statement said.
“Our hearts and prayers are with every employee and every family whose lives have been forever changed. We grieve with those who lost a loved one and pray for the healing and recovery of those who were injured.”
The lives of the families of the victims had been torn apart, Cordero-Stutz told reporters at the news conference.
“[We’re] trying to identify what happened and how it occurred, but for those families, they are going to be living with this for the rest of their lives,” she said.
“So it’s a very difficult time, and it’s very difficult on each and every one of these families.”
Investigators from the NTSB continued their examination of the crash site on Tuesday as the airport began to return to normal operations after three days of cancellations and delays.
At a press conference on Monday afternoon, Homendy said teams were working through a scene of “utter devastation” after the crash, which occurred after a thunderstorm.
The aircraft, she said, traveled about 1,300ft beyond the paved surface at the end of the runway and through a perimeter fence. The crash left a wide field of debris, including airbags and other parts of the destroyed vehicles, sections of the aircraft, and fencing.
“It’s pretty extensive,” she said. “Hard to see, and I’m sure it must have been very difficult for the responders as well. I would describe it in one word as devastating, utter devastation.”
Video showed the plane touched down far along the runway, prompting speculation its speed was too high to be able to stop safely.
Other factors being examined, Homendy said, were weather conditions before and during the landing, and the mechanical condition of the 32-year-old plane that was completing its third flight of the day.
Although the NTSB team would remain on site for about a week, she added, they would focus on recovering as much “perishable” evidence as possible, and not immediately determining a cause.
Some industry experts have said they believe the circumstances of the crash point towards pilot error. They include Robert Clifford, an aviation attorney who has handled cases in numerous commercial aircraft crashes spanning five decades.
“This appears to be a classic tailwind landing mistake where a pilot mistakenly or over-confidently decides to land with a tailwind instead of a headwind,” he said in a statement to the Guardian.
That, he said, “causes excessive touchdown speed and distance from the threshold, leaving inadequate stopping distance for the airplane’s braking and reverse thrust systems to handle”.
Clifford also noted the absence of any arresting devices or fencing at the end of the runway commonly found at other major airports. Homendy said on Monday the NTSB would be looking at that to determine its impact on the severity of the Miami tragedy.
Amazon, meanwhile, said it would work closely with federal investigators on the investigation. Homendy said her team would also examine the relationship between Amazon and 21 Air, the Miami-based aircraft operator.

  Reuters contributed reporting

IN BRIEF
- The 82-year-old died after complications from influenza.
- An acclaimed writer, d'Alpuget published her final novel in 2025, at 81.
Blanche d'Alpuget, the Australian writer and widow of former prime minister Bob Hawke, has died.
D'Alpuget died on Tuesday from complications from influenza. She was 82.
In a statement, d'Alpuget's family remembered her as someone who lived "entirely on her own terms".
"She was full of vitality, generosity and curiosity, with an extraordinary appetite for beauty, ideas, history, new places and spirited conversation. She refused to be confined by convention or by other people's expectations of who she should be," they said.
"We will miss her force, her humour, her curiosity and her love beyond measure."

They shared the words d'Alpuget lived by: “Our highest calling and greatest achievement is love, the rule of life. Love one another."
Having never lost her appetite for life, d'Alpuget refused to be confined by convention or by other people's expectations of who she should be, the family said.
Just two years before her death, at age 80, she swam with whale sharks in Indonesia and a year later published her final novel, a murder mystery entitled The Bunny Club.
She is survived by her son, artist and sculptor Louis Pratt, daughter-in-law Brianna and granddaughter Sienna.
The author married Hawke in 1995 after a tumultuous on-again, off-again affair that ran throughout the tenure of his prime ministership.
The pair, who met at a party in 1970, remained together for 24 years until his death in 2019.
Hawke controversially divorced his first wife, the popular Hazel, in 1994, which caused great family upheaval. She died in 2013.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has shared his condolences, saying Australia has lost "a true one-off".
"As a writer, she was at home in fiction as she was in non-fiction, working in each realm with a keen eye for every telling detail that opened up the humanity of her subject to her readers," he said.
"Blanche’s novels were compelling works of verve and originality, and her biographies comprehensive and definitive – most famously those she wrote of Bob Hawke, who became her great love and ultimately her husband."
Born in Sydney on January 3, 1944, d'Alpuget was shaped by early travels in Indonesia, Malaysia and Europe with first husband and diplomat, Tony Pratt, with whom she had her son.
She began a more than six-decade career as a writer at The Daily Mirror and Woman's Day in Sydney and later at the News of the World in London.
Gaining literary acclaim for her fictional works, d'Alpuget was also a lauded biographer, including a 1982 book on her later husband titled, Robert J. Hawke: A Biography.
She met Hawke in Jakarta in 1970, but reconnected later in life — taking a job writing his biography, work that would later cement her as an award-winning writer.
The pair were married in 1995, and shared over two decades together before Hawke's death in 2019.
Among a flood of tributes were several from prominent figures from across the Labor Party and publishing industry.
Federal minister Chris Bowen said d'Alpuget had cemented herself in the nation's culture and memory.
"Blanche was always delightful company. She lit up a room and was always full of joy and empathy," Mr Bowen said.
A former publicity agent for the author described her "incredible aura, an infectious, positive energy that swept up everyone around her".
"Indefatigable, quick-witted, curious and endlessly interesting, she was one of the most remarkable people we've had the privilege of working with," the agency said.

Ukrainian drones struck Novorossiysk naval base and fuel terminal overnight on Sept. 9, Ukraine's General Staff said.
Fires were reported at the naval base and at the seaport's fuel oil terminal in the southern Russian city of Novorossiysk overnight, according to the General Staff.
The extent of the damage is being assessed, the General Staff added.
The Russian frigate Admiral Essen is burning as a result of the strikes, Ukraine's military intelligence agency (HUR) said on Sept. 9. The Admiral Essen typically carries Kalibr cruise missiles, which Russia has repeatedly used to strike Ukrainian cities and infrastructure.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Sept. 9 that a terminal used for oil shipments, facilities within the military harbor, warships, and Kalibr launchers were hit in Novorossiysk.
"We are responding to Russia's daily terrorist attacks – effectively and across virtually the entire territory," Zelensky said.
A residential building in the city was also damaged in the strikes, not injuring anybody, independent Russian news channel Astra reported, citing eyewitness footage.
Novorossiysk Mayor Andrey Kravchenko confirmed that a Ukrainian drone attack took place, saying that debris from downed drones has fallen on "the territory of enterprises" and near a residential building, without specifying at which sites.
In separate attacks, Ukraine hit 13 of Russia's shadow fleet vessels in the Black Sea, Robert "Madyar" Brovdi, commander of Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces, said on Sept. 9.
Ukraine regularly strikes military infrastructure deep within Russia and the occupied territories in an effort to diminish Moscow's ability to continue waging its war.
Overnight on Sept. 8, Ukrainian drones reportedly struck Russia's Saratov Oil Refinery, according to footage shared by locals on social media and analyzed by monitoring groups.
On Sept. 7, Ukraine's General Staff said that overnight drone strikes hit a railway bridge over the North Crimean Canal in Russian-occupied Crimea near the village of Vladyslavivka, which hosts a key railway junction in the area.
Meanwhile, Russia continues to strike Ukrainian civilians in cities across the country.
A major missile and drone attack targeting Kyiv overnight on Sept. 8 killed at least five people and injured 35 others. The Russian strikes sparked huge fires that filled the morning air across the city with smoke.
