Sharpeville massacre, 66 years on: Families still wait for justice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
00:24:57 UTC
09:24:57 KST

Sharpeville massacre, 66 years on: Families still wait for justice
More than six decades after police opened fire on protesters, survivors and relatives are taking their fight to court.
Sharpeville, South Africa – Paulina Mathinye was five years old when her father left home for a meeting near the police station in Sharpeville, a township south of Johannesburg.
She remembers waiting for him to return.
“I’ll go run to him,” Mathinye recalled thinking. “He will pick me up like daddies always do with their beloved daughters.”
He never did.
On March 21, 1960, Mathinye’s father joined other men from the community at a gathering protesting apartheid’s pass laws, which required Black South Africans to carry documents restricting where they could live and work.
“There was a meeting here at the old police station, so he accompanies those fathers to the meeting. But then he never came back.”
Police opened fire on the protesters that day in what became known as the Sharpeville Massacre.
Apartheid-era police records put the death toll at 69 and the number of injured at 180. Research published in 2024 using police records found that as many as 91 people may have been killed and 238 injured. The higher figures are also cited by lawyers representing Sharpeville survivors and families.
The massacre became a defining moment in South Africa’s struggle against apartheid. March 21 is now commemorated as Human Rights Day, and South Africa’s democratic Constitution was signed in Sharpeville in 1996.
But for the families of those killed and injured, the consequences did not end that day.
More than six decades later, survivors and relatives are seeking redress through the courts.
Lawyers for Human Rights has filed an application in the Gauteng High Court challenging the continued existence of the Indemnity Act 61 of 1961, an apartheid-era law that the applicants say prevented survivors and dependants of those killed from pursuing civil and criminal proceedings arising from the massacre.
The applicants are also seeking certification of a class action involving survivors who were shot and dependants of those killed.
For Mathinye, the legal fight is inseparable from the life that followed her father’s death.
He had been the family’s breadwinner. After he was killed, her mother worked as a domestic worker to support five children.
“We sometimes go to bed with empty stomach. We sometimes go to school and when we come back from school we find nothing to eat.”
There was no electricity, and sometimes her mother could not afford even a candle for the children to study.
“There was no light. There was no library. Struggle even to buy a candle, a mere candle.”
Mathinye wanted to become a teacher.
She stayed in school and applied to study further, but her family could not afford it. She eventually began working while still young to help support her mother and siblings.
When she encounters people she went to school with who became teachers and nurses, she thinks about the life she might have had.
“If my father was not shot, maybe I was going to be one of those people… Maybe by this time I would be a teacher.”
Why now?
The effort to seek redress is not new.
Charne Tracey-Mamdoo, a lawyer in the Strategic Litigation Programme at Lawyers for Human Rights, told Al Jazeera that victims and families attempted to pursue claims soon after the massacre.
“Immediately after the Sharpeville massacre, victims and families did attempt to pursue these sorts of claims, but they were barred because in 1961 the apartheid government enacted the Indemnity Act.”
The applicants argue that the Act created a legal barrier to civil and criminal proceedings arising from conduct covered by the legislation.
The current case challenges that barrier.
Lawyers for Human Rights is asking the High Court to declare the Indemnity Act unconstitutional and invalid. It is also seeking certification of a class action for survivors who were shot and dependants of those killed.
The applicants must first persuade the court to grant the constitutional relief they seek and certify the proposed class action. If the case proceeds, individual claims for damages could then be pursued.
More than 70 survivors and relatives have expressed support for or interest in the proposed litigation, according to Lawyers for Human Rights.
Tracey-Mamdoo said lawyers had spent years locating surviving victims and witnesses, reconstructing claims and gathering historical and expert evidence.
The survivors’ age has added urgency. Many of those directly affected by the massacre are now elderly, and some who spent decades seeking redress have died without seeing the matter resolved.
An inheritance of loss
Ishmael Poho was six years old when his father left home for a community meeting on March 21.
Poho wanted to go with him.
“He said, ‘No, I’ll come back. You need to stay home.’”
Poho saw his father again briefly that day.
“That was the last time I saw my father that day.”
It took his mother three days to find his body.
According to Poho’s account, related partly through an interpreter, his mother searched police stations before eventually finding him among bodies that had been placed in garages.
“At that station, there were vehicle garages as part of the building and the infrastructure. However, bodies were piled up or stacked up in those garages,” the interpreter said.
His father’s death changed the family’s circumstances.
His mother had never worked and did not speak English. She eventually found work as a domestic worker in a nearby white neighbourhood. As the children grew older, they also worked to support the household.
Poho, now 72, thinks about the people he went to school with who became teachers, nurses and other health professionals.
“If my father was alive, I would have been different. My life would have been different from the life I have lived.”
For Mauleen Maine, the loss began before she was born.
Her uncle was 23 when he was killed.
According to family history passed down by her grandmother, he had returned from a night shift, gone to buy bread and then returned to the meeting.
He had been the family’s breadwinner.
After his death, Maine’s grandmother struggled financially and eventually sold liquor to survive. She died without seeing the matter resolved.
Maine’s parents later continued seeking redress. They too died without seeing justice.
Now Maine, 62, is continuing the effort.
She told Al Jazeera through an interpreter that compensation alone would not be enough. Her family also wants better housing and educational opportunities for their children.
For families like hers, the question is not only what was lost in 1960, but what might have been different in the decades that followed.
What would justice mean?
For Vincent Thamae, a member of Voices of Sharpeville who has worked with survivors and families, the case cannot be reduced to compensation.
“It’s not a question of the amount of money. It’s the question of how much does it need for a change in the lives of the victims and survivors?”
Thamae argues that the effects of the massacre reached beyond those who were shot.
“The victims were not only those who were shot,” he said. “We maintain even the whole township was a victim.”
Lawyers for Human Rights says the plaintiffs also want dialogue with the South African government about appropriate reparations and recognition.
The formal court case, however, is narrower. The applicants are challenging the Indemnity Act and seeking relief that would enable the proposed class action to proceed. The court has not yet ruled that the Act is unconstitutional, nor has it determined that the government is liable to compensate the applicants.
That distinction matters because Sharpeville occupies a powerful place in South Africa’s democratic identity.
It is remembered every year as a symbol of the struggle for human rights.
For some of the families who lived through the massacre, however, remembrance has not amounted to redress.
Lawyers for Human Rights says 51 Sharpeville survivors were formally awarded reparations through the Truth and Reconciliation Commission process.
Poho had expected the democratic government to address the concerns of survivors and families.
“We were happy that a Black government had stepped into office, and we were hopeful that our issues would be met and, you know, justice realised, only to realise it became worse. Nothing ever came.”
The government respondents will have an opportunity to respond to the application before the High Court considers the relief sought.
There is no clear timetable for the proceedings.
For Tracey-Mamdoo, the age of the survivors makes the case urgent.
“They’ve already waited a very long time for this to happen and we are doing everything we can to just kind of move that process forward.”
Mathinye is now 71. Poho is 72.
Their fathers died more than six decades ago.
Their families have lived with the consequences ever since.
Children grew up without fathers. Breadwinners were lost. Educational opportunities disappeared. Mothers struggled to keep households afloat. And in some families, the next generation inherited not only the consequences of the massacre but also the fight for redress.
Sharpeville is remembered as a turning point in South Africa’s history.
For these families, the story remains unfinished.
And Mathinye is still asking the question she has carried since she was five.
“Why did they shoot my father?”

Skepticism and Fallibilism,
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
00:23:00 UTC
09:23:00 KST

Scepticism is the view that we know almost nothing. Despite its historical pedigree, and its centrality both as a topic of research and as a staple of undergraduate syllabi, this view has few contemporary defenders. Instead, it is primarily evoked in ways that presuppose its falsity, as when epistemologists debate where particular arguments for scepticism go wrong, or object to an otherwise appealing thesis because of its sceptical consequences.
Skepticism and Fallibilism calls for a different approach: we should develop scepticism into a positive theory of what knowledge is, and what we would have to be like to have it. Occasionally, Kvanvig seems to suggest that this may make scepticism more defensible, giving it tools to resist quick dismissal on the grounds that it is too radical and implausible to be taken seriously (27). But the more consistent theme, adapting Stroud (1984), is that developing a positive sceptical theory will reveal insights that non-sceptical theories should aim to integrate.
The book proceeds as follows. Chapter 2 argues that, if scepticism is to be illuminating, we need to do more than formulate sceptical arguments: mainly because, for broadly Moorean reasons, it will always be more plausible to reject one of the premises of such an argument than to accept its conclusion. Chapter 3 argues that we shouldn’t be satisfied with standard non-sceptical theories: they don’t adequately explain the temptation to think that knowledge is incompatible with the possibility of error. Together, these motivate Chapters 4 and 5, which develop a sceptical conception of knowledge, and defend it against a challenge that Kvanvig regards as particularly significant—more on this below. Chapter 6 then develops a non-sceptical conception of knowledge as suitably approximating the state identified by the sceptic’s conception. Chapter 7 concludes with lessons for the importance of epistemic humility.
This review will focus on Chapters 4 and 5, which serve as the book’s fulcrum, and contain some of its most original ideas.
According to Kvanvig, scepticism is driven by infallibilism, the view that knowledge is incompatible with any risk of error. After rejecting alternatives, Chapter 4 proposes to understand infallibility in terms of control, which is itself understood in terms of abilities. While I couldn’t quite find a canonical statement, I take the proposal to be that a belief amounts to knowledge just in case the facts about which powers and abilities were exercised in forming the belief completely explain why the belief is true.[1] Let us stipulatively refer to such beliefs as i-knowledge; the sceptic/infallibilist’s distinctive claim would then be that knowledge is i-knowledge.
I’m not sure that this really is the right way of articulating a sceptical/infallibilist position, at least if we want a characterization that is neutral on other controversial questions in the area.
Firstly, I worry that i-knowledge may not be enough for knowledge. Perhaps someone could have an infallible perceptual power while having good reasons to doubt that they have such a power (some versions of Bonjour’s (1980) clairvoyant come to mind); if so, it’s tempting to think that their perceptual beliefs aren’t always knowledge, even though they are i-knowledge. Or they could have perfect deductive capacities and working memory, but be uncertain that they do; it’s then tempting to think that the beliefs they form through complex deductive reasoning aren’t knowledge, even though they are i-knowledge. This second version of the concern is closely connected to one of the main challenges to scepticism as a positive position, namely that it becomes unstable or self-undermining once generalized to logical or epistemological domains.[2] Not discussing it thus feels like a missed opportunity.
Secondly, I worry that beliefs that are intuitively “fallible” could amount to i-knowledge, given certain views about abilities. Earlier in the book, Kvanvig briefly considers non-sceptical views sometimes associated with infallibilism, citing McDowell (1994) and Williamson (2000); he suggests that these views aren’t genuinely infallibilist because “they make no pretence of claiming that our epistemic assurances are maximal” (44). However, an important theme in this tradition is that the mental states and processes involved in the “good cases” of knowledge are not of the same kind as those involved in the “bad cases” of error. It seems a small step from there to thinking that they do not involve the exercise of the same powers or abilities, say because the ability exercised in the good case is an ability to know, and one only genuinely exercises an ability when one does so successfully.[3] But if bad cases don’t involve the exercise of the same powers or abilities as good cases, then many of our ordinary beliefs qualify as i-knowledge.
But let’s set those worries aside, and return to the main strand. Having articulated an infallibilist conception of knowledge, Kvanvig introduces a challenge for the sceptic/infallibilist that dominates the remainder of these chapters: that of showing that beings recognizably like us could in principle have powers that enable us to have i-knowledge. In fact, he sets an even higher bar: the sceptic/infallibilist should try to show that, for each of the abilities or powers that we ordinarily think of as producing knowledge, there are recognizable idealizations of those abilities or powers that could result in i-knowledge. If this challenge can’t be met, Kvanvig holds, then i-knowledge is too far removed from our ordinary epistemic concepts and practices to illuminate them.
Kvanvig argues that this challenge is relatively straightforward to meet for many of our modes of inquiry, such as perception, deduction, testimony, and rational intuition. (I’m less sure, but won’t press that point here.) However, Kvanvig worries that the challenge initially looks insurmountable in the case of nonmonotonic (or “defeasible”) reasoning, paradigmatically exemplified by inductive beliefs about the future. This is an interesting, and I think important, observation: unlike most of our other trusted methods of belief formation, defeasible inference seems to wear its fallibility on its sleeve. As such, our willingness to use defeasible inference, and to sometimes treat the products of such inferences as knowledge, pose a distinctive challenge to infallibilism.
Chapter 5 aims to address this challenge on behalf of the sceptic/infallibilist. The solution is framed in terms of defeasible reasoning machines that draw out all of the defeasible consequences of a given set of inputs. What makes the consequences defeasible (or nonmonotonic) is that the machine may not draw conclusions from a set of inputs that it would have drawn from a subset of those inputs: e.g., it may not conclude that all ravens are black when the input consists of a hundred black and one white raven, even though it does draw this conclusion when the input consists of only the hundred black ravens. We can then distinguish inputs according to whether they will result in completion, that is, whether a machine given those inputs will take a stance on every question. Kvanvig’s proposed response to his challenge is that, given other assumptions that the sceptic may legitimately help themselves to, one can ensure that defeasible reasoning never introduces error to one’s belief system “by restricting one’s use of defeasible reasoning to contexts where an initial supposition state leads to completion” (141).
Let’s grant, for the sake of argument, that such a restriction would count as a reasonable idealization. That still leaves the question of whether it is enough to guarantee infallibility. On the face of it, the answer seems to be no. Suppose that the world is extremely simple: all it contains are 100 black ravens and one white raven. I have observed only the 100 black ones, and have thus concluded that all ravens, including the one I haven’t yet seen, are black. I have thus reached completion: I take a stance on every question. My input observations, moreover, were unfailingly accurate. And yet my use of defeasible reasoning has introduced error into my belief state.
What, on Kvanvig’s account, prevents this possibility? It seems to be the assumption that “truth leaves tracks”—that for any truth, (fallible) evidence for that truth can be found; this is an assumption that Kvanvig argues that the sceptic may legitimately help themselves to (115-117) and explicitly appeals to in his argument that completion entails infallibility (138-141). But I don’t see how this assumption helps. We can add to my story that I will eventually examine the final raven and discover that it is white, so that no truth remains hidden from me forever—this does not prevent me from using defeasible reasoning to form a complete but mistaken picture of reality before I do.
Where does Kvanvig’s reasoning go wrong? I suspect it is in his argument that when defeasible reasoning results in completion, there can be no “external” defeaters for the resulting beliefs, i.e., no truths that you are unaware of such that, if you became aware of them, you would have to revise one of the beliefs. (In my example above, the final raven being white is such an external defeater.) Kvanvig argues that the “truth leaves tracks” assumption rules out such external defeaters:
Once this assumption is in place, the tracks created would need to be accommodated by the reasoning program, … and thus tracks that defeat would end up being subsumed in the system of information on which the program operates, thereby counting as internal defeaters. (139)
The reasoning seems to be that the external defeater would have left tracks; that these tracks must be available to the program; and that, therefore, any potential defeating force of the external defeater is already accounted for by the program. But why think that the tracks, even if they exist, are available to the program? This seems to illicitly move from the assumption that evidence for a truth can always be found to the much stronger assumption that all reasoning machines have always already found this evidence.[4] The only fix I can see is to strengthen the idealization, restricting the use of defeasible inference only to contexts where all possible evidence has been obtained. But, at that point, we have surely idealized too far for the result to be anything like our own use of defeasible reasoning.
Overall then, I’m not convinced by the positive theory that Skepticism and Fallibilism develops on behalf of the sceptic. What seems importantly correct, however, is its insistence that developing such a theory as clearly as possible, and exploring how it responds to Kvanvig’s challenge (whether by trying to meet it or by explaining why it is misplaced), would benefit all reasonable epistemologies, sceptical or not.
REFERENCES

McDowell, John (1994). Mind and World. Cambridge MA: Harvard UP.
Millar, Alan (2019). Knowing by Perceiving. Oxford: Oxford UP.
Rinard, Susanna (2018). “Reasoning One’s Way out of Skepticism” in Kevin McCain & Ted Poston, (2018) The Mystery of Skepticism: New Explorations. Boston: Brill. pp. 240-264.
Stroud, Barry (1984) The Significance of Philosophical Skepticism. Oxford: Oxford UP.

ACKNOWLEDGMENTS
Thanks to Brendan de Kenessey and Joshua Thorpe for helpful comments on an earlier draft.
[1] This is adapted from the guiding idea that knowledge requires total control and that “one is in total control of an epistemic situation when the complete explanation of whether one has gotten to the truth and avoided error is given in terms of such powers or abilities [to keep from making a mistake] and whether the person has exercised them” (94).
A different proposal that Kvanvig considers (but isn’t fully satisfied with) is that a belief amounts to knowledge if “there are [no] possible worlds in which one is in error in the same kinds of circumstances as those of the actual situation” (94). In context, the “same kinds of circumstances” are naturally interpreted as those in which the subject exercises exactly the same powers and abilities. This is then very close to the main text formulation, replacing “completely explain why” with “necessitate that”.
[2] See e.g. Wright (1991) and Rinard (2018) for versions of this challenge.
[3] Millar (2019) explicitly defends such an account of perceptual knowledge.
[4] Another problem is that the “truth leaves tracks” principle Kvanvig actually formulates (115) is restricted to truths about the past or present. The question is then whether a truth about the future can count as an external defeater. If yes, what guarantees that there are (already) tracks for all external defeaters? If no, why would the absence of external defeaters for a belief about the future guarantee its truth?

The End of Binaries: How Gender and Sexuality Come in Degrees
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
00:21:00 UTC
09:21:00 KST

The gender binary is a collective effort to divide human beings into exclusive and exhaustive groups of men and women based on their reproductive capacities, and to impose different social expectations on each group. The gender binary is ethically suspect, both because it limits the lives and dreams of men and women, and because it relies on the oppression of those who don’t fit neatly into either category. It’s also metaphysically suspect, because it appears to lack adequate basis in objective reality. Yet, many people continue act in ways that uphold it, both in ordinary life and in their capacity as philosophers.
Kevin Richardson’s book offers a sharp critique of the gender binary, as well as the related sexual orientation binary that divides people into exclusive groups of heterosexuals, homosexuals and (marginally) bisexuals. It documents the way so-called “gender critical” philosophers uphold binaries while claiming to reject them. But most importantly, it develops a positive alternative to binary thinking—the spatial theory.
Geographic location furnishes a handy metaphor for the spatial theory’s central insight: just as your position in physical space ultimately determines the answer to the question “where are you?”, your position in a structured space of properties ultimately determines the answer to the question “what is your gender?” There are many ways of naming locations: a single geographic location might be accurately described with “Boston”, “Somerville”, “Massachusetts”, a street address, or precise latitudinal and longitudinal coordinates, while a single gender might be accurately described with “man”, “trans man”, “masc-of-center nonbinary”, “elder twink”, or “genderqueer demiboy”. Which description we pick is partly a matter of how our culture divides up the terrain, and partly a matter of our communicative interests, but the underlying reality is a location that can be described in many equally accurate ways.
In Part I, Richardson characterizes the gender binary as a system of social norms that encodes three assumptions:
- there are two genders, woman and man, and everybody belongs to exactly one,
- people’s status as women or men is determined by their sex, which is either female or male (with familiar phenotypic stereotypes), and
- everyone must perform a complex set of social roles based on their gender.
He goes on to observe the high stakes of the gender binary: in the US, its advocates want to ban books about queer people from public libraries and queer people themselves from public life. Richardson covers only legislative threats that target queer and trans people—one could expand the list of tactics to include stochastic terrorism, discrimination, social stigma, and conversion “therapy”, and one could expand the list of victims to the many intersex people, cis women, and cis men harmed by gendered violence—but he gives more than enough evidence to establish the political significance of his project. Part I also includes a chapter examining how “gender-critical” philosophers uphold the gender binary—unsurprising, but worth documenting.
By the end of Part I, Richardson has offered compelling evidence that the gender binary is morally bad, but this leaves open the question of whether it’s metaphysically wrong. Part II gathers recalcitrant evidence that the gender binary cannot explain. The chapter begins with a survey of attempts to define gender in terms of biology, social role, and self-identity. Richardson argues that these attempts don’t partition human beings into two exclusive and exhaustive categories, don’t align with each other, and don’t match most people’s intuitive judgments. Instead of a single, unambiguous definition, our gender categories admit of multiple non-equivalent definitions, and when forced to choose among them, we typically pick based on context and pragmatic factors.
He goes on to argue that gender is nonbinary in multiple ways. First, there are non-normative genders—various ways of being genderqueer, fluid, intersex, and so on—that we should see as real in themselves, not as afterthoughts to binary categories. Second, gender is fuzzy—there may be no fact of the matter as to a particular person’s gender (e.g., whether they’re a trans man, a butch lesbian, or nonbinary). This fuzziness includes both vagueness (which Richardson understands as the idea that category membership is a matter of degree) and open texture (where we are confronted with new examples that our categories were never designed to handle). And third, as the survey of definitions illustrates, there’s no good, context-independent way of defining genders using necessary and sufficient conditions.
Part III develops the spatial theory, beginning with the idea of gender prototypes. Richardson draws on the prototype theory of Eleanor Rosch (1988), which models how we grasp concepts without relying on necessary and sufficient conditions. A prototype of an F is an ideal F—not a real individual that happens to be exemplary, but a collection of properties that would be possessed by an exemplary F.[1] The prototypical bird is small, has feathers, flies, and sings; it is more like a robin or a sparrow than a cassowary or a cockatoo with beak-and-feather. Similarly, there are prototypical women and men, though Richardson is circumspect in naming their features. (He points to a lack of empirical psychological data; there’s also a danger of covertly pushing pernicious norms.) Someone counts as belonging to a gender category like woman or man insofar as they are sufficiently similar to its prototype.
Prototype theory raises three questions. First, why assume each category has only one prototype? Richardson’s answer is that we shouldn’t: there can be multiple competing prototypes, or different ones for different contexts. This multiplicity of prototypes explains why gender categories are fuzzy: someone may be sufficiently similar to some prototypes of manhood, but insufficiently similar to others. It also explains why our definitions might shift with context: different practical interests call for different prototypes.
Second, what does it mean to be similar to a prototype? Richardson answers by pointing to an underlying space of gender-making properties. Whether someone is a woman depends in a complex way on many fine-grained features: how often they are marked out for treatment as a woman, how often they are systematically subordinated as a woman, their hormone levels, etc. These features come in degrees: someone can be singled out for a treatment more or less often, and have higher or lower estrogen levels. We can think of the features as axes in a multi-dimensional space, and prototypes as points in that space exemplifying the “ideal” combination of features for each gender. To be similar to a protype is to be near it in this multi-dimensional space.
Third, what counts as sufficient similarity to a prototype? This question presupposes some way of measuring similarity, even when the underlying dimensions differ wildly from each other. How does one trade off sex chromosomes—which seem best represented by a discrete variable with a few values and no natural ordering—against frequency of being singled out for treatment as a woman, which seems best represented by a continuous variable whose values are linearly ordered? Richardson posits numerical degrees of womanhood, manhood, and so on to substantiate judgments like “Demario is much more of a man than Nolan”, but doesn’t offer us concrete ways of measuring these degrees, which (he says) represent how the world is, not what we know or how we should talk.
Part IV applies the spatial theory to sexual orientations by keeping the gendered dimensions for the agent of sexual desire, and adding gendered dimensions for the patient (i.e., the type of person desired). Richardson posits separate dimensions for disposition to feel desire, disposition to engage in sexual activity, and identifying with an orientation label. For example, the prototypical lesbian is a woman (along various dimensions) who is disposed both to desire and to have sex with people who qualify as women (along various dimensions), while not desiring or having sex with people who qualify as men, and who identifies as a lesbian. Other people count as lesbians as long as they are sufficiently similar to this prototype (but they might be nonbinary, or occasionally sexually attracted to men, or celibate.)
Naming new sexual orientations doesn’t change the underlying space, but it introduces new prototypes, thereby creating new sexual orientation categories. The prototypical asexual doesn’t feel sexual desire for anyone, regardless of gender. The prototypical heteroflexible person mostly desires and has sex with people of the “opposite” gender, but is disposed to occasionally desire or have sex with same-gender partners. And so on. As with gender, the property space is the fundamental reality underlying both the prototypes and the categories based on them.
Part V consists of a final chapter theorizing about binary abolition. While it’s okay to keep talking in terms of categories, Richardson argues, we should hold our labels more loosely, remembering that they don’t reflect fundamental divisions in reality, and adapting them to our needs rather than taking them as given.
There’s a lot to like in Richardson’s theory. It’s refreshing to see a philosopher take the messy realities of queer life seriously as data, rather than trying to shove them into a binary mold that tacitly treats heterosexuality as the most natural way of being. It’s particularly nice to see a theory that takes bisexual and trans experiences as central examples rather than embarrassing anomalies. Richardson writes with the sensibilities of a public philosopher, which is to say that he often steps back from the persona of the objective, impersonal reasoner to evince a personality and a sense of humor. Nerds like me (and much of NDPR’s readership, I expect) can enjoy nitpicking his treatment of vagueness and concept possession.
One of my nitpicks is that he commits to specific claims about vagueness and indeterminacy that don’t seem crucial to the project’s goals. I am tempted by bivalent theories of vagueness that don’t posit “joints in nature” (e.g., Raffman, 2005; Fara, 2000), but these theories are at odds with Richardson’s degreed treatment of vagueness. Adopting a sophisticated classical theory like Raffman’s or Fara’s shouldn’t saddle a metaphysician with commitment to the gender binary, and Richardson’s theory should ideally translate across these abstract disagreements. In fairness to Richardson, vagueness is notoriously hard to describe, and even one viable description of gender fuzziness is better than none. I hope that future logicians translate his ideas into other idioms.
Here’s another nitpick in the form of a question: What fixes the underlying dimensions’ gender spaces? Estrogen level is arguably one such dimension, but endocrinologists only succeeded in isolating estrogen in the 1920s (Santen and Simpson, 2019), when the concept of womanhood was well established. This suggests that the space itself is constantly reconfigured in response to changing social pressures. The nature of particular dimensions is also in flux. Consider frequency of being singled out for treatment as a woman; what counts as treatment as a woman depends on shifting social practice. And the binary concept woman is embedded in treatment as a woman, raising doubts about Richardson’s claim that gender space is more fundamental than binary concepts.
Characterizing underlying dimensions seems especially puzzling when it comes to sexual orientation, and Richardson’s choice to characterize it in terms of gender. Some people are mainly excited by sadomasochism, or by feet, or by fictional monsters; why shouldn’t these count as full-fledged sexual orientations? Even among the orientation labels that Richardson discusses, “asexual”, “graysexual”, “demi-sexual”, and “reciprosexual” are fully agnostic about the genders of all parties.
Regardless of the ultimate metaphysical status of gender spaces, they’re invaluable for theorizing gender and sexual orientation. The End of Binaries draws our attention to the fluidity and fuzziness of gender, and makes important headway on systematically theorizing its complexity. We still have a lot to learn, but Richardson helps advance our collective understanding a little farther.
REFERENCES

Building collapses to fires, 33k died in 5 yrs from 2020
NEW DELHI: Between 2020 and 2024, nearly 33,000 people died across the country in incidents involving building collapses, fires and falls into pits and manholes, according to govt data. Most of these deaths occurred in urban areas, pointing to serious gaps in civic governance and enforcement of safety regulations.The actual numbers will be significantly higher as data on road deaths within municipal limits - many on account of potholes - and those due to contaminated water are unavailable.
The data taken from reports by National Crime Records Bureau indicate that thousands of deaths every year are linked to accidents that are largely preventable and often occur due to poor upkeep of public infrastructure, unsafe buildings and non-compliance with safety regulations.While recent incidents in Delhi have caught the attention of people, instances of parts of Gurgaon and Delhi getting flooded and accumulation of piles of garbage are clear indicators of how municipal governance has deteriorated."Every corporator or councillor, municipal officer and mayor needs to take responsibility. ," said former urban development secretary M Ramachandran.Experts and former officials who have worked in the sector also stressed that govt's push for ease of construction and deregulation must follow a balanced approach. "The distinction between deregulating to increase economic activity and deregulation that leads to collapse of civic order is a fine one and has been lost in the rush to deregulate everything. Officers are unable to draw the line and have stopped attending to routine work under the guise of deregulation. An important side-effect has been de-skilling as they are no longer able to decide and act," an expert said.

"I am hereby directing the GSA (General Services Administration), working with the USTR (United States Trade Representative), to take all necessary steps to REMOVE Canadian-origin products from GSA's Multiple Award Schedules unless Canada restores full and fair reciprocity for American Farmers and Companies," Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social.

"From now on, NO RECIPROCITY - NO ACCESS!" Trump declared.
The order comes amid escalating trade tensions between the United States and Canada. The United States imposed 50 percent tariffs on about 20 billion dollars worth of Canadian goods, effective Aug. 22, prompting Canada to retaliate with matching tariffs on an equivalent value of U.S. imports, which took effect Tuesday. ■

In 2016, Jinhu Special Education School launched a home-based teaching program for children with severe disabilities. Over the past decade, teachers involved in the program have traveled nearly 80,000 kilometers across the county to teach students in their homes.
For each child, the teachers develop an individualized education plan covering cognitive development, daily living skills and rehabilitation training, while also providing families with parenting and caregiving guidance. Marco Rubio says US seeks more economic and security ties in Latin America
Unknown

Marco Rubio says US seeks more economic and security ties in Latin America
The US secretary of state visits Colombia, Ecuador and Peru in a bid to enhance cooperation with right-wing allies.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio says President Donald Trump’s administration hopes to ink trade deals with Colombia, Peru and Ecuador soon, as Washington seeks greater ties with right-wing allies across Latin America.
Rubio met with Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella during a visit to Barranquilla on Tuesday, part of a three-nation trip aimed at consolidating relationships with allied governments and expanding US military involvement in the region.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Rubio heads to Ecuador, Colombia, Peru after right-wing victories in region
- list 2 of 3Colombia asks Trump to suspend tariffs as country reels from earthquake
- list 3 of 3Colombia’s far-right government recognises Israeli claim over Golan Heights
“We have a lot of common interest with them, both taking on regional transnational criminal terrorism and also economic engagements,” Rubio said of the three countries before departing. “It’s part of a trend that you’re seeing in the Western Hemisphere of alignment with US and US interests.”
In addition to Colombia, the US secretary of state is set to travel later this week to Ecuador and Peru to meet with their respective presidents, Daniel Noboa and Keiko Fujimori.
Before his departure to Colombia, Rubio explained that Washington was seeking “good, solid” trade deals in the near future with all three countries.
The diplomatic tour also comes as the Trump administration seeks to check China’s growing influence in Latin America.
China, for example, signed a free-trade agreement with Peru in 2009 and has since become the South American country’s top trading partner, beating the US.
The Trump administration has also pushed for greater control over the entire Western Hemisphere as part of a policy platform informally called the “Donroe Doctrine”.
Security has been the centrepiece of that effort. Since taking office for a second term, Trump has authorised lethal military actions in Venezuela, the eastern Pacific Ocean and the Caribbean Sea, which he touted as critical to combat drug trafficking.
De la Espriella took office in August, promising a return to a militarised approach towards crime and armed groups, in line with Trump’s priorities.
He has also pledged to pursue closer relations with the US, after clashes between Trump and former President Gustavo Petro, Colombia’s first elected leftist leader.
“Colombia wants to re-establish itself as the United States’ primary partner in hemispheric security,” De la Espriella said after his meeting with Rubio, which included the signing of agreements on critical minerals and civil nuclear cooperation.
De la Espriella indicated he would seek US support for military operations, including through radar and drone technology.
A political newcomer with no prior experience in elected office, de la Espriella has been part of a wave of right-wing victories across Latin America in recent years.
The Trump administration has buttressed the electoral campaigns of the region’s conservative candidates by pledging financial and political support.
He has also invited them to join the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition (ACCC), or the “Shield of the Americas”, a regional security framework that emphasises US military involvement to combat drugs and crime.
Leftist presidential candidate Ivan Cepeda, a Petro ally, slammed Rubio’s visit to Colombia as an “act of surrendering strategic aspects of our sovereignty”, pointing to Tuesday’s mineral and energy deals.
Cepeda also criticised de la Espriella’s decision to loosen gun restrictions on the same day, a position that echoes Trump administration policy.
“Just how disastrous the ‘memoranda of understanding’ that Rubio and De la Espriella are set to sign must be, given that an equally disastrous decision — the authorisation to carry weapons — is being announced at the same time,” Cepeda wrote on social media.
De la Espriella has defended his decision, however, citing Colombia’s struggles with crime and its six-decade-long internal conflict.
“For years, law-abiding citizens faced restrictions while criminals continued to arm themselves illegally to the teeth. That has to change,” he said in a social media post.
Colombia has asked the Trump administration to lower tariffs imposed on the country in July.

What is celebrated on September 9 in Ukraine and around the world
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
03:13:25 EEST
09:13:25 KST

What is celebrated on September 9 in Ukraine and around the world
Kyiv • UNN
On September 9, Education, Beauty, Electric Vehicle, and FASD Days are observed. Tajikistan celebrates its independence, while churches honor the saints.
On September 9, the International Day to Protect Education from Attack under the auspices of the UN, World Beauty Day, and World EV Day are observed, while Tajikistan celebrates Independence Day. In the church calendar according to the New Calendar, the righteous ancestors of God, Joachim and Anna, are commemorated, while according to the Old Calendar, Venerable Pimen the Great and Venerable Kuksha of the Caves are commemorated, UNN writes.
International Day to Protect Education from Attack
An official UN observance established by a decision of the General Assembly in 2020 at the initiative of Qatar and UNESCO. The day is intended to draw the attention of the global community to the threats faced by students and educators in areas of armed conflict, where schools often become targets of military attacks or are used as bases for armed formations. The event emphasizes the obligation of states to comply with the Safe Schools Declaration and guarantee children continuous access to a safe educational environment even during wartime.
World Beauty Day
The event was established in 1995 at the initiative of the Comité International d'Esthétique et de Cosmétologie (CIDESCO), the world's leading organization in the beauty industry. The celebration is dedicated to aesthetics, harmony, and the perception of beauty in all its diversity, and is also a professional day for cosmetologists, stylists, plastic surgeons, makeup artists, and fashion industry professionals.
International Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorders Awareness Day (FASD Awareness Day)
A global medical and educational initiative launched in 1999. The campaign symbolically begins at 9:09 a.m. on the ninth day of the ninth month, reminding people of the nine months of pregnancy, during which a woman should completely abstain from alcohol consumption. The day's goal is to spread information about irreversible physical and mental developmental disorders in the fetus caused by exposure to alcohol during pregnancy.
World EV Day
An unofficial international observance established in 2020 by the media company Green.TV to promote environmentally friendly transport and sustainable development. The event brings together automakers, charging-station infrastructure providers, and electric vehicle owners to discuss the benefits of moving away from internal combustion engines and accelerating the decarbonization of the transport sector.
Independence Day of Tajikistan
The country's main national holiday, established to commemorate the adoption, on September 9, 1991, at a session of the Supreme Council of the Republic of Tajikistan, of the Declaration of State Independence from the USSR. On this day, solemn military parades, festive processions, celebratory fireworks, and nationwide festivities take place throughout the country.
Foundation Day of the DPRK
The main state holiday of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea, commemorating the official proclamation of the republic on September 9, 1948, under the leadership of Kim Il Sung following the division of the Korean Peninsula. The date is marked by large-scale military parades in Pyongyang, mass gymnastics performances, and state ceremonies.
Day of Remembrance for the Victims of the Holocaust and Racial Violence in Slovakia
An official day of remembrance established to commemorate September 9, 1941, when the government of the First Slovak Republic adopted the so-called "Jewish Code"—a set of antisemitic laws that deprived the Jewish population of civil and property rights and became the first step toward their subsequent deportation to concentration camps.
Day of Remembrance of the Righteous Ancestors of God, Joachim and Anna
According to the New Calendar, the Orthodox and Greek Catholic Churches commemorate the righteous ancestors of God, Joachim and Anna—the parents of the Most Holy Theotokos. Under the church calendar, the commemoration of the holy parents falls on the day after the Feast of the Nativity of the Theotokos. The righteous Joachim and Anna are considered patrons of marriage, family harmony, and childless couples who pray for the gift of children. On this day, Saint Severian of Sebaste, who suffered martyrdom for his faith in Christ in the 4th century, is also commemorated.
According to the old calendar, believers commemorate Saint Pimen the Great, one of the most revered Egyptian Christian ascetics of the 5th century and a founder of monasticism, whose wise sayings became part of the treasury of patristic writings. They also remember Saint Kuksha of the Caves — a hieromonk of the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra, a prominent enlightener and baptizer of the pagan Vyatichi tribes, who, together with his disciple Nikon, suffered martyrdom at the hands of pagans at the beginning of the 12th century

Smithsonian chief Lonnie Bunch steps down amid Trump administration pressure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
00:10:56 UTC
09:10:56 KST

Smithsonian chief steps down amid Trump pressure over how US history is presented
The Smithsonian announced Tuesday that Secretary Lonnie Bunch will leave his post at the end of the year as the institution faces continued scrutiny from the Trump administration over how its museums present US history.
Lonnie Bunch is stepping down from the leadership of the Smithsonian Institution following a tumultuous year in which President Donald Trump tried to remake the portrayal of US history by the Smithsonian museums and other cultural entities.
Bunch said in a news release Tuesday that he was departing the position he had held since 2019 “with very mixed emotions and heartfelt gratitude”. The Smithsonian said he would leave the post at the end of the year.
Bunch’s departure comes two months after a White House report branded the leaders of the Smithsonian Institution, especially at the National Museum of American History, as radical activists who cannot be trusted, an indication that Trump could be preparing to install his own team.
Anthea M. Hartig, the first female director of that museum, faced growing scrutiny from Trump and other Republicans over the summer after the White House Domestic Policy Council’s report saying the museum’s leadership doesn’t tell history “in a way that is inspiring, unifying, and worthy of our great republic”.
Three weeks after the report’s release, Trump ordered his administration to install signs in front of the US history museum telling visitors that some of the exhibits are inaccurate. Hartig pushed back, telling lawmakers during congressional hearings that the report “does not fairly or accurately characterise the full body of work at the museum”.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
There had been speculation that firings were in the offing. Trump doesn’t have the power to fire leaders at the Smithsonian with the swiftness he’s managed at other top cultural institutions in Washington, most notably the Kennedy Center, where a board of his supporters named him chairman.
The Smithsonian operates outside the executive branch and museum directors report to Bunch, who is subject to oversight from a Board of Regents that includes Vice President JD Vance, Supreme Court Chief Justice John Roberts, a bipartisan group of lawmakers and so-called citizen regents.
Roberts, who serves as Smithsonian’s chancellor, said in a release that Bunch had “pursued excellence in the telling of our nation’s story”.
The White House did not immediately return a message seeking comment.
Tony Johnson, membership director of the Heritage Foundation, said Bunch's retirement is just the first stop. “We will fight to ensure that the next Secretary of the Smithsonian will not treat the Institution as a culture-war battleground,” he said.
Bunch is scheduled to speak September 25 at the National Museum of African American History and Culture at an event entitled: “Understanding America: 10 Years of Excellence”. A Smithsonian spokesman said Bunch would be at the event.
The Smithsonian has been under examination by the Trump administration since 2025 as it has focused on the images and messages presented to the public as the nation approached its 250th anniversary.

A March 2025 executive order, "Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History", led to signs being changed at federal parks, exhibits being altered or in some cases removed, and military bases being renamed. Trump specifically cited the National Museum of African American History and Culture and argued that the Smithsonian as a whole was engaging in a “concerted and widespread effort to rewrite our Nation’s history”.
Several months later, the White House ordered a wide-ranging review of the Smithsonian museums and exhibitions before the country’s 250th birthday, with a goal of aligning the institution’s content with Trump’s interpretation of American history.
Watch moreUS history gets a presidential makeover for its 250th birthday
In a letter sent to Bunch at the time, the White House detailed the steps it expected the organization to take as part of the announced review. The examination covers all public-facing content, including social media, exhibition text and educational materials, to “assess tone, historical framing, and alignment with American ideals”, according to the letter.
That review initially focused on eight museums – the National Museum of American History, the National Museum of Natural History, the National Museum of African American History and Culture, the National Museum of the American Indian, the National Air and Space Museum, the Smithsonian American Art Museum, the National Portrait Gallery and the Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden.
California Democrat Senator Alex Padilla praised Bunch in a statement for not shying away from the nation's history. “In the face of Donald Trump’s attacks on the Smithsonian, Secretary Bunch spoke truth to power and reasserted his commitment to defend and uphold American history and values. While I respect his decision to depart, the job now falls to the Board of Regents and Congress to ensure the success of his work will remain for generations to come.”
(FRANCE 24 with AP)

Three people died at the popular Burning Man festival this year
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

Three people died at the popular Burning Man festival this year
Kyiv • UNN
Three men aged between 51 and 60 died during this year's Burning Man. The causes of death are being established; there are no signs of violence.
During this year's Burning Man festival in the Nevada desert, 3 men over the age of 50 died. This is three times the average number of deaths recorded at the festival each year, The Guardian reports, writes UNN.
Details
According to Pershing County Sheriff Jerry Allen, 2 deaths occurred during the festival itself, while another participant died after being taken to Reno for medical treatment.
The deceased were approximately 55, 51, and 60 years old. Local authorities said there are currently no signs of violent death in any of the 3 cases.
Burning Man's audience is getting older
The increase in the number of deaths occurred amid changes in the age composition of festival attendees. According to the Black Rock City census, the share of participants aged 20 to 30 fell from approximately 30% in 2014 to 10% in 2025, while the share of people aged 40 to 50 increased.
The causes of this year's deaths have not yet been established. The final autopsy and toxicology results are expected in approximately 6–8 weeks.
Burning Man ended on September 7. The festival, held in Nevada's Black Rock Desert, has attracted more than 70,000 participants in recent years.

US strikes five Iranian oil tankers, as Iran attacks 10 ships, Jordan base

US bombs five Iranian oil tankers after its navy is attacked
Iran says it has attacked 10 ships near the Strait of Hormuz after the US announced it had sunk five Iranian oil tankers in the Gulf of Oman and near Kharg island after accusing Tehran of launching ballistic missiles at a US warship.
Iran also fired missiles at US forces stationed at the Al-Azraq base in Jordan.

The exchange of fire overnight and Wednesday morning comes amid escalating tensions in the Gulf six months into the US and Israel’s war on Iran, with Tehran closing the Strait of Hormuz and Washington enforcing a naval blockade on Iranian ports.
The hostilities drove oil prices above $100 a barrel in early trading on Wednesday. Iran’s Foreign Ministry condemned US attacks on Iranian tankers, warning of the escalatory consequences of such attacks.
“In response to the US’s aggressive actions against Iranian oil tankers, armed forces, in accordance with their inherent right of legitimate defence, attacked US military bases and facilities located in Jordan, which continues to support US military attacks against Iran, as well as several US vessels,” it said.
In a statement late on Tuesday, the US Central Command (CENTCOM) said Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) had sought to target a US warship twice over the past two days, but that the vessel “successfully evaded the attempted Iranian attacks”.
“No American personnel were harmed,” it said.
CENTCOM said it responded by striking and destroying the Iranian oil carriers, M/T Kaviz, M/T Charminar, M/T Horizon 1, and M/T Riesco in the Gulf of Oman, as well as M/T Derya near Kharg island.
“American forces directed the crews to abandon ship before the vessels were struck and rendered inoperable,” CENTCOM added.
It later published a video that it said showed the M/T Riesco sinking in the Gulf of Oman.
Iran claims attacks on Jordan
The IRGC confirmed that five tankers were targeted. It said it retaliated by subjecting the Al-Azraq base in Jordan to “fierce missile strikes” and claimed that hangars used by US fighter jets were destroyed in the attacks.
The IRGC also claimed ballistic missile attacks on the US Navy DDG-119 and DDG-53 destroyers, saying the strikes caused “significant damage … to these vessels”.
In a subsequent statement, it said its naval forces targeted “two American vessels and 8 tankers in the region, causing great damage to them”. It was not clear if the two “American vessels” were the same destroyers mentioned in the earlier statement.
There was no immediate comment from the US on the Iranian claims.
The ship attacks followed a statement by the IRGC that warned of imminent attacks on oil tankers in Bahrain and Kuwait’s borders. The IRGC said all crews must evacuate immediately.
The IRGC also said a maritime restricted area would extend from Chabahar in Iran into parts of the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea, with its precise coordinates to be announced.
The announcement follows comments on Sunday by Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, saying Iran would establish a restricted zone outside the Strait of Hormuz.
Later on Wednesday, maritime monitor UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said it received a report of an attack on a cargo ship off the coast of Iraq.
The vessel was hit by a projectile 52km (28 nautical miles) southeast of al-Faw, Iraq, the UKMTO added.
The Jordanian Armed Forces, meanwhile, said the country’s air defences engaged 20 ballistic missiles, “successfully intercepting and destroying 18 of them”. Two missiles “fell in unpopulated areas”, it said in a statement.
The attacks did not cause any casualties, and specialised teams “have begun securing the locations where debris and shrapnel fell”, the military added.
Earlier, the chief of staff of Iran’s Armed Forces, Ali Abdollahi, had warned that Tehran would strike US military installations across the region if Iranian tankers were targeted.
‘War crime’
The US had previously attacked three Iranian oil tankers on September 5, causing one of them to sink. Tehran said it responded on the same day by attacking three commercial ships and three US-linked ships.
Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Tuesday condemned the latest US attacks on Iranian commercial vessels as a violation of the United Nations charter, describing them as a “war crime”.
It said the “illegal and aggressive actions” were a continuation of the US’s military “aggression” and “economic war” against the country and warned that Washington and its partners bear full responsibility for the consequences.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio defended the strikes, telling reporters during a visit to Colombia that Washington will not back down. “Iran continues to try to hit US naval ships, and for every time they do that or try to do that, they’re going to lose tankers,” he said.
Al Jazeera’s Mike Hanna, reporting from Washington, DC, said the attacks mark an “escalation” in the six-month-old conflict.
“The US is now finding different targets, new targets, in terms of response to Iranian attacks, or what the US administration says are Iranian attacks,” he said.
“Whether these tanker attacks are part of a formulated strategy or whether it is just a question of circumstance, that is not particularly clear at this point,” he said. “However, there is no doubt that these attacks on Iranian tankers would have an economic impact on Iran, and that does fit into what the US administration has declared is its present strategy, which is to bring economic strangulation to Iran.”
Also on Tuesday, the IRGC claimed the capture of an unmanned US submarine at the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz “in a complex intelligence and operational action”.
But the US military said the submersible drone had “malfunctioned” as it was surveilling regional waters. It said the “defective drone” had not collected sensitive data nor carried any classified sonar or radar equipment.

Suspected smugglers on trial over deadliest migrant tragedy in France
Paris trial begins over deadly Channel tragedy, with 14 facing charges for manslaughter.
The trial for the accident involving at least 31 migrants and asylum seekers killed while trying to reach the United Kingdom has begun, with 14 men facing smuggling-related charges.
Some 114 civil parties, including victims’ families, are involved in the trial that opened on Tuesday. The incident was the deadliest disaster on record involving asylum seekers crossing the Channel separating France and the UK.
Twenty-seven people died after their inflatable dinghy deflated in one of the world’s busiest shipping lanes on November 24, 2021. Two men survived, and four others were left unaccounted for.
The victims were mostly Iraqi Kurds but also included nationals from Afghanistan, Ethiopia, Egypt, and Vietnam, aged between seven and 46.
Investigators say Afghan and Iraqi Kurdish migrant smuggling networks organised the crossing to the UK from camps in northern France.
The 14 defendants face charges including manslaughter and “facilitating illegal immigration as part of an organised gang”. Only nine suspects were present at the opening of the trial in a Parisian court, one of whom was in custody. The trial is expected to last three weeks.
Prosecutors accused the defendants of launching a “substandard small boat, uncertified, unfit for navigation on the open sea, overcrowded and lacking appropriate life jackets”.
Two of the suspects will be tried in absentia after eluding French authorities.
A French fishing vessel alerted authorities after reporting bodies floating in the Channel near the UK, according to a court document.
“Around 2:30am, we began bailing water out. But suddenly, the boat capsized,” survivor Issa Omar said in a statement read out in court.
A UK inquiry published in February found that some of the deaths were avoidable and concluded that a French naval vessel failed to respond to an alert from the UK coastguard.
Despite dozens of distress calls made to the UK and French rescue services, it was nearly 12 hours before the boat was finally found.

Singapore boosts PM’s salary by $1m amid major pay rise for ministers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
00:00:38 UTC
09:00:38 KST

Singapore’s prime minister has been given a $1m pay rise as the affluent city-state announced a dramatic one-off salary boost for government ministers.
The pay increases add more than 60% to what are already the world’s highest ministerial salaries.
Singapore has justified high-end salaries for its political leaders, arguing they attract talent and ensure good governance. The issue is nevertheless politically sensitive, with cabinet members’ income far exceeding that of most ordinary citizens.
Prime minister Lawrence Wong’s benchmark annual salary will rise from S$2.2m ($1.7m) to S$3.6m ($2.8m).
The deputy prime minister’s benchmark will lift from S$1.8m to S$3m. Cabinet ministers will get between S$1.8m and S$2.8m, depending on the seniority and weight of their portfolio.
Wong said he would donate the entire increase of his salary to “suitable good causes” during his term.
Even before the raise, the Singaporean prime minister’s paycheck vastly outstripped the wages of many other leaders, including in the US and other G7 nations. The US president earns $400,000 a year, while the UK prime minister is paid about $230,000 annually.
“Political salaries are a difficult and emotive issue,” said Wong, whose long-ruling People’s Action Party dominates Singapore’s parliament and its 21-member cabinet. “The sums involved are more than what most citizens earn, so I understand why Singaporeans scrutinise them closely, and why many feel strongly about the matter.”
However, the issue is “ultimately about whether Singapore will continue to have the quality of political leadership we need to take our country forward” in the decades ahead, he said.
“Our starting point is this: good government depends on good leadership.”
The South-east Asian nation, which last adjusted ministerial salaries 15 years ago, is regularly ranked among the world’s least corrupt countries.
Wong said the pay raises were recommended by an independent committee, adding that existing office holders would not be moved immediately to the new benchmarks.
They will receive a one-off adjustment of up to 9% from 15 October, depending on individual circumstances, including performance.

He acknowledged that “securing human resources is a major challenge in the context of the declining birth rate and ageing population”, but said the government was instead drawing up plans to address personnel shortfalls by improving conditions and facilities for serving members and their families, offering more support after they had left the armed services and expanding the use of technology such as AI.
Employers across Japan are struggling to find workers and analysts say the military holds little appeal for many young people.
While other countries allow non-nationals to serve – Britain, for example, recruits Commonwealth citizens – Japan has shown far greater reluctance to follow suit, a stance that coincides with hardening public opposition to immigration more broadly.
“There are just too many reasons, from the military, the government and the public, why this suggestion is not going to work,” a government adviser on national security told This Week in Asia.
“All arms of the SDF are understaffed at the moment and they are having problems retaining trained people. But this [proposal] has alarmed people.”

Ukraine has developed a new RK-19 missile to shoot down Russian &quot;Banderols&quot;
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
02:56:19 EEST
08:56:19 KST

Ukraine has developed a new RK-19 missile to shoot down Russian "Banderols"
Kyiv • UNN
The RK-19 has a range of up to 10 km and a 14.3 kg warhead. It was developed to intercept drones and Banderol-type cruise missiles.
Ukraine's KB Luch has unveiled the RK-19 surface-to-air missile, designed for Soviet Osa air defense systems. It is intended to replace scarce standard missiles and can be used against jet-powered drones and cruise missiles, reports Defense Express, writes UNN.
Details
The RK-19 is designed to intercept subsonic and supersonic targets. The missile uses radio-command guidance, proximity fuzing, and is equipped with a 14.3 kg high-explosive fragmentation warhead.
The declared engagement range is up to 10 km, the altitude is up to 5 km, and the maximum flight speed is 600 km/h. The missile's weight together with the transport-launch container is 163 kg.
The RK-19's specifications are close to those of the standard 9M33M3 missile for the Osa-AKM, but it has a higher maximum speed. Due to a shortage of older interceptors, Ukrainian forces had previously been forced to use less effective missiles or integrate air-to-air missiles, including the R-73.
Defense Express notes that the emergence of the RK-19 will allow the continued operation of Osa air defense systems and their use against aerodynamic targets, including jet-powered drones and Bandероль-type cruise missiles.
The cost of the RK-19 and its production volumes have not yet been disclosed.

UNITED NATIONS, September 9. /TASS/. The first meeting of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly has taken place at the UN headquarters.
During the meeting, which lasted just under an hour, Khalilur Rahman, president of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly, addressed delegations on the session’s priorities. These include strengthening peace and security, advancing sustainable development, stepping up efforts to combat climate change, promoting and protecting human rights, ensuring universal access to cooperation in digitalization and new technologies, and restoring trust in multilateralism.

One of the key tasks of the session is to select the next UN secretary general. The term of current UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres expires on December 31, 2026. UN Security Council members are currently considering candidates for the post, after which the General Assembly will hold a vote.

Australians sleep at Heathrow after UK air traffic control failure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
23:52:20 UTC
08:52:20 KST

Australians forced to sleep at London's Heathrow Airport after air traffic control failure
In short:
Hundreds of flights have been cancelled and the plans of tens of thousands of passengers disrupted after an air traffic control failure across the UK.
The fault has been fixed, but Australian travellers are among those facing delays and cancellations as airlines clear a major backlog.
What's next?
UK airports and airlines have warned disruption could continue on Wednesday as aircraft and crews are repositioned.
Australian travellers have been left stranded at one of the world's busiest airports after an air traffic control failure led to flight cancellations across the United Kingdom.
Up to 1,000 flights were cancelled on Tuesday, according to tracking website FlightRadar24, and delays are expected to continue throughout today as airlines work through a significant backlog.
A fault in the flight data processing system operated by the UK's air traffic control provider, National Air Traffic Services (NATS), caused the disruption.
Perth woman Monique Whiting and her partner Frank are sleeping on the floor at London's Heathrow Airport after their flight to Iceland was cancelled.
The couple boarded their Icelandair flight shortly before 1pm local time and remained on the aircraft for more than four hours before being told to disembark.
"We knew pretty early on that there was a bit of a delay, and I could see through the window that there was a bunch of planes lining up to go," Ms Whiting said.
She said the airline provided snacks and water, but later that afternoon passengers were told the flight would not be leaving.
Ms Whiting said Icelandair told passengers to arrange their own accommodation and offered to reimburse them up to a certain amount, but nearby hotels were full.
"A bunch of other things had already been cancelled, and a lot of the close-by accommodation was obviously already booked out," she said.
"You can imagine how busy it is and there's lots and lots of people still at the airport.
"We're all staying here overnight and not getting any sleep."
Debbie Payne was four days into a European holiday when she arrived at Heathrow for an 8:50pm flight home to Australia via Singapore.
After travelling to the airport by car, train and the London Underground, she discovered flights had been cancelled.
"People weren't sure what to do," she said.
"You just had to wait around and hope."
Ms Payne said passengers were initially prevented from passing through security, while some travellers were stranded aboard aircraft on the tarmac.
"There were people on planes who couldn't get off because there were no ramps," she said.
"It was hard to know what was going on.
"I felt sorry for people who didn't speak English and those with young babies."
Backlog to cause further delays
A fault in the flight data processing system operated by NATS caused the disruption.
The system processes flight plans and other operational information controllers use to manage aircraft travelling through UK airspace.
NATS said it had fixed the problem, but warned it was taking longer than expected for normal operations to resume.
Chief executive Martin Rolfe apologised to affected travellers and told the BBC there would be a full investigation.
Flight-tracking website Flightradar24 reported that up to 1,000 flights had been cancelled.
The worst-affected airports included Heathrow, Gatwick, Manchester and Birmingham, while airports in Scotland and Ireland also reported disruption.
EasyJet cancelled about 200 flights, and British Airways cancelled or diverted more than 100.
Ryanair said more than 65,000 passengers experienced delays of up to eight hours.

US increases pressure on Iran with sanctions targeting aviation sector
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
23:51:29 UTC
08:51:29 KST

US increases pressure on Iran with sanctions targeting aviation sector
Trump administration has sought to isolate Tehran through a raft of measures meant to squeeze the country’s economy.
The United States has put forward a new package of sanctions targeting Iran’s aviation sector, as the administration of President Donald Trump seeks to ratchet up economic pressure on Tehran.
On Tuesday, the US Treasury Department announced 36 Iran-related sanctions on commercial and private airlines, part of an effort to isolate Iran dubbed “Operation Economic Outcast”.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Can Iran enforce a restricted zone in the Strait of Hormuz?
- list 2 of 3As fuel prices rise again, Iran’s government urges citizens to cut back
- list 3 of 3Qatar says reopening Strait of Hormuz ‘unconditionally’ is a priority
The penalties expand existing sanctions on the privately owned Iranian airline Mahan Air, while targeting other Iran-based aviation companies, as well as firms that provide them with services.
“Under Operation Economic Outcast, we promised severe consequences for those providing financial lifelines to the Iranian regime,” US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said.
“Today, we followed through on that promise with sanctions on companies that continue to support Mahan Air. Let this be a warning to anyone doing business with Iran’s remaining airlines, all of which we sanctioned today: You are at risk of being cut off from the global financial system.”
Iran has been subject to years of heavy economic restrictions, and Mahan Air has been under sanctions as far back as 2011, when the US government accused it of supporting the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).
But since Trump returned to office for a second term in 2025, he has sought to heighten pressure on the Iranian government.
On February 28, the US and Israel launched a war against Iran that hit its six-month mark in August.
With the war grinding on without a conclusion in sight, Trump last month announced a series of measures designed to further squeeze the Iranian economy. He likened the actions to an “economic D-Day”, referencing one of the turning points in World War II.
Bessent said the project would amount to the “toughest sanctions in history“. Still, the fighting has continued.
As recently as Tuesday, the US struck Iranian tankers, while Iran launched attacks on US military forces in Jordan.
“After failing to achieve its aims through sanctions or war, Washington’s ‘novel’ solution is… more sanctions. Seriously?” Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi wrote in a social media post on Tuesday.
One of the enduring sticking points in the conflict has been the Strait of Hormuz, a key conduit in the global fossil fuel trade.
At the outset of the war, Iran restricted passage through the strait, causing fuel prices to surge in the US and globally.
The Trump administration in turn announced its own naval blockade and enhanced sanctions against Iran in an effort to sever its economic lifelines.
In addition to Mahan Air, the US has accused foreign companies in countries such as Turkiye, the United Arab Emirates, Kazakhstan and Malaysia of providing Iranian airline companies with parts and logistics services.
Washington has previously accused Mahan Air of ferrying weapons and support to armed groups allied with Tehran in countries such as Lebanon and Yemen.
The sanctions extend to countries and companies that do business with the restricted entities, along with freezing any assets they have under US jurisdiction.

The talks in the northern Egyptian city of El Alamein brought together Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi, Greek Cypriot leader Nikos Christodoulides and Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis, according to a statement from the Egyptian presidency.
The three leaders reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening peace, security, stability and prosperity in the Eastern Mediterranean and Middle East while expanding cooperation through their trilateral mechanism launched in Cairo in November 2014.
On maritime boundaries, the statement said agreements and memorandums of understanding concerning delimitation “must be concluded in accordance with international law, including the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea.”
Gaza and Palestinian statehood
The three sides reaffirmed support for an independent, sovereign Palestinian state along the June 4, 1967 lines, with East Jerusalem as its capital, in accordance with UN resolutions.
They emphasized the importance of implementing the second phase of Trump’s Gaza plan and UN Security Council Resolution 2803 to ensure the start of reconstruction and early recovery and the delivery of humanitarian aid to civilians.
The leaders also called for preserving the geographic, political and legal continuity between the West Bank and the Gaza Strip and rejected attempts to separate the two territories or forcibly displace Palestinians.
Lebanon and Libya
On Lebanon, the three sides called for an end to Israeli attacks on Lebanese territory and the withdrawal of Israeli forces. They also supported strengthening Lebanese state institutions, particularly the armed forces, to enable the state to exercise its authority and sovereignty across the country.
Regarding Libya, the statement reaffirmed support for the country’s sovereignty, territorial integrity and national unity as well as a Libyan-led and Libyan-owned political process.
It also called for the withdrawal of foreign forces and mercenaries and the holding of simultaneous presidential and parliamentary elections.
Expanded trilateral cooperation
The leaders discussed ways to strengthen cooperation in trade, investment, energy, tourism, education, culture, migration and labor alongside security cooperation and efforts to combat organized crime and irregular migration.
Sisi stressed the importance of continuing to develop cooperation through the trilateral mechanism, while Christodoulides and Mitsotakis reaffirmed their commitment to deepening ties.
The three sides agreed to hold their 11th trilateral summit in the Greek Cypriot Administration, without announcing a date.
