Iran seizes ‘most modern’ US submarine drone (VIDEO)
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has announced the seizure of “one of the most modern, unmanned, and smart submarines” in the possession of the US military. The Pentagon downplayed the incident, saying it was an old drone without any sensitive equipment.
On Tuesday, the IRGC published a video of what it claimed was the advanced US undersea drone, which could perform a wide range of tasks, from seabed mapping to intelligence and surveillance operations, pipeline inspection, and anti-submarine warfare support.
The footage shows a grey, metallic, torpedo-like cylindrical vessel around 5.8 meters long and 1.2 meters wide, weighing around 2.7 tons. The undersea vessel can spend up to 10 days underwater and reach a maximum depth of 6,000 meters, according to the IRGC statement.
The Iranian military identified it as a Dive-LD drone developed by US defense contractor Anduril Industries that entered service in April 2025.
US Central Command (CENTCOM) sought to downplay the incident, claiming Iran obtained a malfunctioning older-model drone that did not carry any sensitive equipment.
The undersea vessel was surveilling regional waters and “neither collected sensitive data nor carried any classified sonar or radar equipment,” US Navy Captain Tim Hawkins, a CENTCOM spokesman, said in a statement.
The incident comes amid yet another escalation between the US and Iran. Late Tuesday, Iran launched ballistic missiles toward US military bases in the Middle East in what it called retaliation for an earlier US attack on Iranian oil tankers near Kharg Island. The IRGC also issued an “urgent warning” late Tuesday, telling tanker crews around the docks and anchorages of Bahrain and Kuwait to leave their vessels immediately ahead of potential attacks.

From AUKUS to AI: Why Australians are demanding a greater say in policy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
23:41:48 UTC
08:41:48 KST

analysis
From AUKUS to AI: Why Australians are demanding a greater say in policy
Australians still believe in the ideals of their democracy and government, but their declining faith in politicians and the political system is putting that trust at "profound risk".
A clear majority of voters think ordinary citizens should have a greater say in setting the country's policy priorities, with many feeling politicians prioritise their own self-interest and the interests of lobby groups and corporations over the community's desires.
Those are some of the key findings from the latest annual Purpose of Government Pulse, published by the centre-left Centre for Policy Development (CPD) think tank this month.
"It is clear that voters are losing patience with politics as it has always been done," the report warned.
"People are voicing their frustration with the traditional two-party system by branching out to independents and minor parties like One Nation.
"People increasingly feel like the current political system doesn't listen to their concerns and that major decisions are made without their input or consultation.
"[But] despite this frustration, Australians have not given up on their vision for what government and democracy can, and should, deliver," it found.
The data is drawn from 10 survey waves conducted by Essential Research between October 2015 and February 2026.
Huge support for universal health care
The report was published on Friday, but the media didn't cover it widely.
Perhaps its findings weren't considered newsworthy enough, since you can only say the same thing so many times before it loses its novelty, and "everyone knows" Australians are increasingly frustrated with their political system.
But the report had important insights.
First, it found that, despite decades of political messaging about the need for smaller government and less intervention, the overwhelming consensus is that government should play a direct role in improving people's long-term wellbeing.
It found the vast majority of Australians say health, education, and child care must be free or affordable for all, with targeted extra support provided to those who need it most, and that government must maintain the capability to deliver social services directly.
Second, it showed two-thirds of Australians had consistently said for the past decade that voters should have a greater say in setting the government's core policy priorities.
Third, it found that while Australians had clear expectations of what they wanted government and democracy to deliver, they were increasingly sceptical that politicians would deliver it.
Little say over strategic future
Now, if you look for evidence of voters' growing frustration with Australia's political system, you won't be short of examples.
The CPD report didn't mention it specifically, but an obvious example of voters' concerns about their lack of control over Australia's future is manifest in the current public inquiry into the AUKUS deal.
That inquiry is an extremely unusual phenomenon.
Loading...
If you haven't heard about it, the public hearings, which began in June, have no backing from the federal government and are not funded by taxpayer money. The Australian Peace and Security Forum has coordinated them, with former Labor minister Peter Garrett as lead commissioner.
Former public officials, retired military and naval officers, strategists and academics, and lawyers and union leaders have been dedicating their time to the inquiries to try to uncover basic information about the AUKUS "security partnership" that will lock Australia into a particular security arrangement with the United States for decades.
They want to know why ordinary Australians have been largely excluded from one of the biggest defence decisions in Australia's history.
"The AUKUS deal was conceived in secret and with deception — and continues to be shrouded in secrecy despite the incredibly high stakes and massive cost," the inquiry's website says.
It has been asking questions like: Will AUKUS jeopardise our sovereignty? Why are we joining the US to go to war against China potentially, our major trading partner? Will AUKUS make us safer or turn us into a nuclear target?
In a society more responsive to citizens' concerns, one would expect a publicly funded inquiry (rather than a crowd-funded one) to ask such heavy questions about Australia's strategic future.
Loading...
Concerns about AI, data centres, and surveillance
There are examples of voter unease in other areas.
For instance, anxiety is growing across the political spectrum about the pace at which data centres are being built and how little say local communities have over their construction.
"Increasingly, I'm hearing from people from all walks of life how concerned they are with the pace of AI growth," former Labor industry minister Ed Husic told the ABC's Patricia Karvelas in June.
"Again, if we think new One Nation voters are attracted to the idea of giving the system a kick, look how we're managing [the] massive wave of data centre construction.
"Most local communities have absolutely no say about the construction of these centres in their area, leaving average residents fuming.
"When they resist, they're told these data centres are important for the economy. So if they're so important, why aren't they being built in Bellevue Hill instead of Blacktown?" he said.
Concerns about government contracts
And what about the concerns people have about controversial companies winning major government contracts?
In April, journalist Cam Wilson, writing for Crikey (he now works for the ABC) reported that the federal government had spent $60 million on contracts with the Trump-aligned surveillance and intelligence data company Palantir Technologies, with little public scrutiny, and the Future Fund held $165 million worth of the company's shares.
"The company has been mired in controversy for alleged human rights violations, its close association with the Trump administration, and the outspoken pro-American political rhetoric of its co-founder, Alex Karp," Wilson wrote.
It would be interesting to see how Australians would vote, given the opportunity, on whether Australian governments should sign contracts with companies like that, or whether the Future Fund should invest in them.
But Australian voters rarely get a say over that kind of thing.
Last week, Nine newspapers broke the story that Coles Supermarkets will cut ties with Palantir after its three-year contract ends in 2027. The move follows a pressure campaign from the activist group GetUp! and growing public concerns about the company.
We need more than minor policy tweaks
At any rate, when it comes to formal politics, the CPD report says voters' scepticism about Australia's political system is clearly being reflected in the declining primary vote share of our two major parties and the rising popularity of minor parties and independents.
It also said the "core challenge" for governments and politicians was to address the widespread belief that Australia's political system was failing to deliver on the vision voters had for the future.
When the report was released, CPA chief executive Andrew Hudson said voters wanted to be heard.
"They want to know that their concerns are being listened to and that their long-term interests are being prioritised," he said.
"Unfortunately, the majority of Australians currently don't feel that is the case."
And the report said fixing that "disconnect" would require far more than minor policy tweaks.
"The historic fall in the primary vote share for the major parties is a clear, direct message from voters that they are losing patience with government as it has always been done," it said.
"They want a system that prioritises the needs and concerns of communities in decision-making, and a distinct shift away from a system they see as increasingly captured by powerful, vested interests."
Want to have your say? Go to www.abc.net.au/yoursay

Israel, Arab states meet at secretive Washington summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
23:32:11 UTC
08:32:11 KST

Representatives from Israel, the United States and Arab countries, including states that do not maintain diplomatic relations with Israel, gathered in Washington on Tuesday for the fourth MEAD conference, a closely guarded forum focused on regional security and cooperation.
Delegates from 24 countries are taking part in the conference, including representatives from Israel, the U.S. and 12 Middle Eastern states.
The gathering comes amid continued uncertainty over the confrontation with Iran and a series of unresolved regional security questions left by the fighting across the Middle East.
Among the issues on the agenda are shipping arrangements through the Strait of Hormuz, the situation in Lebanon, efforts toward an arrangement in Gaza and the future of Iran's nuclear program. Participants are also examining possible new frameworks for regional security cooperation.
The conference is taking place ahead of elections in Israel and the U.S. midterm elections, political contests expected to influence the future of U.S.-Israel relations and Washington's broader policy in the region.
One of the most unusual aspects of the meeting is the participation of representatives from countries that have no formal diplomatic relations with Israel.
As in previous years, Middle Eastern states without official ties to Jerusalem have chosen to send representatives, participation made possible in part by the conference's confidentiality rules.
In recent years, the MEAD conference has developed into a forum for discussions among senior figures from the U.S., Israel and other Middle Eastern countries on regional policy and security.
The event brings together political leaders, senior policymakers and other officials for discussions intended to strengthen alliances, encourage dialogue and develop strategic approaches to regional challenges.
Discussions cover security, intelligence, technology, business, energy, finance and governance, with a broader focus on strengthening U.S. engagement in the Middle East and encouraging greater regional integration.
Energy security and freedom of navigation are also prominent on the agenda, after both shifted over the past year from primarily economic concerns to major security issues.
A central feature of the conference is its use of the Chatham House Rule, which allows participants to use information shared during discussions but bars them from identifying who made particular remarks or revealing their affiliation.
Organizers say the confidentiality is intended to encourage candid discussions, including exchanges involving sensitive information, without participants having to fear immediate public attribution.
That framework is particularly significant because it allows dialogue between representatives of countries that would rarely, if ever, meet openly within formal diplomatic channels.
At a time when almost every public statement in the region is closely scrutinized, the closed-door setting gives participants greater room to discuss areas of disagreement, test possible policy approaches and build trust away from the spotlight.

New York failed to disclose what it knew on ‘toxic air’ after 9/11, documents show
- New York City released 170,000 documents revealing it withheld information on toxic air after 9/11, as announced by Mayor Zohran Mamdani.
- Over 9,400 people have died from illnesses linked to toxic exposure after the World Trade Center collapse, with officials repeatedly assuring the public the air was safe.
- The documents may implicate former mayors Rudy Giuliani and Michael Bloomberg in concealing health risks and legal liability related to air quality after the attacks.
AI generated
NEW YORK – New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced on Sept 8 the release of tens of thousands of documents showing the city did not disclose all it knew about air toxicity after 9/11.
The release comes ahead of the 25th anniversary of the Sept 11, 2001, attacks that killed 2,977 people in the United States, mostly in the collapse of the Twin Towers in New York.
In the years since, more than 9,400 have died from illnesses linked to their exposure to the area, according to a federal medical monitoring programme.
“These are documents that show what the city knew about the toxic air around Ground Zero, when they knew it, and how they acted to limit liability,” the mayor told a news conference following the online release of 170,000 pages of documents on health concerns, air quality and the city’s response to the attacks.
The release is part of an agreement with 9/11 Health Watch, a victims’ advocacy group that had taken legal action to compel the city to make the documents public.
“For 25 years, four different mayoral administrations kept from the public, the US Congress and the City Council documents showing what the city actually knew about the danger of the toxic chemicals in Lower Manhattan and Western Brooklyn after the World Trade Center collapse, even as city officials continued messaging to the public that the air was ‘safe and acceptable’,” the group’s director Benjamin Chevat said in a statement.
After the initial dust cloud that followed the collapse of the World Trade Center, months of pollution and lingering dust ensued, causing cancers that thousands of New Yorkers still suffer today.
Leaders ‘lied’
When asked about the names of officials who had withheld information from the public, Mamdani said: “This goes across a multitude of those that New Yorkers have trusted.
“People got sick because the leaders they trusted lied and told them they were safe to breathe in toxic air.”
Roughly 173,000 documents released on Sept 8, and additional ones which will be published online in waves over the next 12 months, could implicate two former New York mayors.
They are Rudy Giuliani, in office at the time of the attacks, and then Michael Bloomberg, mayor from January 2002 to December 2013.
Some concern discussions Giuliani’s administration had at the time about its legal liability and health risks, New York City’s chief counsel Steven Banks said on Sept 8.
Giuliani’s spokesman did not return a request for comment.
Another document highlights information provided by Congressman Jerry Nadler during Bloomberg’s tenure regarding concerns from residents of Lower Manhattan about the quality of the air they were breathing.
Bloomberg’s team declined to comment.
On Sept 11, 2001, hijackers seized control of two planes that struck the two World Trade Center towers. A third hijacked jet smashed into the Pentagon and a fourth, which seemed to be headed for the Capitol or the White House, crashed in woodland near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, after passengers fought back and seized control. Ford, US transportation chief spar over company’s China deals
- US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy criticised Ford for relying on Chinese technology and delaying moving Lincoln manufacturing back to the US, citing national security and supply chain concerns.
- Ford denied the accusations, calling them "wrongheaded" and clarified its US ownership and control of the BlueOval Battery Park in Michigan using a limited technology-licensing deal with CATL.
- Ford highlighted its $3 billion investment in US manufacturing, job creation, and praised support from Trump administration officials, emphasising its commitment to American production.
AI generated
NEW YORK - US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy on Sept 8 slammed Ford Motor Company over its reliance on Chinese technology, accusations that the Detroit-based automaker dismissed as “wrongheaded.”
In a letter to Ford chief executive Jim Farley published on the agency’s website, Duffy said the company’s “recent strategic decisions paint a troubling picture of a foundational American brand actively intertwining its future with Chinese state-backed enterprises.”
The Department of Transportation (DOT) is “alarmed” by Ford’s use of technology from Chinese battery manufacturer CATL at its BlueOval Battery Park facility in Marshall, Michigan, Duffy said, adding that the use of Chinese knowhow “challenges the spirit of American national and economic security and supply-chain independence policies.”
Duffy also criticised other Ford collaborations with Chinese companies, such as a joint-venture with China’s Geely in Spain and the company’s “delaying” move to wait until 2030 to shift manufacturing of Lincoln models from China back to the United States.
“When a company intentionally chooses to deepen operational dependencies on strategic competitors, it fails to act as the reliable partner the American public and this DOT require,” Duffy said.
But Ford – which stresses in its marketing that it is number one among automakers in US vehicle assembly – said Duffy’s broadside “contains factual errors” and misstated the company’s operations.
“Had Secretary Duffy reached out before issuing his letter to the press, we would have been happy to share more details about Ford’s US commitment,” the company said, calling the letter “a wrongheaded attempt to capture headlines.”
Ford’s use of CATL constitutes “a limited technology-licensing and services agreement, not a joint venture or foreign-owned manufacturing operation,” the company said.
“Ford owns the plant, controls the operation and employs the workforce.”
Ford also pointed to recent praise of its supply chain decisions from others in the Trump administration.
An Aug 31 White House press release touting Trump’s efforts to “deliver manufacturing renaissance to Michigan” pointed to Ford’s US$3 billion (S$3.79 billion) investment in the Marshall plant, which will create 1,700 new jobs.
The press release was timed with a visit by Vice-President J.D. Vance to Michigan.
Ford also cited comments from Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Fox Business in August praising the automaker.
“Ford is going to rock us with bringing manufacturing back to America,” Lutnick said. AFP

US destroys 5 Iranian tankers after attacks on warship; Iran fires missiles at Jordan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
23:21:17 UTC
08:21:17 KST

U.S. Central Command said overnight Tuesday that American forces had destroyed five Iranian crude oil tankers after Iran's Revolutionary Guard twice tried to strike a U.S. Navy warship with ballistic missiles over the past two days.
At the same time, Iran launched missiles at a U.S. base in al-Azraq, Jordan, with the Revolutionary Guard saying the attack was in response to the strikes on the tankers. Interceptions were seen in the skies over Israel. Watch footage of the U.S. strikes and the interceptions over the Jordan Valley:
According to CENTCOM, the U.S. warship managed to evade the Iranian attacks and continued patrolling waters in the region. No U.S. personnel were hurt. The statement effectively confirmed earlier reports that Iran had attempted to attack Navy vessels.
In response to the attempted attacks, CENTCOM said U.S. forces destroyed four Revolutionary Guard tankers in the Gulf of Oman — Kaviz, Charminar, Horizon 1 and Riesco — as well as the tanker Derya near Kharg Island, known as Iran's "oil island." CENTCOM said the crews were instructed to abandon the tankers before they were attacked and disabled.
U.S. Central Command said the tankers were part of a multibillion-dollar "shadow network" Iran uses to finance the Revolutionary Guard and its proxies across the region. CENTCOM added that Iran "has no means to protect these vessels."
Shortly after the U.S. announcement, Iran escalated its threats in the maritime arena. The Revolutionary Guard warned crews aboard oil tankers near ports in Kuwait and Bahrain to abandon their vessels immediately, saying they could become targets in retaliation for U.S. attacks on Iranian tankers.
Iran has also threatened to establish a "maritime exclusion zone" in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, warned that U.S. "economic warfare" would be met with maritime measures and said Tehran had fundamentally changed its posture toward U.S. warships and military bases in the region.
It was the second time in a matter of days that the United States attacked Iranian tankers following attempts to strike U.S. Navy vessels. On Saturday, CENTCOM destroyed three crude oil tankers after the Revolutionary Guard launched ballistic missiles at a U.S. aircraft carrier and a guided-missile destroyer. According to the U.S. military, the vessels also managed to evade those attacks without casualties.
In all, the United States has destroyed eight Iranian tankers in the two rounds of strikes.
Earlier, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing U.S. officials, that Iran had attacked U.S. Navy ships. None of the vessels was hit, according to the report, but Tehran's recent attempts to strike American maritime assets have raised concerns in Washington that it is using more advanced weapons — as well as the possibility that China or Russia may be helping Iran with information on the ships' locations.
Iran, meanwhile, claimed it had seized an unmanned U.S. military submarine. In a statement, the Revolutionary Guard said the vessel was captured at the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz in a "complex intelligence and operational mission." Iran's Fars news agency later published images of the vessel it said had been seized.
The United States offered a different account of the incident. A U.S. official told Reuters that the vessel was an unmanned craft that malfunctioned while surveying waters near Iran. The official said it was an older model that did not carry classified sonar or radar equipment, and that the malfunction occurred more than a day before Iran announced it had seized the vessel.
Iran also tried over the weekend to strike a U.S. aircraft carrier, prompting the United States to attack three oil tankers. The Journal cited Iranian officials who told Iranian media that the government was using new missiles with advanced capabilities to target U.S. warships.
U.S. officials who spoke with the newspaper said that even with those "new missiles," Iran would need to know the approximate locations of U.S. ships in order to target them, raising concerns that China and Russia could be helping Tehran track their positions.

THE HAGUE, Sept. 8 (Xinhua) -- Dutch semiconductor equipment maker ASML on Tuesday held a ceremony to mark the start of construction of its second major industrial campus in Eindhoven, the Netherlands, as it expands manufacturing capacity to meet growing demand from the global semiconductor industry.
The new site, known as Brainport Industries Campus (BIC) North, will span 350,000 square meters and could eventually accommodate up to 20,000 workplaces, the company said.
"The growing global demand from the semiconductor industry requires continuous investments," ASML President and CEO Christophe Fouquet said.
According to ASML, the first phase of BIC North is expected to be completed in 2029 and will accommodate at least 3,000 employees. The integrated industrial campus will bring together production, logistics and supporting office functions, with the positions primarily filled by teams relocating from existing ASML sites.
ASML, the world's leading supplier of extreme ultraviolet lithography systems, announced plans in January to cut about 1,700 jobs, mostly in the Netherlands, despite reporting record annual results. ■

Roundup: 81st session of UN General Assembly opens
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
07:20:58 CST
08:20:58 KST

Photo taken on Sept. 8, 2026 shows the scene of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly at the UN headquarters in New York. The 81st session of the UN General Assembly (UNGA) was declared open by Khalilur Rahman, the new president of the General Assembly, on Tuesday. (Xinhua/Zhang Fengguo)
UNITED NATIONS, Sept. 8 (Xinhua) -- The 81st session of the UN General Assembly (UNGA) was declared open by Khalilur Rahman, the new president of the General Assembly, on Tuesday.
In his speech at the opening session at the UN headquarters in New York, Rahman said he is assuming his responsibility at a consequential moment for the United Nations.
As the world body enters its ninth decade, many achievements deserve recognition, he said, noting that, at the same time, the world body faces grave challenges.
The United Nations has often fallen short of the expectations placed on it. Conflicts continue to inflict immense human suffering. Development gains remain feeble and fragile. Climate impacts are intensifying, he said.
"Together, these challenges have brought trust in multilateralism under tremendous strain. A widening trust deficit is testing confidence in international institutions and collective action -- a deficit that we must close by working together through dialogue, renewed cooperation and delivery," said Rahman.
He said his main pledge for the 81st session is to work tirelessly to revive trust in this organization, upon which the success of member states' collective action ultimately depends. This conviction is the spirit behind the theme of this 81st session: "Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations that Delivers for All."
Centering on the restoration of trust, the 81st UNGA session will focus its work around six priorities: to strengthen peace and security, accelerate sustainable development, step up climate action, advance human rights, help ensure that technological transformation serves people everywhere, and restore trust in multilateralism, he said.
"Delivering on these six priorities demands that we remain true to the values of our charter while adapting our institution to a world profoundly different from that of 1945. And if the United Nations is to remain indispensable in an ever-changing world, it must also remain fit for purpose -- and fit for the future," he said.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, in his remarks, said the global problem-solving system is more crucial than ever in these tumultuous times.
"We face conflicts, divisions and a risk of nuclear escalation; persistent poverty and inequality; worsening climate chaos; technology like artificial intelligence that offers great promise but also great peril without good governance and transparency around its environmental footprint; and sluggish progress on the Sustainable Development Goals," he said.
Displacement is near record levels. Human suffering is intensifying while funding for aid and development is being slashed. The institutions of the multilateral system, from the UN Security Council to the international financial architecture, are straining to meet the moment. International law and human rights, the core of the United Nations, are too often flouted with impunity. And geopolitical mistrust and suspicion continue to block the effective solutions that are needed, and erode people's faith in the possibilities of global cooperation, he added.
Guterres expressed the hope that under Rahman's leadership, the UNGA, through diplomacy, dialogue and collaboration, can rebuild the trust and good faith that are missing from today's geopolitics, and ensure the people of the world inherit a better, healthier and more peaceful future.
"Our direction is clear. The Pact for the Future and the UN80 Initiative represent a blueprint for action, solutions and bold reforms to carry our organization into the future. The work of this assembly is critical to bringing these commitments to life," said Guterres. "As we embark on the 81st General Assembly, let's meet the moment. Let's live up to the great promise of this organization, and through solidarity deliver the solutions our world needs." ■

Economic Watch: European gold shifts spotlight concerns over U.S. financial credibility
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
07:20:46 CST
08:20:46 KST

BELGRADE, Sept. 8 (Xinhua) -- Moves by several European countries to relocate gold reserves held in the United States have drawn attention to growing concerns over reserve security and geopolitical risks, as central banks worldwide reassess the balance between gold and the U.S. dollar.
The Dutch central bank said on Sept. 2 that it had transferred about 86 tons of gold from New York and Ottawa to London between March and August this year. Following the move, the share of the Netherlands' gold reserves held in New York fell from 31.3 percent to 18.5 percent, while the share held in London rose from 18.1 percent to 32.1 percent.
The move followed a similar adjustment by the French central bank. In April, the bank said it had completed relocating 129 tons of gold previously held at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York between July 2025 and January 2026. The amount represented about 5 percent of France's gold reserves.
Germany has also reduced its gold holdings abroad, repatriating 674 tons of gold between 2013 and 2017, including 300 tons from New York and 374 tons from Paris. This year, further calls for repatriation have resurfaced amid rising geopolitical tensions and transatlantic trade frictions under the current U.S. administration.
Analysts said the moves reflected concerns about the security of overseas reserves and geopolitical risks.
Nader Antar, executive vice president of Brink's Global Services, said that "heightened geopolitical and economic uncertainty, together with the growing role of gold as a strategic reserve asset, appears to have contributed to this trend."
Laurent Schwartz, president of the French gold trading institution National Gold Counter, said central banks had been adjusting the locations of their gold holdings for years, adding that "the current political environment in the United States may prompt some central banks to favor other storage locations."
Frederic Schneider, a senior researcher at the Middle East Council on Global Affairs in Qatar, said the moves reflected efforts to secure greater physical control over national gold reserves. He also noted that the United States' growing use of the dollar, international trade relations and global payment systems as geopolitical tools has prompted many countries to reassess how and where they hold their reserves.
Paul Donovan, chief economist at UBS Global Wealth Management, said measures aimed at increasing the liquidity of gold holdings were "not normal behavior." Given central banks' traditionally cautious approach to reserve management, he said, such adjustments send a strong signal about "trust" and the United States' international reputation.
The moves came as central banks worldwide continue to increase their exposure to gold while reassessing the U.S. dollar's role in their reserves.
The trend has coincided with elevated international gold prices, which reached a record high of around 5,600 U.S. dollars per ounce in January before easing to around 4,400 dollars as of Tuesday.
According to the World Gold Council's 2026 Central Bank Gold Reserves Survey, 74 percent of reserve managers expect the U.S. dollar's share in global reserves to decline over the next five years, while 84 percent expect gold's share of reserves to increase. Meanwhile, 45 percent expect to increase their own gold holdings over the next 12 months.
The survey also showed that central banks had purchased significantly more gold over the past four years than they did a decade ago. ■

Several Portuguese artists have dropped out of a comedy festival in Lisbon headlined by Jerry Seinfeld, citing their support for Palestinians and implying opposition to Seinfeld’s support for Israel.
At least six acts over recent days have canceled their appearances at the MEO Commedia a La Carte Fest, a new international comedy festival in the Portuguese capital. The event from Oct. 29 to Nov. 1 has advertised that it will host Seinfeld’s first live appearance in Portugal.
Though none of the artists who withdrew mentioned Seinfeld by name, some hinted at a boycott against his pro-Israel views. The Jewish comedian has become one of Hollywood’s most prominent advocates for Israel since October 2023.
Actress and comedian Inês Aires Pereira announced on Instagram on Saturday that “one of the names” featured at the festival “persistently defends ideas and acts that I consider indefensible,” adding, “We cannot relativize or normalize a genocide.”
The comedy duo Cebola Mol posted a graphic of themselves with a watermelon, widely recognized as a symbol of solidarity with Palestinians. “We will celebrate justice, freedom and joy with you on another occasion,” they said on Instagram.
The festival announced on Friday that performances by the groups Tributo Pop and Conjunto Cuca Monga were also canceled, but did not provide reasons. Two other acts, comedian Pedro Tochas and visual artist Vhils, shared their cancellations on Instagram without further details.
Seinfeld breaks decades of political avoidance
Seinfeld has aligned himself with Israel during its current conflict in Gaza, following decades of largely avoiding commenting on political issues. He visited Israel in December 2023 to meet with the families of hostages seized by Hamas on Oct. 7 of that year. Since then, he has attracted attention for a series of dismissive remarks toward pro-Palestinian advocates.
During an appearance last year at Duke University, Seinfeld compared pro-Palestinian activists with the Ku Klux Klan, saying, “The Klan is actually a little better here because they can come right out and say, ‘We don’t like Blacks, we don’t like Jews.’ OK, that’s honest.”
Representatives of Seinfeld and producers of the MEO Commedia a La Carte Fest did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Carney touts Canada ‘pivot’ away from US as Trump levels new threat

- US President Trump has threatened further sanctions, including restricting Canadian companies from US government contracts and targeting Bombardier Aviation.
- Canada plans to support affected businesses and workers with a C$7.5 billion aid package while seeking to reduce economic dependence on the US despite challenges.
AI generated
MONTREAL - Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Sept 8 that reducing economic ties with the United States would come at a cost but the benefits were clear, as President Donald Trump threatened new penalties targeting Canada.
Canada’s retaliatory tariffs came into effect earlier on Sept 8, applying to C$27.6 billion (S$25.28 billion) in US imports, covering steel and aluminium products as well as dairy goods such as cheese.
With the trade war between the North American neighbours heating up, Carney said Canada has “everything we need to pivot and prosper.”
“That pivot will come at a cost. There’s always a cost to action. But it doesn’t come close to the cost of standing still.”
Ottawa’s pushback comes after President Donald Trump imposed tariffs on a similar value of Canadian products over what Washington deemed “discriminatory treatment” of US alcohol, automobile, and dairy industries.
Responding to the latest Canadian levies, Trump pledged to restrict Canadian companies from securing US government contracts.
In a social media post, Trump said he was directing officials “to REMOVE Canadian-origin products from GSA’s Multiple Award Schedules,” referring to a General Services Administration programme for long-term contracts.
Contracts through such schedules account for more than US$50 billion (S$63.24 billion) a year, Trump added.
On Sept 7, Trump threatened to try to block sales of Canada’s Bombardier Aviation unless the Quebec-based plane maker moves manufacturing to the United States.
In response, the aerospace company pointed to its creation of tens of thousands of jobs across the United States, with direct employment in more than 20 states, including Kansas, Texas, Arizona, and California.
The two Republican senators representing Kansas said they had conveyed their concerns to the White House.
“I’m going to fight to keep Bombardier’s more than 1,200 Kansas jobs. I’ve already taken that concern inside the Oval Office,” Senator Roger Marshall posted on X, with similar comments posted by Senator Jerry Moran.
US tariffs pose a modestly negative risk to Canada’s overall economy, but analysts note that they have a sharper impact on central Canada’s manufacturing sector.
Trade lawyer Ryan Majerus said Trump’s latest move restricting Canadian access to US government contracts “definitely has teeth to it” and could widen the scope of affected goods beyond those hit by tariffs.
‘Lake America’
“I don’t believe in escalating the conflict. That’s not constructive,” Carney said in his video statement on Sept 7. “But our tariffs are necessary to protect our workers, protect our companies, and protect our communities.
“This is about who we are as Canadians.”
Negotiations between the two sides broke down on Aug 21 after days of meetings in Washington.
At the time, Carney said US negotiators had introduced restrictions on Canadian trade deals with other countries at the eleventh hour.
US officials also made unacceptable “threats” to the French language and “Quebec culture,” he added, referring to the French-speaking province in eastern Canada.
Ottawa and Washington have not resumed talks since, and Trump has continued his attacks.
On Sept 6, Trump posted an illustration of himself towering over Carney as they played ice hockey, with Trump saying, “Get up, governor,” a reference to his determination to turn Canada into another US state.
Trump also signed an order in August to rename Lake Ontario, on the border with Canada, as “Lake America,” sparking fury in Canada amid a broader wave of patriotism triggered by the US president’s hostility.
Although Carney is backed by Canadian public opinion, his country remains reliant on its neighbour.
Nearly 60 per cent of Canada’s imports come from the United States, and about 70 per cent of its exports go to the US market.
To help businesses and workers, Canada’s government has unveiled an aid package worth C$7.5 billion. AFP

Mamdani releases records on toxic air in New York after 9/11 attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
23:14:31 UTC
08:14:31 KST

Mamdani releases records on toxic air in New York after 9/11 attacks
The New York City mayor said the document release shows victims were ‘lied to’ about health impacts from the attacks.
Just days before the 25th anniversary of the September 11, 2001 attacks, New York City has released a trove of previously undisclosed documents suggesting government efforts to downplay – or even mislead – residents about dangerous air quality following the attacks.
At a news conference on Tuesday, Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced the publication of 170,000 pages concerning health issues following the collapse of two skyscrapers in the World Trade Center complex, known as the Twin Towers.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Trial for 9/11 accused, including Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, set for June 2028
- list 2 of 3Timeline: How September 11, 2001 led to US’s longest war
- list 3 of 3September 11 convict renounces terrorism, al-Qaeda
Mamdani said the effort would deliver “accountability around city government’s response to September 11 that New Yorkers have been denied for years”.
His remarks reinforced long-running suspicions that leaders in the United States prematurely allowed workers and residents back into area around Lower Manhattan where the towers fell.
“It would be one thing if government had stood alongside survivors and provided them with everything they needed at every step of the way. And yet, we know that could not be further from what actually happened,” Mamdani said.
“People got sick because the leaders they trusted lied and told them they were safe to breathe in toxic air.”
During the September 11 attacks, the Twin Towers were struck by two hijacked planes, leading to their collapse and the deaths of 2,753 people on site. The destruction sent a cloud of dust across Lower Manhattan. Fires burned in the rubble for months.
Thousands of police officers, firefighters and construction workers spent time working in the soot, often without proper protection.
Within weeks of the collapse, employees and residents were also allowed to return to nearby buildings, including One Liberty Plaza, which had sustained damage during the attacks.
But many of those who worked or lived around the site, known as “Ground Zero”, have seen their health decline in the years since. Some developed respiratory or digestive-system ailments that appeared almost immediately. Others have fallen victim to illnesses that developed over time, including cancer.
What’s in the documents?
Tuesday’s release includes a document sent in October 2001 to then-Deputy Mayor Robert Harding, detailing the city’s potential legal exposure after the 9/11 attacks.
The so-called Harding Memo shows officials anticipated as many as 10,000 lawsuits against the city over issues such as “toxic exposure” due to the poor air quality and “faulty” safety equipment.
The Harding Memo also outlined means through which the city could “limit” its liability, including by appealing to Congress to create a fund for victims and requesting indemnification from the US government.
Another memo, released in February 2002, detailed how officials worried that criticism from US Representative Jerry Nadler could open the city up to “major public relations problems” and a “barrage of lawsuits”.
Ester Fuchs, a former special adviser to then-Mayor Rudy Giuliani, pointed to statements from Nadler accusing the government of quashing documents that “showed higher than acceptable levels of asbestos” in the area around the attack.
Fuchs went on to acknowledge that “there is at least a low level of asbestos in the dust in many buildings in lower Manhattan”. She suggested that, if Nadler’s accusations were correct, the city needed to act.
Asbestos, a mineral used in the construction of the Twin Towers, is also a known carcinogen, linked to scarring of the lungs and mesothelioma, a type of cancer.
“At the least, we should discontinue telling people to clean their apartments with wet mops and rags,” Fuchs wrote, referencing guidance the city had previously released.
Why are the documents being released now?
In the months following the attacks, city and federal officials repeatedly reassured residents, workers and first responders that air-quality levels were safe.
But questions about what – and when – the government knew about air contaminants have persisted in the years after.
The release of Tuesday’s documents addresses a lawsuit brought by advocacy groups like 9/11 Health Watch, which sought to bring to light records about public health after the attacks.
Mamdani highlighted that multi-year legal battle during his remarks on Tuesday, slamming past city governments for failing to act in the public interest.
“Administration after administration has ignored those calling for answers and clarity, instead choosing to bury them in legal arguments and in red tape,” Mamdani said. “We will do no such thing.”
The mayor promised more documents would be shared over the next year, suggesting there could be “millions” of additional pages to come.
Appearing alongside Mamdani were survivors and victims advocates, including comedian Jon Stewart.
Stewart paid tribute to the survivors who fought for government transparency while also battling severe medical conditions.
“I’m not saying that the information may have changed the outcomes, unfortunately, for their families,” Stewart said.
“But I guarantee you it would not have been the struggle that it was to get people to recognise that what they all knew and what we all knew who live in downtown Manhattan: that there was poison in the air and on the ground.”
In a statement, 9/11 Health Watch also praised the records’ release, thanking labour unions, community groups and others for their advocacy work.
“For 25 years, four different Mayoral administrations kept from the public, the U.S. Congress, and the City Council documents showing what the City actually knew about the danger of the toxic chemicals in Lower Manhattan and Western Brooklyn,” Benjamin Chevat, the group’s executive director, said.
He underscored that, even as city officials knew of the dangers, they “continued messaging to the public that the air was ‘safe and acceptable’.”
How many people were affected?
Nearly 3,000 people died in New York on September 11, 2001, which involved four hijacked planes in total. One hit the Pentagon in Washington, DC, while another crashed into a Pennsylvania field after passengers fought the hijackers.
In the decades since, roughly 4,343 victims have died from illnesses related to the event, according to the World Trade Center Health Program.
The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) estimates 400,000 people were exposed to toxic contaminants, stressful conditions and situations that put them at risk of physical injury as a result of the attacks.
Mamdani called Tuesday’s document release “the right thing to do”, though it is likely to trigger a wave of new lawsuits against the city for withholding information.
“We hold an obligation each of those New Yorkers to ensure that ‘never forget’ is not just a platitude, but that it is something material,” Mamdani said, citing a common phrase evoked after the 9/11 attack.
Stewart, meanwhile, said the release isn’t just about exposing what the local government knew. It also marks the start of ensuring victims have better access to healthcare moving forward.
“There’s more work to be done,” he said.

The cost of living-induced crime more Australians are committing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
23:12:18 UTC
08:12:18 KST

IN BRIEF
- Petrol theft is a crime that's "bleeding into" the wider Australian community, crime experts warn.
- Many instances are going without consequences, with police laying charges for petrol theft in 4 to 8 per cent of cases.
Cost of living pressures are driving more people to speed away without paying at the bowser than sky-high petrol prices, a study has revealed.
The NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics has released a report that found higher living costs and decreased wages had a stronger link to rates of petrol theft than fluctuating prices.
The bureau launched its investigation after a sharp increase in petrol theft following the COVID-19 pandemic despite stable fuel prices, executive director Jackie Fitzgerald told the Australian Associated Press (AAP).
"[Cost of living pressure] tends to mount up over time, and that will encourage people to commit these kinds of crimes, but they can weather a short-term fluctuation," she said.
"It's not just a criminal subclass that is involved in these matters. It's kind of bleeding into other parts of the community."
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
According to the report, a 1 per cent increase in petrol price was associated with a 1 per cent increase in thefts.
By comparison, a 1 per cent spike in living costs was linked to a 6 per cent increase in thefts.
Petrol thieves are also rather likely to get away with the crime, Fitzgerald said, with police only laying charges in 4 to 8 per cent of cases.
"People are more likely to engage in crime if they think they can get away with it," she said.
"There's clearly some people … whose economic situation is sufficiently dire that they will start to consider those options."
Rates of petrol theft in NSW peaked in 2024 — even higher than when the price of fuel skyrocketed in early 2026 due to the Iran-Israel-US conflict.
Australasian Convenience and Petroleum Marketers Association chief executive officer Rowan Lee told AAP the spike in thefts had been recorded nationwide, with no single state or territory standing out.
There had also been a rise in aggression towards service station staff, the association said.
Fitzgerald said requiring motorists to pay before filling up could help prevent thefts.
"It's inconvenient for people, but ... this study suggests you could turn on those kind of strategies when the conditions are ripe for an increase in petrol theft," she said.

New map could reshape the way you see the world
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
23:11:44 UTC
08:11:44 KST

New world map adopted by UN could reshape global perceptions of power
For centuries, human understanding of the size, shape and bearing of nations has been laid out by one map based on a single projection of the way the world looks.
The Mercator projection was designed for maritime navigation by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator in 1569.
It has been the most commonly accepted visualisation of the world since at least the 18th century.
But the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) voted this month to change that, approving a new "equal area" map aimed at "a more accurate representation" of continental landmasses.
It's called the "Equal Earth projection" and some experts say it could reshape how people see the world.
But first, what did the UN vote on?
A proposal introduced on behalf of 54 African countries by Togo, in the continent's west, pledged to correct an "imbalance inherited from the past", a UN statement said.
Togolese Foreign Affairs Minister Robert Dussey argued distorted maps could affect education about and global perception of continents, including Africa.
"How do we represent the world? How do we teach it? How do generations learn to see our planet?" he said before the vote on Friday.
"Correcting the map means recognising that every region of the world deserves to be represented accurately and with dignity.
"Our approach is not directed against any nation, any civilisation or any cartographic tradition.
"A fair map does not change the geography of the world; it changes how we see the world."
Of the 171 nations represented during the UNGA vote, 164, including Australia, voted in favour and six abstained.
A single nation, the United States, opposed it. Its representative, Yaryna Ferencevych, described the plan as a "barnacle" and a "reason this institution is losing its credibility".
Among the abstentions, Ukraine said it supported the idea but would not vote in favour because the Equal Earth map showed Crimea in grey as contested territory amid the ongoing war with Russia.
What is the new world map?
The Equal Earth projection "is a relevant option for improving the accuracy of the cartographic representation of the world," according to the proposed UNGA resolution.
Launched by cartographers in 2018, it makes Africa, Latin America, South Asia and Oceania, including Australia, appear much larger.
It also reduces the size and scale of North America and parts of Europe, while placing Africa slightly more centrally.
The projection does not redraw national borders or coastlines, but shows continents in their true proportions, whereas the Mercator projection skews the scale of landmasses the closer they are to the North and South Pole.
Geographer Greg Lauer, from the OSGeo Oceania geospatial organisation, believes the Equal Earth change is mostly symbolic and the Mercator projection "is not wrong".
"It's right, particularly for navigation, but it's wrong for comparison … I'd say it was misused, not mistaken," he said.
Why is there no 'perfect' world map?
Recognisable world maps rely on the accurate projection of four fundamental principles — shape or angles, area, distance and direction — according to geospatial technologist Alex Leith.
He said the challenge for cartographers had always been converting the three-dimensional globe into a two-dimensional map without skewing the appearances of the world's landmasses.
"You have a choice about what you preserve, and you can't preserve all of it," he told the ABC.
"Mercator maps preserved direction, so that's about sailing from somewhere to somewhere else.
"This [new map] preserves area exactly, and approximately the shape."
Mr Lauer also said projection models sacrificed one or more of the key principles, based on what a map was trying to show.
"The Mercator is more distorted to the north and to the south, whereas Equal Earth is more distorted to the east and the west," he said.
"Projection is the maths that decides what gets sacrificed."
Will Equal Earth change how we see the world?
Mr Lauer said he did not expect the UN vote to spark an immediate social shift or for mandates to be rapidly implemented across the world to adopt the map projection.
He said most people's global perception stemmed from an ingrained mental image of the Mercator-aligned world map, which they had seen for most of their lives.
"Most people form their mental images of the world from a single map, and when you see it thousands of times from childhood, you never question it," he said.
Loading...
He also acknowledged that someone's understanding of the significance of certain parts of the world was shaped by the maps they used, and that a new map could alter future generations' outlooks.
"Size reads as importance," he said.
"If Africa looks the size of Greenland, it's easy to say, 'Africa doesn't matter.'
"I would imagine the African Union suggesting it's a representation issue with rural, economic and diplomatic consequences. They want Africa to be seen equally with the rest of the world."
Mr Lauer said that significance also extended to the continent shown at the centre of world maps, meaning less emphasis could be placed on the US.
For much of his second term, US President Donald Trump has sought to alter world maps to reflect growing American power.
He has repeatedly spoken of plans to make Canada the "51st state" of the US and seize Greenland as an American territory.
Mr Trump also signed executive orders renaming the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America and changing Lake Ontario to Lake America.
But the new map projection suggests a shift in the perception of global power away from central Europe and the Americas, according to Mr Leith.
"It's just a reasonable, rational decision that provides a better representation of the world," he said.
"This is about equity and representing data in a more equitable way."
Will Australian school maps change?
While Togo says it will become the first country worldwide to update geography textbooks with the new map, the change is not legally binding and the Mercator projection should still be used for navigation.
Australia's national education curriculum does not specify which maps schools should use to teach students.
The ABC understands some Australian schools may choose to incorporate the Equal Earth projection into their teaching, but no national mandate requires them to use any specific world map.
"While the Australian government plays a national leadership role in school education, it is state and territory governments and non-government education authorities who are responsible for the day-to-day delivery of education programs," a spokesperson from the federal department of education told the ABC.
"This includes decisions about how best to implement the Australian Curriculum, and in this case which maps to use and for what purpose.
"The Australian Curriculum supports students to read, interpret and create maps, developing their spatial reasoning and geographical skills to better understand Australia and the wider world."
The ABC has contacted the Australian Curriculum, Assessment and Reporting Authority for further comment.

Amazon accused in lawsuit of systematic discrimination against pregnant employees
- Amazon is sued for allegedly discriminating against pregnant employees by denying accommodations and firing those who take too much time off, violating federal and New York laws.
- The lawsuit includes claims of wrongful termination after a pregnant worker was hospitalised and then fired for exceeding unpaid leave limits.
- Amazon denies the accusations, stating it approves over 99.9% of pregnancy accommodation requests and emphasises employee health; legal actions in New Jersey and New York continue.
AI generated
NEW YORK – Amazon.com was sued on Sept 8 in a proposed nationwide class action accusing the retailer of systematically discriminating against thousands of pregnant employees, including by firing some it claimed took too much time off.
According to a complaint filed by four former warehouse employees, Amazon routinely violates federal and New York worker-protection laws by denying pregnant workers basic accommodations such as chairs, bathroom and water breaks, and time off for prenatal appointments.
The complaint said Amazon threatens and regularly fires pregnant employees who miss too much work, and illegally demands medical documentation from those seeking accommodations. It said these actions violate the federal Pregnant Workers Fairness Act and New York labour law.
“Amazon is one of this country’s largest employers, it is no surprise that many of its workers become pregnant,” according to the complaint filed in the Brooklyn, New York, federal court. “Yet Amazon violates the law at every turn.”
Kelly Nantel, an Amazon spokesperson, said the retailer provides pregnancy-related accommodations to tens of thousands of employees annually, and approved more than 99.9 per cent of requests in the last year. “Ensuring the health and well-being of our employees is one of our greatest responsibilities,” she said.
The lawsuit seeks lost pay and benefits, punitive damages and an injunction against discrimination against pregnant employees.
Amazon has long faced complaints in court about its treatment of employees, including those seeking to unionise.
The Seattle-based retailer is the second-largest US private employer, trailing Walmart, with 1.58 million full-time and part-time employees at the end of 2025.
Hospitalisation led to dismissal, lawsuit says
The Sept 8 lawsuit was filed by A Better Balance, a non-profit that advocates for workers’ rights.
It came 11 months after New Jersey sued Amazon, accusing it of widespread discrimination against warehouse employees who had disabilities or were pregnant. New York filed a similar lawsuit in 2022.
One plaintiff, Willamina Barclay, said Amazon gave her a termination warning on June 17, 2025, one day after she was taken in a wheelchair out of its Rochester, New York, warehouse and hospitalised with a pregnancy-related emergency.
Barclay said she was suffering severe abdominal pain from lifting heavy objects, but Amazon claimed the hospital visit pushed her over her limit for unpaid time off, and docked her because she “worked partially that day”.
She was fired five days later, the complaint said.
Nantel said the four plaintiffs’ accounts “contain inaccuracies and omit important details”.
The US Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) plans in November to propose changes to regulations underlying the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act.
That agency has aligned itself with US President Donald Trump’s policies, and EEOC chair Andrea Lucas said in 2024 that the regulations for pregnant employees are too broad.
The EEOC did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
New Jersey’s lawsuit is continuing after a state Superior Court judge on July 31 rejected Amazon’s request for a dismissal, a spokesperson for New Jersey Attorney-General Jennifer Davenport said. REUTERS

In a dramatic flare-up in the fighting between the U.S. and Iran, American forces struck and destroyed five Iranian oil tankers Sept. 8, U.S. Central Command said. Iran retaliated by lobbing ballistic missiles toward a major U.S. base in Jordan.
U.S. officials said CENTCOM took the action because Iran had fired ballistic missiles against a U.S. Navy warship twice in the past two days. The ship, which the U.S. military did not identify, was not hit, and no service members were harmed, CENTCOM said.
Nevertheless, the U.S. hit back with a major attack on Iranian shipping.
“CENTCOM destroyed the IRGC crude oil carriers M/T Kaviz, M/T Charminar, M/T Horizon 1, and M/T Riesco in the Gulf of Oman as well as M/T Derya near Kharg Island,” the command said in a statement, referring to ships controlled by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. CENTCOM released a video of the attacks, which shows several ships engulfed in flames.
The Iranian ships were attacked by U.S. Air Force and Navy fighters and drones.
The U.S. military said the crews were directed to abandon ship before the vessels were “rendered inoperable.”
“Iran has used the tankers as part of a multibillion-dollar shadow network that funds the IRGC and its regional proxies,” CENTCOM added. The command also delivered a harsh warning to Tehran: “Iran has no means by which to defend these vessels.”
Repeated, escalating tit-for-tat strikes in recent days have raised the risk that the two sides might resume the all-out fighting that characterized the first weeks of the war, which is now in its seventh month.
The Trump administration has adopted a policy of striking Iranian tankers to deter Iran from firing missiles at the aircraft carriers in the region and other Navy ships. On Sept. 5, Adm. Brad Cooper, who leads U.S. Central Command, warned the U.S. would “impose an even higher economic cost” on Iran by striking a “limited and exposed oil fleet” if Tehran did not cease its attacks on U.S. forces.
But that warning went unheeded.
In response to the latest U.S. attack, the Iranian military vowed to carry out fresh strikes of its own, specifically against long-standing American allies like Jordan, Kuwait, and Bahrain. Iranian officials also warned that it would target commercial oil tankers near ports in these countries. Iranian officials said such attacks would be justified because those ports had been used by the U.S.
Jordan was hardest hit as Iran fired dozens of ballistic missiles at the country. Iran said it was targeting Muwaffaq Salti Air Base, a key hub for U.S. airpower. Dramatic videos from Jordan showed ballistic missiles and interceptors filling the night sky. Without providing evidence, the IRGC claimed it damaged American fighter aircraft at Muwaffaq Salti, known as MSAB. No American personnel were killed in the intense barrage aimed at the base, according to initial accounts from U.S. officials.
The Trump administration has hoped that stepped-up economic sanctions and its ongoing blockade would force Iranians to stop interfering with traffic in the Strait of Hormuz and to make other concessions. But Tehran has shown no sign of backing down.
The U.S. is deploying fresh warplanes to the Middle East amid the fighting. F-35 Lightning II stealth fighters from the 115th Fighter Wing of the Wisconsin Air National Guard are deploying to the region and are set to arrive in the Middle East in the coming days, people familiar with the matter said.
The Wisconsin Air Guardsmen are replacing another F-35 unit, the 158th Fighter Wing of the Vermont Air National Guard. Vermont’s “Green Mountain Boys” wrapped up a roughly nine-month deployment to South America and the Middle East, where it supported the capture of Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro before heading to the Middle East to fight Iran. Airmen from the unit returned home Sept. 6 and were greeted by Chief of the National Guard Bureau Air Force Gen. Steven Nordhaus.
The fresh F-35s are not the only new fighter unit reinforcing America’s posture in the Middle East. F-16s from the Ohio Air National Guard’s 180th Fighter Wing deployed to the Middle East late last week, taking the place of F-16s from the 555th Fighter Squadron of the 31st Fighter Wing, which returned home to Aviano Air Base, Italy. Nicknamed the “Triple Nickel,” the 555th Fighter Squadron had been deployed to the Middle East since last November, a long deployment compared to the Air Force’s typical six-month rotations.
The Air Force has dozens of F-16, F-35, and F-15E Strike Eagle fighters and A-10 Thunderbolt II attack planes deployed to the Middle East, along with support aircraft and scores of tankers. More rotations are expected in the coming weeks.
The U.S. Navy also has two aircraft carriers and their embarked carrier air wings supporting operations in the Middle East: the USS George H.W. Bush and USS George Washington, along with around 20 surface vessels.
Like the Air Force, the Navy has also had extended deployments in the Middle East to carry out operations against Iran. The USS Abraham Lincoln is headed home after a nine-month deployment. Before that, the USS Gerald R. Ford was deployed for 11 months and, like Vermont’s Air Force unit, supported operations against both Venezuela and Iran.
As the U.S. and Iran exchanged blows, the U.S. Treasury Department announced it was imposing new sanctions on companies that support Mahan Air, an airline that U.S. officials say is connected to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
Fresh fighting between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia added to the tension in the region. The Iran-backed Houthis fired missiles and drones at energy facilities in southern Saudi Arabia on Sept. 8.

Iranian state media said the vessel was a Dive-LD, a large autonomous underwater vehicle built by California defense firm Anduril. The 5.8-metre submersible can carry out missions including mine countermeasures, seabed mapping, intelligence gathering and the inspection of underwater infrastructure such as cables and pipelines, the company has said.
"We trapped one of the most modern, intelligent and unmanned submarines of the terrorist American army at the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz. This submersible is equipped with the latest technologies," the Revolutionary Guards Navy said in a statement carried by Iranian state media.
In response, a Pentagon spokesperson said an underwater drone had "malfunctioned more than a day ago."
"It was surveying regional waters in support of ongoing operations. The defective drone was an older model that neither collected sensitive data nor carried any classified sonar or radar equipment," the spokesperson said.
Israel tells British consulate in East Jerusalem to close
Israel has informed the British consulate in East Jerusalem that it must close and that diplomats assigned there will lose their accreditation within 30 days, an Israeli official and a source familiar with the matter told Reuters.
British representatives assigned to a US-led Gaza coordination mission in Israel, as well as British diplomats based in Ramallah, must leave within seven days, the source familiar with the matter said.
UK maritime monitor says it received report involving several merchant ships in the northern Gulf and Gulf of Oman
Several vessels in the Gulf region were on fire, a British maritime agency reported, after Iran said it had attacked 20 ships trying to pass through the Strait of Hormuz.
"Reports indicate the vessels were subject to disabling fire as part of ongoing military activity in the region," the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said.
Lebanon army says Israeli escalation threatens framework deal
Lebanon's army on Wednesday accused Israel of a deadly escalation in the country's south in recent days that threatened a framework deal between the countries and the military's efforts to implement it.
The army said in a statement that continued Israeli attacks in recent days "threaten existing understandings and arrangements, and hinder the army's efforts to establish stability" in the region.
Arab, Muslim nations welcome UK-led sanctions on Israeli settlements
More than half a dozen Arab and Muslim countries, including Saudi Arabia and Turkey, on Wednesday welcomed UK-led sanctions targeting Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, urging other countries to take similar steps.
The foreign ministers of eight countries, which also included Jordan, in a statement said they "welcome the decision of the Government of the United Kingdom to ban the import of goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the Occupied Palestinian Territory", also hailing other Western countries for announcing their intention to restrict trade with Israeli settlements.
In message to Syrian president, Israeli defence minister says troops 'not moving'
Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz addressed a message to Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa on Wednesday during a visit to Israeli soldiers stationed in southern Syria, vowing that troops would not withdraw.
"We are here sending a very strong and clear message to the President of Syria, who sits 35 kilometres away down there in his palace in Damascus: we are here on Mount Hermon, we are in the security zone, and we are not moving from here," he said during the visit with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Israel to open embassy in Slovenia
Israel will open its first embassy in Slovenia on Wednesday in a turnaround in relations between the countries after populist Janez Jansa formed a centre-right government this year.
The rapprochement comes as Israel faces growing diplomatic isolation elsewhere over its West Bank policies, including import bansby Britain, France and Canada on products from Israeli settlements.

- France and 10 other countries said they would join the UK in banning goods from illegal Israeli settlements.

BJP got Rs 1,473cr to fight Bengal, Assam, 3 other assembly polls
NEW DELHI: Total receipts by BJP's central party headquarters during the last round of assembly polls in Bengal, Assam, Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Puducherry stood at Rs 1,472.8 crore, as per the party's election expenditure statements for Assam, Tamil Nadu and Puducherry submitted to the Election Commission.The party's closing balance rose to Rs 7,627.2 crore upon the completion of elections on May 6, 2026, compared to Rs 6,722.6 crore on March 15, 2026.BJP, including the party's central headquarters and the relevant state and district units, spent a total Rs 160 crore on the assembly elections in Assam, Tamil Nadu and Puducherry. Assam accounted for the BJP's highest spend at Rs 96.3 crore, followed by TN at Rs 51.6 crore and Puducherry (Rs 11.9 crore). Almost Rs 130.4 crore was spent on general party propaganda, while Rs 29.6 crore went to candidates as lump sum payments and on the publicity of their criminal antecedents. The election expenditure statements for the other two states of West Bengal and Kerala are yet to be made public by EC.
As per BJP's election expenditure statements for Assam, the party spent Rs 76.7 crore on general party propaganda, which included Rs 23.1 crore spent by its central unit, and another Rs 19.5 crore spent on candidates.
While Rs 27.3 crore was spent on travel expenses of star campaigners in Assam, Rs 37 crore was on advertisements, Rs 8.9 crore on publicity materials and Rs 2.3 crore on other expenses by the state unit. A total lump sum of Rs 19.4 crore was paid to candidates and Rs 16.7 lakh spent on publishing criminal antecedents of candidates. In TN, BJP authorised a total spend of Rs 44.5 crore for general party propaganda. Another Rs 7 crore was spent on candidates.In its expenditure statement released earlier for the same set of elections, Congress had declared a total spend of Rs 248.6 crore.
